words: மற்றும் தொடர்ப்பா(டு) எவன்கொல் பிறப்(பு)அறுக்கல் உற்றார்க்(கு) உடம்பு மிகை

note: Both name the Jain god by his qualities: the Cintamani's ஓவாது நின்ற குணத்து and தேவாதி தேவன், the Charana's litany with குணவதன், குணப்பெருங் கோமான், தேவன், and also சங்கரன் ஈசன் சயம்பு.
teaches: The Silappathikaram's Charana absorbs Saiva and Vedic titles into the Arhat's praise, while the Cintamani's invocation keeps to self-won bliss and qualities, so two Jain epics show two strategies, inclusive litany and bare definition.

note: The thousand and eight and the feet on the head recur: Kavunthi will speak only the ஆயிரத்து எட்டு நாமம் and bear only the flower feet on her head; the Cintamani's god bears ஆயிரத்து எட்டு marks and the poet sets his lotus feet on his head.
teaches: The number 1008 is a fixed token of Arhat worship that one epic attaches to names spoken and the other to marks on the body, while the feet-on-the-head gesture stays the same in a nun's vow and a poet's invocation.

note: Both apologies use the moon's spot for the poet's flaw: the Neelakesi's poet will own a fault since even the moon is not spotless; the Cintamani's asks the learned to wash the spot away with their wit.
teaches: The two Jain poets put the same flaw in different hands: the Neelakesi's poet takes it on himself, while the Cintamani's poet makes cleaning it the learned reader's task.

note: The Kural uses the spot on the moon to say a fault in the well-born is seen from far; the Cintamani uses it for a fault in a moon-full work and asks readers to wash it, not to see it.
teaches: The Kural's moon makes height expose a fault, but the Cintamani turns the same image into a reader's duty of charity, so the exposure the Kural warns of becomes something the audience may decline.

gains.a: the poet's request is seen to answer the expectation, stated in the Kural, that a high thing's fault draws every eye
gains.b: the couplet's warning is shown to depend on the onlooker, who can be asked to clean rather than point

note: Both prize what brackish ground or brine produces: the Naladiyar's salt above rice from good fields, the Cintamani's coral, conch and pearl though they taste of the sea.
teaches: The Naladiyar argues that a person's low origin does not lower his learning, and the Cintamani applies the same reasoning to a poem's faulty diction, so the brine image carries one argument about worth and origin from persons to texts.

gains.a: the apology is seen resting on an argument the ethics books had already made about rank
gains.b: the quatrain's claim about birth is shown extending to the standing of a work and its words

note: Verse 7 praises Saccandan's கோடாத செங்கோல் and unfading victory; verse 9 has the same king, sunk in desire and deaf to counsel, lose the kingdom to a plot.
teaches: The patikam builds the epic's first lesson from its own praise: the unbending sceptre and unfading victory are undone not by a stronger enemy but by the king's private desire.

note: The Kural says a king with no one to rebuke him perishes though he has no enemy; Saccandan had counsel (சொல்லாறு) and would not hear it.
teaches: The Cintamani's king shows that having rebuking counsellors is not enough, since desire can make a king deaf to them, so the Kural's safeguard fails at the point of hearing rather than of supply.

gains.a: the king's fall is given a named failure of rule, not only a lover's weakness
gains.b: the couplet's guard is shown to need a king who listens, which the couplet takes for granted

note: The Kural says those who set their desire on the home do not reach the fine fruit; the Cintamani's whole frame begins with a king whose desire for his queen grew thick and cost him his throne.
teaches: Held against the Kural's warning about desire fixed on the wife, the patikam locates the whole fault in the husband's excess while calling the queen's chastity unfailing (வீடாத கற்பு), and gives the couplet's lost 'fine fruit' a political price, the kingdom itself.

gains.a: the king's fall, told without any doctrine named, gains the Kural's category of being led by desire for the wife as its ethical name
gains.b: the couplet's unnamed 'fine fruit' is given a concrete price: a throne and, in the story, a life

note: The nectar given to the dying dog in verse 14 and the god who comes down to carry Civakan out of prison in verse 15 are, in the story, one being.
teaches: The patikam sets a small mercy and a great rescue one verse apart without naming their link, so the reader learns the epic's working of deeds by noticing that the rescuer is the dog.

note: The Kural weighs help given at the moment of need as greater than the world; Civakan's gift comes at a dying dog's last moment and is repaid by a god at his own.
teaches: The Kural measures timely help by its worth to the one helped, while the Cintamani shows it returned across species and births, so the couplet's weight becomes a debt that the receiver carries into a new life.

gains.a: the dog episode gains the Kural's measure of why so small a gift counts
gains.b: the couplet's timely help is shown being repaid in kind at the giver's own hour of need

note: Verse 14 has Civakan give nectar to a dog dying in the bathing pool; verse 16 has a god free him, arm him with spells and ask to be remembered.
teaches: Set beside each other, the dying dog's gift and the god's rescue show the patikam placing a kindness and its return two verses apart, leaving the reader to see the debt repaid before the story names the god.

note: The spells the god gives in verse 16 are followed by the cure of a snakebite in verse 18, given only as a word of comfort.
teaches: The patikam never says how Civakan cures the princess, but read after verse 16 the cure is the god's gift at work, so his first marriage is won by the rescue, not by his own arms.

note: Verse 10 has the sword-eyed mother keep a vow that her son may live; in verse 23 the grown son, with brother and friends, comes to bow before her.
teaches: The mother's austerity, kept apart from her son, is answered when he returns alive to bow to her, and the patikam places that homecoming just before he turns to win back the kingdom she lost.

note: Verse 13 has Suramanjari, shamed over the scented powder, refuse to look on any male form and shut herself away; verse 25 has her lower her banner.
teaches: Read together, the two verses frame Suramanjari's vow against men as a challenge the plot exists to undo, so her yielding is told as a conquest like the boar and the enemy in the same verse.

note: Verse 9 tells how the king, sunk in desire and deaf to counsel, fell to a plot while the queen fled to the burning ground; verse 25 has the son kill the enemy.
teaches: The usurpation that verse 9 blames on the father's own desire and deafness to counsel is settled only by the son's killing, so the father's fault and the son's revenge frame the whole plot.
audit_text_issue: Verse 25 line 4 (நஞ்சு ஊறும் வேலான்) is ambiguous between Civakan and the enemy

note: Verse 9 has Saccandan, steeped in desire, not hear counsel (சொல்லாறு கேளான்) and lose his throne; verse 27 has his son hear the dharma (அறம் கேட்டு) and give his throne up.
teaches: The patikam opens on a king ruined because he would not listen and closes on his son freed because he did, so hearing becomes the hinge between losing a kingdom and leaving one.

note: Civakan renounces kingship at its height after hearing the dharma; in the Manimekalai the minister tells the king who wants to leave his throne that the Buddha's dharma, which protects others' lives, is not that.
teaches: The two epics weigh the same act differently: the Cintamani's patikam praises a just king's leaving the throne once he hears the dharma, while the Manimekalai has a minister argue that a king who abandons the people he guards departs from the Buddha's dharma.
audit_text_issue: Unit begins mid-sentence (line 115 continues the minister's speech from before the cut).

note: The Naladiyar's best of men renounce house, youth, wealth and strength because they see these do not last; Civakan renounces in full possession of all of them.
teaches: The quatrain grounds renunciation in seeing that goods pass away, while the epic's king renounces while every good still stands and gives fear of kingship, roused by the dharma, as his motive, so impermanence is not the only road to leaving.

gains.a: Civakan's sudden turn is set against the standard ethics-book reason, showing that his motive is moral fear of rule rather than loss
gains.b: the quatrain's list of passing goods is tested on a case where none of them has yet failed

note: The Kural asks what one who keeps household life in dharma could gain by going the outer way; in the Cintamani the whole household, brother, friends and wives, goes that way and reaches a higher state.
teaches: The Kural's question assumes a householder could gain nothing more by leaving, but the epic answers it by having a just king's whole household leave together and arrive at the state that is ever new.

gains.a: the epic's mass renunciation is read as an answer to a Tamil defence of household life, not only as story
gains.b: the couplet's rhetorical question is shown to be contestable from inside Tamil literature, by a narrative that claims a gain beyond the householder's

note: The Kural's lover asks whether the lotus-eyed one's world can be sweeter than sleep in the beloved's soft arms; Civakan, having tasted a nectar-like bliss, no longer wants the pleasure of women whose beauty makes the heavens bow.
teaches: The lover ranks the beloved's arms above heaven, while the epic's hero, having tasted a higher bliss, finds women's embrace unwanted, so the two verses make opposite rankings of the same two goods.

gains.a: the patikam's closing simile gains an opponent: it reads as a rebuttal of the lover's ranking rather than a bare statement
gains.b: the couplet's open question gets an answer from a renouncer, showing what the lover's ranking denies

note: Verse 1 praises the god of gods who reached by himself (தன்னின் எய்தி) the supreme bliss that does not fail; verse 29 ends the patikam with Civakan in a flood of bliss (இன்ப வெள்ளம்).
teaches: The patikam opens on a god who won unfailing bliss by his own effort and closes on a man who reaches a flood of bliss, so the hero's whole story is framed as walking the road the worshipped one walked, not as receiving a gift from him.

note: Pattinathar asks what breasts, union with women and gathered wealth can do against the coming struggle, and says the god put an eyeless needle in his hand; Civakan stops wanting women's pleasure because he has tasted a greater sweetness.
teaches: Both rich men turn from women and wealth, but the Siddhar's ground is their uselessness before death and a sign from Siva, while the epic's is a higher bliss already tasted, so the same turn can be told as a loss seen through or as a lesser pleasure outgrown.

gains.a: the epic's sweet simile is set against a bitter Saiva account of the same turn, showing that the Cintamani makes renunciation a gain of pleasure, not a flight from it
gains.b: the Siddhar's turn, which rests on death and a god's token, is shown to be one motive among others, since a Jain hero leaves the same goods with no god sending a sign

note: Kural 17 states that the sea itself depends on the cloud returning what it took; verses 32 to 38 narrate that loop, from clouds grazing the sea to the flood reaching the sea again.
teaches: Read together, the couplet's abstract dependence becomes a full itinerary, and the epic's long description gains its shape: it is a circuit of giving back, not a string of pictures.

gains.a: a reason for its sea-to-sea ordering: the run enacts a return the couplet says the world depends on
gains.b: the intermediate stages the couplet skips: mountain, falls, sluices and fields through which the returned water passes

note: The Kural likens the wise man's wealth to water filling the village tank; the Cintamani likens the river's flood to the hand of a generous man carrying wealth to those who have nothing.
teaches: The tradition's image ran both ways, wealth explained by water and water by giving, and the epic adds movement and direction toward the needy, where the Kural's tank waits to be drawn from.

gains.a: a moral precedent that makes the river's simile a statement about how wealth should behave
gains.b: an active counterpart to its still tank: wealth that goes out town by town to the needy instead of waiting to be drawn

note: Kural 978 opposes greatness that bows to smallness that admires itself; the paddy simile sets the base man's erect wealth and the learned man's bow in one stalk at two ages.
teaches: The pair shows that the bow and the raised head can be stages of one thing rather than two kinds of people: what stands erect is empty, and the same stalk bows once it is full.

gains.a: a general maxim that its farm image is illustrating, which lifts the last verse of the chapter into a lesson
gains.b: a picture of how the change from pride to humility happens, by ripening, which the couplet's fixed opposition does not show

note: Kural 1033 says the ploughman alone lives on his own, while all others bow (தொழுது) to eat; in the Cintamani the sower himself bows (தொழுது) to the seed as he sows.
teaches: The ploughman whom the Kural sets above all bowing still bows, to the crop on which his independence rests, so his self-sufficiency is itself a dependence.

gains.a: a sense of why its farmers' gesture matters: they are the ones the Kural says need bow to no one
gains.b: a limit: the independence it praises rests on a seed the ploughman must greet with folded hands

note: Both epics walk through rich wet fields; the Silappathikaram's Jain nun warns that a careless step may hurt crab and snail, while the Cintamani's narrator delights as the ploughing herds scatter the fish.
teaches: The ahimsa scruple that a Jain nun in one epic applies to every footstep in the fields is absent from the Jain poet's own celebration of ploughing, so the epics keep that scruple for the ascetic and not for the land's prosperity.

note: The Kural defines a land as where unfailing yield, the worthy (தக்கார்) and the undiminished wealthy gather; the Cintamani's closing verse on Hemangadam makes it a place for those who do penance and those who make wealth, after ten verses of harvest.
teaches: The epic fills the couplet's three-part definition with a whole country, and reads its worthy ones as those who do penance, so the Kural's land is given room for renunciants beside the wealthy.

gains.a: the hyperbole of heaven fallen to earth is anchored in a received Tamil definition of what makes a land
gains.b: the couplet's unspecified தக்கார் receives a concrete reading as ascetics living alongside the rich

note: The Kural calls those lands whose riches need no seeking; the Cintamani's pools are strewn with gold beads from broken girdles that no one troubles to gather.
teaches: Set beside the reapers and threshers of 55 to 59, the gold no one picks up shows the epic taking unsought wealth to mean surplus beyond need after labour, not riches without work.

gains.a: the image of the gold-starred pools is read as a mark of the ideal land rather than as mere ornament
gains.b: the couplet's riches that need no seeking are given a scene where the absence of seeking is visible

note: Puhar's open court leaves traders' bundles unguarded because a thief is made to carry his load and whirl; Hemangadam's pools hold gold that lies untaken because no one wants it.
teaches: Two epics praise a city by its untaken wealth but give opposite grounds, fear of a punishing power in the Silappathikaram and simple satiety in the Cintamani, so the marvel is not one convention but two theories of order.

note: The Sirupanarruppadai paints the kinai bard's hunger in his kitchen, his wife boiling unsalted greens behind a shut door, until a patron's gifts end it; the Cintamani puts the porunar's distress down in half a line, through the carts of paddy and cane.
teaches: The epic keeps the Sangam bard's want only to cancel it at once, and moves its relief from one named patron's gift to the anonymous traffic of a rich land.

gains.a: the stock phrase about the kinai bards is seen to carry a whole earlier genre of hunger and rescue
gains.b: the guide poem's patron-centred relief is set against a later picture where plenty, not a giver, ends the bard's want

note: The Perumpanarruppadai's girls on sky-touching terraces move like peacocks rejoicing on a great hill's slope; the Cintamani's women on the mansion rows look like peacocks spreading their wings in the mist on a high hill.
teaches: The epic inherits the Sangam figure of terrace women as hill peacocks but makes the hill's mist out of the houses' own perfume smoke, turning a natural setting into manufactured luxury.

gains.a: the simile is traced to an older description of a port city's rich women
gains.b: the older image is shown surviving into the epics with its landscape replaced by the household

note: In both the sulking woman's charge turns on eyes: in the Kural all women feast on the man with theirs, in the Cintamani the women say his loves are in his eyes, and refuse him.
teaches: The Kural keeps the eye-charge inside the couple's quarrel, while the epic lets the same charge end in snapped girdles and spilled gold, so the sulk becomes a sign of the city's wealth rather than a turn in a love.

gains.a: the epic's brief quoted words are recognised as a set move of the sulking wife
gains.b: the couplet's private reproach is shown being absorbed into public description of a prosperous land

note: Both picture the bought embrace through a body: the Kural's woman of wealth embraces a stranger's corpse (பிணந்தழீஇ); the epic's net-woman embraces the flesh of wealth (தசை தழீஇ) and throws the body away.
teaches: Set beside the epic's hunter who keeps the meat of wealth and drops the carcass, the couplet's corpse reads naturally as the client handled by the woman, so the disgust in Kural 913 belongs to the trade itself rather than only to the man.

gains.a: the epic's hunting conceit is seen reworking the Kural's own corpse image and verb of embrace
gains.b: the couplet's disputed embracer gains a later poet's figure in which the woman is plainly the one who embraces and the man is the discarded body

note: The courtesan who ruins whoever falls into her net, refused by the citizens in 78, returns in 98 as the moat that ruins whoever falls into it.
teaches: The vice the poet praises the city for shunning becomes, twenty verses later, the figure of its defence, so the same destroying woman is a danger to citizens and a weapon against enemies.

note: The epic arms the wall with self-acting engines and names no defender; the Kural says every excellence of a fort is nothing without men excellent in action.
teaches: The epic's picture of a wall that fights by its own machinery is exactly the kind of fort the couplet calls empty, so the Kural supplies the missing term by which this lavish security can fail.

gains.a: the catalogue of engines gains a standard that shows what it leaves out: the people who must work them
gains.b: the couplet's unnamed excellences of a fort gain a concrete inventory of what a later poet thought those excellences were

audit_text_issue: Catalogue continues into 102; no finite verb.

note: The Cintamani's wall is armed by Yavana engines that throw molten metal, arrows and stones outward; Kural 747 names three ways a fort is taken, the third (அறைப்படுத்தல்) by working on those inside.
teaches: Read together, the two show that the epic's elaborate machinery answers only the outward assaults of the couplet's list, leaving the inside danger by which this city is in fact lost to its own minister.

gains.a: the engine catalogue acquires an ironic edge, since the couplet names the threat no machine can meet
gains.b: the couplet's abstract third danger gets a concrete case of a fully armed city whose defences all face outward

note: Both use வரைவு for the courtesans: the epic says they sell beauty வரைவின்றி, the Kural calls such women வரைவிலா and their arms a mire for base men.
teaches: The same word that the Kural uses to condemn the courtesan becomes in the Jain epic an item in a city's praise, so the reader sees that a heaven-like city could include the trade the ethical book calls a hell.

gains.a: the epic's praise is shown to carry a word the ethical tradition had already loaded with blame
gains.b: the couplet's condemnation is set against a poem that celebrates the same openness as wealth and beauty

note: Verse 109 has kings linger in the courtesans' quarter out of desire; at 206 a counsellor warns the king that many who gorged on women's pleasure fell into sin and blame.
teaches: The pleasure that the city praise lets kings enjoy without comment is the same pleasure that the story will turn into a warning to its own king, so the description quietly prepares the charge.

note: Both cities leave goods unguarded: Puhar's open court keeps bundles safe because a spirit punishes the thief, the Cintamani's merchants leave fallen jewels lying as a matter of their own conduct.
teaches: The pair gives two different accounts of why a rich city's goods are safe, one by fear of a guardian spirit's punishment and one by the citizens' surfeit and habit, so honesty is shown as either enforced or assumed.

note: The Silappathikaram opens its Puhar with the earth as a woman, sea for garment, hills for breasts, rivers for hair; the Cintamani makes the city wall a maiden with the moat for garment and bastions for breasts.
teaches: The same body-map moves from the whole earth to a single wall, and the Cintamani's word கன்னி turns it into a figure of a fortress never entered, which the Silappathikaram's earth-woman does not carry.

note: Kural 215 likens the wise man's wealth to a full village tank everyone draws from; verse 106 has the inner city's families bring wealth from overseas islands and feed many (பலர்க்கு ஆர்த்தி).
teaches: The couplet says shared wealth is like a common tank but not where it comes from; the epic supplies the source in perilous sea trade and makes feeding many the mark that justifies calling the city heavenly.

gains.a: the epic's praise of wealth is given an ethical test, that the wealth is used to fill many
gains.b: the couplet's image of a public tank gains a whole merchant class acting it out

note: The pavilion where the king dwells with desire burning in him is what a minister later names as the liquor of desire in which the king drowned and left the path of justice.
teaches: The lavish pavilion that reads as ornament is the poet's first, unjudged sign of the vice the minister will later blame for the king's ruin.

note: The garden one cannot leave without losing one's life anticipates the king's words that he cannot bear to part from Vijayai, for which he gives his rule to Kattiyangaran.
teaches: The garden's power to hold its owner is the same inability to part that later makes the king hand his kingdom to a minister.

note: The king introduced with a gracious sceptre and a single command is, some sixty verses later, the king who slips from guarding the land to cling to his queen.
teaches: The poet sets out the full catalogue of a just king's marks so that the reader can measure how far this king falls from them.

note: Both epics put a king with his beloved in a built pleasure-park of hills, falls, pools and deer.
teaches: The same crafted royal park is, in the Manimekalai, interrupted by news from the prison that turns the king to charity, and in the Cintamani the setting of a desire that costs the king his rule.

note: Kural 901 says men set on their wives miss the fine fruit and men of action do not want that desire; the epic shows a king whose rule is given up for it.
teaches: The Kural's flat warning becomes in the epic a seductive scene, so the reader is drawn into the very desire the couplet tells the man of action to refuse.

gains.a: The epic verse gets the moral frame its narrator withholds: the king's desire is the kind that a ruler is told to refuse.
gains.b: The couplet's unnamed 'fine fruit' is given concrete stakes: for a king the loss is his kingdom and his life.

note: The Kural's lover says anicham and swan's down are like nerunji to her feet; the epic has a whole city's women whose feet shiver on flowering cotton while they wear anicham.
teaches: A lover's private hyperbole about one woman's feet becomes in the epic a stock trait of a whole class of wealthy women, showing how the Kural's love conceits turned into description.

gains.a: The verse's strange shiver of feet on cotton is legible as a known conceit, so its point is degree of wealth, not novelty of image.
gains.b: The couplet's image is shown to have become public property, attached to a city's luxury rather than one lover's gaze.

audit_text_issue: line 1 குஞ்சி மேல் அனிச்ச hard; sense flagged

note: Kural 81 says all of a household's keeping of goods is for caring for guests; the epic lists eating with guests as one item among the city's perfumes, gold and beds.
teaches: Where the Kural makes hospitality the purpose that justifies household wealth, the epic sets it inside a catalogue of pleasure, so the duty becomes one ornament of a city that will soon fall.

gains.a: The verse's single mention of guests is shown to carry the one moral justification of wealth in a run otherwise given to luxury.
gains.b: The couplet's rule is seen in a setting where wealth has outgrown the purpose the couplet gives it.

note: Tirumanthiram 518 says that if pujas in the First One's temple stop, kings suffer, the rains' bounty falls and theft spreads; the epic says the Jina's shrines everywhere keep the city's wealth from failing.
teaches: A Saiva manual and a Jain epic share the belief that shrines keep a land prosperous, but the Saiva verse ties it to rites that must not lapse while the Jain verse credits only the shrines' presence.

gains.a: The epic's brief claim is set in a wider Tamil belief tying a city's welfare to worship, so it reads as doctrine rather than mere praise.
gains.b: The Saiva warning is shown to be not only sectarian: a Jain text makes the same causal link without the threat of lapse.

note: In 157 the king is fierce as a poisonous serpent's fire; in 290 he is the sun of the Kuru line swallowed by the great serpent of his minister.
teaches: The serpent's wrath that made Saccandan terrible to enemies is turned back on him from inside his own court, so the image of his strength becomes the image of his end.

note: 159 says the whole world rests in the cool shade of Saccandan's umbrella as under a father's feet; 290 says that when the minister swallows him the darkness of the bent sceptre spreads and the people grieve.
teaches: The shade praised as the world's settled condition proves to depend on one man's life, since one betrayal turns the straight sceptre's shade into the bent sceptre's darkness.

note: 167 says Vijayai's eyes are poison and nectar that madden even sages; in 181 Saccandan is caught in the net of her long eyes.
teaches: The descriptive claim that her eyes overturn the self-controlled is cashed in the plot: the first one they capture is the king whose fall drives the epic.

note: The king is an அணங்கு to women (157); the princess is an அணங்கு even to the goddess on the lotus (162).
teaches: The poem sets an afflicting beauty against a greater one before they meet, so the king who wounds others by his looks is the one wounded by hers.

note: The Kural's man sees two looks in her eyes, one that gives the sickness and one that cures it; the epic says her eyes are poison and nectar at once.
teaches: The couplet's private double look of lover's sickness and cure becomes, in an epic, a public force that maddens sages and later unseats a king.

gains.a: the epic's poison-and-nectar image is placed in an older Tamil account of the look as both wound and remedy
gains.b: the couplet's two looks are given consequences beyond the lover, reaching ascetics and the state

note: The Kural's man laments that his might, feared by enemies in battle, broke before her bright forehead; 161 shows a king whose spear killed kings at the height of his fame just before he meets Vijayai.
teaches: Read with the story that follows, the couplet's lover's hyperbole becomes literal history: the warrior whose strength breaks before a woman is a king, and what breaks is his kingdom.

gains.a: the praise of Saccandan's martial peak gains a known pattern that foretells its undoing by beauty
gains.b: the couplet's complaint gains a case where the broken might is public and political, not only the lover's pride

note: The Naladiyar says kings who rode under the umbrella at the head of armies fall when their deeds turn, and enemies take their wives; 161 shows Saccandan at the full of his fame, the starting point of such a fall.
teaches: The quatrain gives the general fall of the umbrella king; the epic fills in one fall step by step, with the king's own infatuation as the turn and his queen driven out, so impermanence works through character and not only fortune.

gains.a: the epic's high point of praise gains the moral frame within which its listeners would hear it as the top of a wheel
gains.b: the quatrain's abstract turn of deeds gains a narrated mechanism, desire and a trusted minister

note: Purananuru 35 tells the Chola his tall umbrella is not for shade but to shelter suffering subjects, and warns him the world blames kings when things go wrong; 159 says Saccandan's umbrella already shades the world like a father.
teaches: The Sangam poet gives the umbrella as a duty the king must be urged to keep, the epic as a state already achieved; set together, the epic's praise lacks the warning that the story will soon need.

gains.a: the epic's settled praise is seen to omit the counsel that in the Sangam poem accompanies the umbrella
gains.b: the poem's admonition gains a later narrative in which a praised umbrella king does lose the world's shade

note: Purananuru 56 equates the Pandya with four gods, one for each of his powers; 160 equates Saccandan with Dharma, Varuna, Death, Vaman and Kama.
teaches: The epic keeps the Sangam form of measuring a king god by god but shifts it from war powers to grace, giving and beauty, and puts the god of desire in the list, which the story makes the king's flaw.

gains.a: the epic's god-list is placed in an inherited praise form, so its departures (Dharma, Kama) stand out
gains.b: the Sangam form is shown surviving into Jain narrative with new gods and an ironic edge

note: Both are the man's first sight of the woman and both reach for அணங்கு; the Kural's lover wavers among goddess, peahen and woman, while Sachchandan, on the likelier reading, takes her for an அணங்கு without doubt (ஐயுறான்).
teaches: The Kural's perplexity at first sight is a lover's healthy doubt; the epic gives a king who does not doubt, and his certainty that she is more than human is the first step of the absorption that later costs him his kingdom.

gains.a: the king's untroubled certainty is seen as a departure from the expected first-sight wavering, marking his surrender as complete
gains.b: the couplet's three-way doubt is shown to hold a check that a man without it, a king, loses

note: The Kural's lover says all five senses find their objects in one woman; verse 194 gathers sound, scent, sight and touch in Vijayai and calls the joy inexhaustible.
teaches: What the Kural states as the joy of union, with no cost named, the epic puts in a king, and four verses later shows the cost: a man whose senses are all fed from one source slips from guarding the land (198).

gains.a: the sense catalogue is read as a deliberate totality, not ornament, setting up the king's neglect
gains.b: the couplet's praise of complete delight is given a setting, kingship, where that completeness becomes a danger

note: Kural 901 says men who fix their desire on the wife miss life's fine fruit; 196 measures the king's wedded intimacy as greater than the sea, and the story goes on to make that desire lose him his realm.
teaches: The Kural's chapter on following the wife assumes a fault in the yielding; the epic gives a blameless, chaste queen (verse 7, வீடாத கற்பின்) and lawful marriage, and still the husband's boundless absorption alone ruins him, so the rule holds without any fault in the woman.

gains.a: the celebration of the wedding season acquires its moral edge from a stated rule
gains.b: the couplet's claim is tested on a case where the wife is beyond reproach, showing the danger lies in the man's desire, not in her

note: Verse 179 praises Vijayai's soles as if made without bone or sinew (என்பொடு நரம்பு இன்றி); Naladiyar 46 lists bone (என்பு) and sinew (நரம்பு) among the parts of the body and asks which of them is the garlanded woman.
teaches: Two Jain works use the same two words to opposite ends: the epic's praise must imagine the beloved's body without bone and sinew, while the quatrain dissolves her into them, so the courtly portrait depends on the very forgetting the ascetic verse is written to undo.

gains.a: the hyperbole of the boneless foot is seen to deny exactly what the renouncer insists on, showing what the praise leaves out
gains.b: the quatrain's list is shown answering a real literary convention of praise, not an abstract desire

note: Verse 192 praises Vijayai's red-cornered eyes as fighting carp (களிக் கயல் பொருவ); Naladiyar 44's renunciant refuses men who call eyes பொருகயல் and sees an eye as a scooped-out palm fruit.
teaches: The Naladiyar's renunciant names the epic's own stock of praise as the temptation he walks past, and the epic shows that praise doing its work on a king who does not walk past it.

gains.a: the stock carp-eye simile is shown to be a recognised snare in the ethical literature, not neutral ornament
gains.b: the quatrain's 'petty men' who praise eyes are given a full instance in a celebrated poem, and a consequence in the king's fall

audit_text_issue: 192 கயல் பொருவ: reading of பொருவ as 'fight' is doubtful

note: 195 has the king linger with his wife as a monsoon cloud lingers; 198 says the king slipped from guarding the earth (மண் அகம் காவலின் வழுக்கி) while joined to her.
teaches: The lingering that the wedding verses present as pure delight is the same act that 198 names as a lapse in the king's guard, so the romantic sequence is already the first step of the political fall.

note: In 190 king and queen drink each other as nectar and wine; in 199 they drink the flood of love without pause while fortune slips from the king of the moon-white parasol.
teaches: The drinking image moves from mutual delight to unceasing consumption: what was a figure of shared love becomes the measure of the time in which the king's fortune leaks away.

note: 188 likens the wedded pair to the three-eyed god and his goddess joined; in 208 a counsellor cites the god's taking the mountain king's daughter into half his body as a great blame (பெரும் பழி).
teaches: The same divine union serves the narrator as the highest praise of the couple and the counsellor as a warning of shame from desire, so the epic lets its own simile be turned against the king within twenty verses.

note: 187 says the two were joined by the பான்மை for joining; 215 says the king followed the way of her mind because a former பான்மை (முனம் ஆகிய பான்மை) sprouted, ignoring all warning.
teaches: If பான்மை in 187 is read as destiny, the marriage and the king's ruinous absorption have one source in the epic's account, apportioned former deeds, while 187 also names the ministers' reasoning: fate and judgment are both given as causes.

note: 183 likens Vijayai in her father's palace to Tirumakal on the lotus; 232 has Tirumakal leave Sachchandan without a word, the king left alone.
teaches: The king wins a woman praised as the goddess of fortune and, through his absorption in her, loses the goddess of fortune herself: the epic turns its own epithet into the measure of the cost.

note: The soothsayer warns that setting power on one man will drive prosperity from the land; in 241 Kattiyankaran, now holding that power, says a deity urges him night and day to kill the king.
teaches: The prophecy names no traitor, only the structure of power, so its fulfilment shows the epic locating the danger in the king's act of delegation before it locates it in the minister's character.

note: Kattiyankaran bows and promises to bear the yoke so that no blame falls on the land; in 241 he asks his council how to kill the king, laying the impulse on a hostile deity.
teaches: The minister who vowed blameless guardianship later disowns his own intent by blaming a god, so the story pairs the king's excuse by destiny (213) with the usurper's excuse by possession.

note: Vijayai's three dreams, which leave her trembling at dawn, are told in 223: the ashoka tree falls and a sprout rises from its root.
teaches: The dream that frightens her is a dream of fall and succession, and when the king reads it (225) he speaks only of the heir and keeps silent on the fall, so her fear at 219 rightly answers the half that is withheld.

note: The narrator says past destiny sprouted and the king followed his heart; the minister of 233 tells the king he left the path of justice and bathed in the liquor of lust.
teaches: The epic gives the king's fall two causes in two voices, destiny in the narrator's and the king's own wrong path in the minister's, and does not let either cancel the other.
audit_text_issue: gloss of 233's speaker rests on the marker

note: Both queens wake from dreams of the king's fall: the Pandya queen sees umbrella and sceptre drop; Vijayai's dream (told in 223) shows the tree that is the king falling and a sprout rising.
teaches: The Silappathikaram's queen dreams only the end of a reign, while the Cintamani's queen dreams an end that carries an heir, so the same omen-form serves tragedy in one epic and a story of restoration in the other.

note: Kural 377 says even the rich enjoy only as the apportioner has apportioned; the king says his pleasures and life-days are measured by past penance and so refuses counsel.
teaches: The couplet's limit on enjoyment becomes, in a king's mouth, a licence to stop listening, which shows that a doctrine of allotted fruit can be turned against the duty to act on advice.

gains.a: the king's refusal is seen to borrow a recognised ethical teaching rather than being bare infatuation
gains.b: the couplet is shown to be open to a fatalist misuse it does not itself guard against

note: Kural 509 bids a ruler trust no one unexamined; the king vouches for Kattiyankaran by love and past victories and forbids further words.
teaches: Loyalty and battle service, the very grounds the king gives, are not the examination the couplet asks for, so the scene shows how trust can feel tested while skipping the test of fitness for power.

gains.a: the king's grounds for trust are measured against a stated rule and found to fall short of it
gains.b: the couplet's bare 'examine' is shown failing in a case where the examiner thinks he already knows the man

note: Kural 448 says a king without rebukers perishes even with no enemy; the king hears Rudradattan's rebuke, rejects it, and the counsellor withdraws.
teaches: The epic shows the middle case the couplet skips, a king who has a rebuker and sends him away, and its ruin comes through the trusted man, so the danger lies in refusing rebuke as much as in lacking it.

gains.a: the counsellor's failure is given the weight of a known rule of kingship
gains.b: the couplet's 'having no rebuker' is shown to include a king who drives rebuke off

note: Kural 901 says men who fix their desire on the wife miss life's fine fruit; the narrator says the king followed his heart to the queen because a past destiny sprouted.
teaches: The couplet treats being led by desire for one's wife as a fault to be avoided, while the epic adds a ripening past deed as its cause, which raises the question the couplet does not face: whether such a man could have chosen otherwise.

gains.a: the king's surrender to desire is named as a recognised fault of rulers, not only a love story
gains.b: the couplet's simple prohibition is set against a story where karma also pushes the man

note: Kural 55 praises the wife who rises worshipping her husband and not a god; Vijayai rises, worships the god's feet, and then goes to her lord's feet.
teaches: A Jain epic keeps the wife's devotion to her husband but sets worship of the god first, so the couplet's exclusive ranking is answered with an order of two duties rather than a choice between them.

gains.a: the queen's morning is seen as a deliberate ordering of devotions against a known ideal
gains.b: the couplet's 'not a god' is shown to be a position a later work could decline while still honouring the husband

note: Rudradattan counts the konrai-wearing god's taking the mountain-daughter as his half as a stain and a great blame; Tirumanthiram 16 names the same god by that half-woman form as the one the gods delight in.
teaches: The same mark of Siva, his body shared with Uma, is a counsellor's example of lust's disgrace in a Jain epic and a title of praise in Tirumular's invocation, so the image itself is where the schools part.

gains.a: the counsellor's slight is seen to strike at a form the Saiva poets hold central
gains.b: the invocation's epithet is shown to be one a rival tradition read as a scandal

note: Rudradattan argues that lust's blame cannot be hidden and is drummed through the world; Naladiyar 89 says lust burns the mind itself, worse than fire or sun.
teaches: The counsellor argues from public disgrace and the quatrain from inward burning, so a reader sees that the ethics of desire had two separate arguments and that the epic, speaking to a king, chose reputation.

gains.a: the counsellor's choice of argument by reputation stands out against an argument he did not use
gains.b: the quatrain's inward harm is set beside the outward cost it leaves out

note: The king reads the crown, garlands and shoot but will not speak of the falling tree; at 267 he tells the queen that all she dreamed that night has come to fruit.
teaches: The withheld half of the dream was the king's own death, so his kindly silence at the reading becomes, at the fall of the city, an admission that he knew.

note: Consoling the queen, the king asks whether a dream's nature is truth; at 267 he tells her the dreams have all come true.
teaches: The king's dismissal of dreams was comfort he did not believe, since the same man had read the dream by the treatise and later concedes its truth.

note: Wisdom's remedy for the king's lost sense is to build a rare machine; at 272 the king tells the queen the vehicle is ready and she must go first.
teaches: The machine ordered as penance for the lust that cost the kingdom becomes the means of saving the heir, so the fault's remedy is escape rather than reform.

note: Dharmadattan argues that Fortune deserts the man who seizes his maker; Madanan answers that he can speak only with the sword, not the mouth.
teaches: The counsel fails not by being refuted but by being refused, so the plot proceeds with its warning on record, which the story will make good.

note: Both use the wood-apple swallowed by the elephant, whole in shell and emptied within: the Cintamani for a king whom Fortune has left, Tirumular for Siva swallowing soul, states and world.
teaches: The same figure of a shell kept whole while its substance is taken means ruin for a king and consummation for a soul, so Tirumular turns a stock image of loss into one of absorption in Siva.

gains.a: the epic's compressed simile is confirmed in its sense of an outwardly intact but emptied reign
gains.b: the Saiva verse is shown inverting an image whose ordinary use in narrative was loss of fortune

audit_text_issue: 232 sense flagged uncertain; TM 2593 திரிய unclear

note: The Kural binds the one at the king's side to speak what is good even to a king who destroys counsel; in the Cintamani the counsel comes from Wisdom as minister, after the realm is already given away.
teaches: With the minister's office handed to the usurper, the duty the Kural lays on the counsellor falls to the king's own wisdom, and it speaks only when advice can no longer save the realm.

gains.a: the figure of Wisdom as minister is placed within the Kural's account of the counsellor's duty
gains.b: the couplet's duty is shown with its limit: counsel that comes too late can only plan an escape

note: Kural 906 says the man who fears his wife's shoulders is worthless though he live like the gods; Dharmadattan says the king valued a woman's pleasure above heaven and nectar.
teaches: The Kural weighs the wife-ruled man against the gods' life and finds him worthless, while the epic's king makes the same comparison in reverse, and the cost falls not on his worth but on the whole realm.

gains.a: the counsellor's charge is seen as the Kural's chapter on being led by a woman, applied to a king
gains.b: the couplet's private failing is shown with a public cost, a world that sinks with its king

note: Kural 110 says there is no escape for one who kills a good done to him; Dharmadattan warns that Fortune will leave the man who seizes the king who made him, and that loyalty secures his line.
teaches: The Kural's 'no escape' for ingratitude is turned into a political forecast, the loss of fortune and lineage, and offered to a would-be usurper as prudence rather than only as virtue.

gains.a: the counsel is grounded in the Kural's ranking of ingratitude as the sin without remedy
gains.b: the couplet's abstract doom is given a concrete form, a usurper whose line will be uprooted

note: In 241 Kattiyangaran claims a great deity hostile to the king possesses him and urges the killing; 250 calls that a deity of his own mouth, after 247 has made the king himself the great deity.
teaches: The usurper's appeal to divine compulsion is answered by moving divinity to the king, so the regicide is recast from obedience to a god into an attack on one.

note: Dharmadattan forestalls the excuse of sending the king to heaven; in 259 Kattiyangaran uses exactly that excuse, dressed as a promise that the earth will brim with gold.
teaches: The counsellor named the usurper's rationalisation before he spoke it, so 259 reads as a man walking into a trap already shown to him.

note: 248 claims the king's splendour guards the world even while he sleeps; 261 shows the king sunk in pleasure, his army given up, and helpless against his minister.
teaches: The story refutes the councillor's extravagant praise of royal power: a king who has let go of rule is not protected by his majesty.

note: In 205 the king refuses the astrologer's warning, saying he has done his part for Kattiyangaran and let him do as he will; 260 lists the king's own grace among the things that will kill him.
teaches: அருள் கொல்லும் names the king's trust in 205 as a fatal fault, so his generosity is counted with lust and wealth among the causes of his fall.

note: The astrologer in 204 warned that if the king put his power in one man the land's fortune would leave; in 263 that man's army surrounds the palace.
teaches: The siege fulfils a warning the king dismissed, so the fall is shown as foreseen and refused, not as blind chance.

note: In 228 the king soothed Vijayai by calling belief in dreams a woman's credulity; in 267 he tells her that all she dreamt has come to pass.
teaches: The king's dismissal of his wife's dream is reversed by his own admission, which turns his later lecture on detachment in 269 into a man correcting his own earlier error.

note: Vijayai's dream in 223 of the ashoka tree falling, its garland crowning a shoot, is what the king says in 267 has now come true.
teaches: The fallen tree of the dream is the king himself, which the earlier verse could only hint at, while the shoot points ahead to the son not yet born.

note: Kural 388 calls the ruler who does justice and protects இறை; Dharmadattan calls the king a great deity because his favour makes and his anger burns.
teaches: The Kural makes the king's divinity a reward for just rule, while Dharmadattan makes it a matter of the king's power, which lets him use it to protect even a king who has abandoned rule.

gains.a: the councillor's claim is seen to drop the condition the Kural sets, which explains why the story can refute it
gains.b: the couplet's condition is shown to be what separates a just king's sanctity from mere fear of his power

note: Kural 547 says the ruler guards the world and justice guards him if he does not falter; 248 says the king's splendour guards the world even as he sleeps.
teaches: The Cintamani's king, who sleeps in pleasure and loses everything, illustrates the Kural's condition by its breach: majesty without unfaltering justice guards nothing.

gains.a: the verse's claim is placed against a rule that names the condition it leaves out
gains.b: the couplet's 'if he does not falter' is shown at work in a king who faltered through pleasure, not cruelty

note: Kural 691 tells those who serve kings to keep to them as men warming at a fire, neither near nor far; 250 says the king's fire burns those who touch it along with their kin and can be nectar or poison.
teaches: The Kural's fire is a rule of prudent distance for courtiers, while Dharmadattan extends it to the minister who would seize the fire, and to his whole family.

gains.a: the councillor's threat is grounded in a known maxim of service
gains.b: the couplet's image is carried from caution in service to the fate of a servant who turns on his king

note: Kural 110 says there is no escape for one who kills a benefit; 253 names a minister who kills the king who raised him among those who sink into hell and leprosy.
teaches: The epic gives the Kural's abstract unforgivable sin a concrete political form, the minister's regicide, and spells out where 'no escape' leads.

gains.a: the regicide is ranked as ingratitude, the sin the Kural puts beyond remedy
gains.b: the couplet's general rule receives its gravest case and an explicit punishment

note: Dharmadattan sends the one who kills and eats flesh to hell; Neelakesi 97 shows hell's tormentors burning beings while naming the sins of killing and eating flesh.
teaches: Dharmadattan files regicide in one list with killing and flesh-eating, the very sins Neelakesi's tormentors name as they burn the damned, so a political crime is set inside the minor epic's catalogue of injuries to life.

note: Kural 559 says that when the king bends justice the sky will not rain; 255 extends the effects to the planets, the hours, harvest, hunger, women's chastity and dharma.
teaches: The Cintamani turns the Kural's warning to an unjust king into an argument against a minister seizing power, treating usurpation itself as the bending of the sceptre.

gains.a: the councillor's list is anchored in the Kural's best-known statement of the bent sceptre
gains.b: the couplet's single effect, failed rain, is shown as the first of a cascade that reaches into household morals

note: Thirikadugam 50 names three separate 'planets' that cut off rain: a greedy king, deceitful men and a woman who crosses her bounds; 255 makes the bent sceptre the one cause from which failed rain and broken chastity both follow.
teaches: Where the Thirikadugam gives the king, the liar and the unchaste woman equal blame for drought, the Cintamani makes women's lapse a symptom of the king's fault.

gains.a: the epic's causal order stands out against a list that treats the three as parallel
gains.b: the verse's planet image, கோள், is shown read in the epic as literal disorder of the planets

note: Tirumular says one who comes to seize the world for others or himself has the nature of a pouncing tiger; 262 shows Kattiyangaran's seizure: kin chained, wealth given to those who submit, one umbrella over the land.
teaches: The Tirumanthiram names the usurper's nature, and the Cintamani shows his method, buying loyalty and chaining kin, and calls the result a lamp of infamy.

gains.a: the narrator's verdict of blame is seen to match a doctrine of kingship outside the epic
gains.b: the verse's tentative line about seizing the world gains a worked case of usurpation by a minister

note: Ilango's patikam says dharma becomes death to those who err in kingship and that past deeds ripen; 260 lists Death, the woman, the king's own fault, his wealth and his grace as what will kill the king.
teaches: The Silappathikaram's king dies for an unjust verdict, while the Cintamani's is killed for lust and misplaced trust, so 'erring in kingship' is shown to include neglect, not only injustice.

note: Naladiyar 110 says what was fixed at the start neither shrinks nor grows, so why grieve in ruin; 269 says birth and death come from one's own deeds and grief is want of understanding.
teaches: Both forbid grief by appeal to a fixed outcome, but the king speaks while his own fault caused the ruin, so in his mouth deed-fruit is also a confession, which the Naladiyar's impersonal fixed mark is not.

gains.a: the king's consolation is placed within the ethical books' argument against grieving
gains.b: the quatrain's fixed fate is set beside a version in which the fixing is one's own past action

note: The Siddhar says weeping and worship are useless because good and evil come as the lotus-born god wrote; the king says birth and death come from the fruit of one's own deeds.
teaches: The two give the same counsel against grief for opposite reasons: the Siddhar's outcome is written by a creator, the Cintamani's by the sufferer's own deeds, with no god in the account.

gains.a: the king's karma is seen as godless by contrast with a fate assigned by Brahma
gains.b: the Siddhar's fatalism is shown to have a rival ground in self-made deed that leaves worship equally useless

note: Purananuru 186 says the world lives by its king, so it is the king's duty to know he is its life; 246 puts kings above the gods.
teaches: The Purananuru turns the king's exalted place into a duty laid on the king, while Dharmadattan turns it into a ban laid on the subject who would harm him.

gains.a: the councillor's exaltation of kingship is seen as one use of a shared idea, aimed at the subject
gains.b: the poem's claim is shown to cut the other way when a minister, not a king, is the one being warned

note: In 256 Madanan's sweating, garlanded chest is likened to the Karthikai lamp lit on a hill; in 262 Kattiyangaran's seizure is a blazing lamp of infamy lit on a hilltop.
teaches: The festival lamp that first flatters the usurper's ally turns, six verses later, into the sign that shows the usurper's shame to the whole land, so the image passes from praise to blame.

note: Dharmadattan names the king's own fault, his woman and his grace among what kills him; the king, consoling his queen, says death and birth come from the fruit of one's deeds.
teaches: The councillor places the cause in faults of this life that the king could have avoided, while the king refers it to deeds in general, so his doctrine of karma softens a blame the earlier verse fixes on him.

note: Vijayai dreamed that the asoka tree fell and was utterly gone; in 289 the king falls to the earth and goes out like the setting sun.
teaches: The half of the dream the king refused to read at 225 is fulfilled in his fall, so the battle is the dream's first image enacted and Civakan, the shoot, is still to come.

note: The பிண்டி whose fall in the dream meant the king's death is in 271 the tree of the Jina whose scripture the king offers his wife as consolation.
teaches: One tree carries both the loss and the remedy: the royal asoka falls, and the Jina's asoka stands as the ground for not grieving that fall.

note: In 281 the discus cuts the king's shield as the snake joins the sun's disc; in 290 the minister is the great snake that swallows the king, sun of the Kuru line.
teaches: The eclipse simile moves from the shield to the man, so a battle image becomes the narrator's verdict that the usurpation is a swallowing of the sun.

note: In 259 Kattiyankaran proposed that the king go to rule heaven as lord of the gods; in 291 the king does go to the gods, as their guest.
teaches: The usurper's euphemism for murder comes literally true, but the narrator gives the king the heaven of a warrior and a Jain devotee, not the throne the usurper mockingly offered.

note: 261 makes the king's surrender of his army in pleasure the opening for the treachery; 290 mourns him as the sun of the just sceptre swallowed by the minister alone.
teaches: In death the narrator moves the blame wholly onto the usurper, so the epic holds both a negligent king and a righteous one and lets the lament forget the first.

note: The couplet says a ruler who does not attend and judge perishes by himself; Saccandan, who gave up rule for pleasure, perishes, but by a minister's treachery, and is mourned as just.
teaches: The epic splits the couplet's single cause: neglect opens the door and another's crime walks through, so the ruin is self-made in the Kural's sense yet not self-inflicted.

gains.a: the lament gains a standard that names the king's own share in his fall, which 290 leaves unsaid
gains.b: the couplet's bare தானே கெடும் gains a mechanism, the trusted minister through whom a neglectful king's ruin actually comes

note: Puram 62 ends with the gods of the unfading flowers receiving many guests from a field where two kings died; 291 says the dead king became a guest of the gods, adding the Jina's feet and the mantra-sandal.
teaches: The Jain epic keeps the Sangam honour of the fallen king as heaven's guest but makes devotion to the Jina part of his passage, so the warrior's heaven is re-founded on religion.

gains.a: the epic's phrase is shown to be the old battlefield honour, which explains why a negligent king's end can still be glorious
gains.b: the Puram formula, which grounds heaven in fighting alone, is shown being given a religious condition by a later school

note: Pattinathar asks how many mothers, wives, children and births he has had and has yet to have, and cries to the lord of Ekambam; Saccandan reckons births past the sands of the shore and tells his wife kinship lasts two days.
teaches: The same reckoning of countless births and passing kin brings the Siddhar to despair and a cry for Siva's help, and brings the Jain king to composure with no god, so the argument's outcome turns on where release is placed.

gains.a: the king's consolation is shown to be the renouncer's argument, turned to comfort a wife at a parting rather than to leave the world
gains.b: the Siddhar's anguished count gains a reader who draws calm from it through scripture, the answer his song looks for only in the Lord

note: Perunkoppendu argues against the elders that the widow's life of plain food and gravel beds is not for her and the pyre is a lotus pool; Saccandan's women make the same choice in a simile and a vow of the other world, without the argument.
teaches: Set beside the Sangam queen's reasoned refusal, the epic's wives choose death as a group and by figure alone, while the one queen who must live, Vijayai, is spared the choice by her unborn son.

gains.a: The epic verse gains the explicit alternative its women reject, the austere widow's life Purananuru 246 describes.
gains.b: The Purananuru poem gains a counter-case in the same scene: a queen (Vijayai) whom motherhood bars from the pyre.

note: Naladiyar 3 says kings who rode elephants under the umbrella fall when their deeds turn and enemies take their wives; here the usurper mounts the elephant to proclaim himself and takes Fortune.
teaches: The quatrain names only the fallen king, but the epic shows the other half of the turn: the enemy who rises on the same elephant, a figure the poem's logic marks for the next fall.

gains.a: The epic scene gains a general frame in which the usurper's elephant-back triumph is itself unstable.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a named winner and a cause the poem leaves out: the fallen king's own neglect of rule.

note: Kural 37 bids the reader look at palanquin-bearer and rider instead of being told what virtue is; 303 offers the queen alone among skulls as sight for those who know sin only by report.
teaches: Both turn visible fortune into evidence for unseen merit, but the epic applies it to one life reversed from palace to burning ground, and the proof falls on a sufferer the poet does not blame.

gains.a: The epic's 'as if to show' gains the general argument from sight that Kural 37 states.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case where rider and bearer are the same person in one life, which exposes the cost of reading misfortune as proof.

note: Manimekalai 6 lists young mothers just delivered and helpless infants among those Death heaps for the burning ground to eat; in the Cintamani a mother gives birth in the burning ground and its deities bow.
teaches: The Buddhist epic makes the burning ground the end that spares no new mother or infant, while the Jain epic makes the same ground the birthplace of a king, so the place teaches impermanence in one and providence in the other.

note: Purananuru 359 gives the burning ground of owls, corpse-eating jackals and ghoul-women dancing by pyre lamps that has received even conquerors; 309 has jackals as drums, pyres as lamps, ghosts dancing and owls praising at a prince's birth.
teaches: The same creatures and lights that in the Sangam poem greet the end of kings serve in the epic as the band and lamps of a future king's birth, turning a warning about death into a grim birth-festival.

gains.a: Vijayai's bitter question gains its weight from the old image of this ground as where kingdoms end.
gains.b: The Sangam image gains a reversal it never shows: the ground receiving a beginning rather than an end.

note: Kural 10: only those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births. Vijayai asks that the Jina's dharma and her newborn son be her raft across a sea of sorrow.
teaches: The epic keeps the Kural's sea and crossing but moves the sea from rebirth to present grief and doubles the raft, placing a mother's hope in a child beside the lord's dharma.

gains.a: Vijayai's plea gains the doctrinal sea and swimmer the couplet fixes.
gains.b: The couplet gains a human raft alongside the divine one, which it does not allow for.

note: In 269 Saccandan consoles Vijayai that birth and death come from one's own deeds and that grief shows want of understanding; at the birth she blames her own deeds for the child's wretched birth and grieves.
teaches: The doctrine the king offered to end her grief becomes, once he is gone, the ground of her self-accusation, so the same teaching consoles the dying and burdens the survivor.

note: Vijayai's dream in 223 showed the asoka tree falling and a crowned shoot rising from its foot; 313 shows her as an evening where the sun has set and a young moon has risen.
teaches: The fall Saccandan would not interpret in 225 is now fulfilled, and the poet restates the dream's double meaning, loss and rising heir, in a new figure of sun and crescent moon.

note: The patikam in 10 says a deity stood at the mother's shoulder as companion and ended her distress; 314 shows how: the deity comes in the shape of the hunchbacked maid who never left her.
teaches: The summary's 'divine companion' turns out to work through disguise, choosing the most familiar servant's form, so the help comes as continuity of the queen's household rather than as a marvel.

note: The deity foretells that one will come right now to take the child and bids the queen hide; in 322 Kantukkatan reaches the child lying in the burning ground.
teaches: The prophecy and the command to hide make the mother's absence in 322 an arranged handing-over, not a desertion, which the finding scene alone would not show.

note: In 316 the deity foretells that one man will come at once and carry the child off; in 320 Kandukkatan appears out of the dark with a sword.
teaches: The foundling's rescue is framed as foretold before it happens, so the merchant's chance night visit reads as the working of the prince's destiny.

note: The hidden voice's blessing சீவ on the child's sneeze becomes, in 361, the name சீவகன் given him by his foster parents.
teaches: The hero's name is his lost mother's unseen blessing, given unknowingly a second time by the people who raise him.

note: Vijayai's blessing that her son will destroy his old enemy (நுன் பழம் பகை) is fulfilled when Kattiyangaran's rule ends in the Manmagal ilampakam.
teaches: The epic's whole plot of revenge and restoration is set down at the cradle as a mother's word, two thousand verses before it comes true.
audit_text_issue: 2323 is flagged uncertain in the last line, but the fall of Kattiyangaran is clear.

note: In 306 Vijayai imagines the royal order that should have opened the gold hoards for suppliants at a prince's birth; in 331 a merchant opens his own hoard like a mountain of red gold for the same child.
teaches: The birth-gifts denied the prince in the burning ground are given after all, but by a stranger who believes the child his own.
audit_text_issue: 331 line 4 (செருநிலம் பயப்பு உற) is unclear as printed | 331 line 4 (செருநிலம் பயப்பு உற) is unclear as printed.

note: Vijayai says she has done no good deeds (நல் வினை செய்து இலாதேன்); in 343 the narrator likens the passing night to evil deeds that leave when old good deeds come forward.
teaches: The mother's self-condemnation is overruled by the narrator a few verses later, who credits her with a store of former merit that now begins to ripen.

note: The deity names the ascetics' hermitage as their refuge; in 347 Vijayai reaches it, and the narrator says she suffered through a deed from a former birth.
teaches: The road to the hermitage is laid by a deity's counsel, but on arrival the narrator explains the exile as karma, so divine help and former deeds are given together as causes.

note: In the Kural the woman's automatic blessing at her lover's sneeze is withdrawn the next moment in jealousy; in the epic the blessing at the infant's sneeze comes from a mother who cannot show herself, and sticks as his name.
teaches: The everyday sneeze-blessing, which the Kural shows can be taken back, here becomes the one bond between the hidden mother and her child that cannot be undone.

gains.a: the epic scene gains the domestic usage behind it: a blessing said by those who love the sneezer, which makes the hidden voice a mother's
gains.b: the couplet's small rite gains weight: the same word can name and protect a life, not only open a lovers' quarrel

note: The Kural pictures the life leaving the body as a bird flying from a nest left empty; the epic pictures ascetics leaving the body as an exchange for an imperishable golden one, and uses it for the merchant leaving his dead son for a living child.
teaches: Leaving the body is loss in the Kural's figure and gain in the epic's, and the difference is the penance done beforehand.

gains.a: the simile gains a contrast that shows what penance adds: without it the body is only an abandoned nest
gains.b: the couplet gains a limit: the epic admits a departure from the body that is not mere desertion but a passage to a better frame

note: The Naladiyar sets the fool who sighs and breaks when deeds ripen against the wise who say 'it is old desert' and go free; Vijayai says exactly that her deeds are to blame, yet sobs (விம்மா) as she says it.
teaches: The quatrain makes knowing one's karma the cure for grief, but the queen shows that naming one's own deeds as the cause can be itself a form of grieving.

gains.a: Vijayai's lament gains a measure: her self-blame is the doctrine the wise hold, held without the calm it is said to bring
gains.b: the quatrain's clean division between fool and wise gains a case that falls between them, a mother who knows the rule and still breaks

note: In 319 Vijayai cries that she has done no good deeds (நல் வினை செய்து இலாதேன்); 343 has the dawn drive off her night like evil deeds' suffering fleeing when old good deeds come forward.
teaches: The narrator quietly contradicts the mother's self-blame: the karma she said she lacked is the image he chooses for her deliverance, so her despair is shown to be mistaken about her own merit.

note: Naladiyar 51 uses lamp and darkness to state that sin cannot stand before austerity and returns when good deeds are spent; 343 makes the departure of darkness at sunrise a figure for evil deeds' suffering leaving when old merit comes forward, on the road to a hermitage.
teaches: The quatrain's doctrine becomes the epic's narrative weather: the dawn that ends Vijayai's flight is the merit-and-darkness image itself, placed just before she enters the very austerity the quatrain says sin cannot face.

gains.a: the dawn simile gains a doctrinal warrant, so the reader takes it as a forecast that her turn to tapas will hold off misfortune
gains.b: the quatrain's abstract lamp gains a dated moment in a life, a widow at sunrise on the way to the ascetics, where its rule is seen applied

note: Kural 378 says drily that the destitute would renounce if only fate let what they must suffer pass them by; 347 has a queen stripped of everything reach the ascetics' grove because a former-birth deed made her suffer.
teaches: The epic takes up the case the couplet treats as hypothetical: the destitute queen does renounce, and the following verses show the couplet's point surviving the renunciation, since her fated grief for her son goes on inside the hermitage.

gains.a: the verse gains a test of whether entering tapas ends the suffering the narrator ascribes to ஊழ்வினை, which the Kural answers in the negative
gains.b: the couplet's ironic 'if' gains a concrete instance in which renunciation is chosen from loss, not from strength

note: Kannaki, her husband killed by the king's error, asks whether she must waste away in grief like the women who keep hard observances when their husbands go to the pyre; Vijayai, her husband killed by a usurper, is led by the ascetic women into exactly such observances.
teaches: Two wronged wives face the same choice and the epics give opposite answers: Kannaki refuses the widow's penance and turns her grief on the city, while Vijayai accepts it and keeps her grief for a son still living, which shows the son as the difference.

note: In Purananuru 253 a wife whose husband fell asks how she can go among her kin raising an empty hand without bangles; in 351 Vijayai breaks her own bangles in a hermitage among ascetic women.
teaches: The widow's bare hand, which the Sangam wife dreads as a sign shown before her kin, becomes in the Jain epic an act the widow performs herself as part of an ascetic initiation among strangers.

gains.a: the breaking of bangles is shown to be the old widow's sign, so the initiation reads as widowhood as much as renunciation
gains.b: the Sangam poem's shame of the empty hand gains a later setting where the same sign is turned into a chosen discipline

note: Kural 341 holds that from whatever one has let go one suffers no pain; Vijayai lets go her ornaments one by one (349 to 353) but ends with a vow for her son, whom she does not let go and for whom she grieves in 355 and 359.
teaches: The piecemeal renunciation the couplet describes is acted out jewel by jewel, and the pain the couplet promises to remove returns exactly at the one tie the queen keeps, which shows the couplet's claim from its other side.

gains.a: the stripping scene gains a rule by which to measure it, so the son's survival in her vow reads as the unrenounced attachment
gains.b: the couplet's 'whatever, whatever' gains an ordered sequence of things given up and one thing held, with the pain located where letting go stops

note: Perunkoppendu refuses the widow's life of plain food, gravel bed and no ghee and chooses the pyre; Vijayai refuses the milk offered her and takes up a widow's diet of greens in the forest.
teaches: The diet the Sangam queen calls the lot of wretched widows and rejects for death is accepted by the epic's queen and renamed divinity (வனத்து உறை தெய்வம்), which shows how the Jain frame revalues the widow's abstinence the heroic poem despised.

gains.a: the verse's greens and refused milk are recognised as the widow's regimen, not only an ascetic's
gains.b: Perunkoppendu's scorn gains its counterpart, a queen who lives on and makes the same regimen a way of holiness

audit_text_issue: Line 4 of 354 is a repaired 8-half-line stanza.

note: In Purananuru 248 the white water lily that was a girl's garment becomes the alli a widow eats; in 355 the stamens of ripe water lilies and wild rice dry in the hermitage courtyard as Vijayai's food.
teaches: The water lily carries the widow's fall from adornment to bare food in both poems, but in the epic the lily-food sits beside a nursing calf that sends her thoughts to her son, so the widow's diet is joined to a mother's longing the Sangam widow does not have.

gains.a: the passing detail of drying lily stamens is identified as the widow's food, so the hermitage scene is read as widowhood
gains.b: the Sangam widow's lily gains a later life in which the same food marks a mother waiting for her son

note: When Kantukkatan sneezed over the child in 323, a voice hidden in the branches said சீவ, 'live'; in 361 the child is named Civakan.
teaches: The hero's name is the fulfilment of an omen at his finding, so the name itself carries the blessing 'live' given over a child left in a burning ground.

note: In 355 the mother in the hermitage sees a forest cow suckling its calf and thinks of her son; in 362 the son drinks the milk of a foster mother and grows.
teaches: The nursing that Vijayai can only watch in a beast is happening to her own son at another woman's breast, so the two halves of the story are tied by the milk she cannot give.

note: In 314 a deity took the form of the hunchback Chanbakamalai, the maid who never left Vijayai's side; in 358 the deity leaves under the errand she gave it, calling its own guise a deceit.
teaches: The disguise that gave the queen comfort in her worst hour is the same means by which she is left alone, and the deity's own word for it, வஞ்சித்தேன், admits the cost of a kindness worked by pretence.

note: In 200 the narrator introduces Kattiyankaran as a man of flawless learning (வெளிறு இலாக் கேள்வியான்); in 385 the teacher, telling the story to the son, calls him the unlearned minister (கல்லா மந்திரி).
teaches: The same minister's learning is affirmed by the narrator at his rise and denied by the teacher after his crime, so the epic counts learning by its fruit in conduct, not by what a man has heard.

note: In 215 a destiny formed before (முனம் ஆகிய பான்மை) sprouts in Saccandan and drives him after the queen to his ruin; in 380 the old deed (ஊழ் வினை) drives his son to refuge in the Arhat.
teaches: The epic uses one mechanism, a ripened past deed pushing a man, to drown the father in pleasure and lift the son to the Jina, and only the son's case adds his own understanding as a second cause.

note: Vijayai dreamt in 223 that the ashoka (பிண்டி) fell and a shoot rose from its foot; in 384 the teacher sits in the shade of an ashoka to tell that shoot of the felled tree.
teaches: The heir learns of his father's fall under the very tree that figured the fall in his mother's dream, so the revelation scene closes the dream's image on its fulfilment.

note: Naladiyar 331 shows people revelling in the world's net while Death waits to seize them, like a turtle sporting in the pot over the fire; Cintamani 376 makes Death the one who laid the net and the revellers people who know it is there.
teaches: Set beside the quatrain, the epic's step is to take away the excuse of ignorance: the turtle does not know its state, but the teacher's 'we' know Death's net and still turn to pleasure, so folly becomes a failure of will.

gains.a: the teacher's irony (பெரியமே) is sharpened by the quatrain's ignorant turtle, against which knowing captives look worse
gains.b: the quatrain's net and killer gain an agent who sets the snare deliberately and an exit it does not name, austerity

note: Kural 348 says that those who have wholly renounced have reached the head and all others are caught in the net; Cintamani 376 names the net as Death's and austerity (நோற்று) as the way out of it.
teaches: The couplet divides men into renouncers and the netted, while the epic shows the netted as knowing their state, so renunciation is not only clear seeing but a doing that knowledge alone does not bring.

gains.a: the epic's net is tied to the Kural's chapter on renunciation, making நோற்று the renouncer's act
gains.b: the couplet's bare 'net' is given an owner, Death, and a cause for staying in it, the pull of pleasure

note: Kural 335 bids good deeds be rushed before the hiccup stops the tongue; Cintamani 377 asks whether anything intended can be done when the fire takes the body, after the teaching that ends birth has been rarely won.
teaches: The couplet's urgency rests on how near death may be; the epic adds that the means of release is already in hand and wasted by pampering the senses, so delay is the squandering of a rare gain and not only a race with death.

gains.a: the teacher's rhetorical question is grounded in a rule, act before the end
gains.b: the couplet's general 'good deed' is specified as using a teaching already obtained, and its limit moved from the death rattle to the pyre

note: Kural 6 says that those who stand on the path of the one who quenched the five senses live long; Cintamani 375 sets those who reach the path that wears away hard deeds in a sea of bliss and those burnt by the five-mouthed snake of the senses in a sea of pain.
teaches: Where the couplet promises long life on the path of one who quenched the senses, the Jain teacher makes the reward the wearing away of karma and the penalty a sea of suffering, turning a blessing of the householder into a choice between release and pain.

gains.a: the epic's senses-snake and its path are tied to the Kural's opening praise of the one who quenched the five
gains.b: the couplet's 'long life' is shown read by a Jain teacher as the destruction of karma, a reading its words allow but do not state

note: Both build a field guarded by a fence against stray beasts: Cintamani 379's crop is life from infancy to old age, its beasts diseases and its fence the vows (சீல வேலி); Pattinattar's field is the heart, its cattle the five senses, its fence calm (சாந்த வேலி), and its fruit Siva's form.
teaches: The shared Tamil figure of the fenced crop carries opposite ends: the Jain teacher fences a life to be kept from harm by vowed discipline, while the Saiva poet fences a devotion that ripens into the god, so the doctrine lies in what each names as fence and fruit.

gains.a: the teacher's brief farm image is seen as a choice: he fences life itself and names no fruit beyond it
gains.b: Pattinattar's devotional field is set against a Jain version where no grace ripens, showing his fruit of the five letters as the Saiva addition

note: Tirumanthiram 1527: when the two deeds stand balanced, grace comes as the guru, and when one's own agency ends the impurities go; Cintamani 380: a past good deed drives Civakan and his own understanding reaches out, and he takes refuge in the Arhat.
