teaches: Both put a teacher at the turn toward release, but for Tirumular the teacher is grace descending once deeds cancel and one's agency ends, while for the Jain epic it is the push of a good deed and the youth's own understanding that bring him to the teacher's Lord.

gains.a: Civakan's conversion is shown to need no descent of grace: karma and his own understanding suffice
gains.b: the Saiva claim that one's own agency must end is set against a release story in which agency is one of its two causes

note: Kural 49 calls the householder's life itself what is named virtue; in Cintamani 382 the teacher, once Civakan has taken the Jain refuge, teaches him the householder's dharma alongside the errors of false paths.
teaches: The Jain teacher does not set renunciation against the household here but gives the new convert the householder's dharma as his first instruction, so the epic holds the Kural's household virtue as a stage inside the path to release rather than its rival.

gains.a: the content of the teacher's instruction, left unstated, is placed against the Kural's account of what household virtue is
gains.b: the couplet's praise of household life is seen kept, but subordinated, by a tradition whose hero will renounce at the end

note: 387 names the birth star Uttirattathi; 404 makes the horoscope the cause of the prince's eloquence and beauty.
teaches: The birth scene's star is not ornament: the teacher reads Civakan's qualities as written at that birth, so the foundling's worth was fixed before his parentage was known.

note: The teacher tells Civakan that his enemy still stands and not to lament; the next verse shows the rage this rouses, which the teacher must then restrain.
teaches: The consolation that turns grief into thoughts of the enemy produces the very anger the teacher at once has to check, so his own counsel makes the year of restraint necessary.

note: The teacher asks Civakan to bear no anger for a year; his own penance had been undertaken so that fierce anger would wane.
teaches: The request for restraint is the teacher's own discipline passed to his pupil, asked by one who knows how hard anger is to wear down.

note: The teacher binds Civakan to a year without anger toward Kattiyankaran, yet before leaving writes into his mind the policy of destroying enemies.
teaches: The ascetic's restraint on his pupil is a postponement of revenge rather than its renunciation: anger is suspended while the means of war are taught.

note: Sin overtook the ascetic in his first penance; at the end he goes to resume penance to wear down old deeds.
teaches: The teacher's life runs in a circle through Civakan's house: a penance broken by the fruit of past deeds is taken up again, with the wearing away of those deeds now named as its aim.

note: The mother left the newborn to aram in the forest; the grown son now says penance was his mother and the teacher his father.
teaches: The child commended to dharma by a departing mother is answered, in the son's own words, by a parentage of penance and teaching, as if aram had taken him up through the ascetic.

note: Both epics give the elephant-fire hunger and both measure it by mountains poured into the sea: here the silver mountain filling the sea, there the hills the monkeys threw into the ocean.
teaches: The Jain and the Buddhist epic share the disease and its image, but the Cintamani cures it with a child's meal in a Jain household while the Manimekalai cures it with the bowl of a renunciant, so each makes its own kind of giver the remedy.

note: Manimekalai traces Kayasandikai's elephant-fire to a named act, crushing an ascetic's fruit, and his curse; the Cintamani says only that sin came upon the ascetic in his penance.
teaches: Set beside the Manimekalai's exact chain of act, curse and term, the Cintamani's unnamed sin shows karma striking even a guileless penitent with no deed in this life to explain it.

note: The couplet ranks the strength of those who relieve hunger above that of those who endure it; the ascetic's endurance fails and a child's feeding saves him.
teaches: The epic stages the couplet's ranking as one scene: the ascetic's strength to bear hunger breaks, and the boy's strength to relieve it restores him and gives Civakan his teacher.

gains.a: the meal gains a moral rank: the boy's act stands above the ascetic's vow, not merely beside it
gains.b: the couplet gains a case in which the endurer is himself rescued by the reliever, so the ranking is shown to be needed, not only stated

note: The couplet defines penance as bearing the pain that comes; the ascetic's penance gives way under the hunger-fire and he goes to the city to eat.
teaches: The epic marks a limit to the couplet's definition: there are pains, sent by past deeds, that a penitent cannot bear, and his penance has to be suspended and later resumed.

gains.a: the ascetic's lapse is measured against a standard, so his leaving the vow reads as failure under pain rather than mere misfortune
gains.b: the definition gains a case where the pain that comes is beyond bearing, raising what penance does then

note: The couplet bids one forget anger at anyone at all; the teacher asks Civakan to hold his anger against one man for one year only.
teaches: Against the couplet's unlimited forgetting of anger, the epic's ascetic sets a term to restraint, so a teacher who renounced anger for himself still leaves a prince's just anger intact for its time.

gains.a: the request is seen to be partial: it is a delay with an end, not the forgetting the ethics books ask
gains.b: the couplet's 'at anyone at all' is tested by the case of a usurper who killed one's father, where even an ascetic does not ask for it

note: The couplet asks what one gains by leaving a household life lived in dharma; the epic holds that once a man resolves to leave home for penance, the wise speak of no other dharma.
teaches: The two meet on a condition the couplet leaves out: the Kural weighs the householder's path before the choice, while the epic speaks of one who has already resolved, for whom the household dharma is no longer an option.

gains.a: the epic's claim is placed against the strongest defence of the household, so its scope (one who has resolved) becomes visible
gains.b: the couplet's rhetorical question gains an answer from a man who has lived both lives, an ascetic who spent years in a merchant's house and returns to penance

audit_text_issue: Speaker of lines 1-3 and referent of line 4 not fixed by the verse.

note: The couplet says the fruit of hospitality is as great as the guest's worth; the merchant's house that fed a hungry stranger gained a Vidyadhara king as the teacher of its son.
teaches: The epic shows the couplet's measure working through time: the guest's worth was hidden when he came hungry to the door, and the fruit appeared only as the education of the boy who fed him.

gains.a: the long stay of the cured ascetic is read as the return on a gift, which the verse itself leaves implicit
gains.b: the couplet's measure by the guest's worth gains a case where that worth was unknown to the host, so hospitality cannot be rationed by it

note: Tirumular has grace come as the guru and end the soul's own doing; in the Cintamani the guru is himself a karma-bound ascetic who goes off to wear down his old deeds by his own penance.
teaches: The two texts set the guru on opposite sides of karma: for Tirumular the guru is the descent of grace that ends one's deeds, while the Cintamani's teacher, having formed his pupil, must still work off his own past by effort.

gains.a: the teacher's departure is seen as a doctrinal statement, release by one's own penance with no grace to end it
gains.b: the Saiva verse's guru as grace gains a clear contrast, a guru who needs release himself, which sharpens what 'guru as grace' claims

note: Both use the rain bubble (மாரி மொக்குளின், படுமழை மொக்குளின்): the Naladiyar for the body that keeps forming and bursting, the epic for the moment the released teacher's form ends.
teaches: Holding the two together shows the bubble used for opposite ends: in the quatrain its bursting is why the wise resolve to end their wandering, and in the epic the bursting is that resolve completed, the last end of a body that will not form again.

gains.a: the epic's simile gains the sense of repeated birth the quatrain gives the bubble, so Accanandi's vanishing reads as the end of the round, not just a death
gains.b: the quatrain's resolve to end the wandering gains a narrated case of someone who did it, and what its end looks like

note: Bhadragiriyar asks when he will cut the sunken root of desire at its base; the epic says Accanandi cut the root of desire (ஆர்வ வேர் அரிந்து) and went on to austerity and release.
teaches: The same image of desire as a root to be cut is a lament of 'when?' in the Siddhar and a finished first step in the Jain epic, where it is only the start of a path that still needs austerity before release.

gains.a: the epic's one-phrase report gains the inner struggle the Siddhar voices, so the reader sees how hard that cutting was meant to be
gains.b: the Siddhar's longing gains a sequel in another tradition: what is said to follow once the root is cut

note: The Kural calls those free of craving the freed (அற்றவர்); the epic has Accanandi cut desire's root and then perform austerities before he leaves the body.
teaches: Set beside the couplet, the verse separates what the Kural joins: being free of craving comes first, but release from the body comes only after austerity at the Jina's feet.

gains.a: the epic's sequence gains the Kural's claim that ending craving is the decisive freedom, which explains why it stands first
gains.b: the couplet's freedom gains a narrative that spells out what still remains after craving goes: penance and the body's end

note: The omen-reader foretells that the king's army will break leaving umbrella and பிச்சம்; in 437 the army breaks, throwing down elephants, peacock-plumed standards, பிச்சம் and banners.
teaches: The first half of the prophecy comes true to the detail of the dropped standards, which gives the reader warrant to trust its second half before Civakan has even set out.

note: The prophecy ends with the raiders broken by one man in a chariot; in 449 the hunters, stunned by the roar of the generous one's chariot, lose heart and give up the fight.
teaches: The poet names Civakan only through the hunters' own omen, so the hero's victory is foretold by his enemies before it is told by the narrator.
audit_text_issue: 416 line 4 is hard to divide and may be corrupt.

note: The hunter boasts that one man in a chariot can do nothing even if he is Death; in 450 the hunters say a chariot-flood has surrounded them, victory is hard, and a hunter lied to them.
teaches: The raiders' contempt for a single foe is reversed by their own words, and 450's charge that a hunter lied shows them blaming a speaker rather than their dismissal of the omen.

note: Both sides consult birds: the hunters' omen-reader reads a bird's cry before the raid, and the herders' announcer warns of an ill-omened bird; each side goes ahead.
teaches: The episode gives an omen to raiders and herders alike and lets both ignore it, so omens here foretell outcomes without ever restraining anyone.
audit_text_issue: பிள்ளை in 420 is read as an omen-bird name; uncertain.

note: The Kural says the cows' yield fails when the guardian does not guard; the epic shows the king's herd driven off while the king sits fanned on his throne, and 437-438 his army breaks.
teaches: The pairing turns the Kural's cows into the actual herd of the realm: the raid becomes the first public proof that the usurper cannot guard, and clears the place for Civakan, who will.

gains.a: the cattle raid gains a political sense beyond adventure: it measures Kattiyankaran as guardian
gains.b: the couplet's abstract link between guarding and the yield of cows gains a concrete scene of what failure to guard looks like

audit_text_issue: 429 does not name the king or the herds

note: Nandagon's drum promises the maiden to whoever brings back the herd; in 479 the herd chief, now naming himself Govindan, offers her with seven golden images to Civakan.
teaches: The public prize proclaimed to all the city's warriors is paid to the one outsider who answered it, which makes Govindai's marriage a contract kept rather than a match made.

note: Kattiyangaran sinks in grief when the herd is lost; when he hears Civakan has recovered it he is enraged as if a spear were thrust into a sword wound.
teaches: The usurper grieves the loss of his herd and rages at its return, showing that what wounds him is a rival's glory, not the people's loss.
audit_text_issue: 455 flagged uncertain; the raging man is unnamed.

note: The hunters claim the forest as their deep water where even the strong will fall; in 453 Civakan alone destroys six thousand of them there.
teaches: The maxim of one's own ground is turned against the very people who invoked it, so the story shows it fails when the opponent is misjudged.

note: The hunters restate the couplet's crocodile, strong in deep water, and apply it to themselves in their forest.
teaches: The couplet's rule of ground is here voiced by the losing side, so the pair shows the rule cannot by itself predict a fight and must be weighed against the enemy's strength.

gains.a: the hunters' boast gains a known maxim of statecraft, so their defeat reads as a misapplied rule and not mere bluster
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where the strong-on-its-ground party still loses, a limit the bare maxim does not state

note: The Pandya's war proclamation in Puram 9 tells cows, brahmins, women, the sick and the sonless to get clear before battle; Civakan names cows, renunciants, women, children and brahmins as those he must protect.
teaches: The same list of the protected is in the Sangam poem those a king spares from his own arrows, and in the epic those a warrior must defend from another's raid, so the duty widens from restraint to rescue.

gains.a: Civakan's oath gains a Sangam pedigree: his list is the old code of who stands outside war
gains.b: the Puram poem's code of sparing gains its active counterpart, an obligation to defend the same people when someone else attacks them

note: Tirumular threatens unending hell to a king who fails to guard cows, women, the virtuous and the holy; Civakan, not a king, binds himself to the same guard on pain of a eunuch's shame.
teaches: Read together, the duty to guard cows, women and the holy passes from the failed king to a private man, and its sanction moves from hell after death to dishonour in this life.

gains.a: the oath gains a measure of what the king himself owed and failed to give, which Civakan supplies
gains.b: Tirumular's rule, framed for the king's office, gains a case where the office fails and the duty is taken up by one who holds no office

note: The patikam's line வஞ்சம் மறவர் நிரை வள்ளல் விடுத்த வாறும் announces that the liberal one freed the herd from deceitful hunters; 451 to 455 tell it, ending with the herd turned by the bow's sound and no man lost.
teaches: The patikam's word வள்ளல் for the rescuer of a herd only makes sense once the telling shows a recovery that is given back to its owners without loss, so the summary's epithet anticipates the bloodless manner of the deed.

note: The city women bless the unknown youth with பூமியும் புணர்க, 'may he wed the earth too'; the patikam's verse 26 puts his marriage to his uncle's daughter and the spread of his umbrella and sceptre over the land in one verse.
teaches: The epic pairs bride and kingdom twice, once as a crowd's wedding blessing on a merchant's son who does not know his birth and once as the outcome, so the blessing works as an unwitting prophecy of his recovery of the throne.

note: The women hold that union with Civakan is the reward of penance (அண்ணலைத் தவத்திற் றந்தார்); the patikam ends with Civakan, as one who has eaten nectar, no longer wanting the pleasure of women.
teaches: The epic plants early the crowd's belief that penance buys the pleasure of this man, and its own close makes the same man's penance the end of all such pleasure, so the word தவம் is turned against the hope it first expressed.

note: In the Vettuva Vari the herds the hunters' brothers brought back from the raid fill the yards of the smith, the drummer and the yazh bards; in the Cintamani the hunters are routed and the herd turns back to the shouting cowherds.
teaches: Held together, the two epics show the one cattle raid from both ends: the Silappathikaram's hunters' seizure feeds a whole village of dependents, while the Cintamani's recovery returns the same kind of herd to its keepers and leaves the raiders faceless.

note: The Purananuru's warrior, with no chariot and no forest fort, watched the enemy's herd go, counted it and turned it with his bow (சிலையின் மாற்றியோனே); Civakan turns the herd by the bow's twang alone (சிலையின் னொலியால் தொறு மீட்டு).
teaches: The epic keeps the Sangam feat of turning a herd with the bow but removes even the drawn arrow and gives the deed to a city's darling, so a poor warrior's unsung skill becomes a prince's proof of worth before the town.

gains.a: the Cintamani's bow-sound recovery is shown to rest on an existing heroic type, the lone bowman who turns a herd, rather than on the poet's invention
gains.b: the Puram poem's quiet single-handed recovery is seen to be the seed of a scene that later poetry could magnify into public triumph and crowd adoration

note: Kural 265 says penance (செய்தவம்) is undertaken because what one wants is got as one wants it; the city women say Civakan's mother must have done penance (செய்தவம் உடையள்) and ask on which mountain to do it so that they too may attain.
teaches: The couplet's frank promise that penance gets what one wants is taken literally by lovesick townswomen, who plan austerity on a mountain to win a man, showing how the Kural's motive can be bent toward the very desire the next couplet condemns.

gains.a: the women's talk is shown to repeat a recognised ethical doctrine of the fruits of penance, not merely a crowd's fancy
gains.b: the couplet's unqualified wording is shown to license a use, penance for erotic gain, that its own chapter would reject

note: In Kural 1214 the woman finds pleasure in dreams because they bring the man who gives no grace when she is awake (நல்காரை); the women of 466 ask Civakan to grace them (அருளி) by coming in a dream tomorrow.
teaches: The Kural's dream comforts a woman for a lover who once was hers and now withholds himself, but the Cintamani's crowd asks the dream for a man they have only seen pass, so the convention turns from consolation for loss into the only union a stranger can hope for.

gains.a: the crowd's prayer is shown to draw on the akam convention that the dream does what the absent man will not
gains.b: the couplet's dream-remedy is shown stretching beyond separation to love that never had a meeting, which the couplet's situation does not cover

note: At 215 the narrator says the king ignored counsel because a destiny formed before sprouted in him; Nandagon, telling the same fall, blames only the king's own desire and choice.
teaches: The epic keeps two causes for Saccandan's fall in two voices, so a former deed in the narrator's account never excuses the choice his subject remembers.

note: Nandagon turned back from suicide hoping, like a banyan seed, that the royal line survived; the patikam at 26 has Civakan spread his just sceptre over the land.
teaches: The cowherd's private hope is the plan of the whole epic, and he states it to the very heir he thinks may be lost.

note: The Naladiyar says that when a banyan is eaten hollow its aerial roots hold it up, as a son covers a weakened father; Nandagon's banyan seed is the hope that a son of the fallen king lives.
teaches: Set beside the quatrain, the herdsman's seed image takes on the son's work of propping a fallen house, which the epic will make a war for a kingdom rather than a household's shame.

gains.a: the obscure seed image is given its point: a hidden son is the root that will hold the line up
gains.b: the household maxim is seen stretched to a dynasty, where the father is dead and the son does not yet know whom he props

note: Nandagon argues from Murukan and Vishnu that lineage should not be thought of in marriage; Civakan at once thinks that a man may not take an unequal wife before one of his own rank.
teaches: The hero answers the herdsman's mythic precedent not by denying unequal marriage but by ranking it, so birth still governs the order of wives in a story that lets him marry across it.

note: The Kural says birth is alike for all beings and distinction comes from the work they do; Civakan holds that birth decides which wife a man may take first.
teaches: The pair shows the Kural's levelling of birth stopping at the threshold of marriage in the epic, where rank of birth remains a rule of conduct even for a hero honoured for his deeds.

gains.a: the hero's private rule is seen against a classic denial that birth confers worth, which makes its reliance on birth visible
gains.b: the couplet's claim is tested on a case it does not name, the ordering of marriages, where birth kept a force the couplet does not grant it

note: At 440 Nandagon had it proclaimed that the maiden would be given to whoever brought back the herd; at 479 he offers her to Civakan, adding seven golden statues.
teaches: The proclamation is kept to the letter, yet the hero's decline at 483-484 shows the prize could be honoured only by being passed to another.

note: Civakan's acceptance in 484 turns on an obscure kinship word; at 489 he receives the gift water on behalf of Padumukan.
teaches: Read from 489, Civakan's quick acceptance was always an acceptance for his friend, which lets him keep both Nandagon's honour and his own rule of rank.

note: In the Kalittokai the herd girl is cried as the prize of whoever takes the fighting bull, and the taker himself has her; here the herd chief's daughter is the prize for recovering the herd, and the winner passes her to a friend.
teaches: The epic keeps the mullai custom of a herd girl won by a public feat, but moves the feat from the herders' bull-pen to a prince's war and lets the prize be transferred, which the bull-catch, where the girl goes to the man who wrestled, does not allow.

gains.a: the herders' wedding is seen to rest on an old custom of the herd girl as prize of a feat, which explains the father's proclamation in 440
gains.b: the bull-catch's bond between feat and husband is shown to be what a later courtly telling could loosen, the girl becoming a gift between men

note: The couplet says the pleasure of love is a sea but its pain, when it strikes, is greater; 491 gives the bridegroom the sea of pleasure that cannot be contained, and no pain.
teaches: The epic uses the couplet's measure of pleasure as a sea but leaves out the greater sea of pain that the woman in the Kural speaks from, because the wedding has no separation in it.

gains.a: the uncontained sea of 491 is seen to be half of a measure, the half that a married union can claim
gains.b: the couplet's first clause is given a scene where it stands alone, which shows its second clause belongs to separation

note: At 216 Saccandan drinks unwearied the nectar of Vijayai and his fall begins; at 491-492 Padumukan drinks Govindai's nectar and loses all awareness in unguarded pleasure.
teaches: The poet gives the bridegroom the very image of the king whose drinking cost him his kingdom, so the epic's warning about pleasure lies under even its happiest wedding, though the narrator blames no one here.

note: In 495 Sitattan calls it a failure of understanding to blame former deeds when fortune turns; in 510, in the storm, he makes the fruit of former deeds the only ground on which the good survive.
teaches: The merchant's creed of effort over fate lasts only until the sea rises; under the storm the same man falls back on karma, so the epic stages the Kural's own pull between effort and fate as one character's change of mind.

note: 497 ends பொய்யில் பொருளே பொருள்; 514 has the shipwrecked merchant tell himself பொருளைப் பொருள் என்று கொண்டாய், as a reproach.
teaches: The wordplay on பொருள் as wealth and as the thing of worth is turned against its speaker, so the wreck reads as a verdict on his creed and not only as bad luck.

note: In 213 King Saccandan dismisses warning by saying pleasures and days of life are measured out in advance; in 510 Sitattan uses the same doctrine of a measured life-span to steady his crew, and alone survives.
teaches: The doctrine of the measured life-span is voiced twice before a disaster, once as an excuse for heedlessness that ends in a king's death and once as courage that ends in rescue, so its worth in the epic depends on what the speaker does with it.

note: 497 restates Kural 759 (make wealth; no steel is sharper against foes) and joins to it the claims of 760 and 751 as a merchant's motto, a few verses before the sea swallows the wealth.
teaches: Put in the mouth of a man about to lose everything at sea, the Kural's praise of wealth as the sharpest steel is shown to say nothing about wealth's own exposure to loss.

gains.a: the merchant's motto gains its source and is seen as a borrowed rule of statecraft applied to trade
gains.b: the couplet gains a test case in which the wealth it praises is destroyed by forces no amount of it can subdue

note: 509 opens as Kural 621 opens and turns the couplet's laughter into a steel that cuts trouble, spoken by a captain to his crew in a storm that drowns them all but him.
teaches: The couplet's laugh in trouble becomes a leader's duty to others, and the scene shows its limit: composure saves the one who keeps it but cannot save the ship.

gains.a: Sitattan's exhortation gains a known maxim behind it, which explains why he speaks in aphorisms at the height of the storm
gains.b: the couplet's private resolve gains a public setting, where the person who laughs is responsible for others who perish

note: 496 holds that a resolute man's effort can bring a flood of wealth in a day and that nothing fails to yield to it; Kural 620 holds that tireless effort sees even fate's back.
teaches: The epic puts the Kural's boldest claim for effort in the mouth of a man whose voyage ends in shipwreck, so the claim is made to depend on the life-span and deeds he later invokes.

gains.a: the merchant's boast gains the weight of a rule from the Kural's chapter on exertion
gains.b: the couplet gains a story in which tireless effort does meet fate head on and loses the wealth while the man survives

note: 498 gives the merchant's reason for the voyage: men born into a weakening lineage must hold it up. Kural 1026 defines good manliness as making oneself able to rule the house one was born into.
teaches: The Kural's manliness of the house is the motive that sends a merchant onto the sea, and the verse adds a division the couplet lacks: restoring the line is the men's part, guarding against shame the women's.

gains.a: the merchant's resolve gains a named ideal, so the voyage reads as family duty and not greed
gains.b: the couplet gains a concrete undertaking and a risk: ruling one's house can mean staking one's life on a voyage

note: 513 shows the wealth Sitattan guarded and gathered (ஓம்பிப் படைத்த பொருள்) swallowed by the sea while he stands unhurried; Naladiyar 93 holds that wealth, however tightly held, leaves when the deeds that sent it run out.
teaches: Read with the quatrain, the wreck becomes the ending of a merit that had held the wealth, and the merchant's calm becomes the right response to a loss that no grip could prevent.

gains.a: the loss of the cargo gains a cause the verse does not give, the exhaustion of the merit that brought it
gains.b: the quatrain's abstract leaving of wealth gains a sudden, visible event and a man who loses it without clutching

note: 496 has the merchant hold that effort alone can bring a flood of wealth in a day; Siddhar 641 tells the heart that the wealth it has came by the order of deeds done in earlier lives and was not got today.
teaches: The two disagree about where wealth comes from, today's effort or earlier lives, and the epic lets its merchant hold the first view only until the storm turns him to the second.

gains.a: the merchant's creed gains its direct opposite, which shows how much it denies
gains.b: the Siddhar's claim gains an opponent who believes the reverse and is then brought round by events

note: Dharan vows to restore all without any deceit (வஞ்சமொன்று இன்றி); in 574 the Vidyadhara lord himself declares the storm was a deceit (வஞ்சம்).
teaches: The word that guarantees the promise is the word later used to explain the whole wreck, so the rescuer's honesty consists in undoing a lie he told.

note: The 'dead companions' Dharan promises to return meet the merchant alive and laugh that what they suffered at sea was a play (நாடகம்).
teaches: The impossible promise to raise the dead is kept only because the deaths were staged, which turns the earlier lament for lost friends into an audience's grief.

note: Kural 292 lets a falsehood stand as truth when it yields good free of fault; Dharan's wreck and his 'no deceit' promise are falsehoods serving his king's purpose of bringing a guardian for the princess.
teaches: The pair tests the couplet's limit: the epic's lie does produce good, but at the cost of a man's real grief for friends he believed drowned, so whether its good is 'free of fault' becomes the question.

gains.a: a measure by which to judge Dharan's staged disaster, which the story itself excuses with laughter in 582
gains.b: a concrete case where the beneficial lie causes real suffering before the benefit arrives, which the couplet's bare rule does not weigh

note: In 514 the shipwrecked merchant is reproached for taking wealth as the one thing of worth; in 533 he enters a city where jewels lie in the street because no one wants them.
teaches: The man who lost everything for wealth is led into a place where wealth has no pull, so the description quietly answers the reproach of the wreck.

note: The astrologer names Rajamapuram as the place of the princess's destined husband; the patikam (11) already tells that the Vidyadhara king's daughter was defeated at the vina.
teaches: The prophecy that sends the princess to earth is the start of the contest the patikam announced, so her defeat at the vina is the means by which her horoscope comes true.

note: The astrologer's reading of her பான்மை is taken up by the king in 554, who refuses every suitor because none can stop a portion when its time comes.
teaches: A horoscope cast at birth becomes, years later, the king's reason for refusing all suitors, so the prophecy governs a political decision rather than merely forecasting a marriage.

note: Kural 376 says what is not one's portion will not stay however guarded and what is one's portion will not leave; the king, told his daughter's portion lies in Rajamapuram, neither gives her to the gift-bearing kings nor tells them so, but keeps them waiting with his intent hidden.
teaches: The pair shows that knowing one's portion in advance does not end action: the king turns the couplet's resignation into policy, managing powerful suitors while waiting for fate to arrive.

gains.a: a general rule of allotted portion behind the king's refusal to accept the suitors' riches
gains.b: a case where the rule is applied to a daughter rather than to wealth, and where the one who knows the portion must still act with craft to protect it

note: The Kural says one remembers for seven births the friendship of those who wiped away one's sorrow; the Vidyadhara king says his people and the merchant's have held friendship for seven generations, bound by fate.
teaches: Side by side, the seven-fold span of friendship rests on two different grounds: in the couplet on gratitude for a single act of rescue, in the epic on an inherited tie that fate fixes and no deed has to earn.

gains.a: the king's claim gains a measure of what such a bond is normally owed for, showing how much he gives in asking nothing of the merchant
gains.b: the couplet's seven births gain a case where the span runs through generations of a family rather than one person's rebirths

note: The Kural's lover asks whether the lotus-eyed god's world is sweeter than sleep on a beloved's arms; the Vidyadhara king says even the endless pleasures of the Jain land of enjoyment are misery alone, and sleep in a lover's lap is the gods' own state.
teaches: The couplet leaves its comparison with heaven as a question, and the epic answers it outright, turning a lover's boast into a father's argument for giving his daughter in marriage.

gains.a: the king's maxim gains the akam voice behind it, the man who first set the embrace against heaven
gains.b: the couplet's open question gains an answer, and a use outside the lovers' scene, as a reason to marry a daughter

note: The Kural says nothing is stronger than fate, which gets ahead of every contrivance; the king says that when the destined time comes no one can stop it, and so refuses every royal suitor.
teaches: Read with the couplet, the king's appeal to fate is not a surrender but a policy: he uses fate's strength as the reason to refuse every suitor and leave the choice to a contest, where the Kural sees fate only as defeating a plan.

gains.a: the king's line gains the Kural's general law, which explains why even begging kings cannot move him
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where acknowledging fate guides a decision instead of frustrating one

note: The Naladiyar likens a miser's hoard, enjoyed by a stranger, to a lovely daughter of the house who goes to an outsider in due season; the king says daughters are like the conch's pearls, which profit others and never the conch.
teaches: The same commonplace, that a daughter is raised to go to another, serves the quatrain as an image of loss through folly and serves the epic as a father's consolation, so the pair shows the saying could carry blame or comfort.

gains.a: the king's saying gains the quatrain's point that the daughter's going is as certain as a season, which is why it can console
gains.b: the quatrain's simile gains a scene in which the daughter's leaving is felt by the father, not only used as an image

note: The Vidyadhara king calls living alone the greatest misery even amid heavenly pleasure; the patikam ends the epic with Civakan, his brother, friends and wives renouncing the senses and going to release.
teaches: The king's praise of married joy over solitary pleasure is one character's view, and the epic's own close, where the household and its pleasures are renounced for a higher state, rejects it as a final value.

note: The king refuses all suitors, citing a seer's word and the destined time; the patikam names among the episodes how the Vidyadhara king's daughter was defeated at the vina.
teaches: The patikam already tells the outcome the king says no one can prevent, so the father's appeal to destiny is answered by the epic's own plan: the destined man is the hero.

note: Sridattan told his crew in the storm that their suffering was the ripening of old deeds; Dharan now says the wreck was his own staged deceit.
teaches: The epic lets the merchant read the wreck as karma and then shows a planned human cause behind it, so the karmic explanation stands beside an agent's plan rather than replacing it.

note: 513 has the sea swallow the merchant's guarded wealth and the loved ones with him; 580 shows the ship and the companions intact.
teaches: The loss that the wreck scene narrates as final is revealed as illusion, so the earlier verse's grief was real while its facts were false.

note: In the storm Sridattan urged laughter in trouble; after the rescue his companions laugh that the wreck was a play.
teaches: The laughter urged as courage before the outcome returns as relief after it, which shows how differently the same laugh weighs once the danger is known to be staged.

note: The astrologer's verdict that the maiden's life lies on the earth is what the king turned into his parting saying that daughters, like a conch's pearls, profit those on the earth.
teaches: The king's consoling maxim at the parting rests on the astrologer's prophecy told only now, so his resignation is obedience to a foretold fate as well as a father's wisdom.

note: The Naladiyar calls those who prattle of astrology the greatest fools; the epic has a king act on an astrologer's word, which proves true.
teaches: Two Jain-tradition texts judge the astrologer oppositely: the quatrain dismisses his lore beside the duty death makes urgent, while the epic makes his reading the hinge of its plot. The tension holds only if the quatrain is read as denying astrology's truth, not just its worth.

gains.a: the epic's trust in the astrologer is set against a strand of its own tradition that scorns that lore
gains.b: the quatrain's scorn is shown to stand in a renouncer's frame that a court narrative does not share

note: The Naladiyar says friends who share joys but not sorrows do nothing for each other; Dharan inflicts sorrow on his king's friend to give him joy.
teaches: The quatrain's test assumes sorrow comes from outside and asks who will share it, while the epic's friend authors the sorrow himself and stands apart from it, a case the rule of sharing does not cover.

gains.a: Dharan's apology is measured against a standard of friendship that his deceit plainly fails
gains.b: the quatrain's rule meets a friend who causes, rather than shares, the grief, which shows its limit

note: In 297 the usurper has the drum beaten in his own name after burning his king and 'takes Fortune'; in 609 the city's drum blesses first the lord who embraces the earth as his bride.
teaches: The same drum that announced a murderer's seizure now opens a wedding proclamation by hailing him as the earth's rightful husband, so the formula of royal blessing shows how quickly usurpation becomes the ordinary order of the city.

note: In 556 the Vidyadhara king asks the merchant to be father and mother to the princess; in 607 the proclamation calls the merchant her father outright.
teaches: The private charge to stand in a parent's place becomes, in the public decree, plain fatherhood, so the trust hides the princess's Vidyadhara birth from the city that will compete for her.

note: The astrologer in 539 places the princess's destined husband in Rajamapuram; 610-612 bring kings from Hastinapuram, Kampili and Varanavasi to win her.
teaches: Read against the horoscope, the far kings' arrival is a journey already in vain, and the open contest is the means by which the prophecy picks its man from the city it named.

note: Kural 263 asks whether others, wanting to provide for renouncers, have forgotten their own penance; the proclamation in 605 bids people give to ascetics and also strive at hard penance themselves.
teaches: The epic's decree answers the couplet's chiding question by refusing the division of labour it criticises: giving to ascetics and doing penance are both laid on every listener.

gains.a: a sharp statement of the danger its double command guards against, that support for ascetics could stand in for one's own penance
gains.b: a public, Jain-framed instance where the couplet's implied rule, that penance is not only for renouncers, is proclaimed to a whole city

note: Kural 55 makes the chaste wife command the rain; the benediction of 604 asks for rain and for women's unswerving chastity side by side as goods of the realm.
teaches: The pair shows two ways of joining chastity and rain: the couplet gives one wife's karpu power over the sky, while the city's blessing wishes for both as gifts and gives women's chastity no power at all.

gains.a: a sense of how strong a link between chastity and rain the tradition could make, which the benediction leaves unclaimed
gains.b: a civic setting where the couplet's single wife becomes all the women of a city, wished steadfast rather than credited with power

note: Tirumanthiram 724 nurtures the body because without it true knowledge cannot be gained; 605 bids all strive at hard penance while still in the body.
teaches: Both make the living body the only place where release can be worked for, but the proclamation spends the body in austerity while Tirumular guards it as the means of knowledge, so the same premise yields discipline in one and care in the other.

gains.a: a statement of why 'while in the body' matters, which the proclamation's compressed phrase leaves unsaid
gains.b: a contrasting use of the body as the seat of penance, in a Jain frame, against which Tirumular's nurture of it stands out as a choice

note: The companion is sure the crowned suitors will drown in the flood of the princess's music; the patikam has already told the story as the Vidyadhara king's daughter losing at the vina.
teaches: The companion's certainty is half right, since the kings do lose, but the one it never imagines losing is the princess herself, so the reader hears her boast through the outcome the poem announced at the start.

note: The Vidyadhara astrologer read in the planets that her destined husband lives in Rajamapuram; here an omen-reader in Rajamapuram fixes the contest's hour from the moon's conjunction.
teaches: The open contest is framed by two readings of the stars, one naming the city and one naming the hour, so what looks like a public trial of skill is staged as the working out of a decree already read.

note: Kaluzhavegan kept the suitor kings in hope without telling them his mind; now the kings of the earth arrive in Rajamapuram, the city the horoscope named.
teaches: The king's hidden purpose turns his daughter's suitors into unknowing escorts to the city where her destined husband lives, so their rivalry serves a plan they were never told.

note: Those who saw the princess, the narrator says, would never look upon the world of release; at the epic's end Civakan, having tasted the pleasure of women whose beauty makes the heavens bow, wants it no more and goes to release.
teaches: The hyperbole that beauty shuts out release is a claim the epic's own ending answers, since its hero is the one who saw all such beauty and still reached release, so the line marks the stake of the story rather than its verdict.

note: The Kural's lover asks whether the lotus-eyed god's world is sweeter than sleep in the beloved's arms; the Cintamani's narrator says those who saw the princess would not look upon the world of release.
teaches: Both weigh a woman's beauty against a world beyond this one, but the Jain epic raises the Kural's god's heaven to release from births and gives the preference to dazzled onlookers rather than a lover, which makes it a danger to be overcome rather than a joy to be asked about.

gains.a: the epic's hyperbole is shown to be a set figure of the lover's voice inherited from the Kural's third book, not a doctrine of the narrator
gains.b: the couplet's open question gets an answer from a tradition for which the other world is release, where preferring beauty is a peril to the soul, which the couplet does not consider

note: The attendants call the princess's eyes not carp but blue lilies sheltering in the moon and line them with kohl; the Naladiyar's renunciant scorns those who call eyes water-lilies, carp or spears and sees the eye as a scooped-out palm fruit.
teaches: The comparisons the Jain quatrain names as the talk of the blind are exactly the ones a Jain epic's attendants weigh and choose between, so the pair shows the same tradition keeping the lover's rhetoric in its epic and rejecting it in its ascetic verse.

gains.a: the epic's ornate conceit is set against a reading in which it is the very speech that endangers the renunciant, which the epic leaves unsaid until its last book
gains.b: the quatrain's anonymous praisers of eyes get a concrete scene, women adorning a bride for a crowd, showing the rhetoric it resists at work in public

note: The Kural's lover cannot tell whether the woman is a goddess, a peahen or a woman; the Cintamani's kings ask how she is not Rambha and then notice that her eyes blink (இமைக்குங்கண் இவையோ).
teaches: The pair shows the lover's doubt can be settled by a sign: where the couplet leaves the heart reeling among three guesses, the epic supplies the blink that separates a mortal from the unblinking gods and ends the doubt.

gains.a: the kings' remark is seen as the closing move of a set doubt-scene whose first move the Kural states
gains.b: the couplet's unresolved question gains a test of the kind its own three guesses never apply

note: The couplet's man says he never knew Death and knows it now in a woman's eyes; the onlookers tell the suitors that her girdle and breasts are Death and bid them flee, 'we have told you'.
teaches: Read with the couplet, the onlookers' warning puts the suitors in the state the Kural's man has left behind, knowing Death only by report, and shows that being told does not save anyone, since the crowd stays.

gains.a: the warning gains its irony from the couplet's contrast between Death heard of and Death met
gains.b: the couplet's private discovery gains a public scene in which the same knowledge is offered as advice and goes unheeded

note: The Kural likens the cloth over a woman's breasts to the face-cloth on a rutting elephant; Vinapati jests that the gods hid her breasts altogether because her eyes already killed.
teaches: The two take opposite sides of one premise, that a woman's breasts are a danger to be covered, and the pedi's jest pushes it to the end by having the gods remove what the cloth only veils, with the eyes left as the whole of the threat.

gains.a: the obscure jest becomes legible as a play on a known figure of the veiled danger
gains.b: the couplet's covering gains its limit case, a body in which the covered danger is absent and the eyes do all the harm

audit_text_issue: 653 stanza 5 lines; TSCII repairs; sense flagged uncertain

note: The couplet says tavam is striven for because it gets whatever one wants as one wants it; the kings vow that if they lose her they will fight, or else do great penance.
teaches: The kings take penance on the couplet's own motive, as a way to the thing desired, and so show the weakness the couplet's next verse attacks: penance offered as the consolation of a failed suitor stays bound to the desire it should end.

gains.a: the kings' fallback is seen as a reading of tavam the Kural itself supplies
gains.b: the couplet's promise of getting what one wants gains a speaker for whom the wanted thing is a woman lost at a contest

note: In 467 the city women say only those whose penance has earned it may drink Civakan's beauty; in 640 the suitor kings say that if they cannot win Gandharvadattai they will do penance.
teaches: The epic gives the same belief to both sexes, that tavam is the price of a beloved, but turns it round: the women look to past penance as the cause of a lucky union, the kings to future penance as the comfort for a lost one.

note: At Gandharvadattai's song the trees bud and the birds fall entranced; at the song of the suitors, called faultless and like Ananga in music, the birds fly off as if laughing.
teaches: The poet lets the birds give the verdict the narration withholds: the suitors' music is praised in words and condemned by nature, so the contest is judged before any human judge speaks.

note: The patikam announces that the Vidyadhara king's daughter was defeated at the vina by Civakan; here the assembled kings, faultless masters of music, fail before her.
teaches: Against the patikam the failure of the kings, praised as masters, shows that the victory announced there belongs to no ordinary skill, and raises the merchant's son above a crowd of crowned musicians before he appears.

note: At Krishna's flute in the Thiruppugazh dry trees in the forest sprout and birds come down to the ground; at Gandharvadattai's yazh the trees of the grove put out shoots and the birds forget themselves and fall.
teaches: The same marvel of music that moves trees and birds is a god's sign in the hymn and a contest's evidence in the epic, where 659 adds the reverse, birds fleeing bad music, so the image becomes a measure as well as a wonder.

gains.a: the epic's marvel is shown to use a stock image of divine music, so that the girl is raised to the level of Krishna's flute
gains.b: the hymn's image gains a version in which nature can also refuse, which the hymn's all-conquering flute never shows

note: In the Kaanal Vari the man sings that a cruel Death with spear-like eyes lives in the shore grove in a girl's form, and that had he known he would not have come; in the Cintamani onlookers tell the suitors that she is Death and bid them run while they can.
teaches: The two epics use the woman-as-Death figure at opposite moments: the Silappathikaram's singer learns it too late and says he would not have come, while the Cintamani's crowd says it beforehand to men who stay anyway, so the warning that comes too late in one comes in time and fails in the other.

note: Kovalan's yazh song praises the Kaveri for not sulking when the Chola unites with the Ganga and calls that a noble woman's karpu; Gandharvadattai's yazh songs show the cuckoo's mate estranged and won back only when the male coaxes her and bows at her feet.
teaches: Two yazh songs on lovers' estrangement take opposite sides: the Silappathikaram's makes the woman's not sulking her virtue, while the Cintamani's makes the man's humbling the end of a just sulk, which fits a heroine who yields only to the man who outdoes her.

note: In 454 Civakan returns from the cattle raid like the full moon the Tall One freed from the planet's mouth; in 665 the defeated kings dim like the full moon seized by the serpent.
teaches: The eclipse image is split between them: the rivals are the moon swallowed and Civakan the moon released, so the poet marks him as the winner before he has touched the vina.

note: In 455 one who hears of Civakan's recovery of the herd rages like a man whose last day has come; in 670 the king, burning like gold in fire, stands ready to kill him.
teaches: The ruler's anger first stirred by the hero's fame now becomes a plan to murder him, so Civakan's public successes are the very things that endanger him.

note: Kattiyankaran tells the suitors that only Kama could win the princess; ten verses later the poet calls Civakan, adorning the dancer, அனங்கன் அன்னான், one like Kama.
teaches: The usurper's boast that no Kama is present is refuted by the man he wants dead, so his taunt unknowingly names his rival.

note: Kural 1115 jokes that her waist will snap if she wears anicham with its stems; the spectators of 679 say the dancer avoids flowers lest her small waist break, and lament that sandal and pearls were hung on her.
teaches: The couplet's lover's joke is turned into a crowd's mock indignation at those who dressed the girl, so the hyperbole of the slender waist becomes a charge against the adorner.

gains.a: a known literary formula of the waist too slight for flowers, against which the crowd's outburst reads as conventional praise rather than real concern
gains.b: a public, theatrical setting in which the private lover's exaggeration is shouted by many and aimed at a culprit

note: Kural 1081: the man seeing her first cannot tell whether she is a goddess, a peahen or a woman; the crowd at the dance names her peacock, swan, golden creeper, lotus goddess or daughter of the gods.
teaches: The couplet's one man's bewilderment becomes a whole audience's at a staged dance, so the doubt about her nature is produced by art and costume, not by a chance meeting.

gains.a: the Kural's frame of first sight, which shows the crowd's guesses as the confusion of love rather than mere compliment
gains.b: a case where the woman's seeming divinity is made by adornment and performance, which the couplet's private encounter does not consider

note: Naladiyar 48 mocks those who praise sandal paste and garlands without knowing what the body is; the crowd of 680 calls the sandalled, garlanded dancer a goddess or a daughter of the immortals.
teaches: The epic stages exactly the admiration the Naladiyar scorns and gives it to the whole city without rebuke, so the two works disagree on whether adorned beauty is a fit object of wonder.

gains.a: a Jain didactic verdict against which the crowd's rapture can be weighed, which the narrative itself withholds here
gains.b: a full scene of the praise it condemns, showing how adornment, music and dance build the illusion the quatrain attacks

note: The spectators of 682 waste away like a butter doll in the sun of desire; in Thiruppugazh 142 the poet, melting like wax in fire for women, asks whether he must stay bound to that shame.
teaches: The same melting is in the epic the measure of a dancer's art and in the hymn a bondage to be prayed away, so the image shows how one bodily figure serves praise and penitence.

gains.a: a devotional reading of the melting as delusion, which the epic, praising the dance, leaves unsaid
gains.b: a narrative where the melting is collective and caused by a staged performance, not only by a woman's body

note: Kural 1100: once eyes agree with eyes, spoken words are useless; Anangamaalai sends her love to Civakan by a 'letter' of her eyes carried by her smile, in the middle of a public dance.
teaches: The epic keeps the couplet's wordless eye-language but makes it one-sided and public, a message sent across a crowd, and shows its cost when the king's enmity follows from it.

gains.a: the Kural's rule that the look can replace speech, which makes the eye-letter a full declaration rather than a flirtation
gains.b: a case where the silent message is unreturned and dangerous, a consequence the couplet's mutual glance does not weigh

note: Kattiyankaran sneers at the merchant's son: is he then king of this city? In 316 the deity tells the queen this child will crush the king who stands against him.
teaches: The usurper's mocking question unknowingly names the rightful king, so the story makes the villain voice the prophecy he means to deny.

note: In 455 an unnamed hearer rages at the news that Civakan recovered the herd with no man lost; in 693 Kattiyankaran, hearing the same deed retold by his men, decides Civakan is the way his kingdom will be taken.
teaches: The anger left nameless at the cattle raid is given its owner and its reason here: the deed that saved the city's herds is what tells the usurper he has a rival.

note: 436 tells how the hunters destroyed the king's swordsmen; in 691 men of that army, speaking to Kattiyankaran, recall that they broke twice before Civakan won the herd back.
teaches: The rout told by the narrator as a battle scene returns as the soldiers' own confession to their king, which is why praise of Civakan reaches the usurper as an indictment of his rule.

note: Kural 701 makes one who knows a mind before it speaks an ornament to the world; Kattiyankaran, once the minister, reads from the dancer's signs that she loves Civakan and turns the knowledge into grudge and seizure.
teaches: The pair shows that reading an unspoken mind is praised in the Kural for a use the couplet assumes, and in a jealous ruler the same skill feeds only his grudge and his violence.

gains.a: a name for the faculty the usurper uses, which the epic shows only in action, and a measure of how far he has fallen from the good counsellor's use of it
gains.b: a case where the sign-reader serves himself rather than the one he reads, which the couplet's praise does not consider

note: Kural 226 says that ending the ruinous hunger of the destitute is where one should store wealth; the usurper's soldiers recall that Civakan fed them in a thousand pots when they were faint, and the telling makes the king fear him.
teaches: The pair shows the couplet's store paying out in loyalty: feeding hungry men lays up for Civakan the hearts of the usurper's own army, which is exactly why the giving is felt as a threat.

gains.a: the ethical frame in which the feeding is a virtue and not merely a political move
gains.b: a case where the return on feeding the hungry is political allegiance, and where that return endangers the giver

note: Kural 265 says tapas is striven for because whatever is wanted comes as it is wanted; the city's women say the princess must have done penance (நோற்றனள்) to enjoy Civakan's beauty.
teaches: The women apply the couplet's promise to a marriage, so the pair shows penance taken in common talk as the merit behind erotic good fortune, the very use the Kural's next verse warns against.

gains.a: the doctrinal basis of the women's idiom, which the epic uses only in passing
gains.b: evidence of how the couplet's motive of getting what one wants was heard in popular speech, where the wanted thing is a beautiful husband

note: Tirumanthiram 346 reads Siva's burning of Kama as the yoga that destroys desire's work; the Cintamani says Civakan is as if the burnt Kama had risen again on earth.
teaches: Set beside the Saiva reading, the Jain poet's simile shows the burning of Kama handled as a story whose victim returns, so the myth becomes a measure of a hero's beauty instead of a victory over desire.

gains.a: the doctrinal weight of the myth the simile borrows, which the simile does not state
gains.b: evidence that the Kama-burning circulated as a stock image outside Saiva devotion, with its yogic sense dropped

note: Gandharvadattai's vow to bind the unknown youth with a garland is kept when she fastens the gold garland on his chest after the contest.
teaches: The garland in 738 is the answer to an inward vow, so the public result of the contest was settled in her heart before a string was touched.

note: The astrologer's reading places the princess's destined husband in Rajamapuram; as Civakan takes the lute the poet calls him கணிபுகழ் காளை, the youth the astrologers praised.
teaches: The epithet at the moment of playing marks the contest as the working out of the horoscope, so the reader hears the song as a prophecy being fulfilled rather than a match in doubt.

note: The lute's wood is born of the earth-maiden and reared by the sky as foster mother; Civakan, born in the burning ground, was handed by Kantukkatan to a foster mother.
teaches: The instrument Civakan chooses has his own hidden history, a mother who bore it and another who reared it, while the ones he rejects are faulted for their origin, so his judgement of pedigree reflects on the birth no one at the contest knows.

note: In both a woman takes the lute after the man's songs and begins her own; the Cintamani's நிலத்தோர் and gods wondering (729) echo the Silappathikaram's நிலத்தெய்வம் வியப்பு எய்த, and both close on பாடத் தொடங்கு-.
teaches: The same turn at the lute, his songs then hers, ends in a garland in the Cintamani and in Kovalan's leaving in the Silappathikaram, which shows that the outcome lies in how the man hears her reply, as yielding or as a hidden intent.

note: The Kural's woman says desire's axe breaks the door of nirai bolted with shame; the princess says the youth has opened the door of her hard nirai and entered her heart's guarded chamber.
teaches: The Cintamani keeps the Kural's door of nirai but changes the breaker from desire to the man and the outcome from lament to a vow of marriage, so the breach of self-containment can be the start of a lawful bond.

gains.a: the princess's image is read with the Kural's exact logic of door and bolt, so her 'hard nirai' is a guarded virtue, not a figure of speech
gains.b: the couplet's breach, spoken by a woman already in love, gains a first-sight case in an unmarried girl, where it leads to the garland instead of grief

note: The Kural's lover says the flood of desire carries off the raft of shame and manliness; the epic's princess has a sea of desire that overruns the fence of shame round her nirai.
teaches: Shame is a raft for the Kural's man and a fence round a prison for the epic's woman, so the same flood threatens a man's means of crossing but a woman's enclosure.

gains.a: the princess's sea of desire is placed in the Kural's account of what desire sweeps away, naming shame as the first loss
gains.b: the couplet, spoken by a man, gains the woman's version, where shame guards nirai rather than carrying her

note: Both describe the lute part by part with the same names, the bowl (பத்தர், பத்தல்), the pegs (ஆணி), the stem (மருப்பு) and the strings (நரம்பு), and both credit its music with power over the hostile and the wild.
teaches: The Cintamani takes over the Sangam bard's catalogue of the lute but makes it gold, coral and diamond, and makes knowing the instrument's parts and faults the contest itself, so the bard's working tool becomes the test of a prince.

gains.a: the epic's list of parts is shown to be an inherited form of praise, which explains why the lute is described before it is played
gains.b: the bard's poor lute, praised to win a patron's gift, gains a later setting where judging its wood and strings decides a royal marriage

note: The Kural says tapas is striven for here because one gets what one wants as one wants it; the bride's falling garland is read as a call to all the world to do tapas.
teaches: The Cintamani takes the Kural's frankly worldly motive for tapas and fixes it on a bridal union, showing how far that motive reaches in a work whose hero will at last renounce such joys.

gains.a: the poet's fancy gains a rule that makes it more than a compliment: the joy is the earned fruit of former tapas
gains.b: the couplet's unnamed 'what is wanted' is given a concrete object, sensual and married, which the next couplet's condemnation of desire leaves out

note: Kattiyankaran tells cowardly kings to leave their crowns and go to the hermits' forest; the patikam says Civakan renounced at the height of his rule.
teaches: In the villain's mouth giving up the crown for the forest is the punishment of a beaten king, while the epic's own ending makes it the free act of a victorious one, so the book stages the courtly contempt for renunciation it will overturn.

note: Dharmadattan warned Kattiyankaran that a king is a fire that burns whoever touches him; Padumukan warns the kings that fire burns when touched.
teaches: The fire that was said to guard the true king now guards his unknown son against the same usurper's tools, so the proverb points at Civakan's royal birth before anyone in the hall knows it.

note: The astrologer read that the princess's destined husband lives in Rajamapuram; Padumukan declares her the chaste bride of Civakan whom no one can take.
teaches: What the horoscope fixed as her allotted portion becomes, once she has chosen, her own karpu, so the fated union is defended in the hall as a matter of the woman's chastity rather than of the stars.

note: Kattiyankaran promises the kings fortune if they kill Civakan; Padumukan says his plan is to let them destroy one another and rule alone.
teaches: Padumukan's reading turns the promise of sovereignty into its opposite, showing the reader that the usurper's incitement of the suitors repeats the method by which he took Saccandan's throne.

note: The Kural counts dividing others among a minister's skills; Padumukan exposes the minister-turned-king's plan to divide the kings so they perish fighting each other.
teaches: The craft of division that the Kural lists without moral comment as a minister's skill is shown here in the hands of a minister who betrayed his king, and the epic names its result as a world made cruel.

gains.a: Padumukan's charge gains a recognised name: Kattiyankaran is practising the minister's art of division, not mere spite
gains.b: the couplet's neutral skill gains a case where it is turned against the realm, which the couplet does not consider

note: In the Purananuru poem a king's demand for a girl her father will not give brings war on the town, and the mother who reared her beauty is blamed; here kings rise to seize a bride already won in an open contest.
teaches: The epic removes the father's refusal that drives the Sangam bride-war, since the bride's father set a fair contest and she has chosen, so the suitors' war stands as bare lust and the blame moves from the girl's rearing to the kings and their instigator.

gains.a: the scene is placed in the old category of the bride-war (மகட்பால்), which shows what it changes
gains.b: the poem's blame of the mother is shown to be one choice of cause, which a later poet assigns instead to the suitors' desire and to a schemer

note: The Kural asks what a sword is to those without courage and what learning is to those who fear the assembly; Padumukan mocks kings who lost at the art and turn to the sword.
teaches: The Kural tests the sword and learning separately, each by its own courage, but Padumukan adds that one who has failed the test of art cannot seek the same prize by the sword, so the second arena only confirms the first defeat.

gains.a: the sarcasm வாழ்க நுங் கலை gains a standard: the kings fail both of the Kural's tests at once
gains.b: the couplet's paired measures gain a rule of contest about moving from one to the other, which the couplet does not state

note: Purananuru 369 sings the Chera's battle as a season of tillage, arrows for rain, heads for crop, ghouls threshing; 757 uses the same sowing-and-harvest field, with ghosts fed on flesh and blood, as a warning to rivals before the fight.
teaches: The bard's after-battle praise image, sung to earn a gift, becomes in the epic a combatant's threat spoken before a blow is struck, so the convention moves from rewarding a victory to predicting one.

gains.a: the full Sangam convention of the battlefield as a farm, which the verse compresses into four lines without naming it
gains.b: a use of the convention outside the bard's request for gifts, as an argument about who deserves a bride

audit_text_issue: Speaker of 757 inferred; sense flagged uncertain.

note: 757 calls the slaughter a harvest that wins the victory; in 820 the victor makes a golden image of the Jina, holds a festival and gives gifts to put away the sin (பாவம்) of the battlefield.
teaches: The same killing is first boasted as a crop and then expiated as a sin, so the Jain epic lets the heroic idiom stand in the speeches and corrects it only after the battle is won.

note: In 759 Civakan tells the princess the kings are already food (இரை) for his arrows; in 798 he greets the kings as guests and feeds (ஊட்டினான்) each of them one or two arrows.
teaches: The consolation's figure of kings as food is carried out as a mock feast in which he is host and the arrows are the meal, so his reassurance to her is kept literally.

note: Kural 463 says the wise do not undertake a deed that loses capital for the sake of gain; the kings tell Civakan, as a merchant's son, that a true trader would save his capital and flee, leaving the girl.
teaches: The couplet's prudence is turned into a class insult, and the battle that follows shows that the rule cannot say what counts as capital: for the kings it is life and goods, for Civakan it is his name and the bride.

gains.a: the general maxim of not risking the principal, which the kings bend into an argument for cowardice
gains.b: a case where the maxim is quoted by the side that loses, showing that it holds only once one has judged what the capital is

note: In 772 the kings foretell that Civakan will lie pierced by arrows, his beauty and youth wasted; in 816 those same kings vanish like lightning in rain and the Vidyadharas praise his victory.
teaches: The kings' prophecy of his death is answered by their own flight, so the scorn they pour on his youth becomes the measure of their defeat.

note: In Purananuru 71 the Pandya swears that if he does not see the backs (புறம்) of the kings who have joined against him, may he be parted from his wife; Civakan swears that unless he sees the kings' backs (புறக்கொடை) and embraces the lady, may his name perish.
teaches: The vow keeps the Sangam form, allied kings and the sight of their backs, but moves the woman from the forfeit to the prize: the Pandya risks his wife, Civakan stakes his name to win a bride.

gains.a: its genre: the வஞ்சினம் of a king facing allied enemies, with the shape of a named forfeit
gains.b: a variant in which the beloved is what the vow wins rather than what it puts at stake, showing the form can serve courtship as well as kingship

note: Civakan vows to see the kings' backs and then embrace the lady; in 817, having seen the field where the enemies fell, he enters his house with her, surrounded by his friends.
teaches: The vow's two conditions are kept in its own order, the routed field first and the bride brought home after, so the marriage is presented as the vow's discharge.

note: In 640 some suitors vowed to plunge into battle only if a man other than the vina's victor took her; in 791 the kings who desired her fight after Civakan has won at the vina.
teaches: The kings' war breaks the very terms they set at the contest, so their fight is shown as desire that will not accept its own rule, not as a defence of the bride.

note: 708 records a king who came and fell in the sea of the vina; 798 has Civakan remind the kings that she beat them at the vina before he serves them arrows.
teaches: Civakan's taunt makes the musical defeat the first round of the battle, so the kings now lose twice to the same bride, once to her skill and once to his.

note: The patikam's 28 says that his brother, companions and wives renounced and the master of the vina went to the unequalled state; here the same hero laughs with delight at a ghoul dressing in the slain.
teaches: The Jain epic lets its hero relish slaughter fully before it turns him to renunciation, so the release it promises in 28 is a turning from a violence he once enjoyed, not from one he never knew.

note: Kural 773 calls help to a foe in trouble the cutting edge of valour; 783 has the companions cripple a chariot and then bid its charioteer yoke fresh horses.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's ஊராண்மை into a battlefield move: the generosity is not mercy that ends the fight but an invitation to go on fighting on equal terms.

gains.a: a concept that makes the companions' strange order a recognised height of valour rather than a jest
gains.b: a concrete act that shows what the help to a stricken foe looks like in a chariot fight

note: Kural 776 counts as wasted the days without a noble wound; 782 has the companions offer their chests to the tusk so the scar may lie beautiful.
teaches: Where the couplet keeps a sober ledger of wounded days, the epic turns the wound into ornament, so the same ethic moves from a reckoning of duty to an aesthetic of the body.

gains.a: the reason a scarred chest should count as beauty: a wound is the record of a day not wasted
gains.b: the place of the noble wound on the body, the chest that faces the foe, which the couplet does not name

note: Kural 202 says evil is to be feared more than fire because evil yields evil; in 799 burning arrows kill the mean-minded kings and warn them off evil even in their next body.
teaches: The epic makes the fire itself the preacher: the burning arrow that kills is only the lesser fire, and its warning points to the evil that will follow the dead into the next birth.

gains.a: the ground of the arrows' warning, that evil breeds evil and so outlasts the body the fire destroys
gains.b: a picture of evil outlasting death, which gives the couplet's comparison with fire a span beyond one life

note: Tirumanthiram 2133 has the subtle body, its old deeds following, take up a new body; 799's arrows warn the slain against evil in the body they will take next.
teaches: Held together, the epic's warning to the dying presupposes the passage Tirumular describes, and Tirumular's mechanism is given a moral use: deeds follow, so the dead are urged to change their conduct across the change of body.

gains.a: the mechanism, deeds carried by the subtle body into a new birth, that makes 'the body you will take' literal
gains.b: an ethical address to the dying that the doctrinal account of transmigration leaves out

note: Naladiyar 3 has kings who rode under the umbrella fall when their deeds give out; 797 shows the kings' white umbrellas overturned by Civakan's arrows.
teaches: The quatrain names only spent deeds as the cause of a king's fall, while the epic shows the immediate cause, an archer and the kings' own desire, and in 799 sorts the fallen by their minds, so karma and the battle are both given as cause.

gains.a: a frame in which the overturned umbrellas are a lesson in impermanence and not only a victory
gains.b: a scene that names the human cause beside the karmic one, which the quatrain's 'other deeds' leaves blank

note: Purananuru 369 sings the battlefield as a harvest where the ghoul-woman holds the corpses and jackals thresh, and the bard asks the king for a gift; in 804 ghouls already fed sing over what was given them.
teaches: The epic hands the bard's role to the ghouls: in the Puram poem the singer asks for a share of the field, while here the scavengers have had their share and their song is thanks, so the field is a patron's gift completed.

gains.a: the kalavazhi frame that explains why ghouls 'sing what was given', as bards sing a patron's bounty
gains.b: the reversal that shows how close the Puram bard stands to the scavengers who share the same harvest of corpses

note: Maduraikkanchi 24-42 sets fat-mouthed demon women dancing the tunangai around a battle-sacrifice whose cook serves flesh-rice to the soldiers; in 803 a pregnant ghoul dresses herself in the field's remains while Civakan watches and laughs.
teaches: The Sangam poem makes the ghouls' feast part of a rite the king performs, while the epic removes the rite and keeps the dance as a spectacle for the hero's delight, so the motif survives as ornament of heroism.

gains.a: the ritual setting from which the battlefield ghoul descends, which makes Civakan's laughter a presiding king's pleasure
gains.b: a later afterlife of its demon women, cut loose from sacrifice and turned into a toilette parody

note: The Vidyadhara king said he would not give his daughter even if kings with sea-like armies fell at his feet and begged; here the kings who fought for her lose their sea-like army, which breaks like a salt hill in flood.
teaches: The father's refusal was spoken before any war, and the battle turns his figure of speech into fact: the same sea of soldiers he would not bow to is now the thing that dissolves.

note: Nandagon promised Civakan to fill the underworld with ghee of red cows, sweet milk and thick curd; here the keeper of the herds brings four hundred thousand pots of curd, milk and ghee to Civakan's wedding.
teaches: The herd chief's boast at his own daughter's giving is paid at Civakan's wedding instead, so the bond made by the recovered cattle carries from one marriage of the hero's circle to the next.

note: Civakan's teacher says those great in knowledge reach the path where hard deeds wear away; after the battle Civakan removes the battlefield's sin by an image of the Jina, a festival and gifts.
teaches: The epic gives the householder prince a route to clearing sin by rite and giving, beside the teacher's route of knowledge that wears deeds away, so the work holds two Jain answers to bad deeds at once and assigns them by station.

note: The Kural says it is not the spear but the ruler's unbent sceptre that gives victory; the epic says victory goes to the virtuous mind, and a betel leaf thrown by such a man becomes a spear.
teaches: The couplet ties victory to the justice of a king's rule, while the epic moves it into each fighter's heart and applies it to a war over a woman, where no sceptre is in question.

gains.a: the epic's moral of battle gains a political form, the rule that a just state wins, which its private quarrel over a bride lacks
gains.b: the couplet gains a test case where the side with fewer arms wins and the cause is put in character rather than in government

note: The Kural says a jackal can kill a war elephant when its feet sink in mud, so ground decides; the epic says a single lion kills a herd of elephants, so the nature of the fighter decides.
teaches: Both answer how the few beat the many, but the couplet credits the place of battle and the epic the strength of the one who fights, two incompatible accounts of the same reversal if each is taken as the cause.

gains.a: the epic's boast gains a rival explanation it does not consider, that its small band might have won by terrain or timing rather than by nature
gains.b: the couplet gains a counter-image in which the elephant is the victim of a stronger beast, not of bad ground, which shows its claim is a choice of cause

note: In the Nedunalvadai the king walks the camp at midnight to look at the sword wounds of the warriors; in the epic the wounded are laid in ghee, have spearheads cut out, and are given purses and ornaments.
teaches: The Sangam poem shows care for the wounded as the king's sleepless looking, and the epic turns that care into a practice of treatment and payment, so the reader sees the duty to the wounded grow from presence into provision.

gains.a: the epic's list of treatments gains a source in the old ideal of the leader who goes himself to the wounded, which it leaves to friends and women
gains.b: the Sangam king's visit gains a picture of what was done for the wounded after he looked, which the poem does not tell

note: The Kural says the two kinds of dark deed do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's true praise; the epic says the Tirthan's feet remove all the sins done, and has Civakan worship there after killing in battle.
teaches: The couplet's claim covers both good and bad deeds and asks only praise, while the epic narrows it to sins and stages it as a rite after a specific act of killing, showing how a general promise was put to work as expiation.

gains.a: the epic's rite gains a measure of how much less it claims than the couplet, which frees from good deeds too
gains.b: the couplet's abstract Lord gains a named object, the Jina's feet, and a concrete occasion, the sin of war

note: Tirumular says the holy waters are within the heart and that those who wander the land without bathing in them do not destroy their deeds; Civakan takes the water of a jewelled conch at the Tirthan's feet as part of putting away his sin.
teaches: Read as part of the sin-clearing rite, the conch water is the outward tirtham Tirumular says cannot destroy deeds, so the pair sets an epic's confidence in rite against a Saiva yogi's insistence on the inward bath.

gains.a: the epic's ceremony gains a sharp critic, who would ask whether the water touched the heart
gains.b: Tirumular's verse gains a case from another faith of the outward practice he dismisses, done sincerely by a hero after war

audit_text_issue: line 2 கூலித் doubtful; sense flagged uncertain

note: In 640 rival kings vow to plunge into war if another wins the vina contest; 844 reports that a wicked one, burning, said she belonged to the strongest spear and made war.
teaches: The suitors' threat comes true not as their own act but through a single instigator who turns their wounded pride into a war, so the contest's law is broken by one man's design.
