note: In 554 the king refused all suitors until the time fate set for his daughter; in 848 he tells the son-in-law that what is to come will come unsought.
teaches: The king who once used fate to wait for the destined husband now uses it to promise that husband his kingdom, so his trust in destiny moves from patience to assurance.

note: Kural 376 says what is not one's own will not stay however guarded and what is one's own will not leave though thrown away; 848 says what is to come comes and what is to go goes, as the sea and river receive unasked.
teaches: The Kural states the rule of fate about possessions, and the letter applies it to a dispossessed heir in the same breath as an offer of arms, showing fate being cited to back an effort rather than to forbid one.

gains.a: the letter's proverbial lines gain the weight of a known maxim on fate and property
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where 'what is yours will come' is a political promise to a man whose throne is held by another

note: Naladiyar 103 says each one's enjoyments are measured by their own course, as no one rounded the vilam fruit; 848 says the sea need not fetch water nor the river beg rain.
teaches: Both argue from unmade nature, but the quatrain's fruit shows a lot fixed in advance while the letter's sea and river show a lot that flows in, so the same proof from nature can counsel content or confidence.

gains.a: the letter's images are placed in the didactic argument that nature's givens prove fate
gains.b: the quatrain's measured lot gains a picture of fate as abundance flowing toward the fortunate

note: Kural 265 says tavam is striven for because what is wanted comes as wanted; in 829 the crowd sees the hero's wedding wealth as the fruit of his tavam and wishes it would come to them.
teaches: The onlookers accept the couplet's premise that tavam yields what one wants, yet only wish for its fruit instead of doing it, which is the very shortcut the couplet rules out.

gains.a: the crowd's wish is shown to rest on the doctrine that good fortune is the wages of penance
gains.b: the couplet gains its counter-case: people who believe its promise and still do not strive

note: Kural 1103 has the lover ask whether the lotus-eyed god's world is sweeter than sleep in the beloved's arms; 836 says even Indra, lord of the gods, could not have had this wedding.
teaches: Both set a human union above a god's world, but the Kural's lover measures it by private sweetness while the epic narrator measures it by public splendour, so the same boast ranks feeling in one and rank and wealth in the other.

gains.a: the narrator's hyperbole joins a known topos of love outranking heaven
gains.b: the couplet's private boast gains a version voiced in public about a wedding rather than an embrace

note: Kural 216 likens wealth in a man of goodwill to a fruit tree ripening in the town's midst; 828 likens the crowd at the hero's house to birds on a tree heavy with fruit.
teaches: The couplet's tree is a figure for wealth that others may share, and the epic shows who actually comes to such a tree: a crowd that gives as well as takes, as 829 and 831 go on to say.

gains.a: the simile gains the couplet's moral sense that the house's wealth is held for others
gains.b: the couplet's fruit tree gains a scene showing the throng that gathers and the exchange of gifts both ways

note: The patikam tells that at the festival bath two young women quarrelled over their powders and swore not to bathe if they lost; here the two, Suramanjari and Gunamalai, sit together in the grove free of grief.
teaches: The patikam's quarrel is set against this calm first sight of the rivals side by side, so the story's discord grows out of an easy companionship and the festival's own luxury.

note: The powder is first held out here; the patikam says Suramanjari's powder was beaten and she withdrew vowing to look on no man.
teaches: A trifle of pleasure called the powder that bears desire becomes the cause of a vow against all men, so the section's marriage turns on a toiletry rather than a battle.

note: Paripadal 12 has Madurai dress, perfume itself and mount she-elephants, horses and chariots in a rush to meet the Vaiyai flood; the Cintamani's city sets out with litters, elephants and carts for its spring water-play by the river.
teaches: The epic keeps the Sangam river festival's order of dressing, mounting and rushing to the bank, but its festival honours no river or god, and is likened instead to the Jina's assembly, so the old civic rite is re-made as pure pleasure under a renouncer's image.

gains.a: a precedent showing that its procession is a set piece of the Tamil river festival rather than an invention
gains.b: evidence that its catalogue of the crowd's preparations survived as a convention into the later Jain epic, cut loose from the river's worship

audit_text_issue: 858 has no main verb; the unit is only a catalogue

note: The Cintamani calls the Jina the lord of faultless kevala; Tirumular calls kevala the soul's sleep of utter stupor under anava, from which karma drives it out.
teaches: The same word for the soul's state 'alone' is the summit of release for the Jain poet and the lowest darkness of the bound soul for the Saiva, so the two traditions disagree on whether the soul left to itself is free or blind.

gains.a: a sense of how pointed its epithet is: kevala names perfection only in a doctrine where the soul alone, freed of karma, is omniscient
gains.b: a rival use of its technical term, showing that its claim that the solitary soul is in darkness answers a school that called that solitude release

note: The patikam says the two women vowed not to bathe in the festival water if they lost; here the wager is spelt out: the loser forfeits the water-play and pays crores of gold.
teaches: The patikam's single vow turns out to be one half of a two-part stake, honour and gold, and only the honour half is followed through the story, which shows which loss the poem thinks matters.

note: The women treat the powder contest as a wager (வெல்வது சூது); the Kural says not to want gambling even when one can win, since the winnings are the hook the fish swallows.
teaches: The epic shows a wager whose real stake is not wealth but pride, and whose cost falls in a vow of seclusion on the loser, so the Kural's warning about winnings is widened to what a wager does to the one who loses face.

gains.a: the women's game is shown to belong to a kind of act the ethical tradition already condemns, which the narrator's mild கண்ணற்றார் only hints at
gains.b: the couplet, which counts gambling's harm in money, gets a case where the harm is a loss of honour that reshapes a life

note: A simile for the maids' eyes mentions Civakan's resolve to cut Kattiyangaran down; much later a voice from the sky proclaims that Civakan will swallow Kattiyangaran's life.
teaches: The revenge is never dropped even in a scene of scents and maids: the poet plants it as an aside here, so the heavenly proclamation reads as the public fulfilment of a purpose already settled in private.

note: The maid cites the praise of the whole city, the merchant included, against Civakan's verdict; the Kural says understanding is seeing the true substance whoever's mouth one hears a thing from.
teaches: The pairing shows the couplet's rule tested where it is hardest, against unanimous acclaim, and shows that the epic does not let the lone judge rest on his authority either but makes him prove the truth by a test both sides accept.

gains.a: Civakan's refusal to follow the city is given a principle, so it reads as discernment rather than vanity
gains.b: the couplet's abstract rule gains a case where the many and the respected are wrong and the truth needs a witness, not a second opinion

note: The maid argues that moisture makes the bad good and drying makes the good bad; the Kural bids one examine qualities and faults, see which prevail, and take that.
teaches: The maid's argument exposes what the couplet assumes, that qualities hold still to be weighed; if condition changes them, weighing by inspection cannot settle a dispute, which is why the epic turns to the bees.

gains.a: the maid's retort is seen to strike at the method of judgement itself, not just at Civakan's verdict
gains.b: the couplet's method gets a limit: it needs qualities that are stable or a test that does not depend on the examiner's eye

note: Civakan proves the powder by what the bees do with it; the Kural says one's own deeds are the touchstone of greatness and smallness.
teaches: Both put the proof in what a thing does rather than in what is said of it, but the epic adds that a touchstone convinces only when both parties accepted it beforehand, as the maid did in 890 and 891.

gains.a: the bee test is shown to rest on a recognised rule of judging by effects, not on a trick
gains.b: the couplet's touchstone, stated of persons, gains a scene showing it must be agreed in advance to settle a quarrel

note: Here the bees prove Suramanjari's powder the lesser; in her own ilampakam a woman says the guarded chastity Suramanjari kept is because the lord dimmed the powder he tested by producing a witness.
teaches: The later verse reads the bee test as the cause of Suramanjari's guarded maidenhood, so a judgement of scents becomes in the story's memory the origin of a chaste seclusion.

note: Suramanjari vows to wait until Civakan comes defeated and worships her anklet-feet; in her ilampakam Civakan sets his head on the anklet of her feet, says the great forgive the wrongs of the small, and ends her sulk.
teaches: The vow is kept to the letter, his head on her anklet, yet the hero turns it by calling his own slight the wrong of a lesser one forgiven by the greater, so her condition is met and her pride still yielded.

note: The patikam says Suramanjari, beaten, resolved to look on no male form and withdrew into the guarded mansion; here she states the vow's condition, his coming defeated to her feet.
teaches: The patikam's 'no male form' is in the verse itself a vow with one exception named in advance, the man who shamed her, so the summary hides that her withdrawal is aimed at Civakan.

note: Shamed by the verdict, Suramanjari withdraws under a vow; the Kural says those like the yak that will not live once its hair is lost give up life when honour is lost.
teaches: The epic offers a third path to the couplet's choice between life and honour: a withdrawal from the world that keeps the wound open and names the act that will restore her honour.

gains.a: Suramanjari's seclusion is seen as a measure of honour like the yak's, not mere sulking
gains.b: the couplet's stark alternative of death gains a case where honour lost is answered by a vow with terms, which the couplet does not imagine

audit_text_issue: நோற்பன் நோற்றனை நீ hard to divide.

note: The patikam sums up Suramanjari as resolving to look on no male form; 908 has her vow already reserve one exception, Civakan.
teaches: The vow the outline reports as a refusal of all men is in the story a vow with Civakan written into it, so her seclusion is a waiting as much as a withdrawal.

note: 908's condition, joining Civakan's chest or no one breaking her nirai, is met when Suramanjari's heart rises to sink into his chest in her own ilampakam.
teaches: The exception she sets in anger becomes the desire that ends the vow, so the epic keeps her nirai intact by letting the one permitted man be the one she longs for.

note: The father has every carved figure made female so no male form is seen; later Civakan is told to hide by the golden image of Kama in the god of love's temple.
teaches: A ban thorough enough to change the sex of statues still leaves the love god's own image standing, and that is the gap through which the excluded man is brought in.

note: Kural 367 says that if craving is cut off thoroughly, unfailing deeds (தவாவினை) come as one wishes; 913 pictures giving to suppliants as damming the sea called அவா, with தவாவினை at its shore.
teaches: The epic takes the Kural's pair of craving and unfailing deed and makes festival giving the practical means of checking craving, where the couplet names only the cutting itself.

gains.a: the doctrinal source of its compressed image: the words அவா and தவாவினை are the couplet's own pairing, which explains why deed and craving share one metaphor
gains.b: a concrete social act, gold poured out to suppliants on a festival day, as the way craving is held back short of renunciation

note: Naladiyar 60 says the higher ones look to the pain within each pleasure and do not cling; in 909 Gunamalai, after the game that cost her a friend, sees that play meant for joy became the cause of sorrow.
teaches: The quatrain's discipline of seeing pain inside pleasure appears in the epic first as a girl's tears over a garden game, an early lesson in a story that ends in renunciation.

gains.a: the ascetic frame in which Gunamalai's private grief reads as the first form of the insight that leads to thuravu
gains.b: a lived case where the pain in pleasure is not bodily or moral but a broken friendship, arising from a contest of beauty

note: The patikam summarizes this episode as the hero giving nectar (அமிர்தம்) to a dog that came to harm at the bathing festival; 947 shows that the nectar is the five padas, swallowed in the heart (பதவமிர்தம் நெஞ்சின் அயின்று).
teaches: The patikam's 'nectar' turns out to be a teaching rather than a drink, so the summary's word is the poem's own metaphor for the mantra and not a miracle of healing.

note: The dog appears as a god in 948; the patikam's next verse tells how a god came down the sky like lightning and carried Civakan out of the king's prison.
teaches: Read together, the hero's kindness at the festival is the cause of his rescue later: the creature he saved by a mantra returns as the god who saves him, so the plot itself runs on karma's return.

note: Kural 30 says those called அந்தணர் are so because they bear cool kindness to every living being; in 934-936 the men skilled in the four Vedas, with minds of fire, beat a dog to death over a heap of rice.
teaches: The epic stages the Kural's definition as a test the Brahmins fail, and gives the cool kindness the Kural requires to the hero instead, so the name and the conduct come apart exactly as the couplet's reasoning allows.

gains.a: a standard, from outside the Jain frame, by which the Brahmins' violence is condemned without the epic having to state it
gains.b: a scene showing what follows when the title is kept and the conduct lost: the couplet's 'because' becomes a charge

note: Tirumanthiram 533 says those who grieve the ascetics who teach the mantra are born as dogs; in 945 a dog dying with no merit hears a mantra and is born a god.
teaches: Both texts tie the mantra to rebirth as a dog, but run the scale in opposite directions: Tirumular uses the dog's birth as the punishment for wronging the mantra's teachers, the Jain epic uses the mantra to lift a dog out of that birth even without merit.

gains.a: the sharpness of its choice of a dog, which in the Saiva text is the very emblem of a fallen birth
gains.b: a view in which the mantra's power reaches the lowest birth directly, not only as a sanction protecting its teachers

note: Tirumanthiram 905 promises that chanting சிவாயநம ends birth, by grace; in 946 the Lord's five padas, taken at death, bring the dog a good state (நற்கதி), a better birth.
teaches: Both are five-part formulas given at the decisive moment, but the Saiva five letters promise an end to birth through grace, while the Jain five padas here promise a better birth by the dog's own letting go of attachment and fear.

gains.a: the measure of how modest its promise is: a good birth, not release, and won by the hearer's renunciation rather than by a god's grace
gains.b: a rival five-fold formula against which its claim that the five letters end birth stands out as a stronger claim

note: Naladiyar 322 says those not disposed to virtue cannot take it in, as a tanner's dog that chews leather cannot take the taste of milk rice; in 944 a dog pricks its ears, weeps and takes in the teaching.
teaches: The quatrain uses the dog as the type of the creature who cannot receive dharma; the epic answers with a dog that hears and consents, so receptivity is made a matter of the moment of hearing, not of the hearer's kind.

gains.a: the force of the inversion: the dog is the proverbial non-hearer, which makes its listening the point
gains.b: a limit on its image: the dog's inability is a habit, which the epic shows can be broken at death

note: In 951 the dog, given the five padas at its ear as it died, is reborn a god; in 3036, in the last ilampakam, those lying at the point of death to whom the ascetic's words are set at the ear appear at once as unaging gods.
teaches: The single rescue of a dog becomes, at the end of the epic, a general working of the teacher's word, so the early episode is shown to be the model case of a rule the work states only at its close.

note: Both make a recited formula the agent of a change of state: Tirumular's சிவாயநம is an alchemist's pill that turns the body's cage to gold; the Cintamani's five padas are water that washes off black karma and bring a new god's body after death.
teaches: Set side by side, the two mantras do different work: the Saiva syllables transmute the body the devotee already has through the Lord's act, while the Jain padas clear karma so that a better body follows in the next birth, with no Lord who acts.

gains.a: a Saiva counterpart in which the mantra changes this body rather than the next, which shows that 951's change comes only with death and a new birth
gains.b: a case in which the mantra works on one who cannot melt or contemplate, a dying animal, so that devotion of the mind is not what gives the formula its force

note: 952 has fire burn away iron's nature and turn it to gold, with Civakan as the fire; 960 repeats the forge, adds mercury piercing the iron, and uses it to answer the doubt that a dog could become a god.
teaches: The image moves from praising the friend as the cause of the change to defending the change itself as lawful, so the narrator relies on one figure first for gratitude and then for doctrine.

note: 959: the god promises to stay like Civakan's shadow and come if he thinks of him in trouble; patikam verse 15 tells how, when the king throws Civakan into prison, a god comes down the sky like lightning and carries him away.
teaches: The patikam's rescue is the promise of 959 kept, so the god's later appearance is not a chance intervention but the return of a debt owed for the mantra.

note: Both use iron turned to gold for a change of being: Tirumular says gold once made never turns back to iron, so one who has the guru's grace is not born again; the Cintamani's iron-to-gold is a dog reborn as a god.
teaches: The same alchemy marks a final release in Tirumular and only a rise within the round of births in the Cintamani, so the image's 'no return' belongs to the Saiva claim, not to the figure itself.

gains.a: a reading of its own image as a step and not an end, since the god of 951 is still embodied
gains.b: an instance where the gold is a higher birth, which shows that the couplet's finality is a doctrinal addition to the metallurgy

note: Tirumular says those who grieve the ascetics who taught the mantra are born as dogs (சுணங்கன்); the Cintamani's dog (சுணங்கன்) is raised to a god's birth by the mantra heard from Civakan.
teaches: Read together, the teacher's mantra decides birth in both directions: offending its teachers sinks a man to a dog, and receiving it lifts a dog to a god, so the same word names the bottom of the scale in both books.

gains.a: the Saiva warning that the dog's birth is itself the fruit of offending the bearers of the mantra, which deepens the narrator's 'no good in it'
gains.b: a story in which the same creature climbs back up the scale by the same means that, in the couplet, cast men down

note: Kural 9 says a head that does not bow at the feet of the one of eight qualities (எண்குணத்தான்) is useless; 961 vows to bow the head to no one but the one who removes the eight karmas (எண்வினை) and gives bliss, and sets aside the gods of desire.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's positive command into an exclusion and fills its unexplained 'eight' with a count of karmas destroyed, so the Kural's open epithet is given a Jain content it does not itself state.

gains.a: a canonical model, the bowing head of the Kural's first chapter, for its refusal
gains.b: one reading of its undefined eight, together with the inference that the bow must be withheld from other gods

note: Kural 24: one who guards the five senses with the goad of firmness is a seed for the finest ground; 962 builds the whole farm, with zeal as the plough, the body as the field, vows as seed, conduct as water and the five senses as the fence.
teaches: The couplet's one image of the guarded self as seed is spelled out as a season of tillage, and its unnamed 'finest ground' gets two harvests, heaven first and release after.

gains.a: a classical root for its allegory, in which the guarding of the five senses already leads to the best place
gains.b: an answer to what வரன் yields, given as a sequence of heaven and release, and a place for vows and conduct beside the guarding of the senses

note: In 962 the practiser yokes the plough, tills his own body and guards it with the senses' fence until release ripens; in Tirumular 1875 the first Lord has taken the poet's soul as his field to plough, and praise and blame fall away.
teaches: The two pictures of the tilled self disagree on who holds the plough: in the Jain allegory release is the crop of one's own labour, in Tirumular the Lord does the tilling, so the shared farm figure carries the dispute between release by effort and release by grace.

gains.a: a Saiva counter-picture that brings out how wholly 962 leaves the work to the practiser, with no god in the field
gains.b: the Jain alternative it implicitly answers, which makes its passive 'he has taken my soul to plough' a claim about grace and not only an image

note: Paripadal 6 sets the river play out as a battle array, with bathers drilling rivalry 'as in war' and carrying syringes (சிவிறியர்); in 966 the bathers spray with syringes (சிவிறி) and the play goes through a campaign's whole course, the enemy's back seen, the offender fined with garlands, tribute taken.
teaches: The Sangam festival's figure of water-play as battle is carried by the epic from the array to the victory and its exactions, and set just before a real terror breaks out (973), so the mock war of desire gives way to a true danger.

gains.a: the Sangam convention of the festival as a war of pleasure, which explains why the verse reaches for rout and tribute
gains.b: a later use of the convention that completes the war figure with conquest and penalty, which the Paripadal's arrays only begin

note: Patikam verse 14 tells that on the same day the hero gave nectar to the dying dog at the bathing festival, he overcame the victorious elephant that had terrified Gunamalai; 973 is the elephant breaking loose as the festival crowd returns.
teaches: The patikam binds the mercy to the dog and the mastery of the elephant as one day's deeds, so the chapter's turn from the god's farewell through the water-play to the rampaging tusker is a single day planned as a pair of the hero's virtues.

note: The patikam gives the episode one line, the victorious elephant that terrified Gunamalai, beaten on the same day Civakan gave nectar to the dying dog; 974-985 tell it as a scene in which the bearers flee, the companion offers to die, and Civakan chooses death over life before he knows who the girl is.
teaches: The patikam's pairing of the dog and the elephant on one day is borne out by the scene's terms: both deeds are mercy to a life in danger, not courtship, and the love follows only afterwards.
audit_text_issue: 985 is in a longer metre than its neighbours; the count ஐஞ்ஞாற்று நால்வர் is uncertain.

note: Kural 969 says the honourable give up life when honour is at stake, like the yak that will not live without its hair; 978 has Civakan reckon death better than life when a stranger woman's life is in danger.
teaches: The epic moves the Kural's honour-death from guarding one's own standing to rescuing another, so that honour is measured by whose danger a man will not stand by and watch.

gains.a: a rule that names the choice Civakan makes in a single line as a settled standard of honour, not a hero's impulse
gains.b: a case where the life given up for honour is risked to save someone else, which the couplet's self-regarding image of the yak leaves out

note: In Akananuru 18 the friend tells the lover that if her friend suffers harm for a single day she will not live after; in 976 Gunamalai's companion, facing the elephant, resolves that it should kill her together with her mistress.
teaches: The akam friend's stock claim that her life hangs on the heroine's is put to the test in the epic by a real beast, and the companion keeps it, so the convention is shown as a loyalty that can be acted on.

gains.a: the akam convention behind the companion's resolve, which makes her offer a known role rather than a passing panic
gains.b: an enacted instance of the friend's pledge, which the poem only states as a warning to the lover

note: In Kalittokai 103 a herdsman wrenching a charging bull by the ear is likened to Mayon tearing the horse's jaw, and the herd girls will embrace only one who falls between the killer bull's horns; in 984 Civakan facing the elephant is likened to the gem-coloured lord facing the elephant sent to kill him, and Gunamalai's love follows.
teaches: Both poems make the man who masters a charging beast a Krishna figure whom a girl then loves, but the herders' bull-catch is a set contest whose price the community names, while the epic's rescue is unplanned and the girl chooses for herself.

gains.a: the older pattern of beast-taming as a bride-winning feat under a Krishna simile, which explains why the elephant fight leads straight into Gunamalai's love
gains.b: a later merchant-city version of the pattern in which the danger falls on the girl and the feat is a rescue, not a sport

note: Naladiyar 30 says kin come unasked and go silently, leaving the body as a bird leaves its nest-tree; 993 says Gunamalai spurns her kin's talk like those who know their births.
teaches: The epic borrows the renouncer's detachment from kin, which the Naladiyar grounds in kin's passing, to picture a girl whose turning from family is love for one man, so the same outward withdrawal is shown to have opposite causes.

gains.a: the reasoning about kin as passing visitors that the simile's 'those who know their births' assumes but does not state
gains.b: a sign that the quatrain's lesson had become a known figure of speech, usable even of a lover's absorption

note: Kural 270 says the have-nots are many because few do penance; 997 has Gunamalai ask whether, like the small folk who did no penance, she has any door to escape her longing.
teaches: The couplet's explanation of want by the lack of past tapas is taken up by a lover as an account of why the man she wants is out of reach, showing the doctrine at work in ordinary speech about desire.

gains.a: the doctrinal sense of her simile: that what one lacks is owed to penance not done, which turns her cry into a judgment on her own merit
gains.b: a reading of the couplet's unspecified 'those who lack' as covering the lover's lack, which the couplet leaves open

note: The Kural praises womanhood that suffers a sea of desire and does not ride the palmyra horse; Gunamalai, with longing like the sea, considers riding it.
teaches: The epic shows the couplet's praised restraint from inside, as a near thing: the heroine reaches the very thought of the madal before turning to a go-between, so the Kural's 'does not ride' names a line held under pressure, not an absence of the wish.

gains.a: Gunamalai's thought of the madal gains its measure: it is the one act the ethical tradition says a woman forgoes
gains.b: the couplet's abstract womanhood gains a woman who voices its praise of herself (998) and then wavers, which a gnomic line cannot show

note: The Kural's wife takes offence even at his adoring gaze, asking whom he is thinking of; Gandharvadattai's sulk blazes at a portrait of another woman painted by her husband.
teaches: The Kural's comedy of jealousy depends on the husband's innocence, and the epic removes it: here the suspected other woman is real and painted by his own hand, so the sulk is no longer love's game but a just grievance.

gains.a: Gandharvadattai's flare is placed in a known type, the wife of the pulavi nunukkam who reads every look as a rival
gains.b: the couplet's baseless suspicion is set against a case where suspicion is right, showing how much its charm rests on there being no rival

note: The Kural's lover says his bond with the girl is that of body and life; Civakan tells his sulking wife they are one life in two bodies.
teaches: Spoken with another woman's portrait still in his arms, the claim of a single life becomes an appeasing formula, so the Cintamani shows the Kural's declaration of union put to use in a marriage that is about to take a second wife.

gains.a: Civakan's line gains the weight of the classic declaration it reworks, which makes its hollowness here visible
gains.b: the couplet, spoken in first love, gains a later setting that tests whether the claim survives a rival

note: Gunamalai stood before the charging elephant looking about with doe eyes and trembling like lightning; Civakan paints exactly her look and her trembling.
teaches: The lover's image of the beloved is the instant of her mortal fear, so what he desires and keeps is the moment he saved her, and the rescue becomes the ground of the love.

note: Gunamalai fears she has no way to live, like little people who have done no tapas; Civakan says her very ornaments did penance to be on her.
teaches: Apart and unknown to each other, both lovers reach for the language of penance: she counts herself among those without its merit, while he grants its merit even to her jewels, so the same idea marks her despair and his worship.

note: Civakan praised Gunamalai so that even her girdle and anklets had done penance; to his wife he calls her the sand of a seep-well beside the Ganges.
teaches: Within a few verses the hero ranks the same woman as worthy of the jewels' penance and as a puddle beside his wife, so the poem lets the reader see his words to each woman fitted to the listener.

note: Gunamalai wasted like a garland in a ghee-fed flame; Gandharvadattai's sulk blazes like fire with ghee poured on it.
teaches: One simile serves both women: the fire that consumed the girl's longing now feeds the wife's jealousy, so the poem sets the two women's passions, love and anger, burning from the same man.

note: Boothappandiyan swears that if he does not see his enemies' backs he may be parted from his wife; Civakan swears that if he does not live with Gunamalai he may be one who turned his weapon on the beaten.
teaches: The vanjinam form stakes one domain against the other in both directions: the king pledges his marriage to secure a victory, and the epic hero pledges his warrior honour to secure a marriage, choosing as penalty an attack on fleeing men, the very thing the king's vow hopes to see.

gains.a: the Sangam vanjinam kaanji as the source of its self-curse, which the epic turns from a battle vow into a love pledge in a letter
gains.b: evidence that the vow's frame outlived the battlefield and that a later poet could read its stake, the beloved, as reversible with the warrior's code

note: The Kural ranks highest the woman who suffers a sea of desire and does not ride the palmyra horse; the parrot says maidens hide their love-sickness from even their nearest, out of shame.
teaches: The silence the couplet praises has a working cost the couplet does not show: because the girl will not speak even to her confidante, the knowledge of her illness has to travel by a go-between who asks the man to diagnose it.

gains.a: a rule stating why Gunamalai must use a messenger rather than speak, which the scene assumes but does not argue
gains.b: a scene showing who carries the woman's unspoken desire once shame forbids her to declare it

note: The Kural's man says the woman who causes his love-sickness is its only cure; Civakan writes that the little parrot she sent has cured his swelling sickness.
teaches: Set beside the couplet's rule that only the beloved herself can heal, the letter shows the cure passing to her token: a sent message relieves the sickness before any meeting, so the remedy can be borne by a proxy.

gains.a: the convention that love's cure is the beloved, against which the parrot's cure reads as a claim about messengers
gains.b: a case of courtship by letter, where the remedy the couplet confines to the woman's presence is carried by a go-between

note: The Kural says penance is striven for because it gains what one wants as one wants it; Gunamalai says that if Civakan refuses she will win him even by penance.
teaches: The girl takes the couplet's motive for தவம் at its word and aims it at a husband, which exposes how far the Kural's argument for penance rests on desire rather than release.

gains.a: a doctrinal ground for her resolve, which the verse states without explaining why penance should work
gains.b: a concrete wish, love for a man, that tests the couplet's open promise of getting whatever is wanted

audit_text_issue: sense of the verse flagged uncertain (word division of காதகா தென்று)

note: Civakan pledges to wed her with his word not falling short (சொற்குன்றா); Gunamalai, having read his letter, offers worship so that he may not fail his word (சொற்குன்றான் ஆக).
teaches: The hero's own phrase comes back as the heroine's prayer, so the pledge he treats as settled she treats as needing divine witnesses, which marks the unequal risk the two carry in a promise of marriage.

note: Gunamalai draws a circle in the sand asking that the union come about without fail; the parrot then lands and she hears the message of his pledge.
teaches: The divination is answered not by the circle closing but by the messenger's arrival, so the story replaces the omen with news and lets the girl's private rite be fulfilled by the man's written word.

note: In 1003 Civakan paints Gunamalai on cloth as she stood trembling before the elephant; in 1047 the nurse says the cousin worships a likeness of her painted on cloth every day.
teaches: The nurse's test gives the rival suitor the very gesture Civakan made, so Gunamalai's refusal shows that what binds her is the man she chose, not the devotion paid to her image.

note: In 978 Civakan, seeing the girl in danger, judges death better than a life that lets her perish and charges the elephant; in 1049 she calls service at his feet the wage for that toil.
teaches: Her refusal of the cousin is set up as repayment of a specific risk, so the epic makes her love the answer to his choosing death over a shamed life.

note: After losing the powder contest Suramanjari vows that none but Civakan shall break her reserve and shuts herself away (902, 908); after winning it, Gunamalai vows death or penance if she is denied him.
teaches: The quarrel Civakan judged ends with both rivals bound by vows only marriage to him can release, the loser by seclusion and the winner by threat of death, so his verdict sets up two of his marriages at once.

note: Kural 54 says nothing is greater than a woman who has the firmness called karpu; Gunamalai shows such firmness before marriage, against her own parents, for a man she has only chosen.
teaches: Read together, the couplet's firmness moves from a wife's fidelity back to a maiden's choice, where it shows itself as resisting her parents with death or renunciation rather than as serving a husband.

gains.a: the Kural's naming of karpu as திண்மை, a strength, which lets her threat read as firmness of virtue rather than wilfulness
gains.b: a case of that firmness exercised before any marriage and directed against the girl's own parents, which a couplet about a wife does not foresee

note: In Akananuru 369 the foster mother laments that her girl refused the rich wedding her kin had prepared and went off across the waste with a youth; Gunamalai, told by her nurse of a match with a rich cousin, names death or penance as her only alternatives.
teaches: Beside the Akam girl who answers an unwanted family wedding by elopement, Gunamalai answers by a vow spoken to her nurse, keeping the refusal inside the house where it can move her parents instead of leaving them.

gains.a: the akam convention of the refused kin wedding, which marks the nurse's report as the familiar trigger for a heroine's flight that this heroine declines
gains.b: an outcome in which the same refusal, voiced rather than acted on, ends in a sanctioned wedding, a path the elopement poem never shows

note: Kurinjippattu opens with the friend disclosing to the mother the marriage the girl chose past her father's guard; in 1052 the nurse who sounded Gunamalai tells the mother, who tells the father.
teaches: The epic runs the akam disclosure through the whole household chain and adds the nurse's verdict that the match ripens from past penance, so a convention of love poetry becomes a step in a karmic marriage plot.

gains.a: the logic of அறத்தொடு நிற்றல், by which the nurse's report reads as a recognised duty to disclose rather than gossip
gains.b: a narrated sequel in which disclosure reaches the father and produces the wedding, which the idyll's speech to the mother can only argue for

note: In 996 Gunamalai says her heart burns like the sacrificial fire; in 1059 Civakan's mother's unfailing chastity is like the flame of the mantra-fed Vedic sacrifice.
teaches: The same ritual fire stands first for a girl's consuming desire and then for a matron's chastity, so the epic uses one Vedic image for passion and for the discipline that marriage is meant to make of it.

note: In 1037 Gunamalai draws circles in the sand, asking whether she will unite with Civakan if his errand prospers; in 1063 the wedding drums sound.
teaches: The sand-circle divination she made in doubt is answered by the wedding within the same ilampakam, so the epic lets a folk rite of the anxious lover come true.

note: In 899 Suramanjari, hearing Civakan call her powder unfit, vows penance until he comes defeated to worship her anklets; in 1069 Civakan asks Gunamalai whether that harsh word is arrow or nectar to him.
teaches: The hero knows his verdict both won him Gunamalai and earned him a rival's vow against him, so his teasing question names the double fruit of one judgement.

note: In Kural 1316 the woman turns the man's 'I thought of you' into proof that he had forgotten her; in 1070 Gunamalai turns his praise of a powder into proof that he forgot her and keeps another in his heart (மறந்தீர், மனத்துள் உறைகின்றாள்).
teaches: The couplet's sulking logic, that any word of the lover proves his neglect, becomes in the epic a weapon aimed at a named rival's beauty, so feigned jealousy is how the epic's wife claims the hero among his many loves.

gains.a: the epic verse gains a recognised move of the ஊடல் convention that shows its accusation is play, not real suspicion
gains.b: the couplet gains a rival woman and a remembered contest as the occasion of the twisted word, which it leaves abstract

note: Kural 1109 names sulking, making up and union as love's rewards; verses 1071, 1072 and 1074 enact the three in order, sulk, appeasement at her feet, embrace.
teaches: The epic plays out the couplet's triad in full and then cuts it off with the king's runners, so love's three rewards are set as the calm the hero's karma-laden story breaks.

gains.a: the three verses gain a frame that makes them one completed movement rather than a string of descriptions
gains.b: the couplet gains a narrative cost: its rewards are shown as fragile, interrupted by a power outside the lovers

note: The patikam (14) tells how Civakan overcame the victorious elephant that frightened Gunamalai; in 1076 that same elephant, ashamed, refuses its food.
teaches: The victory the patikam lists as a rescue becomes, through the beast's shame and the mahout's report, the usurper's pretext for seizing the hero, so a deed of protection ripens into danger.

note: Kural 567 says harsh words and punishment past all bounds file down a king's conquering strength; in 1079 the king, raging over a sulking elephant, orders the hero seized and his strength rooted out.
teaches: The epic shows where such excess comes from: a usurper's envy of a subject's fame finds a trivial cause, and the order that follows is the first stroke of the file that will bring his own fall.

gains.a: the king's order gains a rule by which the reader can judge it as the self-wearing excess of a bad ruler, not just anger
gains.b: the couplet gains a source for excessive punishment in wounded pride, and a story in which the file's work can be traced

note: In the Silappathikaram the Pandya, inquiring into nothing, orders the guards to kill the thief and bring the anklet (கொன்றச் சிலம்பு கொணர்க); in 1080 the angry king's men run to kill and bring Civakan's life (கொன்றுயிர் கொணர) on a mahout's word.
teaches: The same unexamined order to kill and bring yields Kovalan's death and the bent sceptre in one epic but only a binding in the other, because Civakan chooses submission and a god he once helped intervenes; the Cintamani turns the scene of ripened evil into one where restraint and past kindness turn it aside.

note: Kural 895 says those who draw a mighty king's anger will survive nowhere; Kantukkatan reasons that to contend with the king is the work of the doomed (விளிகுற்றார்) and sends his son bound.
teaches: The merchant applies the couplet's prudence to a king who is a usurper and his son's true father's killer, showing that the rule of not provoking the strong counsels submission even to injustice, a cost the couplet does not weigh.

gains.a: Kantukkatan's choice gains the weight of received wisdom, so it reads as prudence rather than cowardice
gains.b: the couplet gains a case in which obeying it means yielding to an unjust king, which tests its scope

note: In 393 the teacher asks as his fee that Civakan bear no anger against the usurper for a year, and he agrees; in 1090, recalling his teacher's word, he lets his arms be bound with his anger quenched.
teaches: The vow made in private as a teacher's fee is what actually disarms the hero before the king's men, so the plot's turn depends on a kept promise rather than on the parents' prudence or the hero's weakness.

note: In 1092 the king's men bind Civakan's shoulders with their belts (கச்சின் வீக்கலின்); the patikam (16) tells how the god removed the flower-belt (பூங் கச்சு) that bound his shoulders.
teaches: The belt that binds the hero here is the very thing the patikam has the grateful god remove, so the eclipse simile's promise of a passing darkness is already answered at the epic's opening.

note: In 1090 Sunandai and her husband call going under the king's protection the right course; in 1093 she falls into a sea of unending grief as he is led away bound.
teaches: The foster mother who counselled submission as virtue cannot bear its result, so the chapter sets the household's prudent counsel against its cost to the one who gave it.

note: The Kural likens death to sleep and birth to waking; Civakan uses the waking from heavy sleep for the soul's appearing in the states of birth, adds release as a third motion, and draws from it a refusal to grieve at his own arrest.
teaches: The Kural's calm figure of sleep and waking only describes the cycle, while the Cintamani makes it an argument for conduct, so understanding birth as waking becomes the ground for refusing grief, and the cycle gains an exit the couplet never names.

gains.a: the hero's consolation is seen to rest on a figure the ethical tradition already held, which makes his calm learned rather than merely brave
gains.b: the couplet's image is shown as the first step of a larger scheme in which knowing the cycle aims at leaving it

note: Both measure a small but fatal thing as a split sesame seed: the Kural an inner enmity that holds ruin, Civakan the least attachment, which he calls a fault.
teaches: The sesame measure moves from a king's household enemy to the attachment inside the self, so the danger the Kural locates in a court the Jain hero locates in the heart that clings.

gains.a: Civakan's rule is given a familiar measure of how little it takes to ruin, transferred from politics to the soul
gains.b: the couplet's warning that a tiny hidden thing contains ruin is extended to attachment, a second enemy within

note: Saccandan, before his death, tells Vijayai that dying and being born come from one's deeds and that grief comes from want of understanding; his son, now seized by the same usurper, tells the women of his house that one who knows births and release will not grieve.
teaches: Father and son meet the usurper's violence with the same doctrinal consolation to the women who love them, but the father dies after speaking it and the son walks on alive, so the teaching recurs as the epic's own answer to tyranny rather than one man's farewell.

note: The city women see Civakan's arrest as the fruit of deeds; the dog beaten at the festival was said to have fallen into the net of strong karma, and Civakan freed it with the five mantras.
teaches: The same karmic explanation covers the beaten dog and the bound hero, but the story has already shown Civakan's own good deed to that dog, so the crowd's 'fruit of deeds' is about to ripen as the god's rescue of him.

note: The Kural says the weak who harm the strong beckon Death with their hand; the city women say the king who seizes Civakan has clapped his hands at Death and will perish with his line.
teaches: The women apply the couplet against the one who holds power, so the 'weak' party is the reigning king and the 'strong' is the bound merchant's son, which makes strength a matter of worth rather than of office.

gains.a: the women's curse is seen to rest on a received rule about provoking the stronger, not on mere anger
gains.b: the couplet is shown to be usable against a king, with the strong one being the person he has in chains

note: The Kural says the many lack because few do penance; the city women say they lose Civakan because they did no penance.
teaches: The couplet's account of why most people lack is turned into a mourner's self-blame, so lack of penance explains not poverty but the loss of a beloved, and the women accuse themselves while blaming the king and the father in the same verse.

gains.a: the lament's first cry is seen to rest on the ethical rule that what one keeps is earned by austerity
gains.b: the couplet's severe claim is shown working as consolation and self-reproach in grief, a use its general form does not show

note: Saccandan, ringed in his palace, was a roaring lion hemmed in at a cave mouth and died fighting; his son, seized by the same usurper, goes as a lion bound with a spider's thread.
teaches: The lion image marks the difference between father and son: the father was caught by force and fought to death, the son could break his bond at will and keeps it, so the son survives the trap the father did not.

note: The patikam tells that the god Civakan once helped untied the flower-cord with which soldiers had bound his arms.
teaches: The bond that holds the lion here is as weak as a spider's thread and is in fact loosed by a god, so the image of 1116 is fulfilled literally: it is never the king's force that holds him.

note: Civakan let himself be bound because his parents asked it and told him his manhood would not be lessened; here he goes bound like a lion held by a spider's thread.
teaches: The thread that binds the lion is the parents' word of 1091, so the spider's thread is the image of consent, and the arrest becomes a test of filial obedience rather than of strength.

note: The Kural tells those who serve hot-tempered kings to be like those warming at a fire, neither too far nor too near; Kantukkatan judges the king's anger a fire that burns all who come near and sends gold to quench it.
teaches: The Kural's fire teaches distance, while the merchant adds a remedy, gold poured like rain, so the pair shows a courtier's caution and a merchant's purchase as two answers to the same burning king.

gains.a: Kantukkatan's payment is seen as a known prudence toward royal anger, not mere fear
gains.b: the couplet's image is shown to allow a means of putting the fire out, which its advice of keeping distance leaves aside

note: Kantukkatan reasoned that opposing a king is the work of the doomed and that sending his son bound would cool the king's anger; now he adds twelve crores of gold to quench it.
teaches: The father's policy of submission is completed by payment, so between these two verses his defiant words to the crowd (1114-1115) stand as consolation only, and his actual answer to the king is obedience bought with gold.

note: The sage foretold that when the graceless king seized Civakan to kill him a yaksha would carry him off; in 1158 a god lifts Civakan and rises away in the storm while the city mourns.
teaches: The rescue the friends are plotting by fire and disguise was already promised to the parents, so the plan of the companions is made needless by a fate a Jain ascetic had foreseen.

note: In 388 the merchant takes up the infant 'as the great ascetic had foretold' (அருந்தவன் முந்து கூற); here, years later, the father tells what that foretelling was.
teaches: The foundling's adoption, told earlier as a bare fulfilment, turns out to rest on a promise given to a mother in despair, and the same prophecy also held the hero's capture and rescue.

note: In 325 the merchant leaves his own dead son at the burning ground and goes off with the royal child; 1124 recalls that Sunandai had borne many children who died before the ascetic came.
teaches: The exchange at the burning ground was the last of a run of dead births, so the merchant's taking of the child answers a grief long prepared for, not a chance find.

note: Padumukan guesses that only Civakan's parents could have bound him; the spy reports that the father embraced him by a stratagem and the weeping mother bound his arms.
teaches: The friend's reasoning from the hero's invincibility is confirmed by the report, so the one force the story allows to bind Civakan is filial obedience, not the usurper's army.

note: In 1116 Civakan is led off bound like a lion caught in a spider's thread; the spy's report explains the thread: his parents' embrace and tears.
teaches: The spider's thread of 1116 is glossed by the scene of 1138: a weak bond holds the lion because he will not break his parents' hold, and he feels the shame of it toward his friends.

note: Kattiyangaran swears to write 'thief' on Civakan's chest; in 1165 he praises Civakan as without equal in grace, strength, learning and generosity and rewards the man who claims to have killed him.
teaches: The usurper's own praise in 1165 shows that his charge of theft was never a judgment, so the bent sceptre here is a king punishing a man he knows to be the best of his subjects.

note: Kural 550 likens a king's putting killers to death to weeding a crop; here the king sentences the youth who stopped the royal elephant from killing a girl.
teaches: The couplet's justice assumes that the king punishes the killer; the epic shows a king whose own beast is the killer punishing the rescuer, so the weeding image fails when the king himself decides what the weed is.

gains.a: a rule by which Kantukkatan's question 'if this is a fault, what is virtue?' becomes a charge of inverted justice
gains.b: a case in which the one who owns the deadly force is the judge, which the couplet's farming image cannot address

note: Kural 269 says that those who attain the power of austerity can even leap past death; here the ascetic's words, remembered, keep the stricken merchant alive.
teaches: The Kural places the power of tapas in the ascetic's own victory over death, while the epic shows it working on householders, through a foretelling whose remembered word revives a father who stood as if dead.

gains.a: a name for the force that holds up the merchant: the power of penance, here exercised through speech
gains.b: a story in which that power reaches beyond the ascetic to the lay people who fed him

note: In Kural 1164 the woman parted from her lover says there is a sea of love but no safe raft to cross it; here Gunamalai, parted from Civakan and near death, crosses the sea of grief on the raft of the ascetic's words.
teaches: The Kural's parted woman has no raft because no one sends word; the epic gives its parted woman a raft from outside love altogether, an ascetic's prophecy, so the same plight is solved by religious authority rather than by the lover.

gains.a: the convention behind its image: the sea and raft are the parted woman's set terms, and Gunamalai's grief is cast as a lover's
gains.b: a case where the raft the couplet denies is supplied, and by whom, which shows what the woman of the couplet lacks

note: The patikam tells that a god came down the sky's path like lightning from a cloud and carried the strong one away from the king's prison; here Sudanjanan feels the omen, learns the danger and descends in storm.
teaches: The patikam's single line is filled out with the god's heaven, his omen and his far-seeing knowledge, so the rescue is shown as the answer of a bond, not a stroke of luck.

note: In 947 Civakan gives the dying dog the five padas and it leaves its body; here the dog, now a god among goddesses, comes down to save the one who gave it the mantra.
teaches: Read together, the two scenes make the mantra given out of pity into the cause of the hero's deliverance, the Jain epic's way of showing a good deed returning within the same story.
audit_text_issue: 1156 does not name the god or the dog; sense uncertain | 1156 மயிலனார்க்குப் படி வைத்து is doubtful.

note: Kural 107 says people remember through seven births the friendship of those who wiped away their sorrow; Civakan, facing death, counts on the friend whose death-sorrow he eased in another body.
teaches: The epic makes the couplet's seven births literal: a dog that became a god still keeps the debt, and the debtor runs to the man who wiped his tears.

gains.a: a moral frame that makes Civakan's appeal to the god a claim of gratitude rather than a call on magic
gains.b: a case where the remembered friendship crosses an actual rebirth from beast to god, which the couplet only asserts as a span of time

audit_text_issue: 1154 does not name the dog; relies on 943-948

note: Kural 903 says stooping before one's wife brings a man shame among the good; Gandharvadattai, able to free Civakan, holds back because being saved by his wife would shame his strength and learning.
teaches: The couplet's shame is a man's fear of his wife's power, but here the wife herself fears it on his behalf and keeps her power idle, so the rule's cost falls on the woman who could act.

gains.a: a source in Tamil ethics for the code that stops her hand
gains.b: a scene showing the rule enforced from the woman's side, at the price of leaving the husband in danger

note: Kural 967 holds it better to be called ruined than to live following those who scorn one; Civakan says he does not want to live if he is set free by his wife's spells.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's preference for ruin over dishonour onto rescue by a wife, so honour can refuse even a loving help, and the story then lets a male friend's help pass as honourable.

gains.a: a name, maanam, for the choice Civakan makes in chains
gains.b: an instance where the dishonourable life is not servitude to enemies but survival by a woman's power, which shows how gendered the couplet's honour could be made

note: Kural 327 forbids taking another's life even to save one's own; Madanan's men, fearing the king, kill a stranger and pass him off as Civakan to save themselves.
teaches: The story shows the exact deed the couplet forbids and shows its source in the tyrant's terror, so the rule against killing is seen giving way first where the sceptre is bent.

gains.a: the Kural's measure for judging an act the narration only reports
gains.b: a case of the forbidden trade of life for life driven by fear of a king, which ties the chapter on not killing to the chapter on oppressive rule

note: The storm the god raises in 1157 to hide the rescue is the rain, darkness and wind Madanan cites in 1164 as the reason he had Civakan cut down.
teaches: The one storm serves two ends: it hides the god's rescue and gives the killers the alibi that lets the usurper believe his rival dead.

note: Buddhisenan's plan in 1140 is to burn the city and free Civakan by force; Civakan here sets both that and his wife's magic aside and waits on his friend.
teaches: The prisoner overrules all the rescues offered him, so his deliverance comes only from the bond he made himself, which is the episode's point about merit.

note: The hero calls his release ஊழ்வினை; five verses later the god who freed him explains that Civakan once eased his suffering as a dog and gave him his body.
teaches: Read together, the 'former deed' the hero blames is no hidden deed of a past birth but his own recent kindness to a dying dog returning to him, so the epic's karma is visible to the reader while the hero speaks of it as unknown.
audit_text_issue: 1172 sense flagged uncertain | 1172 line 1 பிணிக்குலத்து for the race of dogs is unusual.

note: In 943 Civakan promised the dying dog a god's body shining like the sun's disc if it thought on the mantra; in 1172 the god, now in that body, says the man gave it to him.
teaches: The promise made through a mantra is remembered by the one who received it as a personal gift of the man, so the epic lets doctrine (the mantra's power) and gratitude (the debt to the giver) both stand as the cause of the rescue.

note: Kural 379 asks why those who take good fortune as good should grieve when it turns; Civakan, freed after imprisonment, neither grieves nor rejoices and ascribes both to former deeds.
teaches: The epic answers the couplet's question with a stricter ideal: not only bearing ill as one bears good, but declining joy at good fortune too, since rescue is as much karma's working as captivity.

gains.a: the hero's indifference gets a recognised ethical frame, the Kural's reasoning that what fate gives cannot be graded into welcome and unwelcome
gains.b: the couplet's rhetorical question gets a test case in which the good turn comes through another's hand, a god's, and is still referred to one's own deeds

note: Purananuru 192 says good and ill do not come from others, and the speakers neither rejoice that life is sweet nor curse it as bitter; Civakan is freed by a god yet calls the freeing his own former deed and feels neither joy nor grief.
teaches: The pair shows the Sangam sage's 'not from others' being kept even when the rescue plainly does come from another: the epic folds the rescuer into the hero's own deed, the dog he once helped.

gains.a: the hero's two-line equanimity is set against a fuller statement of the same stance, with its image of life carried like a raft by the river
gains.b: the poem's abstract claim gets a narrative in which an outside helper exists and the claim must explain him, which it does by tracing the help back to the self

note: The Caranas at Aranapatham wash away their own karma (தம்வினை கழுவுகின்றார்) by renouncing rule; Tirumanthiram 2422 says the soul is cleaned of its dirt as cloth by a washer, and everything that comes to it is the bond of grace.
teaches: Both use the image of washing a stain from the self, but in the Jain epic the ascetic is the washer and the dirt is his karma, while in Tirumular the washer is grace and even the soul's bonds are its soap; the shared image exposes the rival accounts of who does the cleansing.

gains.a: the Cintamani's brief phrase about karma-washing is shown to carry a doctrine of self-effort that a Saiva reader would contest
gains.b: Tirumular's claim that all is grace's bond is sharpened against a named alternative, ascetics who clean themselves without a god

audit_text_issue: 2422 flagged uncertain, மோசு obscure | tirumanthiram:2422 மோசு is obscure; the verse is marked uncertain.

note: Kural 918 says the embrace of deceiving women is an அணங்கு to those without discerning sense; in 1183 the god warns of ghoul-women who come as pining lovers and, embracing, wring out a man's life.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's metaphor into a literal creature of its geography: the deceiving lover really is a life-drinking demon, and what saves the hero is the god's forewarning, standing in for the 'discerning sense' the couplet demands.

gains.a: the ghoul episode is seen to carry the Kural's ethics of the courtesan rather than being a mere marvel of the road
gains.b: the couplet's அணங்கு, which might be read as hyperbole, gets a narrative that spells out what the word threatens: the embrace that kills

note: Kalittokai 11 gives the three tender creatures of the burning waste: the tusker who lets his mate drink first, the dove that fans its mate with its wings, the stag that gives its shadow to the shadeless doe; 1187-1188 give the elephant shielding its calf, the cock bird sheltering the hen with its wings, and the stag shading the doe with its body.
teaches: The Cintamani keeps the palai triad but changes its use: in the Kalittokai the creatures' care is the heroine's ground for hoping the man will return, while here it only measures the heat for a lone traveller with no beloved at home, so the akam sign of love becomes a road-guide's warning.

gains.a: the god's description is shown to be a set piece of Tamil palai convention, which explains why these three animals and no others appear
gains.b: the Kalittokai's images are seen to outlive their love setting, showing that the triad had become a stock mark of the desert itself

audit_text_issue: Only 1188 is printed; the elephant and bird of 1187 are taken on trust.

note: Konganar's Vaalaik Kummi counts going to foreign lands (தேசாந்திரங்களும் செல்லாதே) among things to avoid, with facing a tiger in the forest and courtesans' ways; Civakan calls those who never leave home fish in a well and sets out, and the god's road then holds elephant forests and ghoul-women.
teaches: On the same question, whether to go to other lands, the Siddhar's caution and the hero's resolve give opposite advice, and the epic's road is made of exactly the dangers the Siddhar lists, so the epic treats them as the hero's schooling rather than a reason to stay; the conflict holds only if the kummi's line is read as general advice and not as a rule for the adept alone.

gains.a: the hero's departure is seen as a choice against a known prudential rule, not a mere plot device
gains.b: the kummi's terse prohibition gets its strongest counter-case, a traveller whom the dangers it names do not ruin

audit_text_issue: Lines 1-3 of 1176 are obscure (விடுத்தன் மேயினார்; கூற்று/காற்றின); the fish-in-a-well reading is the marker's.

note: The patikam tells how the king of the middle country (மத்திம தேய மன்னன்) came out to receive Civakan on seeing his bow; in 1214 the god foretells that meeting (மத்திம தேயம் ஆளும் ... கண்ணுறு குணம்) before the journey begins.
teaches: The meeting the summary reports as the king's response to the hero's bow is, in the god's speech, a fortune already laid out on the road, so the poem frames a political welcome as the fruit of a divine guide's foreknowledge.

note: The patikam compares Civakan's younger brother, desolate, to a star that has lost the moon (மதியம் கெடுத்த வய மீன்); 1215 gives the same image (வெண்மதி யிழந்த மீன்போல்) to all his friends.
teaches: The stars-without-the-moon figure belongs to the hero's whole circle rather than to one kinsman, so Civakan is the moon to every follower and his absence dims them all alike, brother and friends.

note: The patikam says the lion-like royals of the middle country kept Civakan and gave him a girl in marriage; 1215 has the god foretell that the king will give him his daughter while he stays there.
teaches: Read with the patikam, the marriage that looks like the royals' choice to bind a strong stranger was promised in advance by the god, so the hero's marriages come to him as foretold gifts rather than conquests.

note: Kural 916 scorns women who spread a base goodness (புன்னலம் பாரிப்பார்) to all; in 1200 the river, sharing its own goodness to feed the world (தன்னுடைய நலம் பகிர்ந்து உலகம் ஊட்டலின்), is called a courtesan with approval.
teaches: The same act, a நலம் given to everyone, is a mark of baseness in the Kural and of bounty in the epic's simile, which shows that the Kural's contempt lies in the sale of a person and not in the sharing itself.

gains.a: a reminder that the courtesan figure carried moral weight, so the epic's praise of the river is a deliberate reversal and not a neutral image
gains.b: a case where the courtesan's openness is turned to praise once nothing personal is sold, sharpening what exactly the couplet condemns

note: Kural 974 says greatness exists only for one who holds himself as single-minded women (ஒருமை மகளிர்) do; 1208 likens a straight unforking road to the minds of chaste women (கற்புடை மாதரார் மனம்).
teaches: Both texts use the chaste woman's mind as the model of an undivided line, for a man's greatness in one and for a road in the other, showing that karpu was read as singleness of direction rather than as purity alone.

gains.a: a precedent that the chaste mind is a figure of oneness, which explains why the epic chooses it for a road without forks
gains.b: a concrete picture, a straight road strewn with flowers, of what the couplet's single-mindedness looks like in space

note: Kural 329 says those whose work is killing are base in the eyes of the discerning; 1205 calls the forest bowmen who kill travellers embodiments of sin (பாவ மூர்த்தியர்).
teaches: The couplet judges a deed, killing, while the epic fixes the same judgment on a forest people as a class, so the pair shows how the ethics of not-killing could harden into a picture of hunters as sin incarnate.

gains.a: the couplet's ground for the label: the hunters are condemned for the work of killing, not for being foresters
gains.b: evidence of how the principle was applied to whole groups living by the bow, which the couplet's general wording does not show

audit_text_issue: flag: line 1 possible lost vowel sign

note: 1208 likens the straight red road to the minds of chaste women; 1212 likens a road splitting into many forks to the hearts of women on the path of marriage.
teaches: If மணநெறி மகளிர் are married women, the same speech makes women's minds the figure of both the one straight road and the forking one, showing the simile serves the road and carries no settled view of women.

note: The god gives Civakan three mantras because Civakan once whispered the five padas into the dying dog's ear (செல்கதி மந்திரம் செவியிற் செப்பிய).
teaches: The mantra that carried a dying dog to a god's birth comes back to the hero as mantras of power for his road, so the epic lets an act of compassion bear its fruit in this same life through the very being it saved.
audit_text_issue: 945 line 4 குதற்செய்கை unclear | 945 line 4 குதற்செய்கை is unclear

note: A hill chief tells a visitor he cannot keep his body alive without liquor and meat; in the Manimekalai Saathuvan concedes and gives the Naga chief a reduced dharma, while Civakan presses on and wins full renunciation.
teaches: Faced with the same objection from a forest people, the Buddhist epic tailors a lesser rule to what the hearer can bear while the Jain epic refuses any compromise and makes the hunter choose heaven over his body, which shows how differently the two works weigh abstention against a hearer's livelihood.
audit_text_issue: 1234 flagged; compromise side rests on 1235 not in packet

note: The Kural asks how one who eats another's flesh to swell his own can have grace; the hunter says he needs meat merely to keep his body alive.
teaches: The couplet's eater fattens himself by choice, while the hunter claims he must eat flesh to survive at all; the epic thus raises the case the couplet passes over and answers it not with grace but with the threat of hell and the promise of heaven.

gains.a: Civakan's demand gains a measure from the classic statement that flesh-eating swells one's own flesh at another's cost, which is what 1235 line 1 restates
gains.b: the couplet gains a hearer who objects from need, not appetite, which tests whether its rule holds for people who live by hunting

note: The Kural says that if one eats flesh hell does not open its mouth; Civakan sets hell for the meat-eater against a god's birth for one who abstains and makes the hunter choose.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's one-sided warning into a two-way choice with a reward on the other side and has the eater himself pronounce the verdict, so the Kural's rule becomes a conversion by question and answer.

gains.a: the epic's hell gains the couplet's sharper image of a mouth that will not reopen, which makes the threat permanent
gains.b: the couplet gains a positive alternative it does not state, a god's birth bought by the wasting of the body, and a listener who accepts it

note: Tirumular calls flesh-eaters புலையர and sends them to hell; Civakan says the hunters were born low because of former killing and eating.
teaches: Tirumular makes baseness a name earned by what one eats now, whatever one's birth, while the epic makes the low birth itself the fruit of past eating, so the two texts tie the same stigma to flesh-eating from opposite ends of the karmic chain.

gains.a: Civakan's account of low birth is shown to keep birth-rank as real and deserved, which the comparison with Tirumular's moral use of புலையர் exposes
gains.b: Tirumular's after-death punishment gains an earlier stage in the chain, a birth already lowered by flesh-eating, which his verse does not consider

note: The Cintamani's god is worshipped as the one who cut away his own ghati karmas; Tirumular's grace-power comes as guru and removes the soul's bonds.
teaches: On the reading that the Jina is honoured for destroying his own karmas, the two texts disagree about what a god does with karma: the Jain god is the one who freed himself and is a model to circle, whereas Tirumular's Lord is the agent who frees the bound soul, so the worshipper's release comes from his own effort in one and from descending grace in the other.

gains.a: the epic's brief epithet காதி கண் அரிந்த is shown to carry a whole doctrine of self-won release that it states without argument
gains.b: Tirumular's grace gains a rival account in which no god acts on the soul, which sharpens why his verse insists that one's own agency must end

note: The Kural says those who reach the Lord's feet swim the sea of births; Civakan's hymn worships the Jina's lotus feet from within that sea and asks that attachment's bonds be untied.
teaches: Set beside the couplet, the hymn names what reaching the feet is supposed to do in a Jain frame: not a crossing given from outside but the loosening of attachment (பசை), so the same image of feet and sea carries a doctrine of release by unbinding.

gains.a: the hymn's sea and feet are placed in the oldest Tamil statement of the image, which shows that the Jain poet is answering a known formula
gains.b: the couplet's unnamed Lord and unexplained swimming gain one school's account of both: the Lord is the Jina and the swimming is the ending of attachment

note: Tirumular says the three cities Siva destroyed are the work of the three malas; the Jain hymn gives the destroyer of three guarded forts to the Jina, who rose to the world's summit.
teaches: Both a Saiva and a Jain poet read the three-city myth as the destruction of inner bonds, but they give it to different destroyers, so the pair shows the myth as ground the schools contested and allegorised in rival directions.

gains.a: the hymn's bare epithet gains its source: it is Siva's deed, taken over for the Jina, and the allegorical reading of it was already current
gains.b: Tirumular's correction of 'fools' gains a rival who also refuses the literal myth yet keeps no Siva in it, a sharper opponent than literalism

note: Tirumular has grace-power come as guru and end the malas when one's own agency ceases; the Jain hymn praises the Jina who ended karma that cannot be ended and taught the path of no return.
teaches: On the reading that the Jina ended his own karma and teaches others to end theirs, the two verses give opposite answers to who removes karma: in the Saiva verse one's own doing must stop and grace acts, in the Jain verse the liberated one is the one whose own effort ended it.

gains.a: the hymn's 'karma that cannot be ended' gains its contrast: the Saiva text agrees it cannot be ended by the soul alone but supplies a divine agent the Jain hymn does without
gains.b: Tirumular's demand that one's own agency end gains a named rival doctrine in which the agent of release is a man who acted, which shows what the demand is arguing against

note: The Naladiyar says a harlot's love ends when the hand is empty, like a lamp without oil; the Cintamani's dancer calls the saying that chastity breaks for gold a lie and vows herself to one man.
teaches: The dancer answers the very proverb the Naladiyar states, in her own voice, so the pair shows the epic giving the woman of the stage a reply that the didactic tradition never lets her make.

gains.a: the dancer's 'those who said it lied' gains a named target: a saying of this kind stood in the ethical books
gains.b: the quatrain's general rule gains a counter-claim from inside the class it judges, which tests whether the rule is observation or stereotype

note: In Rajamapuram the king saw that the dancer's longing had gone to Civakan and went in with resentment; in Chandirapam the prince follows the dancer's gaze to Civakan and is glad.
teaches: The poem stages the same scene twice, a ruler reading a dancer's eyes fixed on Civakan, and makes the ruler's response the measure of him: jealous enmity in the usurper's city, affection and alliance in the Pallava court.

note: The patikam told in one line that a snake took the king's daughter's face for the moon and bit her; verse 1271 tells the bite in scene.
teaches: The patikam's line already made the bite a praise of her face; the full scene keeps that conceit but sets it at the instant she reaches for a flower she raised, so the compliment and the danger arrive in the same gesture.

note: In the patikam Civakan cures her by saying only 'let not your heart melt'; here he tells the household that she will not die and they must not weep.
teaches: The patikam's bare word of comfort turns out to be the promise of a man who, unlike every healer before him, first diagnoses and then cures, so the comfort is earned by the lore of the next three verses rather than given as a hero's charm.

note: The god freed Civakan and taught him spells, asking to be remembered; Civakan now heals the snakebite by reciting a spell.
teaches: The spells given in return for the nectar Civakan once gave a dying dog become the means that win him a princess, so the chain of gratitude the patikam began pays out as a cure, here reached through the mantra and not through any call on the god himself.

note: The astrologer says the bite, given the hour, is hard to cure even for the Lord; within ten verses the venom leaves her at Civakan's gaze.
teaches: The epic sets a reading of the stars that declares death against a cure that follows at once, so the hour the astrologer trusted is shown not to bind, and the outcome turns on the healer's learning rather than on the time of the bite.

note: The king had proclaimed by drum that whoever cures the girl will have land, wealth and the bride; now Civakan is told to sow fame and reap kinship in this land.
teaches: The public offer of a prize is restated to one man as a bond of kinship, so the marriage that the drum put up for any healer becomes, before the cure, a relationship offered to Civakan in particular.
audit_text_issue: Speaker/addressee ambiguous (நம்பி and கொற்ற வேந்தன் both named).

note: The Kural orders the healer to find the disease, its cause and the means that subdue it, then act; Civakan names the causes and kinds of bite and the snake's type before he recites the cure.
teaches: The epic stages the couplet's order as a contest: a crowd of healers who act first and diagnose in contradiction all fail, and the one who examines cause and kind before acting succeeds, so the rule is shown by the cost of breaking it.

gains.a: Civakan's string of classifications gains a reason for being in the story: it is the diagnostic step the ethics book requires and the rival healers skipped
gains.b: the couplet's three steps gain a scene of failure beside success, which shows what is lost when treatment comes before finding the cause

note: The Kural says the three humours counted by the learned, beginning with wind, cause disease when they exceed or fall short; one healer blames out-of-balance wind, bile and phlegm for the girl's state.
teaches: The humoral theory the Kural states as the general cause of disease is here invoked for a snakebite and fails, so the epic marks a limit the couplet does not: a correct doctrine of illness misleads when the cause is a poison from outside.

gains.a: the healer's line is identified as learned medicine, so his failure is the failure of sound theory misapplied, not of quackery
gains.b: the couplet's account of disease gains a case outside its reach, a harm that does not arise from the body's own balance

note: The Kural says birth is alike for all living beings and distinction comes from the work they do; Civakan's lore sorts even snakes into four varnas known by the smell of their bite.
teaches: Read with பிறப்பொக்கும் as denying rank by birth, the couplet stands against a lore that fixes varna in nature down to snakes; the pairing shows that the Cintamani's hero carries birth-rank as plain knowledge even where the Kural, speaking of all living beings, had set it aside.

gains.a: the snake lore gains its weight as a claim about birth, which in the story passes as neutral technique
gains.b: the couplet's 'all living beings' gains a test case among animals, where the opposing view assigns rank by birth alone

note: The Naladiyar calls those who prattle of astrology the greatest fools; in the epic the astrologer's verdict of death fails while a bird omen of rescue comes true.
teaches: The Jain epic does not dismiss divination wholesale as the quatrain does: it splits it, letting the star-reader's verdict be overturned while an omen pointing to a rescuer is fulfilled, so the scorn of the quatrain falls on fatalistic forecasting rather than on every sign.

gains.a: the omen and the astrologer gain a measure: the epic's tradition holds such readings in suspicion, which makes the success of the one and the failure of the other a pointed choice
gains.b: the quatrain's blanket scorn gains a narrative in which signs are tested against outcome, showing which kind of foretelling the scorn fits
