note: Tirumular lists removing poison among the powers that yoga brings; Civakan removes the venom by a spell he learned, after seven thousand Brahmins with mantras have failed.
teaches: Where the Tirumanthiram makes curing poison a sign of the yogi's attainment, the Cintamani gives it to a young layman as a learned art and lets the ritual mantra-masters fail, so the same power is moved from spiritual rank to skill and from priest to hero.

gains.a: Civakan's cure gains its weight as a power the Saiva tradition reserves for adepts, which makes its ease in a householder's hands notable
gains.b: the siddhi list gains a contrasting account in which poison-cure needs no yoga, only taught knowledge, which sharpens what Tirumular claims for his discipline

note: In 1290 the poison leaves Padumai's body as darkness breaks before the sun; two verses later she is bitten again by the snake of desire.
teaches: The poet makes the cure the cause of a new sickness: the instant the real venom is drawn out, the girl's first look at her healer lets in a second venom, so the rescue and the love are one event told twice.

note: The god foretold that the king who guards the earth would give Civakan his flawless daughter; the onlookers now say the king will give him the maiden today.
teaches: The prophecy reaches the crowd as gossip: what the god told Civakan privately is now guessed aloud by strangers who do not even know who he is, so the story's foreknowledge passes from the divine to the public before the king has spoken.

note: The onlookers guess whether he is a Vidyadhara hero or a prince of the gods; Padumai asks her maidens whether he is Kama or a young god, and says she does not know.
teaches: The question of the stranger's identity, a public puzzle in 1296, becomes in the girl's mouth a symptom of love: her not knowing who he is is now part of her sickness, since she cannot even name the thief.

note: Civakan says desire churns him (கடைகின்றது காமமே); Padumai says her heart is the ocean churned for nectar.
teaches: The poet gives the two lovers, lying apart on the same night, one verb: he says it plainly of himself, and she expands it into the whole churning of the ocean, so the image binds their separate laments into a matched pair.

note: Tirumular's single five-hooded serpent lives in the anthill of enjoyment and, its hoods drawn into one, makes the body its fit home; the epic's snake of desire lives in the anthill of the body ruled by the five senses and bites again.
teaches: Both poets house a serpent of the five senses in the body's anthill, but Tirumular's can be stilled by discipline into one hood while the epic's strikes the moment a spell has cured the real snake, showing that a remedy for poison is no remedy for the senses.

gains.a: a yogic reading of its anthill and five senses, which makes the love-bite a statement about the body and not only an ornament
gains.b: a narrative case where the serpent of the senses is shown striking in a living person, against which its taming is measured

note: The Kural's man says she will not look at him directly but smiles as if narrowing one eye; the epic says Padumai bound Civakan with a look that looked as if it did not look.
teaches: The averted look that the Kural treats as a sign the man must decode becomes in the epic an act with an effect: the same not-quite-glance does not hint at love, it ties the hero fast, so the convention moves from evidence to force.

gains.a: the convention behind its paradoxical look, which shows the line is a known sign and not a fresh conceit
gains.b: a scene in which the half-look is followed by its consequence, the man bound, which the couplet leaves unstated

note: The Kural says penance is striven for here because what is desired is obtained as desired; the onlookers say only women who did rare penance before could be born to sleep on Civakan's chest.
teaches: The onlookers take the couplet's promise at its word and fill 'whatever is desired' with a husband's embrace, showing how the motive the Kural offers for penance could be heard as making penance the price of pleasure in the next birth.

gains.a: a doctrinal rule behind its onlookers' wonder, that what is gained now is the fruit of penance done before
gains.b: a concrete example of what ordinary people wanted penance to bring, which tests how wide the couplet's 'whatever is desired' is meant to be

note: The Acharakkovai sets out the mouth-rinsing the great have seen as the way: three sips, wiping, and touching the face's parts with the fingers; Civakan sips three times, wipes three times and touches his face with his fingers.
teaches: The rule book's after-meal rinse appears in the epic, step for step, as a mark of the hero's breeding, performed under the eyes of a king who will next examine him, so the code of conduct works in the story as a credential.

gains.a: the source of its unusually exact sequence, which shows the poet is narrating a known rite and not inventing detail
gains.b: a scene showing the rite performed by a prince as a sign of refinement, beyond the bare prescription

note: The Acharakkovai lists what one does not do in a great man's house: spit, climb a high seat, chew areca, speak out of turn, lie down; in the king's house Civakan sits on a high flower seat, chews areca and lies on a couch.
teaches: Civakan does three of the five things forbidden in a great man's house, and does them at the king's command, so the pair shows that the rule binds the dependent and the visitor and is suspended for an honoured guest whom the host himself seats, serves and beds.

gains.a: the rule against which its hospitality reads as a deliberate honour and not a mere list of comforts
gains.b: a limit to the rule: the prohibitions assume a lower visitor, and the host's own gift lifts them

note: The Kural's man asks whether her look is Death, an eye or a doe and answers that it has all three; Civakan asks whether it is her bow, her eyes, her speech or her look and says he cannot tell.
teaches: Both men ask the same 'is it this or that' of a woman who wounds them, but the Kural settles the question in her look, while Civakan gives it up and lays the cause on his own desire, so the epic turns the couplet's question about her into an admission about himself.

gains.a: the convention of the bewildered list of alternatives, which shows the force of its refusal to answer
gains.b: an alternative ending to the convention, in which the cause moves from the woman's look to the man's longing

note: The Kural's woman says the herdsman's flute is the burning evening's messenger and a killing weapon; Padumai finds the bull's bell, the moon, the anril and the evening burning like smokeless fire.
teaches: The evening's pastoral sounds that burn the parted wife of the Kural are given to a girl who has not yet been joined or parted, showing that the epic transfers the whole thurai of evening grief to the first night after first sight.

gains.a: the source convention of its list, which shows the bull's bell and the evening as the settled tokens of separation
gains.b: a case where the separation grief is felt before any union, widening the occasion the couplet presupposes

note: The Kural's woman asks why her eyes weep, since they showed him to her and so gave the unending sickness; the epic says Padumai lay sick with the love her own eyes had given her.
teaches: The couplet's blame of the eyes is spoken long after, by a woman left alone; the epic places the same diagnosis on the very first night, so the eyes are blamed before the love has any history.

gains.a: the convention that the eyes are the cause and so the culprit, which gives தன் கண் தரு its edge
gains.b: an instance of the eyes' guilt at the start of love, where the couplet knows it only in separation

note: The question who she is, goddess or woman, is answered in the next verse by the fading garland, blinking eyes and feet on the ground.
teaches: Read together the two verses make the doubt and its clearing a single step of the kalavu sequence, in which the man must establish she is human before he may approach her.

note: Both are the man's first sight of the woman and his doubt whether she is a goddess.
teaches: The couplet leaves the heart reeling in doubt, while the epic expands the doubt into a list of named goddesses and settles it in the next verse, so the Kural's moment becomes the first stage of a scene that ends in union.

gains.a: the epic verse gains the Kural's frame for reading its list of goddesses as the lover's conventional doubt (ஐயம்) and not as worship
gains.b: the couplet gains a sequel the Kural never gives: the doubt is resolved by signs of humanity and acted on

note: Both say the woman who causes the lover's sickness is its only cure.
teaches: The Kural states the paradox as a lover's hope, but the epic puts it after the union and makes the remedy bodily, the sandal on her breasts, so the cure is something already taken.

gains.a: the epic verse gains the couplet's paradox of cause and cure, which shows its compliment is a set argument of love and not a stray conceit
gains.b: the couplet gains a time and a body: the cure it promises is shown applied, after the meeting rather than before it

note: In both the man asks bees to judge whether any flower matches the woman, and both name her teeth and hair.
teaches: The epic keeps the Kuruntokai's appeal to the bee as the expert in flowers but asks about her teeth against the mullai, and its bees already live in her hair, so the witness the Sangam poem sends out to the flowers has been drawn inside the woman's own beauty.

gains.a: the epic verse gains a known model, which shows its address to the bees as a learned borrowing of the oldest Tamil praise poem
gains.b: the Sangam poem gains a later reading that moves its test from her hair's fragrance to her teeth and puts the bee in her hair

note: Both compare a woman and her lover's view of her with the moon and its mark.
teaches: The Kural uses the moon's mark as the flaw her face does not have, while Civakan uses it as the figure of a bond that cannot be parted, so one image carries opposite values according to whether the lover is praising her face or swearing to their union.

gains.a: the epic verse gains the contrast that shows its moon-and-mark pledge reverses the usual praise, making the mark the point and not the blemish
gains.b: the couplet gains a counter-use that shows its image of the spot as a flaw is a choice, not the only reading of the moon

note: The father decides to give Padumai to Civakan just after the two have united in secret in the grove.
teaches: The father's reasons, royal marks and a saved life, lead him to the marriage the secret union already requires, so the kalavu of the grove turns into wedlock without the lovers having to ask or confess.

note: In both a father gives his daughter to the man who has done a deed for him: Nandagon to whoever recovers the herd, Padumai's father to the man who saved her life.
teaches: Nandagon offers his daughter in advance as a public prize for any warrior, but Padumai's father reasons afterwards from the hero's bodily marks and makes the gift wait on his consent, so the epic's brides-for-deeds are not all of one kind.

note: In 1296 the onlookers say that he alone restored her remaining life and that the king will give the girl to the spearman; here the king, on his minister's counsel, decides exactly that.
teaches: The marriage is first the crowd's verdict on the cure and only then the king's decision, so royal policy here ratifies a public judgment that the healer has earned the bride.

note: In 1294 Civakan strokes her whole body as a cure, thinking her life will stay if she is seen, spoken to and touched; here the narrator cites that touch, with the maxim that a woman belongs to the one who touched her, as the ground of the marriage.
teaches: Read together, the physician's touch made to save a life becomes after the fact a claim on the woman, showing how the epic fuses healing and betrothal into one act of fate.

note: The patikam says he delighted in her for two months and then took the road again; this verse gives the two months, the night departure, and his destiny as the chariot that carries him.
teaches: The patikam reports only the length of the stay, while the narrative adds that the leaving is driven both by the hero's own rising heart and by fortune, which the summary line never says.

note: In 1340 the king reads the match as having come by destiny; in 1359 the hero's destiny (பொறி) is the chariot that takes him away from the same bride after two months.
teaches: The same fate that the king cites to make the marriage is what carries the husband off, so in this epic destiny grants a union without promising that it will last.

note: The couplet says all five senses find their objects in one bright-bangled woman; the epic names the same five, smell, taste, music, the sight of dance and her touch, as the round of the hero's pleasure.
teaches: Where the couplet gathers all five senses into one woman, the epic spreads them over perfumes, food, string music and dance with only touch left to her, showing a prince's pleasure as a court of arts rather than the single person the couplet praises.

gains.a: the verse's list of senses is recognised as the Kural's fivefold scheme of the lover's delight, not a random catalogue
gains.b: the couplet's claim of concentration is set against a scene where the senses are served by many things, which shows how strong its claim that one woman suffices really is

note: The couplet says the bond between the lover and the girl is that between body and life; the epic has the husband leave his sleeping wife as a good life leaves the body.
teaches: The couplet's simile is a promise that the two cannot part; the epic takes the same simile literally, so the husband's going is a death for the wife, which is the cost the couplet's image leaves unstated.

gains.a: the departure simile is read as the turning of a known love image, the lovers as body and life, into a picture of loss
gains.b: the couplet's image is shown to cut both ways: if he is her life, his leaving makes her a lifeless body

note: The couplet likens the bond of body and life to a bird flying off and leaving its nest alone; the epic has the abandoned wife as a body searching for its departed life and as a bird searching the nest for its mate.
teaches: In the couplet the forsaken body is an empty shell that feels nothing, which is its lesson on impermanence; the epic gives the left-behind body and nest a longing of their own, turning the image of death's indifference into one of grief.

gains.a: the double simile is seen to rework the Kural's figure of body, life, bird and nest, so its pathos rests on a known image of death
gains.b: the couplet's bare picture of the life leaving gains a view from the side of what is left, which the couplet passes over

note: In the Kuruntokai poem the woman prays that even when this life turns into the next he may be her husband; the epic's narrator calls the couple's love one joined through seven births.
teaches: What the akam speaker can only pray for, the epic narrator states as fact, yet ten verses later the hero leaves this bride in the night, so the seven-birth bond in the epic marks the depth of love without securing its continuance.

gains.a: the phrase எழுமையும் இயைந்து is seen as the old wish for a husband across births, which the plot then strains
gains.b: the poem's prayer is set beside a story where love across births is granted and still does not stop separation, which shows why the woman must pray rather than assume

note: The patikam says only that Civakan delighted in her for two months and then cut through the mountains and swiftly took the road; this run gives the night of that leaving from the side of the wife left behind.
teaches: The patikam's swift departure is told from the hero's road, and only here does the epic count its cost, a wife who blames birds, lamps and her own eyes and falls to the floor.

note: Pleading with Gunamalai, Civakan asked whether a swan that delighted in the flowering Ganges would go near the white sand of a seep-well; here Padumai is a hen-swan left by a dry stony pool after her mate has quit the Ganges lotus bed.
teaches: The hero's own image of a constancy that never leaves the Ganges is turned against him: the swan does leave, and the one stranded at the poor water is the wife he swore by it to another.

note: Gunamalai's parrot answers her plea and flies as her envoy to Civakan; Padumai's myna, swan, peacock and lamp neither stopped him nor will tell where he went.
teaches: Set beside the parrot that carried Gunamalai's love, Padumai's mute household creatures show the same convention emptied: the love-messenger exists only when the lover is still within reach.
audit_text_issue: 1000 speech division is the marker's reading (என்றதே)

note: The Kural's woman says her eyes do not sleep whether he is away or near; Padumai told her eyes not to sleep so she could keep sight of him, and they slept, and he went.
teaches: The couplet's sleepless eyes are the lover's watch against loss; the epic shows the watch failing once, so the eyes are blamed not for their suffering but for the one night they rested.

gains.a: a reason, from the Kural's chapter on the eyes, why the night's sleep is a fault and not a mercy
gains.b: a case where the eyes' vigilance actually lapses and the feared parting happens, which the couplet only fears

note: In the Kural the bangles slip from the wasting wrist and so announce the parting; Padumai pulls her bracelets off herself, blaming them for having come between her and his embrace.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's involuntary sign into a deliberate act: the bangle no longer reports the grief but is punished as one of its causes.

gains.a: the convention of the bangle as the body's witness to separation, which makes her gesture legible
gains.b: a scene where the woman acts on the sign herself, so the bangle becomes a culprit rather than a gossip

note: Kural 1154 asks whether those who trusted the assuring words of one who was gracious can be at fault if he leaves; Padumai calls Civakan one who walks by grace and speaks dharma, and asks why he shows her no grace.
teaches: The couplet sets the fault on the gap between the lover's word and deed; the epic sharpens it by making the deserter a man praised for grace and dharma, so his own virtue becomes the charge against him.

gains.a: a moral frame in which her reproach is not mere grief but an accusation of broken assurance
gains.b: a deserter whose public virtue is named, so the gap between word and deed is measured against a whole character, not one promise

note: The Kural's man finds one pain inside the sulk, the worry that union may be delayed; Padumai says that if a husband leaves even in the sweet hour of the sulk, the wife's life leaves her.
teaches: The game of sulking assumes the lover stays to be won back; the epic names the case the couplet only worries about, where the partner leaves during the sulk and the delay becomes loss.

gains.a: the Kural's view of the sulk as a sweet risk, which explains why she names the sulk-time as the worst moment to be left
gains.b: the risk carried to its end from the woman's side, where the delay the man fears becomes desertion

note: The Manimekalai's teacher sets out the forward chain from contact to craving, clinging, becoming and a birth whose fruit is aging, death and grief; the friend's tree runs from the seed of ignorance through deeds and desire to the fruit of death.
teaches: The two epics share the shape of a causal chain from ignorance to death, but the Cintamani makes it a single growing tree with love and elation among its branches and uses it to dry a lover's tears, where the Manimekalai gives it as a doctrine of release with named links.

note: The Kural calls craving the seed that yields unceasing birth; the friend's tree has ignorance as its seed and desire as its root.
teaches: Put beside the couplet, the verse shows a different order of causes: craving is not the first cause but what anchors the tree once ignorance has sown it, so cutting desire alone would not uproot it.

gains.a: a known single-cause maxim against which its own order of seed and root stands out
gains.b: an account of what lies behind craving, which the couplet leaves unasked

note: The Kural promises distinction to one who takes what hurts as pleasure; the friend says that bearing sorrow as joy is harder than weeping or dying.
teaches: The couplet's discipline for a man in adversity becomes, in a deserted bride's chamber, the hardest thing in the world, set above death itself in difficulty, so the epic measures the cost the couplet only rewards.

gains.a: a recognized rule of endurance, which shows its consolation to be ethical counsel and not just comfort
gains.b: a test case in grief over a loved one, where the rule is admitted to be harder than dying

note: Naladiyar 23 has wedding drums turn into funeral drums in the same hall the same day; the friend sees parting within union, age within youth and sickness within health.
teaches: The quatrain shows one reversal as an event; the verse turns it into a rule that every good state already holds its opposite, and uses that rule to forbid even a blink of grief.

gains.a: a concrete scene of union turned into loss that grounds its abstract list
gains.b: a generalization of its single reversal into four, with parting from kin named among them

note: In 1360 Civakan slips from Padumai's sleeping arms in the dark like a good life leaving the body; here the friend teaches that parting and death both belong by nature to human birth.
teaches: The narrator's simile of departure as death is taken up as doctrine: the parting that was likened to the soul's leaving is now said to be of the same kind as death, and as little to be grieved.

note: The friend says she once foretold a cruel trouble from a fanged snake; 1271 tells how a snake living in the grove bit the princess.
teaches: Her old warning, proved by the snakebite that brought Civakan to Padumai, is what gives her new omen of his return its weight.

note: The friend reads the owl's paired call as a sign that he has not left her; Civakan, unrecognized, sends word that her beloved will be seen within ten months.
teaches: The omen is confirmed out of the absent man's own mouth, and given a term, so the chapter closes the friend's consolation with the hero's pledge.

note: Kuruntokai 174 says that if he leaves her for wealth across the waste, then wealth alone is wealth and grace exists nowhere; Civakan's saying makes leaving for deeds and wealth a man's duty and staying a woman's.
teaches: The Sangam woman's voice hears the man's going for wealth as the end of grace, while the epic puts the same convention in the hero's mouth as a duty, and uses it, untruly, to cover a departure that is neither for work nor for wealth.

gains.a: the akam convention it quotes, with the woman's protest that the hero's maxim leaves out
gains.b: the man's own statement of the rule as duty, which the woman's lament answers

note: Civakan's hymn praises the Jina for teaching that a deed's fruit reaches its doer and no other; the Manimekalai names fierce vow-keepers who hold that a deed reaches its doer even without intention, and tells of a seat built to answer them.
teaches: Seen from the Buddhist epic, the doctrine the Cintamani's hymn takes for granted has a disputed edge, whether a deed done without intention still binds, which the Jain hymn never raises.

note: The hymn says the soul is not from anything other than itself; the Neelakesi's sage asks whether a child is the body, made of the parents' blood, or the soul, which came to a human birth by its own former deed.
teaches: The Neelakesi spells out what the Cintamani's brief formula denies: the soul is not produced by the parents or the elements but brings itself into each birth by its own deeds.

note: The Kural bids one cling to the one free of clinging in order to let clinging go; the Cintamani's hymn says love wears the karmas away and yet, being love, cannot end them.
teaches: The couplet makes attachment to the unattached the way out of attachment, while the Jain hymn admits that very attachment and counts it still a bond, so the two disagree on whether devotion can itself be the final cause of freedom, on the reading of காதல் as love of the Jina.

gains.a: a sharp foil showing that its paradox denies what the couplet affirms, devotion as the last step to freedom
gains.b: an objection the couplet does not face, that clinging to the unattached remains a clinging

audit_text_issue: Verse flagged uncertain: காதல் and மறைதி open.

note: The Kural says neither shaving nor long hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns; Civakan says matted hair, robes and the skull bowl are seeds of a mean birth.
teaches: Where the couplet sets the marks aside as unnecessary, the epic counts them as harmful, sowing rebirth, so the pair shows two degrees of the same critique of outward signs.

gains.a: a neutral maxim that makes plain how much further its own judgment goes
gains.b: a case where the marks are not merely superfluous but are taken for the path itself and so mislead

note: Pattinathar calls vows, Vedas, Agamas, fire rites, offerings, mantras and pujas all pretence; Civakan mocks standing in the five fires and eating grass, but goes on to urge austerity in the Jina's form (1435).
teaches: Both reject the Vedic ascetic's fire and diet, but the Siddhar rejects observance as such, while the Jain hero rejects one school's austerities only to set up his own, so the pairing separates a critique of ritual from a rivalry of disciplines.

gains.a: a contrast that shows its polemic is not anti-ritual in general, since it keeps tapas
gains.b: a reasoned reductio, the beast that already lives the practice, where the Siddhar only lists and dismisses

note: Civakan says that if plunging in water won release the bear would gain it; Tirumular says the holy waters are within the heart, and those who do not bathe there so their deeds perish wander the land.
teaches: Both deny that outer bathing destroys deeds, but Tirumular keeps the bath and moves it inward, while the Jain hero drops it and replaces it with knowledge, vision and conduct, so the two show different ways out of the same criticism.

gains.a: an inward alternative its own mockery does not offer, which shows its answer is substitution rather than interiorization
gains.b: a blunt test, the bear in the pool, for the outward bathing its verse dismisses

note: Pattinathar asks what forest life, eating wind, rags and the bowl avail without inner love, and says the Lord's true lovers reach release even living at home beside their women; Civakan says sin born of desire for women cannot be removed by union with women.
teaches: The two agree that going to the forest is nothing in itself, but they part on the household: the Saiva poet lets love free one beside one's wife, while the Jain hero makes leaving the wife a condition, so the shared attack on outward renunciation hides opposite views of the married life.

gains.a: a rival conclusion from the same premise, which shows that its demand to leave women is a doctrine of its own and not implied by its critique
gains.b: the strongest objection to its claim, that sin born of desire cannot be cleansed while desire continues

note: The Neelakesi praises those who leave home for forest and hill and strive with knowledge to wear away their deeds; Civakan says leaving the house of women for the forest does not wear away old sin carried within.
teaches: Read together, the two Jain epics place the cause of release not in the forest but in the knowledge the Neelakesi names (ஞானமொடு), which the Cintamani's ascetics lack until Civakan supplies it in 1436.

note: Civakan says the body will drop at once like a ripe fruit from its stalk; the Naladiyar warns that a harsh wind can drop the green fruit while the ripe stays on the tree.
teaches: The epic's ripe fruit makes death a ripening that comes in order, but the quatrain's fallen green fruit warns that it need not wait for age, and the two urgings to act now rest on different pictures of when the body falls.

gains.a: a caution that its own image of ripeness understates the danger to the young
gains.b: a renouncer's use of the falling fruit that turns the urge to do good into a call to austerity

note: The Kural says one whose mind ponders and knows what is with certainty need not think again of birth; Civakan says knowledge, right vision and right conduct must all three be full before both kinds of deed pass.
teaches: Where the couplet lets true knowing alone end rebirth, the Jain formula makes knowing only one of three and insists on vision and conduct of non-harm as well, so the pair shows the Kural's chapter on true knowledge as a narrower account of release.

gains.a: a single-cause claim against which its insistence on all three, each made full, stands out
gains.b: a fuller account of what knowing must be joined with before birth ends, which the couplet leaves unsaid

note: In 1432 Civakan mocks the ascetics who leave soft beds only to lie with women in leaf huts; in 1437 they put away their households and go to the Jina.
teaches: The jibe was not only abuse but a charge the converts accept, so the poem counts their earlier forest life as no renunciation and their conversion as the first true leaving of home.

note: 1436 names knowledge, right faith and conduct whose fulness ends both kinds of deed; 1437 has the hearers rise and take the path of release.
teaches: The doctrine of the three jewels is tested at once by its hearers, and the epic settles the debate by conversion rather than by any further argument from the ascetics.

note: 1438 calls Civakan the man whose body bears the true marks; from 1460 the marks are listed one by one.
teaches: An epithet that seems mere praise on the road becomes the evidence by which a stranger is recognised as a destined husband, so the body itself carries the plot.

note: The astrologer foretells that Kemasari's husband is the man at whose sight she will feel sudden shame; in 1472 at first sight her restraint and shame give way and she melts.
teaches: The prophecy names shame as the sign, but its fulfilment is shame overwhelmed by desire, so the virtue that should guard a maiden is made the very place where the destined bond shows itself.

note: Both brides' fathers wait on an astrologer's word about the destined husband: Gandharvadattai's says he lives in Rajamapuram, Kemasari's that she will know him by her own shame.
teaches: Set side by side, the two horoscopes show the epic varying one device: the Vidyadhara princess's husband is found by place and contest, the merchant's daughter's by a sign in her own body that no contest can stage.

note: The couplet praises the host who tends the departing guest and watches for the guest to come; Subhadran feeds a thousand and eight guests a day for twelve years watching for one guest who will be his son-in-law.
teaches: The epic takes the couplet's watching for the coming guest literally and turns it to a private end, so hospitality becomes a search, rewarded with a husband in this life rather than with welcome among the gods.

gains.a: the father's twelve-year feast is given the standing of a recognised householder's virtue rather than a mere device of the plot
gains.b: the couplet's 'watching for the guest to come' is shown to admit a host whose care has a hidden aim of his own, a case the couplet does not weigh

note: 1460 lists Civakan's bodily marks without saying who sees them; in 1465 the father, having examined them, decides he is his daughter's husband and takes him in his chariot.
teaches: The catalogue that reads as the poet's praise is revealed as a merchant's inspection, so the marks of a great man work as a test of a bridegroom alongside the astrologer's sign.

note: 1453 tells how the merchant fed 1008 people daily for twelve years for the sake of the திருமகன் who would be his daughter's husband; in 1465 he reads the stranger's body and names him திருமகள் கணவன்.
teaches: The twelve years of feeding were a long wait for a sign, and the sign comes as a body to be read, so the epic turns the merchant's charity into the means by which the fated groom is found.

note: In 1339 Padumai's royal father gives her because Civakan bears marks fit to rule the earth (பொறியினன்); in 1465 the merchant Subhadran gives his consent on the same kind of reading of the body.
teaches: Two fathers of different rank, a king and a merchant, both choose the stranger by reading his body rather than asking his birth, which shows that in the epic the hero's hidden royalty is legible on his skin to anyone trained to look.

note: Kural 84 says the fair goddess dwells in the home of one who tends good guests with a glad face; Subhadran, who has kept a great guest-feeding for years (1451, 1453), receives a guest he calls திருமகள் கணவன்.
teaches: The Kural's promise that fortune lives in the hospitable house is made literal: the guest the merchant takes in is the lord of fortune himself and becomes the son of the house.

gains.a: a reason, in the ethics of hospitality, why the long feeding is rewarded by the arrival of Tirumagal's husband
gains.b: a story in which the goddess's dwelling in the host's house arrives as a person, a guest who joins the family

note: Kural 10 says those who do not reach the Lord's feet cannot cross the sea of births; 1467 says those who do not praise the Jina with flowers and tongue do not reach the world of release.
teaches: The Kural leaves the Lord unnamed and the means as reaching his feet; the Jain hymn names him by the pindi tree and the triple umbrella and makes the condition a concrete act of worship, so the same exclusion becomes sectarian and ritual.

gains.a: the general frame of the couplet, which shows that the hymn's threat belongs to a shared Tamil form of praise
gains.b: an instance of how a Jain reader could fill the Kural's unnamed Lord with the Jina and its reaching with flowers and song

note: Kural 6 praises the one who quenched the five gates of sense (பொறிவாயில் ஐந்தவித்தான்) and promises long life to those who keep his path; 1468 calls the Jina lord of those who slew the five senses (ஐம்பொறியும் அட்டு) and promises heaven to those who sing his feet.
teaches: The Kural's sense-quencher is a teacher whose path is followed; in the hymn he is the head of a class of victors, and the reward moves from long life on earth to the world of the gods.

gains.a: a named model for the Jina's epithet, which shows the hymn speaking the Kural's language of sense-conquest
gains.b: evidence that the couplet's sense-quencher was read in Jain circles as the Jina and his followers

note: In Tirumanthiram 1775 worship of the Lord's feet brings grace by which the worshipper's own five senses are conquered; in 1468 the Jina conquered his own senses, and the worshipper's singing earns heaven, not sense-conquest.
teaches: Both tie the five senses to praise of holy feet, but the conquest is done by different hands: Saiva grace subdues the devotee's senses for him, while in the Jain hymn the conquest belongs to the Jina alone and remains the worshipper's own task.

gains.a: a contrast that shows the hymn gives the worshipper no grace that does the work of restraint
gains.b: a Jain counterpart in which the feet are praised for a conquest already achieved by their owner, not for one they bestow

note: Kural 9 calls the one to be worshipped எண்குணத்தான், the one of eight qualities, and calls a head that does not bow useless; in 1469 those who do not praise the Jina have the eight qualities taken from their souls by their deeds.
teaches: The eight qualities that the Kural gives to the one worshipped are, in the Jain hymn, the soul's own, lost to karma by those who will not praise, so the failure to worship costs the self what the god possesses.

gains.a: a source for the term, which shows the hymn reworking a couplet every Tamil hearer knew
gains.b: a Jain reading in which the eight qualities are the soul's nature, so the couplet's god is what the freed soul becomes

note: Tirumanthiram 444 gives the eight qualities (குணம் எண்குணம்) to matted-haired Siva who keeps the world; 1469 has them seized from souls by the robber deeds.
teaches: On my reading of 1469, the two texts disagree about whose the eight qualities are: for Tirumular they are the attributes of a God who protects, for the Jain hymn they are the soul's own and are lost to karma, with no protector named who restores them.

gains.a: a Saiva rival that sharpens the hymn's claim that the qualities belong to the soul
gains.b: a Jain counter-reading in which the eight qualities are not a divine possession but a human one under siege

audit_text_issue: line 4 வெண்குணனும் is probably எண்குணனும்; sense uncertain

note: In 1420 Civakan praises the Jina who teaches that the eight karmas (எண்வினையும்) pass through love and yet do not pass because of love; 1469 shows the eight qualities of the soul seized by those karmas.
teaches: The two hymns of this ilampakam make a pair: the eight deeds of 1420 are the robbers of 1469, so the reader sees what the soul loses before the paradox of love and release in 1420 can be weighed.

note: In 1456 Subhadran consoles the grieving mother that the man of merit will meet her daughter's eyes tomorrow (கண்ணுறு நாளை); in 1471 their gazes meet as Civakan enters the city.
teaches: The meeting of the eyes is the fulfilment of a precise prediction, so the first-sight love of the next verses is framed as a fate announced in advance rather than a chance encounter.

note: Kural 1251 says the axe of desire breaks the door of restraint bolted with shame; in 1472 Kemasari's inner restraint and modesty (உண்ணிறை நாணும்) break together at the first sight of Civakan.
teaches: The Kural's woman says this in separation as a confession of defeat; the epic makes the same breaking happen at first sight and treats it as the sign that the destined man has come, turning a lament into an omen.

gains.a: the frame of நிறை as a door with நாண் as its bolt, which explains why the two words break together
gains.b: a scene that moves the breaking of restraint from the end of a love to its first instant

note: Kural 1082 says her returned look is like a striking goddess (தாக்கணங்கு) bringing an army; in 1473 Kemasari's look becomes an afflicting goddess (நோக்கணங்கு) and Civakan wonders whether she is a தாக்கணங்கு or a mortal.
teaches: The Kural settles that the woman is human and keeps the goddess as a figure for her look; the epic stops at the doubt and stacks அணங்கு on lute, look and woman, so the hero's own art is made one of the goddesses that strike him.

gains.a: the term and its sense of a look that strikes back, which the verse expands in its triple pun
gains.b: a narrative moment in which the man's doubt is left unresolved and he sinks under it

note: In 1327 Civakan settles that Padumai is no goddess by three marks (her garland fades, her eyes blink, her feet touch the ground); in 1473 he asks whether Kemasari is a goddess or a daughter and does not settle it.
teaches: The hero who coolly tested a woman's humanity by signs in one ilampakam is in the next too struck to test, which shows the epic varying the same first-sight doubt from a clear-headed proof to helpless wonder.

note: In 1451 the astrologer foretells that the man at whose sight Kemasari instantly feels shy (கதுமென நாணப் படுவான்) will be her husband; in 1475 she looks at Civakan and turns her eyes away.
teaches: The averted glance is the very sign the astrologer named, so a lover's ordinary modesty becomes the proof of fate, and the reader knows the marriage is sealed before anyone speaks of it.

note: Kural 1086 says her eyes would not cause him trembling pain if her curved brows would straighten and screen them; in 1482 her brow is a strong bow bent at the middle that beats him.
teaches: In the Kural the brows could be the eyes' restraint if only they were straight; in the epic the bent brow is itself a weapon in league with eye, hair and breast, so the hope of a screen is gone.

gains.a: the idea that the brows might have held the eyes back, which shows what the epic's brow-as-bow has abandoned
gains.b: an extended scene of capture in which the brow joins the eyes as attacker

note: Kural 1087 likens the cloth over her firm breasts to the face-cloth over a rutting elephant's eyes; in 1483 her breasts are bound by a bodice as cruel things must be bound.
teaches: Both treat the covering of the breasts as a restraint put on something dangerous; the epic adds that the binding fails, since the bound breasts still wreck her waist and him, while the Kural's cloth only warns.

gains.a: a reading of the bodice as a restraint on a dangerous force, which explains why the verse calls the breasts கொடியன
gains.b: a sequel to the image, in which the covering does not hold and the danger it marked comes to pass

note: The Kural's man asks whether Vishnu's world is sweeter than sleep in the beloved's arms; the epic answers by likening the lovers to those beyond birth and death.
teaches: Set beside the Kural's open question, the Jain epic lends sexual bliss the very vocabulary of release, then ends that bliss within the chapter by the hero's leaving.

gains.a: the epic's simile is shown to answer a known question about whether love can rival the gods' world
gains.b: the couplet's question receives a narrative test, in which the answer 'yes' holds only for two months

note: The Kural's lover says the beloved is life when present and death when she leaves; Civakan offers to live serving her or leave his body, then is himself the one who leaves.
teaches: The couplet assumes the woman is the one who departs and the man the one who dies of it; the epic reverses the roles, so the parting the man dreads is the parting he chooses.

gains.a: Civakan's live-or-die hyperbole is shown to be a formula of the lover's art, not a vow
gains.b: the couplet's life-and-death image is seen from the side of the one who goes rather than the one left

note: Civakan asks her to command whether he lives to serve her or goes; six verses on he goes without a word to her.
teaches: The hero's offer to let her decide his going is contradicted by a departure she is not even awake to know of.

note: Naladiyar makes the sun Death's daily measure of one's days; the epic tells one day's sun as a whole life from infant to desireless old man, and the lovers go to bed.
teaches: The epic uses the Naladiyar's moral image of the sun as a life measured out, but withholds its moral, letting the lovers' indifference to the dying sun foreshadow the night that ends their union.

gains.a: the sunset's life-stages carry the ethical charge of the day as a portion of life eaten by Death
gains.b: the quatrain's abstract measure gains a concrete picture of a day as infancy, youth and old age

audit_text_issue: 1503 flagged repaired; Naladiyar 7's last line read variously

note: The patikam sums up the Takka episode as living with the merchant's daughter as one life and then leaving her; here the leaving is told.
teaches: The patikam's bare 'he left her' becomes a stealthy departure from a sleeping bride, so the summary's single verb hides the secrecy the story stresses.

note: The Kural's woman demands to be told whether her man will go; Civakan leaves while Kemasari sleeps, so that she cannot ask.
teaches: The secret night departure is the hero's way of avoiding exactly the plea the couplet voices, and the couplet names what Kemasari is denied: the chance to speak before the going.

gains.a: Kemasari's silent loss is given the words she never gets to say
gains.b: the couplet's plea is shown its counter-move, a leaving timed so the plea cannot be made

note: Here the lovers' delight is called the eating of the good of their deeds; in 408 the teacher leaves to do penance that wears away old deeds.
teaches: Within one Jain epic, pleasure counted as the good fruit of deeds is still deeds, the very store that the renouncer's penance sets out to wear away.

note: She now says she did not grasp the words about the bee that Civakan spoke before he left.
teaches: Read together, the bee speech that sounds like idle love-play in 1502 proves to be his only farewell, and her failure to decode it becomes part of her grief.

note: She holds back her life on the strength of the bee words, in which the mate stays on without grief when the other goes.
teaches: The pairing shows the covert message doing its work: the image of the mate who waits without grieving, left in place of a goodbye, becomes the rule by which she chooses to live.

note: The life she says in 1509 is leaving her body is held back in 1530.
teaches: The two verses frame the lament between a life about to go and a life restrained, and show that what turns it is not his return but her fear of harm to him.

note: Love said to cling like a shadow in 1511; her actual reflection taken for a companion in 1524.
teaches: The love she said should cling like a shadow has gone, and what stays is her literal image, which she then comforts as a friend, so the simile becomes her situation.

note: Both are a deserted woman weighing the assurance of the man who left.
teaches: The couplet asks whether those who trusted an assurance are at fault, and the epic heroine answers both ways at once, calling his word a lie and naming herself the one of evil deeds.

gains.a: the epic verse gains the couplet's moral question, so her cry that he lied reads as a judgment on who answers for a broken assurance
gains.b: the couplet gains the promise in its exact words and a speaker who does not acquit herself, which it never shows

note: Both make the woman's shoulders the record of union and parting.
teaches: In the couplet the shoulders betray the parting to onlookers, while the epic woman questions her shoulders as witnesses of where he went, so the body that tells the secret becomes a confidant.

gains.a: the epic verse gains the convention that the shoulders bear the sign of union and parting, which explains why she turns to them
gains.b: the couplet gains a reason the shoulders should know: he painted them, and they are asked rather than read

note: Both put the parted woman at night with no companion but herself.
teaches: The couplet's woman mocks the night for having only her as companion, and the epic's woman, as alone, makes her own reflection the companion and consoles it, so the loneliness turns inward on the self.

gains.a: the epic verse gains the Kural's frame of the night that has no companion, which shows her talking to her image is the extreme of that solitude
gains.b: the couplet gains a scene where the absence of any companion is acted out, not stated

note: The companion appeals to the deity that dwells in the house; Kemasari then installs the bees as the gods of her house.
teaches: The house god that the household turns to for her survival is answered by her own choice of new household gods, the bees of his parting words, so worship shifts from the family's deity to the creature his parting words named.

note: The mother warns that dying of separation loses both worlds; the narrator says Kemasari lives only by his words to the bee.
teaches: Holding the two together shows the doctrinal consolation failing: what keeps the bride alive is not the threat of losing both worlds but one covert sentence of love.

note: Both use the water bubble for what forms and bursts.
teaches: The impermanence figure that in the quatrain moves the wise to end their wandering is used by the epic's mother to keep a bride steady in the household until her husband returns.

gains.a: the mother's simile gains the quatrain's renunciant force, which shows how strong a medicine she is giving for a lover's absence
gains.b: the quatrain gains a domestic use of its argument, as comfort rather than a call to leave the world

note: The couplet calls children a man's wealth; the riddle says children of the body are others' and only merit is one's own son.
teaches: On the reading that line 4 denies ordinary children are one's own, the Jain riddle answers the Kural's householder by taking the very word மக்கள் and giving it to merit.

gains.a: the riddle gains the Kural's claim as the view it overturns, so its paradox reads as a reply
gains.b: the couplet's crux over whose deeds and whose wealth is sharpened by a text that assigns the only lasting gain to one's own deeds

note: Both speak of householders who provide for renouncers.
teaches: The couplet chides those who give to renouncers in place of doing austerity themselves; the epic's householder does both, counting the gift to renouncers and his own fasts as two of four equal duties.

gains.a: the epic gains the Kural's worry that giving to ascetics can stand in for austerity, which its fourfold scheme answers
gains.b: the couplet gains a worked-out lay discipline in which its implied rivalry of giving and tapas is resolved

note: Both define tavam.
teaches: The Kural defines austerity as enduring pain and harming none, with no rite named, while the epic's lay teacher defines it as fasting on fixed moon days: the pair shows the same word as an ethic and as a calendar.

gains.a: the epic's fasts gain the Kural's ethical core, the bearing of hardship, which gives them their point
gains.b: the couplet gains a concrete practice by which a householder can take up its definition

note: Civakan once bade the forest hunter give up meat, honey and toddy; now a wayfarer bids him give up lust, drink and meat.
teaches: The teacher becomes the taught, and the triad changes as it is aimed at him: honey drops out and lust comes in, the vice of a man who has just left a bride.

note: Both turn on eating flesh to swell one's own flesh.
teaches: The couplet asks how the flesh-eater can have compassion; the epic adds the end of the fattened body, carried only to feed vultures, so the cruelty is shown to profit no one but the birds.

gains.a: the epic verse gains the couplet's moral charge that flesh-eating defeats arul, beyond its picture of waste
gains.b: the couplet gains an ending for the body it fattens, which it leaves unstated

note: Both bid people take provisions for the journey because Death is coming.
teaches: The quatrain's bundle carried on the shoulder stays a figure; the epic sets it against the food anyone packs for a visit to kin, and says it to a man actually on the road, so the figure is pinned to an everyday act and to the hearer's own journey.

gains.a: the epic gains the quatrain's warning that Death takes even the unborn, which makes the provision urgent
gains.b: the quatrain gains the comparison with the ordinary traveller's food that shows why neglecting it is folly

note: Both warn men against women's smiles.
teaches: Tirumular's etti fruit says only that the smile is poison under a fair surface; the Jain sermon says what the poison does, endless rebirth in states of sorrow, and in 1555 offers heaven to those who refuse it.

gains.a: the epic gains Tirumular's image of fair leaves over a poisoned fruit, which explains why a smile should be distrusted
gains.b: Tirumanthiram 204 gains the karmic consequence it does not state, in the Jain terms of the gatis

note: Both say deeds do not cling to those devoted to the Lord.
teaches: The Kural's unnamed Lord, to whose devotees the two deeds do not cling, is given a Jain identity in the epic, the Great One under the asoka and triple umbrella, so the couplet's claim is read as one about the Jina.

gains.a: the epic's hard verse gains a clear parallel for its claim that karma will not cling, which supports the reading of line 4
gains.b: the couplet gains an early reader who names its Lord, showing one tradition's reading of the Kural's opening chapter

note: The simile of 1557 sets Civakan's leaving beside men who renounce dancer and wife; 27 tells his final renunciation at the feet of the Knower.
teaches: Read together, the narrator's simile for a lover's journey is an early rehearsal of the end the patikam promises, so the hero already leaves his marriages in the manner of a renouncer long before he renounces.

note: In 1574 Civakan, tempted, asks his heart whether a world of women's pleasure ending in death is good; in 27 he hears the dharma and renounces.
teaches: The pair shows that the hero's renunciation has a rehearsal mid-story, but here the reflection serves only to keep his restraint against one woman, and he goes on to marry again, so the epic separates thinking renunciation from doing it.

note: Both list the body as a thing of filth with nine openings that dazzles the deluded; Naladiyar's fool is the lover, Civakan uses the inventory to refuse a woman.
teaches: The epic shows the Naladiyar's anatomy of the body being used by a man at the very moment of seduction, as a defence rather than a sermon, and by a hero who will still take wives, so the disgust is a tool of restraint, not a rule for life.

gains.a: Civakan's catalogue is placed in a known tradition of meditating on the body's foulness to cure desire, which marks it as a deliberate discipline and not a passing mood
gains.b: the quatrain's general mockery of the fool gets a speaker, a woman before him and a test, which it lacks, and the test is passed by one who is no ascetic

note: Arunagirinathar calls the nine-gated body a house Brahma built; the Cintamani's hut of flesh is built by a carpenter that 1578 names as the deed (வினை).
teaches: Holding the two together shows that the same anatomy of the body serves opposite accounts of its maker, a god in the Thiruppugazh and one's own deeds in the Jain epic, and that the disgust can be shared while the theology differs; the contrast rests on reading 1577's builder through 1578.

gains.a: the epic verse's unnamed builder is shown to be a doctrinal choice, since a devotional text with the same inventory names a creator god instead
gains.b: the Thiruppugazh's attribution to Brahma is shown not to follow from the inventory itself, since a text with the same list of body parts gives the work to karma

audit_text_issue: Depends on 1578 for the builder; 1577 line 4 can divide as நல்லன் or அல்லன்.

note: Tirumular's dead man has his nine gates shut while the loving ones weep and leave; the Cintamani's dying lover has his eyes closed by the beloved and goes.
teaches: The epic turns Tirumular's unnamed mourners into the very women of the man's pleasures, so the lovers who melt in his arms are those who close his eyes, which joins the critique of desire to the meditation on death.

gains.a: the epic's refrain gains the Saiva verse's frame of the body's impermanence, showing the lover's death as one case of a general account of the body's end
gains.b: Tirumular's 'loving ones' (அன்புடையார்) are given a particular identity, the beloved of the bed, which makes his mourning scene a rebuke to desire as well as to attachment

note: The couplet holds that one's own understanding prevails however many subtle books one learns; the epic says the deed blinds those who have swum through learning.
teaches: The epic gives the limit of learning that the couplet states a cause and a scene, the deed covering one's eyes at the moment of desire, so the 'own understanding' that overrides books becomes the karma that defeats even the learned.

gains.a: the epic's claim that learning gives no protection is set against a known ethical rule about learning's limit, sharpening its point that knowing is not seeing
gains.b: the couplet's unstated reason why learning fails is supplied as karma at work in desire, one answer to the question its nuance leaves open

note: Naladiyar 46 lists entrails, fat, blood, bone, sinews, skin, flesh and grease and asks which part is the garlanded woman; 1583 gives nearly the same list (குடர்கள், வழும்பு, நரம்பு, தோல்) but starts from the adorned hair and adds the three humours.
teaches: The Naladiyar's renunciant catalogue is put in the mouth of a hero who is not renouncing, as a weapon against another man's wife, so the meditation on the foul body becomes a householder's defence against adultery rather than a step out of the world.

gains.a: a recognised ascetic form, the list of tissues, that tells the reader Civakan's reply is a teaching and not merely a rebuff
gains.b: a dramatic occasion: a particular woman pressing a particular man, against whom the list is used and proves effective

note: Siddhar 301 also strips the body to wind, bile and phlegm and foul matter, but the poet confesses he still runs after women and begs the Lord's grace to free him; Civakan recites the catalogue and simply refuses.
teaches: The same catalogue that the Saiva poet finds powerless without grace is, in the Jain epic, enough by itself to master desire, which shows the two traditions disagreeing about whether self-knowledge alone can free a man from lust.

gains.a: a contrast that brings out how self-reliant Civakan's restraint is: no god is asked for help
gains.b: a case where the catalogue works without grace, which makes the Siddhar's plea a claim about his tradition and not a fact about the body

note: Naladiyar 41 says that if skin the size of a fly's wing is torn from the body a stick is needed to drive off crows; 1584 opens the body and sets crows at the eyes.
teaches: Both poets end the lover's gaze with crows at the body, but the epic uses the image on the living woman standing before the hero, turning a general memento into a refusal spoken to her face.

gains.a: a traditional image whose force a Tamil reader already knows, which lets the hero's rebuff be brief
gains.b: evidence that the crow at the torn skin was a stock figure that a narrative poet could place in a scene

audit_text_issue: 1584 lines 2-3 (தடிதடித் கீழ்ந்த, பிள்ளையார் கண்ணுட்) hard | 1584 lines 2-3 (தடிதடித் கீழ்ந்த; பிள்ளையார் கண்ணுட் காக்கை) are probably corrupt

note: At 1577 Civakan reflects to himself that the body is a flesh-filled hut (ஊன்பயில் குரம்பை) of bone, sinew, blood and skin with nine gates; at 1584 he tells the woman it is a worm-filled hut (புழுப்பயில் குரம்பை).
teaches: The hut image moves from the hero's private thought when the woman first appears to his spoken answer to her, so the reader sees that his rebuff was prepared in silent meditation before she spoke.

note: At 1585 Civakan says the kavya poets have dressed up the flesh to kindle desire; at 1482, lying in Kemasari's house, he himself laments that her hair, brows, eyes and breasts kill him.
teaches: The hero who now condemns the poets' painting of the body was a few scenes before its most eloquent practitioner, so the epic sets its own love poetry under judgement and leaves the reader to weigh whether desire for a wife differs from desire for another's.

note: Naladiyar 44 refuses the petty men who call eyes water-lilies, carp and spears; 1585 blames the poets of kavya by name for painting brows, eyes and nose on a bag of skin.
teaches: Where the Naladiyar's opponents are anonymous fools, the epic names its own craft as the source of the illusion, so the critique of the simile becomes a self-critique of the epic genre.

gains.a: a precedent that makes Civakan's attack on poets part of an older ascetic argument rather than a passing jibe
gains.b: an identification of who the praisers of eyes are: the poets of the great poems, not only foolish lovers

note: At 1580 the woman tells Civakan that a Vidyadhara carried her off and his wife made him drop her in the forest; at 1592 her husband says she sent him for water and was gone when he came back.
teaches: The husband's plain account exposes the woman's story as a lie told to the hero, so the reader learns that her helpless plight was itself part of the seduction.

note: Pavadattan swears that after seeing him his wife never looked at another man; at 1581 she has begged Civakan to take her or let her die.
teaches: The husband's certainty about his wife's chastity is false in the reader's sight, and Civakan's silent laugh, not exposure, is how the epic lets the household survive the truth.
audit_text_issue: identification of 1581's speaker is not in the verse

note: Kural 414 says listening to the learned is a support in one's faltering (ஒற்கத்தின் ஊற்றாந் துணை); 1595 says learning is a companion to the heart in its weakness (மெலிவிற்கோர் துணை) and asks the learned Pavadattan why he grieves.
teaches: The epic applies the Kural's promise to a man of many treatises and shows it failing: his learning does not console him, and he is comforted only when a mantra returns his wife.

gains.a: the authority of a Kural teaching, which makes Civakan's rebuke to the grieving scholar a reasoned one
gains.b: a test case in which the support learning offers is tried against the loss of a wife and found insufficient

note: Kural 57 says the guard of confinement is useless and the best guard is the one women's own நிறை keeps; 1597 says women do not hold their restraint within (உண்ணிறை யுடைய வல்ல) and yield to pressing.
teaches: The Kural trusts the guard inside a woman, the epic's hero denies most women have it, and the story of this chapter is offered as his proof, so the two texts disagree on whether a woman's restraint can be relied on at all.

gains.a: a precise contrary, the Kural's நிறை, that shows the hero's view as a position taken against a known teaching
gains.b: a narrative challenge to its trust, in which a wife thought steadfast is not

note: Kural 55 promises that the wife who rises worshipping her husband commands the rain; 1598 describes chaste wives who live worshipping their husband's hands (கணவற்கை தொழுது வாழ்வார்) as a few against the many of 1597.
teaches: The epic keeps the Kural's figure of the husband-worshipping wife but makes her a rare exception within women's general frailty, and drops the rain, so her power shrinks to ending her husband's distress.

gains.a: a known ideal against which the hero's two-part teaching on women can be measured
gains.b: a reading in which the husband-worshipping wife is defined by her renunciations in his absence, not by power over nature

note: Siddhar 910 calls the mountain of Ekambar the one that removes the hard deeds of those who bow (பணிவாரருவினை தீர்க்கும்); in 1603 women climb a hill so that their accumulated evil deeds may leave them (நிரைத்த தீவினை நீங்க).
teaches: A Jain epic and a Saiva poet share the belief that a sacred hill wears away karma, which shows a common practice of pilgrimage beneath the doctrinal quarrel over how deeds are destroyed.

gains.a: evidence that the pilgrims' purpose is a widely held Tamil belief and not a doctrine peculiar to the epic's hill
gains.b: a parallel from another faith that shows the hill's power over karma as shared ground rather than a Saiva claim alone

note: Siddhar 696 says the poet wandered over every forest and hill until his legs ached without seeing the Lord who moved within his body; 1603 shows crowds climbing a hill to shed their sins.
teaches: Within the Saiva tradition itself the climb that the epic describes approvingly is mocked as wasted walking, so the pairing shows the Siddhars turning against a practice that Jains and Saivas otherwise held in common.

gains.a: a critic's view that shows what the epic's narrator takes for granted in describing the pilgrims
gains.b: a picture of the very pilgrimage the Siddhar rejects, with its anklets, lac and crowds

note: Two hymns to the Jina in neighbouring episodes: the woman's song in 1467 warns that those who do not praise will not reach release; Civakan's hymn argues that praise follows from what the Lord is.
teaches: Held together, the two hymns show the epic grounding worship two ways, as a condition of release in the singer's warning and as the only fitting answer to the Lord's nature in Civakan's reasoning, so praise is both means and response.

note: The Jain hymn calls the Jina the one who scorched Kama; Tirumular makes the destruction of Kama's work Siva's yoga at Korukkai.
teaches: The pair shows two traditions claiming the same feat for their own lord and reading it the same inward way, as desire overcome in austerity, so the rivalry is over who did it, not over what it means; the tension holds only if the epithet is read as a title one lord alone may bear.

gains.a: the epic hymn gains the Saiva background against which giving the Kama-burning to the Jina is a pointed claim, not a stock epithet
gains.b: Tirumular's verse gains a rival who claims the same conquest of Kama without a god's grace, by the Jina's own discipline and compassion

note: In 1488 Civakan says one woman's beauty made her an enemy to Murugan, Kama, himself and the matted-haired god; here he praises the Jina who scorched Kama.
teaches: The same hero who, newly in love, ranked Kama among those a woman's beauty conquers, now, having left that woman, praises the one who conquered Kama, so the hymn marks the swing in Civakan between desire and its mastery that the ilampakams keep repeating.

note: In both a hen swan is misled by a reflection in the water.
teaches: In the Kalittokai the hen swan runs to the moon's reflection thinking it her mate and is shamed when he appears, an image of a wife who welcomes a straying husband; in the epic the hen takes her own reflection for a rival and sulks, so the same mistake that there yields shame here yields jealousy of herself.

gains.a: the epic scene gains the akam convention in which a swan deceived by a reflection stands for a wife's misjudgment of her husband
gains.b: the Kalittokai's image gains a version in which the false image is the bird's own, which turns misplaced longing into baseless jealousy

note: The quarrelling pair of swans: in 96 the drake leaves the flock after a quarrel and sits alone like an ascetic; here the drake ends the quarrel and unites with his mate.
teaches: The epic uses the swan's quarrel for opposite ends, the drake's withdrawal as a picture of the yogi's solitude in 96 and the drake's reconciliation as the sight that draws Civakan back into longing here, so the one image holds both the renunciant's and the lover's path.

note: The couplet names quarrel, reconciliation and union as love's rewards; the epic stages that sequence in the swans and has the hero watch it.
teaches: The couplet lists oodal, understanding and union as what lovers gain, and the epic shows that sequence complete in birds before a man who is parted, so the reward the couplet promises becomes, for the onlooker who lacks it, the cause of pain.

gains.a: the epic verse gains the couplet's order of quarrel, reconciliation and union, which explains why the swans' episode ends in union and not in the sulk
gains.b: the couplet gains a watcher outside the pair, for whom the rewards of love seen in others turn into longing

note: Both are a man describing the girl's averted gaze: when he looks she looks down.
teaches: The couplet catches the girl's averted look in the present as a sign of love, and the epic hero recalls the same look from the past while parted from her, so the gesture that once told him she loved him is what memory hands back in separation.

gains.a: the epic verse gains the couplet's reading of the downcast look as a sign of love, not coldness, which is why Civakan treasures it
gains.b: the couplet gains a later moment, in which the shy look survives as a memory and returns unbidden to a husband far away

note: Civakan fears his absent wife will die in the fire of separation; Kemasari, whom he has just left, held back her own life in 1530.
teaches: The man who imagines a wife dying of separation has just left another wife who, contrary to his fear, chose to live for his sake, so the pairing shows the deserter's imagination of grief running behind what the deserted woman actually did.

note: Civakan imagines his wife wasting and burning on her bed; in 1509 Kemasari, left by him, cries that her life is leaving her body.
teaches: Read together, the lament the epic gave Kemasari in her own voice returns here as the hero's guess about another wife, so the poem lets the reader measure his pity for the absent Tattai against his silence toward the wife he has just left.

note: 1627 fears she will die in the fire of parting; 1631 argues she cannot have, since he lives.
teaches: Together they show the hero answering his own fear with an argument rather than news, using the lovers' shared life as evidence, so that separation grief turns into reasoning.

note: Kemasari cited his doctrine that lovers' lives become one to reproach him for leaving her; he now uses the same doctrine to reassure himself about Gandharvadattai.
teaches: Held together, the verses show one premise serving opposite ends: for the wife he has just left it proves his desertion wrong, for the absent first wife it proves she is safe, so the doctrine binds him only where it comforts.

note: The couplet calls the bond with the girl that of body and life; the epic draws an inference from it during separation.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's simile into a test a separated lover can run, that one life cannot end while the other goes on, and so shows the image used as reassurance rather than praise.

gains.a: the epic verse gains the couplet's settled formula, so the hero's inference rests on a known saying about lovers
gains.b: the couplet gains a situation of separation and a consequence drawn from its image, which it never states

note: Both say lust breeds the evil that ends in hell; Manimekalai puts it in an ascetic's sermon on the five things to shun, the Cintamani in the hero's thought about his own wife.
teaches: The Buddhist epic uses the rule to say lust must be renounced and only ascetics manage it, while the Jain epic lets a married hero apply it mid-romance and simply turn his mind, so the same doctrine works there as a householder's brake, not a call to the robe.

note: The couplet allows a falsehood that yields faultless good; the narrator excuses the hero's false name in similar terms.
teaches: The epic gives the couplet's exception a concrete case, a fugitive prince hiding his name from a usurper, and shows a narrator reaching for the exception to keep his hero truthful.

gains.a: the epic verse gains a recognised rule under which its awkward excuse of the hero's lie can be judged
gains.b: the couplet gains a test case where the 'good' is the liar's own safety, which leaves open whether its strict condition is met

note: The couplet tells courtiers to keep near a king like men warming at a fire; the epic gives the same fire conduct to pupils with their teacher.
teaches: The epic moves the rule from court to schoolroom, and since the teacher is a hidden king, the princes unknowingly keep the courtier's rule toward a real king.

gains.a: the epic verse gains the couplet's reason for the distance: the one served can burn as well as warm
gains.b: the couplet gains an application beyond kingship, to any one whose favour is sought, here a master of an art

note: Her resolve to bind him with her garland is fulfilled when he takes it.
teaches: Together they show the binding she plans in private take effect only through his hesitant consent, so the exchange of garlands becomes a mutual tie rather than her gift alone.

note: The hero's garland as her raft: first in her own lament, then in the narrator's account of failed remedies.
teaches: The raft she claims in despair in 1663 is confirmed by the narrator in 1674 after every cooling remedy fails, so the image moves from a lover's hope to the story's fact.

note: Love explained by a former deed: Civakan's father ran after his queen because an earlier disposition sprouted; Civakan takes the garland saying it comes by ūzhvinai.
teaches: Set beside the father's fatal infatuation, which the narrator blames on former deed, the son's acceptance under the same explanation shows the epic marking each of his loves as karma at work, but here with a pause of scruple the father never had.

note: The raft (புணை) on the deep sea: in 380 the Wise One to whom the youth goes for refuge, here the hero's garland on the sea of night.
teaches: The Jain epic uses one image for refuge from the sea of births and for a girl's hold on her lover's token, so the reader sees desire offering a false copy of the refuge the teacher gives.

note: The Kural's woman says there is a sea of love but no safe raft to cross it; Kanakamalai finds her raft in the garland Civakan made.
teaches: The pair shows that the raft the couplet denies can be supplied by a token of the beloved, but only as a raft through the night, not a way out of the sea.

gains.a: the epic's raft is read against a known claim that love has none, which makes the garland's comfort pointed
gains.b: the couplet's abstract missing raft is given a concrete candidate, a love gift, and the epic's later failures of cooling test whether it holds

note: Both women swim love's flood alone in the night watches (யாமம்).
teaches: Where the couplet's woman sees no shore and is simply alone, the epic adds the watchers who laugh at her, so the solitude of the night becomes public shame by day.

gains.a: Kanakamalai's 'sea of the night' is placed in the Kural's convention of the midnight flood of love
gains.b: the couplet's bare 'I alone' gains a social side, the women who mock the lovesick girl

note: The Kural's lover says love's flood carries off the raft of modesty and manliness; Kanakamalai says she sold her modesty to buy a garland.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's loss into a trade: modesty is not swept away but given in exchange, and what it bought, the garland, becomes the new raft of 1663 and 1674.

gains.a: her bargain is read as the woman's version of the loss the Kural gives to a man
gains.b: the couplet's image gains a sequel in which the lost raft of modesty is replaced by one of love

note: Evening as what eats the lives of the separated: the couplet's woman says it is not evening but the hour that devours; Kanakamalai sees it as a demon gaping to swallow her.
teaches: The epic makes the couplet's figure of devouring evening into a visible monster, the moon its tooth and the red sky its mouth, showing how a Kural conceit was expanded into scenery.

gains.a: her terror of evening is placed in the Kural's convention of the devouring hour
gains.b: the couplet's bare 'eats life' is given a body and features drawn from the evening sky

note: The Kural condemns those who clung to dice (கவறு) and the gaming hall (கழகம); the epic makes the woman's body a board, dice and gaming hall for love.
teaches: Borrowing the Kural's own words for ruinous gambling, the epic frames love as a game one should give up for penance when it cannot be won, so the condemned dice become a figure for the pleasure renunciation replaces.

gains.a: the conceit's choice of dice gains the Kural's moral weight against gaming, which prepares its turn to restraint
gains.b: the Kural's dice and hall are shown entering a love conceit, a use the couplet does not foresee

note: The Kural's lover says he once had modesty and manliness and now has only the palmyra horse; the epic's maxim says restraint is the beauty of manliness when love fails.
teaches: Against the Kural's man who says love has taken his manliness, the epic defines manliness as the restraint that remains when love is denied, so the same word marks opposite outcomes of desire.

gains.a: the epic's maxim is seen as a reply to the Kural's account of love overcoming manliness
gains.b: the couplet's despair is set against a path the lover does not consider, restraint through penance

audit_text_issue: Soolamani flagged sense uncertain; Cintamani 1657 marked uncertain

note: The king says such excellence belongs only to a king or a twice-born; the couplet says the learned low-born outrank the unlearned high-born.
teaches: Read together they show the epic using learning as a sign that betrays hidden royal birth, the reverse of the Kural's use of learning to override birth rank; the conflict holds on reading the king's line as a general rule rather than a compliment.

gains.a: The king's remark is exposed as a claim about birth that the Kural explicitly denies, not just praise of a teacher.
gains.b: The couplet meets a narrative where its opponent's view is spoken by a sympathetic king and even happens to be right about the man in question.

note: Both speak of a help weighed against earth and heaven: the couplet says they cannot repay it; the king says the help itself gave him earth and heaven, and finds no requital.
teaches: The pair shows a king accepting the couplet's verdict that such a debt is unpayable and answering it with a daughter, so the unpayable gift becomes a bond of marriage instead of a repayment.

gains.a: The king's 'I see no requital' is placed within the Kural's doctrine of gratitude, which explains why he does not offer wealth.
gains.b: The couplet's abstract measure of earth and heaven gets a case where the debtor still acts, choosing kinship over payment.

note: Both have the bangles slip as the sign of the man's leaving, and both use the verb துற for his going.
teaches: Where the Kural's bangles announce that he has left, the epic's refrain makes the bangles leave as he left, so the body imitates the desertion it reports.

gains.a: The epic princess's song is placed in the Kural's grammar of separation, showing the convention it is varying.
gains.b: The couplet's single image is unfolded into a three-stanza refrain that links his former tenderness to the bangles' going.

note: The crowd grieves at the binding of Civakan in Rajamapuram and again at the king's threat of fetters here.
teaches: The poet replays Civakan's arrest as comedy: the crowd that once wept for real bonds now weeps for a fetter that proves to be a bride, so the second scene answers the first.

note: Kemasari's birth reckoning names her husband by a sign; Kanakamalai's names him as a master of the bow.
teaches: Held together they show the Cintamani's pattern of licensing each marriage by a birth horoscope, so the hero's many brides are presented as fate fulfilled rather than conquest.

note: Gandharvadattai's horoscope placed her destined husband in Rajamapuram; Kanakamalai's names him by his bow.
teaches: The first bride's horoscope and this one frame the series: from the first marriage the stars, not the hero's pursuit, name his wives, and here Civakan's teaching of arms itself becomes the sign.

note: The patikam foretold that the younger brother, like a star that lost the moon, would come at a woman's bidding; here the image returns and Gandharvadattai appears.
teaches: The pairing identifies the patikam's unnamed woman as Gandharvadattai, whose song follows, and shows the brother's search starting exactly as the patikam framed it.

note: In 351 the widowed Vijayai strips her pearls, bangles and rings; here Nandattan reasons from Gandharvadattai's unremoved ornaments that Civakan lives.
teaches: The stripping of ornaments that the epic first showed as a widow's grief becomes, read backwards, a sign a kinsman can read, so jewels on a wife are public evidence of a living husband.

note: Thirikadugam lists a husbandless woman's adornment among things unfit; Nandattan argues from the same norm that a wife still adorned has a living husband.
teaches: The ethical list states the rule as unfitness, while the epic turns that rule into a piece of inference, showing the norm was strong enough to serve as proof of a fact.
