gains.a: the Cintamani's argument gains a stated norm outside the story, so Nandattan's reasoning rests on a known rule and not on a guess
gains.b: the bare rule gains a scene in which someone actually relies on it to learn whether a man is dead

note: Puram 246's queen rejects the widow's austerities and chooses the pyre; Nandattan names penance and the fire as two equal courses for a widow.
teaches: Where the Sangam queen ranks the fire above the hard widow's life, the Jain epic's speaker leaves the two as alternatives, so the pair shows the choice the queen made was one of two recognised paths.

gains.a: Nandattan's passing phrase gains the weight of a real choice argued for in the Sangam queen's own voice
gains.b: the queen's refusal gains a later witness that the austere path she scorned stayed a full alternative to the fire

note: The Kural praises the manhood that does not look at another's wife; Nandattan, who must meet and speak to his brother's wife, keeps his eyes on her anklet.
teaches: The couplet forbids the look outright, and the scene shows how the rule is kept when a man must face and address the woman: the gaze goes to her feet, where looking becomes reverence.

gains.a: Nandattan's lowered eyes gain a named virtue, so the verse reads as conduct and not only courtesy
gains.b: the couplet gains the case it does not cover, a kinsman's obliged meeting, and the bodily form its restraint then takes

note: In 1147 Gandharvadattai's recited spells bring armed powers to free Civakan; here her spell shows Civakan far away and then sends his brother to him.
teaches: Her vinjai, first a weapon of rescue, becomes a means of sight and passage over distance, so the Vidyadhara wife is the household's power to reach Civakan wherever he goes.
audit_text_issue: 1709 flagged uncertain; the woman is not named.

note: The patikam says the younger brother, desolate as a star that has lost the moon, came to join Civakan at a woman's bidding; here Civakan sees that Nandattan has come with the peacock-like woman's word.
teaches: The patikam's 'by a woman's command' is shown to mean Gandharvadattai's spell and bargain, so the summary's single phrase hides a whole scene of grief, vision and magical travel.

note: Gandharvadattai's promise to bring him to his lord's feet is kept when the chapter opens with him lying at Civakan's feet.
teaches: Read after 1747, the opening tableau of the brother at the feet is the exact fulfilment of a Vidyadhara's spoken promise, so the reunion the narrator showed first was her doing.

note: Buddhisenan would die after killing the king; Nandattan resolves to die alone if he cannot find his lord.
teaches: The same either-find-him-or-die resolve is a public war vow in the companions' mouths and a private one in the brother's, and it is the private one, aimed at no enemy, that brings him to the woman who can reunite them.

note: Gunamalai reproaches him for being able to eat without his lord; at Kanakamalai's table he eats beside him.
teaches: Held together, the two meals show that for the women of the epic eating is a measure of grief: the brother's meal without Civakan reads as betrayal, his meal with him as reunion.

note: Civakan's own account of being led bound names his reason, to please his father, and adds what he saw of his kin.
teaches: The narrator showed him yielding to his parents' plea; his own retelling turns that yielding into filial choice and adds a sight the earlier scene did not report, kin armed and ready to die.

note: Both console a waiting woman by saying the flowers have been fooled by a false rain; in the epic the thunder is an elephant's trumpet and the song is overheard by warriors.
teaches: The akam friend's denial that the season has come is lifted whole into the epic and read by men as an omen that their lord lives, so a love convention becomes a sign in a war story.

gains.a: the epic verse gains its key: the Kuruntokai poem shows that the song is the friend's claim that he has not yet broken his word, which is why it comforts
gains.b: the Kuruntokai poem's consolation is shown working outside the love situation, as a formula strangers could overhear and apply to their own loss

note: The couplet defines a king as one who weighs a case before punishing; Devadattan asks the same of companions planning to punish a king.
teaches: The pair shows the rule of inquiry before penalty binding not only the ruler but those who would avenge themselves on him, and its first question is not guilt but whether the wrong has happened at all.

gains.a: Devadattan's caution gains the couplet's standing as the definition of just punishment, not mere prudence
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where the punishers are subjects and the punished a king, outside the royal court it assumes

note: Pisirandhaiyar and many others sit fasting with the Chola; Buddhisenan would follow Civakan in death, but only after vengeance and without knowing he is dead.
teaches: Against the Purananuru's companions who die beside a living king by his own choice, the epic's vow to follow a lord in death rests on an unverified death and a killing first, and the next verse checks it.

gains.a: Buddhisenan's vow gains its model, the companion who dies with his lord, which shows what kind of loyalty he is claiming
gains.b: the Purananuru poem's sitting-with gains a contrast in which the same loyalty is armed, hasty and turned outward

audit_text_issue: PN 219 sense flagged uncertain; epic verse repaired from 8 half-lines

note: Gandharvadattai held back her spells lest a wife's rescue shame him; Civakan says he himself preferred death to being saved by a woman.
teaches: Put together, the wife's restraint and the husband's choice turn out to be one scruple about his honour, held by each without the other's knowing, which is why the rescue had to come from the god and not from her.

note: The god promised to come if Civakan thought of him in trouble; in his account Civakan thought of him and he came.
teaches: The retelling shows that the god's promise worked as a pact of thought: Civakan's only act in the crisis is to think and praise, and the friendship made with the dog he once helped is what saves him.

note: The narrator says Civakan relieved the elephants hemmed in by fire; Civakan's own account says rain fell while he stood grieving.
teaches: The narrator credits the hero with the rescue, while the hero credits a holy rain that came as he stood helpless, so his compassion is shown to act without any deed and he does not claim it.

note: Padumai, left behind, called him a deceiver; Civakan himself says he left her by deceit.
teaches: The epic lets the hero confirm the abandoned woman's charge in his own word வஞ்சித்து, so her bitterness is not a lover's exaggeration but a judgment he accepts without excuse.
audit_text_issue: 1756 line 1 வாவிப்புண் அடையினாளை unclear; 1405 sense uncertain

note: The god foretold that the king of the middle country would give him his daughter; Civakan reports that he has.
teaches: The god's itinerary is fulfilled step by step, and the pairing shows that the marriage, which Civakan reports as a fee for teaching archery, was already fixed as his fortune before he set out.

note: The god foretold the friends would come to him drooping like stars that have lost the moon; they waste at home and set out.
teaches: The friends' wasting like a burnt summer hill is the drooping the god foresaw, so their grief is part of the plan that brings them to him, not a delay in it.

note: The friends suspect Gandharvadattai because her body does not waste; she has already sent his brother to him by her spell.
teaches: Read against 1747, the calm the friends take for deceit is knowledge: a wife who knows by her arts where her husband is has no cause to pale, and the convention they judge her by misleads them.

note: The couplet makes the parted woman's pallor spread the moment the man goes; the friends treat its absence as proof of deceit.
teaches: The epic turns the Kural's sign of parting into a test applied by men to a wife, and shows the test failing, since a wife who knows her husband is safe does not pale.

gains.a: the epic verse gains the rule behind the friends' suspicion, that pallor follows the lover's going at once
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where its sign is read from outside as evidence and its absence is misjudged

note: The couplet says nothing that can be gained equals wise children; Civakan counts children among the gainable and sets a brother beyond gain.
teaches: Civakan's list puts children with wealth and wives among the things a man can acquire, and names the brother as the one bond that cannot be got at all, a value the Kural's ranking of gains has no place for.

gains.a: the epic verse gains the Kural's frame of 'things that can be gained', which shows how far his praise goes in placing the brother outside it
gains.b: the couplet gains a rival answer, from kinship by birth rather than by begetting, to its question of the greatest gain

note: The couplet says giving and sweet speech gather kin around a man; Civakan says friends and wives can be gained but a brother cannot be made.
teaches: Set beside the Kural's way of winning kin by gifts and kind words, Civakan's saying separates the circle that can be won from the brother who can only be born, so not all kin answer to the Kural's means.

gains.a: the epic verse gains a contrast with the Kural's claim that kin can be drawn by giving, which sharpens what 'cannot be made' means
gains.b: the couplet gains a limit: the kin it gathers are the acquired circle, not the brother of one's birth

note: The ochre-dyed fine cloth (கல் தோய் நுண் கலிங்கம், 353; நுண்டுகில் கல்லரத்தம், 1783) that Vijayai put on 'that the strong one's son may rise'.
teaches: The robe she took as a vow for her son's rise is still on her years later and is now listed beside the son as a burden, so the renunciation proves to have been made for him rather than from him.

note: In 359 she watches the road for news of her son; in 1785 she still sits thinking of his lot when the news walks in.
teaches: The waiting begun in 359 is answered not by her messenger but by strangers who stumble on her, so the news she longed for comes unsought and unrecognised.

note: In 356 the deity hid her land and lineage when commending her to the ascetics; here she herself refuses to tell her clan.
teaches: The concealment first done for her by the deity has become her own habit, so that she withholds her identity even from her son's companions and the recognition must wait on their story.

note: 785 says the companions were born on the very day Civakan was born; 1793 says that day was also the day the king perished, through their own deeds.
teaches: The birthday the battle verse gave as a warrior's pedigree is retold to the king's widow as a day of death, and the companions take the guilt of it on themselves.

note: In 334 Vijayai heard her son's future greatness foretold; in 1796 his first deeds are recited to her by one who does not know she is his mother.
teaches: The prophecy she took on faith returns to her as report of deeds done, and the irony that the reciter does not know his listener lets the mother hear her son's fame as a stranger would.

note: The couplet promises that those who reach the feet of the one without liking or aversion have no suffering anywhere; Vijayai worships at the Jina's feet and in the next verse weeps for her son.
teaches: Placed beside the couplet, the scene shows worship at the passionless one's feet asked to remove a fault while the grief of attachment to a child runs on, so the promised freedom from suffering is a goal still far off, not a present state.

gains.a: the epic's silent worship gains a standard, the couplet's 'no suffering at any time', against which her tears in 1785 read as the distance still to go
gains.b: the couplet gains a case of a worshipper at the right feet whose suffering persists, which tests whether 'reaching' the feet means worship or attainment

note: The Puram queen refuses to be one of the widows who go unanointed, eat cooked leaves and sleep on gravel, and chooses the pyre; Vijayai lives that very widow's life, unanointed, on greens (354), as a Jain ascetic.
teaches: The life the Sangam queen scorns as the wretched alternative to the pyre is the one the Jain epic gives its queen as a penance lived for a son, so the two show the widow's choice valued in opposite ways.

gains.a: the epic's unanointed ascetic gains the older measure by which her survival was the lesser choice, sharpening why she lives on: for her son
gains.b: the Puram poem gains a widow who takes the 'leaf-food' life deliberately and turns it into austerity, a reply its speaker does not imagine

note: In 225 the king reads the dream's crown as her son and leaves the falling tree unexplained; here she says that reading was the raft that kept her alive.
teaches: The half-told dream reading the epic first showed as the king's tact becomes, years later, the single hope a widow lived by, so the omitted part of the omen proves the part she could not afford to hear.
audit_text_issue: 1803 line 4: whether என்னரசே ... இறந்தனையே addresses the dead king or the son is unclear.

note: At the burning ground in 309 she asked the newborn whether this was how kings are born; here she remembers that same birth as the son appearing as her companion.
teaches: The birth among corpses, first lamented as a disgrace to a king's son, is remembered as rescue, and the loss she now fears is told as the loss of that companion of the cremation ground.

note: In 260 the councillor says the king will be killed by Death, by the woman and by his own fault; here the queen says he died through the love he fixed on her.
teaches: The cause the councillor named in passing, the woman, is accepted by the woman herself, so the epic's verdict on the king's fall is confirmed by the one it blamed rather than by the narrator.

note: At the birth the deity foretold that the boy would crush the king who stood against him; here the friends, learning his birth, hail him as the life that will be Death to the usurper.
teaches: A prophecy spoken only to a hidden mother passes, through her grief, into the mouths of armed men, which is how the epic moves a foretold fate from secret knowledge to a plan of war.

note: The proverb says one's suffering is one's own old deed and the foe only the sent servant; the friends see the usurper's deed ripen and the heir become its agent of Death.
teaches: Read together, the two show the sent-servant idea from both ends: the proverb tells the sufferer not to rage at the agent, while the epic shows men rejoicing to become the agent of another's ripened deed.

gains.a: the friends' cry gains a stated account of how a ripened deed uses a human hand, which explains why they can call Civakan Death without calling him the cause
gains.b: the proverb's consoling rule gains a scene from the agent's side, where the instrument of the deed is glad and armed, which the proverb never considers

note: The Kural forbids trusting anyone unexamined but bids trust after examination; Vijayai bids the friends trust no one at all with the secret except Civakan.
teaches: The Kural's two-step rule of trust assumes time to examine people, and the epic shows a mother hiding an heir from a usurper dropping the second step altogether, so that danger turns examined trust into blanket silence.

gains.a: Vijayai's charge gains a rule against which its absoluteness can be measured, showing how far beyond ordinary prudence her fear has pushed her
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where its own first clause, தேறற்க யாரையும், is held without the second, marking the limit of the time to examine it presumes

note: The Naladiyar's eel-like doubleness belongs to women who sell intimacy; Vijayai, the faithful queen, puts the hearts of girdled women in general among things that do not go straight.
teaches: The quatrain confines double dealing to a class of women and blames the men who embrace them, whereas the epic's chaste widow extends the suspicion to all women when a secret is at stake, so the pair shows the charge widening from a trade to a sex.

gains.a: the queen's maxim gains a narrower ethical source, which shows how much she generalises the doubleness the moral books assigned to courtesans
gains.b: the quatrain gains a woman speaker who uses its suspicion as practical counsel, testing whether its warning was about trade or about women

note: The Kural praises those who keep the path of the one who quenched the five senses; the epic gives Vijayai that sense-restraint (பொறிதவ நெருங்க நோற்று) in the verse that sends an army out at her word.
teaches: The couplet makes quenching the senses the way to a long, settled life, while the epic shows the same restraint in a widow who still commands a war of revenge, so ascetic control of the senses is shown sitting with, not ending, worldly purpose.

gains.a: Vijayai's penance gains the weight of the Kural's opening ideal, so her austerity reads as the highest discipline and not mere widowhood
gains.b: the couplet's ideal gains a case where it is kept by a householder's widow with an unfinished duty, showing it need not mean withdrawal from affairs

note: In 454 Civakan turned back the hunters' raid on the king's herd; here his friends plan a raid on a king's herd to make him ride out.
teaches: The cattle raid that first made Civakan a public hero becomes a signal his friends can send him, so the epic treats his response to niraikol as a known trait that others can plan on.

note: Mastering a king's must elephant brings Civakan the usurper's threat to brand him a thief with the elephant's tusk in 1121, and a lawful king's assembly's acclaim here.
teaches: The same feat earns punishment under Kattiyangaran and honour under Tadamittan, so the epic makes the court's response to Civakan's prowess a measure of the ruler, not of the deed.

note: With Asanivegam Civakan only dodged between the tusks and drove the beast away; here he mounts, harnesses and pats the must elephant until it obeys gladly.
teaches: Set side by side, the two elephant scenes show the hero's mastery grown from escaping a beast to commanding and calming one, the step from youthful daring to the skill a king's court rewards.

note: The Kural trusts the concurring word of three spies who do not know one another; the friends' three spies come back together (ஒன்றி) with one report.
teaches: The epic keeps the Kural's number three but drops its safeguard of mutual ignorance, showing a band of friends using the statecraft rule loosely, with trust in place of cross-checking.

gains.a: the friends' three spies are seen to follow a recognised rule of intelligence rather than a chance number
gains.b: the couplet's condition that spies not know one another stands out once a story shows three who arrive together

note: The Kural says to think before resolving, since rethinking after resolving is a fault; Buddhisenan says that once the raid is made, turning back brings blame, so weigh it first.
teaches: Buddhisenan supplies the reason the Kural leaves unstated: in war, the deed once begun shuts off retreat through blame, which is why the thinking must come before the resolve.

gains.a: Buddhisenan's caution gains the standing of a general maxim of deliberate action, not mere timidity
gains.b: the couplet's bare 'lapse' gains a concrete cost, the blame of retreat before a king's army

note: The Kural's huge tusked elephant fears the tiger's attack; Civakan comes at the elephant like a lion (1833), but it ends not in fear but in one mind with him.
teaches: Against the Kural's picture of the strong beast cowed by a fiercer one, the epic's elephant is won into agreement, so mastery here is shown as concord after force, not fear alone.

gains.a: the epic's claim that rider and beast share one mind gains force against the common image of the elephant ruled by terror
gains.b: the couplet's image of fear as the end of the contest gains a counter-case in which the stronger spirit ends in rapport

note: Maduraikanchi lists a must elephant that kills its goad-men, breaks its post and roams, beside horses drilled in circling courses; 1831 and 1839 give the same post-breaking elephant and the same circling drill.
teaches: The Sangam city poem sets the rampaging elephant and the drilled circles side by side as separate noises of the capital, while the epic joins them as two stages of one hero's mastery, riot turned into drill.

gains.a: the epic's set piece is seen to draw on a Sangam catalogue of the capital's elephants and horses
gains.b: the catalogue's separate items gain a story in which one man turns the first into the second

note: Neduncheliyan swears that if he fails to take the kings who scorned him, the poets led by Mangudi Marutan may cease to sing of his land; Civakan swears that if he fails to bring the raiders to bow before the king, his name may not go out in the world of song.
teaches: The epic keeps the Purananuru's vanjinam form, a war vow whose penalty is the loss of poets' praise, but its hero swears it for another man's king and against raiders who prove to be his friends, so the oath of fame becomes a set piece the plot quietly empties.

gains.a: Civakan's vow gains its form: the vanjinam kanchi self-curse, which shows his oath stakes the same thing a Sangam king staked, fame in song
gains.b: the Purananuru vow gains a later life in which the curse is softened into a love simile and sworn by a hero in exile on a host's behalf

note: Civakan swears to bring the raiders to the city with their crowns at the king's feet; three verses later the raiders fall at his own feet as his companions and ride into the city honoured on elephants.
teaches: The vow is kept to the letter and reversed in substance: the raiders do come to the city bowing, but as friends at the hero's feet rather than captives at the king's, so the epic turns a war oath into a reunion.

note: In the first cattle raid Civakan swears that if he does not protect cows, renunciants, women, children and brahmins he may become like a shameless eunuch; here he swears by his fame to bring raiders to a foreign king.
teaches: Set beside the first raid's vow, which rests on the duty to protect the helpless, the second vow rests on fame and loyalty to a host, and the friends' choice of a cattle raid to draw him out repeats the very scene that first made his name.

note: Both kings, told of a cattle raid, order the army to go swiftly and turn back the herd (விரைந்து தொறுமீட்க, 432; வல்லே படுநிரை பெயர்க்க, 1858).
teaches: The repeated order scene makes Tadamittan stand where the usurper Kattiyangaran stood, but where the usurper's army was routed by real hunters, this king's whole army rides out against a raid staged by friends, so his rage meets no enemy.

note: The Kural's spy goes in the guise of renunciants (துறந்தார் படிவத்தர்) and gives nothing away; Padumukan's spies (படிவ ஒற்றாளர்) have found Civakan in disguise and are rewarded on their report.
teaches: The Kural writes spying as a king's instrument against enemies, while the epic turns the same disguised spy to a band of friends searching for their lost lord, which shows the technique is a means that serves loyalty as well as statecraft.

gains.a: the epic's spies gain from the couplet the sense of படிவம், a borrowed and often ascetic guise, which the verse names but does not explain
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where the spy's master is not a king and his search is for a friend, not for hidden enemies

note: The companions, taking a passing song as a sign that Civakan lived, put off revenge and scattered to search for him; here they find him and their grief ends.
teaches: The search the companions began in place of revenge ends in this verse, so the grief that had nearly turned into killing the king is finally discharged by a bow at the hero's feet.

note: The companions seized the king's herd as a ruse to bring Civakan out; the princess greets them as the thieves to be punished.
teaches: Read against the staged raid, her mock sentence shows the household already knows the theft was a summons, so the crime against the king becomes a joke at his table.

note: Gandharvadattai sealed the letter with her earring and handed it to the companions; here it reaches Civakan and the seal is broken.
teaches: The pair closes the errand she began: the earring-seal that made the leaf hers is the thing Civakan must remove to read her, so the seal guards her words until they reach the one reader they were for.

note: The couplet asks a wife to guard the good name of the house; Gandharvadattai guards her husband's name among her people by sending a false message.
teaches: Together they show the wife's duty of guarding the good name pulling against truthfulness: Gandharvadattai keeps the couplet's charge by deceiving her own father's envoy, and names the couplet's duty as her reason.

gains.a: her deception gains the standing of a wife's recognised duty, the guarding of the house's name, rather than mere cunning
gains.b: the couplet's சொற்காத்து gains a hard case in which keeping the name requires a wife to tell something other than what happened

note: Nandattan found Gunamalai wasting and reproaching him; Gandharvadattai's letter now reports her worse, unable to tell sun from moon.
teaches: Set beside the brother's account, the letter shows Gunamalai's grief growing in the interval and makes the co-wife, not the brother, the one who carries it to Civakan.

note: The couplet makes one day pass like seven for those waiting for a return; the epic's girl, told 'tomorrow', asks her parrot whether tomorrow is near or far.
teaches: The pair shows that a promised day of return does not shorten the wait but makes it measurable, and the epic turns the couplet's arithmetic into a question the waiting woman cannot answer.

gains.a: Gunamalai's question gains the couplet's rule that the fixed day itself is what lengthens time for the one who waits
gains.b: the couplet's general waiting is given a scene, a comforter's 'tomorrow' and a parrot asked to say when it comes

note: The couplet's lover says he would recall her if he forgot, but he knows no forgetting; Gandharvadattai says she need not recall her husband, since he never leaves her heart.
teaches: The conceit that one who never forgets has nothing to remember becomes, in the abandoned wife's letter, a reproach: the same words that pledge constancy remind the new bridegroom that she has not moved and he has.

gains.a: her line gains its source in the Kural's play on remembering and forgetting, so the sulk is a known figure of love
gains.b: the couplet's lover's boast is turned around into a wife's, said to a husband who is with another woman, where it carries blame as well as love

note: The companions bowed at the feet of Vijayai in her penance grove before setting out; now they tell Civakan whom they met.
teaches: The pair shows the companions' news running in the order the story requires: the mother's ascetic state, seen first by others, reaches her son only as their report, and he must ask to hear it twice.

note: Vijayai fell lamenting that she had seen her son once and failed to see him again; hearing of her, Civakan weeps.
teaches: Read together, the mother's and the son's tears are the two halves of one grief, each learning of the other only through the companions who carried the story between them.

note: The king had asked Civakan for his clan when the alarm of the raid broke in; now the companions answer the question for him.
teaches: The interrupted question is finished by others: Civakan's birth, which he was about to tell, is declared by his friends, so the hero's lineage reaches the king as testimony rather than his own claim.

note: The companions told Vijayai they would bring Civakan to her feet within a month; he now leaves Kanakamalai's city with them.
teaches: The departure answers the mother's charge: what moves Civakan to leave a new wife is the promise his friends made to his mother, not any call of his own.

note: In 201 Saccandan hands his kingdom to Kattiyankaran out of trust; here the son's brother warns that those who trusted have died.
teaches: The brother's rule against trusting anyone is drawn from the family's own ruin, so the epic makes prudence an inheritance learned from the father's fatal trust.

note: The verse takes up the couplet's hands joined in worship and weeping tears that hide a weapon, adds hair and jewel caskets, and ends with those who trusted being dead.
teaches: The couplet names where a weapon hides; the epic turns it into a bodyguard's order and adds the outcome, showing the rule read as a practical protocol against poisoning.

gains.a: the brother's warning gains a known authority, so it reads as received wisdom rather than a young man's fear
gains.b: the couplet gains a situation and a consequence, a prince among strangers and the death of those who trusted

note: The couplet says to cut a thorn tree while young; the verse says no enemy, however soft and small, should be called small, using the snake that kills an elephant.
teaches: The couplet's remedy is to strike early, while the epic's is to guard always, so the same fear of a small foe yields attack in one and vigilance in the other.

gains.a: the verse's warning gains the couplet's point that a small foe grows, which explains why softness is no safety
gains.b: the couplet gains an alternative to striking first, the defence of a man who cannot yet fight his enemy openly

note: The couplet puts the lotus goddess in the effort of the unslothful; the verse says she will not embrace those who slip.
teaches: Where the Kural earns fortune by effort, the epic loses it by a lapse, so prosperity is shown as something kept by conduct and not only won by work.

gains.a: the blessing gains the couplet's account of what Lakshmi rewards, so the warning becomes a condition
gains.b: the couplet gains its negative side: fortune can be lost by one slip as well as missed by sloth

audit_text_issue: line 4 has a stray letter; lines 1-2 hard to construe

note: Neelakesi argues in debate that trees live, as their change with the seasons shows; the Cintamani's narrator says the same from their flowering at a woman's glance.
teaches: The Jain thesis that plants live appears both as a debater's proof and as a narrator's aside in a love scene, showing the doctrine was common enough to be argued from a poetic convention.

note: In Neelakesi 370 the Buddhist Mokkalan likens those who give trees life to men in madness; the Cintamani calls those who deny it madmen or ghouls.
teaches: The same charge of madness is thrown from both sides of the dispute over plant life, so the insult marks a live sectarian quarrel and not a settled view.

note: In 359 Vijayai, failing in spirit, watches the road for news of her son; here her watching ends when Padumukan announces him.
teaches: The long wait set up at the hermitage is closed by omens and then a messenger, so the mother's watch that began at his birth is fulfilled by the son's own coming rather than news of him.

note: In Akananuru 289 a wife waiting for her husband prays at each chirp of the lizard; here Vijayai reads the lizard's call, a dream and a throbbing eye as signs of her son.
teaches: The lizard omen of the akam wife waiting for her lover is given to a widowed mother in an ascetic's robe, showing that the epic carries the akam signs of reunion over to a son.

gains.a: Vijayai's omens gain their conventional sense from the akam waiting, which makes her longing read as near-erotic in intensity
gains.b: the akam image gains a non-erotic use, showing the omen signals any longed-for return, not only a lover's

note: In 318 Vijayai suckles the newborn, puts her husband's ring on him and leaves him; here the grown son falls at her feet.
teaches: The parting at birth and the reunion are linked by the son's self-naming as her servant, so the child she gave up returns as a worshipper of the renouncer she has become.

note: At 310 Vijayai, alone in the burning ground by a hostile city, says she does not know how the child could be raised; at 1913 she names herself the base woman (கயத்தியேன்) who left him there.
teaches: The mother who was shown as helpless now judges the same act as her own baseness, so the reunion is weighed down by a guilt the narrator never laid on her.

note: At 465 the townspeople say the mother who bore Civakan must have done great penance; at 1912 the mother herself, now an ascetic, speaks of her penance as having seemed fruitless until this meeting.
teaches: The crowd's easy inference from a splendid son to a fortunate mother meets the real mother's view from inside the hermitage, where penance felt barren for years.
audit_text_issue: 1912 lines 3-4 (தாளையா... றோளையா) are hard to divide; the sense is a reading.

note: At 473 the foster father, more to Civakan than a mother, receives him home; at 1915 the birth mother herself declares Sunandai his mother and Kandukkatan his father.
teaches: The foster bond the story showed in action is ratified by the one person entitled to dispute it, turning the merchant's care into a parenthood the queen confers.

note: The patikam's 24 says only that Civakan took counsel with his mother (தாயொடு எண்ணி) before entering the city; 1918 to 1931 give that counsel as a full lesson in kingcraft.
teaches: The summary's two words turn out to hold the epic's most compact statement of royal policy, placed in the mouth of a widowed ascetic queen.

note: The patikam's 9 says Saccandan would not hear counsel (சொல்லாறு கேளான்) and was beaten by a plot (சூழ்ச்சியில் தோற்ற); at 1925 his son asks what need a lion has of strategy (சூழ்ச்சி).
teaches: The son's first reply to his mother repeats his father's fatal contempt for counsel, so the lesson of the patikam must be learned again within the family.

note: 1925 makes Civakan a thunder-voiced lion who needs no stratagem against a jackal; 1928 has a cave lion, roaring and leaping, fall into the hunters' net.
teaches: The counsel defeats the hero with his own image: the lion stays a lion, but the reply shows that strength without judgment is just what a net is made to catch.

note: Kural 497 says no ally is needed but fearlessness, provided one thinks everything through and acts by the place; at 1925 Civakan claims no strategy or allies are needed because he is strong.
teaches: Civakan keeps the couplet's conclusion and drops its condition, and the mother's next verses restore exactly the weighing of place that the couplet made the price of going alone.

gains.a: Civakan's boast is shown to be a half-quoted rule, which explains why the mother answers with place and time rather than with doubts about his courage
gains.b: the couplet's proviso (எஞ்சாமை எண்ணி இடத்தால் செயின்) is shown to be the part a brave young man leaves out, so it reads as a warning and not a licence

note: Kural 481 says the crow beats the owl by day and that kings need the right time; 1927 tells of one crow that went among the owls in their own place and killed a thousand crore.
teaches: The couplet's even match, decided by the hour, becomes in the epic one against countless decided by time, place and cunning together, so judgment is shown to multiply strength and not merely to time it.

gains.a: the mother's fable gains the authority of a known royal maxim, so it reads as counsel from the books of kings rather than a nursery tale
gains.b: the couplet's image gains a story in which the crow's advantage is pressed home by stratagem in the enemy's own ground, beyond what daylight alone gives

note: Kural 500 has the jackal kill the fearless elephant once its feet sink in the mire; 1928 has the roaring lion caught in the hunters' net in the forest.
teaches: Both reverse the strong beast by its setting, but the epic puts the reversal in a mother's answer to a son who has just called himself the lion, so the maxim is aimed at a person and not at kings in general.

gains.a: the epic's lion gains the couplet's structure, in which ground and not courage decides, so the net is read as the place chosen by weaker men
gains.b: the couplet gains a living addressee, a young claimant who must hear that his own strength is what the trap relies on

note: Kural 445 says a king walks with his counsellors as his eyes and must choose them with care; 1921 has Vijayai give the same rule, and at 1924 she says there are no learned counsellors here.
teaches: The couplet assumes a court to choose counsellors from; the exiled prince has none, so the rule becomes a measure of what he lacks and throws the choice back on his own resolve.

gains.a: Vijayai's lament gains force from the rule it cannot meet, showing why she asks what he himself has resolved
gains.b: the couplet gains its limiting case, a ruler without a court, where the eyes it requires must first be found

note: Kural 751 says nothing but wealth makes people of no account into people of account; 1922 says wealth makes the diminished into mountains, and 1924 names the speaker and her son as those diminished in lineage and treasure.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet, often read as a dry observation about upstarts, onto a fallen royal house, for whom wealth is the way back to the standing birth once gave.

gains.a: the mother's maxim gains a sharper edge, since the Kural's rule about the lowly is applied to princes who have become lowly
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where wealth restores rather than creates standing, which tests whether its rule is only about the low-born

note: Kural 760 says that for those who have made bright wealth the other two aims, virtue and pleasure, come together; 1923 makes gold yield army, army land, land wealth, and wealth everything.
teaches: Where the couplet makes wealth the way to virtue and pleasure, the mother's chain loops wealth back into power and more wealth, and only her own first condition in 1920, wealth got by justice, ties it to அறம்.

gains.a: the chain gains a measure: set against the couplet, it shows how far political counsel has narrowed wealth's ends to power
gains.b: the couplet's ஒண்பொருள் gains a contrast case, a cycle of wealth for power whose brightness depends wholly on how it was got

note: 1919 counts taking the daughters of hill and forest chiefs as the settled custom of kings whose rule stands; Purananuru 336 shows a king hot for a girl whose father will not give her, and the war that waits on it.
teaches: The epic's 'custom' is the king's side of a transaction that the Purananuru shows from the chief's side as a demand refused and a battle coming, so the policy's cost becomes visible.

gains.a: the mother's maxim gains the cost it leaves unsaid: a chief's daughter is not always given, and the alliance may first be a war
gains.b: the Purananuru's refusal gains the ruler's reasoning, marriage as policy for a firm throne, which the poem's anger does not state

audit_text_issue: line 4 ends in a doubtful word

note: The patikam promised that Civakan would enter the city's sky-high streets and fall into the sea of nectar of a maiden born by a boon; 1951 brings him into the street and shows her at her ball.
teaches: The patikam's figure of him falling into her sea of nectar is set up with a reversal: in the street it is the other women who shoot their eyes at him, while the destined maiden is first seen paying him no attention at all.

note: Routed kings cried that Civakan was Murugan on his peacock; the city's women now ask whether he is Murugan or Kama.
teaches: The likeness to Murugan that the defeated kings shouted in terror returns as a question of desire in the women's mouths, so one image carries both his name in war and his effect in the street.

note: Kural 1081's man cannot tell whether the woman is a goddess, a peahen or a woman; here the women cannot tell whether the man is Murugan or Kama.
teaches: The epic gives the first-sight bewilderment of the Kural's lover to a crowd of women looking at a man, and narrows the choice to two gods, so the doubt is no longer whether the beloved is mortal but which divine lover he is.

gains.a: the epic verse gains a recognised convention, the lover's dazed question at first sight, which marks the women's cry as love struck at a glance rather than plain praise
gains.b: the couplet gains a case with a plural female speaker, showing its doubt is a form of first sight that the tradition could turn round, not something tied to the man's voice

note: The epic praises the city's women for drawing back even minds bent on release; the Siddhar reproaches his heart for sinking into lust for women after keeping the company of ascetics.
teaches: The same lapse, a seeker of release pulled back by women, is the epic's yardstick of beauty and the Siddhar's confession of madness, so what one poet spends as a compliment is the very failure the other's renunciation is built to fight.

gains.a: the epic's hyperbole gains the view of the seeker it uses as a measure, for whom being drawn back is ruin and not a tribute to anyone's beauty
gains.b: the Siddhar's self-reproach gains the voice of the world he turns from, where the same pull is celebrated as a city's glory, so his struggle is against a culture's praise as well as his own heart

note: Kural 1085 asks whether the maiden's look is Death, an eye or a doe; Civakan asks whether her eyes are swords, mango slices, lilies, lotus, spears, arrows, carp, eyes, or Death come to kill.
teaches: Set beside the couplet's three-way doubt, the epic's ten guesses show the question turned into a catalogue that closes by choosing Death, where the couplet leaves the look holding all three at once.

gains.a: the verse's list gains a model: it is the couplet's riddle of the look, widened, not a loose string of comparisons
gains.b: the couplet gains a voiced scene, a hero dazed on a merchant's step, in which its question is asked of one particular woman

note: Kural 1083: the man never knew Death and now knows it in a woman's warring eyes. Civakan: those who named her called her woman; had they called her Death, men would flee the city.
teaches: The pair shows two steps of one discovery: the couplet's man learns that Death has a woman's form, and the epic adds that the name 'woman' hides it, so no one is warned in time.

gains.a: the epic's joke about naming is grounded in the couplet's discovery that Death and a woman are one
gains.b: the couplet's private discovery is made public: if it were known, a whole city would empty

note: Vimalai calls desire the one sickness with no medicine; Kural 1102 says the woman who causes the sickness is herself its cure.
teaches: Read together they show the two sides of one sickness: to the sufferer who cannot speak of it, it has no cure, while the couplet, spoken from the side of union, finds the cure in the beloved, which the story will supply by marriage.

gains.a: Vimalai's despair is shown to be a stage, not a verdict, since the couplet names the cure her story reaches
gains.b: the couplet's paradox gains a woman's voice, where the Kural gives the man's, and the cure turns out to be needed on both sides

note: Kural 1091: her eyes have two looks, one that gives the sickness and one that is its cure. Civakan, shot by her brows, asks what medicine there is for the wound and looks back at her.
teaches: The couplet's two looks are both hers; the epic gives the second look to him, so the exchange of glances, not one woman's eyes, carries both the wound and the hope of a cure.

gains.a: Civakan's question gains an answer the verse does not state: the cure lies in the look itself
gains.b: the couplet's single-eyed paradox is staged as a mutual exchange in which both lovers fall sick at one glance

note: Kural 1180: the town reads the secret of those whose eyes are beaten drums. Vimalai: her pallor beats out her desire like a drum (பறையாய் அறையும் பசப்பு).
teaches: The drum that proclaims a hidden love sits in the eyes in the couplet and in the skin's pallor in the epic, so the pairing shows the body as a whole betraying what restraint tries to keep.

gains.a: Vimalai's drum image is placed in an old line of thought about love that cannot be hidden
gains.b: the couplet's eyes gain a partner: the skin too announces the secret, and at first sight, not only after long love

note: In 1963 Vimalai holds that restraint and desire cannot coexist; in 1964 she stands steadying herself with restraint while desire seizes her.
teaches: Her rule that restraint and desire exclude each other is contradicted at once by the story, which shows a woman holding restraint and burning with desire at the same moment.

note: Kuruntokai 40's lover marvels that strangers' hearts mingled like rain and red earth; Civakan asks whether the woman who took his heart with one look knew him in a former birth.
teaches: Facing the same mystery of a stranger's sudden hold, the Sangam lover lets the merging stand without cause, while the Jain epic's hero reaches for a past birth, so the pair shows rebirth entering the love lyric as an explanation.

gains.a: Civakan's question is seen as a choice: the old poetry had answered the same wonder without any former life
gains.b: the Kuruntokai's uncaused union is set against a later frame in which love itself has a karmic past

note: Pattinattar lists the body as a feast thrown to the pyre's fire (ஈமக் கனல்) and a leaf scorched in the fire of desire (காமக் கனல்); Civakan's body, called a pyre (ஈமம்), burns in desire's fever (காமக் கடுநோய்க் கனல்).
teaches: The same pairing of pyre and desire's fire is a reason to renounce the body in Pattinattar and a lover's complaint in the epic, so the image does not carry its lesson with it: the hero who will one day renounce here uses it only to say how much he burns.

gains.a: the epic's hyperbole is shown to borrow the renouncer's figure, which the Cintamani will later take back seriously when Civakan renounces
gains.b: Pattinattar's figure is seen to be older than his use of it: in love poetry the pyre-body burns without teaching contempt for the body

note: In 1973 Sagaradattan suddenly sells six crores of goods while Civakan sits at his step; in 1977 the merchant tells that it was written at Vimalai's birth that goods would sell when her destined husband sat at his shop.
teaches: The unexplained sale is the fulfilment of a birth-sign told only afterwards, so the narrator lets the reader see the sign come true before learning that it was one.

note: In 1948 the city's women ask whether he is Murugan or the five-arrowed Kama; in 1961 Vimalai decides he is the son of the five-flower-arrowed god come down to earth.
teaches: The question the crowd of women asked and left open is answered by the one woman who will marry him, and for her the answer costs her modesty and restraint.

note: The sign written at Vimalai's birth, that the unsold cargo will sell when her husband climbs onto the shop, is the sale of 1973, made while Civakan sat lovesick at the shop front (1966).
teaches: The sale the merchant boasted of turns out to be a sign he had waited for since his daughter's birth, so Civakan's idle lovesick sitting is retold as the fulfilment of a prophecy he did not know.

note: Both brides have their husbands fixed by astrologers: Gandharvadattai's horoscope names the city where her destined groom lives (வந்தடை பான்மை), Vimalai's names the sign he will give.
teaches: Read together, the two horoscopes show the epic making each of Civakan's marriages a destiny read in advance, and fitting the sign to the father's world: a king's question about a place, a merchant's about goods that sell.

note: Here the narrator makes the couple one life in two bodies; in 1510 Kemasari, deserted, throws back at Civakan his own saying that love makes two lives one.
teaches: The oneness the narrator grants Vimalai is the formula Kemasari already turned against Civakan after he left her, so the reader knows before the dawn music that this union too ends in his going.

note: With Kemasari he rose while she slept and slipped out through the door unseen (1504-1505); with Vimalai he tells her he is going and promises a quick return.
teaches: Against the silent night escape from Kemasari, the open farewell to Vimalai looks kinder, yet it ends the same way in a departure, so the change lies in how he leaves, not in whether he stays.

note: The Kural's woman (or her friend) refuses a promise of speedy return: tell it to those who will still be alive. Civakan makes exactly that promise, quicker than an arrow, and Vimalai answers only with tears.
teaches: The epic stages the very speech the couplet refuses to accept, and the bride's silent tears in 1994 are the wordless form of the couplet's retort.

gains.a: Civakan's light promise is shown to be the stock comfort the Kural's speaker has already judged worthless.
gains.b: The couplet's retort gains a concrete farewell scene with the promise spelled out and a listener who cannot answer it.

note: The Kural's lover says his bond with the girl is that of body and life; the narrator says Civakan and Vimalai became one life in two bodies because they never parted.
teaches: The epic makes the couplet's body-and-life bond conditional on never parting, and then has the husband part at the next dawn, which tests the image the couplet offers as a pledge.

gains.a: The narrator's formula gains the force of a pledge, so his departure in 1994 reads as a breach of it.
gains.b: The couplet, a lover's pledge with no sequel, is given a sequel that shows what such a pledge is worth when the lover is a wanderer.

note: The narrator reports that the pleasure of Vimalai's breasts is worth the three worlds; the Naladiyar, a Jain didactic work, lists entrails, blood and bone and asks where among them the garlanded woman is.
teaches: The epic gives full voice to the valuation that the Jain didactic tradition exists to unmask, and hedges it as hearsay, so the praise stands as the worldly view that Civakan's later renunciation will have to undo.

gains.a: The hyperbole is placed as the very error a Jain reader is taught to dissolve, which gives it weight in the epic's arc toward renunciation.
gains.b: The quatrain's dissection gains a live instance of the praise it attacks, made within a work of the same religion.

note: The companion dares Civakan to win a girl who would refuse even Kama; in 908 Suramanjari had already excepted Civakan alone from her vow of self-containment.
teaches: The dare the companions think impossible was settled in advance by the girl herself, so the reader sees the conquest as a meeting she has already allowed and the hero's oath as courage spent on an open door.

note: In 899 Suramanjari vows to wait until the generous one comes defeated and worships her anklet feet; in 2012 Civakan arrives bent, panting and begging at her gate.
teaches: Her vow's terms are fulfilled to the letter in comic form, since the proud judge of the powder contest comes stooped and humbled, but in a guise he chose himself, so her victory and his stratagem are the same act.

note: In 907 her father buys a royal order with a priceless necklace that ends men's coming and going and even makes the carved figures female; in 2013 the guards let a man in out of pity for an old Brahmin's hunger.
teaches: A ban bought with the three worlds' worth of jewels fails not by force but through the guards' compassion for hunger and age, showing that the exclusion was drawn against young men's bodies and could not see past a guise of decay.
audit_text_issue: 907 line 3 வாள்வழக்கற்ற read as ஆள் வழக்கு அற்றது

note: Naladiyar 13 condemns the old who lean on a staff, toothless and tottering, yet keep their eyes on desire; Civakan, young, puts on that very figure with staff and white hair for love of a woman's beauty.
teaches: The quatrain's figure of shame, the old man still ruled by desire, becomes in the epic a costume a young lover wears to reach a woman, so the image meant to turn men from desire is used as an instrument of it.

gains.a: the comic disguise gains a moral shadow: the narrator's 'became even a ghost' reads as the quatrain's verdict on desire that will not let go
gains.b: the quatrain's staff and failing body are shown to be imitable signs, so its warning rests on a look that a lover can counterfeit and that guards pity rather than scorn

note: Kural 586 sends the spy into closed places in the guise of renunciants, undiscovered whatever is done to him; Civakan enters a house closed to men in the guise of an old Brahmin and holds his part under the women's threats (2014-2015).
teaches: The statecraft couplet's method, borrowing a status no one guards against, is shown working in love, and its clause 'whatever is done to him' is tested when armed women surround the disguised man and he keeps silent.

gains.a: the trickster scene gains a named technique, the spy's guise of the harmless, which explains why the Brahmin disguise works where force could not
gains.b: the couplet gains a demonstration of the guise's real lever, the protector's scruple, since the women spare him because harming a Brahmin is sin (2016)

note: In 2008 Civakan judges the gate easy to pass if he goes as a Brahmin; in 2016 the women hold back their weapons because touching an old Brahmin is sin.
teaches: The plan's premise is confirmed by the guards' own ethics: the protection owed a Brahmin is what admits the intruder, so a religious scruple becomes the hero's key.

note: Both name bathing at Kumari to be rid of a bodily affliction; the Thiruppugazh poet asks not to go there and be laughed at by many as a diseased wretch, and the epic's old brahmin goes there and is laughed at (பெரிது நக்கு, 2021).
teaches: Holding the two together shows that the afflicted pilgrim to Kumari was a stock figure of ridicule, and that Civakan chooses that figure as a disguise precisely because a man so laughable is trusted inside a guarded house.

gains.a: the epic's pretext is shown to be a recognisable, mocked practice rather than an invented whim, which explains why Suramanjari laughs instead of suspecting him
gains.b: the shame the Thiruppugazh poet fears is seen acted out, the laugh given by the very person asked for help, and turned to the trickster's profit

note: The Naladiyar warns that grey hair will come and youth will not return; Suramanjari scoffs that those who think a dead tree revives by rain are mad.
teaches: The Naladiyar's truth that age is irreversible becomes, in the epic, the very certainty a schemer relies on: because everyone knows the old cannot become young, no one looks for the young man inside the old one.

gains.a: Suramanjari's scoff is shown to rest on a sober didactic commonplace, so her being deceived is not folly but the misuse of a sound belief
gains.b: the quatrain's warning acquires a social use it never considers: the general certainty about age is a cover that disguise can exploit

note: The Kural says the fruit of tending a guest has no fixed measure but is as great as the guest's worth; Suramanjari feeds a guest she takes for a poor old brahmin.
teaches: The couplet assumes the host's offering and its fruit are reckoned by the guest's true worth; the epic shows a host who cannot see that worth, so the fruit she reaps, the end of her vow, is far beyond what she thought she was giving.

gains.a: the feast gains a frame in which its unforeseen consequence is the guest's hidden worth returning on the host
gains.b: the couplet's measure by the guest's worth is tested where that worth is concealed, showing that the return is fixed by what the guest is, not by what the host believes

note: In 899 Suramanjari vowed to hold out until Civakan came beaten and worshipped her anklet-feet; here he is inside her house as a begging old brahmin, singing to bring on the wedding.
teaches: Her condition is met in mockery: he does come to her low and dependent, a supplicant fed at her hands, yet the humbling is a mask he wears to win her, so the vow is kept in form and defeated in substance.

note: In 908 she resolved that only union with Civakan could break her nirai; here her women hear the song and praise the youth wrought into her mind.
teaches: The single exception she allowed in her seclusion is the one man already inside it, so the guard she set against all men admits the very one it was kept for, unrecognised.

note: At Gandharvadattai's contest his song shamed Kama (அனங்கன் நாண, 729); here his song makes him seem none other than the god of spring himself.
teaches: The music that won one bride openly, before kings, is now used covertly to win another, and the comparison moves from surpassing the god of love to being taken for him, as the singer's aim shifts from victory to seduction.

note: In 899 she vows to keep her vow until Civakan comes defeated and worships her anklet-feet; in 2056 she sets her own head on the temple floor and joins her hands to pray for him.
teaches: The prostration she demanded of the man who shamed her is performed by her, in his hidden presence, so the vow is undone in its own terms of who bows to whom.

note: 908 left one exception in her refusal: union with Civakan's gold-bright chest; 2057 asks Kama for exactly that chest (சீவகன் அகலம் சேர்த்தின்).
teaches: The exception hidden inside her vow of self-containment becomes the whole content of her prayer once a disguised song has worked on her, so the refusal was a waiting all along.
audit_text_issue: 908 line 2 பொன்றுஞ் சாகம் unclear; 'gold chest' not in the Tamil; 2057 repaired

note: In 885 the maid disputes Civakan's powder verdict to his face; in 2043 she repeats the grievance to him in his disguise, and he condemns the young man who gave it.
teaches: The judge of the powder contest now hears his verdict judged by the loser's household and joins in cursing himself, which is how the disguise wins their trust.

note: In 2052 she resolves to worship Anangan and win a boon; in 2058 the boon is granted aloud, by a man's voice she takes for the god's.
teaches: The boon she set out to win is granted, but by Civakan's companions, so the plot turns the god's grace into a human contrivance the narrator names as deceit.

note: Kural 1228: the herdsman's sweet flute is evening's envoy and a killing weapon to the woman whose lover is away; 2050 is a sweet vina-song whose evening enters like a spear into a wound.
teaches: In the Kural sweet music wounds a woman because her lover is absent, while in the epic the lover himself plays the music to a woman who has no lover yet, so the evening-song creates the sickness it laments.

gains.a: the epic's song gains the Kural's figure of music as evening's weapon, which explains why a lament can work as a seduction
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where the weapon has a wielder with a purpose, turning the woman's complaint into a strategy someone else can use

note: Sivavakkiyar asks whether a planted stone will speak; in 2058 a worshipper hears the shrine speak, and the narrator says the voice was a man's trick.
teaches: The Siddhar's scorn assumes the stone is silent; the epic shows a voice supplied to it by a hidden man, so the credulity he mocks can be steered by whoever stands behind the image.

gains.a: the comic oracle gains a doctrinal edge, since the Siddhar names the error of taking an image for a speaking god
gains.b: the Siddhar's rhetorical question gains a narrative case of what follows when worshippers do believe the image speaks: they can be deceived

note: Suramanjari vowed that no one but Civakan would break her restraint; now Civakan says her beauty has carried off his.
teaches: The vow that guarded her நிறை against all men is answered by the loss of his, so the restraint the story set out to test breaks first on the man's side.

note: She knelt in Kama's shrine and begged the god for Civakan's chest; he now bows to her feet as to a goddess and begs her grace.
teaches: Worship runs both ways in one shrine: the girl's prayer to Kama for the man is turned into the man's prayer to the girl, so the deity she addressed is replaced by the lovers themselves.

note: Civakan swore to join her tomorrow on pain of becoming a king who lets dharma go; her father gives her to him in marriage.
teaches: The oath sworn in secret is kept through the father's public gift, so the secret union is made lawful by the kin rather than by the lovers alone.

note: Kural 560 says that if the guardian does not guard, the cows' yield fails and the learned forget their books; Civakan's oath calls such a guardian's fate down on himself if he fails her.
teaches: The bent sceptre that the Kural treats as a public disaster becomes, in a lover's oath, the worst private penalty a man can name, which shows how deep the guardian's duty sat as a measure of shame.

gains.a: the oath gains its weight: without the couplet's picture of a land ruined by an unguarding king, the curse Civakan names would read as a stock phrase
gains.b: the couplet gains a use as an oath-penalty, showing that failing to guard was held a dishonour fit to stake a promise on, not only a policy failure

note: The father bought a king's order to keep men from his daughter; now that a suitor asks for her he can neither accept nor refuse.
teaches: His wealth could shut out a whole city's men but cannot settle a single proposal, and he falls back on the lack of past penance to explain a bind his money made.

note: Kural 270 says the destitute are many because few do penance; the rich merchant says he and his daughter have done none.
teaches: The couplet ties lack to the absence of penance; the epic puts the same reasoning in a rich man's mouth, so the want that penance would have prevented is a want of good fortune in a child, not of wealth.

gains.a: the merchant's cry gains a doctrine behind it, that misfortune is the fruit of austerity not done, which makes his helplessness a moral account rather than a complaint
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where the one who lacks is wealthy, showing that its இலர் need not mean the poor

note: Kural 1251 makes restraint a door bolted by shame, broken by desire's axe; Suramanjari drives off the bee of shame and waves the garland of chastity.
teaches: In the couplet restraint stands only while shame bars it; the epic has a woman put shame away in order to keep her chastity, so the two virtues the couplet binds together are parted and ranked.

gains.a: the epic image gains a known structure to depart from, so that her casting off shame reads as a choice for chastity rather than a fall
gains.b: the couplet gains a counter-case in which shame is given up without restraint failing, which shows its door-and-bolt bond is not the only order of the two

note: In Kuruntokai 333 the friend asks what harm there would be in revealing their secret; in the epic the girl discloses it to her friend, who carries it to the foster mother, then the mother, then the father.
teaches: The Sangam friend only proposes disclosure; the epic plays out the whole chain of telling through friend, foster mother and mother to the father, which ends in marriage the same day.

gains.a: the epic scene gains its name and purpose: it is the akam move of disclosing so that kin will arrange the marriage, not a confession
gains.b: the Sangam poem's single question gains the full sequence it sets going, showing who carries the secret and to whom

note: The mother dreamed that a flower pond ran dry and reads it as the girl's maidenhood gone; the secret union of 2063 is the event.
teaches: The dream is read after the event it pictures, so it serves the mother as confirmation of what the foster mother reported rather than as a warning.

note: The mother once told the father that their daughter burned with anger at Civakan's verdict on her powder; now she tells him the same man has won her.
teaches: The grievance that made the girl shun all men is reread as the cause of her chastity for one man, so the anger and the love are shown to have had one object.
audit_text_issue: 2077 line 2 obscure | 2077 line 2 பெருவளைப் பிட்டு is obscure.

note: Akananuru 86 recalls a wedding of rice, sand, lamps, water poured with petals and paddy by four mothers, and the kin giving the bride; the epic father gives his daughter before the fire with a dowry he announces.
teaches: Set beside the Sangam wedding, which names no fire and no dowry, the epic's gift before the flame with women, gold and villages shows the giving of a bride recast as a fire rite with property declared.

gains.a: the epic verse gains a measure of what is new in it, the fire and the declared dowry, against an older Tamil wedding
gains.b: the Sangam poem gains a later counterpart that shows by contrast what its rite lacks: a sacred fire and a stated transfer of wealth

note: Suramanjari vowed in 899 to keep apart until Civakan came defeated (தோற்று) and worshipped her anklet feet; in 2088 he lays his head on her anklets and her sulk ends.
teaches: Her vow is kept not by a defeat he admits but by a lover's bow inside a quarrel he says he did not cause, so the pride that began in a contest is satisfied by the rites of love.

note: The Kural says the loser of a lovers' quarrel is the winner, as union shows; Civakan casts himself as the small one who erred, yields, and wins her.
teaches: The epic gives the couplet's paradox a plot: a woman who swore to see the man defeated gets his surrender, and his surrender is exactly what wins him her.

gains.a: the hero's bow at her feet reads as a known strategy of oodal rather than humiliation
gains.b: the couplet's abstract loser and winner become a named pair whose defeat had been sworn as a vow

note: Naladiyar 77 says the great bear faults hard to bear, which is why their friendship is sought; Civakan uses the same maxim to plead with a sulking wife after denying any fault.
teaches: A maxim about the forbearance of the great in friendship turns, in a lover's mouth, into flattery that makes the angry woman the great one and so obliges her to forgive.

gains.a: the hero's maxim is seen to be a borrowed rule of friendship pressed into love's service
gains.b: the quatrain's rule is shown working as rhetoric: naming someone great lays on them the duty to forbear

note: In Kural 1311 the woman refuses his chest because all women feast on him with their eyes; Suramanjari refuses a chest many embrace like the Ganges.
teaches: The Kural's sulking pretext is that other women merely look at him, but in a polygamous epic where the hero has already married several wives the same refusal names a fact.

gains.a: Suramanjari's complaint is placed in the oodal convention, so it reads as play that leads to reunion
gains.b: the couplet's mock charge is seen with a literal referent, which shows how close the convention runs to real grievance

note: In Kural 1320 she is angry even at his gaze, asking whom he thinks of; here she is angry at his gaze on a painted figure, and he claims he took the picture for her.
teaches: The epic supplies the object the couplet leaves imagined, a painted woman on the wall, and turns the lover's defence round: his gaze was faithful because he mistook the picture for her.

gains.a: the epic scene inherits a precise oodal type, the jealousy of the gaze
gains.b: the couplet's suspicion gets a concrete rival and an answer the man can give, which it never offers

note: Kural 1269 says one day is like seven to those waiting for the absent one's return; Civakan tells Gunamalai the day he was parted from her was like an aeon.
teaches: The epic moves the measure of absence from the waiting woman to the returned man and inflates it from seven days to an aeon, said only once the parting is over and as a gift of words.

gains.a: Civakan's hyperbole is placed in the Kural's tradition of time stretched by longing
gains.b: the couplet's longing, which commentators argue about assigning to the man, is here plainly spoken by a man to the wife he left

note: The sage foretold that Civakan would be seized, carried off by a yaksha, and seen again after some days; in 2095 he comes home and his mother's grief ends.
teaches: The prophecy promised only that he would be seen again, and the return shows its cost: the mother was comforted by the word yet still wept herself thin until he stood before her.

note: In 1132 Gunamalai, near death with grief, clung to the sage's words as a raft; in 2099 Civakan says he survived by her penance.
teaches: The grief that the narrator showed Gunamalai surviving by holding to a prophecy is renamed by the hero as தவம், so her endurance becomes the cause of his rescue rather than only her consolation.

note: Kural 233 says nothing in the world stands undying except towering fame; 2107 takes the same unstable world and fame that stands, and uses the fame-seeker's wealth as a figure of what vanishes fast.
teaches: The pair shows the price side of the Kural's maxim: the fame that alone stands is bought with wealth that goes as fast as a desert crossed in a day, so lasting renown and fleeting riches are one transaction.

gains.a: the simile's ground, why a fame-seeker's wealth should be the very type of the fleeting, which the epic leaves unstated
gains.b: a concrete measure of how quickly the giver's wealth leaves him, which the couplet's praise of fame never shows

note: Kural 29 speaks of the anger of those who stand on the hill of virtue, held even for a moment; 2107 counts the anger of the holy among things that do not stay.
teaches: Read together, the couplet's crux over whether such anger lasts only a moment or is unbearable for a moment is settled one way in the epic, which takes its brevity as proverbial enough to serve as a simile of speed.

gains.a: a source and authority for the figure of the holy man's short-lived anger, which the epic uses without explaining
gains.b: an early reader's construal of its disputed second line, showing the brevity reading in use as common speech

note: The women of another city asked whether Civakan was the Vel of the kadamba or the son of the five arrows; Videham's crowd hails him as both, the spear-bearer who slew the mountain and Kama.
teaches: What was a puzzled question of desire in one city becomes a public litany of titles in the next, so the likeness to Murugan and Kama hardens from a woman's doubt into the name a whole city gives him.

note: In 2124 the women claim they learned their gait from the she-elephant and plead for a slow walk; in 2125 others call the same beast no she-elephant for its rough gait.
teaches: The two verses turn one convention, woman's gait as a she-elephant's, against itself: the beast that is the model of womanly walking is scolded for failing womanhood when its speed takes the hero from their sight.

note: The patikam lists Civakan's winning of his maternal uncle's daughter beside the spreading of his just sceptre; 2133 shows the first look between them in the uncle's palace.
teaches: What the patikam pairs as a dynastic gain alongside the sceptre begins here as a private exchange of looks before any council has met, so the marriage is grounded in love before it serves the war.

note: Vijayai once wept alone in the burning-ground forest for her lord; in her brother's palace she is the one who ends the household's weeping.
teaches: The widow whose solitary grief the poem dwelt on now stands among her own kin and stops their lament, so her restraint marks the turn from mourning to the counsel of revenge.

note: Kattiyankaran wept and joined his hands over Saccandan's body; his letter now protests that the blame of that death is false.
teaches: The usurper's tears at the pyre and his wounded innocence in the letter are one performance in two forms, which is why the reader, and Govindan, can see through the letter at once.

note: The narration says the minister, a great snake, swallowed Saccandan; the letter says an elephant threw and killed him and the sceptre merely slackened.
teaches: Setting the narrator's account against the usurper's shows the epic staging propaganda: the same death is a cruel sceptre spreading darkness in one telling and a stable accident in the other.

note: Kattiyankaran bowed and vowed to bear the yoke of rule blamelessly for Saccandan; now he offers his life and owns Govindan as lord.
teaches: The minister's vow of loyal service, already broken once, is reused word for word in spirit as bait, so the story teaches the reader to weigh his pledges by what followed the first one.

note: Kattiyankaran plotted to send the king to rule heaven and keep the earth himself; Govindan now resolves to take his life by the same kind of guile.
teaches: The guile that won Kattiyankaran the throne becomes the means of his own destruction, as Govindan names the symmetry outright, so the plot's justice is shown as treachery turned back on its maker.

note: The Kural warns that honouring one's own spy openly lets out the secret; Govindan honours Civakan's companions exactly as his own men so that the enemy's spies cannot pick them out.
teaches: The couplet's insight that visible honour leaks a secret works in reverse too: honour spread evenly conceals, so a king can hide his guests by treating them like everyone else.

gains.a: the epic verse gains a statecraft rule that explains why the even-handed gifts are a security measure and not plain hospitality
gains.b: the couplet gains the inverse case, where the same logic of visible favour is used to defeat an enemy's spies rather than to protect one's own

note: Kural 827 says the humble words of an enemy are like a bending bow; Kattiyankaran's letter bows, offers his life and calls Govindan lord.
teaches: The letter shows the bowed bow of the couplet in a full text, and Govindan's laughter (2148) shows the reader the couplet applied: the humbler the words, the plainer the threat.

gains.a: the epic letter gains a rule by which its humility is read as menace before the story confirms it
gains.b: the couplet gains a concrete instance with its parts in view: the professed loyalty, the false excuse, the invitation to come close

note: Kural 830 counsels befriending a feigned friend with the face while letting go in the heart; Govindan proclaims through the city that he has become one with Kattiyankaran while mustering his army.
teaches: The couplet speaks of an individual's face and heart; the epic turns the face into a public proclamation and the hidden heart into a state secret guarded by threat, so the mask needs the silence of a whole city.

gains.a: the epic proclamation gains the Kural's licence for a face of friendship toward a false friend, which makes the king's feint a known policy and not mere cunning
gains.b: the couplet gains its political scale: when a king wears the friendly face, his people must wear it too, and the cost is a gag on every tongue

note: In 2149 the Videha king tells his counsellors that as the usurper meant to kill him by deceit, they will take his life by deceit, and bids them keep it secret; 2176 has the narrator announce that very plan, with love as its sword.
teaches: The secret the king swore his counsellors to keep is opened to the audience but not to the victim, so the listener watches the gifts of 2174 and 2175 knowing what the usurper cannot, and the narrator names the plan deceit without blaming it.

note: In 2148 the king laughs at the letter that the wretch is calling Death with his own hand; in 2174 the usurper does not know that Death has come and camped outside.
teaches: The king's jest becomes the narrator's description: the Death the usurper summoned by letter now sits at his gate, and the gifts he sends out are his welcome to it.

note: The king's right eye throbs as a good sign and his drums roar as he sets out; in the usurper's palace the women's right eyes throb, owls cry by day and the victory drum falls silent.
teaches: The poet gives the two camps the same signs with opposite values, the throbbing right eye good for the marching king and bad for the palace women, the drum loud in one and dumb in the other, so the omen code is read by sex and by side.

note: Kural 830 counsels that when a foe must be treated as a friend, one should befriend with the face and drop friendship within; the Videha king makes himself one with the usurper so as to kill him by the sword of love.
teaches: The couplet's face-friendship is a defensive mask with an exit, while the epic turns it into the method of a killing and calls it வஞ்சம் even on the hero's side, so the pair shows how far the Kural's permission can be stretched once the foe is a usurper.

gains.a: the epic's ruse gains a rule of statecraft that makes a just king's deceit look like prudence rather than treachery
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where the outward friendship is not a passing shelter but the weapon itself, which its own wording does not reach

note: Kural 882 bids one fear the bond with enemies who are like kin more than enemies like swords; the usurper delights in the kinsman-like gifts of the king who means to kill him.
teaches: The couplet's warning is spoken to the potential victim, and the epic shows that victim praising the gift that should have frightened him, while placing the kin-like enemy on the side the story favours.

gains.a: the scene gains a name for the usurper's error: he guarded against the sword but not against the friend
gains.b: the couplet gains a plot in which its danger is visible to everyone but the one it warns, and in which the false friend is not the villain

note: Purananuru 20 says the Chera's guard is not shaken by omen birds coming or going; in the usurper's palace owls cry by day, blood rains and earth and sky shake.
teaches: Read together the two make portents a measure of rule: the praised king's realm is not shaken whatever the birds do, while the usurper's palace is shaken by every sign, though the epic does not itself say his usurpation is the cause.

gains.a: the epic's portents gain a puram standard by which a secure realm is one omens cannot move, which marks the usurper's as already lost
gains.b: the poem's claim gains its counter-case, a palace where the omens do strike, which shows what the praise of immunity is set against

note: The patikam's summary joins the shooting of the boar to the killing of the enemy in one line; Govindan's proclamation starts the scene that keeps that pairing.
teaches: Read against the patikam, the bride-contest was never chiefly about a bride: the work announced from its opening that the boar and the death of Civakan's enemy come together.

note: The proclamation that the man who shoots the boar shall marry the princess is fulfilled when Civakan brings down machine and boar together.
teaches: The impossible condition set in 2177, tested by a catalogue of failing kings, is what makes Civakan's single shot read as proof of a destined claim rather than mere skill.

note: The Kural calls not looking at another's wife the great manhood; the epic's simile grants that the heart goes out to her and places virtue in the wise man's recalling it.
teaches: Set beside the couplet's ideal of never looking, the simile shows a working form of the virtue the Kural allows only as perfection: the desire arises and understanding turns it back.

gains.a: the simile gains a fixed ethical rule, so the turning arrow is measured against the standard the Kural names as manhood
gains.b: the couplet gains a picture of restraint as a movement out and back, a second chance the couplet's flat 'not looking' leaves out
