note: The Kural says austerity is practised because it brings what is wanted as it is wanted; the narrator explains the kings' six days of failure by their ignorance of the greatness of ripened austerity.
teaches: The pair shows the couplet's promise worked out as a plot: what the kings want, they cannot get by wanting, and the one who wins does so by merit of austerity, so tapas becomes the hidden cause of a marriage.

gains.a: the narrator's aside gains a known maxim behind it, making the failures a lesson rather than a joke
gains.b: the couplet's general 'whatever is wanted' gains a concrete case where desire and skill fail and only earlier merit succeeds

note: Madanan swore to the king that he had split Civakan's chest and rolled him over; Kattiyangaran now sees Civakan alive and names Madanan's failure as his ruin.
teaches: Together the two verses show the usurper undone by his own system of lies: he rewarded a false report of a killing, and the man he believed dead returns to the very contest set as his trap.

note: In 1137 the soldiers who hem in Civakan scatter like deer that have seen a killing tiger; here Kattiyangaran himself cries out like a deer that has seen a tiger.
teaches: The same simile moves up from the king's soldiers to the king: the fear Civakan once struck in the men sent against him now reaches the man who sent them, and his own words in 2197 call Civakan the tiger.

note: Kattiyangaran fears that the escaped 'tiger' will crush him; in 2206 a voice from the sky proclaims that the lion Civakan will swallow the life of the elephant Kattiyangaran.
teaches: The usurper's private dread in 2197 is answered by a public sky-voice in 2206 with the same beast imagery, so his fear turns out to be accurate foresight rather than panic.

note: The failed kings laugh, asking whether the boar will break and fall of itself; in 2204 Civakan's shot brings down the machine and the boar together.
teaches: The mockers' jibe is answered in a few verses: what they said could not happen without effort happens at one shot, so their laughter becomes the 'fire' 2201 says they lit against themselves.

note: The prologue's summary joins two acts in one line, that Civakan shot the boar and killed the enemy; 2204 performs the first.
teaches: The prologue binds the contest shot to the killing of the usurper, so the reader knows the winning arrow here is the opening blow of the war, not a feat for a bride alone.
audit_text_issue: Both verses flagged uncertain; 25 line 4 subject unclear.

note: The epic likens the hero's arrows to the straight minds of the refined; the couplet holds that the straight arrow is cruel and that form proves nothing about worth.
teaches: Read against the couplet, the simile shows the epic choosing the arrow's straightness as a sign of virtue at the very moment the arrow starts a war of slaughter, which the Kural warns is the arrow's real nature.

gains.a: a check on its own praise: the straight arrow it calls a refined mind is, by the couplet, a killer's shape
gains.b: a case of exactly the misreading it warns against, where an admired shape stands in for goodness in a famous poem

note: The epic gives the usurper the larger host, and the couplet says that many steadfast men make no army without leaders.
teaches: The counts set Kattiyangaran's bigger force against Civakan's smaller one, so the coming defeat of the larger host turns the couplet's rule about leadership over numbers into a plot.

gains.a: a rule that explains why the counted advantage of the usurper will not decide the battle
gains.b: a story where the two armies are counted unit by unit and the larger one is the one fated to lose

note: Both make the Earth a woman on the battlefield: the Kalavazhi's Earth is wrapped red as in a fine cloth by the king's slaughter, the Cintamani's beats her breast and pines.
teaches: The same personified Earth that the praise-poem dresses in the victor's blood becomes in the epic a mourner, so the pair shows the one figure serving both the glory and the grief of a war.

gains.a: a sense of how pointed its grieving Earth is, set against the battle-praise convention that adorns her
gains.b: a counter-voice that turns its red-robed Earth from ornament to wound

note: The Purananuru poet asks whether the Pandya's spear did not stop short of ruin when it saw women made widows beat their breasts and shear their hair; the Cintamani names the widows' lost adornment as what the hero's spear will bring.
teaches: In the Sangam poem the sight of widows is what checks the spear, while in the epic the widows are counted in advance as the spear's work, so the pair shows grief for the enemy's women moving from a limit on war to its foreseen price.

gains.a: an older measure of a just warrior, who stops at the widows' grief, against which its raging spear is judged
gains.b: a later story where the same grief is foreseen and does not stop the fighting, which sharpens how rare its king's restraint was

note: Both set war as a sea with ships: in the epic the two armies meet as two seas with elephants as ships, in the Kalavazhi the blood drags elephants and drums like boats meeting on the sea after the slaughter.
teaches: The epic uses the sea at the moment of the clash, the Kalavazhi uses it for the blood that remains after, so together they show the sea image passing from the armies' living mass to the flood of their dead.

gains.a: the aftermath its own image points to: the seas that meet become a sea of blood
gains.b: the moment before its blood-sea, when the boats it shows were the living elephants of two hosts

note: In 257 Madanan told the council he settles things only by the sword, never by the mouth; in 2245 he falls at the mouth of a sword (வாளின்வாய்) in the war that the usurpation he urged has brought on.
teaches: The man who refused talk for the sword dies by the sword's 'mouth', so the epic answers his boast with its own wording and makes his death the fruit of his counsel.

note: Madanan falls like the moon swallowed by Rahu plunging into the sea; the Kalinga king falls like the sun dropping into the sea with a planet.
teaches: The two eclipse similes make the enemy's captains the moon and the sun of their side, so their two deaths together read as the setting of both lights of Kattiyangaran's host.

note: In 803, at his first battle, Civakan watches a ghoul dress herself in the slain and laughs with delight; in 2235 the same ghoul's feast is made from bridegrooms whose wedding garlands their brides had strung.
teaches: Where the first battle offers the ghoul's feast as spectacle for the hero's laughter, the final war sets it against the brides' garlands, so the same image now carries the cost of war to the women left behind.

note: Kural 780 calls a death that fills the eyes of one's patron with tears worth begging for; 2240's warriors have paid their debt of the red rice, and the only ones who cry over them are jackals.
teaches: The epic keeps the Kural's logic of a death owed to the lord but removes the weeping patron who gave that death its worth, leaving the debt paid with no one to mourn it.

gains.a: the Kural gives the epic's 'debt of red rice' its moral frame, a death owed in return for being sustained
gains.b: the couplet's patron's tears are shown to be absent on the actual field, where the howling of jackals takes their place

note: Puram 26 praises a Pandya who cooked a battlefield sacrifice with crowned heads for the hearth, blood for water and bangled arms for ladles; in 2235 the slain warriors themselves are the ghoul-woman's feast, their wedding garlands replaced by entrails.
teaches: The Sangam battlefield-feast is the victor's rite and his glory, while the Cintamani tells it from the side of the slain, as bridegrooms whose wedding garlands become entrails.

gains.a: the epic's ghoul-feast is placed in the old genre of the battlefield sacrifice it inherits
gains.b: the Puram's feast, sung only from the victor's side, is shown from the dead men's side, where it costs a marriage

note: In Puram 19 Death itself runs away ashamed from the field where mothers of old houses weep over their sons; in 2233 the Earth goddess, unable to look at the cruelty, veils herself in a red blanket of blood.
teaches: Both poems make a cosmic power recoil from the field, but the Sangam poem turns the recoil into praise of the king's valour, while the epic gives it to the Earth the hero fights to win, so the prize cannot bear the war waged for her.

gains.a: the conceit gains an older pattern in which a cosmic witness flinching from the slaughter measures its scale
gains.b: the Puram's recoil, used there to praise the victor, is shown able to judge the war instead, when the one who flinches is the land being won

note: Naladiyar 48 asks those who praise sandal and garlands whether they have not seen vultures tear the body once it breaks; 2244 sets the sandal-smeared chest that women embraced in the blood, embraced now by the sword.
teaches: The Naladiyar uses the ruined body to turn a man from desire, but the epic shows the same ruin of the beloved body in battle and draws no lesson from it, keeping beauty and slaughter in one image without preaching.

gains.a: the epic's image gains a name for what it shows, the body's adornment undone, which it leaves unspoken
gains.b: the quatrain's argument meets a case where the body is broken by war rather than age, and the poet still sees it as beautiful

note: The Kural's hero pulls the spear from his own body and laughs; Ulokapalan plucks the arrow from his forehead and the gushing blood is likened to the dawn sun's first ray.
teaches: Together they show the wound pulled from the body as a fixed sign of the hero, and that the epic turns the Kural's psychological shock, a laugh, into visual glory, so the same act is valued as composure in the one and as splendour in the other.

gains.a: the forehead-arrow is recognised as a stock heroic act, not a chance detail, which explains why the verse lingers on it before the kill
gains.b: the couplet's bare gesture gains a full scene with its consequence: the man who pulls the arrow is the one who kills in the next verse

note: The Kural says help to a foe in misfortune is the cutting edge of valour; Nabulan, seeing the Magadha king flinch, holds his blow, reassures him and goes elsewhere.
teaches: The couplet calls kindness to a stricken foe valour's sharpest point, and the epic shows what drives it in the moment: shame in the stronger man (நாணி), so that sparing is felt as a duty to one's own honour rather than as pity.

gains.a: Nabulan's laughing restraint is given a name as the height of valour, so it is not read as weakness in the middle of a battle
gains.b: the couplet's abstract ஊராண்மை acquires a motive and a gesture, the laugh and the word 'do not fear', that it does not describe

audit_text_issue: line 1 ஏந்தறன் is read, not certain

note: The Pandya Kudumi warns cows, brahmins, women, the sick and the sonless to take shelter before he shoots; Vipulan will not strike beasts, the wounded, the young or the old.
teaches: Both armies spare the weak, but on different grounds: the Purananuru's warning is the way of right (அறத்துஆறு) protecting those who cannot fight, while the epic grounds each refusal in the striker's own glory, so the same restraint can rest on dharma or on pride.

gains.a: Vipulan's code is seen as the epic's version of an old battle rule, and its distinctive turn, honour rather than protection, stands out
gains.b: the Pandya's proclamation gains a contrast that shows how particular its reason is: it names the protected by their vulnerability and their rites, not by what striking them would cost the warrior

note: The Kural prefers a spear that missed an elephant to an arrow that hit a hare; Vipulan will not strike even a rutting elephant, since a beast brings no distinction.
teaches: The Kural ranks quarry by size and danger and puts the elephant at the top; the epic's warrior ranks by kind and puts every beast below a man, so the two measures of a worthy target diverge exactly at the elephant.

gains.a: the oddity of refusing an elephant in war is sharpened against the proverb that makes the elephant the noblest mark
gains.b: the couplet's scale of targets is shown to be one of several: a code of honour among men can rank the elephant as no target at all

note: Nabulan will not strike an unarmed youth or even his elephant; two verses later the narrator states the code of not striking beasts, the wounded or the young.
teaches: The scene acts out first and the rule is stated after, so the code of 2261 reads as a summary of how this whole company fights, not as one man's quirk.

note: Vipulan offers the enemy heaven in exchange for leaving fame on earth; the challenger who answers him is killed and received into heaven by the celestial women.
teaches: The taunt turns out to be a literal promise kept: the one man who takes up Vipulan's offer gets exactly the heaven it named, so the challenge is courtesy as well as threat.

note: Purananuru 287 says warriors who do not run, if they die, enjoy the weddings of flawless women in the higher world; in 2265 the slain challenger is showered with flowers by celestial women and reaches heaven.
teaches: The Purananuru's reward is promised to one's own unflinching men to steady them; the epic grants it on the field to an enemy killed by the hero's companion, so the heaven of the brave is shown to belong to the fallen of either side.

gains.a: the apsaras' welcome is read as the old Puram reward for the unflinching dead, not a passing ornament
gains.b: the poem's promise, a speech to warriors before battle, is seen fulfilled as an event, and extended to the man who loses a fair duel

note: The Kural says one who tends his guests becomes a good guest of those in the sky; Vipulan calls his challenger a guest and gives him the first blow, and it is the guest, killed, who goes to heaven.
teaches: Read with the couplet, the duel inverts its exchange: in the Kural the host earns heaven by feeding the guest, while on the battlefield the host's hospitality is the first stroke, and heaven goes to the guest he kills.

gains.a: the word விருந்து in a duel is shown to carry the full weight of the guest-ethic, so the courtesy is not a figure of speech
gains.b: the couplet's tie between hosting and heaven is seen working in a setting it never imagines, where the guest is an enemy and the welcome is death

note: The Kampili king dies by arrows in the chest that women's breasts had ploughed; later the warrior whose chest is flushed from pressing women's breasts scatters burning arrows.
teaches: The chapter uses the lover's chest twice, once as the place where death enters and once as the source of the killer's fire, so the same mark of love signals both the victim and the victor.

note: The Kural's hero pulls the spear from his own body and laughs; the epic's youth plucks out the spear that fed on his flesh and laughs (பறித்து நக்கான்).
teaches: The epic gives the couplet's laugh a cause the couplet leaves open: the spear had been thrown by a man who kept his spear for elephants, so the wound is an honour and the laugh is the pride of having been judged worth it.

gains.a: the youth's laugh is placed in a known code of valour, so it reads as a canonical act rather than bravado
gains.b: the couplet's bare gesture gets a situation, the foe's choice of target in 2289, that explains why a wound is a matter for joy

note: The Kural calls it flight when a fierce man blinks at a flung spear; the epic's warrior does not blink at all (இமைத்திலன்) as the spear comes, and takes it on his chest.
teaches: Set beside the couplet, the verse shows where its standard leads: the unblinking eye is kept to the end, and the warrior who will not blink is the one the spear kills, so the code costs the life it measures.

gains.a: the stillness of the eye, one detail among many, is shown to be the decisive proof in the code of courage
gains.b: the couplet's test is followed to its consequence, a death embraced like a garland, which the couplet's question stops short of

note: The Kural prefers a spear that missed an elephant to an arrow that hit a hare; the epic's thrower would not cast except at a young elephant, and spends that spear on one warrior.
teaches: The couplet ranks targets; the epic shows the ranking used as a courtesy between enemies, a man of the elephant-only code paying a foot soldier the honour of the elephant's spear.

gains.a: the thrower's habit is recognised as the standard the couplet names, so his choice reads as tribute to the youth
gains.b: the couplet's private scale of glory becomes something one warrior can confer on another

note: In Purananuru 284 a warrior straightens his twisted sword with an elephant's tusk as lever (மிறையாக ... திருத்தா) and laughs at the fleeing back; Salanidhi straightens his elephant-bent sword in a lever (மிறைக்கொளீஇ திருத்துவான்) and the kings flee.
teaches: The pair shows the epic taking over a Sangam war vignette in its own words, the sword-straightening and the enemy's flight, but turning the Sangam hero's laugh into the foe's fear and making the man a spear-pierced warrior who dies in the next verse.

gains.a: Salanidhi's obscure gesture is clarified by the older poem's clearer picture of a sword set against a lever
gains.b: the Purananuru vignette is shown to have lived on as a set piece of heroic poetry long after the Sangam

audit_text_issue: 2293 line 3 மிறைக்கொளி corrupt; line 2 unclear | 2293 line 3 prints மிறைக்கொளி, read as மிறைக்கொளீஇ; line 2 வான் புண்ணுள் நீட்டி is unclear.

note: Purananuru 290 tells a king to give toddy to the warrior whose forefathers died for his, because he will shield the king from the spear; the epic's warrior says it is for a day like this that lords keep their men.
teaches: The two show the same exchange of sustenance for service from both ends: the Sangam poet urges the lord to pay in advance, and the epic's warrior, arming, counts himself as that payment falling due.

gains.a: the warrior's brief remark is seen as part of an old covenant between lord and fighter rather than a passing thought
gains.b: the bard's plea to the king is answered by the warrior's own voice accepting the debt

note: A warrior advancing laughs that men bold among women but trembling in battle have no manliness; Arichandan shames fleeing warriors whose heads women's feet have kicked.
teaches: The same taunt, the lover who yields to women must not yield in war, is spoken by an attacker scorning cowards and by a captain stopping a rout, which shows the epic's measure of martial shame is drawn from love and serves either army.

note: Kural 780 says a death that fills with tears the eyes of those who sustained one is worth begging for; Ariccandan's speech promises rewards to men who die helping the leader who raised and kept them (தற்புறந் தந்து வைத்த தலைமகற்கு).
teaches: Together they show the couplet's patron-bond being used as a battlefield appeal, and that it can be spent on a bad master: the leader these men are asked to die for is the usurper, and the speech wins only their deaths.

gains.a: Ariccandan's speech is seen to rest on the moral claim of the sustained man's debt, not merely on bribes of heaven
gains.b: the couplet's ideal is shown with its blind spot: it weighs the bond to the sustainer and not whether the sustainer deserves the death

note: The Purananuru poem says warriors who stand under arrows care nothing for fields because, dying, they wed flawless women in the high world; Ariccandan offers the same heavenly women (கடியரமகளிர்) and adds the poets' praise and the hero-stone.
teaches: The pairing shows the Sangam promise of heavenly brides surviving into the Jain epic as a commander's rallying formula, now stacked with fame and stone into a three-world reward, while the following verse turns its hearers into food for the hero's arrows.

gains.a: the speech is placed in a long tradition of the warrior's reward, which explains why the beaten men return to the fight
gains.b: the poem's confident claim is set in a story where those who believe it fight for the losing, unjust side

note: Dharmadattan warned Kattiyangaran that a king is a fire that turns nectar or poison as it will; at his end Kattiyangaran says it is good or bad deeds that turn poison to nectar and nectar to poison.
teaches: The same nectar-and-poison figure moves from the wronged king's power to impersonal karma, and the shift lets the usurper blame his fall on deeds in general rather than on the king he wronged, as he was warned.

note: Kural 380 holds nothing is stronger than fate, which forestalls any scheme; Kattiyangaran says the wise do not think of killing or being killed because deeds decide.
teaches: The epic gives the couplet's fatalism to a schemer whose own plot made the war, so the reader sees how the doctrine that fate outruns all devices can also serve to excuse the devices one has already used.

gains.a: the speech is seen to quote a sanctioned teaching, so its self-serving use is the point and not an error of doctrine
gains.b: the couplet gains a test case where fate is invoked by the guilty party at the moment of reckoning

note: The Naladiyar quatrain says that as darkness rushes back when the lamp's oil runs out, evil settles in when good deeds are spent; Kattiyangaran says that as a lamp dwindles when ghee and wick are gone, wealth perishes when the two kinds of deed wear away.
teaches: Both make karma the lamp's fuel, but the quatrain teaches renewing merit by austerity while the epic's usurper uses the image to explain the loss of a throne, so the lamp shows its political use: a fall can be read as fuel run out instead of a wrong repaid.

gains.a: the speech is seen to draw on a renunciant teaching image, sharpened by counting both good and bad deeds as fuel
gains.b: the quatrain's image is applied to kingship and wealth in a story, where it can be heard as self-excuse

note: Kural 775 counts it flight for the fierce to blink when a spear is thrown; Kattiyangaran says that if he blinks when a spear comes, Civakan may laugh.
teaches: The king splits outcome from courage: he grants victory to fate yet stakes his honour on the couplet's unblinking eye, so the pair shows the unblinking gaze as the one part of valour fate cannot take.

gains.a: the boast is read against a fixed measure of valour, which answers Civakan's taunt of fear
gains.b: the couplet's standard is shown held by a man who believes the battle's result is not his to decide

note: Kural 904 says the man who fears his wife gains no distinction from his deeds; Kattiyangaran's self-curse is that if he loses in valour he may become a base man who fears his wife (இல்லாளை அஞ்சி) and slights a guest.
teaches: The vow ranks fear of one's wife as a disgrace equal to defeat in battle, which shows the couplet's household fault serving as a warrior's measure of shame, the worst a king can wish on himself.

gains.a: the oath's odd household content is explained: it names a vice the moral tradition already marks as ruin of a man's action
gains.b: the couplet's fault is seen weighed against cowardice in war, which places it among the gravest failures of manhood

note: Boothappandiyan's vow wishes on himself, if he fails, separation from his wife, a weak sceptre and the loss of friends; Kattiyangaran's vow wishes on himself fear of his wife and the shame of slighting a guest.
teaches: Both are conditional self-curses whose penalties are drawn from household and court rather than the field, so the pair shows the vanjinam form keeping its structure into the epic while the epic gives it to the losing usurper, who dies at once.

gains.a: the speech is identified as a vanjinam of a known form, with its self-curse clauses
gains.b: the Sangam vow is seen in a story where it is not fulfilled, so the vow's force is shown as a matter of the speaker's cause

note: Dharmadattan warned that if Kattiyangaran seized the king who made him, Fortune would turn from him; here his rule, called a Kali-reign, perishes and the war is declared over.
teaches: The usurper's fall fulfils the councillor's warning given before the crime, so the story names his own deed as cause even though, dying, he gave everything to karma at 2314 to 2316.

note: Vijayai asked that her son be told all the evil she suffered after her lord died and be brought to her; here hearing his victory her tear-filled eyes grow cool.
teaches: Her grief, laid on the son as a charge, is answered by the victory, so the battle closes the mother's wrong and not only the father's loss of the throne.

note: At 2308 Civakan is likened to the white moon seized by a serpent; at 2324 he is the young sun that splits the serpent's mouth after many days.
teaches: The eclipse image moves from moon in the serpent's grip in the thick of the fight to sun breaking free after the king's death, so the hero's figure grows brighter as the usurpation ends.

note: Kattiyangaran promised to guard the earth so it would brim with gold once the king had gone to heaven; at the end the Earth goddess, bathed in his allies' blood, is taken by Civakan.
teaches: The usurper's claim to be the earth's guardian is reversed by the closing marriage of earth and rightful heir, which shows the ilampakam's title answering his first speech of seizure.

note: Vijayai's blessing at Civakan's birth, that he would utterly destroy his old enemy, is fulfilled when the city's women say he has killed the deluded one with all his sons.
teaches: The blessing spoken alone in the burning ground is fulfilled in public speech: the city, not the mother, now announces the destruction she foretold.

note: Kattiyangaran had told the suitors that only Kama himself could beat Gandharvadattai at the vina and that no such man was present; the women now call the king's slayer the vina-master.
teaches: The usurper's own boast that no rival existed names the man who would kill him, so the vina contest becomes the first sign of his fall.

note: Vijayai went from a sky-touching palace to the burning ground alone after the usurper killed her husband; now the usurper's women go from flower-cushions to the bare hot ground after his death.
teaches: The epic gives the usurper's household the very fall it gave the queen he wronged, and 303's reading of that fall as sin made visible is left for the reader to carry over.

note: The Kural says the tears of those who cannot bear oppression wear away the oppressor's wealth; when the usurper falls, the tears in the story are those of his own women.
teaches: The ruin that the tears of the oppressed bring on a bent sceptre falls in the story on the oppressor's women, who now weep in their turn.

gains.a: the women's tears get a cause beyond the scene: the wealth they lose was worn away by the tears of the city in Saccandan's fall
gains.b: the couplet's abstract 'wealth' is shown to include people, and its justice is shown to land on those who did not themselves oppress

note: The Naladiyar says kings who rode in state fall when their deeds give out and their foes take the wives they married; the Cintamani's victors break into the fallen king's palace and drive his women out.
teaches: The epic stages the quatrain's fall of a king but changes its last turn: the victors expel the dead king's wives rather than take them.

gains.a: the expulsion, which the verse narrates without comment, gets the quatrain's frame of a fall that comes when one's deeds run out
gains.b: the quatrain's 'foes take the wives' is shown not as the only end: a victor of the Jain epic sends them away instead

note: After killing Saccandan the usurper had his own name drummed from an elephant and, the poet said, the dark-hearted man won the goddess of fortune; now he and his sons lie dead and no one can say which of his women wore the queen's fillet.
teaches: The fortune the usurper seized in 297 is shown at its end as an empty title, and the ilampakam named for that goddess opens by taking her back.

note: Vijayai, hearing the usurper's victory drum, fainted like a doe struck by a spear (எஃகு எறி பிணையின் மாழ்கி); the usurper's queen, hearing of his death, sinks like a doe that has taken a spear (வேலேறு பெற்ற பிணை ... மாழ்கி) and dies.
teaches: The epic gives the usurper's wife the very simile it gave the queen he widowed, so the wrong done at the start comes home in the same figure, except that Vijayai survived to bear the avenger and this woman does not survive.

note: Saccandan's women stripped off their necklaces, garlands and ear-rings and cried that the king's cruelty was cruel; now the usurper's women put off ear-rings, bangles and garlands as a burden.
teaches: The stripping of ornaments that opened the epic as the price of the usurper's deed closes his reign on his own women, showing that the widowhood he caused is the widowhood his household inherits.
audit_text_issue: 295 sense uncertain; whose women in 2349 not stated

note: After the first great battle Civakan made a gold image of the Jina, gave wealth and put away the sin of the battlefield with lament; after the final battle he bows to the Jina and flings out gold before putting on his royal ornaments.
teaches: Read with 820, the morning worship and gift of 2357 are not ornament but the same rite of expiation after killing, now made the first act of the new king's day.

note: After the earlier battle Padumukan tended the wounded with ghee and cloths and sent them to beds; here Civakan himself charges his uncle with the care of the wounded before he rests.
teaches: The care of the wounded moves from a friend's improvised kindness to a king's first order, so the epic marks Civakan's kingship by who is told to look after the men who bled for him.

note: The Nedunalvadai's king walks the camp at midnight, a few men with him, looking each wounded man kindly in the face; Civakan tells his uncle to have the wounded tended and lies down to rest with women stroking his feet.
teaches: Set beside the Sangam king who goes out in the cold to see the wounds himself, the epic's victor delegates the duty and sleeps, which shows how far the later court poem has moved the king's care from presence to command.

gains.a: an older measure of royal care for the wounded against which Civakan's delegation and rest stand out as a choice
gains.b: a contrast in which its king's personal midnight round reads as a distinct ideal, not the only way a poet could honour a king

note: The Mullaippattu's king cannot sleep for thinking of the elephant with its trunk cut, the men who fell and the wounded horses; Civakan sleeps through the noise of wounds, weeping women and drums as if he heard none of it.
teaches: The two kings face the same night after battle with opposite responses, the one kept awake by the wounded and the other asleep amid their cries, so the epic's sleep is a sign of a war ended where the Sangam king's waking is a sign of one still going on.

gains.a: a reason to read Civakan's undisturbed sleep as the peace of a finished war rather than mere indifference
gains.b: a view of its king's sleeplessness as tied to an unfinished campaign, which the poem alone does not test

note: Kalladanar asks whether the Pandya's spear did not stop short when he saw the widows of his enemies beating their breasts and cutting their hair; Civakan's anger stops at the usurper's death and he offers the widows a living in the city or gold to leave with.
teaches: Where the Sangam poem praises the conqueror only for holding back his spear at the sight of the widows, the epic makes restraint into provision, the victor feeding or endowing the women his war has widowed.

gains.a: an older warrior ethic of sparing the enemy's women, which shows Civakan's speech as the fulfilment of a known ideal
gains.b: an example of how far the restraint it praises could be carried, from not killing to giving the widows a livelihood

note: Purananuru 194 sets the dirge drum in one house beside the wedding drum in another and concludes that the maker of the world is unkind; in 2356 one band of women swims in a sea of sorrow and another in a sea of joy on the same morning, while the hero washes his face.
teaches: The epic puts the Puram poet's split world of grief and joy inside one palace and makes one man's victory its cause, so what the Sangam poet blames on the world's maker is shown here as the plain consequence of a deed.

gains.a: a reflective frame that names what is unsettling in its quiet line about two seas of feeling side by side
gains.b: a concrete case in which the division of grief and joy is made by a human act, not by an unkind creator

note: The patikam opens with Saccandan, king of the unbending sceptre; Civakan's first order from the throne is to clear his realm of afflictions and have the drum announce it.
teaches: The son's first act as king is the sceptre's work that his father's reign set at the start, so the epic sets his crowning as the repair of the wrong the story began with.

note: The patikam says that Civakan renounces while kings bring tribute and his sceptre runs just; this verse ends the ilampakam on the people's peace and turns to what befell the king of kings.
teaches: The peace of 2377 is the height from which the patikam says he turns away, so the praise of his rule is the setup for the renunciation, not the end of the tale.

note: Kural 390 names giving, kindness, a straight sceptre and care of the people as the four that make a king a light; the proclamation of 2375 turns them into acts: remission of dues and the end of hunger, disease and enmity.
teaches: The couplet's four virtues become a single proclamation with named relief, which shows what giving and care of the people cost a treasury and who is to benefit.

gains.a: The proclamation gains a standard by which its remission and the ending of hunger are measured as the work of a king.
gains.b: The couplet gains concrete acts, a remitted tax, for virtues it only names.

audit_text_issue: பதிளை யாண்டை and குறுகடன் readings uncertain

note: Kural 557 says a king's lack of grace is for those who live what the lack of rain is for the earth; 2376 has the king's wealth go as grace to the blind, the sick and the wives abandoned.
teaches: The couplet states the cost of a king's lack of grace in the language of rain, while the epic names those who would be left dry, showing who counts as the people the sceptre owes.

gains.a: The proclamation gains the couplet's picture of grace as rain: help that reaches those who cannot ask.
gains.b: The couplet gains named sufferers, the blind, the sick and the abandoned wife, who are the dry land of its simile.

note: Naladiyar 3 says that even kings who rode in state under the umbrella fall when their deeds turn against them; 2371 seats the victor on the lion throne in the full pomp of such a king, after the usurper's fall.
teaches: The throne scene stands on the ground the quatrain describes: the pomp the winner now enjoys is what the usurper lost, so the crowning is shown as one turn of a wheel, not a rest.

gains.a: The enthronement gains a warning that the seat is held only while deeds support it.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a case in which the fallen king's rival, not death, is the agent of the fall.

note: In 2366 a god crowns Civakan with gold and sea-water; Tirumanthiram 1601 says that those who rule the three worlds wear crowns, but the bliss of the kings of the Lord's feet has no measure.
teaches: The Cintamani lets the crowning be the height of splendour, while the Saiva verse ranks the same crowned kings below those who serve at the feet, so what counts as the highest state is exactly what the two texts divide on.

gains.a: The coronation gains a rival measure of rank, in which crowns do not count, against which its splendour can be weighed.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram verse gains a full scene of a crowned king receiving the highest earthly honour, so its contrast has a concrete case.

note: In 1062 the astrologers fix the day and the party sets out for a bride; here the astrologer lays out the days for the elephant-lord and the wedding is carried out on the day named.
teaches: The astrologer's fixing of the day is the Cintamani's regular first step in a royal marriage, and here it gains a royal scale: a hundred and eight dressed elephants and a seven-day city festival.

note: 1687 has the wedding announced with the drum and the whole world knowing; 2388 shows how it is done, with the proclaimers dressed in white and sandal and carried on a battle elephant.
teaches: The wedding drum is a royal herald's act with its own costume and mount, which the earlier wedding announcement only names.

note: Naladiyar says a wife married on a fixed day, with the drum beaten that many may know, is the wife a man should keep to; the epic shows that drum beaten from an elephant and the day set by an astrologer.
teaches: The Naladiyar's drum and fixed day are the public face of a marriage, which the epic acts out as a city-wide command.

gains.a: the epic's drum is given its moral weight, since a bond announced to all is the bond that shuts the husband off from another's wife
gains.b: the Naladiyar's drum and fixed day, only named in the quatrain, get a full royal scene: the herald, the elephant, the seven days of orders

note: The Akananuru man remembers a wedding of sand spread under a pandal, lamps and garlands at an auspicious dawn; the Cintamani's order has plantain and areca, aloe pots, lute and dance and golden flags across the city.
teaches: The same wedding adornments grow from a household's sand pandal to a king's command that the whole city be decked, and so show how rank changes the scale and not the parts.

gains.a: the epic's royal decking is seen to rest on the household's pandal, sand and lamps, which it enlarges and does not replace
gains.b: the Akananuru wedding, remembered only in the bride and groom's house, is set beside a city-wide wedding and shows how small and private it is

note: In 605 the drum proclaims alms to ascetics and hard penance while still in the body; in 2389 the drum cries to wear pearls and sandal and dress in fine cloth.
teaches: The one royal drum serves both a call to wear away the body in penance and a call to adorn it, so the epic's ideals of renunciation and of festival sit side by side without being reconciled.

note: The Naladiyar says the same wedding drums that sound in the hall may be funeral drums that very day; here a wedding drum thunders for seven days and the city is told to live.
teaches: The Cintamani's wedding drum is heard here only as joy, while the Naladiyar hears in the same sound the fragility of the groom's life, so the two give opposing readings of the same instrument.

gains.a: the epic's drum gets a shadow of impermanence which the Jain poet leaves unspoken here but may mean the reader to carry from the epic's end
gains.b: the Naladiyar's warning is given a concrete scene of seven days of festival to be undone, not only the bare image of a drum

note: The city's wealth is compared to a grove of wish-granting trees with honey-dripping garlands and ambrosia in the first ilampakam; here the festival goods held up in incense smoke make the city look as if the golden wish-trees and the wish-creeper had taken it.
teaches: The same wishing-tree figure that praised a city's standing wealth is now used for the wealth brought out for a wedding, so the epic's image of plenty follows the occasion.

note: The wedding instruments sound and the carp-eyed women go to the bath; the Naladiyar quatrain says the drums that sounded as wedding drums may sound that day in that place as funeral drums for the bridegroom.
teaches: The epic gives the drums only their joyful sound, and the quatrain reminds the reader that a hero's wedding festival is not yet a safe ground for pride, which matters in a poem that ends with its hero leaving the throne.

gains.a: The festival's drums and blessings, which the verse sounds only for joy, gain the warning that the same drums can turn funereal, which the verse never says.
gains.b: The quatrain's general rule gains a long, fully dressed wedding of a hero who will later fear kingship, so the lesson meets a concrete story.

note: The king reads Vijayai's dream of the shoot and crown as her son's rising fortune; at the ghee-anointing the women now bless him to be lord of the wheel and to abide with Fortune.
teaches: The fortune that the king foretold from the dream is voiced as a blessing in the rite, so the reader sees the prophecy being fulfilled step by step.

note: After the cattle-raid the women wished that the young elephant of a man wed the earth too; at the anointing they now wish that he be wheel-lord and live in Fortune.
teaches: The earlier, offhand wish for him to wed the earth returns as a formal blessing in a rite, so the epic marks how far his standing has risen since the cattle-raid.

note: After the last battle he is called a Kama even to the wise as he sits like a lion in his silk; at the wedding bath he again becomes Kama to the women of fragrant hair.
teaches: The poet gives the hero the Kama figure in victory and again in his wedding dress, so the epic ties his beauty first to conquest and then to marriage.

note: The guards wave countless whisks and the festival's wealth is beyond count; the poem's summary says that while kings brought tribute and fortune stayed, Civakan heard the dharma, feared kingship like a snake struck by thunder, and renounced.
teaches: Read with the closing renunciation, the countless whisks mark the height of the splendour he will later flee, so the poem's praise of kingship is held against its end.

note: The onlookers of 637 say the bride's girdle and breasts are Death upon Death and that the anklet bells cry to the suitors to run and save their lives; here Death has come in the king's daughter's form and her girdle, anklet and bells cry to the onlookers to go and guard their hearts.
teaches: The cry that was gossip at Gandharvadattai's contest becomes the ornaments' own speech at Lakkanai's wedding, so the adornment itself is made the warning.

note: Kural 1083 has a man say he never knew Death and now does, it being a woman's grace and large war-eyes; 2451 says Death has come in a king's daughter's form and her own jewels bid the onlookers flee.
teaches: The couplet turns Death into one man's private discovery, while the epic makes it a public warning given by the jewels, so a figure of suffering becomes a danger announced to a crowd.

gains.a: a source for the figure of the woman as Death, which shows the jewels' warning is a figure for the pain beauty gives and not an idle boast
gains.b: a scene of bride, ornaments and a watching crowd that shows what in her dress the poet reads as a weapon, which the couplet leaves to the word பெண்டகை

note: The dresser nips flowers with her curved nail to print the bride's forehead mark, the opening of a householder's life; Vijayai, turning ascetic, takes the mark off with her finger, with the ear-rings and pearls, to close it.
teaches: The same mark and the same ornaments are put on to begin a marriage and taken off to end a life in the world, so the epic shows adornment as the sign of entry and renunciation as its undoing.

note: The dresser takes off the bride's tusk studs and plain ear-rings and sets wedding ear-ornaments (கடிப்பு); the herdswomen take off the herd girl's gold ear-studs and gem pendants and set the same auspicious கடிப்பு with a small simple adornment.
teaches: The same step in the rite is done in the same words for a king's daughter and a herd girl, showing the rite fixed while the stuff of the ornaments shows the wealth of the house.

note: Civakan adorns the dancer by the stage rules, tying the band, crowning, setting sandal and jewels; the bride's dresser, who knows every treatise, dresses the bride's hair by the hand-books.
teaches: Both scenes make dressing a learned craft with its manuals, so Lakkanai's toilet is told as an art practised by a master and not as vanity.

note: Gandharvadattai is bathed in scented water brought in gem pots on elephants' heads; the king's daughter is bathed with water in a jewelled pot on a white musth elephant.
teaches: The bath on an elephant's pot is the royal bride's rite in two marriages, which marks Lakkanai's wedding as one in the line of the contest bride's.

note: The city women take Civakan for Kama who has put down his arrows and come in person; here Kama himself forgets his bow and arrows before the adorned bride and hides.
teaches: The poem gives the hero the god's looks, then lets the bride overcome the god, which sets her beauty above the hero's.

note: The dresser draws the creeper of desire in sandal paste on the bride's breasts; the Naladiyar asks whether those who praise sandal and garlands have not seen vultures tear the body when the axle of its cart breaks.
teaches: The painted creeper is told as a high art at its best, so the Naladiyar's corpse image is shown to answer not coarse adornment but the finest.

gains.a: the other side of the sandal-paste art, the body that lies under it, which the tender scene never looks at
gains.b: a worked scene of sandal and garland laid on with great skill, which shows what its warning is aimed at and why it needs saying

note: The narrator says her adorned beauty would bewilder even the steady; the Tirumanthiram tells the heart to turn from women who smile and show their breasts, as the etti tree's fruit is good to look at and not to eat.
teaches: The narrator and the Saiva teacher agree that adorned beauty overcomes the heart, but the narrator offers it as wonder and the teacher as a poison to resist.

gains.a: a remedy, the turning away of the heart, which the narrator names as a sickness but does not prescribe for
gains.b: an instance of beauty so dressed and so praised that the warning is tested against the strongest case, not left as a general rule

note: The bangled women stand desiring the bride's eyes, breasts, hips and hair; the Naladiyar tells the reader not to desire a woman for her spear-like eyes, for she too will stoop and walk with a staff for eyes.
teaches: The gaze that the epic lingers on is the one the Naladiyar answers with the staff of old age, giving the scene's longing a time it will pass through.

gains.a: a limit of time on the beauty so intently looked at, which the scene itself does not offer
gains.b: a particular pair of eyes, hips and hair worth the longing the quatrain says to resist, so its warning has something to weigh against

note: After the ornaments cry that Death has come, the chowries, sandal fans and white parasol hide the girl for fear of what the graceless would do to the rolling world.
teaches: The screening is the household's answer to the danger the ornaments announce, so the verse before it is read as a threat to be guarded against and not praise only.

note: Verse 26 in the opening summary has Civakan winning the nectar-like beauty of his maternal uncle's daughter; 2460 brings that daughter, from Govindan's mountain, to the sacrificial hall to be given.
teaches: The poem's opening promise of this marriage is kept here with Vedic rite and a king's gift-water, so the reader sees the match as one planned from the start with the uncle's daughter given by her father's house.

note: Verse 29 says Civakan will no longer want the pleasure of women; 2477 shows the pleasure he had in marriage in its fullest.
teaches: The full wedding night shows what the hero gave up at the end, so his later renunciation of pleasure counts for more than a hero who never knew it.

note: In Kural 1146 the woman says gossip spread like the serpent seizing the moon after one sight of him; in 2461 the shy bride's hidden face is the moon in the serpent's grasp.
teaches: The same moon-and-serpent figure stands for exposure in the Kural and for modest hiding in the epic, so the figure is a flexible one for a face that is partly seen.

gains.a: The bride's shyness gains a ready sign of what is hidden, a shame that the Kural's woman does not have because her secret is out.
gains.b: The Kural's couplet gains a contrast in which the same image means a lawful, guarded display, not a scandal.

note: The wedding verses lay out darbha, sticks and ghee for the fire with care; siddhar 372 lists observances, vows, the Vedas, fire rites and water offerings as among the outward forms the Siddhar puts aside.
teaches: A Jain poem makes the fire rite the centre of a happy wedding while the Siddhar counts the same fire rite among forms to be left behind, so what counts as a sacred act depends on whether the aim is a household or release.

gains.a: The rite's careful detail gains a sceptic who judges all such rites as outward.
gains.b: The Siddhar's list gains a case of the rite performed for a wedding, a purpose the Siddhar does not address.

note: 2466 reports the fire rising right as an omen of fortune; Tirumanthiram 551 says the way of sacrifice has no way through while the eight-limbed yoga path leads to samadhi.
teaches: The epic reads the fire as a sign of worldly fortune, while Tirumular reads the same fire path as a dead end for release, so the same rite is a good for the household and no good for release.

gains.a: The omen of fortune gains a view that the fire gives no release.
gains.b: Tirumular's dismissal gains a scene in which the fire's use is worldly luck and not a claim to release.

note: In 2467 drums, conches and kings roar as the bridegroom takes the water; Naladiyar 23 says the same wedding drums can sound as funeral drums that very day.
teaches: The roar of the wedding drums sets Naladiyar's warning on how soon joy turns, and the epic's later turn to renunciation is its own answer.

gains.a: The wedding's loud joy gains the reminder that it may not last.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a full wedding in which the drums actually sound.

note: Kural 1251 says desire's axe breaks the door of restraint barred with shame; 2477 shows the bride's shame giving way within a sanctioned marriage.
teaches: The Kural treats the fall of shame as a defeat, while the epic shows it fall inside a rite-bound marriage, so shame is given up here without the loss the Kural fears.

gains.a: The bride's drained state gains a rule against which shame's giving way is not a fault.
gains.b: The Kural's couplet gains a case in which the bar of shame lifts lawfully.

note: The bride's ornaments protest that the 'king of kings' turned cruel-sceptred will not look into or hear their clamour (ஆய்ந்து கேட்டு மருளான்); the couplet says the ruler who does not examine daily and do justice loses his land.
teaches: The poet borrows the courtroom picture of the deaf king who spurns a plaint to make a lovers' jest, which shows how familiar the Kural's failed-hearing image was as a figure.

gains.a: the jest gets its edge from a standard of judging that the verse never states and the couplet supplies
gains.b: the couplet is shown being used by a poet to joke about, not to condemn, the king who will not hear, which its own grave tone cannot show

note: The wedding dresses the bride in a necklace that seems to own her body; the quatrain says nothing goes with a person but their deeds, and the body they guarded and adorned is no use when Death seizes it.
teaches: Set beside the quatrain's warning, the wedding's lavish adornment of a body reads as the thing the Jain moral is aimed at, which the festive verse itself does not say.

gains.a: the adornment gains a counter-voice that questions what the necklace and razor-work are for
gains.b: the quatrain gains a concrete, joyous scene of body-adorning to push against, where it only names the body in general

audit_text_issue: 2502 grammar of lines 2-3 hard | 2502 lines 2-3 are syntactically hard.

note: The patikam promises that Civakan wins the maternal uncle's red-eyed daughter; here he sits beside the spear-eyed bride on the wedding couch.
teaches: The patikam's one-line promise is cashed here as a full wedding in which the groom is shaved, bathed and seated, so the reader sees what 'winning her' came to in rite.

note: The wedding spends its verses on adorning the body and delights of marriage; the patikam says that Civakan, afraid of kingship, hears dharma and renounces at the Knower's feet.
teaches: The lavish bodily pleasure of this marriage is the very life that the patikam says Civakan will at the end put down, so each wedding adds weight to the later renunciation.
audit_text_issue: 2502 sense uncertain; grammar of lines 2-3 hard

note: Kural 1320 has the sulking woman accuse a man who only sits gazing at her of thinking of someone else; here Civakan's unblinking gaze and watering eyes make Ilakkanai say he weeps thinking of others.
teaches: The epic shows that the suspicion in the couplet can grow from the very rapture of the gaze, so the quarrel is a love's misreading and not a sign of a wandering heart.

gains.a: the sulk is placed in the Kural's recognised pattern of a wife who suspects her husband for what he does with his eyes
gains.b: a story in which the suspicion is false and ends in laughter, which the couplet does not tell

note: Kural 1329 has the man wish the sulk would go on and the night lengthen so he might keep pleading; Civakan, pleading through the bees, calls her anger the fruit of his own past sin.
teaches: Where the couplet relishes the plea as part of love's game, the epic lets the husband feel the quarrel as an undeserved punishment, so the same scene reads as pleasure or as pain by the speaker's mood.

gains.a: his plea is shown to be, in the Kural's terms, a stage of love's play that he has not yet found pleasing
gains.b: the cost of the pleading, which the couplet leaves out, the fear that one's love is being punished for a past wrong

note: Kural 1327 says the one who yields in a lovers' quarrel wins; Civakan yields first, but the quarrel ends when the parrot threatens to hang itself.
teaches: Yielding does not by itself end the sulk in the epic; it takes the comic shock from a third party to break it, which limits the couplet's rule that the loser wins.

gains.a: Civakan's earlier abasement is shown to be only half of what wins her, as the Kural's rule would suggest
gains.b: a case where a rule about the two lovers alone needs an outside agent, here the pet

note: Naladiyar 384 praises a wife who knows when to sulk and relents sweetly; Ilakkanai relents only when the birds' scene makes her laugh, and gives the smile as her reward.
teaches: The quatrain's wife relents of her own judgment, while the epic's wife is brought round by a joke at her own expense, so the ideal is softened by what the story shows of how quarrels actually end.

gains.a: Ilakkanai's smile is read as the sweet relenting the quatrain prizes in a wife
gains.b: the quatrain's ideal is given a scene that shows what makes a sulk melt

note: Gunamalai's red-beaked parrot, her only refuge, was made her go-between in love; here the household parrot, with its mock death, becomes the go-between that ends a lovers' quarrel.
teaches: The parrot appears again as the love-story's helper, but at Gunamalai's side it carries a plea across a distance while at Ilakkanai's it mends a quarrel within the bed-chamber.

note: 2326 had the victor bathed as for anointing with the blood of crowned kings, joined to the Earth goddess; now, riding Culamani, he treads on the crowns of kings.
teaches: The anointing promised in the battle's aftermath is fulfilled in the procession, where the defeated and allied kings' crowns are laid beneath the hero as a public sign of his rule.

note: After the victory, 2327 had him enter the old city worshipped by its people; now, wedded, he rides into the street among kings with whisks and drums.
teaches: The victor's private return becomes a king's state procession, with the same city now seeing him as a husband and sovereign.

note: The verse measures a breast's shrinking against a king who will not hear justice; Kural 553 says such a king loses his land day by day.
teaches: The poet treats the sceptre's decline as a stock yardstick to measure the shape of a body, so the epic's court ethic works as common knowledge rather than argument.

gains.a: A known doctrine of the king's loss that makes the simile of shrinking legible without explanation.
gains.b: A sign the couplet's rule was assumed outside moral discourse, used even in description of a woman's body.

audit_text_issue: Sense flagged uncertain; the simile's grammar is unclear.

note: The verse says the people honour only the rich and the poor have no kin, using it as a simile; Kural 752 states that everyone scorns the poor and honours the rich.
teaches: The Kural states the world's partiality as a fact and the epic applies it as a simile, showing the poet treats it as shared knowledge and as a cost on the neglected waist.

gains.a: A flat statement of the rule that the simile of the neglected waist depends on.
gains.b: A case of the rule seen in an unexpected place, the jewelling of a body, not in money.

note: The women speak a desire and beg with their eyes, while Kural 1100 says that when two pairs of eyes agree, mouth-words are of no use.
teaches: The Kural's silent agreement of two pairs of eyes needs the other side's glance; the women here ask in words and eyes for what he has not yet answered.

gains.a: A standard that shows the women's begging as one-sided and so not yet the eye-agreement the Kural names.
gains.b: A counter-case where eyes and words both ask, showing the couplet's agreement needs two parties.

note: The kings in the battle cried that Civakan's chariot was the peacock and he was Murugan; the women now call him Murugan's younger brother.
teaches: The same god-likeness that struck the kings with terror strikes the women with desire, showing the epic fits one figure to two audiences.

note: In 473 his foster father Kantukkatan receives him lovingly as if Indra's son had come; here the women call him a lion fed by Kandukkan.
teaches: The merchant's rearing, hidden in the early books, is now the credential in the city's praise, showing his birth in a merchant house is part of how he is seen as a king.

note: Padumai, after one look at Civakan, lost restraint, bloom and bangles; the women of the city now say they lose their bloom and bangles after seeing him.
teaches: What Padumai suffered alone is now the whole city's lot, so his beauty is shown to unsettle a crowd as well as one girl.

note: The people of Govindai's ilampakam said that the good mother who bore the lord must have done great penance and asked on which hill she did it; here the women of the city again set a mother's penance behind the son's glory, and name Sunandai as the great vower.
teaches: The street's guess that a hero's greatness is a mother's earned penance is first a wonder at his youth and is now a verdict on his rule, and the woman named for it changes from the one who bore him to the one who raised him.

note: At the birth in the burning ground the child shone like the sun from the sea, gem lamps drove off the dark and the place's deities bowed; the people now call up that same birthplace beside his rise as a merchant's son and kings' lord.
teaches: The burning-ground birth that was a picture of desolation becomes the first term of a turn of fortune that the epic offers as a reason to take up tapas.

note: Kattiyangaran took the land by a gift of law that was no true gift (வஞ்சம்) and gathered its wealth; Civakan now picks out all that belonged to him and gives it to Govindan, the uncle who stood with him.
teaches: The usurper's hoard is not destroyed but passes to the kin he had wronged, so the plot closes the fraud of 240 by moving the goods, not by punishing anything beyond the man.

note: Civakan whispered the five mantras into the dying dog's ear, seed that frees one of former karma, and the dog became a yaksha; the friend whose story he now has danced and whose golden image he sets up is, if the friend is that god, the debt repaid for that mercy.
teaches: A kindness to a dying animal is paid back in a rescue and then in the first public memorial the epic records, so the charity of 945 outlasts the dog's death in the city's own ritual.
audit_text_issue: line 1 of 2573 corrupt | 2573 line 1 நீக்கிப் யாய is corrupt (for நீக்கிய); 945 line 4 குதற்செய்கை is unclear.

note: The world asks 'what penance must he have done' and the king repays the one who reared him with a queen's title; the couplet makes that very kind of question the repayment a son owes his father.
teaches: The couplet's repayment is a sentence the world speaks; the epic adds a repayment made in rank and land and paid to the nurse, so the debt to one who raised a child need not stay in words and is not only the father's.

gains.a: the couplet's frame that the world's astonished 'what penance did he do' is itself the son's gift, which the verse leaves as bare talk
gains.b: a case where the debt is paid in rank, land and the title of queen, and to a rearing mother, which the couplet's wish for a father's good name never reaches

audit_text_issue: Sense flagged uncertain; recipient of the feast unnamed.

note: Wealth does not come across seas and mountains without fortune, and may come home to those who go not a cubit; the couplet says what is not one's own will not stay and what is will not leave.
teaches: The epic draws the practical conclusion the couplet leaves unsaid: if wealth is the share fortune gives, the effort spent seeking it is better spent on tapas.

gains.a: the couplet's flat rule about fate that grounds why effort for wealth is not the safe course
gains.b: a seafaring merchant's world of crossings and sickness, which the couplet gives no instance of, and a use for the rule in recommending tapas

note: Poison, hiding and the elephant's tusks are the dangers the strong in tapas escape; the couplet says austerity's power lets one even leap past Death.
teaches: The Kural states the power of tapas at its limit and the epic lists the particular harms it turns aside, and adds that when tapas is spent no flight saves.

gains.a: the couplet's claim that tapas power reaches even to Death, beyond poison and tusks
gains.b: named perils (poison, the tusker) and the warning that spent tapas leaves no hiding place, which the couplet's bare 'even leaping past death' lacks

note: Civakan lays his endowment at the feet of the one who walked on the red lotus; the Kural's opening couplets name the one who walked on the flower and promise long life to those who reach his feet.
teaches: The epic names the lotus and puts a temple and a gift at the feet, filling in the figure the couplet leaves open, so it shows one tradition's reading of the lotus-walker as the Jina's temple god.

gains.a: the couplet's idea that to reach the lotus-walker's feet is the aim of the faithful and not only a courtesy
gains.b: a worshipper's act of endowing the feet with lamp, towns and chariots, and a reader who takes the lotus-walker as the Jina, which the couplet does not say

note: Civakan raises a golden image and a dance to the friend who wiped away his trouble, and that friend was once a dog who changed birth; the couplet says the friendship of those who wiped away sorrow is remembered for seven births.
teaches: The Kural's memory across births becomes a literal chain from dog to god, and the epic makes the memory public and material in image and dance where the couplet leaves it in the heart.

gains.a: the couplet's measure that a rescue is owed memory beyond one life, which explains why a gold image is not too much
gains.b: a case where the friendship does cross births and is kept up in public ritual, which the couplet has only as a promise

note: The people see the hero's birth in the burning ground, rearing as a merchant's son and the kings' worship and ask why one should not do tapas; the quatrain has the best renounce home, youth, beauty, repute, wealth and strength because none lasts.
teaches: The Naladiyar argues renunciation from the failing of goods in general, and the epic argues it from one life in which a single man has held every state, so the argument rests on a case the hearers have seen.

gains.a: the quatrain's list of what fails (home, youth, wealth, strength) as the reason that makes tapas the sensible answer to his rise
gains.b: a named life that has lived through desolation, rearing and kingship, which the quatrain's list of goods never shows in one person

note: Civakan says he will not be born again, having found the unborn one; Tirumular says that after he renounced and saw the light the lord of the gods set him here so that he would not die and be born again.
teaches: Both end births by reaching a lord who is not born, but the Saiva verse makes the lord the one who sets the seeker free while the epic verse puts the claim in the worshipper's mouth and does not say the Jina acts.

gains.a: the Saiva verse's mechanism, a lord who sets the seeker beyond birth, which Civakan's cry of certainty lacks
gains.b: a parallel from a worshipper of the unborn Jina who rests his claim on reaching the feet, which shows how the end-of-birth language is shared and the cause differs

note: In 683 the dancer wrote a letter in figure, calling her streaked eyes the letter and her smile the friend who carried it; in 2586 she hands over a letter in the proper manner and he reads it.
teaches: The earlier letter of eyes only hinted; the written letter now makes the same appeal in words, which shows the epic turning a figure into a document, so her love must now be answered in the open.

note: In 686 the usurper closes on the garlanded dancer and strips her; in 2587 she recounts that, once she had bowed to Civakan, the cruel spearman threw her off the stage and jailed her.
teaches: The letter gives the dancer's own account of what 686 told from outside, which shows the violence as something she carries as an injury against Civakan, not only as the usurper's crime.

note: In 687 the captive cried out unceasingly to Civakan, the bowman who took her maidenhood; in 2593 the king, now secure, answers 'how could I forget you?'.
teaches: The cry in the usurper's grip is answered only after the usurper's fall and a letter, so the epic shows that the king's help comes late, long after her call.

note: In 676 her eyes and brows moved as she danced and the watchers were overcome; in 2594 the same eyes and brows play while the king himself watches, his garland opening.
teaches: The dance that once undid a crowd of strangers now undoes the one man it was aimed at, which shows how the same art, once open to all, has been turned to a single patron.

note: In 684 the dancer rejoiced that his hand had touched her hip and that the toil of bearing young breasts was over; in 2598 the ripened love is enjoyed as a harvest.
teaches: The joy in 684 was only a promise made on being touched; 2598 shows what became of it, which is the epic's picture of love as a field worked for a harvest.

note: Tirumanthiram 207 says that union with young women is sweet cane juice in the hand and turns bitter neem in the body; 2598 sets the same pleasure as a sweet harvest of love enjoyed in peace.
teaches: Set against the Saiva warning, the epic's closing image of the king resting in love reads as a stage in a life the epic itself will end in renunciation, not a conclusion.

gains.a: a counterweight inside the poem's praise of enjoyment, to set against the epic's later turn to the Jina's path
gains.b: a worked scene of the pleasure it warns against, drawn at its sweetest, which shows why the warning is needed

note: Anangamalai pleads that she not be left outside the shade of Civakan's white umbrella, which she calls the shade of dharma; Purananuru 35 tells Killivalavan that his tall umbrella is not for shade but to shelter suffering subjects who may come to him for justice.
teaches: The Sangam poem tells a king to keep his umbrella for the sufferer, and the epic shows a sufferer actually using it, which puts the claim to the test of whether a king's sheltering reaches a woman's private petition.

gains.a: an older standard of the umbrella as the king's duty to the suffering, which her petition invokes but the epic does not itself state
gains.b: a petitioner who stands in the position it only imagines, which shows what it asks of a king in practice

audit_text_issue: 2590 repaired from 8 half-lines; sense flagged uncertain

note: Kural 545 says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who wields the sceptre by its nature; 2583 says that under Civakan killing and miserliness are banished and the land becomes like Uttarakuru, with fish leaping into the fishers' yards.
teaches: The couplet's rule is carried to its extreme here, where just rule ends killing and scarcity as well as drought, but the epic offers it only as praise, so the couplet's causal claim remains unproved.

gains.a: the Kural's measure by which the praise is read, rain and harvest as the sign of a just sceptre
gains.b: a case where the sign is raised from rain to a golden age, which shows the couplet's limit: it names the sign but not how far a king's rule can reach

note: Naladiyar 371 says the friendship of harlots ends when the hand is empty, as the lamp's light ends when the oil runs out; in 2588 Anangamalai, a woman of the stage, is jailed and released and keeps worshipping a painted image of Civakan with no payment.
teaches: The quatrain's rule is a claim about women of her station, and her story tests it, which shows the epic treating constancy as the person's, not the profession's.

gains.a: a hostile frame that makes her constancy a deliberate answer to a standing charge against dancers
gains.b: a counter-case in which a woman of the stage keeps love without income, which shows the rule as a generalisation about types, not a law

note: Vijayai says that no return can match those who ended her distress and gives them every delight; the Kural says that help given when none was given before cannot be paid back even by earth and sky.
teaches: The Kural states that such help is beyond repayment, and the epic shows what a queen does about it: she gives all she has and still says the debt remains.

gains.a: the verse's claim that there is no requital is shown as an ideal measure, with the Kural giving the rule that explains why gratitude must outrun the gift
gains.b: the Kural's rule for gifts in need is tested against a person with a whole kingdom's power to repay, who still declares it not enough

note: In 302 Vijayai grieves alone in the burning ground and has no fear; in 2603 she turns the place of her fall and rescue into a painted memorial on her mansion, with a town granted to her rescuer.
teaches: The burning ground that was her lowest place is made at the end into a thing gratefully remembered, so the reader sees grief turned into a debt honoured.

note: In 223 Vijayai dreamed of a tree falling and a shoot growing with a crown for eight pearl garlands; in 2607 she tells the eight queens they came as that eight-garland crown in her dream and begs them never to part.
teaches: The dream of the shoot and the crown is shown fulfilled in the eight wives, and the reader sees that the dream's fruit is the Cintamani's marriage-chain, now held together by the mother who dreamed it.

note: In 261 the usurper planned to kill the king who was sunk in pleasure with his queen; in 2610 Vijayai tells her son that the king was swallowed by pleasure as the moon by the serpent and would not take counsel.
teaches: The ruin that the poet told as a plot is retold by the survivor as the king's own failing, so the reader sees that the epic gives both the plotter's cunning and the king's desire as the cause.

note: In 299 the queen, riding the peacock machine, faints like a struck doe as the usurper's drum sounds; in 2614 the same machine is called the deed's peacock (வினைமயில்) that sent her away while he went to the sky.
teaches: The carpenter's flying peacock of 235-239 is named here as fate's instrument, so what was a clever device comes to be read as the working of deeds.

note: Vijayai says no one knows how many days are given and that the dead cannot be recalled; the Kural says good must be done before the hiccup rises and stops the tongue.
teaches: The Kural's urgency is made a mother's plea to a king at the height of pleasure, showing the rule's cost: it must be heard just when it is least welcome.

gains.a: the verse's general lament about the span of life gets a concrete deadline of the final hiccup
gains.b: the Kural's call to hurry is placed in a scene where the one urged is a king surrounded by wives and enjoyment

note: Vijayai says deed's force scatters us like clouds and there is no lasting fellowship; the Naladiyar says kin arrive unasked and leave wordless, leaving the body as a bird leaves its nest.
teaches: The Naladiyar says parting happens at death; Vijayai says it is the working of deeds even in life, which is why she can ask her son to loosen his own attachments now.

gains.a: the verse's cloud image of scattering gets the further picture of the bird leaving the body
gains.b: the Naladiyar's kin-leaving is given a cause in deeds, which it itself leaves unstated

audit_text_issue: line 3 அத்தை unfixed; sense flagged uncertain

note: Vijayai urges penance and giving before black hair turns white; the Naladiyar says the wise renounced in childhood, knowing grey hair would come, and the youth-lovers later lean on a staff.
teaches: The pairing shows that the call to act before age is made both to a king in his prime by his mother and as a general rule, so the epic's mother is speaking the Naladiyar's counsel in her own household.

gains.a: the verse's address to the young gets the image of the staff in old age that makes the urgency felt
gains.b: the Naladiyar's general advice is given a speaker who has lost a husband and knows how fast it comes

note: Vijayai says the body is a fire of disease with life as ghee, and urges giving and good before Death leaves; Tirumular says give out the rice before the pot burns near, since the days slip away.
teaches: Both turn the household fire and the measure of rice into a warning that gifts must go out now; the epic frames it as the end of a king's pleasure, the Saiva verse as ordinary housekeeping.

gains.a: the verse's body-as-fire gets a plain rice-pot image for what is given up first
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's counsel to give is placed under a Death who drinks the household, with the Jain epic's warning of disease and awareness as fuel

note: Vijayai tells diners to think of austerity, not riches, as they eat milk-rice from gold bowls; the Naladiyar says the fool who hoards his wealth and dies is laughed at by the wealth itself.
teaches: The epic says wealth is not a thing to rely on at the table; the Naladiyar says what wealth does to the hoarder, and together they show that gifts and penance are what the dying keep.

gains.a: the verse's call to austerity gets a figure of wealth laughing at its owner
gains.b: the Naladiyar's hoarder is set at a banquet table in a king's palace, where the temptation is not stinginess but ease

audit_text_issue: 2623 line 3 அடகிடுமின் ஓட்டகத்து hard | 2623 line 3 is hard to divide (அடகிடுமின் ஓட்டகத்து)

note: Naladiyar 1 shows men who ate six-flavoured meals served by a willing wife and then beg gruel here and there; 2624 shows a woman who drank boiled milk from a golden bowl and now holds out a wide bowl for alms.
teaches: The Naladiyar's quatrain draws the rule that wealth cannot be counted on, and the Cintamani turns the same beggar's fall into a sight the preacher points to while urging the hearers to turn to dharma.

gains.a: the sermon verse gets an old, general proof (those who ate richly and then beg) behind its single sight, so the woman reads as a type and not a pity
gains.b: the quatrain gets a woman, her hunger and the posture of begging bent like a creeper, which it lacks as an anonymous list of eaters, and the sermon's turn from the picture to dharma

note: The woman of 2624 would give anything for boiled milk in a golden bowl; in 354 the good women offer milk-nectar in a gold vessel to Vijayai in the ascetic's hermitage, and she will not even look at it.
teaches: The milk in the gold vessel is the same thing wanted by one and refused by the other, so the epic puts the beggar's lack and the nun's refusal on one object to show what renunciation means as a choice.

note: In 303 the woman who once went into sky-touching palaces like a heavenly maiden is left alone in a forest of white skulls and is said to be shown so that hearers may see sin; 2625 offers another woman in a half-covered rag as the same lesson.
teaches: What the epic first set before the eye as Vijayai's own fall is later handed on as a spoken example, so the story and the sermon the story ends in draw on one fund of images.

note: Naladiyar 13 shows those whose speech fails, who lean on a staff and lose their teeth, yet stay in the house with their eyes on desire; 2626 shows a youth in a garland and spear who comes to lean on a staff and drool.
teaches: The sermon shows the young man whose decline the Naladiyar describes only from its end, and so makes the same warning about desire outliving the body's strength.

gains.a: the epic's youth gets the Naladiyar's charge that the old man who lingers in the house is blind to the road to safety, which the sermon only implies
gains.b: the quatrain gets the garland-and-spear picture of the youth before, which it lacks, so its old man is someone who was once the Kama of women's eyes

note: The patikam says that while kings paid tribute and his sceptre ran, Civakan heard the dharma and was afraid of kingship like a snake; in 2627 Sunandai says she will renounce too and Civakan melts.
teaches: The turn the patikam gave in one line is shown here as it happens, in the answer of a mother and the dissolving of a king, not as a decision of his own.

note: 2628 has the matrons go in palanquins to their renunciation; Tirumanthiram 153 has the lord of the town mount for the last time a palanquin of the burning ground.
teaches: One kind of vehicle is shown going two ways: a rich woman's palanquin carries her to a life given up while still alive, and the lord's palanquin carries him to the burning ground whether he chooses or not.

gains.a: the epic palanquin gets the Tirumanthiram's irony that the ride of honour ends in the burning ground, so the matrons' ride reads as taking that last ride first and by choice
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's palanquin gets a counter-case in which the ride is boarded willingly before death, which its picture of the lord's last journey leaves out

note: Kural 47 puts the householder who lives the household life rightly first among all who strive; 2632 has the nun say that penance is hard and that a gift sown with virtue yields fame and then the pleasures of the gods.
teaches: The Jain nun grades the gift of the householder as a fruit of fame and heaven and keeps the harder penance above it, so the Kural's 'first among strivers' is put against a ladder of fruits.

gains.a: the nun's rule that gift watered with virtue gives fame and heaven gets a rival ranking that puts the householder at the head of all effort
gains.b: the couplet, which does not say what is striven for, gets one answer: for the Jain the striving is for fame and heaven by gift, or for more by penance
