note: 2635 has the women fling off garlands and ornaments and sow thorns on Kama's road; Siddhar 19 asks when the singer shall leave silk clothes, gold ornaments, pretence and evil deeds and desire the Lord's feet.
teaches: Both strip off ornament, but one is done as a rite with no god in it and the other is a longing aimed at a god's feet.

gains.a: the epic stripping gets the Siddhar's aim, the Lord's feet, which the verse leaves blank, and shows that its rite aims only at closing Kama's road
gains.b: the Siddhar's longing gets a finished ritual, a fixed hall and day, where the song only asks 'when shall I'

note: In 350 Vijayai takes off the tilaka, earrings, neck ornaments and the pearls on her breasts when she is received into the hermitage; 2635 has the women scatter garlands and ornaments in a prepared hall.
teaches: What one forlorn queen did alone in a forest is done here as an ordered rite for many, so the epic shows renunciation first as a refuge and last as an institution.

note: Kural 280 says neither shaving nor long hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns; 2637 has the matrons pluck out their own dark hair and enter renunciation pondering the settled meaning of the Lord's book.
teaches: The Jain rite of plucking the hair is joined to inward thought in the verse, which is the answer to the Kural's doubt whether the shorn head means anything without giving up.

gains.a: the plucking is given a test, whether it comes with giving up what is condemned, which the epic verse supplies only as pondering the scripture
gains.b: the couplet gets a rite that is neither shaving nor matting, hair plucked by one's own hand, which it does not consider

note: In 349 Vijayai takes off the gold garland and necklace while her musk-dressed hair grieves; in 2637 the matrons themselves pluck their dark hair without a flinch.
teaches: The grief of the hair in the forest is replaced by an act done without bowing, so the epic shows the same hair going first with sorrow and then with composure.

note: The patikam says that his younger brother, friends and richly adorned wives all renounce the things of sense; 2640 shows the new nuns studying the Anga books and shining as tilaka of the order.
teaches: What the patikam announced as a bare fact is shown here as a life of learning and equanimity.

note: After the last battle Civakan bows to the Jina and flings out gold before putting on his royal ornaments (2357); in 2641 he takes flowers and touches his crowned head to the nuns' feet.
teaches: The crown is lowered twice, first before the Jina in victory and last before the women who have given up, so the epic marks the end of his kingship by whom he bows to.

note: In 1915 Vijayai tells her son that his mother is Sunandai, always, and his father Kandukkatan; in 2646 Sunandai is called 'no mother' for leaving.
teaches: The mother whom the epic made the true one by love is accused of not being a mother when her vow takes her away from her son.
audit_text_issue: 2646 speaker uncertain; sense flagged | 2646: speaker not fixed by the verse (marker flagged uncertain).

note: The queen puts away pleasure for austerity; Naladiyar 53 says the best of people consider slowly and give up home, youth and beauty without delay.
teaches: The epic shows the quatrain's counsel taken by a woman at the court while her husband is still held by pleasure, which makes giving up one's own household look like a path that is left open and not forced.

gains.a: The queen's austerity, narrated in one verse, gets a stated reason: the things she gives up are the short-lived goods of the quatrain.
gains.b: The quatrain's counsel of quick renunciation meets a case from a royal house, where the one who gives up is a wife and not the head of the family.

note: In 1946 the breasts of the sandal-painted women turn even those who think of release back; in 2651 a woman of the court puts pleasure down and goes to austerity.
teaches: The poem keeps both outcomes in front of the reader: the same world of women that can undo a renouncer can also be left by one of its own members.

note: The king wins the love-god's war in play, with garlands and streams; Naladiyar 17 says youth drops like fruit and the woman desired for her spear-like eyes will walk with a staff.
teaches: The epic's delight at its brightest is the thing the quatrain tells the hearer not to desire, so the water-sport is set to be read against the old age it will bring.

gains.a: The verse's triumph over the love-god gains a time limit: the women who yield are those who will one day lean on staffs.
gains.b: The quatrain's warning gains a concrete scene of the pleasure it warns against, with garlands, powder and a king at play.

note: The women dress, steam and garland themselves after the play; Naladiyar 16 likens the joy of youth to a lamb nibbling at the garland held out before the slaughter.
teaches: The same garland that is the sign of pleasure in the Cintamani is the bait of the sacrifice in the quatrain, and the reader sees both uses of one object.

gains.a: The garland-wearing at the end of the sport gains a darker reading, in which the adornment is what precedes the loss.
gains.b: The quatrain's lamb and garland gain a courtly setting where the garland is a gift of love and not a rite.

note: The couch scene rubs off the sandal and tears at the garlands; Naladiyar 48 mocks those who praise sandal paste and garlands without knowing the body they decorate.
teaches: Both pass through sandal, garland and body, one to delight in them and one to say the body is the cart that vultures will tear at.

gains.a: The sandal rubbed off the women's breasts gains the quatrain's view of what lies under it, the body that decays.
gains.b: The quatrain's sandal and garlands gain a scene in which they are being worn and spoiled in the way that it mocks.

note: In 67 women plunge into the country pools and their girdle strings break and scatter; in 2662 the defeated women in the king's pool give up their girdles and earrings to him.
teaches: The scattering of gold that the landscape verse shows as nature's wealth is shown here as a gift laid at the king's feet, which changes whose ornament it is.

note: In 1996 Civakan praises Vimalai's breasts as enough to make the released fall; in 2671 the king, with women skilled in writing, song and dance, is called the love-god of the love-god.
teaches: The poem moves from a lover's praise of one woman to the poet's claim for the man among many, the height of pleasure just before the hero's renunciation.

note: The king is set above the love-god among women; Tirumantiram 203 says even those who hold knowledge are infatuated with women who bewilder and cannot change a mind once bewildered.
teaches: The epic's compliment to the king and the Saiva verse's warning describe one hold, and the reader learns the praise is also a statement of how firm that hold is.

gains.a: The praise of the king as the love-god's love-god gains a hint that those who hold such knowledge are no safer than the ignorant.
gains.b: The verse's general warning gains a named king, a court and a chapter just before his own turning away.

note: The sulk of 2678 is answered by the consoling words and embrace of 2679.
teaches: The quarrel turns on one conceit: her sulk makes the moon a paled rival, and his answer keeps the moon and makes it pale before her face.

note: The husband tells his wife the moon pales before her face and thereby ends her sulk; Kural 1118 tells the moon it would be loved if it shone like her face.
teaches: The face-and-moon compliment is shown at work in a quarrel as a way to end a sulk, not only as praise.

gains.a: The conceit of the moon outshone by her face has a well-known formulation in a Kural couplet.
gains.b: A scene in which the same compliment is used to win a wife back from a sulk, which the couplet's address to the moon does not show.

note: The south breeze is sent as envoy to prepare the groves for spring; in the Silappathikaram's song the same breeze is the messenger who announces spring to the land.
teaches: The breeze as spring's herald serves different ends: the Cintamani uses it to dress the groves as a host's welcome, the Silappathikaram to bring the news to a Tamil land.

note: Spring's feast-dance in the groves rests on the loosened bangles of forsaken women; the Silappathikaram's closing venbas make spring the command that sulking lovers unite.
teaches: The same spring brings reunion for sulkers in one telling and shows the cost to women left apart in the other, so the season's joy is not shared by all.

note: The women of the verse are worn and pale from love itself; Naladiyar 17 tells a man not to crave a woman's spear-like eyes, since age will bend her.
teaches: The Naladiyar waits for age to wear a woman's beauty, but the epic shows love's own use wearing it at the bed, long before old age.

gains.a: The wan lips and thin shoulders read as the body's early decline, not just tiredness after love.
gains.b: A young case of the wearing it foretells, where no staff or grey hair is needed to show the same loss.

note: The sons learn arts, weapons and horse-riding at five; Kural 61 prizes children who come to know what should be known.
teaches: The couplet names knowing as the child's worth, while the epic's lesson is the skills of a warrior's house, so what is 'known' differs.

gains.a: A measure that asks whether the princes' skill in arms and arts is the knowing a father should prize.
gains.b: A concrete household where the child's gain is skill at arms, which tests whether the couplet means moral knowing only.

note: 1435 tells the listener not to gaze on pleasure like a sick old monkey; here a lusting monkey stands in an actual grove.
teaches: The sermon's monkey of appetite becomes a scene a king may watch, so the lesson reaches him as sight, not speech.

note: The mate who saw the pair in 2721 now speaks, rebuking the male and refusing his chest.
teaches: The tryst of 2721 is answered here, so the wrong and its rebuke are told in two steps, and the injured mate's voice is heard.

note: The mate refuses a chest that has lain with courtesans; Kural 1311 has a woman refuse a husband's chest, calling him a philanderer.
teaches: The Kural's refusal rests on a seen glance, while the monkey's rests on a proved infidelity, so the sulk is shown with a real cause.

gains.a: A named, human form of the refusal that makes the monkey's speech a wife's quarrel rather than animal noise.
gains.b: A case where the fault is real, which tests the couplet's sulk against a cause beyond being looked at.

audit_text_issue: 2722 sense flagged uncertain | 2722 line 2 (the bath of clear water) is not clear as printed.

note: The mate asks who would take bitter neem after mountain honey; Tirumanthiram 207 says the sweet of young women turns to neem within the body.
teaches: The same pair of sweet and bitter serves a wife's refusal and a sage's warning, showing the image works both for pride and for renunciation.

gains.a: The honey-and-neem pair gains a second use, as the ascetic's verdict on pleasure, behind the wife's refusal.
gains.b: A lived case of the image, in a quarrel where bitterness is what the mate will not accept, not the end of pleasure.

note: 2614 tells in Vijayai's words how Kattiyangaran conquered the kings and sent her off by the peacock machine; in 2726 Civakan sets him beside the monkey who seized the fruit and himself beside the one who lost it.
teaches: The old usurpation, told as injury in the mother's tale, becomes in the monkey scene an instance of seizing and losing that teaches the hero how little taking or holding is worth.

note: The Kural warns one who is about to oppress the weak to think how he stands before the stronger; Civakan sees that the strong seize the weak's wealth and draws not a rule for the strong but a reason to leave.
teaches: The warning that assumes a ruler who will listen is answered by a ruler who, having seen the same fact, withdraws from rule altogether.

gains.a: the verse's remark on the strong and weak gets a moral measure it lacks, a rule against oppressing the weak, so Civakan's renunciation reads as a response to a recognised wrong
gains.b: the couplet's appeal to a fear of the stronger is tested against a hero who owns power and finds that no fear or fairness but only leaving settles the matter

note: In 213 the king says that pleasures and days of life are measured out for those who guarded penance; in 2728 Civakan names wives and children as the fruit of that merit and says the wind of sin will bring the tree down.
teaches: The earlier remark that pleasure is a measured ration of merit becomes here a reason to give it up before it runs out.

note: Naladiyar 130 tells the heart that attachment to home and children is idle since nothing but good done goes with it; 2728 names the family itself as the fruit of that good and says it will be lost.
teaches: The quatrain makes the family a hindrance beside merit, while the verse makes the family a result of merit, so the reader sees that giving up the fruit and keeping the merit are different acts.

gains.a: the verse's tree of good deed, which only reports loss, gains the quatrain's directive that the heart should stop clinging and put its hope in good done
gains.b: the quatrain's contrast of home against good deed gains a case in which the home is itself the earlier good deed's yield, so renouncing it is spending, not rejecting, merit

note: In 233 the king's wisdom rebukes him for bathing in the liquor of lust and losing his senses; in 2729 Civakan names desire as toddy drunk on the tongue and turns back like an elephant to the goad.
teaches: The same intoxication that unmade Saccandan and cost him his throne is seen by his son in time to leave it by choice, which sets father and son side by side.

note: In 1245 the hymn asks who rose to the summit of the worlds and answers that it is the Lord; in 2739 the question is turned on the worshippers, who are those that wear his feet, and the answer is the honour they receive.
teaches: The question-and-answer form that named the Lord in the young Civakan's hymn is now used to name the reward of devotion, so the hymn teaches why one worships and not only whom.

note: Kural 10 says that those who reach the Lord's feet swim the sea of births; 2741 praises the Lord who crossed the sea of karma and makes his praisers lords of the wheel under the three umbrellas.
teaches: The couplet promises crossing the sea of births, while the verse promises kingship to the worshippers of a crosser, so the two disagree about what a follower gains.

gains.a: the verse's reward of sovereignty is set against the couplet's promise of escape from birth, which shows that the hymn's worldly reward is short of the end that the sermon later takes up
gains.b: the couplet's Lord, whom the Kural leaves unnamed, gets a form here, a crosser of karma under three parasols, and a stated fruit for those who praise him

note: In 1240 the young Civakan goes round the temple of the god who cut the ghati karmas and passes on; in 2743 he circles the Charana lord's shrine as an old king and stays to be taught.
teaches: The circling that was a stop on a road is here the last one, and what it leads to is a teaching and not a journey.

note: 1247 praises the god of the asoka as the one who ended karma that cannot be ended; 2745 asks the ascetic's grace to end the darkness of the karma Civakan himself did.
teaches: The hymn's praise of a Lord who ended karma becomes Civakan's own request to have his karma ended, so doctrine turns into a personal petition.

note: Naladiyar 51 says that sin cannot stand before austerity as darkness dies when a lamp comes, and returns when the oil runs out; 2745 asks for grace as a flame that will clear the darkness of the evil deed.
teaches: The quatrain gives the lamp's work a limit, since the dark returns, which raises the question whether the grace Civakan asks is a lasting cure.

gains.a: the verse's flame of grace gains the quatrain's warning that a lamp clears darkness only while it burns, which makes the plea more urgent
gains.b: the quatrain's lamp of austerity is put into the mouth of a king asking for it, and is thus a gift sought from another and not only a thing one earns

note: Tirumanthiram 114 has Nandi cut away the tarnish and open the eye of grace so that a light shows that nothing can darken; 2745 asks a Jain ascetic's grace to clear the darkness of karma.
teaches: Both ask a teacher's grace to clear a stain, but Nandi gives it as a lord who acts on the soul, while the Jain sage is only asked and is a teacher, not a god.

gains.a: the verse's plea, which does not say how the darkness goes, is given the Saiva picture of a god who cuts the tarnish, against which the sage's role looks much smaller
gains.b: the verse's image of Nandi's gift is set against a request made of a man who is no god, so grace is shown there as something that a teacher can only point toward

note: Kural 543 makes the king's sceptre the origin of the books of the learned and of virtue; 2746 gives the ascetic the duty of telling the king dharma and leaves the king with the sceptre.
teaches: Where the couplet makes dharma depend on the king, the verse has the king come to the ascetic to hear it, so the two disagree about which gives the other its authority.

gains.a: the verse's two duties, scripture and sceptre, are put against a couplet that derives the first from the second, which exposes the ranking that the verse leaves open
gains.b: the couplet's claim that the sceptre is the source of dharma gains a story in which the sceptre's holder goes to be taught and leaves the sceptre

note: In 2616 Vijayai tells Civakan in a few lines that we are born not knowing our days and that the past cannot be recalled; in 2748 the sage lists the rare body, its end, the pain of leaving and the release as the subjects of a full teaching.
teaches: What the mother says as a warning is turned into the heads of a doctrine, so the reader sees which of her points the sermon will take up.

note: Tirumanthiram 307 calls life and body a close support and the mind on Siva's feet the firm support that ends birth; 2748 lists the body hard to gain and its destruction among the sermon's topics, with release.
teaches: Both begin from the body, which the Saiva verse treats as a support to be used, while the Jain sage announces it as a thing that is rare and must end.

gains.a: the announced sermon gains a Saiva view in which the body is a means that is used on the way and not merely lost
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram verse's body-as-support is set against a view that treats it as hard to get and bound to end, which adds the Jain sense of its loss to the claim

note: In 377 the poet laments that the nectar that ends birth is rarely won and yet men pamper the senses; in 2749 the teacher shows the rarity itself, a human birth as unlikely as a drifting pole finding a yoke-hole in the sea.
teaches: The earlier complaint is given its measure here, so a reader sees that wasting the human birth is wasting a one-in-a-sea chance.

note: Naladiyar 34 tells one who has this rare body to take its full fruit, as juice from cane; 2749 gives the odds that make the body rare, the pole in the yoke-hole.
teaches: The quatrain's advice to use the body gets a reason in the epic's image of how improbable it is, and the epic's image gets a use to put it to.

gains.a: the verse's picture of chance gains the plain duty the rarity implies, to use the body's fruit
gains.b: the quatrain's word 'rare' gains a concrete measure, with a drifting pole and an unlikely yoke-hole in place of the bare word

note: Kural 338 says body and life part like a bird leaving its nest; 2754 says the life may be lost even before it leaves the womb, as a bubble bursts.
teaches: The Kural's picture begins at the nest-leaving; the epic starts earlier, with the embryo itself already at risk, so the loss is not only a late one.

gains.a: the verse's tale of the embryo gains the bird-and-nest image of parting that gives the loss its shape
gains.b: the couplet's parting of body and life gains an earlier start, in the womb, so the risk is shown to begin at conception

note: Naladiyar 25 says the man who sees kin wailing at a corpse and yet marries and expects joy is answered by the funeral drum; 2758 shows men in the heart of pleasure cut off by Death while the living beat their faces.
teaches: The quatrain shows the lesson refused, the epic shows the death that teaches it, and together the reader sees that pleasure and mourning are the same scene seen at different times.

gains.a: the verse's death in pleasure gains the quatrain's voice of the one who watches and still does not learn
gains.b: the quatrain gains the verse's scene of pleasure at its height, with the jewelled women and their anklets, so the cost of ignoring the drum is made concrete

note: Naladiyar 33 sets the fool who sighs when the fruit of past deeds arrives against the wise who accept it; 2762 says the evildoer sows deeds in the soul and eats their harvest.
teaches: The quatrain names the response to the fruit, the epic names how the fruit is formed, so karma is shown as both cause and the way to meet it.

gains.a: the verse's farming image of sowing and eating gains the quatrain's wise way of facing the harvest, which the hell scenes never show
gains.b: the quatrain's 'fruit of past deeds' gains the hell-sermon's scale, which shows how severe that fruit can be

note: Tirumular says the subtle body eats the fruit in heaven and hell and then takes another body with the old deeds following; 2762 says the evildoer eats the harvest of deeds sown in the soul.
teaches: Both let the deeds ripen as an experience of hell, but the Saiva verse carries the sufferer on into a new birth by a subtle body, which the Jain verse does not say here.

gains.a: the verse's farming image of deeds gains the Saiva account of what survives to carry the deeds, the subtle body
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram verse gains a vivid account of what 'eating the fruit' means, in the hell scenes that follow

note: In 347 Vijayai's distress comes because a deed of a former birth stood waiting; in 2763 the same ripening is told of all who do evil, with fruits dropping from the palm.
teaches: The single case of the queen's fate and the general teaching that deeds come to fruit are placed side by side, so the reader sees the sermon as the rule behind a plot he already saw.

note: Tirumanthiram 198 has Death's servants bind and drive the killers into fire-mouthed hell; in 2764 the hell-beings rise and fall on the blades with no jailer named.
teaches: The Saiva verse puts Yama's servants in charge, while the Jain verse leaves the pain to the deeds and the place, so the two show different views of who runs hell.

gains.a: the verse's hell gains the contrast of a judge's servants at work, which brings out its own lack of any
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram verse gains a hell without servants as a rival picture, in which the ground itself does the work

note: Siddhar 16 hopes to avoid being called a sinner and falling into the barren hell, by knowing the breath-thread; 2766 shows what that fall would be, the stake and the fire.
teaches: The Siddhar's wish to avoid hell gains a picture of what he flees, and the epic's picture of hell gets a way out the Siddhar names, knowledge of the breath rather than the Jain sermon's virtue.

gains.a: the verse's torture gains a different way to avoid it, by a yogic knowing, in place of conduct
gains.b: the Siddhar's hope gains a precise picture of the hell, so the escape is not a vague wish

note: Naladiyar 84 asks the adulterer what pleasure he had, since the act brings disgrace, a cut leg and long hell; 2769 sets the adulterer in hell with a glowing copper woman in his arms.
teaches: The quatrain names the price of the act and the epic shows the price paid, so the pleasure is seen turning into the pain it earned.

gains.a: the verse's embrace gains the quatrain's question about what pleasure was gained, which turns the scene into an argument
gains.b: the quatrain's phrase 'long hell' gains a specific image, the copper woman

note: Kural 255 says that if one eats flesh hell does not open its mouth; 2770 shows the killers of beasts and fish thrown daily into a seething pit.
teaches: The couplet says that hell waits, and the epic shows what its mouth holds, so the reader sees the rule enforced by the pain of the killer, not by a judge's word.

gains.a: the verse's hell for killers gains the couplet's plain rule that eating flesh is itself the reason
gains.b: the couplet's 'hell' gains the epic's concrete view of the pit that waits for killers

note: 2764 shows hell-beings rising and falling on blades; 2770 shows that the same beings are tormented daily by others who throw them in a boiling pit.
teaches: The sermon moves from the bare place of hell to those who work in it, so a reader sees that hell has both a ground that hurts and agents who add to the hurt.

note: 2774 gives hell's tortures by molten copper and the oil-press without a cause; Tirumanthiram 198 binds those who urged 'kill, stab' and sets them in fire-mouthed hell.
teaches: Together they show hell as the fruit of a named sin and as a daily mechanical punishment, which neither shows alone.

gains.a: the verse names no crime for its tortures, and gains the sin of urging killing
gains.b: 198 gives only a fiery pit, and gains the machines and repeated daily torment

note: 253 names killing and eating flesh among the sins that sink into leprosy and hell; 2776 names the killers and the deniers of the next world as those who go.
teaches: The reader sees the Cintamani widen the list of sinners from conduct (253) to belief, since the one who denies the next world is sent there too.

note: 2776 sends those bent on killing into hell on the cars of their sins; Kural 321 says killing brings all other evil deeds with it.
teaches: The couplet states killing as the root of other wrongs, and the epic adds the journey to hell as its end.

gains.a: the verse gains a rule naming killing as the first of all sins, which it presupposes
gains.b: the couplet gains a picture of where such deeds lead, which it leaves unsaid

note: 2780 attacks the sacrifice of a lamb for the gods' pleasure with the recompense in Yama's world; Kural 259 weighs a thousand oblations against not killing and eating one creature.
teaches: The epic condemns the sacrificer by his punishment while the Kural condemns by comparison of worth, so the reader sees two ways to refuse sacrifice.

gains.a: the verse gains a measure of worth for sacrifice set against not killing
gains.b: the couplet gains a consequence after death and a scene of blood, which it lacks

audit_text_issue: 2780 நான்மடங்கு uncertain in sense | 2780 நான்மடங்கு is uncertain (fourfold or a fourth).

note: 2781 asks whose eyes would look on the creature cut apart and wailing; Kural 257 says flesh would not be eaten by those who saw it as another's wound.
teaches: The epic stages the very seeing that the couplet only wishes for, and shows it fails when appetite rules.

gains.a: the verse gains a name for what is being asked, seeing flesh as a wound
gains.b: the couplet gains a scene of the wounded animal, where it states only a condition

note: 2789 sends those who revile ascetics and the sinful to animal birth; 943 tells a dog that, leaving its dog's body, it will gain a god's body through the mantra.
teaches: The same Cintamani shows rebirth moving down by sin and up by holy words, so an animal body is not final.

note: 2791 shows the body as a skin of filth swarming with worms; Siddhar 41 calls it a worm-nest from which excrement and urine flow.
teaches: Both teach disgust at the body, one to warn of birth, the other to leave the body for the feet of Siva.

gains.a: the verse gains a goal beyond disgust, which the Siddhar names as the feet
gains.b: the Siddhar song gains the womb and birth as the origin of the body's filth

note: 2794 says the householders' wealth is a yoke of toil and pain; Kural 46 asks what one gains by going outside the household life if it is lived by dharma.
teaches: Whether household life is a yoke or the best path depends on the claim of 2794, and the two works cannot both hold it.

gains.a: the verse gains the Kural's own defence of the householder, which it argues against
gains.b: the couplet gains a counter-view that names the householder's wealth as the pain

note: 2796 says taking and guarding the earth is pain for kings; 27 says Civakan, fearing kingship like a snake struck by thunder, renounces after hearing dharma.
teaches: The hero's renunciation is the answer to this teaching, so the reader sees what the teacher's argument was meant to do to him.

note: 2797 says the body is a grove burned by the fire of disease; Siddhar 63 says this life has no standing, like a bubble on water.
teaches: Jain teacher and Siddhar agree that the body does not stand, but one asks escape from disease and the other from rebirth by grace.

gains.a: the verse gains a prayer for release, which the Siddhar adds
gains.b: the Siddhar song gains a concrete picture of how the body ends, in disease

note: Vijayai urged her son, before bright youth lapses and black hair greys, to do hard penance and give; the teacher now lists the lapse of youth and the coming of old age as one of the standing sufferings of men.
teaches: The mother's household warning about youth is shown here as one item in a Jain account of suffering, so her urging reads as the doctrine put plainly for a son who might delay.

note: The epic lists unmet wishes, parting, lost youth and old age as suffering; the quatrain lists home, youth, beauty, repute, wealth and strength as things that do not last and the best therefore renounce at once.
teaches: The epic names the pain of loss where the quatrain names its passing, and the quatrain supplies the action, renouncing without delay, that the epic verse leaves unsaid.

gains.a: The epic verse gains the Naladiyar's practical conclusion, to renounce at once, which it does not draw itself
gains.b: The quatrain gains the Jain account of why passing things hurt: wishes unmet and the loved parted from, not mere decay

note: The gods watch the goddesses dance and still take their fill of fortune without being content; the opening of the ilampakam says the hero has lost his wish for women whose beauty makes the heavens bow.
teaches: The sermon's heavenly pleasures supply the reason for the hero's turn from women in the opening: even the gods' unlimited enjoyment does not satisfy.
audit_text_issue: 2806 line 4 மானார் read as 'not satisfied' by the marker, not stated | 2806 line 4 ஆனார் / மானார் division is uncertain

note: The epic gods, with fifteen days left, blink and see their garlands fade and grieve like those who ate poisoned nectar; the Saiva verse says countless gods have died while the one with the forehead eye stays.
teaches: The two texts share the mortality of gods but part on the cure: the Jain verse leaves no god to rest on and moves the hearer to release, the Saiva verse moves him to the one undying Lord.

gains.a: The epic gains a rival answer to the fall of the gods: an unchanging Lord to rest on, which a Jain account of gods without such a Lord lacks
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram gains a concrete picture of how a dying god feels, the signs, the regret at wasted pleasure, that it only states in a line

note: The poet announced early that the hero hears the dharma and, afraid of kingship like a snake struck by thunder, renounces; the sermon's lesson that all embodied life, even a god's, is suffering is the content of that dharma.
teaches: This unit is the first body of the doctrine whose effect on the hero the early verse reports in a line, so it shows what the renunciation was a reply to.
audit_text_issue: 2811 line 2 (மணிகமாப் பணிகள்) garbled | 2811 line 2 (மணிகமாப் பணிகள்) is garbled.

note: The epic teacher says all who have a body suffer, even gods bowing to higher gods; the quatrain says parting, grievous illness and ruin come together to all who take a body and bids the heart cling to the wise.
teaches: The quatrain's advice to cling to the wise is shown to need the epic's wider claim, that no heaven escapes the suffering it names, before it becomes more than comfort.

gains.a: The epic verse gains from the quatrain a remedy, to cling to the wise who see through birth, where the epic only states the diagnosis
gains.b: The quatrain gains the extension to the gods: if even heaven is under suffering, no birth, however high, is a place to rest

note: On the sea the merchants are told not to weep over the suffering ripened deeds have brought but to think on the flower-feet of the lord; here the lotus feet of the Lord under the asoka are praised and wished upon the head.
teaches: The sea-scene told the crew to take refuge in the feet of the Lord, and this sermon names whose feet they are and why they save.

note: The Kural's one who walked on the flower and his noble feet and the epic's wheel-king who walked on the open lotus and his feet which the virtuous praise; both give the lotus walker as the object of devotion.
teaches: The epic names what is learned at those feet, five, six and nine, where the couplet names only the reward of long life on earth.

gains.a: The epic verse gains from the couplet the promise attached to reaching the feet, long life on the earth, where it states only knowledge
gains.b: The couplet gains a lotus-walker with a doctrine, who teaches what is to be known, in place of an unnamed figure

note: The epic uses the same compound அறவாழி for the lord of dharma ('wheel of dharma' with வேந்தன், king, set against the Kural's reading of the Lord as a sea of virtue).
teaches: The epic's use of ஆழி with a king points to the wheel of dharma rather than the sea as the compound's meaning, which the couplet's other seas set against it leaves open.

gains.a: The epic verse gains the couplet's claim that nothing else can carry one across, which makes devotion the necessary way
gains.b: The couplet gains an early reading of அறவாழி as the king's wheel of dharma, tied to a doctrine of five, six and nine, not left abstract

note: Vijayai said that, like clouds struck by wind, we are scattered by the force of deeds; the teacher says that Indra himself and a small monkey alike eat what their deeds have made.
teaches: The mother's saying of parting by deeds becomes a rule with no exemption, since it covers heaven's king, so no rank of birth can be claimed as a refuge.

note: The couplet says the two deeds born of darkness do not cling to those who praise the Lord; the epic says that those who have understood both deeds and the Lord's scripture neither exult nor scorn, because every being eats its fruit.
teaches: The epic sets the escape in understanding, in a world where even Indra eats his deeds, while the couplet sets it in devotion, so the two give different accounts of how the deeds stop clinging.

gains.a: The epic verse gains the couplet's promise that the deeds can fail to cling, which it does not state
gains.b: The couplet gains an account of the mechanism, understanding the two kinds of deeds, and the equal reach of karma over Indra and a monkey, that devotion alone does not give

audit_text_issue: verse is flagged repaired but readable

note: The epic says every being from Indra to a monkey eats the fruit of its own deeds, with release by understanding; the Saiva verse says the Lord stands beyond the two deeds and is the seed of the world.
teaches: The two give opposite places to the divine in karma: for the Jain verse no one, however high, stands outside deeds, for the Saiva verse the Lord alone does.

gains.a: The epic verse gains the Saiva claim of a Lord beyond the two deeds, a figure its own teaching of universal karma has no place for
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram gains a direct rival: that the highest being is also bound to eat his deeds, and that knowledge, not the Lord's stance, ends them

note: The epic says those who eat the wounds of other creatures and honey with worms destroy their inner knowledge and are beasts; the couplet says that if men saw flesh as another creature's wound they would not eat it.
teaches: Both call flesh another creature's wound, but the epic adds the charge that eating it destroys the eater's discernment, so the loss is the eater's own.

gains.a: The epic verse gains the couplet's single image of flesh as a wound, which makes the grammar of its பிறவற்றின் புண் clear
gains.b: The couplet gains an account of what the eater loses, inner discernment and the name of beast, rather than only what the eaten suffers

note: The epic defines sila as giving up what the great condemn, and the couplet says neither shaving nor long hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns.
teaches: The two agree that sila is the giving up of what is condemned, but the epic's ascetics keep the plucked hair as discipline (2820) where the couplet makes the mark unnecessary.

gains.a: The epic verse gains the couplet's insistence that the test of renunciation is what one gives up, not an outward mark, which tests its own list of marks
gains.b: The couplet gains a Jain case where the mark, plucked hair, is itself an austerity borne with patience, so its dismissal of marks is not complete

note: Vijayai urged her son to give and said people never give a handful to the poor; the teacher now gives the reason, that a gift in good soil grows like seed and one in barren soil withers.
teaches: The mother's plain call to give is answered by an account of why it matters who receives, so giving is a sowing whose crop depends on the field.

note: The epic compares gifts to seed in good and poor soil; the quatrain compares even a small virtuous deed that reaches worthy hands to a banyan seed whose shade makes the sky seem small.
teaches: Both make the recipient decide the harvest, but the epic adds the poor-soil case, where the gift is lost, which the quatrain's banyan does not show.

gains.a: The epic verse gains the quatrain's picture of a tiny gift that grows greatly, which gives the good-soil half its scale
gains.b: The quatrain gains the opposite case, seed in barren soil that yields little, which shows what a gift to the unworthy costs

note: 2824 names what the ascetics do to quench the five senses (wither them, keep from four sins); Kural 25 says only that the strength of one who has quenched them is witnessed by Indra.
teaches: The Kural gives the strength of one who has quenched the senses without the practice, and the verse gives the practice without the strength, so the two together show both sides.

gains.a: the verse's practice of withering the senses gets a measure of what it wins, a strength that heaven's king himself would witness
gains.b: the Kural's quenching of the five gets a concrete discipline (withering the body, keeping from lying, killing, theft and lust) that its praise leaves open

note: 2824 has the ascetic wither the five senses and so subdue them by effort; Tirumanthiram 140 says the senses come under control of themselves once the Lord is met.
teaches: One text holds that the senses are conquered by the ascetic's own labour, the other that they are conquered by meeting the Lord, so the two disagree on who does the work.

gains.a: the verse's effortful mortification is shown to be one of two ways to the same end, and the one that leaves out a god
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram verse's claim that no effort is needed meets its rival, a school that does not wait for grace

note: 2831 says merit is measured by the gift as iron takes water in proportion to its heating, a gift for the next birth; Purananuru 134 says Ay is no trader who buys virtue with gifts for the next life.
teaches: The verse sets a gift's reward in an exact ledger, and the Sangam poem names that ledger as what its patron does not do.

gains.a: the doctrine of measured merit, shown from outside, looks like the trade it is accused of in the Sangam poem
gains.b: the poem's refusal of a 'trader's' giving gains a worked-out doctrine of gift-for-fruit that makes the refusal pointed

note: 2841 says the middle sort of gift is paid by whatever one wishes in the land of enjoyment; Kural 222 says giving is good even if there were no higher world.
teaches: The Cintamani ties each gift to its reward, while the Kural cuts giving loose from reward by a hypothetical.

gains.a: the verse's rewards (wishing trees for the middle gift) are shown as one of the things the Kural's hypothetical sets aside
gains.b: the Kural's hypothetical gets a full account of the other-worldly rewards it asks us to imagine away

note: 2842 ranks gifts by the receiver, with a debased birth for a gift to the unrestrained; Kural 221 says only giving to those who have nothing is giving.
teaches: The Kural names the needy as the only true recipient, but the Cintamani's sage names the restrained, so who deserves a gift is answered in opposite ways.

gains.a: the verse's grading of recipients by restraint is set against the Kural's grading by need
gains.b: the Kural's 'the destitute' is shown as one possible answer, where the sage answers 'the restrained'

note: 2845 defines release's path as knowledge, faith and conduct together; Kural 356 says those who learned here and saw the real thing reach the path of not coming back.
teaches: The Kural pairs learning and seeing, and the Jain verse adds the third (holding it in conduct), so the two give different recipes for the same release.

gains.a: the verse's triad is shown as a larger version of the Kural's learning and seeing
gains.b: the Kural's two-part path is given a third part that the verse insists cannot be left out

note: 2846 says knowledge, faith and conduct together are a fire that burns the tree of deeds; Tirumanthiram 117 says the malas burn only in the sun's presence, as the sunstone burns cotton only in the sun.
teaches: Both burn the impurity by fire, but one fire is the seeker's own three virtues and the other needs the Lord's sun.

gains.a: the verse's fire of karma is shown to burn on its own, which the sunstone image says it cannot
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's sunstone gets a rival that claims the stone burns without a sun

note: 2847 names what the freed soul has (endless knowledge, seeing, power and joy); Kural 362 says to want, want not to be born.
teaches: The Kural describes release as an absence of birth and desire, and the Cintamani's sage describes it as a fullness, so one calls release emptying and the other filling.

gains.a: the verse's release is set beside the Kural's, which describes it only as not being born again
gains.b: the Kural's release by not wanting gets an account of what the one released then has

note: In 2622 Vijayai says that all who are born are greedy, never give a handful, and should give their wealth away; in 2829 the sage promises to tell what gifts to the worthy yield.
teaches: The mother's plea to give and the sage's account of what giving earns are two halves of one argument, one urging, one promising.

note: In 2840 the pair are bound by the garland of desire in the pleasure that their gifts earned; in 2610 Saccandan, swallowed by pleasure, would not come out and fell.
teaches: Pleasure that is the fruit of merit is still a bond, and the story of the old king shows what happens when one stays bound.

note: In 2619 Vijayai tells the people to do hard penance and give before youth lapses; in 2848 the king bathes in the sage's dharma-water and loses the stain of sorrow.
teaches: The mother's exhortation and the sage's sermon reach the same hearer in the same ilampakam, and the sermon is what makes the king act on them.

note: 2849 has the hearer bid the people bow to the lord's feet to be clear of sins of earlier births; 2846 gave the sermon's release as three together burning the tree of deeds.
teaches: The sermon sets release as a burning of deeds, and the hearer answers with worship as the first step, so the doctrine becomes a practice.

note: 2861 has the swan chicks hide in the lotus and the prince find them; 2867 has the king speak of the pains of parting from kin.
teaches: The play with the chicks is read back as an act of parting kin, so a pleasure-scene becomes a moral one.

note: 2824 names lying, killing, theft and lust as what ascetics guard against; 2868 to 2873 teach these to a prince as duties of a layman.
teaches: The four sins the ascetic keeps from are given to a layman with their fruits, so the rule is seen to reach a king's son.

note: 2868 says killing a life brings great suffering; Kural 321 says not killing is virtuous action and killing brings all other evil.
teaches: One tells the rule and the other the fruit, so together the rule has a reason.

gains.a: The verse's warning of suffering gets a plain statement of the rule behind it, that not killing is the chief virtue
gains.b: The Kural's rule gets a scene, a king giving it to a prince who has just scattered the swans, to show who must hear it

note: 2868 teaches against killing as a cause of suffering ripening from deeds; Tirumanthiram 200 names killing, theft, lust and lying as sins great as mountains whose giving up reaches Siva's feet.
teaches: The same sins are shunned in both, but one pays out as karma and the other as arrival at a god's feet.

gains.a: The Jain king's rule, which has no god to reach, shows the Saiva reward as a different end for the same practice
gains.b: Tirumular's giving-up of the four sins, which says what is gained, shows the Jain view that the fruit is only the working of deeds

note: 2869 says the true word lifts to the towers of the upper world and the lie to hell; Kural 293 says that after lying your own heart burns you.
teaches: The Kural puts the punishment of a lie within and the verse sets it in the next world, so the two give two places for the same cost.

gains.a: The verse's heaven and hell for speech get an inward witness, the liar's own heart
gains.b: The Kural's burning heart gets a cosmos, in which what the heart knows is carried to a birth

note: 2870 says theft is punished by kings and drops the thief into a fallen birth; Kural 290 says the thief loses his footing and the one who does not steal does not lose the world of the gods.
teaches: The verse spells the two punishments the Kural gives in one line, in this world and in the next.

gains.a: The verse's king-tortured thief gets the Kural's measure that the loss is of the very footing of life
gains.b: The Kural's lost footing gets a picture, the elephant's tusk and then the fallen birth

note: 2870 teaches the giving up of theft and gambling to the prince; Naladiyar 157 says those of faultless vision do not steal, drink, scorn others or lie.
teaches: Both put the vows in a list for a lay hearer, so the list of vows seems a common teaching form.

gains.a: The verse's vows get a more general frame, the sort of man who keeps them, 'of faultless vision'
gains.b: The Naladiyar list gets a speaker, a king who gives it to a son with the cost of each breaking

note: 2871 says the one who goes to another's wife is like a bright sword over his own neck and falls into heavy suffering; Naladiyar 84 says if caught the leg is cut, the family shamed and hell follows.
teaches: Both put the cost of adultery in a worldly punishment and a future one, with the same image of a blade.

gains.a: The verse's blade image gets the actual penalties it stands for, caught, maimed and shamed
gains.b: The Naladiyar's list of penalties gets one picture that holds them, the sword that hangs over him

note: 2871 puts another's wife as a sword over the neck and heavy suffering; Kural 146 says enmity, sin, fear and blame never leave one who crosses another's threshold.
teaches: The Kural lists four worldly costs and the verse gives one inward one, so the verse adds fear and the Kural adds blame.

gains.a: The verse's suffering gets named costs, enmity and blame, and not only pain
gains.b: The Kural's costs get the Jain view that adultery is also a deed that sends one downward

note: 2873 tells the prince to abandon wealth got with lies, deceit and dice; Kural 283 says gain got by stealth seems to grow and then perishes.
teaches: The Kural says the ill-gotten gain will not last and the verse adds that the greed behind it is itself what to drop.

gains.a: The verse's abandoning of greed gets a reason from this life, the loss of the gain
gains.b: The Kural's lost gain gets the cause it leaves out, the lie and the dice that win it

note: 2875 sets caged birds crying for their kin and warns the captors that they will be parted from theirs; Naladiyar 122 says those who cage partridges and quails will go as slaves to strangers in irons.
teaches: Together they show the same crime repaid in two forms, loss of kin and loss of freedom, which neither names alone.

gains.a: the verse's warning of parting from kin gains a second, bodily form of repayment, irons and service under strangers
gains.b: the quatrain's repayment for caging gains the grief of the caged, the birds' separation from their flock, that its sentence mirrors

note: 2875 warns that those who cage birds will be parted from their kin; in 2880 the prince who heard the dharma sets the captured cygnet free in the pool.
teaches: The warning and the release show a sermon changing a deed within a few verses, which a rule on its own does not.

note: 2876 says the deed clings to the soul like a thread in a lotus stalk and follows it into each body; Naladiyar 120 says nothing goes with a person but the deeds done.
teaches: One gives the thread image of how a deed follows, the other the fact that only deeds follow, so each answers what the other leaves open.

gains.a: the verse's following deed gains the plain statement that it is the only thing that goes with the person, body and wealth being left
gains.b: the quatrain's 'what goes with a person' gains a picture of how it goes: an unbroken thread that burns as it follows

note: 2876 gives the old deed as a thread that cannot be torn away and burns the soul; Tirumanthiram 117 says the malas burn like cotton only when the sunstone meets the sun's presence, and not before.
teaches: The Jain verse leaves the deed unbroken and the Saiva verse says what ends it, so the Saiva verse limits the Jain one's permanence.

gains.a: the thread that follows through every body is shown to have, in a Saiva view, an end at the coming of grace
gains.b: the malas that grace burns gain a rival account in which the burden is a clinging deed that no god is said to remove

note: 2883 has the father tell the youth who wants to renounce to rule and pass on the kingdom first; Kural 342 says to renounce while there is time.
teaches: The Kural leaves open what counts as time, and the father fixes it as the time after the duties of a king are done.

gains.a: the father's delay gains the Kural's urgency, which makes his 'first rule' a hard answer and not a mild one
gains.b: the Kural's 'while there is time' gains a worked limit, the discharge of a kingdom's duties, that its bare phrase does not give

note: 2883 tells the youth to rule first and give the kingdom to a son before renouncing; Naladiyar 11 says the wise renounced in childhood, knowing grey hair will come.
teaches: One praises renouncing at the earliest, the other puts duty before the vow, so they mark two views of when the right time begins.

gains.a: the father's order of duties gains the opposing view that foresight, not age, marks the wise and that waiting is the fool's course
gains.b: the quatrain's praise of early renunciation gains a king's reason for delay, the kingdom that must be handed on

note: 2884 asks whether the kin he cannot be rid of are kin or enemies; 2885 answers that they are neither, being strangers in past births and in those to come.
teaches: The answer is a rebirth argument and not a complaint, so the question of kin turns on how many lives one counts.

note: 2885 says kin were strangers in past births and will be strangers in births to come; Naladiyar 30 says kin come unasked and go wordlessly, leaving the body like a bird its nesting tree.
teaches: The quatrain holds within one life and the verse extends the same estrangement across births, which turns a sad fact into a ground for cutting the bond.

gains.a: the verse's no-kin argument gains the plain picture of kin arriving and leaving unasked in a single life
gains.b: the quatrain's passing kin gain a reach into past and future births, and with it a reason to cut the tie

note: 2885 has the prince reason that there is no kin and cut the bond of love; Siddhar 55 wishes to put kin away, like a lotus leaf on water, with the mind far off.
teaches: The Siddhar states a wish for detachment and the prince acts on an argument, so together they show the wish and its grounds.

gains.a: the prince's cut gains the Siddhar's image of being among kin without being wetted by them
gains.b: the Siddhar's wish to put kin away gains the argument that kin were strangers across births, which the song never gives

note: 2886 compares the body to a doll that falls apart joint by joint when its pins are loosed; Siddhar 42 asks when the puppet taken up to match the two karmas will be thrown down.
teaches: The epic shows the doll's falling as a mechanism and the Siddhar wants to throw it down, so one explains how the body fails and the other why it is to be cast off.

gains.a: the doll's failing joints gain the Siddhar's reason for the body, a payment for two deeds, to be thrown down
gains.b: the Siddhar's puppet gains an account of how it comes apart, each pin loosing the rest

note: 2887 shows a clinging that holds like the monitor's grip broken by a single word; Kural 350 says to cling to the clinging of the one without clinging in order to let clinging go.
teaches: The Kural names the means as a right object of clinging and the verse names a single word, so the means can be a sentence from a teacher.

gains.a: the single word that broke the prince's clinging gains the Kural's account of why a word can work: it points to the unclinging one
gains.b: the Kural's command to cling in order to let go gains a case where one saying did it

note: 2901 gives Nandan the heritage of the army; 2902 declines it together with heaven and release.
teaches: Nandan answers a plain offer of a throne by ranking his brother's feet above every prize the work weighs elsewhere.

note: 2902 has Nandan turn away from release to worship a brother's feet; Tirumanthiram 284 has devotees who bow in devotion given release in return.
teaches: One text makes devotion the door to release, the other makes devotion a choice that outweighs release.

gains.a: the verse's refusal of release reads as a break with the devotional bargain, which gives the refusal weight it lacks alone
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram claim that devotion earns release meets a devotee who does not ask for the reward

note: 2904 calls the handsome body hollow and moves at once to choose an heir; Naladiyar 42 asks the viewer to look at a body whose skin hides its openings as a bag turned inside out.
teaches: The quatrain teaches the contemplation and the verse shows it driving an abdication.

gains.a: the verse's bare word 'hollow' gets a concrete picture of what lies under the handsome surface
gains.b: the Naladiyar's meditation on the body gets a king who acts on it by giving up his throne

note: 2904 has Civakan act on the body's hollowness by handing on the realm; Siddhar 642 warns the heart that Yama takes the body from a golden throne and the gold stays behind.
teaches: The Siddhar only warns that the throne cannot be carried away, while the epic king acts on the warning and descends from it.

gains.a: the verse's choice of an heir is shown as an answer to the death the Siddhar says takes the throne's owner
gains.b: the Siddhar's warning to the heart meets a ruler who actually leaves the gold throne before Yama comes

audit_text_issue: Lines 2-3 of 2904 (the tusk and thunder similes) are obscure.

note: 2906 tells the heir to guard the earth with the sceptre unbent and calls the guarding of dharma a king's highest joy; Kural 546 says the unbent sceptre, not the spear, wins victory.
teaches: The Kural says the straight sceptre wins, and the epic gives the heir a motive beyond winning, that it is the best joy a king can have.

gains.a: the verse's unbent sceptre gets a stated effect, victory, that it does not name
gains.b: the Kural's unbent sceptre gets a motive from inside the king's own heart, a joy of keeping dharma

note: 2907 sets the elephant fed balls of ripe paddy against the elephant that grazes the field and perishes; Purananuru 184 uses the same two elephants for a king who takes his due against one who grabs.
teaches: Both poets reach for the fed and the loose elephant, and the epic puts the old Sangam figure in the mouth of a king handing on power.

gains.a: the verse's image is shown to be an older figure of the taxing king, not the poet's own
gains.b: the Sangam poem's counsel to a king gets a speaker who is himself a king instructing his successor

note: 2907 says a king who takes revenue in measure keeps the treasure flowing; Kural 552 says a sceptred king's asking is like a robber's demand at spear-point.
teaches: The Kural condemns heavy taking as robbery, and the epic gives a prudent reason for lightness: the field that is grazed bare yields nothing.

gains.a: the verse's advice to take in measure gains a moral name for the opposite, robbery under a sceptre
gains.b: the Kural's charge of robbery gains a worldly argument that the grabbing king ruins his own treasury

note: 2908 says that of rice and water, both life, the king is the world's good life; Purananuru 186 says neither rice nor water is life, the wide world lives by its king.
teaches: The poem makes the king life by denying that rice and water are, while the epic keeps them as lives and adds the king beside them.

gains.a: the verse's ranking of the king above rice and water is shown as a traditional claim
gains.b: the Sangam poem's flat denial that rice or water is life gets a gentler form in which they remain lives and the king is a further one

note: 2909 compares a king to a driver who must know the ground his chariot runs on; Purananuru 185 compares the realm to a cart that sinks if its driver cannot steer.
teaches: Both set a skilled driver against one who does not know the way, and the epic ties the skill to knowing the land.

gains.a: the verse's chariot is shown to belong to an old comparison of kingship with driving
gains.b: the Sangam poem's cart gains the condition that the driver must know the ground, not only steer

audit_text_issue: The marked reading's 'ploughed field' for நேர்நிலத்து should be 'level ground'; this does not touch the link.

note: 2910 says learned kings put away anger with mercy and keep what they desire hidden; Kural 590 says a king who honours a spy openly lets out his own secret.
teaches: The Kural treats concealment as a rule of spycraft, and the epic treats it as a trained temper in which anger is put away and wishes are kept back.

gains.a: the verse's hiding of desire gains a working case in which showing favour betrays a secret
gains.b: the Kural's rule gains a temperament behind it, mercy that has put anger aside

note: 2911 forbids a king even one false syllable for fear of losing fame; Kural 292 allows falsehood to stand as truth if it yields good free of fault.
teaches: One text bars all falsehood from the king, the other lets a blameless good justify it.

gains.a: the verse's total ban is shown to be stricter than the Kural's exception allows
gains.b: the Kural's exception gains a counter-case in which a king's word is watched by all and cannot be bent

note: 2904 orders the youth who will guard the world brought; 2912 shows the king dressing a youth and making him crown prince.
teaches: The call for a successor is answered by the king's own hands adorning him.

note: 2913 decrees that the boy become the great lord; 2914 crowns him and seats him among elephants.
teaches: The decree is kept in a crowning that shows the whole court's weight behind the boy.

note: 2906 tells the heir to keep dharma with learned poets; 2916 sets the learned, blameless sons of his father's comrades beside him.
teaches: The advice to rule with the learned is carried out by the old king before he leaves.

note: 2906 calls guarding dharma the king's highest joy; 2922 turns to the women and asks them to hear the lasting good.
teaches: The same speaker ranks the joy of ruling highest for the heir and then offers a different good to those he leaves.

note: 2918 orders the women brought without saying why; 2923 shows them fading once they read the king's intent.
teaches: The summons hides its purpose, and the women's withering shows that his intent is a farewell.

note: 2923 has the women wither like garlands on a burning vine when they read the king's intent; Naladiyar 392 has women without their companions hear the rain's thunder as a funeral drum.
teaches: The Naladiyar's grief comes after the absence, while the epic's grief comes before it, from the husband's choice.

gains.a: the verse's withering is shown as the same grief of parting that the Naladiyar describes, felt in advance
gains.b: the Naladiyar's sorrow of parting gains a case in which the man leaves by choice and is not away by chance

note: 2929 shows a man who never gave now begging in cold rags; 2624 shows a woman who drank boiled milk from a gold bowl now worn by hunger and cut off from her fortune.
teaches: The first pictures the beggar's state and names his past failure to give, the second pictures a fall from wealth, so together they show beggary as both the fruit of not giving and a turn of fortune.

note: 2929 says the beggar stands begging because he never gave; Naladiyar 107 says those who stand begging at great gates are living out their former deeds without saying which.
teaches: The epic names the former deed behind the begging, a life of not giving, where the quatrain leaves the cause as deeds in general.

gains.a: the beggar of the epic gains the Naladiyar's plain statement that begging in public is the working out of earlier deeds, not an accident
gains.b: the quatrain gains a named cause, never giving, for the former deeds that fill the begging bowl

note: 2927 makes food to the hungry a well in heaven and guarding life a title to earth and sky; Kural 222 says that even if there were no higher world, giving alone is good.
teaches: The epic gives the reward of heaven for giving, while the Kural says giving is right even with no reward, so the two differ on whether the gift needs a world to come.

gains.a: the heaven-reward of the verse is shown to be an extra, since the Kural holds giving good without it
gains.b: the Kural's no-heaven giving is given a school's account, Jain karma, in which giving does bring fruit

note: 2941's speaker, who ate rich ghee-scented food, fears the begging that renunciation brings; Naladiyar 1 says those who once ate six-flavoured food served by a willing wife may end up begging for gruel, so wealth is no support.
teaches: The quatrain uses the fall to beggary as the argument for renouncing, while the epic's speaker uses the same fall as the reason to fear renouncing.

gains.a: the speaker's fear of alms is answered, since the quatrain says such beggary comes anyway to the rich
gains.b: the quatrain's warning about lost wealth meets a person who feels it and still hesitates

note: 2938 strips the body of its sandal and flower to fat, blood, pus and soiled skin; Naladiyar 46 lists entrails, fat, blood, bone, sinew and skin and asks which part is the woman.
teaches: Both teach desire away by breaking the body into its parts, and the epic does it to the very women who are the audience.

gains.a: the verse's list of fluids gains the quatrain's question of where the woman is to be found among the parts
gains.b: the quatrain's analysis is placed in a scene where the one who is analysed is listening

note: 2934 follows the embryo through the channel and into muddy water where it falls weeping without provision for the road; Tirumanthiram 451 has the Lord stay within the womb and form the embryo.
teaches: One text lets the body come into the world helpless and left to its deeds, the other has a Lord who forms it, so the same birth is read without and with a maker.

gains.a: the epic's helpless birth meets a verse that says a Lord forms the embryo within the womb
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's Lord within the womb is set against a Jain account of birth with no one forming it

note: 2940 shows the body's colour, breasts and eyes fading with age as the women watch; Siddhar 23 asks when the speaker will see the bones within as white bones and see himself lowered like a cast-off corpse.
teaches: The epic shows the body's fading from the lover's side, the Siddhar from the renouncer's, so one is a loss and the other is a practice.

gains.a: the verse's fading colour gains the Siddhar's practice of looking through the flesh to the bones
gains.b: the Siddhar's look at the bones gains a view of the same body as it loses its beauty to a lover

note: 2939 says we begin dying from the day we are born and knowledge is useless when one shakes at the end; 2616 has Vijayai say we are born not knowing our days and cover our eyes only when the cow is milked.
teaches: The mother's warning in the first sermon returns in the king's own words to his wives, so the doctrine is passed down rather than invented.
audit_text_issue: 2939 line 4 is compressed and flagged uncertain; line 3 தனிச்சித்தம் வைத்தறேற்றாம் is hard | 2939 lines 3-4 are compressed and hard to construe (தனிச்சித்தம் வைத்தல் தேற்றாம்)

note: 2957 recalls the rescue of Gunamalai from the elephant, which 1068 shows Civakan teasing her about in the early love.
teaches: The wives hold his old rescue against him, so a joke between lovers turns into a debt called in at the parting.

note: 2958 recalls Padumai restored after the snake bite that 1285 shows him curing with his spells.
teaches: The cure that made him a hero is cited as the proof that his love gave life, so leaving takes it back.

note: 2951 has the wives ask whether he will cast them off, while 1097 has him say he will not melt in grief and that even a sesame-seed of attachment is a fault.
teaches: His own earlier teaching to weeping women is now turned on him by wives who ask for what he then refused to grant.

note: 2962 asks whether a husband may give up the wife he took, while Naladiyar 56 says a husband cannot easily put away a wife even if she lacks good qualities.
teaches: The wife's plea is that the bond cannot be cast off, which the Naladiyar says too but only to praise those who avoid marriage.

gains.a: the wife's plea that a husband is bound gains the support of a rule from the moral literature that she does not cite
gains.b: the Naladiyar's argument that marriage binds hard gains a case where the bond is felt by those left, not by the husband

note: 2960 asks whether renouncing wives can be worthy, while Naladiyar 53 says the best renounce home, youth and beauty without delay.
teaches: The Naladiyar's praise of the best renouncers leaves out the people left behind, whom the wives put forward as the cost.

gains.a: the wives' question is given the opposing view that the best of men renounce what they love without delay
gains.b: the Naladiyar's praise of renouncing gains the weeping wives that its list of things given up does not name

note: 2965 shows the wives stripping bangles and weeping at the king's going, while Tirumanthiram 157 has the wives and kin who wailed turn back at the town's edge.
teaches: The epic shows grieving women at a living man's leaving, where the Tirumanthiram shows the same women turning back at a dead man's bier.

gains.a: the wives' grief gains a Saiva reading in which wives, kin and children turn back at the edge of town
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's turning back gains a living scene where the same grief ends in a king's choosing to go

note: 2964 and 1104 both show women beating and weeping at the going of Civakan, once into prison and now into renunciation.
teaches: The same hero's leaving is wept over twice, first as a captive and then as one who goes freely.

note: 2977 compares the vanished smoke of incense and garlands to the fame of misers who gave nothing; Naladiyar 9 says the miser who guards his wealth is already counted as one who has lost it.
teaches: Together they show the miser losing twice, his goods in the Naladiyar and his name in the epic, so hoarding gets a fate in memory as well as in wealth.

gains.a: the simile of vanishing smoke gets its ground, that the miser is already counted as a loss
gains.b: the Naladiyar's loss of the hoarder gets a trace in memory, his fame disappearing like the smoke

note: Kural 333 tells the possessor of wealth to do at once what stays because wealth does not; 2983 adds that Fortune stays with the one who is not attached and never clings to the one who is.
teaches: The Kural treats wealth's going as a fact to act on, while the epic makes clinging the cause of its going, so a reader sees what each assumes about why wealth leaves.

gains.a: the verse's claim about Fortune and attachment gets the plainer rule that wealth by nature does not stay
gains.b: the Kural's rule gets a reason for the going: wealth is lost through the very clinging that tries to keep it

note: In 232 Fortune leaves the clinging king without a word; in 2983 Civakan says she never leaves the one who lets go.
teaches: The goddess of fortune who abandoned the grasping king in the first ilampakam is shown in the last to stay with the king who gives up, so the story's arc on wealth reverses.

note: 2985 calls the fruit of good deeds poison and says only crossing the flood of deeds gives bliss; Tirumanthiram 258 makes penance and virtue the boat that carries one across the sea of deeds.
teaches: Both see deeds as a sea to cross, but one holds virtue's fruit to be poison and the other makes virtue the boat, so the two disagree on whether good deeds help or only bind.

gains.a: the epic's claim that merit too binds meets a text that sets virtue and austerity as the crossing itself
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's boat of virtue meets the Jain view that its fruit is a poison to be crossed

note: 2846 says the three jewels burn the tree of deeds and release is freedom from deeds; 2985 applies this to Civakan's wives, saying even the fruit of good deeds is poison.
teaches: The sermon's doctrine of freedom from deeds is turned into advice to the wives, and it is made to include good deeds that the sermon does not single out.

note: 2984 sets wealth against the funeral rice and the wife's tears at the burning ground; Tirumanthiram 149 gives the man's public mansion, palanquin and three crores and then his silent going.
teaches: The Tirumanthiram shows a life of building and giving with no look back; the epic shows what the household is left with, so together they give the whole before and after.

gains.a: the funeral picture is set after a life like the man's, in which a mansion and palanquin were all in public view
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's man who did not turn back gets a household to leave, with a widow's tears and a funeral rice

note: In 2607 Vijayai begs the eight wives, who came in her dream as eight garlands on the king's crown, never to part; in 2987 they decide to renounce.
teaches: The dream's garlands that were never to part are parted by the story's end, showing the epic setting a mother's wish against the wives' own turn from the household.

note: 2727 has Civakan reflect that to subdue oneself in time, do penance and reach a world without affliction is better; in 2988 he speaks it to his wives and calls them to come.
teaches: The reflection made alone in the earlier chapter becomes an invitation, so the resolve is seen first as thought and then as something shared.

note: Kural 346 says the one who cuts 'I' and 'mine' enters a world higher than the gods'; 2988 calls the wives to cross old deeds and reach bliss at the top of the world above.
teaches: The Kural names the pride to be cut and the height, the epic names the deeds to be crossed and the place, so each gives what the other leaves open.

gains.a: the summit above the world gets a condition the verse does not state, the cutting of 'I' and 'mine'
gains.b: the Kural's higher world gets a location at the top of the universe and a means in crossing old deeds

note: 2988 has the wives cross old deeds by leaving the household and gives no god; Tirumanthiram 219 has the worshipped fire rise and burn the diseases of deeds.
teaches: One text frees from old deeds by the renouncer's own crossing, the other by a fire that burns them when worshipped, which is the split between Jain effort and Saiva rite.

gains.a: the call to cross old deeds on one's own meets a text where a worshipped fire does the burning
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's fire that burns deeds meets a rival route with no fire and no god

note: In 2607 Vijayai begs the wives never to part from the king; in 2991 he entrusts them to her as he goes.
teaches: The mother who wished the wives to stay with her son is the one who now receives them as he leaves, so the wish is kept in a changed form.

note: 2992 has the wives lay aside their ornaments like a vine shedding flowers; Siddhar 19 asks when the speaker will leave silk and gold ornaments and desire the feet.
teaches: The Siddhar's wish to leave ornaments is shown done by women who give them up, but without the god's feet as its aim.

gains.a: the stripping of ornaments gets an aim in a god's feet that the epic's scene never names
gains.b: the Siddhar's wish to leave silk and gold gets a scene where it is carried out, with the cost to those who give up beauty

note: Kural 221 says giving to the destitute is true giving and the rest a loan with return; 2995 has the king give to those who ask in great want on the eve of leaving.
teaches: The king giving just before he leaves the world where any return could come is the case the couplet's test points to, so the epic shows the rule in its purest form.

gains.a: the farewell gift is shown to be of the kind the Kural calls true giving, with no return possible
gains.b: the Kural's test of no return gets a case where the giver leaves the world in which returns could come

note: In 2628 the matrons go in palanquins to renounce and the king is left; in 2998 he boards a palanquin himself and the gods carry it.
teaches: The palanquin of renunciation first carried the mothers by men, and now carries the son by gods, so the epic shows the same vehicle changing in meaning from parting to ascent.

note: In 2998 the king mounts a palanquin that the gods carry; Tirumanthiram 153 has the lord of the land mount the burning ground's palanquin for the last time.
teaches: The same royal vehicle is a bier in one and a god-borne chair to release in the other, so the reader sees how renunciation and death can wear the same procession.

gains.a: the king's palanquin gets the contrast of the bier in which a king is carried to the burning ground
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's royal bier gets a counter-case where the royal palanquin leads to release

audit_text_issue: 2998 uses the same vehicle word as a different thing

note: 2555 has the city say that anyone who sees how Civakan was born in the burning ground, grew up a merchant's son and was worshipped by kings must ask why live heedless instead of doing penance; 3016 has the Jina tell the king that renunciation is the excellent thing.
teaches: The people's question about heedlessness at the crowning is answered by the lord's own word here, so the end of the book fulfils what its hero's rise had begun to pose.

note: 2560 has Civakan circle the shrine and say he has been born and will not be born again; 3017 has a worshipper at the end say he was born in a fearful course and feared his deeds, and that those who circle the feet do not suffer.
teaches: The coronation-day boast of no more births is brought to its ground at the end, where the fear of deeds, not the pride of a king, is what sends the worshipper to the feet.

note: 2563 hymns the lord as the one who understood without fault, the wheel that removes stain, and who set bounds to the senses; 3023 hymns the same lord as the sea of virtues and the wheel of dharma that clears hunger, hatred and disease.
teaches: The same epithets, wheel and a sea of virtues, recur at the king's last bow, so the earlier hymn's titles are seen to be the book's one settled form of praise.

note: Kural 342 says renounce while there is something to renounce, and many things come after; 3016 has the Jina tell a king, who has the most to give up, that renunciation is the excellent course.
teaches: The Kural counsels renunciation in general and never says who it is hardest for, and the verse sets it before a crowned king as the hardest case.

gains.a: the Jina's counsel to the king gets a general rule that one can renounce only what one still holds, which is why the king's case is the gravest
gains.b: the Kural's bare 'renounce while it is yours' gets a concrete test, a ruler with a whole kingdom to give up

note: Kural 10 says those who reach the Lord's feet swim the sea of births and others cannot; 3019 says those who do not reach the lord are kicked by their deeds into the sea of sorrow and whirl like thread on a shuttle.
teaches: The Kural states the crossing and the failure to cross but gives no cause or picture for the failure, and the verse supplies deeds that beat the swimmer down and a turning that never ends.

gains.a: the verse's sea of sorrow is given the Kural's single condition for crossing it, reaching the lord's feet
gains.b: the Kural's 'cannot swim' is given a cause (deeds that strike) and a picture (thread wound without end on a shuttle)

note: 3020 praises the Jina as the master whose spoken word frees those who repeat it from suffering; Tirumanthiram 105 has the Lord stand beyond the two kinds of deed.
teaches: Jain release comes by hearing and keeping the word of one who went before, while the Saiva text puts the Lord beyond deeds so that deeds cannot reach him, and the two disagree on whether a liberated one also helps.

gains.a: the praise of a teacher whose word wears away deeds is shown as a path with no god above it who removes them
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's Lord beyond both deeds meets a rival in which the one beyond deeds is a teacher who shows a way and does not grant grace

audit_text_issue: Sense flagged uncertain; line 4 is repeated in 3021.

note: 3022 has the king bow to the feet that walked over the lotus with its bees; Kural 3 praises those who reach the feet of the one who walked on the flower.
teaches: Both place the object of worship on the lotus, the Kural without a name and the epic with a figure the king can bow to, so the stock image is shown being used as a scene.

gains.a: the verse's lotus-treading feet are shown as the stock image of the Kural's opening praise, so the king's bow is the act the couplet commends
gains.b: the Kural's 'one who walked on the flower' gets a staged scene, a lotus in an assembly with a king bowing before it

note: Kural 9 says a head that does not bow at the feet of the one of eight qualities is as useless as a dead sense; 3022 has the king bow with his gem crown, ear-rings and bands shining on the ground.
