teaches: The Kural gives the cost of a head that does not bow, and the epic shows the most ornamented head in the book putting its crown to use by bowing.

gains.a: the king's crown, ear-rings and garlands are given their one use, the bow, which the couplet makes the measure of a head
gains.b: the Kural's useless head gets its opposite, a head heavy with ornaments that is not useless because it bows

note: Kural 8 says other seas are hard to swim except for those who reach the feet of the one called அறவாழி; 3023 uses அறவாழி for the wheel of dharma and also calls him a sea of virtues.
teaches: The Kural's single word அறவாழி can be a sea or a wheel, and the epic shows the lord named as both in one verse.

gains.a: the verse's wheel of dharma and sea of virtues are read as the two sides of one name, so its praise echoes the couplet's term in both senses
gains.b: the Kural's compound அறவாழி gets a use in which it is a wheel and the sea is named separately, so its single word is seen to carry two images

note: 3036 says the mantra heard at the hour of death brings birth among the gods; 945 shows Civakan whispering it to a dying dog.

note: In 3037 the god Sutanjanan praises Civakan's feet, whom in 945 he met as the dying dog taught the five mantras.

note: 3027 has the king take off jewels and garlands because the world is a drop of milk; Kural 345 says that for those cutting off births even the body is excess.
teaches: The epic stages the stripping as a royal act step by step, while the Kural makes the body itself the last thing to be let go.

gains.a: the king's removal of ornaments is shown to be the first step of a series that reaches the body
gains.b: the Kural's rule that even the body is excess gets a worked case of a king who has things to lose

note: 3030 has Civakan pluck his hair like a lion shedding its mane; Naladiyar 53 says the best renounce home, youth, wealth and strength at once because none lasts.

gains.a: the verse's act of tonsure gets the reason the Naladiyar gives, that none of these things lasts
gains.b: the quatrain's advice to renounce without delay gets a worked case at the height of a king's power

note: In 3033 the bees mourn the cast-off hair and garland; Siddhar 329 lists a loincloth, a porch and leaves to eat as all one needs once ornament is gone.
teaches: The Jain epic gives the loss of ornament a lament by those who lived on it, while the Siddhar counts it as pure gain.

gains.a: the bees' lament shows the cost of renunciation that the king's calm stripping leaves out
gains.b: the Siddhar's cheerful poverty is tested against those who lose by it

note: 3039 has the ascetics shed the milk of kindness on every life; Kural 30 names the virtuous, clothed in cool kindness to every being, as the true brahmins.
teaches: Both define the ascetic by his kindness to all lives, not by any robe or rite.

gains.a: the verse's milk of kindness gets a name for the sage whom it makes
gains.b: the Kural's kindness to every living thing gets the practice of an order that has put away hatred

note: 3039 has the freed ascetic reach it by wholly dropping attachment and hatred; Tirumanthiram 497 has the siddhas free of the bonds by becoming Siva and destroying the five malas.
teaches: The Jain epic makes release the result of the ascetic's own dropping of passions; the Saiva text has it come by becoming Siva.

gains.a: the verse's self-made release is set against a release by becoming the Lord
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's grace-based freedom meets a school that gives no role to a god

note: 3044 has King Senikan call for a feast to the Jina's feet with kings gathered; Purananuru 134 has a patron who does not give to buy merit for the next birth.
teaches: The king's feast here is made an act of worship whose fruit the next lines of the work will tell, and so the poem's patron who gives without bargaining is set against it.

gains.a: the king's feast to the Jina gets a foil in a patron who refuses to give for reward
gains.b: the poem's refusal of trade-giving meets a king whose gift is plainly an act of worship

note: 2846 names knowledge, faith and conduct together as the fire that burns the tree of deeds; 3064 has Civakan cut the eight karmas himself by the firmness of his mind.
teaches: The sermon gives the means of release as three jewels and a fire; the life shows the one quality of mind that does the cutting, so release is both taught and done.

note: 28 says only that Civakan goes to the ever-new state; 3073 gives the ending of the austerity by which he gets there, with his family waiting.
teaches: The opening summary states the destination in a half-line; the closing shows the cost, the family watching and the hand held back from food.

note: 2844 says release lies in the scripture of the Lord under the three umbrellas and the pindi tree; 3051 shows that same Lord preaching to kings who leave their retinues outside the golden wall.
teaches: The sermon only names the Lord as the source of the doctrine; the assembly shows what following him costs a king, who leaves his army at the gate.

note: 2843 promises that virtue makes gods in heaven; 3056 says the heaven-dwellers of the enjoyment lands renounce nothing and see nothing but what the Lord's word has said.
teaches: Heaven is the reward of virtue in one verse, and in the other it is a place where renunciation, and so release, is not done.

note: Kural 267 says austerity burns pain as fire burns gold so that it shines; 3070 has the sun's own fire ring burn on Civakan for four months while he stands on the elephant of knowledge.
teaches: The couplet gives the gold-and-fire image of austerity in general; the verse sets it in a particular season of heat and ties the shining to knowledge, not to appearance.

gains.a: the verse's four months of burning sun are given the principle that the heat is what makes the ascetic shine
gains.b: the Kural's gold in fire becomes a named ordeal, a season of heat with an ascetic standing in it

note: 3072 has Civakan spend four cold months in the open field, using the body up for release; Tirumanthiram 724 says if the body perishes the life perishes, so the body is nurtured to win knowledge.
teaches: One text treats the body as the means to be spent, the other as the means that must be kept alive, so they disagree on what a body is for.

gains.a: the verse's exposure of the body is set against a school that says release needs a body kept alive
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's nurturing of the body meets an ascetic who spends his on release

note: Naladiyar 51 says austerity drives sin out like a lamp but that sin returns when the oil of merit runs out; 3064 has the eight karmas cut to pieces by one firm mind.
teaches: The quatrain's lamp-and-oil picture makes the effect of austerity last as long as its merit; the epic claims a final cutting, so the two differ on whether it can return.

gains.a: the verse's total destruction of karma is tested by the rule that austerity only keeps sin away while the merit lasts
gains.b: the quatrain's returning darkness meets a claim that the cut is final

note: 3064 has Civakan cut the eight karmas by the strength of his own mind; Tirumanthiram 120 has deeds made into seeds that have touched fire and will not sprout, by the one who parts milk from water, the Lord or guru.
teaches: The seeds will not sprout in both, but one makes the ascetic himself the burner and the other leaves the burner a god or teacher.

gains.a: the verse's self-won end of karma is set against a Saiva reading in which the burning is done for the soul
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's burnt seeds meet a Jain account in which no one else burns them

note: Kural 261 defines austerity as bearing the pain that comes and causing none to living beings; 3072 has Civakan live four months in the cold open field and guard sweet life.
teaches: The couplet joins the endurance and the harmlessness in one definition, and the verse shows them in one season, if the 'guarded life' is the lives of creatures.

gains.a: the verse's four months in the open are measured against a rule that endured pain counts only with harmlessness
gains.b: the Kural's two-part definition is given an ascetic who lives it out in one cold season

note: 2845 gives knowledge, faith and conduct as the three that make release; 3074 turns knowledge into the chariot, mercy into armour and virtue into the sword.
teaches: The ilampakam's plain teaching of the three jewels is here made into an army, so the reader sees what the three do and not only that they are three.

note: 2819 makes virtue (sila) the armour of warring kings; in 3074 mercy is the armour and sila the sword.
teaches: The same virtue moves from a guard to a weapon, showing that in this ascetic war sila both protects and wins.

note: 2846 says knowledge, faith and conduct together are a fire that burns the tree of deeds; 3082 shows the fire's end: the four destroying kings fall and the three worlds are known.
teaches: A teaching that the three burn deeds is fulfilled in the hero's own omniscience, so the doctrine is shown as an event in a life.

note: 2847 lists the four infinites of the liberated, and 3082 lifts the banner of the fourfold infinite.
teaches: The list of what release gives is shown as something one person takes, with the world swallowed, and not only a catalogue.

note: 3082 has Civakan win omniscience by his own war on the karmas; Tirumanthiram 113 has the Lord come down in a body, set his feet on the devotee's head and cut away the stain.
teaches: One text has the soul win release by its own battle, the other has it given from above, so the two disagree on whose act cuts the deeds.

gains.a: the war of the passions is set against a release that is given and not fought for, so its self-reliance becomes a choice
gains.b: the grace that cuts the stain is set beside a release won by effort, so its giver is seen to be what the Jain refuses

note: 3093 repeats 3082's swallowing of the three worlds, there as the narrator's victory, here as praise in the worshippers' mouths.
teaches: The same image is first an event and then a creed, and the hymn shows how a story becomes what a community says.

note: Kural 360 names three roots of pain, desire, anger and confusion; 3080 names four passions, Anger, Pride, Deceit and Greed, as warriors who must be slain.
teaches: The Jain list of four widens the Kural's three, showing that one counts the roots of pain differently depending on the school.

gains.a: the four passions, as warriors, get a rule that when their very names perish pain perishes
gains.b: the Kural's three roots get a fourth and a fighting form: pride and deceit, and a weapon against them

note: Kural 10 says those who reach the Lord's feet swim the sea of births; 3091 prays 'let our birth end' to the Lord who destroyed Desire and Death.
teaches: The Kural says the feet carry across, and the verse names who the Lord has beaten (Desire and Death) and why they should be prayed to.

gains.a: the prayer for the end of birth is given a wider rule that reaching his feet is the way to cross
gains.b: the Kural's Lord, who is left unnamed, is shown as one who has killed Desire and Death

note: Kural 9 praises the one of eight qualities; 3092 praises the one who has cut four deeds together and knows the three times.
teaches: One text counts a Lord by eight qualities and the other by four deeds cut, so the reader sees two different measures of the same worshipped figure.

gains.a: a Lord counted by four destroyed karmas is seen beside a Lord counted by eight qualities
gains.b: the Kural's eight qualities, left unnamed, can be compared with a Jain account of what is cut and known

note: 3082 tells the cutting of the four destroying karmas and the knowing of the three worlds; 3092 sings it as the Lord's own deed.
teaches: The event of 3082 becomes the praise of 3092, so the narrator's story is shown as the hymn's ground.

note: 3081 fires the arrow of pure meditation like a roaring fire to destroy the foes; Tirumanthiram 219 has deeds burnt by the fire that is worshipped and fed with ghee.
teaches: One text burns deeds by an inner meditation like fire, the other by an outer fire kindled in worship, so the two disagree on where the fire is.

gains.a: the meditation that burns is seen as an inner fire beside the Saiva fire kindled in ritual
gains.b: the ritual fire that burns deeds is set beside a Jain fire that burns them with no offering

note: 3098 gives the bad deed a child nursed by anger and desire; 3099 gives the good deed a child nursed by compassion.
teaches: The two verses pair the same upbringing image so that the difference between kinds of deed lies in what feeds them.

note: 3101 has the Lord's feet cut through the hard-gathered karma like a blade; Kural 5 says the two deeds do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's true praise.
teaches: The verse gives the means by which the deeds are removed and the Kural gives the assurance that they will not cling.

gains.a: the verse's cutting spear is given an outcome, that the deeds do not attach to the one who praises

note: 3101 has worship of the feet cut karma like a weapon; Tirumanthiram 219 says the fire worshipped and risen burns the deeds of ages.
teaches: Both promise that worship removes karma, but one gives the cutting to an enlightened teacher's feet and the other to a worshipped fire.

gains.a: the Jain feet-as-spear gets a rival agent of the same removal, a burning fire that the Jain verse does not use
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's burning fire gets a rival that cuts by the feet of a liberated one who does not answer prayer

note: 3105 pictures desire as grass that lures souls into the four-state pen and says reaching the pure one's feet lets one go to release; Kural 10 says those who reach the Lord's feet swim the sea of births.
teaches: The verse supplies the trap that the Kural's sea leaves unnamed, and the Kural supplies the crossing the verse only names as going.

gains.a: the verse's pen of four states gets the picture of a sea crossed, which turns the escape into a swim
gains.b: the Kural's sea of births gets a reason people are in it, the grass of desire, and a price for crossing, love sold

note: 3107 says that guarding all lives as one's own brings a high birth; Kural 327 says not to kill even if one's own life is the price.
teaches: The verse makes non-injury pay in a later birth, and the Kural cuts the rule loose from payment even at the price of one's life.

gains.a: the verse's reward for protection is tested by the case where protection costs the protector his life
gains.b: the Kural's absolute rule gets the Jain account of what the careful guarder wins in later births

note: 3108 has the one who harms for food thrown by two deeds into burning flame; Kural 320 says pains rest on those who caused pain.
teaches: The verse names the form the returning pain takes, a hell of fire, which the Kural's general law does not.

gains.a: the verse's hell is shown as one case of a general law that pain returns to its cause
gains.b: the Kural's law gets a specific place and fire where the pain lands

note: 3117 pictures omniscience as a maiden embraced by the king at the top of the worlds, the self still distinct; Tirumanthiram 134 says those who feel the teacher's word become the reality, like ghee mixed in milk.
teaches: Both end in bliss, but the Cintamani keeps lover and beloved two, while the Tirumanthiram dissolves the self into what it meets.

gains.a: the verse's embrace is shown as release that keeps a separate self, which the milk-and-ghee image of union would remove
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's merging gets a rival picture where the freed one stays apart and enjoys

note: 3118 has the king live with a woman who has no old age or death; Naladiyar 14 has the once-desired woman bent over a staff and a torment.
teaches: One text shows what the loved woman will become, and the other the woman who never becomes it.

gains.a: the verse's ageless bride is shown as the answer to the old woman the quatrain describes
gains.b: the Naladiyar's bent old woman gets the Jain promise of a partner who does not age, offered to those who give up the first kind

note: 3120 has the women see the dirt on their adorned bodies and think of ending woman-birth; Naladiyar 46 breaks the woman into entrails, fat, blood and bone and asks which part she is.
teaches: The quatrain gives the analysis of the body's parts and the verse shows women applying a like seeing to themselves.

gains.a: the verse's women get the reasoned list of parts that grounds their disgust, so their turn is more than a mood
gains.b: the Naladiyar's list, offered to men about women, gets a case where women use it on their own bodies

note: 3106 tells the women to hate the body kept for desire; 3120 shows them doing it, seeing their adorned bodies as stained.
teaches: The sermon's advice to hate the body and the women's act of seeing it as dirt are the same turn, the teaching and then its keeping.

note: 3116 has the pyre burn the Lord's jewel-bright body with gods circling and rejoicing; Naladiyar 24 has the drums beat three times and the corpse be covered and the fire taken up.
teaches: The same flame ends an ordinary corpse in grief and a Lord's body in festival, so the pyre's meaning depends on who is burning.

gains.a: the festival pyre is shown in contrast with the common corpse's plain burning, which the gods' honours dress up
gains.b: the quatrain's grieved burning gets a body whose burning is celebrated because nothing of the person is lost

note: 3105 says that giving up clinging at the pure one's feet lets one reach the state of release; 3121 shows the women, free of desire and love, reaching heaven.
teaches: The promise to the women's sermon is kept, though what they reach is heaven rather than the release the verse named.

note: 3121 sends the women who gave up desire to heaven as Indras; Kural 346 says one who cuts off 'I' and 'mine' enters a world higher than the gods'.
teaches: The verse ends in the gods' world and the Kural says release lies above it, so the same renunciation is given two different ends.

gains.a: the verse's heaven is shown as a stop below where the Kural puts the one who has left 'I' and 'mine'
gains.b: the Kural's world above the gods gets a case of renouncers who stop at the gods' world

note: 3132 has Nandan and his friends piling up penance by effort; 3134 ends their lives on the mountain with rebirth as gods.
teaches: The penance begun in one verse comes to its fruit two verses later, so the story shows the deed ripening into a heavenly birth and not into release.

note: 3133 says fasting and meditation wash off evil deeds; 3145 closes on the Lord's feet as the way across the sea of deeds.
teaches: The first verse gives the ascetic's own washing of deeds, the last the worshipper's crossing by the Lord's feet, so the work ends by joining effort and devotion.

note: 3122 sets the lovers as wishing-trees wrapped in creepers; 3141 puts the gods in a sea of the senses, so one pleasure is drawn at two levels.
teaches: The poet writes human and heavenly love with the same figures, so the heaven reached by penance is a purer form of the bed that penance left.

note: 3133 says fasting and meditation wash off evil deeds; Naladiyar 51 says austerity drives off sin as a lamp drives off dark, but only while the good deeds last.
teaches: The story shows the ascetics' fast washing deeds away, and the quatrain adds that the lamp burns only while its oil of good deeds holds.

gains.a: the verse's washing of deeds acquires a limit, that austerity works only while the store of good deeds lasts, which is not said in the verse
gains.b: the quatrain's lamp and oil acquire a case in which a company of ascetics is seen to carry the austerity through to their deaths

note: 3134 has the penance end in birth as gods; Kural 346 says one who cuts off the pride of I and mine goes to a world above the gods.
teaches: The epic's ascetics end among the gods, but the couplet puts above the gods a world reached only by cutting off the self, so heaven is not the last goal.

gains.a: the rebirth among gods is shown as not the top of the scale, which the verse itself does not say
gains.b: the couplet's world above the gods is given a case of ascetics who stop at heaven short of it

note: 3145 ends on the Lord's feet as the way over the sea of deeds; Kural 10 says those who reach the Lord's feet cross the sea of births.
teaches: Both place the Lord's feet beyond a sea, but the Cintamani names the water as deeds and the Kural as births, so the epic fixes on karma as the thing to be crossed.

gains.a: the sea is placed in a fuller tradition of birth as the sea to be crossed, so karma and rebirth are read together
gains.b: the couplet's sea of births is given a cause by the epic, since the water is made of deeds

note: Verse 2 says the slips of speech of one praising the faultless are no slips; verse 17 says a fault stays a fault even in those who have reached truth and in a god.
teaches: The fragments hold two standards side by side: the poet excuses faults by the worth of what is praised, while the moral verse refuses to let any height excuse a fault, so the apology rests on devotion, not on a rule about faults.

note: Both poets apologise for faults in their work: the Kundalakesi poet says faults in praise of the faultless one are not faults; the Neelakesi poet says the moon itself has a spot and he will own any fault.
teaches: The two rival works answer the same assembly in opposite ways, the Buddhist denying that his slips count and the Jain conceding them, so the debate between the books begins in how each poet stands toward his own fault.

note: Verse 2 praises the one who cut off the three faults without naming them; Kural 360 names three, desire, anger and confusion, whose very names must perish for pain to end.
teaches: Read with the couplet, the epic's unnamed three faults take on a Tamil list already current, and the couplet's goal of ending the three is shown as the very mark by which a Buddhist poet recognises his lord.

gains.a: the fragment's bare 'three faults' gets a known Tamil naming
gains.b: the couplet's triad is seen used as a title of the one who has achieved it, not only a goal for the seeker

note: Kural 280 says neither shaving nor long hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns; Kundalakesi 4 dismisses a longer list, nakedness, ash, cold, fire, alms and matted hair, as words, and calls tapas a subdued life.
teaches: The couplet sets aside only the hair, and tests the renouncer by the world's blame; the fragment sets aside the whole repertoire of bodily austerity and puts the test in inner restraint, so the two differ on where the renouncer's proof lies.

gains.a: the fragment's dismissal is seen to extend a point the Kural already made about outward marks
gains.b: the couplet's narrow example is shown to open onto a general attack on bodily penance

note: Kural 1148 says thinking gossip can put out love is like thinking ghee can put out fire; Kundalakesi 5 asks whether a fire-pit can be put out with ghee, of those who would end desire by enjoying it.
teaches: The same proverb of ghee on fire serves the lover, for whom nothing will quench love and that is its strength, and the ascetic, for whom indulgence only feeds desire and that is its danger.

gains.b: the couplet's image is shown to carry a warning against desire that the love-speaker does not draw

gains.b: the quatrain's 'the dying' is given a measure: one dies at every stage of growth

gains.b: the couplet's bare command gains a reason a hearer can test on his own body

gains.a: the fragment's denial is extended past death to every scavenger
gains.b: the Siddhar's after-death scene is shown to have begun in the living body, which sharpens his question of what gain the rearing brought

note: Kural 957 says a fault in the well-born stands out like the spot on the moon; Kundalakesi 17 says a fault stays a fault even in those who have reached truth, as the stain on the god's throat is still a stain.

gains.b: the couplet's one-sided rebuke is shown to stop short of the full equanimity its premise allows

note: Purananuru 192 says good and ill do not come from others, we neither delight in life nor call it bitter, since life moves by its order like a raft on a river; Kundalakesi 18 says what is due comes, so the wise neither grieve nor exult.
teaches: The Sangam poet draws from the same certainty a rule about others, neither marvelling at the great nor despising the small; the fragment draws only the inner rule, so the pair shows one premise yielding a social ethic in one book and a private discipline in the other.

gains.a: the fragment's maxim gains an older Tamil statement of the same order of things
gains.b: the Sangam poem's equanimity is shown carried into a later religious setting where it becomes a teaching on grief and joy

note: Verse 18 states that the wise neither grieve nor exult because what is due will come; verse 19 shows a man unmoved both by a king's pardon and by a plot to kill him, naming all of it the fruit of deeds.
teaches: The maxim of 18 is put to its hardest test in 19, a reprieve and a death plot, and 19 names the cause 18 left unnamed: deeds.
audit_text_issue: Verse 19's sense is flagged uncertain; who plots the killing is not stated, but the link does not depend on it. | 19's event is unclear (who plotted கொலை சூழ்ந்த is unstated), but the link does not depend on it. | Fragments in an editor's order; adjacency is editorial.

note: Pattinathar asks what use weeping is, since good and evil will not come otherwise than as the lotus-born god wrote; Kundalakesi 19 has a man stay unmoved by pardon and death because all that befalls is the fruit of deeds.
teaches: Both counsel the same steadiness, but the Siddhar grounds it in what a god wrote and the fragment in one's own deeds, so the same calm rests on incompatible accounts of who decides what comes.

gains.a: the fragment's karma is set against a theistic account of the same events
gains.b: the Siddhar's appeal to Brahma's writing is shown to be one choice among Tamil grounds for equanimity

audit_text_issue: The marker flags the verse's sense as uncertain; who plotted the killing (கொலை சூழ்ந்த) is not stated.

note: Silappathikaram's patikam ends with Ilango graciously telling and Saathan the grain merchant hearing (அடிகள் அருள ... சாத்தன் கேட்டனன்); Manimekalai's ends with Ilango graciously hearing and Saathan setting out the work (இளங்கோ வேந்தன் அருளிக் கேட்ப ... சாத்தன் ... அறிய வைத்தனன்), each in thirty parts.
teaches: The two patikams frame the twin epics as one exchange between the same two men, each the listener of the other's poem, so the tradition joins them by their frames and not only by Madhavi's daughter continuing the story.

note: Pattinappalai opens on the Kaveri that does not fail though the white star strays south and the sky withholds rain; the patikam calls the Kaveri the Tamil maiden who does not leave her course though the planets stray and summer lengthens (கோள் நிலை திரிந்து கோடை நீடினும் தான் நிலை திரியா).
teaches: The epic takes the Sangam praise-formula for Puhar's river and turns it into a person, a Chola daughter who bows to the city's goddess and gives the city its second name, so a boast of the land's yield becomes a founding story.

gains.a: the epithet in line 24-25 is shown to be an inherited Sangam formula, placing the epic's Puhar in the Chola praise tradition of Karikalan's city
gains.b: the idyll's unfailing river gains a myth of origin (Agastya's pot, the king's request) and a person who acts, which the idyll's description does not have

note: The narrator states as event that at the jewel seat Manimekalai came to know all her former births (பழம் பிறப்பு எல்லாம் ... உணர்ந்ததும்); in kaathai 27 she asks whether no one has known a former birth, and the materialist answers that such knowledge is the delusion of those led by a god or by dreams. The tension holds on the reading that 281-283 are the materialist's.
teaches: The materialist's dismissal names exactly the route by which the patikam says her knowledge came, a goddess carrying her to an island, so the epic lets the one school it answers attack the very ground of its heroine's conversion.
audit_text_issue: manimekalai:27:281-283 speakers are unnamed and assigned from sense

note: The patikam's line for kaathai 27 is that she asked them to state the faultless truth and heard (கேட்டதும்) the schools' doctrines; kaathai 27 lays the schools out one by one and she answers only the materialist.
teaches: The patikam's own word for the chapter of the schools is hearing, not defeating, which supports reading most of kaathai 27's accounts as reported views left for the Buddhist teaching of the later kaathais to answer.

note: Kural 225 ranks the strength of those who bear hunger below the strength of those who remove it; in the patikam the renunciant who begs with a bowl is the one who ends Kayachandigai's hunger-fire.
teaches: The Kural sets the one who endures hunger and the one who relieves it as two kinds of strength in rank, while the epic gives both to one person, a begging ascetic whose bowl feeds others, so its Buddhist renunciation removes the Kural's ranking rather than falling under it.

gains.a: the bowl scene gains a standard from the ethics books by which the heroine's begging is a higher strength than ascetic endurance, not a lower one
gains.b: the couplet's contrast between enduring and removing hunger is shown not to be exclusive, since a renunciant can hold both

note: Kural 362: if one must desire, desire not to be born, and that comes by desiring not to desire; the patikam closes with Manimekalai, having heard the dharma, vowing that becoming be cut off (பவத் திறம் அறுக என ... நோற்றதும்).
teaches: The Kural allows one desire, for birthlessness, and reaches it by turning desire on itself; the epic makes that one desire a vow kept with austerity after hearing a teacher, so the end the Kural states as inner paradox is reached in the epic through instruction and practice.

gains.a: the heroine's closing vow is seen to be the single desire the Kural permits, not a lapse from desirelessness
gains.b: the couplet's wish for birthlessness gains a path, a teacher's dharma and a vow, which the couplet does not name

note: The Purananuru poet names the ancestors who destroyed the hanging fort as a deed so great that killing is no longer the living Chola's own fame; Manimekalai's opening makes the hanging-fort Chola the founder of Puhar's festival of Indra.
teaches: Holding the two together shows the epic taking a Sangam war-memory of the Chola line and turning it into a sacred charter, so that a city's yearly rite rests on an ancestor's feat rather than on the reigning king.

gains.a: the epic's unnamed founder gains a lineage: he is the ancestor the Sangam court already cited by this one feat
gains.b: the poem's bare allusion to the fort-breaking ancestors gains a story in which that ancestor is Indra's ally and the patron of a festival

note: The assemblies warn that a forgotten festival will bring the guardian spirit's affliction on the city; in kaathai 25 the king, searching for his lost son, neglects the festival and Manimekala deity curses the city to the sea.
teaches: The opening warning is the plot's first prophecy, but its fulfilment shifts the punisher from the city's guardian spirit to Manimekala deity, so the epic keeps the civic threat while giving the punishment to its own Buddhist-protecting goddess.

note: Both epics place in Puhar a spirit that seizes the wicked with its noose, beats them and devours them; in the Silappathikaram it punishes named sins, in Manimekalai it is one of the powers the festival keeps appeased.
teaches: The same noose-bearing spirit changes office between the two epics: a moral police against hypocrites and false witnesses in the first becomes, in the second, a power whose goodwill depends on the city keeping its festival.
audit_text_issue: manimekalai:1:10-34 is flagged uncertain at line 34.

note: The Kural states that when the king bends justice the sky withholds rain; the drummer's blessing wishes three rains and an unswerving king in the same sentence, as things the festival must secure.
teaches: The Kural makes rain follow from the king's justice alone, while the festival treats both rain and just rule as gifts to be prayed for from the gods, so the epic's city does not leave the causal chain to the king.

gains.a: the paired wish in lines 33-34 gains its logic: the Kural explains why rain and the sceptre belong in one blessing
gains.b: the couplet's rule gains a ritual setting in which a city, not trusting the king alone, asks the gods for both ends of it

note: The drummer proclaims the good day of the island's rite of peace (தீவகச் சாந்தி); in kaathai 24 a charana tells the king that on the day the rite is not performed his city will enter the sea, by Manimekala deity's word and Indra's curse.
teaches: The same rite named in the festival proclamation becomes, twenty-three kaathais later, the condition on which the city's survival hangs, so the decorations of the opening are already the terms of a covenant the city will break.
audit_text_issue: 24:64-65 (மணிமேகலை தன் வாய்மொழியால் அது தணியாது இந்திர சாபம்) is ambiguous on whose word and whose curse.

note: The Kural defines a land as one that goes on without crushing hunger, unceasing disease and destructive enemies; the drummer ends the proclamation by wishing that hunger, disease and enmity leave the city.
teaches: What the Kural states as the mark of a true land, the epic's city asks for once a year as a festival blessing, showing that the freedom from the three ills was felt as a gift to be renewed by rite, not a settled condition.

gains.a: the herald's closing wish gains a political measure: these three ills are exactly what decides whether Puhar is a land at all
gains.b: the couplet's definition gains a public voice and an occasion, a drum proclamation in which the city itself asks to meet it

note: The Kural advises not to do harm in hostility even when others act against you; the drummer bids the schools' debaters part without hatred or quarrel even from those who do not accept their view (பற்றாமாக்கள்).
teaches: The epic carries the Kural's rule of non-retaliation from private enmity into public doctrinal debate, making civility between rival schools a law of the city's festival.

gains.a: the herald's rule for debaters gains an ethical ground beyond festive peace: hostility harms the one who nurses it
gains.b: the couplet's counsel gains a concrete arena, the debating hall where disagreement is expected but enmity is forbidden

note: The festival bids the debaters of the schools mount Puhar's debating hall and part without quarrel; in kaathai 27, after Puhar is lost, Manimekalai goes among the schools of Vanji in disguise and hears each in turn without dispute.
teaches: The public hall of debate promised at the opening is never shown in Puhar; it returns only in another city as one renunciant's quiet hearing of the schools, so the epic moves doctrinal inquiry from civic festival to private search.

note: The town lists the arts set down for dancing women that Madhavi mastered; Silappathikaram 3 opens on her seven years' training in dance, song and beauty for her first performance before the king.
teaches: The training that the earlier epic presents as the making of Madhavi's fame becomes in the town's mouth its argument against her leaving that life, so the courtesan's accomplishments bind her to her trade as a claim others hold on her.

note: Kural 1017 says those ruled by shame give up life rather than shame for life; Madhavi says that by staying alive after hearing of her lover's suffering she gave up her shame.
teaches: Read against the couplet, Madhavi's confession places her among those who kept life at the cost of shame, so the shame the town sees in her tapas already lay in her survival, and her renunciation becomes the answer of one who has failed the rule rather than a new disgrace.

gains.a: the general rule that makes her confession intelligible: the couplet says why outliving the news of Kovalan's suffering counts as giving up shame
gains.b: a person who has failed the rule and lives on, which shows a way of answering lost shame, by tapas, that the couplet's choice between shame and death leaves out

note: Madhavi recounts Kannaki twisting off her breast and setting the king's city aflame; Silappathikaram 21 tells the act.
teaches: Madhavi retells the burning as the deed of the mother she assigns to Manimekalai, so the earlier epic's vengeance becomes a lineage by which a courtesan's daughter is claimed for tapas instead of her mother's trade.

note: Perunkoppendu tells the elders holding her back that for her, her husband dead, a lotus pond and the pyre's fire are one, and scorns the widow's life of sparse food and bare ground; Madhavi's second kind of pathini enters the blazing fire as into a cool-water pool, and her third wears the body down in vows.
teaches: The queen's single act of defiance, in which the pyre is a cool pond and the austere widowhood she refuses is worse than fire, becomes in the epic a ranked typology of the chaste wife where entering the fire is only the second kind and the vowed austerity she despised is admitted as the third, and all three are then set beneath Kannaki.

gains.a: the source of the fire-as-cool-pool figure in a widow's own speech against the elders, so that Madhavi's kinds are seen to be drawn from remembered acts and not invented as a scheme
gains.b: a later frame in which the queen's choice is one recognised option among three, with the widow's austerity she scorned now counted as a path of chastity, which shows how the poem's personal refusal was absorbed into a norm

note: Madhavi says Manimekalai will be brought to great tapas and never to the courtesan's trade; at the close of kaathai 30 Manimekalai takes up tapas and vows to end the course of births.
teaches: The mother's claim made for her daughter in the third kaathai is fulfilled only in the last, and by the daughter's own vow after hearing the whole doctrine, so the epic runs between a claim made over Manimekalai and her own assent to it.

note: Aravanar's four lines to Madhavi set suffering for the born, bliss for the unborn and attachment as the cause; in kaathai 30 he sets out the twelve links, with attachment (பற்றே) one link among them, and says the born who know them gain the great reward.
teaches: The same teacher gives the grieving mother a single cause and five precepts, and the daughter the full twelve-link chain, so the epic shows the doctrine scaled to its hearer: consolation and lay discipline first, the analysis of release later.

note: Kural 349 says that when attachment ends it cuts off births; Aravanar says suffering comes from attachment, bliss to those free of it, and that birth itself brings growing suffering.
teaches: The couplet ties the end of attachment to the end of rebirth but sets no value on birth; Aravanar's lines add that birth is itself suffering and offer a bereaved lay woman five precepts as the way in, not the renouncer's clean cut.

gains.a: a bare causal statement, attachment to rebirth, against which the teacher's added judgment that birth is suffering stands out as the Buddhist addition
gains.b: a scene where its renouncer's rule is given as consolation to a grieving woman still in the world, with lay precepts as the first step

note: Tirumular says the Lord who made birth for joy shut it in the suffering of the bond; Aravanar says the born meet growing suffering, the unborn great bliss, and suffering comes from attachment.
teaches: Both trace suffering to a binding, attachment or the bond, but they disagree about birth itself: for the Buddhist teacher birth is the suffering and not being born is bliss, while for Tirumular birth was made for joy and the bond was laid on it by the same Lord; the conflict holds on reading இன்பப் பிறவி as birth made for joy.

gains.a: a theist account in which a maker lays the suffering on birth, which shows that Aravanar names no maker and makes attachment alone the cause
gains.b: an opposed claim that birth is itself suffering, which shows that the verse's birth made for joy is a position taken, not common ground

audit_text_issue: Tirumanthiram 432 is flagged uncertain; the variant அடைந்தனன் would change its sense.

note: Sudhamathi warns that no man who sees the weeping Manimekalai could turn away; in the next kaathai Ettikumaran's glimpse of her faded face entering the grove sends the prince after her.
teaches: The warning is fulfilled by exactly the beauty it named, a face dimmed by grief rather than adorned, so the renunciant's sorrow, not her old trade, is what draws the prince into the story.

note: Both have a vidyadhara fly down from the sky to see Puhar's festival for Indra; in the Silappathikaram he brings his beloved as a spectator, in the Manimekalai Marutavegan seizes a brahmin girl and abandons her.
teaches: The heavenly visitor whom the first epic uses as an admiring eye on Puhar's festival becomes in the second a seducer who strands a girl there, so the same festival that showed Madhavi's art is now a danger to an unguarded girl.

note: Kural 34 makes a spotless mind the whole of virtue; the Uvavanam seat shows that a flower laid without intention goes nowhere, as proof that a deed without intention bears no fruit.
teaches: The couplet puts the mind first in judging virtue; the seat pushes that principle to the disputed case of the unintended act and makes it a point on which schools divided, which the couplet never has to face.

gains.a: a general ethical statement, free of any school, behind the Buddhist side of the dispute
gains.b: a hard case, the deed done without any thought, that tests how far the mind-first rule reaches

note: Kural 929 says reasoning with a drunk is like searching with fire under water; here the drunk reasons with a sober ascetic, arguing that toddy kills nothing.
teaches: The epic reverses the couplet's direction, letting the drunk be the one who argues, and his argument from non-harm shows that the drunkard's reasons can borrow the ascetic's own principle and still be worthless.

gains.a: the rule that makes the drunk's reasoning absurd without the narrator having to answer it
gains.b: a scene where the drunk himself offers reasons, showing the futility runs both ways

note: The drunk calls toddy-drinking a yoga whose fruit the ascetic should taste; Tirumanthiram 566 says breath-control gives the intoxication of toddy without drinking it.
teaches: The equation of drink and yogic ecstasy runs in opposite directions: the Tirumanthiram borrows toddy's joy as an image for breath-discipline, while the epic's drunk borrows yoga's name to sell toddy, so the pair shows the figure was common enough to be turned either way.

gains.a: evidence that 'the yoga of drink' was a live figure the epic could parody
gains.b: a satirical counter-use that shows the risk in its image of yoga as intoxication

note: Kundalakesi 4 calls nakedness, ash, fire and fasting mere talk and tapas a restrained life; the epic shows a naked fasting ascetic in the street, cared for unseen lives and begged to drink by a drunk.
teaches: The two Buddhist works keep their distance from bodily austerity by different means, argument in the fragment and street scene in the epic, and the epic allows the naked ascetic a real virtue, his pity for unseen lives, that the fragment's dismissal leaves out.
audit_text_issue: kundalakesi:4 is a fragment, and its last line's division is uncertain.

note: The Silappathikaram lists Kama's eunuch dance and the pot dance in Bana's city among the eleven dances Madhavi performs at Indra's festival; here a street performer dances the eunuch dance, named in nearly the same words (வாணன் பேர் ஊர் மறுகிடை ... நீள் நிலம் அளந்தோன்), as her daughter passes in robes.
teaches: The dance that was Madhavi's art on the royal stage at one festival is a street show at the next, watched by the crowd while her daughter walks past it to the Buddha's grove, so the repeated formula marks how far the family has moved from that stage.
audit_text_issue: The Manimekalai merges Bana's city (the pot dance in the Silappathikaram) with Kama's பேடி dance.

note: In the last kaathai the town's talk, brought by Vayantamalai, calls Madhavi's tapas shameful; here the festival crowd says it to Manimekalai's face and calls the mother cruel.
teaches: The gossip that reached Madhavi indirectly becomes a crowd around the daughter, and its charge shifts from the mother's shame to her cruelty to the girl, so the town's judgment follows the renunciation from one generation to the next.

note: The quatrain mocks the fool who calls a body of nine oozing openings 'broad-shouldered one'; Sudhamathi answers the prince's love-poetry questions about Manimekalai with the same inside-out view of the body.
teaches: The epic stages the quatrain's cure as speech to a lover just after he has used the love-poem epithets, and then shows it failing: the sight of the girl reaches him before the words do.

gains.a: Sudhamathi's catalogue is placed in an existing ethics genre that answers love poetry's epithets one by one.
gains.b: The quatrain's sure contempt for the fool gets a test case in which the cure is spoken in time and still loses to sight.

note: Pattinattar calls the body the enjoyment of deeds, gone the moment deeds end, and sends the mind to Siva's feet; Sudhamathi calls it born of deeds and the field where they ripen, and asks only that it be known and turned from.
teaches: The two share the premise that the body exists to eat karma but part on the remedy: the Saiva poet needs Siva's feet, while the epic's speaker names no god and puts release in seeing the body truly.

gains.a: Sudhamathi's godless remedy stands out once set beside a Saiva statement of the same premise.
gains.b: Pattinattar's appeal to Siva's feet is shown to be an addition to a premise that a Buddhist epic holds without it.

note: The proverb verse tells of the young Chola who tied on grey hair and judged a case (உரைமுடிவு) to prove that a family's craft comes half-known; Sudhamathi names the same act (உரை முடிவு காட்டிய உரவோன்) to shame his heir.
teaches: The proverb says the line's judgment is inborn, and the epic turns the same story against the line's heir, who must be lectured by a woman, so the inherited craft is invoked because it is missing.

gains.a: The allusion at 108 is fixed to a known story whose point is wisdom in youth, which sharpens Sudhamathi's rebuke of a youth acting unwisely.
gains.b: The proverb's claim that a family's craft comes by birth meets a heir of the same line who lacks it.

note: Kaathai 3 says the crystal pavilion lets no voice out but shows the body outside (விளிப்பு அறைபோகாது மெய் புறத்து இடூஉம்); Sudhamathi hides Manimekalai in it.
teaches: The hiding place was announced as one that hides speech but shows the body, so the shelter Sudhamathi picks is the one that will display the girl to the prince while she preaches against the body.

note: Manimekalai hears the prince's chariot with fear and asks what to do; in the next kaathai, after he has gone, she confesses that her heart followed the stranger who had scorned her.
teaches: The crystal wall kept her body from his hands but not her heart from him, so the flight here and the confession after it show the girl's renunciation is not yet secure.
audit_text_issue: 4:61 and 4:69-70 readings flagged uncertain by the marker.

note: Kovalan tamed a rogue elephant that had seized an old Brahmin; his daughter's pursuer Udayakumaran tames his own elephant gone mad in Puhar.
teaches: The father's deed of rescue returns as the prince's feat of strength on his way to chase the daughter, so the same heroic act is shown serving compassion once and desire the second time.

note: The couplet says crushing foes comes through tapas if the ascetic so intends; Sudhamathi warns the prince that Manimekalai's fated austerity carries a curse for an arrow.
teaches: The couplet's power of tapas is invoked here as a shield for a girl who has barely begun austerity, and the prince's shrug at line 21 shows the threat carrying no weight until it is backed by practice.

gains.a: Sudhamathi's warning is read as an appeal to a recognised Tamil belief that tapas can harm an enemy, not an empty boast.
gains.b: The couplet's claim gets a case where the power is asserted on another's behalf and fails to deter, which the couplet's confident statement does not consider.

note: Sudhamathi tells the prince the girl is given to fated austerity; in kaathai 18 he reports that a golden woman appeared to him at night with a sceptre and told him to forget the girl who had taken up tapas.
teaches: The warning comes twice, first from a woman he brushes aside and then from a divine figure, and the prince repeats the second to Chithirapathi without obeying it, so his ruin is shown as a refusal of a warning he understood.

note: The couplet is a woman's admission that the axe of desire breaks the door of restraint; the prince asks whether any restraint exists once desire takes hold.
teaches: The same claim that in the Kural is a woman's confession of her own defeat becomes, in a prince's mouth, a licence to press on a woman who refuses him, so the epic shows how the love-book's lament can serve as an excuse.

gains.a: The prince's maxim is recognised as borrowed from the love poets' woman's voice, which shows how far he has moved it from its place.
gains.b: The couplet's resignation gets a test: said by the stronger party about another's body, the same words stop being a confession and become a threat.

note: The couplet says the அந்தணர் are the virtuous, because they wear cool kindness toward every life; Sudhamathi's Brahmin father, turned off by Brahmins and Jain monks alike, cries for any அறவோர் and is answered by a Buddhist monk, called மறையோன் at 68.
teaches: The epic tells the couplet's redefinition as a story: those who hold the title by birth or by vows fail the dying man, and the title of one who knows the sacred lore passes to the stranger who shows kindness to him.

gains.a: The cry அறவோர் உளீரோ gets the couplet's measure of virtue, kindness to every life, which explains why the monks of spotless form fail it.
gains.b: The couplet's definition by conduct is shown working against real holders of the status, and across a sectarian line the couplet does not name.

note: The couplet says those sick with love cannot know the dignity of not going after one who has turned hostile; Manimekalai says her heart went after the stranger who had scorned her, and asks if this is the nature of desire.
teaches: The couplet's lovesick woman knows her loss of dignity and keeps loving, while Manimekalai, meeting the same fact in herself on a single sight, answers it with a curse on desire (91), the renunciant's reply the love chapter never gives.

gains.a: Manimekalai's question is shown to have a known answer in the Tamil love tradition, so her surprise marks how new desire is to her.
gains.b: The couplet's diagnosis is applied to a girl vowed to austerity, which shows it holding even where the speaker has renounced the love it describes.

note: The Purananuru poem says the world endures because there are those who strive not for themselves but for others (தமக்கென முயலா ... பிறர்க்கென முயலுநர்); Sudhamathi calls the Buddha one who lives not for himself but belongs to others (தனக்கு என வாழாப் பிறர்க்கு உரியாளன்).
teaches: The epic takes the Sangam formula for a class of honourable men who hold the world up and makes it the mark of one being whose living for others is the turning of the dharma wheel, moving the ideal from social honour to religious compassion.

gains.a: The epithet at 73 is heard as a Tamil ideal already named in puram poetry, so the Buddha is praised in terms a Tamil audience held as the highest human worth.
gains.b: The poem's unnamed many who strive for others are given a single founder as exemplar, whose motive is compassion for all beings rather than fear of blame and love of fame.

note: The prince leaves saying Manimekalai may yet come to him through Chithirapathi; in kaathai 18 Chithirapathi vows to put the girl in the prince's golden chariot or be shamed among the dancers.
teaches: The prince's passing remark becomes the grandmother's public vow, so the plot against the girl is shown to be carried by her own family's trade rather than by the prince alone.

note: The couplet says none but those who reach the feet of the அறவாழி அந்தணன் can cross the other seas; the goddess praises the Buddha's feet marked with the thousand-spoked wheel (ஆயிர ஆரத்து ஆழி), whom Sudhamathi has just called the one who turned the wheel of dharma (அறக் கதிர் ஆழி, 76).
teaches: The same words, அறம், ஆழி and the lord's feet, name the Buddha's wheel of dharma in the epic, which shows that ஆழி in the couplet's epithet could be heard as wheel as well as sea, and that a Buddhist hearer would find the Buddha in a verse that names no one.

gains.a: The goddess's praise of the feet is set in the Kural's opening frame, where reaching the feet is the way across.
gains.b: The couplet's unnamed epithet is shown in use for a named founder, which opens a second sense of ஆழி that the sea reading alone hides.

note: The Silappathikaram brings evening on Puhar with the earth weeping as if her king were lost, lamps lit by women, the cowherds' mullai flute, and evening 'came and encamped' (மாலைவந்து இருத்தென); the Manimekalai's evening on Puhar has the lamps, the mullai flute and evening that came and encamped (வந்து இறுத்தனளால்) as a woman widowed in battle.
teaches: The sequel reuses its parent's evening on the same city almost item by item but moves the grief from an earth that has lost her king to a woman who has lost her husband and goes home to her kin, so the evening of Kovalan's daughter carries the bereaved woman's figure that the first epic gave to the land.

note: The couplet says a fault in the well-born stands out like the spot on the moon; the epic's moonrise says the moon's spot shows like a fault in the worthy.
teaches: The epic can use the couplet's moral as the familiar term of a comparison for the sky, which shows the saying was common enough to be turned round.

gains.a: The odd simile of a moon's spot shown like a worthy man's fault gets its source and its direction.
gains.b: The couplet is seen working as a known saying that a narrative poet could invert in passing.

note: Sudhamathi's sermon on the body did not reach the prince before the sight of the girl; here the goddess reports that his gaze has not abated and sends the women into refuge.
teaches: The epic marks the failure of the sermon on the body as a fact the plot acts on: after argument fails, protection becomes a matter of place and then of flight.

note: Madhavi ranks first among pathini women those who give up their lives when their husbands die; the cemetery holds brick shrines for women who died together with their husbands, sorted by varna beside ascetics and kings.
teaches: The death Madhavi praises as the highest kind of chastity ends, in the goddess's tour, as one more class of memorial in a field whose lesson is that no death is exempt.

note: The Purananuru poem describes the same burning ground of owls, corpse-eating jackals and dancing demon women, which has taken even conquerors, and urges the patron to give freely and win lasting fame; the goddess draws from it that revelling in wealth instead of desiring dharma is the height of folly.
teaches: The same memento mori leads the puram poet to gift and fame that outlast the body, and the Buddhist epic to dharma, with no word of fame: the cemetery's lesson changes with what each tradition thinks survives.

gains.a: The goddess's verdict is seen to drop the fame and the patron that the older use of the scene required.
gains.b: The poem's turn from the burning ground to fame is shown to be a choice, since the same scene could argue for renunciation.

note: The quatrain's speaker, having seen teeth and bones scattered in the burning ground, will not listen to talk of teeth like pearls; the demon woman eats the eyes without asking 'tooth or pearl', and Sarngalan, seeing it, dies of fright.
teaches: The sight of the burning ground that steadies the Naladiyar's renouncer kills an unready boy, so the contemplation of the dead body is shown to need a prepared mind and not merely a sight.

gains.a: Sarngalan's death is read as a failed contemplation of the body, not only a ghost story.
gains.b: The quatrain's confident resolve gets a counter-case in which the same evidence destroys the one who sees it.

note: The quatrain warns that merciless Death stalks and takes even the child while its mother wails; Gotami wails over her son and asks whether a spirit took him, and Champapathi answers that no spirit takes a life, only the boy's former deed.
teaches: The epic gives the quatrain's wailing mother a voice and an answer, and the answer removes the stalking agent the quatrain imagines: what takes the child is his own deed, with fright as its occasion.

gains.a: Champapathi's denial of a killing agent stands out against the ethics book's ready personification of Death.
gains.b: The quatrain's figure of Death as a thief is shown to be one account among others, which a Buddhist epic replaces with karma.

note: The couplet sets not killing one creature above a thousand sacrifices; Champapathi calls 'killing is dharma' a false word and counts a mother's offer of her own life for her son's under it.
teaches: The epic extends the couplet's rule against killing to giving one's own life in exchange for another's, which the couplet, concerned with animals and sacrifice, does not consider.

gains.a: Champapathi's sharp refusal of a mother's offer is seen to rest on the ethics of not killing, not on want of pity.
gains.b: The couplet's rule is carried to the case of self-offering, where its scope is tested by a sympathetic petitioner.

audit_text_issue: Lines 162-166 are terse; who 'those whose trade' is, and the sense of 164, are uncertain. | Unit flagged uncertain; 164 reading uncertain.

note: In Puhar's festival warriors set their own heads on the altar praying that the offering be a bulwark of the king's strength, and the narrator does not judge it; Champapathi says lives have been given for kings, yet the burning ground holds a thousand kings' shrines.
teaches: On the plainer reading of lines 164 to 166, the second epic denies what the first epic's rite assumes, that a life given for the king protects him, and it does so in the same city.

note: Maalathi carries a Brahmin household's dead baby to every shrine, Saathan says the gods give no boon to those without tapas yet hands her a child by becoming it; Gotami, a Brahmin's wife with a dead son, appeals to the gods' boons and every god of the Chakravala says none can give back a life.
teaches: The two epics tell the same story of a grieving mother at Puhar's shrines with opposite endings: a god supplies a living child by illusion in one, while in the other the gods together refuse even that, and the mother dies.

note: The couplet says that for those who have gained the power of tapas even leaping past Death becomes possible; Champapathi, the old ascetic goddess, shows her power by proving that no god can give back a life.
teaches: The power over death that tapas earns, in the epic, stops at the one who earned it: even the oldest ascetic goddess and all the gods cannot pass it to the dead.

gains.a: Champapathi's display of power is seen as a demonstration of a limit, not a failure of her tapas.
gains.b: The couplet's 'even' is given a firm boundary: tapas may carry one past death but cannot bring another back.

note: The couplet says that when the king bends justice the sky withholds rain; the goddess gives the same chain with the planets inserted between sceptre and rain, and aims it at the heir's desire for a nun.
teaches: The pair shows the rule's reach being widened: what the Kural ties to judging wrongly the epic applies to a prince's private lust, so the sceptre is bent by desire, not only by a verdict.

gains.a: The goddess's warning is grounded in a known rule of kingship, which shows she argues from ethics shared beyond her own creed rather than from her power.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case in which the wrong is not a judgment and the wrongdoer not yet king, which tests how far its bending of justice extends.

note: The Purananuru poem says rice and water are not the world's life, the king is, and he must know it; the goddess says the king's swerving kills life through the failing of rain, so the standing of being the beings' life is lost.
teaches: The epic turns the poem's title into a conditional one that a king's own fault cancels, and routes his power over life back through the rain the poem had set below him.

gains.a: Lines 11-12 are read against an old formula of kingship that the goddess is citing in order to take away.
gains.b: The poem's claim that the king, not water, is the world's life gains its limit: in the epic the king governs life only by way of the rain.

note: The goddess warns the prince to give up his intent on the ascetic girl; he does not, and is cut down by the vidyadhara Kanchanan as he goes to the girl in her disguise.
teaches: The warning threatened failing rain and perishing beings, but the fruit comes as one man's sword on the prince alone, so the cosmic stakes she named collapse into a private death.

note: The goddess says only that the cause for the girl's entry into dharma has ripened; at the jewel seat Manimekalai learns that in her birth as Lakshmi a sage foretold that on the day of her trouble the goddess Manimekala would carry her to an island in the south.
teaches: The bare 'ripened cause' of this kaathai is revealed later as a prophecy made in a former birth, so the goddess is fulfilling an old word, not deciding afresh.

note: Maadalan tells how Kovalan named Madhavi's daughter after the sea goddess who saved his ancestor with the words வந்தேன் அஞ்சல் மணிமேகலை யான்; here the goddess, speaking the same words, adds that on that naming night she told Madhavi in a dream that the child would be a creeper of tapas.
teaches: The pairing shows the Manimekalai turning a name given in gratitude for merit of giving into a vocation for renunciation, revealed only now by the goddess herself.

note: The goddess's dream foretold a creeper of tapas that would leave Kama helpless; in the Silappathikaram's last kaathai Madhavi gives her daughter to the dharma at the Bodhi seat while Kama throws his bow and arrows on the bare ground.
teaches: The earlier epic's closing image of Kama disarmed turns out, read with this dream, to be the fulfilment of a prophecy spoken at the child's naming.

note: Both have warriors at the bhuta's altar in Puhar crying that the victorious king take victory (கொற்றம் கொள்க) with a thunder voice as they offer bali; the Silappathikaram stages it as the festival's central rite, the Manimekalai lists it among the night noises a grieving woman hears.
teaches: Set side by side, the same offering formula moves from the heart of a royal festival to one sound among drunk shipwrights and mantra-men, which shows how the later epic pushes the blood rite to the margin of its story.
audit_text_issue: Manimekalai 7:76-77 (தீர் வினை மகளிர்; ஆடவர் இன்றியும்) are of uncertain sense; the link does not rest on them.

note: The painted image on the pillar of the hall speaks at night to frightened Sudhamathi; later the same image speaks to Kanchanan just after he has killed the prince, telling him the woman he sought was Manimekalai in disguise.
teaches: The pillar's voice comes once in time, to comfort with knowledge of past births, and once too late, to tell a killer what he did not know, so the same speaking image marks both the gift and the failure of right knowing.
audit_text_issue: 7:85-97 ends before the image's speech begins at 98.

note: The image addresses Sudhamathi with இரவிவன்மன் ஒரு பெரு மகளே, துரகத் தானைத் துச்சயன் தேவி and promises that Lakshmi will come knowing both births; returned from the island, Manimekalai addresses her mothers with the same lines and names them Tarai and Virai.
teaches: The prophecy is fulfilled in the very words of the image, now in the girl's mouth, and the later scene supplies what the image left out: Madhavi too was a sister, Tarai.

note: Madhavi tells how the teacher Aravanar taught her that suffering comes of attachment and freedom from it of letting go; here, a renouncer, she sits like a body without life because her daughter has not come.
teaches: The pair shows the epic letting its own renouncer fall short of the teaching she received, so taking robes does not by itself end attachment to a child.

note: In the next kaathai Manimekalai, remembering her former birth as Ilakkumi, recalls the sage's word that on a day of grave sorrow the goddess Manimekala would come, lift her up in the dark night and set her on an island in the south.
teaches: The waking that she meets as abandonment and a strange rebirth is the foretold step of a prophecy she has not yet remembered, so the epic makes her terror on the shore the unknowing half of a plan the reader learns only afterwards.
audit_text_issue: The b end is a span over two marked units (9:31-41, 9:42-57).

note: The sage's prophecy, recalled in kaathai 9, bids her go to the radiant seat where the healer of the disease of birth sits and preaches, where the Naga kings cleared anger and the stain of mind, and worship it, and that very day know her birth.
teaches: The seat that the narrator first presents as the prize of a war over 'ours' is named in the prophecy by what it did to the warring kings, purging their anger and opening their ears to dharma, so the place that cured possession becomes the place where a grieving girl recovers her past.

note: Silappathikaram 16 tells how a drunken guard's sword cut Kovalan down as the king's sceptre bent and his former deed came in wrath; his daughter's lament on the island recalls the sword on his chest and the cruel deed ripening.
teaches: The earlier epic gives two causes for Kovalan's death, the bent sceptre and the ripened deed, but his daughter's memory keeps only the deed and stretches it over her own plight, so the sequel's first word on the killing drops the king's guilt and makes karma something a family suffers together.

note: Naladiyar 101 says an old deed seeks out the one who did it as a calf finds its mother among many cows; Manimekalai says the cruel deed ripened so that her father went to a foreign land and died by the sword, and that it casts 'us' into misery.
teaches: The quatrain's deed that hunts down its own doer explains how karma found Kovalan far from home, yet the daughter's 'us' lets the same ripening fall on her too, which the one-doer rule does not allow, so the pair opens the question whether a deed's fruit can be shared by kin.

gains.a: a stated rule that the deed seeks out its own doer, against which her claim to share her father's ripening becomes visible as a widening
gains.b: a case in which the deed finds its doer in a strange land, and a survivor who counts herself in its fruit, a limit the calf image leaves untested

note: Kural 350 bids one cling to the clinging of the one who has no clinging in order to let clinging go; the two Naga kings, unable to let go of their great attachment to the seat each calls 'ours', stop their war when the great sage calls it 'ours' and preaches from it.
teaches: The couplet's paradox, giving up attachment by attaching to the unattached one, is staged as a scene: the sage does not tell the kings to own nothing but sets his own claim, 'this is ours', in place of theirs, and their war ends because a claim of the one without clinging displaces a claim of clinging.

gains.a: a doctrinal key to why the sage answers the kings with the very words of possession they used, instead of a call to give the seat up
gains.b: a concrete case of the clinging the couplet means (kin kings at war over an object neither can lift) and of the moment the substituted clinging takes hold

note: Manimekala told the sleeping Sudhamathi that within seven days Lakshmi, her younger sister, would come knowing her own birth and Sudhamathi's; here Manimekalai rises from the seat knowing that birth.
teaches: The goddess's promise to a third person is kept before Manimekalai knows it was made, so the recognition at the seat is staged as the second prophecy fulfilled in the chapter, not a private vision.
audit_text_issue: manimekalai:7:100-115 is not a marked unit; it spans 7:98-109 and 7:110-134.

note: In both a Buddhist ascetic foretells that a city will be swallowed, Idavayam by earthquake and Kaveripattinam by the sea, and those who trust the word act on it and are saved from the ruin.
teaches: The epic repeats the drowned city as a test of trust in a seer's word: the survivors in both are those who believed a forecast before any sign, which makes heeding the ascetic the epic's form of escape from a city's fate.

note: Manimekalai remembers the camp at Kayangarai as a day of worship and the sage's compassionate teaching; the deity of the pillar in kaathai 21 tells that on that same visit Rahulan killed the cook who stumbled with the sage's food.
teaches: The recovered memory is partial: what the seat restores to her is the piety of that day, and the deed that will kill her husband has to be supplied later by a god, so knowing one's birth in this epic does not yet mean knowing one's karma.

note: The sage foretold that on a day of sorrow Manimekala would lift her in the dark night and set her on an island in the southern quarter (தென் திசை மருங்கில்); kaathai 6 tells it in the same words: at midnight the goddess carried her south and left her on Manipallavam.
teaches: Read back from this prophecy, the abduction of kaathai 6 that seemed a goddess's rescue from the prince is shown to be an appointment fixed a birth earlier, which turns chance into the ripening of a cause.

note: The sage foretells Rahulan's death by a glance-poison snake without a cause; the deity of kaathai 21 gives the cause, his killing of the cook, and says Lakshmi's loving refusal to leave him could not turn the deed aside.
teaches: Together the passages show the epic's karma working in two steps: the prophecy fixes the fruit as certain, and only later is the deed named, with the added point that a wife's devotion, even unto the pyre, does not share or lighten a husband's deed.
audit_text_issue: 21:61-62 and 67-69 are compressed and flagged uncertain.

note: Perunkoppendu insists against the elders that her husband's pyre is to her a lotus pool; the sage tells Lakshmi as a plain fact that she will sink into Rahulan's fire, and the epic sends her, through that fire, to a new birth still bound to him.
teaches: The Sangam queen's choice of the pyre is her last word and her karpu's proof, while the Buddhist epic treats the same act as foretold and as no end at all: the bond she dies for carries into the next birth as the attachment that must be undone.

gains.a: Lakshmi's foretold death in the fire is set against a known Tamil model of the wife who chooses the pyre, which shows how flatly the sage reports it, without praise.
gains.b: The queen's claim that the fire and the lotus pool are one meets a work for which the fire leads not to union but to rebirth with the same longing.

note: The sage promised that the goddess who brought her would appear and say 'this is your husband'; in kaathai 10 Manimekala comes and names Rahulan as Udayakumaran, telling the story of Lakshmi's past.
teaches: The husband she longs to be shown turns out to be the prince she has been hiding from, so the promised reunion is delivered as a reason to understand her pull toward him and turn from it.

note: In the Silappathikaram the goddess of Madurai tells the grieving Kannaki she will see her husband within fourteen days, but only in a god's form; here the grieving Lakshmi is told a goddess will show her husband in a later human birth.
teaches: The two epics answer the same plea of a widow to see her husband again in opposite ways: the first through a heavenly reunion after death, the second through a new birth in which the man shown is the one she must learn to leave.
audit_text_issue: Silap 23 unit flagged uncertain; M9:64 repaired.

note: The epic calls the teacher whose seat this is the physician of the disease of birth (பிறவிப் பிணி மருத்துவன்); Arunagirinathar calls Murugan of Thiruttani the physician of the disease of becoming (பவரோக வயித்திய நாத) and asks his grace to cut birth's root.
teaches: The same title names two cures: in the Buddhist epic the physician heals by teaching dharma to those who have cleansed their minds, and his seat alone is left to be worshipped; in the Saiva hymn he heals by grace given to one who calls his name.

gains.a: The epithet at line 61 is shown to be a contested title, and the epic's choice to name no god while using it becomes visible.
gains.b: The hymn's physician-god is seen against an older Tamil use of the title for a teacher whose cure is a doctrine heard, not a grace received.

note: The goddess foretells that Manimekalai will hear the false words of the many schools and gives her a mantra to take another form; in kaathai 27 she goes among the reckoners of Vanji in an ascetic's borrowed form and questions them one by one.
teaches: The debate chapter is set up as a test prepared for in advance: the disguise exists because the goddess expects no one to tell a young girl the truth, so the schools are heard under a mask chosen against their condescension.

note: Sudhamathi's sermon on the body born of deeds failed to turn Udayakumaran once he saw Manimekalai; the goddess now reveals that he is her husband of a former birth and that her heart, too, still clings to him.
teaches: The failure of the grove sermon is given a cause in karma after the fact: the pull between the two was not mere sight but a bond carried across births, which is why words could not break it and a goddess had to carry her away.

note: The akam heroine asks that, when this life turns into the next, the same man be her husband and she the one close to his heart; the goddess tells Manimekalai that exactly this has come about, her heart still bound to her former husband, and calls it seed falling on scorched saline ground.
teaches: The bond across births that the akam poem asks for as the highest pledge of love is, in the Buddhist epic, the very danger to the merit that would end births, so the same wish is fulfilled and judged a loss.

gains.a: The goddess's verdict is seen to overturn a fixed ideal of Tamil love poetry, not just a passing desire of the prince.
gains.b: The heroine's vow gets a sequel in which it is granted, and its cost, the turning of rebirth into a trap, is shown.

note: The quatrain says a small act of virtue that reaches worthy hands spreads like a banyan from a tiny seed; the goddess says Lakshmi's meal to a sage will not go to waste but will cut off her births, and also that the giver herself, as a seed of dharma, could be lost on barren ground.
teaches: The epic agrees that a gift to the worthy grows, but changes its harvest from a covering shade of merit to the end of rebirth, and adds that the giver's own attachments can still waste what the gift has sown.

gains.a: The goddess's claim at 41 is placed within an ethics-book teaching on giving to the worthy, which marks how far its promised fruit goes beyond that teaching.
gains.b: The quatrain's growth image is shown to depend on the giver as well as the receiver, a condition it does not state.

note: Tirumular bids the seeker hold to the Lord's feet, by whom strong deeds perish, and says the Lord will set him among the gods; Aravanan calls the Buddha's footprints on the hill the feet that destroy faults, and the next unit says the sisters who worshipped there were reborn beside Lakshmi.
teaches: Both give the feet power over past deeds, but the Saiva feet belong to a Lord who acts now and places the soul, while the Buddhist feet are the trace of a teacher who left long ago, and their fruit comes from the worshippers' own act ripening in the next birth.

gains.a: The footprint hill is seen as a Buddhist answer to the feet-devotion of Tamil theism, with the giver of grace replaced by a place and a remembered teaching.
gains.b: The verse's agent, the Lord who sets the soul among the gods, stands out as the thing a rival tradition does without while keeping the image of the feet.

note: Kudapulaviyanar tells the Pandya that food makes the body (உண்டி முதற்றே உணவின் பிண்டம்), so those who bind water to land give body and life, and bids him build tanks; the goddess uses the same phrase, the body is a lump of food, to give Manimekalai a mantra that cuts off her own hunger.
teaches: The same maxim drives two answers to hunger: the Sangam poet makes it a king's duty to feed a people by irrigation, the epic turns it into an ascetic's private release from hunger, the first step before the bowl that will feed others.

gains.a: The goddess's sudden afterthought at 90 is heard as a known saying about kings and food, which foreshadows Manimekalai's later role as feeder of the hungry.
gains.b: The poem's maxim is shown carried from the king's public works to a single renouncer's body, where the remedy is a mantra, not water.

audit_text_issue: manimekalai:10:71-93 flagged uncertain at 83-85, which the link does not use.

note: The couplet ranks the strength of enduring hunger below the strength of removing others' hunger; the goddess gives Manimekalai the first strength by mantra, and the patikam (manimekalai:0:51-68) says the bowl for feeding others comes next.
teaches: The epic follows the couplet's order of rank but removes the effort from the lower strength: enduring hunger is granted as a gift, so the renouncer is freed for the higher task the couplet values, feeding others.

gains.a: The hunger mantra is seen as a step in a known scale of virtue rather than a magic convenience.
gains.b: The couplet's ranking is shown worked out in a life, where the lesser strength is a means to the greater rather than a rival to it.

note: Aputhiran, stranded on Manipallavam, let the bowl into Gomukhi bidding it rise once a year and enter the hand of anyone who keeps compassion and guards lives; here it rises into Manimekalai's hand on that day.
teaches: The bowl's arrival is not a goddess's gift but the meeting of a condition laid down by its last owner, so the kaathai tests Manimekalai before the reader is told what the test was.

note: Deepathilakai says Aravanan will tell Manimekalai the bowl's nature (52); in the next kaathai Aravana Adigal says she has the bowl and gives the one dharma common to men and gods, curing hunger.
teaches: The goddess hands over the object and defers its meaning to a human teacher, so the epic places authority over the bowl's use with the Buddhist monk rather than the island's deity.

note: The Naladiyar's ascetic's bowl (தவசி கடிஞை) is filled slowly at door after door by householders' small gifts; Manimekalai's bowl, held by a renunciant, never fails and only the takers' hands tire.
