teaches: Set together, the two bowls reverse the flow between householder and ascetic: the quatrain's begging bowl is the image of a giver's merit filling, while the epic's is an ascetic's vessel that gives without end.

gains.a: the bowl's inexhaustibility is seen against the ordinary begging bowl it inverts, which the epic never needs to describe
gains.b: the quatrain's image of the slowly filled bowl gains its opposite, which shows that its point is about the giver's accumulation, not the bowl

note: Kural 10 says those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births; Deepathilakai calls the feet of the Lord of dharma on Samantam the ship of dharma that frees from the great sea called birth (23-25).
teaches: The Buddhist epic takes the Kural's unnamed Lord and his feet as the Buddha's footprint on a named peak and turns swimming into being carried by a ship, so the couplet's open theism becomes a pilgrimage relic served by the gods.

gains.a: Deepathilakai's image is shown to rest on the Kural's opening chapter, giving the Buddhist claim the Kural's wording of release
gains.b: the couplet's இறைவன் is shown open to sectarian claiming, read here by a Buddhist work as the Buddha

note: Purananuru 18 tells a Pandya king that those who give food give life (உண்டி கொடுத்தோர் உயிர்கொடுத் தோரே) and that land waiting on the sky does not serve its ruler, so he must build tanks; Deepathilakai gives the same line (96) after a famine ended only by a god's rain.
teaches: The maxim moves from a king's public works to a renunciant's alms-bowl, and the remedy for a failing sky moves from tanks a ruler digs to a god's gift and a bowl that never empties.

gains.a: line 96 is shown to be a borrowed Sangam maxim, so the goddess's sermon carries the authority of old royal counsel
gains.b: the poem's maxim gains a later life in which the duty to feed passes from the state to a single compassionate giver

note: Kural 225 ranks the strength of those who endure hunger, read by its commentators as ascetics, below that of those who remove it; here a goddess tells a girl who has just renounced that removing hunger is beyond praise and the true way of the world.
teaches: The epic dissolves the couplet's ranking of giver over ascetic by putting the bowl in a renunciant's hand, so the one who endures hunger becomes the one who ends it.

gains.a: the sermon's praise of the hunger-curer is seen as an answer to the Kural's ranking, not only a commonplace
gains.b: the couplet's opposition between ascetic and giver is shown not to be fixed, since a renunciant may be the giver

note: Kural 1042 calls poverty 'a sinner' (இன்மை எனவொரு பாவி) that comes with this world and the next both lost; Deepathilakai calls hunger 'the sinner' (பசிப் பிணி என்னும் பாவி, 80) that destroys birth, learning, modesty and beauty.
teaches: The Kural speaks to the poor man about what poverty takes from him, even merit for the next world; the epic speaks to the one who can cure it, so the merit the poor man loses becomes the giver's highest dharma.

gains.a: the list of hunger's ravages is seen to extend a Kural formula, which places the sermon within the ethics books' account of want
gains.b: the couplet's loss of the next world gains a remedy outside the poor man, in another's gift

note: The goddess told Lakshmi that the dharma of the meal Saathusakkaran ate would not leave her and would end her births; here Manimekalai names this bowl as that meal's fruit (105-106).
teaches: The prophecy's fruit arrives first not as release but as a means of further giving, so in the epic merit ripens into the power to make more merit before it ends births.

note: The Naladiyar calls liberality milk a cow yields gladly to its calf, against the base who yield only when squeezed; Manimekalai wants the bowl to flow at the hungry's faces as a mother's breast flows at her newborn's (114-118), and Deepathilakai says it flows only for those who feed from compassion (120-121).
teaches: The epic turns the quatrain's distinction between glad and forced giving into a property of the vessel itself, which will not yield to a giver whose gift is not compassion.

gains.a: the mother's-breast simile and the bowl's condition are seen to rest on an old ethics image of giving as lactation
gains.b: the quatrain's moral distinction gains a story in which the manner of giving decides whether anything is given at all

note: Tirumular says joy and sorrow are settled by former deeds and that those who see their joy and still do not give know no dharma; Manimekalai sees the prosperous enjoying the fruit of dharma sown (108-109) while the hungry stand ragged at their gates.
teaches: A Saiva and a Buddhist text agree that karma explaining who is fed does not excuse withholding, and the epic adds that the giver's own gift is the deed that will return as a means of giving.

gains.a: the unit's view of the rich at their gates is seen to be shared doctrine across the schools, not a Buddhist peculiarity
gains.b: Tirumular's argument gains a case in which the deed of giving returns, the bowl that is the fruit of a past meal

note: The goddess told Sudhamathi, as Veerai, Tharai's younger sister, that in seven days Lakshmi would return knowing her birth; Madhavi cries that the seventh day has come and Manimekalai arrives to name Tharai and Veerai.
teaches: The promise and its keeping frame Manimekalai's island journey as a timed rebirth-recognition, and Madhavi's near loss of faith on the last day sets the goddess's truthfulness against a mother's fear.

note: The goddess says Tarai and Virai were reborn beside Manimekalai because they worshipped at the Padapankaya hill when Aravanar bade them; Aravanar now tells that afterwards one died drunk under an elephant and the other leapt from a terrace.
teaches: Held together, the two accounts show the epic letting one act of worship outlast a drunken death and a suicide: the manner of dying does not cancel the merit, which is why the two women now stand beside the heroine.

note: The quatrain says that knowing people still do blameworthy things because of deeds done before; the epic calls Virai's drunken death and Tarai's fall the ripening of a cruel deed.
teaches: The epic applies the quatrain's explanation to a death and then, at 46 to 48, names the drink and the leap, so a past deed is the cause behind the act while the act itself stays on the record.

gains.a: the epic's bare phrase வெவ் வினை உருப்ப gains a stated mechanism: the old deed works by producing the fault itself
gains.b: the quatrain's abstract puzzle gains a named case in which the blameworthy act is fatal and its doer is reborn

note: The couplet asks why those who welcome good fortune grieve when it turns; Aravanar tells a king who has lost both queens not to grieve, since it is the fruit of old deeds.
teaches: The couplet grounds equanimity in consistency toward one's own fortune; the epic's monk grounds it in karma and speaks it to a mourner, showing the same counsel turned from self-discipline into consolation for another's loss.

gains.a: Aravanar's curt consolation gains the Kural's argument from consistency, which keeps it from sounding like indifference
gains.b: the couplet gains a hard case: bereavement, where the counsel must be said by one person to another

note: Tirumular bids refuge in the shade of the feet of the one God present in all ten directions, so that the sea of deeds will not reach; Aravanar goes to worship the footprints of the First Lord on one hill because they wash away hard deeds.
teaches: Both texts make worship of feet dissolve karma, but the Saiva feet are everywhere because their Lord is, while the Buddhist feet are a print left on a particular hill by a teacher of the past, so the shared gesture rests on opposite accounts of where the cleansing power lies.

gains.a: the epic's footprint worship is shown to use a devotional idiom the Saiva texts also use, against which its relic-and-place character stands out
gains.b: Tirumular's claim that the feet are in every direction gains a contrast with a rival tradition whose sacred feet are fixed in one place

note: The couplet says only those who reach the Lord's feet cross the great sea of births; Aravanar says those who hear the Buddha's dharma pass beyond painful birth and vows to praise the Bodhi Lord's feet in every birth.
teaches: The epic names the couplet's unnamed feet as the Buddha's but moves the crossing onto hearing his teaching, and its worshipper expects many more births before that hearing, so the feet become a lifelong devotion rather than the crossing itself.

gains.a: Aravanar's vow gains a reading against the Kural's opening chapter, which shows how much of the shared idiom a Buddhist could take over
gains.b: the couplet's unnamed Lord gains a test case: a reader of another faith who fills the name and changes the means

note: Freshly aware of her past birth, Manimekalai hails the Buddha at his seat as a young sun risen over a world that had lost its light; Aravanar foretells the next Buddha as a sun rising to clear the stain of minds.
teaches: The sun image moves from praise of a Buddha already come to prophecy of one yet to come, so the epic places its heroine between two dawns, in the age of mist that Aravanar describes at 63 to 65.

note: Aravanar tells Manimekalai she will not take up the teaching until the events her presence causes have happened; seventeen kaathais later she asks him for the true doctrine and he begins with the two means of knowledge.
teaches: The deferral is kept: the epic withholds its doctrinal core until its heroine has fed the hungry, emptied a prison and heard the other schools, so experience is made the condition of hearing the Buddha's logic.

note: The couplet ranks the strength of those who endure hunger below that of those who end others' hunger; an ascetic here names ending hunger as the one dharma equal for men and gods and calls it the dharma of tapas.
teaches: The epic answers the couplet's ranking by giving the higher strength to a renunciant: with the bowl, the one who has left the household can feed others instead of only enduring hunger, and feeding becomes the ascetic's own discipline.

gains.a: Aravanar's claim gains the Kural's prior ranking of feeding above endurance, which explains why he can call feeding a form of tapas
gains.b: the couplet's opposition between ascetic and feeder gains a case where one person holds both roles

note: The cow that licks, suckles and guards the abandoned infant here is the cow in whose womb Aputtiran is reborn after he dies on Manipallavam.
teaches: The mother who would not pity her child is replaced across two births by the cow, which first nurses him and then bears him, so the name 'cow's son' that the brahmins throw at him as an insult becomes literally true and honoured.

note: Aputtiran begs with an ordinary bowl to feed the helpless and eats the leftovers; in the next kaathai, unable to feed travellers who come in the rain, he is given the inexhaustible bowl by Chinthadevi.
teaches: The divine bowl goes to someone already living as a beggar who feeds others before himself, so the epic presents it as answering an alms-giving done with nothing rather than as the source of his charity.

note: The couplet ranks not taking one creature's life above a thousand oblations; the boy takes the cow from a sacrifice and is caught, beaten and called a thief.
teaches: The couplet weighs abstention against sacrifice as a private choice of merit, while the epic shows what acting on it costs inside a sacrificing community: the rescuer is branded a thief and expelled from his caste.

gains.a: The boy's theft gains a recognised ethical rule behind it, which the brahmins' charge of theft leaves out.
gains.b: The couplet's comparison gains a case where refusing the sacrifice carries a social price, which the couplet does not count.

note: The quatrain calls good and bad caste mere words and makes lineage depend on austerity, learning and effort; Aputtiran cites the brahmins' own seers born of cow, deer, tiger and jackal.
teaches: The quatrain denies birth rank from outside by naming what truly makes a line, while Aputtiran denies it from inside the brahmins' tradition, so the critique becomes a charge of inconsistency rather than a rival standard.

gains.a: Aputtiran's retort is given the general principle that his examples only imply.
gains.b: The quatrain's bare assertion gains an argument that defenders of birth rank cannot dismiss as foreign to their own books.

note: The couplet says a brahmin's birth is ruined when his conduct fails; the brahmin witness declares the boy an outcaste because his mother confessed she acted unlike a brahmin wife.
teaches: The couplet lets a man's own conduct unmake his birth, and the witness stretches this into a son's birth unmade by his mother's conduct, a step the couplet does not take and one Aputtiran then turns back on the Vedic seers' own mothers.

gains.a: The witness's verdict is seen as a twisting of a recognised rule rather than plain prejudice.
gains.b: The couplet's rule is shown to be open to use as hereditary taint once conduct is read through a mother.

note: The couplet says nothing shames the tongue more than begging, even water for a cow; Aputtiran, the cow's son, begs from house to house to feed the blind, the deaf and the lame.
teaches: The couplet holds that even the worthiest cause cannot make asking honourable, while the epic makes begging on others' behalf its hero's virtue and the ground of the divine bowl; the conflict depends on reading the couplet's cow example as covering begging for another's need, which it seems to.

gains.a: Aputtiran's begging stands out as a choice made against a known ethic of shame, not mere want.
gains.b: The couplet's limit case meets a story that answers it by honouring a beggar for others' sake.

note: The Siddhar says he has resolved to beg from any caste and lacks nothing; Aputtiran, driven from caste with stones in his bowl, begs from every house to feed the helpless and eats what is left.
teaches: Begging across caste lines is the Siddhar's chosen freedom and his sufficiency, while for Aputtiran it is what is left after caste expels him, and he turns it outward to feed others, so the same act carries renunciation in one and charity in the other.

gains.a: The epic beggar's stripped life is seen as close to a renouncer's, though he claims no renunciation.
gains.b: The Siddhar's self-sufficiency is seen to leave out the feeding of others that the epic puts at the centre of begging.

note: Kural 225 ranks the strength to bear hunger below the strength to remove it; Aputhiran, who lives on begged food, grieves not at his own hunger but at finding no means to remove the travellers', and it is then that the goddess gives him the bowl.
teaches: Together they show the couplet's higher strength given to a man with no wealth at all: the epic makes the power to end others' hunger a gift answering grief, not a store of means, which the couplet's comparison of two strengths leaves unexamined.

gains.a: a rule that explains why the goddess answers his grief at not feeding others rather than his own need
gains.b: a case where the higher strength is wanted by one who has only the lower, so the couplet's ranking becomes a longing rather than a description of the rich

note: Kural 25 makes Indra the witness to the power of one who has quenched the five senses; in the epic Indra's throne trembles at a beggar's feeding of all creatures, and he comes in person to reward it.
teaches: The epic moves the test that brings Indra down from the ascetic's restraint to a giver's feeding, and then shows the witness turning rival, since the god's reward will undo the giving it acknowledges.

gains.a: the known Tamil rule that Indra's disturbance testifies to a human's power, so the shaken throne reads as a verdict on Aputhiran
gains.b: a story in which Indra's witness is followed by Indra's interference, which the couplet's bare 'witness enough' does not foresee

note: Kural 222 says giving is good even if there were no higher world; offered heaven's reward, Aputhiran laughs that heaven is a place where no one does dharma or gives, and asks what its king could give him.
teaches: The couplet's hypothetical, giving is good even without heaven, becomes in Aputhiran's mouth a judgment that heaven is worse than earth for a giver, because there is no hunger there for giving to meet.

gains.a: a statement of the principle on which his laughter rests, that giving is valued apart from any reward
gains.b: an argument the couplet does not make: heaven is not merely unnecessary to giving but excludes it

note: Kural 19 says that if the sky gives no rain, neither giving nor austerity will last; Indra's abundant rain leaves Aputhiran's bowl idle for want of takers, and the hall of giving becomes a gambling den.
teaches: Rain is the condition of giving in the couplet, but the epic shows that rain in full measure can end giving too, since giving needs someone in want, so plenty sustains the giver's means and destroys his occasion.

gains.a: the Kural's rule that giving depends on rain, against which Indra's rain reads as a pointed reversal
gains.b: the other limit of its rule: too much of what makes giving possible makes it pointless

note: Puram 173 praises Pannan's house, where the noise of eating (ஊணொலி அரவம்) sounds like birds in a fruiting tree, as the home of the doctor of hunger; the epic uses the fruit-tree birds for the crowd at Aputhiran's hall (26 to 27), then tells how the hall's noise of eating (ஊண் ஒலி அரவம், 60) fell silent once rain removed hunger.
teaches: The epic takes the Sangam praise of a patron's noisy kitchen and shows its condition: the sound that proves a giver's fame lasts only as long as others are hungry, so the doctor of hunger is unmade by a world without the disease.

gains.a: the phrase ஊண் ஒலி அரவம் is shown to be the Sangam patron's formula, so its silencing marks the end of Aputhiran as a patron of the poor
gains.b: Pannan's praise gains a counter-case in which the same sound stops, exposing that the patron's glory depends on the hunger he cures

note: Deepatilakai tells Manimekalai that in a famine Indra's rain brought plenty and saved the brahmin about to eat dog's flesh; here Indra's rain, sent as a retort to Aputhiran, leaves his bowl idle and his hall to gamblers.
teaches: The epic gives Indra's rain two faces, the mercy that ends a famine and the spite that ends a giver's work, and in both tellings sets the human hand that feeds above the god's plenty, which Deepatilakai's praise alone does not show.

note: Kural 230 says nothing is more bitter than dying, yet even death is sweet when giving is out of reach; alone on an uninhabited island with no one to feed, Aputhiran will not keep his own life with the bowl, gives it away and starves himself to death.
teaches: The epic takes the couplet's hyperbole literally: a giver cut off from anyone to give to chooses death, and refuses even the means of life that giving had put in his hands.

gains.a: a general rule that turns his fast from despair into a judgment on a life without giving
gains.b: a case where the couplet's ranking is acted on, together with the refusal to turn a giving-vessel to one's own use, which the couplet does not state

note: Aputhiran lets the bowl go into the Gomukhi pool to rise one day a year into the hands of one who wears compassion and dharma; in kaathai 11 it rises from Gomukhi into Manimekalai's hands as she circles the pool with Deepatilakai.
teaches: The receiving scene is the fulfilment of a test set by the bowl's first owner, so the bowl's coming to Manimekalai is a verdict on her compassion as well as a gift.

note: Aputhiran dies on Manipallavam with the purpose of sustaining lives and is born in Savakam, where he had meant to carry the bowl against a famine; in kaathai 25 the minister tells the king that before his birth Savakam lost its rain for twelve years, and that since he was born the sky has not failed and no creature has known hunger.
teaches: The famine Aputhiran set out to relieve with the bowl is ended by his birth instead, so the purpose held at death is fulfilled by what he becomes rather than by what he carries.
audit_text_issue: 14:103-104 attachment of சாவகம் ஆளும் தலைத் தாள் வேந்தன் is unclear.

note: Both epics use one formula for death by fasting: Kavunthi 'gave up her life by the vow of not eating' (உண்ணா நோன்போ டுயிர்பதிப் பெயர்த்ததும், 27:83) asking whether the couple's deeds had struck at her too; Aputhiran dies by the same vow (உண்ணா நோன்போடு உயிர் பதிப் பெயர்ப்புழி, 95).
teaches: The twin epics give the same fasting death opposite fruits: Kavunthi's ends a life overtaken by others' karma in grief, while Aputhiran's is a passage to a birth in which his purpose of feeding goes on.

note: In kaathai 14 Aputhiran hears that rain has failed in Savakam and sets out to carry his bowl there; here the cow's sage foretells, in Savakam itself, a protector born to make the rain abound and guard lives (மழை வளம் சுரப்பவும் மன் உயிர் ஓம்பவும்).
teaches: The errand the shipwreck cut short is fulfilled by rebirth: Aputhiran reaches the rainless land not as a beggar with a bowl but as its rain-bringing king, so the epic moves his charity from alms to kingship across a death.
audit_text_issue: The b end is a span over two marked units (14:49-64, 14:65-78).

note: Kaathai 14 says he left his body on Manipallavam with the intent to sustain unappeased lives and arose from a cow's womb in Savakam; here the cause of that womb is that his unwavering heart never let go of the cow that had guarded him (ஒல்கா உள்ளத்து ஒழியான் ஆதலின்).
teaches: Read together, the two passages give rebirth two causes at two levels: compassion for all lives decides the land and the work, while a personal debt of gratitude decides the very mother, so a private bond shapes the birth inside a universal vow.

note: In kaathai 14 Indra's gift of plenty left Aputhiran's bowl with no takers and his hall silent; here Aravanar says want has come again despite the Kaveri and forbids laying the same bowl aside.
teaches: The bowl's worth is shown to depend wholly on there being hunger: plenty once made it useless and drove its keeper to death, and now a season of want is the reason it must come back into a girl's hands.

note: The couplet calls relieving the destitute's ruinous hunger the place where a man of wealth should store it; Aravanar likens laying aside the hunger-ending bowl to the gods keeping back their leftover nectar, and calls it unfit.
teaches: The couplet keeps a giver's profit in view by making charity a kind of saving, while the epic's bowl has no owner to profit and treats any keeping back as the gods' hoard, so feeding the hungry is pressed past prudence into a duty with no return.

gains.a: Aravanar's rule against laying the bowl aside gains a contrast with the ethics book's view of charity as a store for the giver, which shows how far the bowl's keeper is from any owner's interest.
gains.b: The couplet's banking image gains a case with no depositor at all, a bowl whose holder gains nothing, which exposes the self-regard the image keeps.

note: The couplet says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who wields the sceptre rightly; Aravanar asks whether the king of heaven or the just-sceptred king has failed, and says want has come though the Kaveri flows. The link holds on the reading that the questions at 46-47 clear both.
teaches: The epic grants the Kural's premise that a just king brings plenty and still finds hunger in his land, so hunger becomes a want no sceptre cures and the place where the renouncer's bowl, not the king, must act.

gains.a: The rhetorical questions at 46-47 are explained: they answer the Kural's doctrine that want betrays a bent sceptre, which is why the speaker must clear the king before calling for the bowl.
gains.b: The couplet's promise of plenty under a just king gains a counter-case where both god and king are blameless and the people still hunger.

audit_text_issue: the sense of துய்ப்பிலன் (46) is uncertain

note: When Aputhiran's hall fell silent in plenty, rakes, libertines and idlers (விடரும் தூர்த்தரும் விட்டேற்றாளரும்) took it over with dice; here the same rakes and libertines (விடரும் தூர்த்தரும்) crowd round Manimekalai as she enters the street with the bowl.
teaches: The town's idlers mark both ends of the bowl's story: they fill the hall when the bowl is useless and gather in pity when it returns, so the bowl's renewed use is first met by the very crowd that had displaced it.

note: The Udayana Kumara Kaviyam tells how Yugi, feigning madness and sense by turns, passed along the great streets with crowds about him to the prison where the Vatsa king was held; the Manimekalai likens the crowd's pity for Manimekalai with her bowl in the great street to the pity felt for Yugi's feigned sickness when he freed the Vatsa king.
teaches: The simile reads the nun's garb as a disguise like Yugi's, pitied by onlookers yet hiding a purpose of release, and the later Jain epic's street scene shows the crowd and the prison that the Manimekalai's one-line allusion assumes its hearers know.

note: The couplet says nothing is more degrading to the tongue than begging, even water for a cow; Manimekalai enters the street with a begging bowl and, at 71-74, calls receiving a chaste wife's alms a thing of great worth, while the crowd grieves at the sight.
teaches: The town's grief voices the Kural's shame of asking, and the nun's claim answers it with a begging that asks nothing for herself and seeks the worthiest giver, so the two disagree about whether all asking shames the asker.

gains.a: The crowd's pity (சிந்தை நோய் கூர) is shown to rest on the ethics books' contempt for begging, which the nun's alms round has to overcome.
gains.b: The couplet's limit case, begging even for a cow, meets a beggar whose bowl came down from a cow-born king and feeds others, a case its absolute rule does not consider.

audit_text_issue: The claim the tension rests on (71-74) falls just after the unit's end at 70.

note: Kayasandigai sends Manimekalai to Athirai's house as the one wife of rain-giving chastity; the next kaathai ends with Athirai putting the first food, the 'medicine for life', into the bowl (ஆதிரை இட்டனள் ஆருயிர்மருந்து).
teaches: Manimekalai's rule that the bowl's first alms must come from a pathini is carried out at once, and the giver chosen is a wife whose husband had left her for a courtesan, so the courtesan's daughter's bowl is first filled by such a wife.

note: The couplet says the wife who worships her husband and not a god can bid the rain fall; Kayasandigai praises Athirai as standing alone among the house-dwelling wives of rain-giving chastity (வான் தருகற்பின் மனை உறை மகளிரின்) and so the right giver of the bowl's first alms.
teaches: The epic takes the couplet's rain-giving wife as a known type and makes it a rank, one supreme among many, and a qualification for feeding a Buddhist bowl, so domestic chastity is set to work for the renouncer's charity.

gains.a: Kayasandigai's phrase is shown to rest on the Kural's claim, so her choice of Athirai appeals to a test the hearers already accept.
gains.b: The couplet, which speaks of any such wife, gains a use: chastity's power over the rain becomes a standard for whose alms are worthiest, a ranking the couplet does not make.

note: In the Silappathikaram Kannaki lists the chaste wives of Puhar and their wonders as she turns on Madurai; here Kayasandigai names Athirai as the one who stands alone among Puhar's rain-giving wives.
teaches: The pathinis of the same city serve the twin epics in opposite ways: Kannaki calls on them to back a curse that burns a city, while Manimekalai seeks one of them to give the first food to a bowl that feeds it.

note: The voice in the burning ground names the merchant Chandradattan and his ship; at the end of the tale Saathuvan comes home on Chandradattan's ship, as foretold.
teaches: The prophecy that stopped Aathirai's death is kept only after Saathuvan has converted his captors, so the voice in effect promised a return that his own learning and argument had still to earn.

note: Madhavi listed the ways of the pathini: die at once with a sigh, enter the blazing fire as if it were a cool pool, or wear down the body in vows; Aathirai takes the second way, and the fire will not have her, and she leaves it like a woman coming back from a bath (16:46).
teaches: Madhavi's list assumes the fire completes the pathini's choice, but Aathirai's fire refuses her, so the epic shows that a pathini's power can overrule even her own resolve to die and makes Madhavi's simile of the cool pool literally true.

note: Saathuvan argues from the insensible corpse and the dream journey that a life leaves the body and enters another fitted by its deeds; the materialist of kaathai 27 holds that awareness ends when the elements part, that inference is no means of knowledge, and that a next world of fruits is a lie.
teaches: The materialist's challenge is met eleven kaathais before he states it, by a merchant using exactly the inference the materialist refuses to accept, so the pair shows that the epic's case for rebirth stands or falls on whether inference counts as knowledge.

note: Saathuvan tells the Naga chief that the dying of the born and the birth of the dead are like sleeping and waking, the simile of Kural 339 in other words, and draws from it that good deeds lead to a good world and ill to hell.
teaches: The couplet's simile is a calm statement of impermanence, but Saathuvan turns it into the premise of an argument against liquor and killing, showing that the image of sleep and waking implies a self that wakes again and must answer for its acts.

gains.a: Saathuvan's premise gains a formulation already familiar as a saying, which is why he can offer it to a sceptic without proof
gains.b: the couplet gains a moral consequence it never draws, that what one does before sleeping decides where one wakes

note: Saathuvan is ruined by a courtesan and by dice and cast off penniless; among the Nagas he refuses the woman and liquor offered him, and comes home with treasure.
teaches: The couplet names double-minded women, liquor and dice as the company of those Fortune has left, and the story runs the rule both ways: two of the three strip Saathuvan of wealth, and his refusal of a woman and liquor on the island is what brings fortune back.

gains.a: the tale's two halves gain a single rule that ties his ruin to his later refusal
gains.b: the couplet gains a reversal it does not state, that leaving the three restores what keeping them lost

note: The couplet's highest wife commands the rain; here the chaste wives who bring down the rain themselves worship Aathirai, whom fire would not burn.
teaches: The epic places a rank above the Kural's summit of wifely power, and grounds it not in daily worship of the husband but in a wife's readiness to die for a husband who had deserted her for a courtesan.

gains.a: Aathirai's praise gains a fixed measure, the rain-bringing wife, against which her rank can be stated
gains.b: the couplet gains the sign that its power is not the highest, and that it can be tested against a husband who did nothing to deserve it

note: The Kural argues that no one would sell flesh if no one killed to eat; Saathuvan, told the Nagas cannot live without meat, lets them keep only the flesh of beasts that die of age and bids them harm no living thing.
teaches: The couplet treats the eater as the cause of all killing, while Saathuvan finds the one flesh no killing supplies and so gives people who cannot give up meat a way to keep the Kural's end without its whole demand.

gains.a: Saathuvan's concession gains the reasoning that makes it a principle: what is wrong is the killing that eating causes
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where its rule must bend to what a people can bear, and a shape the bending can take

note: Saathuvan argues that the departing life enters the body its deeds put on, as a reason for the Nagas to do good; Tirumular bids the reader seek the way by which, leaving this body, one does not enter another.
teaches: The same passage of the life into a new body is good news in the epic, a reason to act well for a better world, and the thing to be escaped in Tirumular, so the pair shows that a merchant's ethics of rebirth stops short of the release both traditions put beyond it.

gains.a: Saathuvan's argument gains the reminder that a good rebirth is still a rebirth, which the epic leaves to its later teaching
gains.b: Tirumular's verse gains a reasoned account, from the corpse and the dream, of the entry into another body that it simply assumes

note: The Kural says the evil disease called hunger will not touch one used to sharing his food; Aathirai fills the inexhaustible bowl saying 'may the disease of hunger be cut off from the whole earth'.
teaches: The couplet promises that sharing guards the sharer from the disease of hunger, while Aathirai's gift, poured into a bowl that never empties, aims to cure the disease for everyone, so the pair moves from the giver's safety to a cure for the world.

gains.a: Aathirai's phrase பசிப் பிணி gains the couplet's account of hunger as a disease that sharing keeps away
gains.b: the couplet gains an image of sharing that no longer protects one household but is meant to empty hunger from the earth

note: The couplet says the fire-disease of hunger seldom touches one who habitually shares food (பாத்தூண்); the unit opens on a bowl first filled with a chaste wife's share (பாத்தூண், 1) and on a woman with the elephant-fire disease whose hunger came from old deeds.
teaches: The couplet's protection covers only the sharer's own body, while the epic shows a fire-hunger that no habit of one's own sharing could have kept off because a former deed sent it, so the cure has to come from someone else's share.

gains.a: the epic's alms bowl gains the Kural's name for hunger as a fire-disease that sharing holds off, which makes the bowl a medicine
gains.b: the couplet gains a case beyond its reach: hunger sent by karma, curable only by another's gift and not prevented by one's own

note: The couplet ranks the strength of those who endure hunger below that of those who remove it; Viruchikan eats once in twelve years, and when his fruit is crushed his fasting power becomes a curse of hunger on another, which Manimekalai's bowl removes.
teaches: The story stages the couplet's ranking and adds a reason for it: the endurer's power, once offended, can itself manufacture hunger in others, so only the giver's power ends suffering rather than moving it about.

gains.a: the epic's sage and girl gain a stated rule that ranks them, the faster below the feeder
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where the endurer's strength is not merely lesser but harmful, causing the very hunger the giver must remove

note: Kavunthi's penance-given curse (தவம்தரு சாபம்) turns two scorners into jackals for twelve months; Viruchikan's curse binds Kayasandigai to hunger for twelve years. Both are ascetics' curses with a fixed term, but here the cursed woman names her own ripening deed as the cause and her husband calls the curse causeless.
teaches: Set beside the Silappathikaram, where the curse simply answers an insult, the Manimekalai makes the ascetic's curse an instrument through which the victim's own karma ripens, and lets one voice call it unjust, so the curse is no longer self-justifying.
audit_text_issue: The husband's line (17:54) falls outside the unit printed.

note: The goddess gives Manimekalai a mantra to travel the sky and another that cuts hunger, since the body is a lump of food; Kayasandigai has lost the mantra for going through the sky (55, and அந்தரம் செல்லும் மந்திரம் 43) and suffers a hunger no food fills.
teaches: The two women are drawn as mirror images: the very powers granted to Manimekalai by mantra, flight and freedom from hunger, are those the curse stripped from Kayasandigai, and Manimekalai restores the second to her by charity, not by mantra.

note: In the Purananuru poem the bard hears the noise of eating (ஊணொலி அரவம்) at Pannan's house and asks where the house of the physician of hunger (பசிப்பிணி மருத்துவன்) is; the epic closes with the same noise of eating (ஊண் ஒலி அரவத்து ஒலி, 97) at the public hall, after Kayasandigai has called Manimekalai physician of life (மருத்துவி, 15).
teaches: The epic borrows the Sangam scene of the hunger-healer's feast word for word but moves it from a patron's house, reached by a bard's praise, to a public hall with a gate open to all where anyone who will receive is called in.

gains.a: the epic scene gains a Sangam lineage: the girl with the bowl takes the old title of physician of hunger and the very sound of the patron's feast
gains.b: the poem's question of where the healer's house is, near or far, gains an answer the Sangam world lacked: a public hall that needs no patron and no praise-song

note: Madhavi described the pathini widows who die, enter fire as a pool or waste themselves in vows, and confessed she had lived on; Chithirapathi repeats the same figures and phrase to say a courtesan was never bound to any of them.
teaches: The same list of widow's deaths serves the daughter as a measure she has failed and the mother as proof that their caste is exempt, so Madhavi's renunciation is attacked from below as well as judged from above.

note: The quatrain says a harlot's love goes out like a lamp when the money is gone; Chithirapathi says courtesans leave a drained flower like bees and leave men like Fortune when their merit ends.
teaches: The moralist's charge against the courtesan is spoken in the epic by a courtesan as her house's rule, and she uses it to forbid her daughter's grief and renunciation, so the faithlessness the quatrain condemns turns out to be enforced on the women themselves.

gains.a: Chithirapathi's boast is shown to be the very account outsiders give of her profession, which she presents as her own code.
gains.b: The quatrain gains the cost to the woman who tries to leave the life it describes, which its warning to men never considers.

note: In kaathai 7 the goddess tells the prince that a bent sceptre unsettles the planets, the rain and the people's lives, and bids him drop his designs on the ascetic girl; here he recalls only a woman showing a sceptre and wonders if she was a god.
teaches: The warning that tied the prince's lust to the kingdom's rain reaches him only as an image he cannot interpret, which is what lets the courtesan laugh it away and sets up his ruin.

note: The couplet honours the wife who worships her husband and no god; Chithirapathi describes the families whose women worship no god but the man who took them, to say Manimekalai is not of them.
teaches: The epic shows the couplet's ideal working as a boundary of birth: women outside the families it describes are declared fair game, so praise of the chaste wife becomes an argument for coercing a woman who has chosen celibacy.

gains.a: Chithirapathi's argument rests on a standard of womanhood the audience already reveres, which is why it can persuade a prince.
gains.b: The couplet gains a reading of its exclusions: it says nothing of the women it leaves out, and here they are claimed as the prince's to take.

note: The couplet warns men off women who weigh the gain and speak of virtue; Chithirapathi describes dancers who take many gains with sweet speech and leave like bees, and tells the prince to bind such a woman.
teaches: The couplet's advice is to avoid the profit-weighing woman, while the courtesan who describes the same woman advises the prince to seize her, so a portrait meant to protect men becomes a licence to coerce a girl who has left that life.

gains.a: The courtesan's self-portrait gains the weight of a recognised moral description, which makes her case for force seem like common sense.
gains.b: The couplet's type gains a case where the woman so labelled is no longer what the label says, showing how the description outlives the conduct.

note: Sudhamathi told the prince in the grove that the human body is born of deeds, ages, dies and holds disease and grief; Manimekalai now tells him in nearly the same words why she renounced.
teaches: The lesson that did not reach the prince's heart from the companion (4:122-123) is repeated by Manimekalai herself as her own reason, and she expects it to fail again, so the teaching is a test the prince keeps failing rather than an argument he has not heard.

note: The goddess told Manimekalai that Udayakumaran is her Rahula and that her mind has not left him; here she bows to him as her former husband and admits her heart goes to him.
teaches: The attachment the goddess predicted is admitted openly rather than denied, and Manimekalai turns the former husband's claim on her obedience into the occasion for her refusal.

note: The quatrain says the best of people reflect on impermanence, disease, old age and death and do their real work; Manimekalai says she understood the body's birth, ageing, disease and death and chose dharma.
teaches: The same reflection that the quatrain treats as a private discipline of the wise is here a defence a woman must speak aloud to a man pursuing her, and she doubts he will listen.

gains.a: Manimekalai's Buddhist reason is shown to rest on a reflection the Tamil ethical tradition already commends, not on a doctrine peculiar to her school.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a scene where the reflection must be argued before someone who does not share it, which its address to the wise leaves out.

note: The goddess gave Manimekalai a mantra to change her form so that no one would dismiss her teaching as a young girl's; here she uses it to take Kaayasandigai's form and hide from the prince.
teaches: The power given for teaching rival schools is first used to escape a pursuer, so the epic's protection of her celibacy and its preparation for debate run through the same gift.

note: Manimekalai's disguise as Kaayasandigai leads Kaanchanan, Kaayasandigai's husband, to think the prince is courting his wife and to kill him; the pillar goddess then calls the death ஊழ்வினை and blames Kaanchanan.
teaches: The disguise that protects Manimekalai's vow becomes the means of the prince's death, and the epic assigns the death to past deeds while still holding the killer guilty, so her innocent act is one link in a chain of karma.

note: The prince describes Manimekalai quoting old wisdom (முதுக்குறை முதுமொழி எடுத்துக் காட்டி) as the goads that tamed him; in kaathai 20 Kaanchanan sees the disguised Manimekalai doing the same and takes it for a wife's flirting.
teaches: Her act of teaching is read twice as desire, once by the man it is meant to turn away and once by the jealous husband, and the second misreading is fatal.

note: In the grove the prince asked whether any restraint holds once desire takes root; here evening pursues him 'with an aspect that destroys restraint' and he leaves burning and sighing.
teaches: The prince's line that no நிறை survives rooted desire was his licence to pursue; two kaathais on, the same loss of restraint is drawn as a beast that hounds him away from her, so his excuse becomes his torment.

note: The goddess gave her a mantra to take another form and travel the sky so that no one would refuse her teaching for her youth; here she first uses the other form to evade the prince and enter a prison with the bowl.
teaches: The power given so she could hear doctrine as an adult is first spent on escaping desire and feeding prisoners, so the epic puts charity and self-protection before debate in the order of her training.

note: The patikam tells that Kanchanan, taking her for Kayachandigai, approached her and killed the prince; here she chooses that form to keep the prince away.
teaches: The disguise she takes to be free of Udayakumaran is what brings Kayachandigai's husband upon him, so her flight from the prince is the cause of his death, which the patikam names and this kaathai does not yet show.

note: The couplet calls taking bad even if it were a good path and giving good even without heaven; Manimekalai cites the learned that for an alms-seeker both taking and giving are duty, and going to give is better still.
teaches: The couplet's flat ranking of giving over taking leaves no place for the mendicant, while the epic makes taking a duty when it serves giving, so the beggar's bowl is let in under the couplet's rule rather than condemned by it.

gains.a: Her maxim gains a sharp statement of the view it must answer: that taking is bad whatever the path.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case it does not cover, the one who takes only in order to give.

note: The herdswomen dance the kuravai of Mayavan, his elder brother and Pinnai to ward off the omens before Kovalan's death; the Chola king sees that same kuravai in birds whirling in his pleasure grove.
teaches: Across the two epics the one divine dance is first a rite of fear performed by herdswomen over coming disaster and then a pleasantry of a king at play, while Kovalan's daughter works in his prison, so the image measures how far the court stands from the suffering it governs.

note: The quatrain's ascetic's bowl (தவசி கடிஞை) fills slowly by alms at door after door; the guard reports a begging bowl (ஐயப் பாத்திரம்) that, taken into the prison, makes food flow for a crowd.
teaches: The quatrain uses the begging bowl as the image of slow accumulation in the giver, and the epic reverses its direction, making the ascetic's bowl the source that pours out, so in the Buddhist epic the mendicant is the giver and the city the receiver.

gains.a: The marvel of the one bowl gains the ordinary picture of a begging bowl it overturns.
gains.b: The quatrain's image gains a counter-case where the bowl's fullness belongs to the beggar, not the donor.

note: The couplet likens a king's punishing the cruel to weeding a crop; the Chola king, at a beggar's request, empties his prison and makes it a house of dharma.
teaches: Held against the couplet, the epic's king does not deny that the cruel must be punished but turns the instrument of punishment itself into an instrument of charity, so the sceptre is shown by feeding rather than weeding.

gains.a: The king's act gains the standard view of royal punishment it departs from.
gains.b: The couplet's weeding image gains a royal alternative it does not consider, in which the prison is abolished rather than filled.

note: Kudapulaviyanar tells the Pandya that those who give food give life and urges him to build tanks; the disguised girl tells the Chola her bowl is life-medicine for embodied beings and asks him to give the prison to the righteous.
teaches: Both poems set a counsellor before a king to teach that feeding is giving life, but the Sangam poet asks for waterworks that bring fame and the other world, while the epic's beggar asks the king to give up a prison, so the duty to feed passes from royal works to a renouncer's bowl the king only endorses.

gains.a: The girl's plea gains a Tamil royal precedent for the claim that food is life.
gains.b: The poem's counsel gains a later scene where the one who feeds is not the king, which shifts who holds the life-giving power.

note: Aravanar called the Amudhasurabhi life-medicine (ஆர் உயிர் மருந்து) and said many events would come to the city through her; she tells the king the bowl is life-medicine (உயிர் மருந்து) and the prison becomes a house of dharma.
teaches: Her words to the king repeat her teacher's phrase, and her first public act fulfils his prophecy of events in the city, so the epic shows the teaching passing into civic change through the disciple's voice before she has formally taken the dharma.

note: The goddess Manimekala warned the prince that a swerving sceptre ruins rain and life and told him to drop his wrongful intent toward one who has taken up tapas; here he resolves to seize her even against the wise and the king.
teaches: The prince's death is set up as the end of a refused warning: he was told in advance that his desire for an ascetic was a fault of the sceptre, and he now names the king's anger as one more thing he will override.

note: Chithirapathi vowed that she would have the prince carry Manimekalai off in his golden chariot; here the prince himself plans to set her in his golden chariot.
teaches: The courtesan mother's plan becomes the prince's own wish in the same image of the golden chariot, so the reader sees the abduction as her design working through him rather than a whim of his alone.

note: The sage Viruchikan cursed Kayasandikai to twelve years of burning hunger; Kanchanan comes to Puhar because the twelve years are over and she has not come home.
teaches: The twelve-year term set in the curse is what brings the husband to the city on the very days Manimekalai wears his wife's form, so the curse that seemed to end with her cure sets up the killing.

note: Freed of her hunger, Kayasandikai told Manimekalai she would go to her city in the sky; the pillar image reveals she was seized over the Vindhya on the way and swallowed by its goddess.
teaches: The cure that Manimekalai's bowl gave Kayasandikai did not bring her home: the release she announced ends in a second death, and her husband's search ends in a killing over her likeness.

note: At their first meeting in the hall Manimekalai told the prince in words that the human body is a vessel of birth, age, disease and death; here she shows him an old woman's body feature by feature.
teaches: Manimekalai moves from stating the doctrine of the suffering body to making the prince look at one, which shows that she treats his desire as a failure of seeing that a statement did not cure.
audit_text_issue: The b span 18:124-141 is not a marked unit; the marked unit runs to 142.

note: The prince praised Manimekalai for setting out 'wise old sayings' (முதுக்குறை முதுமொழி) as part of her allure; Kanchanan sees her setting out the same wise old sayings to the prince and takes it as a lover's talk.
teaches: The same words of wisdom are read by both men as courtship, the prince as charm to be won and the husband as proof of betrayal, so her teaching is misheard twice in the way most fatal to each hearer.

note: The prince goes at midnight to the hall to take Manimekalai and dies; the next kaathai's report to the king sets his death among those of men who approached chaste wives or ascetic women and died as their evil deed ripened.
teaches: The midnight approach is later read as one case in a city's record of such deaths, so the narrative's private intrigue becomes a public precedent that the court uses to explain a prince's death to his father.

note: The pillar says the prince died by his own former deed; in the next kaathai the deity tells Manimekalai that deed: in a former birth he cut down a cook with a sword for spoiling a meal for the sage Brahmadharman.
teaches: The bare claim of ripened karma is given its content one kaathai later, and the content matches the form of the death, a sword for a sword, so the epic makes its karma traceable rather than merely asserted.

note: The quatrain warns men not to desire the spear-eyed woman because she too will stoop and walk with a staff; Manimekalai, the woman desired, points her pursuer to an old woman and shows him eyes and face already changed.
teaches: The quatrain's warning against desire is spoken by a man to men about a woman, while the epic puts it in the mouth of the desired woman as her own defence, turning the lesson on aging into a refusal.

gains.a: Manimekalai's demonstration gains a recognized ethical topos, so her act reads as instruction rather than mere evasion.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a case where the warned man ignores the lesson and dies of the desire, which tests what the warning can do.

audit_text_issue: The marker flagged the sense. | LINK header carries no Gains line; gains_holds set to null

note: The quatrain asks whether spices, flowers in the hair and false finery can remove a foulness the great saw and gave up; Manimekalai says the flowers, paste, cloth and jewels that hide the flesh are a deceit 'those of old' devised.
teaches: The quatrain credits the great of the past with seeing through the body's adornment, while the epic blames those of old for building it, so the same disguise is a personal vanity in one and an inherited social custom in the other.

gains.a: The epic's charge against custom gains a parallel in which tradition is on the side of seeing through adornment, which sharpens how unusual its blame of 'those of old' is.
gains.b: The quatrain gains an account of where the false finery comes from, which it treats only as something individuals put on.

note: The quatrain's renunciant refuses talk of teeth like jasmine buds and pearls because he has seen fallen teeth and bones in the burning ground; Manimekalai shows teeth once like a row of pearls now loosened in a living mouth.
teaches: The quatrain needs the cremation ground to refute the pearl simile, while the epic finds the refutation in a living old woman, so the argument against the body moves from death to aging that every lover can see in the street.

gains.a: Manimekalai's catalogue gains the Naladiyar's frame of rejected similes, showing it answers the praise-poets' language point by point.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a version of its proof that does not wait for death, which widens it from the funeral ground to ordinary life.

note: Sivavakkiyar's man, having taken a woman for her form, would cut down any rival who desires her, though his own body will stink and be handed to the cremation keeper; Kanchanan cuts down the prince over a form that is not even his wife's, whose body is already gone.
teaches: The epic gives the Siddhar's jealous husband a case where the form (வடிவு) he guards belongs to another woman and his wife's body has already perished, so the jealousy is shown wrong both about whose body it is and about its lasting.

gains.a: Kanchanan's killing gains a general diagnosis: it is jealousy over a body, the most perishable of possessions.
gains.b: The Siddhar's hypothetical gains a narrated case in which the rival is actually killed and the killer's price is named as a deed that clings, beyond the body's decay.

note: The quatrain says an old deed finds its doer as a calf finds its mother among many cows; the pillar says the prince's ripened deed came here and took his life, and that Kanchanan's deed will reach him too.
teaches: The epic shows the old deed finding its doer across a change of birth and through a stranger's hand, which gives the quatrain's search image a path: the deed reaches the prince by way of another man's mistake.

gains.a: The pillar's statement gains the image of the deed as an active seeker, which explains why a chance misidentification could deliver it.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a case in which one deed's arrival creates a new deed with its own doer, a chain the calf image does not show.

note: The couplet says the ruin of evil-doers stays at their feet like a shadow; the pillar tells Kanchanan his cruel deed will not leave him, even though the prince died by his own former deed.
teaches: The couplet considers only the doer, while the epic adds that being the instrument of another's ripened karma does not lift the deed from the one who kills, so karma explains the victim's death without excusing the killer.

gains.a: The pillar's warning gains the couplet's image of a consequence that never leaves its doer's feet.
gains.b: The couplet gains a hard case, a killing the victim's own deed called for, in which its rule still holds.

audit_text_issue: The marker flagged line 122 (கைம்மை கொள்ளேல்) as uncertain.

note: The couplet says unguarded anger kills the one who has it; Kanchanan's anger, kindled by misread signs, kills the prince, and the pillar then tells him the deed will cling to him.
teaches: The epic traces how anger turns on its owner: it begins in a misreading of another's signs, kills someone else first, and returns as a deed that will not leave the angry man, which the couplet states as a single blow.

gains.a: Kanchanan's rage gains the couplet's judgment that the angry man is his own first victim.
gains.b: The couplet gains the route by which anger kills its owner: through the deed done to another and its clinging consequence.

note: Brahmadharman foretold that Rahulan would die of the snake's poison glance; the pillar deity now names the deed that set his deaths in motion: the cook he killed in anger at the sage's meal.
teaches: The prophecy of kaathai 9 gave only the event; paired with this unit it shows the epic withholding a cause for twelve kaathais and then placing it inside an act of service to the very sage who made the prophecy.

note: To the killer Kanchanan the same deity said that karma took the prince's life yet his own cruel deed would not leave him; to Manimekalai it says the prince's death is the fruit of his own killing.
teaches: Together the two speeches show the epic's karma as a chain in which every link is also a fresh wrong: the victim's old deed ripens only through a new killing whose doer is held to account in turn.
audit_text_issue: 21:61-62 and 67-69 are compressed; the link rests on 66 and 70-71, which are clear.

note: The Naladiyar's old deed finds its doer as a calf finds its mother among many cows; the deity says the cook's killing came 'here' to strike the man reborn as the prince.
teaches: The quatrain's deed that seeks out its doer becomes in the epic a deed that crosses a death and a new body, so the 'doer' it finds is a person with another name who does not remember the act.

gains.a: an image for the deed's active search, which the deity states only as a bare claim
gains.b: a case that sets the search across births, which the quatrain does not say

note: The couplet says harm done to others comes back on the doer of itself; the deity applies this to a killing done in zeal to serve a holy man and denies that the service exempts it.
teaches: The couplet does not ask whether a good motive changes the return of harm; the epic answers that it does not, and names the excuse it rejects, that the master served will protect his servant.

gains.a: a general rule against which the deity's denial of the pious excuse is measured
gains.b: a test of whether intention to serve dharma can stop harm from returning, which the couplet leaves open

note: The deity foretells that the materialist will call her knowledge of a former birth a dream sent by a deity; in Vanji he says those deluded by a god or by dreams have changed minds.
teaches: The prophecy foretells the opponent's very objection, so when the debate comes the reader already knows the materialist's charge is aimed at a real divine intervention that the epic itself narrated.

note: Sivavakkiyar mocks the planted stone called a god and asks whether it will speak while the Lord is within; the pillar deity grants that stone and wood do not speak but says deities the wise install in them stay and speak to men.
teaches: Both start from the same premise, that the stone itself is mute; they part over whether a power can be lodged in it, the epic answering yes for guardian deities of a city and the Siddhar answering that the Lord is found only within.

gains.a: a sharp statement of the sceptic's objection that the deity's account is built to meet
gains.b: evidence that the 'speaking stone' it mocks had a worked-out defence, the deity bound to its place, rather than naive idol worship

note: Thuvathikan foretells famine in Kanchi and Manimekalai's coming with the bowl; when she arrives, the Kanchi king says all the pillar image's words have come true (கந்திற்பாவை கட்டுரை எல்லாம் வாய் ஆகின்று).
teaches: The epic closes its own prophecy by having a king cite the pillar image by name, so the deity's claim at 112 to 129 that installed gods speak true is confirmed inside the story, not only asserted.
audit_text_issue: The 28:183-203 span is not a marked unit; it overlaps 28:162-183 and 28:184-206.

note: The couplet says that if the sky fails, hunger stays and torments the wide world; the deity foretells the bowl of dharma that gives rain's plenty to a parched world.
teaches: Where the couplet treats hunger after drought as beyond remedy, the epic answers it with organized charity, the begging bowl standing in for the failed rain.

gains.a: a statement of the stakes: drought brings hunger even to a world ringed with water
gains.b: a remedy the couplet does not consider, feeding by alms when the sky fails

note: Tirumular's grace-power descends as the guru when good and bad deeds are balanced and the soul becomes Siva; the epic's Manimekalai, after births of compassion, becomes a disciple and is saved by cutting dependence herself (சார்பு அறுத்து உய்தி).
teaches: Both put a teacher at the threshold of release, but in Tirumular the teacher is grace that ends the soul's own agency, while in the epic the great one only gives dharma and the disciple does the cutting, so they disagree over who acts in release.

gains.a: a sharp contrast that shows how far the epic keeps release in the disciple's own hands
gains.b: a Buddhist counter-model of the teacher-disciple bond without descent of grace

note: Both scenes bring a death before a king with the same approach formula (கோயில் மன்னனைக் குறுகினர்/குறுகினள் சென்று): Kannaki to the Pandya, the ascetics to the Chola.
teaches: Kannaki uses the audience to accuse the king of her husband's death, while the ascetics, bringing a father news of his son's death, hide the body and wrap the news in blessing and old stories, so the same entrance shows two ways of telling a king a truth he is implicated in.

note: The couplet says enmity, sin, fear and blame never leave the man who crosses into another's home; the ascetic says such men die when their evil deed ripens, and adds those who set their hearts on women ascetics.
teaches: The couplet's offence is entering a married woman's home; the epic extends it to desire for a renunciant woman, who has no husband's home to violate, and makes death, not lasting disgrace, the outcome.

gains.a: The ascetic's general charge gains the Kural's account of what such a man carries while he lives.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case beyond the married woman, the woman of penance, which its home-centred wording leaves out.

note: Sudhamathi, carried off by a vidyadhara, became unfit for the brahmins yet her father kept her; Maruthi, only desired by a youth, declares herself unfit for her husband's fires.
teaches: The epic twice lets the brahmin purity rule fall on a woman who did nothing; in Sudhamathi's case the father stays by her, while Maruthi excludes herself before anyone else does, so the rule is shown working inside the woman's own conscience.

note: The Bhuta quotes the couplet to Maruthi and explains her lost power by her worship of gods, festivals and talk.
teaches: The couplet states the wife's power as a fact; the epic uses it as a test a chaste woman fails, reads தெய்வம் தொழாஅள் literally as a ban on worshipping gods, and adds festivals and gossip, so the couplet becomes a rule with conditions that can be broken.

gains.a: Maruthi's loss of power gains a named authority, the poet who never lies, behind the Bhuta's verdict.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case that spells out what not worshipping a god excludes and what happens to the power when it is not kept.

note: Devanthi urges Kannaki to bathe in the sacred tanks and worship to win her husband back, and Kannaki refuses; the Bhuta tells Maruthi that worship of gods is what cost her the rain.
teaches: The Manimekalai's Bhuta supplies the doctrine behind Kannaki's refusal of the tanks in the Silappathikaram: a pathini's power rests on not turning to gods, so Kannaki's refusal is part of what makes her word able to burn Madurai.

note: In the Silappathikaram the Bhuta of the crossroads nooses and devours unchaste women who hide their wrong and men who desire others' wives; here the same Bhuta tells Maruthi its noose will not bind her and that it acts only after the king's seven days.
teaches: Read together, the two show the spirit's justice as a reserve behind the king's: it binds the hidden offender, spares the woman who was only desired, and waits seven days for the king to punish the man before acting itself.

note: The image on the pillar (கந்தின் ... பாவை) of the Ulaka Aravi proclaims Visakai chaste here; in kaathai 20 the same image tells Kanchanan that the woman before him is Manimekalai in disguise.
teaches: The pillar image is the city's witness for women: it once cleared a slandered virgin by declaring her a rain-bringer, and later declares the truth about a disguised renunciant, but in the second case its word comes after the sword has fallen.

note: The Silappathikaram's image in the court weeps without speaking (நாவொடு நவிலாது) when the king's sceptre bends; the Manimekalai's speaking image (நா உடைப் பாவை) proclaims a woman's innocence to the city.
teaches: Puhar's images serve as witnesses of justice in both epics, but one only weeps silently at a bent sceptre while the other speaks and clears a woman, so the pairing shows the speaking image as an active judge where the weeping one is only a sign.

note: Visakai vows in youth to be her cousin's wife only in the next birth; at sixty she tells him again she will not come to his feet in this birth but will serve him in the next.
teaches: The vow made to silence a slander outlives the slander by forty years, so what began as a defence of her name becomes the form their love takes, kept apart in body and joined in shared charity.

note: The couplet says women who obtain their husbands win great distinction in the world of the gods; the brahmin says men without a chaste wife do not enter it.
teaches: Taken together, the couplet and the brahmin's maxim make the wife and husband each the other's way to heaven, but the epic gives the maxim to a man urging a sixty-year-old to marry and then has Visakai deny it, so the reciprocal rule is shown as a pressure rather than a truth.

gains.a: The brahmin's maxim gains its counterpart in the couplet, which ties a woman's heaven to her husband.
gains.b: The couplet gains the reverse claim about men, and a scene in which that claim is answered.

note: The brahmin says men without a chaste wife do not enter the world of the gods however much good they do; Visakai says sons do not give that world and only great virtue is a companion.
teaches: The same phrase, புத்தேள் உலகம், is used for opposite conditions within twenty lines: the brahmin makes a wife necessary, Visakai makes virtue sufficient, and the narrator sides with her by counting their charity above the stars.

note: The couplet calls virtue the companion that does not perish when one perishes; Visakai calls great virtue the true companion (விழுத் துணை) in place of youth, body, wealth and sons.
teaches: Visakai uses the couplet's idea of virtue as companion to replace the wife-companion the brahmin demanded, so a teaching about virtue outlasting death becomes an answer to the claim that a man needs marriage for heaven.

gains.a: Her answer gains the couplet's reason why virtue alone survives.
gains.b: The couplet's companion gains a concrete rival it displaces: the wife and the sons a householder is told he must have.

note: The quatrain says the wise, knowing grey hair will come, renounce in childhood; Visakai points to Dharmadattan's grey hair and turns him not to renunciation but to giving.
teaches: The quatrain offers only two paths, early renunciation or clinging to youth; Visakai, who has kept a vow of chastity since youth, shows a third for the grey-haired householder: shared charity without marriage.

gains.a: Visakai's appeal to his grey hair gains the quatrain's standard of what the wise do before it comes.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a case where the one who saw age coming chose a vow and charity rather than the robe.

note: The couplet says evils will not touch a man for seven births if he has children of good character; Visakai says sons do not give heaven.
teaches: On the reading that the seven births are the parent's own, the couplet credits good children with protecting the parent beyond this life, which Visakai flatly denies, so the pair marks a point where the epic's teacher rejects a household hope the Kural endorses.

gains.a: Visakai's denial gains its target: a recognised claim that children carry merit to their parents.
gains.b: The couplet gains a direct contrary in a text that counts only one's own virtue.

note: Kakandhan, though grieving, kills his elder son with his own sword for seizing Visakai's garland; the present Chola says the vidyadhara did to his son what he himself should have done.
teaches: The ascetic's stories prepare the king's verdict: Kakandhan executes his sons with his own hand, and the Chola, faced with a son already dead, claims that act as his own duty, while also hiding the body from other kings, which Kakandhan never did.

note: Tirumular calls killing, theft, lust and lying sins as great as mountains, whose giving up leads to Siva's feet; the ascetic names toddy, lying, theft, killing and lust as the five to be shunned and threatens hell to those who keep lust.
teaches: Two traditions share nearly the same list of sins but use it differently: Tirumular makes their giving up a path to Siva's feet, while the ascetic names no god, singles out lust as the one that contains the rest, and uses the list to warn a king of hell.

gains.a: The ascetic's list gains a parallel that shows how far it is shared across schools.
gains.b: Tirumular's verse gains a godless version of the same discipline, where shunning is an end in itself and its failure leads to hell rather than away from Siva.

note: The prince follows Manimekalai like a shadow (நிழல் போல், 185); the couplet says ruin stays at the evildoer's feet like his shadow.
teaches: The epic inverts the couplet's shadow: the prince makes himself Manimekalai's shadow, but his own evil deed is the shadow at his own feet, and it catches him in the hall where he followed her.

gains.a: The prince's pursuit gains the couplet's image of what was following him.
gains.b: The couplet's shadow gains a scene where the pursuer is himself pursued, so the image shows how the ruin comes.

note: In kaathai 20 the pillar image tells Kanchanan that ripened karma took the prince's life; here the ascetic tells the king that the prince's evil deed itself struck him by the vidyadhara's hand.
teaches: The killing is told twice as the work of karma, but the deity also tells Kanchanan his act was a cruel deed that will follow him, while the ascetic, speaking to the father, leaves the killer's guilt out, so the same explanation is shaped by who hears it.

note: The pillar image tells Kanchanan he has done a cruel deed whose fruit will not leave him; the king says the vidyadhara did what the king should have done.
teaches: The same killing is a cruel deed with consequences in the deity's eyes and a royal duty done by another's hand in the king's, so the epic sets karmic judgment and royal justice side by side without reconciling them.

note: Kannaki cites the Chola who put his own son under the chariot wheel to shame the Pandya; the Chola king here fears it will be said that in that king's line an evil-doer was born.
teaches: The memory Kannaki used to accuse another king becomes a weight on the Chola's own line: he accepts his son's death as justice, but his first thought is to keep the stain on Manu's line from other kings, so the ancestor's example breeds concealment as well as justice.

note: The couplet says that if the guardian does not guard, the cows' yield fails and the brahmins forget their books; the king says that without the guardian's guarding there are no ascetics' vows and no women's chastity.
teaches: The king adapts the couplet's list of what fails without a guardian to ascetics' vows and women's chastity, the two things his son violated, so the general rule becomes the reason he must count his own son's death as just.

gains.a: The king's maxim gains the couplet's frame of the guardian's duty, which shows it as a known rule rather than a private excuse.
gains.b: The couplet's list gains vows and chastity, and a case where the guardian's duty runs against his own son.

note: Both give the rite of laying a king who died of sickness on darbha grass and cutting him with a sword with the words 'go where the warriors go' (செல்வுழிச் செல்க in both); Avvai uses it to praise Athiyaman's battle wounds, Vasanthavai to console and rebuke a queen whose son died in neither war nor old age.
teaches: Held together they show the rite outliving its Sangam use as praise: in the epic it becomes the standard by which a dead prince is found wanting, so that the warrior code is used to stop a mother's grief rather than to honour a king.

gains.a: the Sangam source of the custom, which shows that Vasanthavai is quoting an old royal code of the warrior's death and not inventing a comfort
gains.b: a later witness that the rite was remembered as a royal custom and could be turned from praise of the wounded against a prince who died without honour

note: The Manimekala goddess gave Manimekalai mantras to take another form, travel the sky and end hunger, warning that people would not tell a young woman the truth; here the form-changing mantra defeats the queen's plot.
teaches: The pair shows why the goddess's gifts were defensive: the mantra of another form, given against those who would not trust a young woman, is first used to save her from a slander about her body.

note: The sage foretold that Rahulan would die of the serpent's venomous gaze within sixteen days and that Lakshmi would burn with him; Manimekalai now uses that death to ask the queen why she did not weep for the same life then.
teaches: The prophecy of a death in the former birth becomes, in this kaathai, the ground of an argument against grief: the same life has died before unmourned by its present mother, so her grief is for this body only.

note: Tirumular describes the whole town wailing, renaming the dead man a corpse, burning him and bathing to forget; Manimekalai asks the queen whether she weeps for the body, since mourners themselves cast it into the burning ground, or for the life, whose next dwelling is set by deeds.
teaches: Tirumular's observation that mourners burn and forget the body they weep for becomes in the epic the first horn of a dilemma whose second horn turns grief for one life into pity for all lives.

gains.a: a plain picture of the mourners' contradiction that her terse question 'who cast him into the burning ground?' assumes
gains.b: a use for the observation: the Buddhist teacher draws from it an obligation of compassion, not only the impermanence the verse leaves the reader with

note: The Silappathikaram's patikam sets as a moral that the deed of the past comes in wrath and feeds its fruit (ஊழ்வினை உருத்துவந்து ஊட்டும்); Manimekalai uses the same verb of the prince's former killing of a cook (உருத்து எழும் வல் வினை).
teaches: The pair shows the sequel taking its companion's moral from the frame into a mechanism: here the wrathful deed is named, traced across two births and two deaths, and offered to a mourner as consolation rather than as a verdict on a king.

note: The pillar deity told Manimekalai that the prince's death came from his killing of the cook who broke the vessels meant for the sage Brahmadharma; Manimekalai now passes that revelation to the prince's mother.
teaches: The same account of a past killing changes use between the two kaathais: revealed to the lover as the reason for his death, it is retold to the mother as the reason not to hate the woman she blamed for it.

note: Kural 284 says that a love grown in stealth yields at harvest a sorrow that does not die; Manimekalai tells the queen not to think that the harsh suffering of those who live by stealth is for thieves alone, since these ways bring sorrow to all who live in the world.
teaches: The couplet assigns undying sorrow to the thief; the epic refuses to let a listener file that sorrow under a class of criminals and extends it to a queen whose fault was deceit, making the rule about theft a rule about all concealment.

gains.a: a known rule on the fruit of stealth, which gives force to the phrase she will not let the queen keep at a distance
gains.b: a scene in which the couplet's reader is warned against using it to sort the guilty from herself

note: The narrator says the queen hid her grief with helpless heart (கையாற்று) and false conduct (பொய்யாற்று ஒழுக்கம்); Manimekalai's maxim says those who take falsehood as their way never pass beyond helpless grief (பொய்யாற்று ஒழுக்கம், கையாற்று அவலம்).
teaches: Read together, the maxim is not general advice but the queen's own conduct described back to her in the narrator's words, so the teaching names her deceit without accusing her.

note: Kural 2 asks what learning is worth if the learned do not bow at the feet of the one of pure knowledge; Manimekalai says learning that is merely learned is not learning, and names the learned as those who curb hatred, end hunger and love all creatures.
teaches: Both refuse learning its own worth, but the couplet completes it in worship while the epic completes it in compassion and the ending of others' hunger, so the pair shows two answers to the same question of what learning is for.

gains.a: a classic statement that learning needs a further end, against which her list reads as a choice of ends
gains.b: a Buddhist answer to its question that puts the further end in conduct toward beings rather than in reverence to a lord

audit_text_issue: Unit starts at 131, after the line 130 statement about learning that the link depends on.

note: Gotami, mourning her son at the burning ground, begged the goddess to take her life for his and was told a life gone goes by its deeds; the queen, mourning her son, is taught the same and her grief is quenched.
teaches: The epic answers a mother's grief twice with the same doctrine but to opposite ends: Gotami, refused, dies beside her son, while the queen, taught to turn her love to all lives, is cleared and bows to her son's supposed enemy.

note: The Silappathikaram gives Madhavi's descent from the maiden cursed to earth when Urvasi's dance failed before Indra as the pedigree of her art; Chithirapathi counts the same heavenly dancers, Urvasi of her own line, to measure her shame now that Madhavi begs.
teaches: The curse-myth that certifies the courtesan's art in the first epic becomes, in the second, the yardstick by which the courtesan house judges a daughter's renunciation as the worst fall of the line.
audit_text_issue: Who exactly was cursed in Silappathikaram 6:20-24 is syntactically unsettled.

note: In the Silappathikaram, when Madhavi gives her daughter to the dharma, the king and city grieve as men who have dropped a gem in the sea and the ascetics speak kind words; Chithirapathi says such a turn earns a courtesan only laughter.
teaches: Held together they show that the courtesan's renunciation has two publics: the city mourns the loss of beauty while the courtesan house reads the same act as ridicule, so neither epic's report of the town's reaction can be taken alone.
