note: Both are a sage's warning that a city will sink: Brahmadharma gives Attipathi a fixed day and the king leads his people out, while the charana makes Puhar's sinking hang on a rite that must never be forgotten and that the goddess cannot override.
teaches: The pair shows the epic's two kinds of prophecy of ruin: a Buddhist sage's fixed fact that is escaped by leaving, and a curse tied to Indra's festival that is escaped only by unbroken observance, which is why the city's fate turns on the king's memory.
audit_text_issue: 24 line 66 (ஆங்குப் பதி அழிதலும் ஈங்குப் பதி கெடுதலும்) is hard to place.

note: Kural 920 groups double-minded women with drink and dice as the company of men Fortune has left; the queen turns the charge on the courtesan house itself, a life built on drink, lies, lust and deceit, and from which a courtesan's own daughter flees in fear.
teaches: The couplet sees the courtesan only as a danger to the man, while the epic shows the same house as a danger to the women born in it, so that renunciation is a courtesan's escape, not only a patron's.

gains.a: a short traditional judgment that frames the queen's list as the old ethical verdict on the courtesan's world
gains.b: a case from inside the courtesan's house, where the harm falls on its daughter, which the couplet's man-centred warning never considers

note: Kural 351 says a base birth comes from the confusion that takes the unreal as real; Aravanar puts ignorance first in the chain of birth and defines it as trusting hearsay that a hare has horns.
teaches: The couplet names unreal things taken as real without saying which; the epic gives the error a mechanism, hearsay preferred to what is seen, and a place, the first of twelve links, so the couplet's one step to birth becomes a chain.

gains.a: an older Tamil statement that ignorance is the root of birth, which shows the Buddhist chain speaking in a known idiom
gains.b: a definition of its மருள் by a stock example of an unreal thing (the hare's horn) and a causal sequence from error to birth

note: Tirumular nurtures the body because its perishing ends the life before true knowledge is won; when the queen wishes Aravanar's aged body long life, he answers that ageing and death are the nature of the born and turns to teaching.
teaches: The pair sets the Saiva siddha's body kept alive for knowledge against the Buddhist teacher's body let go because knowledge has been reached and must be passed on, so the worth of a long life depends on whether knowledge is still to be won.

gains.a: a contrary view that makes Aravanar's refusal of the blessing a position, not just an old man's modesty
gains.b: a teacher who has the knowledge and still declines the body's prolonging, which tests whether nurturing the body is a means or an end

note: Tirumular says those who give up killing, theft, lust and lying reach Siva's feet and its bliss; Aravanar counts the same sins among ten and says that leaving them, with precept and giving, wins only birth as god, human or Brahma.
teaches: The same abstentions are release in the Saiva verse and only a better birth in the Buddhist sermon, which places release in knowing the twelve links rather than in conduct; the pair shows that the two schools agree on the list and disagree on what it buys.

gains.a: a rival claim that abstaining from the great sins reaches the highest, which sharpens the epic's limit on what good deeds can do
gains.b: a finer count of the sins by body, speech and mind and a denial that abstention alone ends birth, against which its promise can be weighed

note: Aravanar tells Manimekalai that after she has heard the other doctrines he will teach her fully; in kaathai 27 she goes among the schools in Vanji and asks the Vedic logician his doctrine.
teaches: The survey of schools in kaathai 27 is set up here as a stage of instruction the teacher prescribes, so the rival doctrines are heard as preparation for the Buddhist teaching, not as free inquiry.

note: At Kannaki's shrine in Vanji the maid asks the pathini whether she has heard of Madhavi's and Manimekalai's renunciation; Manimekalai here resolves to go to Vanji and do good deeds for the great pathini.
teaches: The two epics meet at the Vanji shrine from both sides: the Silappathikaram brings news of the girl's renunciation to the pathini, and the Manimekalai sends the renounced girl to make merit for her.

note: Indra, to idle Aputhiran's bowl, sent rain until the land had no hungry; Aputhiran, reborn as Punniyarajan in the city of Indra's descendant, is a king since whose birth the rain has not failed.
teaches: The plenty that once mocked Aputhiran's charity by leaving no one to feed is now the sign of his merit as king, so the epic turns Indra's rival gift into the reward of the charity it tried to make useless.

note: Kural 545 says rain and harvest gather in the land of a king who rules by the sceptre; the ascetic credits Nagapuram's unfailing rain to Punniyarajan's birth, before any rule.
teaches: Where the couplet makes a land's rain the fruit of a king's just rule, the epic makes it the fruit of his former birth's charity, moving the cause of plenty from the sceptre to karma.

gains.a: the rule against which the ascetic's claim stands out as a claim about birth, not governance
gains.b: a case where the king's plenty precedes any act of rule, showing a second source of the link between king and rain that the couplet does not name

note: Aravana Adigal told Manimekalai that Aputhiran died with an unquenched purpose of sustaining lives and was born from a cow's womb to rule Savakam; here Manimekalai tells that king that, bewildered by wealth, he knows neither that birth nor the cow's womb of this one.
teaches: Rebirth carried Aputhiran's purpose into a king's body but not his knowledge of it, so the purpose has to be handed back to him by one who heard his story from outside.

note: Kural 335 urges good deeds before the hiccup stops the tongue; the sage of Kayankarai urges dharma before death that cannot be turned back (49 to 50), but adds that good deeds win only better births and that none escape birth except those who hear the coming Buddha.
teaches: The sermon separates what the couplet joins: haste in good deeds before death decides the next birth, but release waits on a teacher not yet come, so urgency to do good is not urgency to be free.

gains.a: a measure of what is shared Tamil ethics in the sermon, so that only its claim at 47 to 48 stands out as Buddhist doctrine
gains.b: a limit the couplet does not state: good deeds rushed to before death lead on to heaven or a human birth but do not end birth

note: In kaathai 9 the sage foretold that on the island seat she would know her birth and find his word clear; at her second visit Manimekalai says the sage's word of that day has come true today, after recalling his account of why the seat reveals births.
teaches: The second visit adds the ground of the seat's power, Indra's order made for the coming Buddha, so the fulfilment rests on the Buddha's future presence and not on the seat itself.

note: The king declares it good to renounce kingship wholly, crediting Manimekalai as the cause; Manimekalai, whose call woke him, sends him back to rule and tells him a king's dharma is food, clothing and shelter for all.
teaches: The epic of renunciation turns its heroine against a king's renunciation: the waking she causes is meant to make him a giver on a throne, not an ascetic, so renunciation is not the right end for everyone it moves.

note: Kural 545 says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who wields the sceptre rightly; the minister says rain returned to Savakam after twelve years when the king was born, before he wielded any sceptre.
teaches: The epic moves the cause of a land's plenty from the king's rule to his birth, that is, to merit carried from a former life of giving, so a king can bring rain before he governs at all.

gains.a: a Tamil rule that makes the minister's report a claim about kingship rather than a bare wonder
gains.b: a case its link between rain and right rule cannot explain: rain that follows a king's coming and precedes his rule

note: Puram 186 says the world lives not by rice or water but by its king, who must know he is its life; the minister tells the king that if he leaves, his land will cry like an infant whose mother is gone (110 to 111).
teaches: The Sangam duty that a king know himself the world's life becomes, in a Buddhist epic, the argument that holds a king back from renunciation, so the poem's maxim sets a limit even on seeking release.

gains.a: a Sangam warrant that makes the minister's plea a statement of a king's duty rather than a courtier's flattery
gains.b: an application the poem does not foresee: the king's being the world's life binds him against leaving it for a higher world

note: Kural 244 says one who sustains lives (மன்னுயிர் ஓம்பி) and holds to grace need fear no deed for his own life; the minister says the Buddha's dharma is not to pity one's own life and to protect other lives (பிற உயிர் ஓம்பும், 116), and charges the king with seeking a higher world for himself.
teaches: The couplet promises the protector of lives safety for his own; the minister makes indifference to one's own life the protector's mark, so a king's wish for his own release counts against his grace.

gains.a: a Tamil rule that makes protecting others' lives the core of grace, so the minister's appeal reads as more than Buddhist piety
gains.b: a reversal of its reward: in the epic the protector of lives is the one who does not seek safety for himself, not the one granted it

audit_text_issue: The unit opens mid-speech at line 115 (பெறுதி விரும்பினை).

note: Aravana Adigal told Manimekalai that Chintadevi gave Aputhiran the bowl on a rainy night saying it would not fail though the land did; the reborn king, his birth shown him by the seat, recalls the same night and the goddess's words almost word for word.
teaches: The teacher's story and the seat's revelation agree to the word, so the king's restored memory works in the epic as proof that the seat shows births truly.

note: Kural 327 says not to take another's life even at the cost of one's own; the island goddess tells Aputhiran that by starving he killed his own life and that the merchants who came back and died where he lay died for his sake, so that he is a killer.
teaches: The couplet treats giving up one's own life as a price that may be paid to avoid killing; the epic counts giving up one's own life as itself a killing, and one that draws others to die.

gains.a: a known Tamil rule against which the goddess's charge reads as a judgment about killing, not only grief for the dead
gains.b: a case its two lives cannot keep apart: one's own death that becomes the cause of others' deaths

note: Aravana Adigal told Aputhiran's death by fasting as a sun that sets in the west to rise again, with an unquenched purpose of sustaining lives; the island goddess calls the same death a killing of his own life that led others to kill theirs.
teaches: The epic gives two endorsed voices opposite verdicts on one death, the teacher's passage to a sustaining birth and the guardian's charge of killing, and leaves both standing beside the king who is its fruit.

note: Pathirakiriyar asks when he will see the bones within as white bones and himself lowered like a cast-off corpse; the king digs up his own former body, bones held together as if coated in white lime, and is bewildered.
teaches: The epic grants literally the sight the Siddhar longs for, one's own body as white bones, and shows that the sight alone does not free: the king is bewildered until Manimekalai tells him what it is for.

gains.a: a frame in which seeing one's own corpse is a discipline of release, against which the king's bewilderment is a failure to read it
gains.b: a test of its longing: the sight given in full, without the knowledge that would make it freeing

audit_text_issue: siddhar:23 line 2 is corrupt (போல்இ ழிந்து); manimekalai:25 lines 207-212 compressed

note: Puram 189 measures every man's need, king or hunter, by one measure of food and two cloths and concludes that wealth's use is giving; Manimekalai tells the king that dharma for all lives is nothing but food, clothing and shelter.
teaches: The Sangam measure of human need, used to tell a rich man to give, becomes the entire content of a king's dharma toward every life, and the king at once extends it to other kingdoms.

gains.a: a Sangam ground for reducing dharma to three material needs, so the definition reads as a measure of need and not a slight on doctrine
gains.b: a widening of its argument: what each person needs becomes what a king owes all lives, in his land and in others'

note: Madhavi lists what pathinis do when a husband dies (give up life in grief, enter the fire, or wear the body down in vows) and says Kannaki was of none of these kinds; Manimekalai, praying at the image, says her mother neither held to the debt of love nor took the way of penance but took on the debt of chastity.
teaches: The daughter repeats her mother Madhavi's typology in her own prayer, so that the family keeps Kannaki outside every ordinary path of the widow, and the next lines let Kannaki herself call the path she did take a sin.

note: Senguttuvan has the image of the pathini goddess carved from the Himalayan stone and installed in her shrine; the Manimekalai's shrine holds an image of both Kannaki and Kovalan, and the goddess in it speaks.
teaches: Where the Silappathikaram's royal shrine sets up Kannaki alone as a goddess of the realm, the Manimekalai makes the image a family one with the father beside her, fit for a daughter's prayer, which reshapes the cult toward the household the later epic cares about.

note: Both tell Neeli's curse and close it with the same words, உம்மை வினை வந்து உருத்தல்; the Silappathikaram adds that penance does not help the unrighteous when the old deed comes and calls Bharatan a vow-breaker, while the Manimekalai calls him a doer of evil work and Sangaman faultless.
teaches: The later epic keeps the karmic verdict word for word but moves it into Kannaki's own mouth and sharpens the contrast of guilty and faultless, so the explanation that consoled her in Madurai becomes in Vanchi her own testimony against her husband's former self.

note: The quatrain says an old deed seeks out its doer as a calf finds its own mother among many cows; Mathurapathi's word traces a killing done as Bharatan in Kalinga to Kovalan's death in Madurai, and says the former deed does not fail to come.
teaches: The pair shows how far the calf can walk: the quatrain gives the deed a homing instinct, and the epic gives it a road across a birth, a kingdom and a change of name, with a widow's curse as the means by which it finds Kovalan.

gains.a: the epic's account of a curse crossing births gains a plain maxim that explains why the curse cannot miss its man
gains.b: the quatrain's abstract seeking deed gains a named case with a route, an agent (Neeli's curse) and a distance of a whole lifetime

note: In the Silappathikaram Kannaki says she raged at the city as one without fault (சீறினேன் குற்றமிலேன்) and the fire god burns Madurai at her command; in the Manimekalai the same Kannaki says she destroyed the city in anger (சீற்றம் கொண்டு ... சிதைத்தேன்) and calls it the sin of murderous anger, whose fruit awaits her.
teaches: The two epics judge the same act in the same woman's words in opposite ways: the earlier makes the burning the faultless power of chastity, the later makes it a sinful deed that will ripen, and the conflict turns on whether provoked anger can be free of karmic fruit.

note: The couplet says anger left unguarded kills the one who holds it; Kannaki says her anger at Madurai, though it followed a just grievance, is a sin that will reach her after her heavenly merit ends.
teaches: Kannaki is the hardest case for the couplet, a woman whose anger an earlier epic praised as just, and the Manimekalai applies the rule to her anyway while stretching its reach across births: the self that anger kills is a future self, after heaven.

gains.a: Kannaki's confession gains a stated rule that anger turns on its holder, which explains why a goddess fears her own deed
gains.b: the couplet gains a test case of righteous anger and a time scale beyond one life, which its two lines do not give

note: The venba says gods worship the woman who worships her husband and that Kannaki has become the guest of the women of heaven; Kannaki here says she reached heaven by former good deeds and will leave it when that merit is spent.
teaches: The Manimekalai accepts the Silappathikaram's heavenly welcome for Kannaki but makes it a stay that ends, so the earlier epic's final honour becomes one stage of a samsaric account whose real end is still to come.

note: In the Silappathikaram Kannaki appears in the sky, declares the Pandya faultless and a guest in Indra's palace, and says she will not leave Murugan's hill; in the Manimekalai she foretells her own rebirth, her hearing of the Buddha and her release, while meanwhile working wonders for all.
teaches: The Buddhist epic does not deny the Pattini cult: it keeps Kannaki present and helpful as the earlier epic does, but makes that presence a long interval before a birth in which she must still hear the Buddha, so the goddess becomes a future disciple.

note: The couplet says only those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births; Kannaki, though a goddess in heaven, says she must swim the hard sea of births (40) until she hears the Buddha's dharma and leaves birth.
teaches: Read with the couplet, the epic shows that even a deified woman is still in the sea, and it names the means of crossing as hearing a teacher's dharma, which the couplet's 'Lord' leaves unnamed and which here replaces devotion with understanding.

gains.a: Kannaki's prophecy gains the Kural's image of the sea of births as the frame for her long passage to release
gains.b: the couplet's unnamed Lord gains a rival reading in which the crossing is made by hearing the Buddha's teaching, and in which gods too are swimmers

note: The Manimekala goddess foretold that Manimekalai would hear the false words of many schools and gave her the mantra to take another form because no one would tell a young girl the truth (79-80); here the same two lines are recalled and she chants the mantra and becomes an ascetic.
teaches: The disguise is set off by two voices together: the Manimekala goddess supplied the means long before, and Kannaki now supplies the order of study, so the Buddhist sea goddess and the Tamil pathini goddess both direct the girl to the debates.

note: The Silappathikaram tells how the stone for the pathini goddess, taken from the Himalaya, was set on the crowns of Kanaka and Vijaya and the goddess bathed in the Ganga; the Manimekalai names the same stone on the same crowns in a line of praise for Senguttuvan's city.
teaches: The stone that in the Silappathikaram makes Kannaki a goddess becomes in the Manimekalai a mark of the king's glory and the name of the city where Kannaki's daughter will learn that her mother's goddesshood is not release.

note: The preface to the Patitruppattu's fifth decade says Senguttuvan went through the forests to take a stone for the goddess Pattini, defeated the Aryan lord and bathed it in the Ganga; the Manimekalai names the stone, the Ganga crossing and the defeat of Kanaka and Vijaya.
teaches: The pair shows the stone-taking already fixed as the defining deed of this Chera in two different kinds of text, and shows the Manimekalai using that known deed only to date and dignify the city where its own Buddhist story continues.

gains.a: the epic's brief royal praise gains a second witness that its Senguttuvan is the Chera of the Sangam decade's preface
gains.b: the preface's one line on the Pattini stone gains the names of the defeated kings and the crowning detail that the epic tradition attached to it

note: The logician's perception grasps name, class, quality and action and sits among ten means; Aravanar's Buddhist logic keeps two means and takes name, class, quality and action out of perception.
teaches: The epic stages the theory of knowledge as a reply across two kaathais: what the Vedic logician packs into seeing, the Buddhist teacher moves into inference, so the dispute is over where conceptual labels enter knowledge.

note: Comparison, scripture, presumption and the rest are independent means for the logician; the Buddhist teacher folds all other means into inference.
teaches: Read together, the two lists show the Buddhist reduction is aimed at a named opponent: scripture's unseen worlds lose their standing as a separate source once they must be inferred.

note: The logician pairs the Buddhists with சினன் and with two means of knowledge; kaathai 29 has ஆதி சினேந்திரன் teaching exactly two.
teaches: The later kaathai confirms that சினன் in the list of schools names the Buddha, so the rival's account of Buddhism here is accurate on the count of means.
audit_text_issue: The pairing of schools, teachers and means in 78-85 depends on reading the three lists in parallel; the marker flagged the unit as uncertain. | Unit 57-85 flagged uncertain.

note: The logician files 'these are your parents', taken on another's word, as a false semblance of knowledge; Manimekalai offers knowing one's parents as an inference no one can refuse.
teaches: The chapter's opening list and its closing argument use the same example in opposite ways, so the heroine's rebuttal is also a correction of the logician's classification.

note: The Saiva debater defines God as the eight forms; Pattinathar reads the eight forms and Siva's other emblems as teachings, and mocks those who whirl in word and meaning.
teaches: Set beside the debate hall, Pattinathar's verse shows the Saiva poets turning the same eight-form creed from a debating thesis into a teaching the arguers fail to grasp.

gains.a: the Saiva's bare list gains a Saiva reading of what each form is meant to teach
gains.b: Pattinathar's scorn for word-proud disputants gains a scene of such disputants at work

note: Brahma-vadin, Vaishnava and Saiva each name a different maker or keeper; Tirumular says the three gods are one in continuity and that those who divide them quarrel.
teaches: Manimekalai rejects the theistic schools for disagreeing with truth, while Tirumular faults only their division, so the same sectarian quarrel is read as error by the Buddhist and as a misunderstanding by the Saiva.

gains.a: the epic's row of competing creators gains an insider's verdict that they need not compete
gains.b: Tirumular's 'those who divide quarrel' gains a staged instance of the quarrel he condemns

audit_text_issue: The unit is cut at 96, so the Saiva speaker the note counts falls outside it.

note: The Ajivika holds the elemental atoms to be without beginning; Sivavakkiyar says the elements and senses, and even the soul, are not beginningless, and only the truth mingled with them is.
teaches: The question of what is beginningless divides the two: for the Ajivika matter itself is eternal, for the Siddhar matter and soul are both made, and only the one truth is without beginning.

gains.a: the Ajivika claim gains a direct contrary from a later Tamil voice using the same word
gains.b: Sivavakkiyar's denial gains a named opponent who held the elements beginningless

note: The Ajivika says everything a life meets is fixed at conception by prior fate; the Kural says those who strive without flagging see fate's back.
teaches: Against the Ajivika's fixed course, the couplet's claim that effort can rout fate stands out as a deliberate limit on oozh, which the Kural elsewhere (380) calls the strongest power.

gains.a: the epic's rival doctrine of total fate gains the Tamil ethical tradition's answer
gains.b: the couplet gains a full statement of the fatalism it resists

note: Both end with the two deeds turned back; the Jain does it by blocking new deeds and exhausting old ones, Tirumular by keeping the Lord's feet in mind.
teaches: The pair shows Jain and Saiva agreeing that release needs both good and bad deeds stopped, and parting over whether the stopping is one's own labour or follows from holding the Lord.

gains.a: the Jain account gains a Saiva parallel that isolates what is distinctive in its godless method
gains.b: Tirumular's line on the two deeds gains a rival technique for the same end

note: The Sankhya speaker has space, wind, fire, water and earth unfold from intellect; Tirumular gives the same chain from மான் (mahat), in his chapter on creation.
teaches: The same sequence of elements serves the Sankhya as nature unfolding by itself and Tirumular as part of the Lord's creating, so the cosmology was shared while its cause was disputed.

gains.a: the Sankhya account gains a Tamil Saiva reuse of its sequence
gains.b: Tirumular's uncertain verse gains a fuller statement of the chain it compresses

audit_text_issue: Tirumanthiram 385 கான், தேன் are hard to fit and may be corrupt. | Tirumanthiram 385 flagged uncertain (கான், தேன்).

note: The Sankhya speaker counts twenty-five principles with no maker; Tirumular says the Lord makes the twenty-five within the womb.
teaches: Tirumular keeps the Sankhya count and adds a maker who shapes the twenty-five for each embryo, which is the step the Sankhya account leaves out.

gains.a: the count of twenty-five gains a later life inside Saiva doctrine
gains.b: Tirumular's twenty-five gains its source in a school that counted them without a god

audit_text_issue: Both ends flagged uncertain by the marker.

note: The materialist's awareness arising from the elements like intoxication from mixed ingredients appears in the Neelakesi's materialist as well.
teaches: Buddhist and Jain polemic both put the liquor simile in the materialist's mouth, which suggests it was the standard Tamil way to state his theory of mind.

note: The materialist makes awareness a product of the combined elements; Sivavakkiyar asks whether the dancing self is the five elements and answers with release into open space.
teaches: The tension depends on reading Sivavakkiyar's questions as rhetorical denials: the self that sees the house of release is not the elements, against the materialist for whom nothing survives their parting.

gains.a: the materialist's claim gains a Siddhar who puts the same question and answers it the other way
gains.b: Sivavakkiyar's question gains the explicit doctrine it rejects

note: The materialist calls knowledge of former births the delusion of possession or dream; in kaathai 9 Manimekalai, carried off by the deity in sleep, knew her former birth without error.
teaches: The materialist's objection names the very conditions of the heroine's own knowledge, so the epic's story stands as her unspoken answer to him.
audit_text_issue: Speakers of 278-283 are unnamed in the Tamil; the attribution is inferred.

note: In kaathai 26 she is told to hear each school's doctrine, see it lacks truth, and only then follow the Buddha's way, and she takes an ascetic's form to do so.
teaches: The debate chapter carries out a method laid down beforehand: hearing the schools is a prescribed stage of her training, not an open inquiry.

note: Here the materialist explains away dream and possession as the mind changed; the Neelakesi's Jain asks him how his elements account for dreams, mantras and omens.
teaches: The two epics use dream against the materialist in opposite directions: Manimekalai's opponent uses it to dismiss rebirth, Neelakesi uses it as evidence his elements cannot explain.

note: The Kural says the fivefold sense-knowledge is fruitless without true understanding; Manimekalai tells the materialist, who trusts the senses alone, that true things are hard to know without true understanding.
teaches: The couplet's general claim becomes a debating move: the heroine uses its contrast between sense-knowledge and true understanding to show that a perception-only rule cannot reach even one's parentage.

gains.a: Manimekalai's rebuttal gains a classical Tamil statement of the same limit on the senses
gains.b: the couplet gains a concrete opponent, the materialist, whom its limit refutes

note: Having heard the schools in an assumed form, she later tells Aravanar that the five kinds of religion are not right and she has not kept them in mind.
teaches: The closing line's 'she learned the five kinds of religion' is completed by her verdict in kaathai 29, which turns the survey into a rejection.

note: Manimekalai learns the five kinds of religion on her way to the Buddha's truth; Tirumular says those who saw the six sects did not see him.
teaches: Both texts make a survey of the sects a stage to pass through, but Manimekalai's ends in reasoned teaching and Tirumular's in clarity about a Lord the sects miss.

gains.a: the epic's tour of the schools gains a Saiva verdict on the same exercise
gains.b: Tirumular's dismissal of the sects gains a detailed record of what the sects said

note: Maadalan reports that Kovalan's father, grieving, gave great gifts and renounced in Puhar's Indra viharas before the sky-walkers; in the Manimekalai the same man, in a Vanji monastery likened to an Indra vihara of sky-walkers, gives his own reason.
teaches: The Silappathikaram tells his renunciation as a grief-driven act seen from outside; the sequel gives it from inside as doctrine, home as illusion and wealth and body as passing, so one renunciation is told first as a mourning and then as a conversion.

note: The quatrain has the best of people renounce home and wealth after slow reflection on impermanence; the ascetic renounces when the news of his son's death by evil deeds reaches him.
teaches: The pairing shows impermanence learned two ways: the quatrain's sage reasons his way to it, while the epic's merchant has it forced on him by bereavement and only then states it as the doctrine.

gains.a: the ascetic's turn gains a known ethical type, the renouncer who sees nothing stands, against which his grief-driven timing stands out
gains.b: the quatrain's unhurried reflection gains a case where the same insight comes suddenly, through a son's ruin

note: The Akananuru remembers Cheralathan who carved his bow on the Himalaya and heaped tribute at Maanthai; the epic's Chera of the carved bow feeds Buddhist sages in a Vanji grove. The Tamil shares only the epithet of the carved bow and the Chera line, not a name.
teaches: Holding them together shows the epic borrowing a Sangam conqueror's epithet to give Vanji's Buddhism a royal founder, turning the king remembered for hoarded tribute into a king remembered for a gift to monks.

gains.a: the nameless king of the epic gains a Sangam identity as the bow-carving conqueror, which the epic leaves unstated
gains.b: the poem's image of the conqueror's hoard gains a later legend in which the same line gives food rather than piles treasure

note: The Vanji ascetics foretell that the sea will take Kaveripattinam; in kaathai 25 the sea swallows it by the Manimekala goddess's curse and the ascetic and the mothers go to Vanji.
teaches: The flood of Puhar is given two causes in the epic, a prophecy the seers already knew and a goddess's curse on a negligent king, so foreknowledge and a moral cause sit together without either cancelling the other.

note: Kannaki's image says the two went to the gods by former good deeds, the evil deed will still come, and they will wander until the Buddha appears at Kapilai; the Vanji seers foretell the same and add that Kovalan's merit came from austerity under an earlier Buddha's Bodhi.
teaches: The second witness confirms the first and supplies its missing cause, so the couple's heaven is traced to a past Buddhist austerity, not to Kannaki's chastity alone.
audit_text_issue: manimekalai:28:141-142 compressed and line 148 overlong (may join two lines)

note: The Silappathikaram ends Kannaki's story with her ascent in the gods' car with Kovalan; the Manimekalai says that this heaven only defers the evil deed, and that release waits for the Buddha at Kapilai.
teaches: Read together, the apotheosis that closes the first epic becomes a way station in the second: a Buddhist sequel re-reads the pathini's reward as a heaven still bound by deeds.
audit_text_issue: Mani 28 lines 141-142 are compressed, and line 148 is overlong.

note: Both hold that heaven belongs to the round of deeds; Tirumular frees the soul from heaven, hell and earth by grace, while the seers have Kovalan freed by hearing the Buddha's dharma after he has eaten his deed.
teaches: The two agree that heaven is no escape from karma and part exactly on the way out: Saiva release is given by grace, while the Buddhist release comes after the deed is spent and the teaching heard, with no giver.

gains.a: the seers' prophecy gains a rival account of release that makes plain it involves no god
gains.b: Tirumular's verse gains a named case, Kovalan in heaven still owing his deed, of the soul turned through heaven by karma

audit_text_issue: Tirumanthiram 2313's அறங்காண் and கிரங்கா are unclear

note: The couplet says that without rain neither giving nor austerity lasts; the ascetic reports that Kanchi's ascetics, finding no almsgivers in the drought, have left for Vanji.
teaches: The epic shows the couplet's rule as a chain: the drought ends giving first, and austerity, which lives on gifts, then has to leave the land.

gains.a: the monks' migration gains a stated principle that explains why drought drives out ascetics
gains.b: the couplet gains the mechanism it leaves implicit, that austerity fails because giving fails

note: Thuvathikan foretold the drought in Kanchi and that she would bring rain there with the bowl; Kovalan's father now gives the same charge and asks whether she did not learn it from Thuvathikan.
teaches: A goddess's foretelling becomes a human teacher's command, so her mission to Kanchi rests on two witnesses, one divine and one from her own family.

note: The couplet says the sky withholds rain when the king bends justice; the Kanchi king names the bent sceptre as only one of three possible causes and cannot tell which holds.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's law into a king's anxious self-examination, and then sets it aside: the deity names no fault and sends a renunciant's bowl instead of a reform of rule.

gains.a: the king's question gains its source, the received rule that ties rain to the sceptre
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where the rule cannot be applied, since the drought comes and the ruler cannot find his fault

note: The couplet gives the chaste wife power to bid rain fall; the king asks whether failed chastity among women withheld it.
teaches: The pair shows the couplet's power run in reverse: if a wife's chastity can command rain, the community's women can be suspected when it fails, and the epic records the suspicion without confirming it.

gains.a: the king's third cause gains the couplet's claim that underlies it
gains.b: the couplet gains its darker corollary, that drought can be laid at women's door

note: In Puhar Aravanar asks whether Indra or the king of the just sceptre is at fault for the famine, in the words அலத்தல்காலை ஆகியது; the Kanchi king uses the same words about his own land and adds women's chastity.
teaches: The question first put by the teacher about another's kingdom is put by a king about himself, and both times the epic's answer is the bowl, not a judgment on the ruler.

note: In Puhar she appears with the bowl like a rain cloud over a scorched bamboo forest; in Kanchi the chamberlain says she has come like a great rain cloud.
teaches: The simile becomes literal: in Puhar the cloud is only food for the hungry, while in Kanchi her coming brings real rain to a land in drought.

note: On Manipallavam the bowl rises from the Gomukhi pool before the Buddha's seat once a year into a fit hand; in Kanchi the king builds a copy of the pool and seat and she sets the bowl on it for all beings.
teaches: The holy island is reproduced in a royal city, and the bowl that came out of it to one worthy hand is now placed on the copy of the seat and offered to everyone.

note: The couplet asks whether the host who feeds guests need even sow his field; the epic likens the bowl's plenty to alms in ascetics' hands and to seed sown with the right water, soil, season and tools.
teaches: Both make feeding others a kind of sowing, but the couplet promises the giver's field yields unsown, while the epic makes the yield depend on conditions, the worth of the receiver among them.

gains.a: the epic's image gains a contrast that shows how conditional its sowing is
gains.b: the couplet's unconditional promise gains a rival view in which a gift's fruit depends on where and how it is sown

note: Thuvathikan foretold that her bowl of dharma would give rain's plenty to a parched world; here the bowl feeds Kanchi and the rain returns.
teaches: The fulfilment shows the epic treating feeding as the cause of rain, reversing the usual order in which rain must come before there is food to give.
audit_text_issue: வசித் தொழில் (28.233) is a rare word whose reading as rain's work is not certain

note: Aravanar, in Thuvathikan's foretelling, blesses her with வாய்வதாக நின் மனப்பாட்டு அறம்; at Kanchi she says it of herself, வாய்வது ஆக என் மனப்பாட்டு அறம்.
teaches: The teacher's blessing becomes the pupil's own vow in the same words, marking the point where she stops being foretold and begins to will her path.

note: The Chera king washes the charanas' feet and serves them six-flavoured food of four kinds; Manimekalai washes Aravanar's feet and serves the same.
teaches: The lay gift that founded Buddhism in Vanji is repeated by Manimekalai in Kanchi, so her entry into the order is staged as the same act of royal hospitality to monks.
audit_text_issue: Unit 101-119 ends mid-sentence at பிறப்பின் துன்பமும் பிறவா இன்பமும்.

note: Kaathai 1 has the assembled sages warn that if the festival is forgotten the guardian spirit will bring harm; here a king searching for his lost son forgets the festival, and the curse follows.
teaches: The warning of the first kaathai turns out to name the cause of Puhar's end, and the lapse comes not from neglect but from a father's grief, so the city falls through the king's love rather than his vice.

note: In kaathai 7 the goddess says Kovalan named the child after her and that she told Madhavi in a dream that the child would be a great ascetic; here Aravanar gives the reason for the naming, the goddess's rescue of the Bodhisattva ancestor.
teaches: Read together, the name Manimekalai is a debt of the family line to a goddess who serves a future Buddha, so the renunciation foretold at her birth is the line's old bond coming due.

note: The goddess foretold that Manimekalai would hear the false teachings of many schools and gave her the mantra to take another form; here Manimekalai reports having heard them so, in Vanji.
teaches: The tour of the schools in kaathai 27 was a prescribed stage, not a chance encounter: the goddess set it up so that Manimekalai would reject the schools herself before the teacher speaks.

note: Both turn from the noise of the schools to a teacher; Arunagiri asks Murugan for an upadesam and a vision past the logicians' quarrel, while Manimekalai's teacher answers with the rules of valid argument.
teaches: The pair shows two answers to the same fatigue with the schools: the Buddhist epic trains the hearer to argue rightly, the Saiva hymn asks to be lifted beyond argument by grace, and the tension holds as long as the logic is read as a path and not only as a tool.

gains.a: the epic unit gains a contrast showing that its turn to a teacher leads into more reasoning, not out of it
gains.b: the hymn's list of quarrelling schools gains a case where one of those schools, the Buddhist, is seen from inside, offering method rather than clamour

note: The couplet makes understanding the power to find the true substance in whatever one hears from anyone; Manimekalai has heard every school and judged them wanting, but asks a teacher for the true doctrine.
teaches: The epic shows the limit of the couplet's test: a hearer can reject what she hears from many mouths and still lack the means to find the truth, so the teacher gives her a method of knowing rather than an answer.

gains.a: Manimekalai's refusal of the schools gains a general standard by which her judgment is measured
gains.b: the couplet gains a case showing that discernment can stop at rejection, and needs the means of knowledge to go further

note: The couplet bids one see the true thing whatever nature (தன்மை) a thing appears to have; the Buddhist teacher strips perception of name, class, quality and action and assigns them to inference.
teaches: On the Buddhist account the 'nature' the couplet looks past is largely the mind's own labelling, so seeing the true thing becomes a matter of separating bare perception from what inference adds.

gains.a: the technical definition of perception gains a moral aim: the true thing the couplet calls understanding
gains.b: the couplet's open word தன்மை gains one precise reading, as the class, quality and name the mind lays on what it sees

note: Aravanar told her that she would not take up the teaching until the events caused by her had come to pass; now, after the prison, Aputhiran's land and the tour of the schools, she asks him for it.
teaches: The long middle of the epic is framed as the waiting time Aravanar named, and her request now marks that the conditions he set have been met.

note: Tirumular says the wise gave up logic and debate (தர்க்க வாதம்), recited the Veda and gained release; the Buddhist teacher folds scripture into inference and makes logic the first part of the true doctrine.
teaches: The two disagree on the same question, whether scripture stands as its own source of truth above argument, and the Buddhist answer explains why the epic's road to release passes through debate rules that the Saiva verse tells the wise to leave behind.

gains.a: the epic's quiet reduction of all other means to inference gains a clear statement of the position it denies
gains.b: the verse's dismissal of தர்க்க வாதம் gains a concrete instance of the logic it dismisses, taught as a path to release

note: The couplet says that taking what is not a thing for a thing breeds an unworthy birth; the teacher gives a test for absence, that a thing which exists appears like a gooseberry in the hand, and the hare's horn does not.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's warning into a procedure: what would appear if it were there and does not appear may be judged absent, which gives the confusion the couplet fears a check in method.

gains.a: the logic of non-appearance gains a moral stake, since the couplet ties the error it guards against to rebirth
gains.b: the couplet's மருள் gains a means of correction, a rule for deciding what is not there

note: The Vedic logician listed false appearances of knowing (shell for silver, post or man); the Buddhist teacher lists false theses, reasons and examples.
teaches: Set side by side, the two lists show the Buddhist teacher moving error from the senses to argument: what goes wrong is less a mistaken seeing than a thesis put in terms the other side cannot grant.

note: In kaathai 27 the Sankhya speaker describes the person as awareness itself; here 'the soul has consciousness' is the stock example of a thesis whose subject a Buddhist does not accept.
teaches: The doctrine Manimekalai heard laid out without reply in kaathai 27 returns as a lesson in debate, answered not by a counter-argument but by the rule that a debater cannot assume a soul his opponent denies.

note: The quatrain mocks debaters who do not know how to make what they learned reach the hearer; the teacher's false theses are exactly theses that cannot reach the hearer, because he does not grant their terms or already holds the conclusion.
teaches: The epic gives the quatrain's complaint a precise form: an argument fails not only by poor delivery but when its subject or conclusion is foreign or already granted to the one it is aimed at.

gains.a: the technical rules gain an ethical frame, as the duty of a speaker to the one he addresses
gains.b: the quatrain's 'not knowing how to make it reach' gains named cases showing what such a failure is

note: The Sankhya speaker of kaathai 27 tells every stage of the world as வெளிப்பட்டு, becoming manifest; here 'because it is produced' is a reason a Sankhya does not accept, since for him things are manifested, not produced.
teaches: The pairing shows that the epic's logic lesson is built on the doctrines Manimekalai heard in Vanji, so the account of the schools in kaathai 27 is accurate enough to be used as the test case here.

note: The Vaisheshika of kaathai 27 counts space among the nine substances and sound among the qualities; here 'space is a substance by its quality of sound' is a thesis whose subject an opponent may deny.
teaches: The doctrine stated as settled fact in kaathai 27 is shown here to rest on a subject not every school grants, so the teacher answers the Vaisheshika by the form of debate rather than by contrary doctrine.
audit_text_issue: 27 line 249 gives earth sound among its qualities, an oddity in the account.

note: Kaathai 27's Sankhya speaker gives the person as one, pervading and eternal awareness; here the argument for that person from the senses serving another is shown to prove a composite self.
teaches: The epic answers the Sankhya two kaathais later without denying it outright: its own proof for a partless self, followed through, yields a self with parts, so the refutation is internal.

note: The Vaisheshika says generality gives being (உண்மை) to substance, quality and action; here the argument that being is other than substance, quality and action is shown to make being nothing.
teaches: Read together, the units show the Buddhist teacher taking the Vaisheshika's own words for being and showing that its category, argued as the Vaisheshika argues it, empties itself.
audit_text_issue: Lines 321-325 of manimekalai:29 are compressed and the sense of கருத்தாவுடைய கிரியையும் குணமும் is uncertain.

note: The Vaisheshika counts space among the nine substances; the teacher judges examples built on space under both views, that it is a thing and that it is not.
teaches: The pairing shows the logic lesson deliberately leaving the schools' quarrel over space unsettled: a proof is faulted on either view, so the method does not depend on deciding the rival's ontology.
audit_text_issue: manimekalai:29 lines 443-444 look corrupt (missing negative; அன்ன்று)

note: The Vedic logician lists eight false semblances of knowledge, errors of seeing and remembering; the Buddhist teacher ends with the semblances of inference, errors in a stated proof.
teaches: The two catalogues of error divide the ground differently: the logician locates falsehood in a mistaken cognition, the Buddhist teacher in a badly built argument, which can be checked rule by rule.
audit_text_issue: Line 29:463 (என்றால் என்று நின்ற இடத்து) reads awkwardly and may be corrupt.

note: The Kural says that a mind which examines (ஓர்த்து) and knows what is with certainty (ஒருதலையா) need not think of birth again; Aravanar closes with examine (ஆய்ந்து) and know without doubt (ஐயம் இன்றி).
teaches: The couplet names examination and certainty as the way out of birth but gives no procedure; the epic supplies one, and its technical word for certainty, ஏகாந்தம், is the couplet's ஒருதலை in Sanskrit dress.

gains.a: the fallacy list gains a stated end beyond winning debates, the certainty the Kural ties to release
gains.b: the couplet's bare 'examine and be certain' gains tests for when an argument has earned certainty

note: Tirumular says the wise gave up logic and disputation (தர்க்க வாதம்) and gained release by reciting the Veda; Aravanar, who folds scripture into inference, ends his teaching of dharma with the rules of disputation.
teaches: The two give opposite answers to whether argument leads toward release: for Tirumular it is what the wise leave behind, for the Buddhist teacher it is the discipline that sorts true from false before doctrine is heard.

gains.a: the epic's logic lesson gains a named Saiva rejection of the very method it teaches
gains.b: Tirumular's dismissal of argument gains a full example of the argument he dismisses, from a school that grants the Veda no separate authority

note: The Kural promises the sky to those who have left doubt and become clear; the teacher describes two sound-looking proofs of opposite theses that together leave only doubt (சங்கயம்).
teaches: The epic shows a doubt that more argument cannot remove, since each side's reasoning holds, so the clarity the couplet praises cannot come from matching proofs alone.

gains.a: the stalemate fallacy gains its stake: doubt is what the Kural says bars the way to the sky
gains.b: the couplet's 'leaving doubt' gains a precise case of doubt that reasoning itself produces

note: The Kural calls taking what does not last for what lasts the lowest understanding; Aravanar's model rule is 'whatever is made is impermanent', valid only in that direction.
teaches: Set beside the couplet, the textbook rule shows impermanence as something proved from being made, with the warning that the converse fails, so knowing the passing is a matter of inference as well as of seeing.

gains.a: the stock example gains the moral weight the Kural gives to knowing impermanence
gains.b: the couplet's demand to see the passing as passing gains a stated form of proof and its limit

note: Arunagirinathar lumps Buddhists with the followers of Kapila and Kanada as clamouring disputants whose books cannot give the teaching; here a Buddhist teacher takes apart arguments of the Sankhya and the Vaisheshika by formal logic.
teaches: The pair shows the same quarrel from inside and outside: what the devotee hears as noise of books, the epic presents as a disciplined refutation, and it is the Buddhist the devotee counts first among the noisy.

gains.a: the epic's refutation gains a later Saiva verdict that its whole contest misses the point
gains.b: the song's list of disputants gains a working example of how those schools actually argued against each other

note: The goddess hails Manimekalai for recovering her former birth at the Buddha's seat; here that knowledge of the former birth, in which she held to giving and the precepts, is what she brings to her taking of refuge.
teaches: Read together, the two show that the memory of a former birth is not the end of her awakening but its qualification: what she recovered on Manipallavam is cashed here as the two practices that make her fit to take refuge and hear the doctrine.

note: Aravanar told her that events would happen in the town because of her and that only after they had happened would she take up the teaching; the last lines show her hearing dharma and vowing to end becoming.
teaches: The pairing shows that the epic frames its whole middle, from the prison to the debates of Vanji, as a foretold delay, so that this lesson fulfils a prophecy made eighteen kaathais earlier rather than starting a new episode.

note: The Ajivika says all gain, loss, pleasure, pain, birth and death are fixed at conception by fate laid down before; the teacher says the chain has no fixed fate (ஊழ்பாடு இன்றி) and runs by conditions that can be reversed.
teaches: Kaathai 27 leaves the Ajivika's fixed fate unanswered, and this line supplies the Buddhist reply: the same goods and ills are conditioned links, so cutting a condition can stop them, which fixed fate rules out. The tension depends on reading ஊழ்பாடு as fixed fate.

note: The Brahma-vadin says the world is an egg laid by one god; the teacher says the chain is made by no maker and is not a made thing (பண்ணுநர் இன்றிப் பண்ணப் படாதாய்).
teaches: The pairing shows that the creator Manimekalai dismissed without argument in Vanji is excluded here by the structure of the doctrine itself, since a chain in which each link supports the next leaves no place for a maker outside it.

note: The Sankhya speaker holds the person to be the one eternal awareness that knows all; the teacher says no thing has a self and makes awareness (உணர்வு) a link conditioned by action.
teaches: Held together they show where the Buddhist answer to Sankhya lies: not in denying awareness but in making it the third link of a chain, born of action and ceasing with it, so the eternal knower of kaathai 27 is answered three kaathais later.

note: The Kural says a joyless birth comes from the confusion that takes what is not real as real; the teacher names ignorance first of twelve links that end in birth and defines it as holding hearsay clear, as that a hare has horns.
teaches: The pairing shows that the Kural's மருள் can be given a precise epistemic fault, trusting report over what has been established, and that for the Buddhist teacher this confusion reaches birth only through ten links between, which the couplet's direct cause compresses.

gains.a: a Tamil ethical precedent that already makes confusion about the real the cause of birth, so the first link reads as more than a Buddhist technicality
gains.b: a concrete instance of the unreal taken as real, the hare's horn believed on hearsay, where the couplet names no example

note: The Kural calls craving the seed that gives unceasing births to all beings; in the chain craving (வேட்கை) gives clinging, karma and birth, but itself arises from feeling and contact and ceases only when ignorance ceases.
teaches: Both make craving the seed of birth, but the chain gives the seed its own seed: craving depends on feeling and, eleven steps back, on ignorance, so the Buddhist cure begins with knowledge where the Kural's chapter begins with cutting craving.

gains.a: evidence that the Tamil ethical tradition placed craving, not ignorance, at the root, which shows the chain's order as a doctrinal choice
gains.b: an account of where craving comes from and how it is stopped, which the couplet's image of the seed leaves out

note: The Kural says pain perishes when the very names of desire, anger and delusion perish; the teacher names the same three, in the same order, as the cause of all he has taught and gives a separate remedy for each.
teaches: The Kural names the three roots and promises the end of pain but gives no method; the epic, using the same three words, assigns each root its own discipline, contemplation of impermanence for desire, friendliness for anger, hearing and reflection for delusion.

gains.a: the Kural's claim that pain ends wholly when even the names of the three go, a stronger end-state than the remedies alone state
gains.b: a separate practice for each of the three, where the couplet says only that they must perish

note: The teacher says bondage and release have their own causes and no one exists to grant them; Tirumular says grace put the soul into bonds and grace gives release.
teaches: The two name the same pair, bondage and release, and give opposite answers to who brings them about: the epic denies any giver, and Tirumular makes one grace the giver of both, so the Buddhist and Saiva accounts of release divide exactly at line 251.

gains.a: a named rival position, a giver of both bondage and release, that line 251's denial excludes
gains.b: a counter-position that shows Tirumular's claim that binding itself is grace is the very claim a causal account without a giver rejects

audit_text_issue: Tirumanthiram 1802 line 4 is compressed; the link rests on lines 1-3, which are clear.

note: The teacher's ten bad deeds include killing, theft, lust and lying, as Tirumular's yama does, but the epic sorts them by body, speech and mind and counts coveting, anger and wrong view as deeds, while Tirumular adds sharing food and shunning drink.
teaches: Set side by side, the two lists of ten show the same core abstentions serving different ends: for the epic they decide the next birth, for Tirumular they are the first step of yoga toward Siva, and only the epic counts states of mind as deeds.

gains.a: a Saiva counterpart showing the same abstentions used as the first limb of yoga rather than as the ledger of rebirth
gains.b: the epic's body, speech and mind sorting, which shows that the yama list has no item for coveting or wrong view

note: Naladiyar says craving enters by five gates, body, mouth, eyes, nose and ears, and whoever guards them reaches release; the teacher counts six gates, with the mind among them, and places craving three links after the gates.
teaches: The pairing shows two models of the senses: the quatrain makes the five gates the entry of craving and guarding them the path, while the chain adds the mind as a sixth gate and puts contact and feeling between gate and craving, so guarding the gates is not where the chain is cut.

gains.a: an ethical practice of guarding the gates that the chain's definitions do not state
gains.b: the mind as a sixth gate and the steps between sense and craving, which the quatrain's five gates leave out

note: The Kural says griefs keep hold of those who keep hold of attachment; the teacher's truths say sorrow is caused by birth and clinging, and release, which is joy, by not clinging.
teaches: The Kural's one-verb picture of grip and grief becomes the second truth, and the epic adds its mirror, release as joy caused by not clinging, so the couplet's warning is shown to be half of a four-part formula.

gains.a: a Tamil saying in which the grip one keeps and the grip of sorrow are one act, which the formula's dry causal statement lacks
gains.b: the positive half the couplet omits: that not clinging is the cause of release, named as joy

note: The kuravar's report of a one-breasted woman taken to heaven under a flowering vengai by the retinue of the king of the gods is the event the Katturai Kaathai narrates at its close, where Kannaki climbs the hill, stands under the vengai and boards the heavenly car with Kovalan.
teaches: The patikam gives the ascent as seen by strangers who call it a wonder, while the kaathai gives it from inside, with Kannaki naming herself one who did the deed of fire, so the pair shows the poem framing as a marvel what its heroine felt as guilt.

note: The goldsmith names Kovalan the thief (கள்வன்) of the anklet; in the Vazhakkurai Kaathai the king, seeing the gem fly from the broken anklet, says that he, who heard the goldsmith, is the thief (யானே கள்வன்).
teaches: The word thief passes in the course of the poem from the accused stranger to the goldsmith's own hidden act and finally to the king's mouth about himself, so the patikam's first accusation is set up to be reversed by the one who acted on it.

note: The patikam says the Pandya did not inquire because the time of the deed's ripening had come; Kannaki addresses him as தேரா மன்னா, the king who did not inquire, and says ஊழ்வினை drove her husband to Madurai.
teaches: The patikam makes karma the reason the king failed to inquire, but Kannaki uses that failure as her charge against him while giving karma only as what brought Kovalan to the city, so the epic keeps karma and royal fault as two causes and assigns blame only to the second.

note: The couplet says a ruler who does not examine (ஓரா) and do justice falls by himself; the patikam has the Pandya fail to examine (தேரானாகி) and fall, but says he failed because the time of the deed's ripening had come.
teaches: The couplet treats the failure to examine as the king's own fault and the ruin as its consequence, and the epic keeps the consequence but places the failure itself inside a karmic order, which raises the question the couplet does not face of how a fated lapse can still be the king's guilt.

gains.a: the epic's double cause gains a precise rule from outside the story against which the king's lapse is a fault in law and not only a misfortune
gains.b: the couplet gains a test case in which the lapse it condemns is said to have been brought on by a past deed, so its self-caused ruin is shown with a second cause behind it

note: The couplet says the wife who worships her husband rather than a god commands the rain; the patikam says that because Kannaki was a pathini she burned Madurai and brought down its king.
teaches: The power the couplet gives the devoted wife is a blessing on the world through rain, and the epic turns the same power into fire against a city once her husband is wronged, so the pair shows the chaste wife's word as a force that can destroy as well as nourish.

gains.a: Kannaki's burning of the city gains a source in the ethics book's claim that a wife's devotion commands nature
gains.b: the couplet's promise gains its dark counterpart: the same command over nature used for punishment, which the couplet's rain never suggests

note: The patikam names only the curse of Sangaman's wife from a former birth; the Katturai Kaathai tells that Kovalan, then Bharatan, a king's servant, seized Sangaman as a spy and had him killed, and that his widow Nili, finding no refuge, cried for justice.
teaches: Read together, the curse is seen to repeat its cause exactly: a merchant falsely taken and killed by royal order, a wife left with no ground to stand on, so Kovalan's death mirrors the one he caused and Kannaki's lament repeats Nili's.

note: The quatrain says an old deed finds its doer as a calf finds its mother among many cows; the patikam has a deed of a former birth in Singapuram find Kovalan in Madurai, and says it has run its course for both of them (நுங்கட்கு).
teaches: The quatrain's deed seeks the one who did it, but the epic's curse reaches across a birth and a country through the word of the victim's widow and falls on the doer's wife as well, so the pair shows the epic widening the quatrain's single doer into a household.

gains.a: Saathan's report gains a general law stated without story, that a past deed actively seeks its doer, which makes the goddess's word an instance and not a private verdict
gains.b: the quatrain gains a case showing how the seeking works, through a curse spoken by another, and that it can fall on one who did not do the deed

note: The patikam's first moral is that dharma becomes death to those who err in kingship; the first venba after the Pandya's death calls this the saying of many assemblies, that dharma is death to wrongdoers, and turns it on the queen as well.
teaches: The patikam narrows the saying to kings and claims it as the poem's own thesis, while the venba gives it back to common opinion and extends it to the queen who dies with the king, so the pair shows the poem's moral both resting on a proverb and making it a rule of kingship.

note: The couplet says nothing is stronger than ஊழ், which arrives first even when one devises (சூழினும்) another way; the patikam says the ஊழ்வினை comes in wrath and makes one eat it, through the finely made (சூழ்வினை) anklet.
teaches: The couplet's fate outruns any plan, and the epic gives the plan a body: the anklet Kovalan meant to sell to start life again becomes the instrument of the fate it was meant to escape, and the epic adds that fate comes in anger and feeds its fruit, which the couplet does not say.

gains.a: the epic's moral gains a sharper claim about scheming, that devising against fate is itself overtaken, which explains why Kovalan's fresh start ends in his death
gains.b: the couplet's abstract race between fate and plan gains a concrete object, the anklet, and an emotional colour, the wrath of the returning deed

audit_text_issue: The marker flags uncertainty about who speaks 55-60; the link does not depend on it.

note: The patikam states as a thesis that the deed of the past comes in wrath and makes one eat it; the Tirumanthiram says that by Siva's grace deeds do not cling (வினை சேரகிலாமை).
teaches: If the patikam's line is read as admitting no release, the two give incompatible accounts of whether a past deed must be eaten, and the epic offers no grace that could stop it, since even the gods appear only to honour Kannaki after the deed has run its course; the Tirumanthiram puts grace before the fruit.

gains.a: the epic's moral gains its sharpest contrast, which shows that its karma is unmediated: no god in the patikam intervenes before the fruit
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's claim gains a rival from the same language and land in which deeds do cling and must be eaten, so its grace is seen as an answer to a live view

note: The benediction likens the Chola's bounty to the rain pouring from above; the couplet makes rain itself depend on the king's not bending justice.
teaches: Read against the couplet, the opening simile of rain and royal grace is not mere flattery but the old belief that the sky's giving follows the king's justice, which the epic will put to the test when a Pandya's crooked verdict brings fire rather than rain on his city.

gains.a: the simile gains a causal ground: rain and royal grace are linked because a just king's realm is the one the sky waters
gains.b: the couplet's rule gains a ceremonial setting, sung at a wedding as praise rather than stated as a warning

note: Both see the king's white umbrella as the moon; the benediction praises the moon for resembling the Chola's sheltering umbrella, the quatrain says every king under such an umbrella has been carried off as dead.
teaches: The same moon-umbrella serves the epic's opening as a sign of rule that shelters the world and serves the Naladiyar as proof that such rule ends, so the pair shows the epic beginning in the confidence the ethics book was written to undercut.

gains.a: the hymn's royal moon gains a shadow: the image it uses for lasting shelter is the Naladiyar's stock image of the king who dies
gains.b: the quatrain's umbrella gains an instance of the praise it answers, the court poet's moon that is meant to outlast the king

note: The epic opens saying the learned speak of Puhar only as standing unshaken, never of its decline; the Manimekalai tells how the city was swallowed by the sea when the Indra festival was neglected and Manimekala Deivam cursed it.
teaches: Taken together, the two epics make the city whose permanence the wise affirm at the first wedding the city the sea takes in the next generation, so the opening's confidence becomes the first instance of the impermanence the sequel preaches.

note: Kovalan's father is introduced as the master of great wealth who pours out his riches for others; in the Manimekalai Manimekalai finds him in a Buddhist monastery (பள்ளி) as one who has taken up great austerity (மா தவம்).
teaches: The merchant whose giving is praised at his son's wedding ends as a renouncer, so the pair traces in one man the passage from the householder's generosity to the renunciation the Manimekalai holds higher.

note: The wedding women bless Kannaki never to be parted from her lover nor loosen her embrace; two kaathais later Kovalan buys Madhavi's garland, cannot leave her and forgets his home.
teaches: The blessing names the very loss the story brings within two kaathais, so the wedding song works as an unknowing forecast, and the separation reads as a reversal of a rite performed with fire and Veda.

note: The couplet asks whether the lotus-eyed god's world is sweeter than sleep on the beloved's soft arms; the epic likens the newly married couple to those who enjoy in Uttarakuru the fruit of completed austerity.
teaches: Both weigh a couple's joy against a heavenly world, but the couplet ranks love above heaven while the epic makes the couple's joy itself a heaven earned by past austerity, and so something that can be used up, which is how the epic prepares its turn from pleasure to karma.

gains.a: the epic's simile gains a contrast: love here is not set above heaven but counted as heaven's wage, a measure of merit rather than a rival to it
gains.b: the couplet's rhetorical question gains an answer it does not give, that the beloved's arms may be a heaven only for as long as the merit behind them lasts

note: The couplet says the woman who wore anicham flowers with their stems will hear no good drums for her waist; Kovalan asks why her attendants loaded her with garland, musk and pearls, making her small waist suffer.
teaches: The epic takes the Kural's single joke of a waist too fine to bear flowers and spreads it over a whole toilette, moving the lover's praise from the secret meeting into the marriage chamber, where it is the husband who speaks it and the maids who are blamed.

gains.a: Kovalan's catalogue gains a known convention behind it, so its reproach of the attendants reads as praise in the established form of நலம்புனைந்துரைத்தல்
gains.b: the couplet gains a speaker and setting it lacks, a husband in the first days of marriage, showing the convention used outside the lovers' secret union

note: The elder lady sets Kannaki up in a household for charity and the hosting of guests; in Madurai Kannaki says she has lost giving to the virtuous, tending Brahmins, receiving ascetics and welcoming guests.
teaches: The household the second kaathai founds for its charity and hospitality is named, duty by duty, as what Kannaki has lost, so the pair shows her grief in Madurai as the loss of a household's dharma, not only of a husband's company.

note: In the bridal chamber Kovalan calls Kannaki gold and doll (பொன்னே, பாவாய்) for her beauty; in Madurai, after she has followed him, he calls her gold, creeper and doll of modesty for the steadfastness that brought her with him.
teaches: The same endearments return with a new ground: the words that praised her body in the chamber praise her chastity and endurance on the road, so the pair traces Kovalan's turn from admiring Kannaki's beauty to recognising her virtue.

note: The couplet says all of keeping a house is for tending guests and doing good; the epic's household is set up so that its charity and hospitality may be seen, and the story later takes both away.
teaches: The epic founds Kannaki's household on exactly the couplet's purpose, then lets a husband's absence and exile empty it, showing that the householder's dharma the couplet assigns to the house depends on the pair staying in it.

gains.a: the narrator's brief line on the household's purpose gains the weight of a stated rule, so its later loss reads as the loss of the household's whole reason
gains.b: the couplet's rule gains a case of its failure: a wife ready to keep it who cannot once her husband leaves the house

note: The quatrain mocks one who sees a corpse carried to the burning ground yet marries and thinks there is joy here; the venba says the newly married couple enjoyed every pleasure like people who had seen the world's impermanence.
teaches: The same knowledge that nothing on earth lasts is, for the Naladiyar, a reason to give up marriage and its joys and, in the epic's venba, a reason to take them while they last, so the pair sets out the two lessons impermanence can teach.

gains.a: the venba's last line gains a rival reading of its own premise, so its haste for pleasure is seen as a choice the ethics book condemns
gains.b: the quatrain gains the voice it argues against: not a fool blind to death but lovers who claim to have seen it and draw the opposite lesson

audit_text_issue: The marker flagged the venba's sense; தூமப் பணிகள் is uncertain. | 2:91-94 flagged uncertain; தூமப் பணிகள் unsure.

note: The venba says husband and wife, joined like coiled serpents, never parted; in the next kaathai Kovalan buys Madhavi's garland, cannot leave her and forgets his home.
teaches: The closing praise of a union that never parts is reversed within one kaathai, and the venba's own hint of impermanence turns out to be about the marriage itself rather than about the world.
audit_text_issue: தூமப் பணிகள் (2:91) is uncertain in its first word. | 2:91 தூமப் பணிகள் is uncertain in its first word; the marker flagged the sense.

note: Madhavi's line is traced to heavenly women freed from a sage's curse, shared with Indra's son, at the place of the talaikkol; the talaikkol staff she later receives is worshipped as Jayanta, Indra's son.
teaches: The staff of honour Madhavi wins is the figure of the curse's release that her own descent goes back to, so her investiture re-enacts that release at the very moment she enters the bond that will undo Kovalan.

note: Kovalan buys Madhavi's garland at the price of the king's 1008 kazhanju and forgets his home; returning to Kannaki, he says that sporting with a deceiver (சலதி) has wasted the mountain of wealth his line gave him.
teaches: The narrator tells the purchase as a rule-bound custom and blames no one, and only later does Kovalan himself call Madhavi a deceiver and the purchase a ruin, so the epic lets the buyer, not the poet, put the blame on the seller.

note: The Silappathikaram tells Madhavi's seven years of training to be shown to the king; in the Manimekalai, Vasantamalai lists her arts item by item, opening with the same pair வேத்தியல் பொதுவியல், and reports the town saying her turn to tapas is shameful.
teaches: The accomplishment that the first epic crowns with the king's title becomes, in the sequel, the inventory of what Madhavi has given up, so the length of her training is what makes the town read her renunciation as a disgrace.

note: Kovalan, infatuated, knows no letting go (விடுதல் அறியா விருப்பினன்) once he buys the garland; in the Manimekalai, Madhavi tells how Aravana taught her that the great sorrow of the born comes from attachment (பற்றின் வருவது) and gave her the five precepts.
teaches: The sequel's Buddhist teaching names as attachment the cause that the first epic's narrator only shows as an infatuation that cannot let go, so the garland scene becomes the case the doctrine later diagnoses, told to the woman who sold the garland.
audit_text_issue: The Manimekalai end is a span over units 2:42-57 and 2:58-75.

note: The couplet warns that the sweet words of bangled women who want wealth and not love bring harm; in the epic the garland priced at the king's reward is sent into the street by the doe-eyed woman, Madhavi speaks no word, and Kovalan buys it of his own infatuation.
teaches: The epic splits the couplet's single figure into a household that sets the price in the king's own coin and a dancer who is silent, so the harm the couplet lays on the woman's sweet speech here comes from a public custom and from the buyer's own desire.

gains.a: the scene gains a rule against which Kovalan's purchase can be judged, which the narrator withholds
gains.b: the couplet gains a case in which no sweet word is spoken and the harm still follows, so its warning must reach the custom and the buyer, not only the woman's speech

audit_text_issue: Repaired line 158; the marker flagged the sense.

note: At the wedding night Kovalan asks why her admirers decked her with other ornaments besides the flawless auspicious one (மறுஇல் மங்கல அணியே அன்றியும் பிறிதுஅணி); alone at evening she delights in no ornament but the auspicious one (மங்கல அணியின் பிறிதுஅணி மகிழாள்).
teaches: The husband's compliment that she needs no ornament but the marriage one comes true literally as the mark of his desertion, so the poet builds her abandonment out of his own flattery.
audit_text_issue: The b end is a span over two marked units (2:28-52, 2:53-72).

note: The anklets Kannaki leaves off in grief (அணிசிலம்பு ஒழிய) are the anklets she offers with a smile when Kovalan returns ruined and sees her wasted body (சிலம்புஉள கொண்மின்).
teaches: The epic's fatal anklet enters the story as an ornament set aside in loneliness, and that unworn state is what lets it become the capital for the journey to Madurai.

note: The crescent is praised as founder of the Pandya line and as ruling the stars without swerving from its nature (பான்மையில் திரியாது); in kaathai 20 a Pandya, umbrella drooping and sceptre slack, calls himself the thief.
teaches: The epic's first word on the Pandya line is a praise of unswerving rule set over a scene of Kovalan's straying, and the later verdict turns that praise against its own king; the tension rests on reading the moon's constancy as the line's.

note: The benediction hails the moon because it is like the Chola's cool white umbrella sheltering the world; the venba makes the moon like a guardian king's white umbrella that is shade to the joined and heat to the rest.
teaches: The umbrella that the opening praised as sheltering everyone is here given its second edge, and the edge falls on Kannaki: royal protection, like love, covers only those inside the bond.

note: Both have women parted from their lovers at evening (காதலر்ப் பிரிந்த, nearly the same half-line), and both liken their breath to air blown in a smith's furnace.
teaches: The epic takes a Sangam paalai heroine's evening lament nearly verbatim and turns it from one woman's crisis into a class of Puhar's women, one entry in a survey of the city's nights.

gains.a: the epic's brief list gains the depth of a full lament, the friend, the fear of death in the evening, that its two lines only gesture at
gains.b: the Akananuru poem gains evidence that its furnace image and half-line had become stock diction a later poet could cite as a type

note: The Kural's woman hears the herdsman's flute as evening's envoy and a killing weapon; the epic sets the herdsmen's music and the humming bee over an evening that grieves the parted and delights the joined.
teaches: Heard together, the two show that the flute's cruelty lies in the listener's separation, not in the sound, since the same pastoral music opens a night of delight for others in the epic.

gains.a: the epic's impartial evening gains the inside of one parted listener, for whom its music is a weapon
gains.b: the couplet gains a wider scene in which its deadly flute is, for other hearers, simply the sign of nightfall

note: The Kural's woman says the whole town reels in sorrow when evening spreads; the venba says the same moonlit night is cool to Madhavi with her lover and hot to Kannaki without him.
teaches: The parted woman's sense that the whole town suffers with her is set against a city where one night divides two women of the same house's story, which shows her claim is the projection of grief.

gains.a: the venba's neat sorting of two women gains the parted woman's own conviction that evening is a public calamity
gains.b: the couplet's town-wide sorrow is shown to be a single woman's view, since the epic's city is split by the same hour

audit_text_issue: Kural 1229's sense (whose bewilderment) is uncertain. | Kural 1229 flagged uncertain.

note: The epic's line 21, வளம்தலை மயங்கிய நனந்தலை மறுகும், is the Pattinappaalai's line 193 on the same city's streets of mingled wealth.
teaches: Pattinappaalai uses the line to close a map of goods arriving from every mountain and sea, while the epic attaches it to a census of Puhar's own craftsmen and traders, so the borrowed praise moves from what flows into the port to who works in it.

gains.a: its catalogue is anchored in an older poem's praise of the same streets, which tells the reader this is the canonical Puhar
gains.b: the older line gains a list of the people behind the wealth, whom its own poem leaves out

note: Pattinappaalai's Thirumavalavan makes the northerners wilt among many regional conquests; the epic's Thirumavalavan marches to the Himalaya and brings back gifts from three named northern kings.
