teaches: Read together, the two show a Sangam king's memory being enlarged: one line of the older poem about the north becomes a whole campaign whose trophies are buildings in Puhar, so the epic makes the conquest serve its picture of the city.

gains.a: the epic's past king gains a Sangam record under the same name, showing the episode draws on remembered praise
gains.b: the poem's brief line on the northerners gains a later tradition that turned it into a Himalayan expedition

note: Purananuru 66 praises Karikal Valavan's victory at Venni but says the defeated king who fasted to death for shame at his back wound is better than he; the epic's Valavan is checked by no rival, only by the Himalaya.
teaches: The Purananuru sets a moral limit on the victor through the vanquished man's honour, while the epic removes every human limit and lets only a mountain halt him, so the later memory of the Chola has lost the Sangam poet's check on royal glory.

gains.a: the epic's war-lust with no rival left gains a contrast that shows what its praise omits
gains.b: the poem's lesson that the defeated may be the better man gains a later portrait in which no such man remains

note: The blessing பசியும் பிணியும் பகையும் நீங்கி வசியும் வளனும் சுரக்க is uttered in both: here by possessed old women at the spirit's altar, in Manimekalai by the royal drummer announcing the festival.
teaches: The same two lines pass from the trance speech of warrior women at a spirit's altar to the official proclamation of the king's crier, showing the sequel turning a possessed blessing into the festival's civic formula.

note: Manimekalai's councils warn that if the festival is forgotten, the spirit that relieved the king and the spirit that beats and eats wrongdoers bound in its noose will not stay.
teaches: The Silappathikaram presents the crossroads spirit as a standing marvel of Puhar, while the Manimekalai makes its presence depend on keeping Indra's festival, so the city's moral guard becomes something that can be lost by neglect.

note: The spirit's first victims are those who hide behind penance (தவம்மறைந்து ஒழுகும்); Kural 274 likens hiding in penance to a hunter hiding in a bush to snare birds.
teaches: The Kural shows why the false ascetic's concealment is dangerous, that it lets him prey on others, but names no penalty; the epic imagines a city where the concealment is publicly broken and punished with death, setting a sanction beside the couplet's diagnosis.

gains.a: the spirit's list gains the couplet's reason why the hidden ascetic is the worst of wrongdoers
gains.b: the couplet gains a civic answer to the hidden hunter, a power that sees through the bush

note: Puhar has an image that weeps when the sceptre bends; in Madurai the Pandya's sceptre bends and he himself declares 'I am the thief' and dies.
teaches: Puhar's check on a bent sceptre is an image that can only weep, while Madurai has no such image and the king must find and judge his own fault at the cost of his life, so the epic moves from a ritual sign of injustice to its full price.

note: Kural 559: if the king bends justice the sky bends and withholds rain; the epic's image weeps when either the king's sceptre or the judge's reading bends.
teaches: Both make a mute power answer a bent justice, but the Kural's answer punishes the whole land through the rain while the epic's image only grieves, and the epic adds a second culprit, the judge who twists the law-book, which the couplet does not consider.

gains.a: the weeping image gains the Kural's claim that a bent sceptre has consequences beyond the court
gains.b: the couplet gains the point that justice can be bent by the king's judges as well as by the king

note: Kural 1083's lover learns that Death has a woman's form; the epic says Death took a woman's form because the king's just sceptre forbade its killing.
teaches: The Kural's conceit of the deadly beauty is a lover's discovery, while the epic gives it a political cause, the sceptre that holds Death in check, so a love-figure is turned into praise of the king.

gains.a: the epic's wonder gains the Kural's established conceit of Death in a woman's grace
gains.b: the couplet's figure gains a reason inside a just kingdom, why Death must disguise itself

note: Kannaki's left eye throbs at the festival; in Kaathai 9 a servant announces that Kovalan has come home.
teaches: The good omen is fulfilled in Kovalan's return, but the return leads at once to the journey to Madurai, so the sign of reunion is also the first step toward his death.

note: Madhavi's right eye throbs at the festival; at the end of the Kaanal Vari Kovalan, his former deeds come to fruit, lets go of her and leaves.
teaches: The bad omen given to Madhavi on Indra's festival is fulfilled at the seashore at the festival's end, where the story names former deeds as the cause, so the omen and the karma explanation frame the same parting from two sides.

note: The fifth kaathai shows Puhar's warriors and women making offerings at the guardian bhuta's altar that Indra sent; here the vidyadhara tells why it was sent: a Chola guarded Amaravati against the asuras and received the bhuta and the five halls as Indra's gift.
teaches: Read together, the townspeople's worship and the outsider's origin story show the festival as heaven repaying a Chola's service, which the city's own rite does not explain.

note: The third kaathai says a sage's curse on Indra's son and a celestial woman was lifted at the dance stage, and introduces Madhavi; here a celestial dancer is cursed to earth for failing before Indra, and Madhavi is of her line.
teaches: Madhavi's art is given a heavenly genealogy rooted in a fall: the courtesan's dancing on earth is the continuation of a curse that her first performance was said to end.
audit_text_issue: The syntax of 6:20-24 (who is cursed, Urvasi or a second dancer) is not settled; the marker flagged both units as uncertain.

note: Lines 66-67 repeat the formula of Madhavi's training (பதினோர் ஆடலும் ... விதிமாண் கொள்கையின் விளங்க) from the third kaathai, now as the dances a heavenly watcher sees her perform.
teaches: The repeated formula marks what was learned as a girl's curriculum turning into a public festival performance watched even by beings of the sky.

note: The epic tells Siva's burning of the three cities as an event (the gods asked, the fiery arrow obeyed) and the origin of a dance staged at a city festival; Tirumular calls those who say Siva burned the three cities fools and makes the cities the three impurities.
teaches: The same myth stands in one text as a literal victory reenacted by a courtesan for a crowd and in the other as an inner allegory whose literal telling is folly; the conflict depends on reading the epic's account as a statement of event.

gains.a: the epic's festival myth is shown to be one available reading, the literal and performative one, which a Saiva yogic text explicitly rejects
gains.b: Tirumular's 'fools' get a concrete target: a public culture in which the Tripura burning was danced on a stage as history

note: The couplet's man says sulking is love's sweetness and the embrace after it sulking's sweetness; the epic says Madhavi gave Kovalan both union and sulking, after he had sat in a sulk.
teaches: In the epic the two halves of the couplet's cycle are things a trained woman gives, so ūdal becomes an art supplied to a lover rather than only a mood that lovers fall into.

gains.a: Madhavi's giving of ஊடல் and கூடல் is placed in the Kural's account of love, where sulking followed by union is love's fullest pleasure
gains.b: the couplet's private cycle is shown inside a courtesan's house, where it can be practised and offered, which raises the question the couplet does not ask, whose feeling it is

note: The quatrain says the harlot's love is like a lamp that dies when its oil is spent; here Madhavi, a courtesan, gives Kovalan union and sulking and herself asks for the outing, and in the story it is Kovalan, not she, who breaks off (silappathikaram:7:286-300).
teaches: The epic's courtesan breaks the quatrain's rule from the other side: the love ends, but by the man's suspicion on the shore, not by her turning away when his wealth runs out.

gains.a: Madhavi's devotion in this unit is set against the moral literature's verdict on her class, which makes it pointed rather than merely decorative
gains.b: the quatrain's general rule meets a counter-case in the classical story most read by Tamil readers, which limits it to a type rather than every courtesan

audit_text_issue: The parting itself is in kaathai 7, outside the unit.

note: The Pattinappalai's fishermen count the coloured lights of Puhar's mansions at night; the epic counts the shore's lamps by trade, from perfume-sellers and hawkers to the lighthouse, fishing boats and foreign traders.
teaches: The idyll's lights are a spectacle watched from the boats, while the epic's are a roll of the port's livelihoods, showing how the later poem turns the same harbour of lights into a social survey.

gains.a: the epic's catalogue gains a Sangam precedent for Puhar as a city known by its lights, which marks it as a set piece of the port, not a passing detail
gains.b: the idyll's anonymous lights gain owners: the epic names who keeps each lamp, filling in the trades behind the glow

audit_text_issue: silappathikaram:6 lines 145-147 obscure; the link does not rest on them

note: Both use the phrase of Karikal 'taking the cool water' (தண்பதம் கொள்ளும் / தண்பதம் கொண்டு): in the Akananuru a courtesan recalls how at Karikal's water festival at Kazhar the Kaveri carried off the dancer Atthi, and likens her lover's loss to it; the epic likens the joyful crowd on the shore to the first day of that festival.
teaches: The festival the epic uses as a simile of joy is, in the Sangam poem, the scene of a dancer lost and a courtesan abandoned, which is what this shore day will become for Madhavi.

gains.a: the simile carries a buried memory of loss at the same festival, so the epic's joyful shore is shadowed before the songs begin
gains.b: the Akananuru's water festival gains a fuller picture of its crowds, costumes and noise and of its standing as a byword for Puhar's festivity

note: The Pattinappalai's speaker, in the poem for Karikal, swears he will not leave his long-haired woman even if given all of Puhar; the epic, invoking Karikal's festival, seats Kovalan beside Madhavi on Puhar's shore, where before evening he will leave her (silappathikaram:7:286-300).
teaches: The idyll's vow that no city outweighs the beloved is tested on the very shore it praised, and the epic's lover fails it amid Puhar's full splendour.

gains.a: Kovalan's coming desertion is measured against a famous Sangam refusal to leave a woman for Puhar, which sharpens its cost
gains.b: the idyll's hyperbole gains a narrative counter-case showing that leaving was the choice it imagined refusing

note: Here the lute passes into Madhavi's hand in a bower set up for pleasure; in the next kaathai the songs she sings on it make Kovalan think her false, and, his ūzhvinai coming to fruit, he leaves her on the shore.
teaches: The instrument and the place prepared for the lovers' pleasure become the means and site of their parting, which the next kaathai assigns to karma acting through the lute's music.

note: Madhavi hands Kovalan the yazh and he chooses the songs; at the kaathai's close the narrator says his old deed came to fruit over the yazh music and he left her.
teaches: The pairing shows the narrator placing the first turn of the story's karma not in a crime or a curse but in a lute passed between lovers at play, so the moral of the patikam that past deeds come to fruit begins with a song chosen for pleasure.

note: Kovalan's Kaveri proves her chastity by not sulking when the Chola unites with the Ganga; Madhavi's Kaveri walks as she does because her husband's sceptre never bends.
teaches: Sung back over the same river, the two stanzas put the burden of fidelity on opposite partners: Kovalan asks the wife to bear the husband's other union, Madhavi makes the river's grace the sign of a husband who keeps straight, so the exchange is a quarrel about who owes faithfulness.

note: The song praises a wife who does not sulk at her husband's other love; Madhavi hears in Kovalan's songs a hidden intent and takes up the yazh in a sulk disguised as pleasure.
teaches: The song's ideal of the wife who never sulks is answered at once by the courtesan's sulking, so the kaathai shows the praise of patient chastity working as a provocation on the one woman who is not his wife.

note: In the Ainkurunuru the wife begins to push away her husband's chest, broad as the Kaveri's full flood, in sulking; in the vari the Kaveri herself is the wife who never sulks at the Chola's other unions.
teaches: The Sangam marutham gives the Kaveri's flood to the straying husband and lets the wife sulk at it, while the epic song makes the river the wife and her not sulking the highest chastity, so the same river image moves from licensing the wife's oodal to forbidding it.

gains.a: the stanza's demand for a wife without oodal stands out against the older convention in which the wronged wife's sulking was expected and even loved
gains.b: the quatrain's playful river-chest gains a later reading in which the river is no longer the husband's breadth but the wife's patience

note: The couplet makes sulking love's salt, good in right measure and spoiling only when overdone; the stanza calls not sulking at all, even at the husband's other union, a woman's great chastity.
teaches: Where the Kural sets a measure for oodal, the epic song sets it at nothing and names that karpu, so together they show the measure of sulking turning from a matter of love's taste into a test of a wife's virtue.

gains.a: the stanza's praise gains a standard to be measured against: by the couplet it asks for no salt at all
gains.b: the couplet's measure gains its limit case, a song that would remove sulking entirely from a wife's part

note: The Akananuru friend asks the lord of the shore whether the oath he swore when his chariot crushed the girls' sand dolls was false too, with the sea as witness; the vari asks how simple girls could know that the man who swore by the sea god would break it.
teaches: The pair shows the epic lifting the neithal friend's charge, an oath with the sea as witness and the girls' sand-play spoiled, out of the courtship plot where it pressed for marriage and into a sung entertainment, where the charge of broken faith is performed by the man who will himself walk out at the song's end.

gains.a: the stanza gains its source situation: the sea-oath and the spoiled sand-play were a friend's demand for marriage before they were a song for a courtesan
gains.b: the Akananuru poem gains evidence that its situation had become a fixed piece of Puhar song, recognisable enough to be sung by a merchant at the shore festival

note: Kovalan sings the girls' blame of a man who swore by the sea god and broke his word; when Madhavi answers in song, he decides she is the deceiver and leaves her.
teaches: The singer who voiced the charge against the oath-breaking man ends the kaathai by abandoning his woman and calling her the one full of lying tricks, so the story turns the song's accusation back on the one who sang it.

note: The couplet says this woman is herself the cure for the sickness she brings; the vari asks whether the sickness her face and eyes gave can be cured only by her breasts.
teaches: The song splits the couplet's paradox across the body, the eyes and face causing the sickness and the breasts curing it, which shows how a later lyric turned the Kural's single riddle into a scene of parts.

gains.a: the stanza's closing guess gains a known paradox behind it, that the beloved breaks the rule of medicine by being both cause and cure
gains.b: the couplet gains a concrete setting and a division of roles within the woman's body that it leaves unstated

audit_text_issue: The marker flags 75 (தீர்க்கும் போலும்) as hope or supposition; either way the split holds.

note: The couplet's man says he never knew Death before and now knows it in a woman's warring eyes; the vari's man says he did not know Death lived in the shore grove, and had he known he would not have come.
teaches: Both men learn Death in a woman's eyes, but the Kural's man ends in recognition while the song's ends in the wish never to have come, so the pair separates knowing love's danger from wanting to have avoided it.

gains.a: the stanza's refrain gains a contrast that shows its regret as a choice: the couplet's speaker accepts what he now knows
gains.b: the couplet's moment of discovery gains a sequel in which the knowledge comes too late to act on

note: The couplet asks whether the young woman's look is Death, an eye or a doe and finds all three in it; the vari asks whether her eyes are fierce Death and answers that Death has become an innocent girl.
teaches: Where the Kural holds Death and the doe's innocence side by side in one look, the song makes one the form of the other, so the innocent girl is Death in disguise, a step from mixture to transformation.

gains.a: the stanza's turn gains a reference point: it resolves into one being what the couplet leaves as three natures
gains.b: the couplet's list gains a storytelling form in which its opposites are joined by the god of death taking a girl's shape

note: The Thinaimalai man says the girl guarding drying fish turns weapon-eyes on him and it is he, not the fish, she guards; the vari says the goddess who afflicts those who see her driving birds from drying fish has taken a woman's form.
teaches: The same fish-guarding girl is a wry reversal of guarding in the akam verse and a goddess in disguise in the epic song, so the pair shows the neithal scene moving from the lover's joke to a performance piece of supernatural praise.

gains.a: the stanza gains its plain source scene, in which the girl's task and the man's capture are human and comic
gains.b: the akam verse gains a later form in which its girl is lifted into an anangu, showing how the stock scene was elevated in courtly song

audit_text_issue: silappathikaram:7:99 அலவநோய் and Thinaimalai 32 கடிபொல்லா are uncertain.

note: The couplet calls those whose work is killing base in the eyes of the discerning; the vari tells the fisher girl that her elders live by killing lives in the sea and she by killing lives in men's bodies.
teaches: The ethics book brands killing for a living as base, while the coastal song takes the fishers' killing as the plain inheritance of a family and makes it a compliment, so the pair shows a whole people's livelihood that the Kural's judgment would fall on and that the poetry of the shore never questions.

gains.a: the stanza's easy wit about killing gains an ethical weight it does not register: by the Kural's standard the father's trade is base work
gains.b: the couplet's judgment gains a concrete people it would condemn, the fishing families the epic sings with admiration

note: The couplet says her eyes would not make him tremble if her bent brows would straighten and screen them; the song says she takes lives with her bending brows, as her brothers take lives with boats.
teaches: In the Kural the curved brow is the eyes' failed guard, which could save him by straightening, while the song makes the curve itself the killer and the killing a family trade, so the pair shows the same conceit shifted from a hope of rescue to a charge of hereditary guilt.

gains.a: the song's brow-as-weapon gains the couplet's sense that the brow's bend is a fault, கோடு, the word for a bent sceptre too
gains.b: the couplet's private plea gains a social frame, a fisher girl whose people kill for a living, so the lover's charge of murder is cast as inherited rather than chosen

note: Kovalan tells Kannaki in their bridal chamber that the swan, beaten by her gentle gait, hid among the lotus pools; in the kaanal vari he tells the swan not to follow a fisher girl, whose walk it cannot match.
teaches: The same compliment Kovalan gave his bride is given, with Madhavi listening, to an imagined shore girl, so the pair shows how readily his praise moves from one woman to another, the very thing Madhavi then reads as a hidden meaning.

note: Madhavi reads a hidden intent into Kovalan's songs and sings as if she had one too; at the end Kovalan says she sang with her mind on another, and leaves her, the narrator saying his former deed had come to fruit.
teaches: Set together, the two passages give the break two causes: a pair of mutual misreadings of songs that the poet marks as seeming, and the ஊழ்வினை the narrator names when Kovalan goes, so choice and karma are both offered for the same parting.

note: The Purananuru poem tells Killivalavan that the land of the just sceptre on the Kaveri gets rain when it asks, and that kings are blamed when rains fail; Madhavi's stanza reads the Kaveri's easy flow as proof that the Chola sceptre does not bend.
teaches: The Sangam counsel makes plenty a duty the king must earn and warns he will be blamed for drought, while the epic song takes the river's plenty as already proving his justice, so the pair shows the counsel hardened into a courtly praise that can no longer imagine the failure the older poem warns of.

gains.a: Madhavi's figure gains its political doctrine, that a straight sceptre shows itself in the land's fertility, from an older address to a named Chola
gains.b: the poem's conditional warning gains a later reception in which the same link between sceptre and Kaveri is sung as settled fact, the form the epic later breaks with the Pandya

note: The couplet says it is not the spear but the unbending sceptre that gives a king victory; Madhavi's paired stanzas say the Kaveri's grace shows first her husband's unbending sceptre, then the strength of his spear.
teaches: The Kural ranks the sceptre above the spear and removes the spear as a cause, while Madhavi's song sets them side by side as equal signs of one prosperous river, so the pair shows the court song keeping the force the ethical couplet sets aside.

gains.a: the stanza's turn from sceptre to spear gains a measure: the Kural shows the spear stanza is the one an ethicist would refuse
gains.b: the couplet gains a contrary witness, a praise-song that will not drop the spear when it praises the just king

note: Pattinappaalai says the Kaveri does not fail even when the star goes south and the sky withholds rain; Madhavi's stanza says the Kaveri's unceasing help that sustains life is the grace of the ruler of the wheel.
teaches: The idyll makes the river's reliability its own, a guarantee standing even against a failed sky, while the epic song moves that same unfailing gift under a ruler's grace, so the pair shows the Kaveri's bounty passing from a fact of the land to a token of the king.

gains.a: the stanza's ஒழியாய் gains its older ground, the Sangam guarantee that this river does not fail when the rains do
gains.b: the idyll's praise of the river gains a later reading in which its constancy is no longer self-standing but credited to the sun-like Chola

note: In Kovalan's sarthu vari the shore girl asks how simple folk could know that men who broke their oaths before the sea-god are without dharma; in Madhavi's, she asks how they could know that girls' slipping bangles proclaim the men who married them in secret.
teaches: Both songs use the same refrain of feigned simplicity, but Kovalan's names the man's broken oath as the wrong while Madhavi's shows the cost landing on the woman's body, whose loosening bangles make the secret public, so the exchange moves blame from the oath to its visible price.

note: Madhavi's stanza tells of a shore lord who looked at the crab with its mate and at her and then went away, leaving her senseless; at the kaathai's end Kovalan, hearing her songs as aimed at another, lets go of her and leaves.
teaches: The persona's lament for a lover who left after seeing a scene of union is followed, within the evening, by the singer's own lover leaving her, so the pair shows Madhavi's song turning from a role into her situation.

note: The couplet's woman asks what would become of her if she forgot, since she knows no forgetting and even remembering burns; Madhavi's woman says to the adumbu and the swans, let him go, we will not forget those who forgot us.
teaches: In the Kural not forgetting is a helpless bind, since memory both burns and keeps her alive, whereas in the song it is announced as a choice with an audience, a reproach to the forgetter, so the pair shows the same refusal to forget used as a lament and as a charge.

gains.a: the stanza gains the couplet's inner cost, that the vow not to forget is also a burning she cannot escape
gains.b: the couplet's private bind gains a public turn, the same memory declared to witnesses as an accusation against the one who forgot

note: The couplet's woman lives because she sees in dreams the man who gives no grace awake; Madhavi's woman, whose eyes cannot sleep in the evening, asks the sleeping neythal whether it sees the cruel man coming in its dreams.
teaches: The Kural's comfort depends on sleep, and the song removes it: the sleepless woman is shut out of the dream that keeps the couplet's speaker alive and can only ask a flower for it, so the pair shows the dream-comfort as a privilege of those who can sleep.

gains.a: the stanza's question gains its stake: in the Kural the dream is what keeps a deserted woman alive
gains.b: the couplet gains a limit it does not state, that its consolation fails the woman who cannot sleep at all

note: The Ainthinai Ezhupathu heroine asks whether the sea, like her, does not sleep because the same shore lord took his fill of it and left; Madhavi's woman tells the neythal that, unlike her, it sleeps free of pain.
teaches: The two neythal women look to the shore for company in sleeplessness and reach opposite answers, one finding in the restless sea a fellow sufferer, the other finding in the closed flower only a sleeper who does not share her pain, so the pair shows the same evening shore read as sympathy and as indifference.

gains.a: the stanza's envy of the flower gains a contrast with the older convention in which the shore suffers with the woman
gains.b: the Sangam poem's consoling fellow-sufferer gains a counter-case in which nature sleeps and the woman is alone

note: The Ainthinai Aimpathu heroine begs the crab not to walk over the tracks of her lover's chariot so she can look at them her fill; Madhavi's woman tells the tide that it has already broken up every trace of that path.
teaches: The Sangam heroine still holds the wheel-track and pleads with a small creature to spare it, while in the song the sea has already wiped it out and she can only ask what to do, so the pair shows the same last trace of the lover first guarded and then lost.

gains.a: the stanza gains the older poem's sense of what the track meant, all that is left to look at
gains.b: the quatrain's plea gains its sequel, the loss it feared, done not by a crab but by a tide no one can beg

note: The patikam states that a former deed comes in wrath and makes its doer eat its fruit; here the narrator uses the same words (ஊழ்வினை, உருத்து) for the moment Kovalan leaves Madhavi.
teaches: The first time the narrative names the patikam's third moral at work, the deed ripens not in a crime or a court but in a lover mishearing a song, so the epic's karma enters the story through a private misjudgement long before Madurai.

note: Here the narrator gives Kovalan's break with Madhavi to his ripening deed; when he returns to Kannaki he gives his ruin to his own play with a deceitful woman (சலதி) and is ashamed.
teaches: The same break has two causes in two voices, karma in the narrator's and Madhavi's deceit in Kovalan's, so the epic lets its hero blame the woman while its own frame says the fault came from his past deed.

note: The couplet says a fate of loss makes a man foolish; the epic shows Kovalan, his deed ripening, take a sung convention for a confession and leave.
teaches: The epic supplies the mechanism the couplet only asserts: ripening fate does its work by making a man misread what is in front of him, here a song in an assumed voice, so the folly is the means of the loss.

gains.a: the epic's ஊழ்வினை gains a precise maxim for how it works on Kovalan, through a loss of judgement rather than an outside blow
gains.b: the couplet's abstract 'fate that makes foolish' gains a concrete case of what the folly looks like and what it costs

note: Kovalan sang the girls' charge that a man who swore by the sea god and broke his oath is without virtue; Madhavi's last song bows to the sea god and asks it to bear a false oath.
teaches: The two singers take opposite stances to the same broken oath before the same god, his to condemn and hers to plead for pardon, and the plea, left without a named oath-breaker, is what Kovalan hears as her guilt.
audit_text_issue: Line 284 கனலில் may be a corruption of கானலில்.

note: In the Ainkurunuru the friend says the girl's sickness is not the ford-spirit's doing but the man's oath; Madhavi's heroine asks the sea god not to punish the false oath sworn in the grove.
teaches: Both rest on the belief that a water deity punishes a false love-oath, but where the Sangam friend turns that belief against the man, the epic's heroine asks the god to spare him, so the same belief serves blame in one and loyal forgiveness in the other.

gains.a: the epic song gains the background belief that makes its plea meaningful: an oath sworn at the water draws the god's affliction
gains.b: the Ainkurunuru poem's belief gains a second use, as something a wronged woman can ask the god to withhold

audit_text_issue: silappathikaram:7 line 284 கனலில் is probably கானலில் (in the grove); the link does not depend on it

note: The Kural's woman asks the bewildered evening whether its mate is as hard as hers; Madhavi's heroine asks whether this bewildering evening (மருள்மாலை) exists in the land of the man who left.
teaches: Both put to evening a question that is really about the absent man's hardness, and the epic sets that question in a performance before a lover who is present, showing how the convention can be heard as a personal charge.

gains.a: the epic stanza gains a known form, the address to evening, which marks it as a conventional lament rather than Madhavi's confession
gains.b: the couplet gains a dramatic setting in which its question is sung aloud and misheard, with consequences for the singer

note: The Kural says that when evening comes the whole town reels and suffers; Madhavi's heroine says the world shuts its eyes and, if evening and her husband are such, the world has become poor.
teaches: Both widen one woman's evening grief to the whole settlement, and the epic adds the lover himself to the cause, so the poverty of the world is laid as much on the husband's nature as on the hour.

gains.a: the epic stanza gains a Kural precedent for making the world share the lament
gains.b: the couplet's reeling town gains a named cause in the husband, which the couplet leaves out

note: The Kural makes the herdsman's flute evening's envoy and killing weapon; Madhavi's heroine says evening has struck the fishers' palai and bids it, if so skilled in melody, take her life.
teaches: In both the music of dusk is the instrument that kills the parted woman, but in the epic the song is sung on a yazh by a musician, so the deadly melody of evening is the singer's own art turned on herself.

gains.a: the epic stanza gains a precedent for evening's music as a weapon, which explains why the singer offers her life to a melody
gains.b: the couplet's image gains a second landscape, the fishers' shore in place of the herders' pasture, and a singer who is herself the musician

note: Kovalan sang of a conch that ploughed through a girl's sand-play and left her grieving; Madhavi sings of a man who came by the backwater, spoiled their sand-play and went.
teaches: Madhavi takes Kovalan's own image and puts a man in place of the conch, so the spoiled sand-play changes from a picture of a girl's charm into a charge of desertion, the answer-song turning his playful scene against the lover.

note: At the end of the Kaanal Vari the narrator says Kovalan let go of Madhavi because his ஊழ்வினை rose to bear fruit (line 289); here the same departure is recalled as Kovalan sulking and leaving without union (கோவலன் ஊடக் கூடாது ஏகிய).
teaches: One act is given two causes a kaathai apart, past karma ripening and a lover's pique, so the epic's fate does not replace Kovalan's own temper but works through it.

note: Both letters are sent through Vasantamalai with the same formula for Madhavi's state (பசந்த மேனியள் படர் ..., line 68 here; 13:67-68), and in both she writes with her own hand.
teaches: The repeated wording marks the second letter as a rerun of the first, so the reader can see that what changes between a refused and an accepted letter is Kovalan's state, not Madhavi's message.

note: Here Kovalan refuses Madhavi's letter, filing her every sign of love as a dancing woman's role; reading her second letter in the forest he decides she is without fault and the fault is his (தன்றீ திலளென ... என்தீ தென்றே, 13:94-95).
teaches: Kovalan's verdict that a dancer's grief is only art is withdrawn by Kovalan himself once he is ruined and far away, so the story shows the judgment came from his sulk and not from anything in her.

note: The couplet says sulking is like salt, and drawing it out a little too long is like a little too much; Kovalan's sulk, begun at the shore, is here drawn out into a refusal of her letter.
teaches: Past the couplet's 'little too much' the quarrel stops being a spoiled sweetness and becomes a verdict on the beloved's whole nature, which is how a lovers' sulk turns into the epic's break.

gains.a: the refusal gains a measure by which it is an excess of an ordinary lovers' sulk rather than a reasoned judgment of Madhavi
gains.b: the couplet gains a case showing what the excess it warns of looks like, a rereading of all past tenderness as pretence, with a cost it does not name

note: In the akam poem the wife refuses the bard sent to plead for her husband because he is a deceiving philanderer (மாயப் பரத்தன்); here the man refuses the go-between sent by the courtesan because her love is a dancer's art.
teaches: The epic stages a marutham refusal of the go-between with the roles turned round, so that the charge of false love the convention lets the wife bring against the man is brought by the man against the courtesan.

gains.a: the scene gains its genre: Kovalan's answer is a வாயில் மறுத்தல், and its harshness reads as a convention used against Madhavi
gains.b: the poem gains a view from the other side of the same convention, where the one refused is the woman and the charge of deceit is shown, later in the story, to be wrong

note: Madhavi lies down saying that though he will not come in the evening she will see him in the morning (காலைகாண் குவம்); in the next kaathai Kovalan comes instead to Kannaki's door (கடைத்தலையான் வந்துநம் கோவலன்).
teaches: The morning Madhavi waits for is the morning Kovalan returns to his wife, so her hope and Kannaki's dream are the two ends of one night, and the courtesan's loss is the wife's recovery.

note: Madhavi lies with a helpless heart (கையறு நெஞ்சமொடு, line 116); her second letter ends asking Kovalan to take away the helpless heart (கையறு நெஞ்சம் கடியல் வேண்டும், 13:91).
teaches: The phrase carries one night's grief into the later letter, showing that what Madhavi asks of Kovalan there is to undo the state this refusal left her in.

note: The couplet says sulking is love's pleasure and its pleasure is to come together and embrace; the venba has the cuckoo proclaim love's command to all who have sulked (ஊடினீர்) to unite (கூடுமின்), and chides the one who spurned the letter.
teaches: The couplet's pleasure rests on a condition, that union follows, and the venba shows that condition failing even under love's own command, so the sulk the Kural treats as seasoning becomes the start of a separation.

gains.a: the venba's command gains a stated rule of love, so Kovalan's refusal is a breach of love's own order and not only of Madhavi's hope
gains.b: the couplet's closing condition பெறின், 'if one gets to', gains a case where one does not get to, and what follows then

audit_text_issue: silappathikaram:8:119-126 flagged uncertain; addressee of அலந்தாய் not named

note: Saathan's rule that gods grant no boon without tapas uses the couplet's own word செய்தவம், and then he grants Maalathi a child she has not earned.
teaches: Read with the couplet, the tale shows that the rule linking tapas to its reward is the god's to state and also the god's to override, so grace in the epic stands beside the merit rule rather than inside it.

gains.a: the general law behind Saathan's line 17, which shows his gift to Maalathi as an exception to it
gains.b: a scene where the law is spoken by a god to a woman without tapas and then not applied

note: Saathan says gods give no boon to those without tapas; the goddess of Madurai later says that when a former deed comes in wrath, tapas does not help those not upright.
teaches: Together the two divine sayings set limits on tapas from both sides: without it no boon, and with it no shield once an old deed has ripened against one who was not upright.

note: Devanthi, whose husband is a god, keeps worship at his shrine to have him back; the couplet sets worship of a god against worship of a husband.
teaches: Devanthi's case dissolves the couplet's either-or, since her god is her husband, and so throws Kannaki's refusal of the shrine in the next unit into relief as a choice the couplet's terms describe exactly.

gains.a: a measure for Devanthi's piety as the reverse of the couplet's wife, which prepares the contrast with Kannaki
gains.b: a case the couplet did not foresee, a wife whose husband is himself the god she worships

note: The dream's plea before the king (காவலன் முன்னர் யான் கட்டுரைத்தேன்) is fulfilled when Kannaki stands before the Pandya and argues her case.
teaches: Set beside the plea, the dream shows that Kannaki's speech before the king was foreseen as her own act from the start, not a chance turn of grief, and that she already knew it would bring harm to the city.

note: The 'good' that would be laughed at if told is the ending in which Kannaki, after fourteen days, rises to heaven with Kovalan.
teaches: The pairing explains why Kannaki calls the dream's ending laughable: a reunion that comes only after death and in the form of gods sounds absurd as a blessing to a living wife.
audit_text_issue: Lines 51-54 are dense and the referent of உறுவன் is not certain.

note: Offered bathing and Kama's shrine as a way to keep her husband, Kannaki says it is not worthy; the couplet praises the wife who worships her husband rather than a god.
teaches: The scene shows the couplet's wife as one who refuses a rite offered for her own good, at the cost of the remedy, and that the refusal is framed as dignity (பீடு), not as doubt about the gods.

gains.a: the rule that explains Kannaki's refusal without making her a sceptic about the tanks
gains.b: a lived test in which the wife turns down divine help for her marriage at the moment she most needs it

note: Devanthi blames a vow Kannaki broke to her husband in a former birth; the goddess of Madurai later traces the disaster to a curse on Kovalan's former self, who had Sangaman killed.
teaches: The poem offers two former-birth causes for the same ruin and gives the authoritative one to a goddess, so the friend's guess that the fault was the wife's own is left standing as a mistaken reading.
audit_text_issue: Line 55 (கைத்தாயும் அல்லை) is obscure. | Line 55 கைத்தாயும் அல்லை is obscure.

note: Kannaki declines to worship at Kama's shrine for her husband; the Katturai venba says the gods themselves worship her who worships her husband and no god.
teaches: The early refusal and the later venba make one arc: the wife who would not seek her husband through a god ends as one the gods receive, so the poem pays out the refusal in the Kural's own terms.
audit_text_issue: The marker flagged 9:55 (கைத்தாயும் அல்லை) as obscure. | 9:55 கைத்தாயும் அல்லை is obscure; the link does not depend on it.

note: Kovalan devises a remedy for his ruin, to trade with the anklets in Madurai, and in the same line the narrator says the deed was driving him; the couplet says fate gets there first even when one plans another way.
teaches: The pairing shows fate overtaking a plan by using the plan itself: Kovalan's scheme to recover is the very road by which the deed reaches him, a case the couplet's bare 'it gets there first' does not picture.

gains.a: a rule that explains why the narrator credits Kovalan's sensible plan to the deed (line 78)
gains.b: a concrete mechanism: the counter-plan becomes fate's vehicle rather than being outrun by it

note: Kovalan blames a deceitful woman for the poverty that shames him; the couplet ranks double-minded women with drink and dice as the company of those Fortune has left.
teaches: Kovalan speaks the couplet's judgment of himself, but the closing venba and the narrator put his ruin down to the old deed, so the epic lets the Kural's verdict on courtesans stand as a ruined man's account rather than as the cause.

gains.a: a standard of the age against which Kovalan's blame of Madhavi sounds conventional and self-excusing
gains.b: a speaker who applies it to himself in the moment of loss, while the story he is in names another cause

note: The venba says the old deed drove Kovalan out of Puhar before dawn; the quatrain says an old deed finds its doer as a calf finds its mother among many cows.
teaches: In the quatrain the deed seeks the doer; in the venba the doer is moved toward the deed, so together they show karma working from both ends, the deed seeking and the doer being sent.

gains.a: an image for why the venba gives the deed the active verb கடைக்கூட்ட
gains.b: a narrative case where the search ends by bringing the doer to a distant city, not by the deed arriving at his door

note: The venba's மூதை வினை is unnamed here; the goddess of Madurai later names it as the curse of Sangaman's widow on Kovalan's former self.
teaches: Read together, the venba sets the deed moving with no content and the later speech fills it in, so the departure from Puhar is the first step of a debt whose terms the reader learns only after the death.

note: The ஊழ்வினை that drives the couple out of Puhar before dawn is the deed whose ripening time (வினைவிளை காலம்) the patikam gives as the reason the Pandya failed to inquire.
teaches: The epic names the past deed both at the first step out of the house and at the hour of the killing, so the whole journey is framed as one deed's ripening, while the travellers themselves give wealth as their reason.

note: The couplet says fate outruns any other plan; the narrator puts ஊழ்வினை behind a journey Kovalan plans, by his own word at line 51, to win back wealth.
teaches: The epic shows the couplet's claim working from inside a person's own scheme: the plan to recover wealth is not overtaken by fate but is the road fate travels.

gains.a: its passing word ஊழ்வினைக் கடைஇ gains the force of a stated rule that no counter-plan can outrun the deed
gains.b: the couplet's abstract 'it gets there first' gains a case where the victim's own design is the vehicle

note: The couplet says all living beings join hands to the one who does not kill and refuses flesh; the epic shows lay votaries worshipping the stone seat set for the flesh-renouncing Charanas even when none is there.
teaches: The couplet's hyperbole of universal worship becomes an institution in the epic: a built seat honoured in the ascetics' absence, which then becomes the place where a Charana actually appears at line 161.

gains.a: the empty seat gains its reason: the refusal of flesh is what earns such worship
gains.b: the couplet's worship gains a concrete form, a lay cult of the renouncers' seat

note: The couplet defines the good path (நல்லாறு, நெறி) as the way that keeps not killing anything in view; Kavunthi's road counsel makes that literal, warning that a careless step on the shore may harm the crab and the snail.
teaches: Read together, the couplet's path metaphor turns into an actual walk where every footfall must be watched, and the nun counts harm to a snail as a grief equal to the dangers to the traveller herself.

gains.a: the nun's warning gains its principle: the attention she asks for is the couplet's சூழும், a constant watch
gains.b: the couplet's யாதொன்றும் gains a case showing it reaches even crabs and snails underfoot

note: Both open on Venus straying south as the sign of drought and say the Kaveri still brings its flood.
teaches: The epic borrows the Pattinappalai's drought omen for the Kaveri on the road out of Puhar, so the couple's departure from the city is set in the same praise that once opened a poem about the city's wealth.

gains.a: the epic's omen list gains its source and sense as a Chola praise-formula for the river
gains.b: the Sangam formula gains a later use in a travel scene, where it marks the plenty the travellers are leaving behind

note: Both list Saturn smoking, a comet showing and Venus running south; Kapilar credits the rain that never failed in Pari's land to the king's straight sceptre, while the epic credits the Kaveri's flood to the river.
teaches: Holding the two together shows the same omen formula assigning the land's safety to different powers: to a just king in Purananuru 117, and to the river itself in the epic.

gains.a: the epic's omens gain their weight as signs that normally ruin a land unless something stronger holds
gains.b: Kapilar's poem gains a counter-case where the formula is used without any king's virtue as the cause

note: The patikam's third moral, ஊழ்வினை உருத்துவந்து ஊட்டும், reappears with the same verb ஊட்டும் in the Charana's sermon on the strong deed that will not go.
teaches: The poet's announced moral is put into the mouth of a Jain sage within the story, who adds what the patikam does not: that the Jina's word can end the births the deed feeds.

note: The quatrain says not even ascetics (உறுவர்) can remove what must befall; the epic shows an ascetic who sees the couple's coming fate by his inner lamp and tells them the deed cannot be put off.
teaches: The pair shows the quatrain's limit on ascetic power from the ascetic's side: the Charana knows, does not grieve, and states the rule himself instead of trying to avert the fate.

gains.a: the Charana's silence about the couple's fate gains a reason: by the quatrain's rule his knowing could not change it
gains.b: the quatrain's general uruvar gains a named scene where a seer meets those whose fate he foresees

audit_text_issue: Lines 174-175 are compressed; the unit is a run of epithets from 176 to 189. | Marker flagged lines 174-175 as compressed.

note: The Charana says the strong deed cannot be put off once it clings and that release from births comes through the Jina's spoken teaching; Tirumular says that by Siva's grace deeds do not cling at all.
teaches: The two give incompatible accounts of whether a ripening deed can be stopped: for the Charana only the cycle of births can be ended, by teaching, while the deed must still be eaten; for Tirumular grace prevents the deed from clinging.

gains.a: the Charana's sermon gains a clear rival: what it denies is precisely the grace that removes karma
gains.b: Tirumular's verse gains a contemporary opponent for whom no god's grace stops a deed once sown

note: The couplet calls a head that does not bow to the eight-qualitied one as useless as a sense organ without sense; Kavunthi vows each organ, ears, tongue, eyes, body, hands, head and mind, to the Arhat alone.
teaches: The couplet's single comparison between the bowing head and a dead sense is worked out by the nun into a vow for every sense in turn, and the eight-qualitied one is named in the preceding sermon as the Jain Lord (எண்குணன், line 188).

gains.a: the nun's vow gains its root: a sense not turned to the Lord is as if it did not work
gains.b: the couplet's எண்குணத்தான் gains a reading in which a Jain voice claims the title for the Arhat

note: Both curses are told in the same formula, a curse given (இட்ட சாபம்) that took hold (கட்டியது); the former-birth curse on Kovalan has no term and ends in his never again being seen in human form, Kavunthi's has a term of twelve months and a return to former shape.
teaches: Just before Madurai the epic shows a curse that the wronged can soften and that ends in a restored body, so the reader meets the bounded curse first and the unbounded one, which no plea can term, at the story's end.

note: The couplet ranks those who fast below those who bear the harsh words of others; Kavunthi, whom the mockers address by her fasting body, curses them, and it is the insulted couple who ask that the words be taken as ignorance.
teaches: The epic splits the couplet's two figures between two people: the faster answers insult with a curse, and the forbearance the couplet ranks higher comes from the young couple who were insulted.

gains.a: the couple's plea gains a ranking: by the couplet their forbearance stands above the nun's austerity
gains.b: the couplet gains a scene showing that fasting and forbearance can come apart, with the insult aimed at the ascetic's wards and not at herself

note: The couplet says that crushing foes and raising those one loves come by tapas if one so intends; Kavunthi's penance gives her curse its hold and her word of release its power.
teaches: The epic shows both halves of the couplet in one act of one ascetic: the same tapas that turns the mockers into jackals sets the day they become human again.

gains.a: the phrase தவம்தரு சாபம் gains its doctrine: the curse is a use of the power tapas confers
gains.b: the couplet's 'if one intends' (எண்ணின்) gains a case where the ascetic does intend, and is then moved to limit what she intended

note: Both praise the Chola land of Puhar through its water; the Pattinappalai grants that the sky may fail and makes the Kaveri the river that never fails, while the epic's summary sets the divine Kaveri beside a sky that itself never fails (பொய்யா வானம்).
teaches: The Sangam poem rests Puhar's plenty on the river precisely because the sky can fail, and the epic's summary removes that concession, making the sky unfailing too in a line it reuses unchanged for the Pandya land, so the pair shows a Puhar-specific boast about the Kaveri turning into a stock praise that any crowned line receives.

gains.a: the summary's unfailing sky gains a point of contrast: in the older praise of the same city it was the river, not the sky, that could be trusted
gains.b: the Pattinappalai's claim about the Kaveri gains a later form in which the river's distinction has been levelled into a formula shared by the three kingdoms

note: The two summaries share their opening lines word for word (aram, maram, the old city, festivals, the gods' visits, food, the unfailing sky), with the Vaigai for the Kaveri; the Madurai summary ends by viewing its book as one with the Pandya Nedunjeliyan who died on his throne with his chaste queen, the Puhar summary names no king.
teaches: Because the praise of righteousness and unfailing rain is a fixed frame granted alike to the Chola line and to the Pandya whose verdict burned his city, the epic's judgment of a kingdom lies not in that praise but in what each summary sets at its centre: for Madurai a king who died of his own wrong, for Puhar no king at all but its arts.

note: The couplet says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who rules with the sceptre as it should be; the summary lists the Chola line's righteousness beside the unfailing sky and abundant food, and the Madurai summary gives the same lines to the Pandya line.
teaches: Set beside the couplet, the summaries' line of unfailing rain reads as the Kural's sign of just rule, yet the epic grants it equally to the line whose king it shows killing an innocent man, so the pair shows the epic keeping the sign as ceremony while placing the real test of the sceptre in a single verdict.

gains.a: the formula's rain line gains the political meaning the couplet gives it, as a claim that the realm is justly ruled
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where its sign of good rule is ascribed to a kingdom whose sceptre the story will show bent, which shows that the sign alone cannot vouch for the king

note: The venba wishes Puhar, made by fame for the earth whose moat is the sea, to live like the sun and the moon; the Manimekalai tells that when the king, searching for his lost son, left off the Indra festival, Manimekala Deivam bade the sea take the city.
teaches: The sea the venba names only as the earth's protecting moat is the agent that takes the city in the sequel, and the festival the summary counts among Puhar's glories is the rite whose neglect brings it, so the blessing of lasting life holds the terms of its own reversal.

note: The Puhar book opens hailing the moon, the sun and Puhar for resembling the Chola's umbrella, wheel and line, and closes wishing Puhar to live like the morning sun and the evening moon.
teaches: The book is framed by the same sun, moon and city, but at the opening the heavenly bodies are praised as likenesses of the king, and at the close they are the measure of the city's own life with the king gone from the comparison, matching a summary that names the Chola line but no Chola.

note: The brahmin hails a Pandya who, when the thundering clouds withheld rain, bound them and made the harvest unfailing (மழைபிணித் தாண்ட மன்னவன்); the couplet says rain and harvest gather together in the land of the king who rules by the sceptre's nature.
teaches: The couplet makes rain the natural consequence of just rule, while the epic's praise makes the king compel the clouds, so the same belief appears once as a law and once as a dynastic feat that this epic will test when the Pandya's sceptre bends.

gains.a: the praise gains a stated rule by which the dynasty's rain-making can later be judged as a duty rather than a marvel
gains.b: the couplet gains a royal legend showing its abstract link between sceptre and rain told of one named line of kings

note: On the road the brahmin blesses the Pandya line as one of faultless fame (தீதுதீர் சிறப்பின் தென்னனை); in Madurai the reigning Pandya pronounces himself the thief (யானோ அரசன் யானே கள்வன்) and falls dead.
teaches: The journey to Madurai opens with a blessing of a flawless lineage, so the king's self-condemnation reads as a fall from inherited fame and not only as one wrong verdict.

note: Nettimaiyar wishes the Pandya years more than the sands of the Pahruli river of the ancient Pandya; the epic's blessing says the sea took the Pahruli river (பஃறுளி யாற்றுடன்) with the Kumari peak.
teaches: The Sangam poet measures a king's life by a river that still flows, while the epic remembers the same river as drowned and makes its loss the occasion of a northern conquest, so the river turns from a figure of endurance into a figure of loss.

gains.a: the epic's legend gains evidence that Pahruli was a living name in Pandya praise before it was told as lost
gains.b: the Purananuru blessing gains a later memory in which the river it swore by has vanished, sharpening its wish for long life

note: The brahmin likens the summer that turns mullai and kurinji into paalai to a wide land that has lost its royal order when its king bent with his officers (கொற்றவன் கோடி); the couplet says that if the king bends justice the sky will not pour rain.
teaches: The couplet states that a bent king dries the sky, and the brahmin's simile reads a drought landscape as the look of a misruled kingdom, so the waste Kovalan crosses already pictures the bent sceptre waiting in Madurai.

gains.a: the simile gains a doctrine that makes the drought the fruit of misrule rather than only a likeness of it
gains.b: the couplet gains a picture of what its rainless land looks like: forest and hill twisted out of their nature into waste

note: The brahmin promises that bathing in Bhavakaarini brings knowledge of one's former birth (பழம்பிறப் பெய்துவிர்); Kavunthi asks whether he does not see in this birth what was gained in past births (இறந்த பிறப்பின் எய்திய வெல்லாம் பிறந்த பிறப்பிற் காணா யோநீ).
teaches: The Jain ascetic answers the pilgrim's offer point for point, moving knowledge of past lives from a sacred pool to the reading of one's present life, so the chapter sets two routes to one end side by side without letting either deny the other.

note: The brahmin tells the traveller to recite the mantras of five and eight letters and bathe in the pool he wants, though better to fix the heart on the god's feet; the Siddhar asks those seeking a holy water where the bathing is, and says the holy water is the five letters within.
teaches: Both move from outer water toward an inner formula, but the brahmin keeps the pool and makes the letters its key while the Siddhar dissolves the pool into the letters, so the pair shows two stages of one turn from pilgrimage to recitation.

gains.a: the epic's rite gains a later voice that removes the pool it still keeps and shows where its own ranking of devotion over water could lead
gains.b: the Siddhar's attack gains an early literary witness of the practice it rejects, recitation of a letter-formula as the key to a sacred pool

audit_text_issue: Lines 128-132 are compressed and flagged uncertain.

note: Kavunthi asks whether anything rare is out of reach for those who never swerve from truth and protect living beings, against the brahmin's pool that grants every wish; the couplet says austerity is pursued because it gains whatever is wished as it is wished.
teaches: Kavunthi uses the Kural's promise that discipline gains every wish against a pool that also grants every wish, and grounds that discipline in truth and non-harm, so the couplet's motive of attainment becomes an argument for ethics over pilgrimage.

gains.a: Kavunthi's rhetorical question gains a stated rule that a disciplined life yields whatever is wished
gains.b: the couplet gains a rival, the wish-granting pool, which shows what its claim for austerity competes with

note: The brahmin warns of a goddess on the hard way who appears gently and holds travellers back; at the pool Kovalan recalls that the wondrous brahmin said a deluding goddess haunts the forest (மயக்குந் தெய்வமிவ் வன்காட் டுண்டென) and unmasks her with a mantra.
teaches: The pilgrim's road knowledge, which Kavunthi had set aside as unneeded for the cave, is what saves Kovalan in the forest, so the chapter does not let either guide be simply right.

note: In the Venil kaathai Vasantamalai reports that Kovalan refused Madhavi's letter and Madhavi lies sleepless saying she will see him at dawn; the goddess in Vasantamalai's form tells him Madhavi turned in anger, condemned her calling, tore her pearls and dismissed her maid.
teaches: The illusion is built on the one unfinished thread in Kovalan's past, the refused letter, so the forest goddess tempts him with his unresolved bond to Madhavi rather than with a stranger's charm.
audit_text_issue: 11:176-177 is hard to divide between speakers.

note: Saalini, possessed, calls Kannaki a goddess and the jewel of the world, and Kannaki hides behind her husband; at the Pandya's gate the gatekeeper can describe Kannaki only by saying she is not Kotravai on the bleeding pedestal, nor Kali who tore Daruka's chest.
teaches: The divinity a hunter priestess proclaims in a desert shrine, and which Kannaki herself laughs off as confusion, becomes visible to a stranger at the palace door, so the pair shows the story turning Saalini's words into what others see, and the shy wife into a figure that can only be named by the war goddess she is denied to be.

note: The patikam opens with the hill kuravar telling Ilango of the one-breasted pathini taken to heaven before their eyes; the vari has desert hunters' priestess first naming Kannaki divine.
teaches: Both the frame and the first sign within the story put Kannaki's divinity in the mouths of forest and hill folk, before any king or sage acknowledges it, so the pairing shows the epic consistently letting the people of the wilds be the first witnesses of the pathini.

note: The Ainkurunuru friend asks whether it is a kindness if the old velan of an unerring tradition casts his beads and says the girl's sickness is Murugu; the epic's old wise woman of the clan's ancient duty, possessed, declares Kannaki divine and Kannaki calls it confusion.
teaches: In the akam convention the possessed diviner of an old line is the one who gets it wrong, mistaking love for a god's seizure, while in the epic the possessed old woman's word is the true one and the hearer's doubt is the mistake, so the pairing shows the epic reversing the Sangam irony about divination to make it carry prophecy.

gains.a: Kannaki's dismissal of the speech as பேதுறவு reads as a known stance, the akam scepticism toward the diviner, which the story will overturn
gains.b: the friend's mockery of the unerring velan gains a later counter-case where the same kind of possessed elder speaks truly

note: The Murukatruppadai hails Murugan among his titles as son of the banyan god, son of the mountain's daughter, and child of Kotravai of victorious war; the vari heaps on Kotravai herself the names of Gauri, Shiva's emblems and the title of Mal's younger kin.
teaches: The Sangam guide poem joins Kotravai to the Saiva household through her son, listing her beside the mountain daughter as Murugan's mother, while the epic's hunters make Kotravai herself absorb Gauri, Shiva's emblems and Vishnu's kinship, so the pair shows the war goddess of the wilds drawn into the great gods' family by two different routes.

gains.a: the epic's fusion of names appears as the later step of a joining already begun in the Sangam praise of Murugan as Kotravai's son
gains.b: the bare title கொற்றவை சிறுவ gains the full portrait of the mother it names, with her mount, weapons and the cult that worships her

note: Tirumular lists the goddess's names (Tripurai, Sundari, Narani, Manonmani and others) and says by them the great one stands as many; the vari lists Amari, Kumari, Gauri, Samari, Shooli, Neeli and others for the hunters' goddess of the stag.
teaches: Both pile names on one goddess, but the hunters' names come from her weapons, mounts, hides and battle with the asura and end in a rite where a girl wears them, while Tirumular's end in the doctrine that one power stands as many, so the pair shows the same device of the name-chain serving a public rite of costume and possession in one text and an inner theology of a single Shakti in the other.

gains.a: the vari's chain of names is seen to make no doctrinal claim of oneness; it names a goddess to be worn and worshipped
gains.b: Tirumular's doctrine that the one stands as many gains an older, folk chain of names (குமரி, கவுரி, நீலி) that it gathers into his single Shakti

note: Tirumular makes knowledge of the First, the meaning of the Veda, together with Parashakti abiding in his half, the mark of the one in niyama; the vari makes the hunters' war goddess the woman's form in the half of the forehead-eyed god, praised by the Veda, while carrying Vishnu's conch and discus.
teaches: The half-woman form that Tirumular holds as an object of contemplative knowledge is, in the hunters' song, a goddess with Vishnu's weapons on a fighting mount, so the pair shows the same Saiva image serving yogic discipline in one text and a war cult that will not keep her to one god in the other.

gains.a: the stanza's line on Shiva's half is shown to be the Saiva doctrinal image, and its addition of Vishnu's weapons stands out against it
gains.b: the verse's பாதியுள் மன்னும் பரசக்தி gains an early witness outside the Saiva canon, worshipped by hunters with offerings rather than known in niyama

note: The couplet says birth is alike for all beings and distinction comes from the difference in deeds; the vari credits a girl's penance with her glory and then declares her birth-clan, the bow-wielding hunters, the clan among clans.
teaches: The song agrees that distinction comes from a deed, the girl's penance, but hands that distinction straight back to the birth-group, the move the couplet's rule forbids, so the pair shows how a low-ranked clan claims rank through one daughter's merit rather than by denying that birth confers it.

gains.a: the hunters' boast is shown to rest on a deed and not on birth alone, and to turn that deed into a clan's rank
gains.b: the couplet's rule gains a case that tests it, where an individual deed's distinction is claimed for a whole clan of a lowly calling

note: Both tie the cattle raid to toddy: in the Purananuru the jar is kept for the raider who will bring a herd; here the toddy seller's refusal sends the hunter out.
teaches: Read together they show toddy as the raid's credit: the poem's kept jar is advance pay, and the epic's refusal is the unpaid debt the seized herd later settles in the seller's yard.

gains.a: the epic's brief motive (a refused drink) gains the Sangam custom behind it, where the raider is paid in toddy before he goes
gains.b: the Purananuru poem gains the other side of the trade: a seller who will not pour and is paid afterwards in cattle (lines 132-135)

note: The Purananuru raider takes herds yet his own pot shows no curd; the epic names whose yards the seized herds fill.
teaches: The poem's pitied raider who keeps nothing is explained by the epic's list: the herd goes to smith, drummer, bards, augur and toddy seller, so a raid's wealth is a gift economy that leaves the raider poor.

gains.a: the list of yards gains its point: giving the herd away is the raider's honour, as the poem's empty curd-pot shows
gains.b: the poem's riddle (why a cattle-taker has no curd) gains the epic's answer in named receivers

audit_text_issue: The augur and toddy seller named in teaches come from lines 132-135, outside the unit.

note: The hunters pay for victory with blood at the goddess's feet; the Kural ranks not killing above a thousand oblations.
teaches: The conflict is about what an offering is worth: the hymn makes killing itself the price that buys the goddess's favour, while the couplet holds that no offering outweighs one life spared; it holds if the throat-blood of line 144 is a slain creature's.

gains.a: the hymn's blood price gains a measure from outside the cult, one by which the payment is a loss
gains.b: the couplet's comparison of oblation and abstention gains a live case where the offering is not ghee but blood

audit_text_issue: marker flags the stanza's sense as uncertain

note: The hunters owe the goddess a bali as a debt; Tirumular, having nothing to show the god who eats oblations, offers a song as his food offering.
teaches: The vari is itself a song sung over the bali, so the hunters give both the blood and the song that Tirumular offers in its place, which shows the song offering was a companion of the blood rite before it was a substitute for it.

gains.a: the hunters' debt-offering gains a contrast that shows its song as a second offering, not mere accompaniment
gains.b: Tirumular's song-oblation gains a scene of the older rite in which song and blood were offered together

audit_text_issue: Tirumanthiram 1824 lines 1-2 are compressed and flagged as uncertain.

note: Tirumular praises the lord who swallowed the poison and shares half his body with the lady; the hunters give the poison-swallowing to the goddess herself.
teaches: The hymn moves Siva's defining act of grace to his consort through the shared body Tirumular names, and makes it the ground on which a goddess who eats the pitiless hunters' offerings still grants grace.

gains.a: the hymn's attribution gains its basis: the goddess is the half of the poison-eater's body
gains.b: Tirumular's half-body formula gains a use outside Saiva devotion, where it lets a forest goddess claim Siva's deed

note: The Kural says wealth that comes without grace and love should be let go; the hunters name themselves graceless takers of wealth by wounding and ask the gracious goddess to eat their due.
teaches: Where the couplet tells the getter to let graceless wealth roll away, the hymn shows a community whose living is exactly such wealth offering a share of it to a goddess of grace, who is asked not to refuse it; the tension rests on reading the due as paid from the plunder.

gains.a: the hunters' self-description gains the ethical name for what they live by: wealth that comes without arul
gains.b: the couplet's rule gains a case where graceless wealth is not let go but sanctified by offering

note: The hunters close their rite praying that the Pandya of Pothiyil wear the vetchi and ruin other lands; in Madurai the same king's sceptre fails and he falls dead before Kannaki.
teaches: The blessing asks for victory over others' lands, but the king's ruin comes from within his own court; the forest rite that hailed Kannaki as the goddess has, unknowing, blessed the king she will undo.
audit_text_issue: silappathikaram:12:165 மறைமுது முதல்வன் பின்னர் மேய is obscure.

note: On entering the Pandya land the travellers rely on the fame that the Pandya's straight sceptre keeps even beasts and thunder from harming those who depend on it; in the court the same Pandya, having killed Kovalan, finds himself the thief and his sceptre bent.
teaches: The pairing shows the epic letting the travellers stake their lives on a king's reputation for protection and then making that king's failure fall on exactly the stranger who trusted it, so the praise of the sceptre at the border is the premise his own verdict on himself overturns.

note: The couplet says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who rules by right; the epic's fame says that in the just Pandya's land even beasts, serpents and thunder spare those who depend on it.
teaches: Held together, the two show the claim that nature answers a just sceptre turning, in the epic, into a traveller's reason to trust a stranger king, a reputation the story then puts to the test with the travellers' own lives.

gains.a: the border praise gains its doctrinal ground: the fame rests on the Kural's teaching that a just reign orders nature itself
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where its promise is taken as a guarantee by outsiders and so becomes something a king can betray

note: The couplet likens a king's lack of kindness to the world's lack of rain; the epic likens travellers waiting out the scorching sun to subjects waiting for a cruel king to set.
teaches: The Kural pictures the bad king through the weather and the epic pictures the weather through the bad king, so the pair shows the image of misrule running both ways, and the epic placing it, unprompted, at the first step into the Pandya's land.

gains.a: the simile gains the couplet's moral weight: the cruel king is a drought to all that lives, not just a passing discomfort
gains.b: the couplet gains a hope its subjects do not voice: that a cruel reign, like a summer day, has an end to wait for

note: On the road Kovalan, reading Madhavi's letter, says the fault was his own; before the king, Kannaki says ஊழ்வினை drove him to Madurai.
teaches: The pair shows the epic giving Kovalan's ruin two causes in two voices: his own confession of fault, made privately to clear the courtesan, and his wife's public appeal to former deeds, made to indict the king, so neither account stands alone as the poem's verdict.

note: The couplet says the sweet words of women who seek a man's wealth and not his love bring him harm; here a courtesan writes to a man who has lost his wealth, asking only what her fault was, and he judges her blameless and himself at fault.
teaches: The pair sets the Kural's rule that a courtesan's sweet words are for wealth against a courtesan's letter written after the wealth is gone, so the epic tests the rule on the one case it cannot explain and has the man himself withdraw the charge.

gains.a: Kovalan's verdict that Madhavi is faultless gains force from the rule it overturns: he clears her against the expected judgment of her class
gains.b: the couplet gains its limit case, a courtesan whose plea comes when the man has nothing left to give

note: Maduraikkanchi's dawn in Madurai has the Brahmins chanting the Veda, the elephants fed and the horses in their stalls (பணைநிலைப் புரவி); the epic's travellers hear the same dawn, the Vedic chant and the stalled horses' neighing among it, from outside the walls.
teaches: The epic reuses the Sangam catalogue of Madurai's dawn, phrase for phrase in places, but moves its hearer from the king the idyll counsels on impermanence to the strangers whom the city will destroy, so the idyll's warning that such splendour passes is carried out on the city itself.

gains.a: the catalogue gains its pedigree: Madurai's dawn is a set piece of the Sangam city, heard in the epic as the city's settled glory
gains.b: the idyll's counsel that wealth and splendour do not last gains a story in which this very Madurai, with its stalled horses and chanting Brahmins, is burned

note: The Paripadal fragment asks whether Madurai's fame can ever prove false as long as the Vaigai flows; the epic calls the Vaigai the never-failing (பொய்யா) creeper of the clan and has her hide her tears for the wife the city will wrong.
teaches: The Paripadal makes the flowing Vaigai the pledge that Madurai's fame cannot fail; the epic keeps the river unfailing but makes her the first to know that the city's justice will fail, so the pledge passes from the city to the river alone.

gains.a: the epic's 'never-failing' river gains the old pledge it echoes, which shows what the river's hidden grief is a grief for
gains.b: the fragment's confidence gains a story that separates the river's constancy from the city's fame

note: The Vaigai hides tears as if knowing the young wife's fate; in the court the king, called the lord of the Vaigai, loses his life at the hearing of her words.
teaches: The pair shows the river grieving at the entry for the wife and the river's lord dying at her word in the court, so the Vaigai frames Madurai's story from the woman's arrival to the king's death, siding with her in silence before he hears her.

note: At the moat the flowers weep and the flags wave as if saying 'do not come'; in the palace the queen dreams of the umbrella and sceptre falling and the gate bell shaking.
teaches: The pair shows the epic sending warnings to both sides of the coming wrong, to the strangers at the walls and to the queen in the palace, and having neither heeded, so the catastrophe is foreseen in nature and in sleep yet still unfolds.

note: The patikam announces as the epic's third moral that the deed of former birth comes in wrath and feeds its fruit (ஊழ்வினை உருத்துவந்து ஊட்டும்); Kavunthi says the hard deed feeds its fruit and that the unlearned are bewildered when the evil deed comes in wrath (உருத்த காலை).
teaches: The moral Ilango states from outside the story is first spoken inside it by a nun who uses it to console Kovalan for a hardship already past, so the reader hears the thesis as comfort just before it becomes the account of his death.

note: Kavunthi assures Kovalan that, unlike the dice-ruined king who left his wife in the forest by strong karma, he has a life never parted from his wife; in the Pandya's court Kannaki says her husband came to Madurai driven by ஊழ்வினை and was killed.
teaches: The nun's karma, invoked to show that Kovalan's lot is better than the exiled king's, is the same force Kannaki names when she stands parted from him for ever, so the consolation becomes the epic's irony: the karma Kavunthi uses to excuse a parting is already moving toward a worse one.

note: The couplet asks why those who take good fortune as good grieve when ill fortune comes; Kavunthi says the learned do not despair when they eat the fruit of their deeds, while the unlearned are bewildered when the evil deed ripens.
teaches: The couplet's argument for calm rests on consistency between good and bad fortune, while the nun rests it on learning and adds a cause, desire for women and food, so the pair shows the Kural's equanimity before fate being turned into a renouncer's diagnosis of where suffering comes from.

gains.a: Kavunthi's counsel gains a compact general rule behind it, so her talk of the learned not despairing reads as a recognised teaching rather than private comfort
gains.b: the couplet gains a hearer and an occasion, a ruined husband in a strange city, and a second argument for calm that it does not make, that the suffering was earned by desire

note: The quatrain says that because a wife cannot be put away even if she lacks virtue and bears no child, the learned called marriage கடி; Kavunthi says the pains of parting and union belong only to those joined with women, not to the strong who live alone.
teaches: Both make marriage a source of suffering from which the solitary are free, but the Naladiyar argues it to recommend renunciation while Kavunthi states it to a married man and then sends him on with his wife, so the pair shows the renouncer's diagnosis offered without its prescription.

gains.a: the nun's claim gains the ethical tradition's own argument for why the bond brings pain, that it cannot be undone
gains.b: the quatrain gains a case where its view is spoken to a husband who is not told to leave his wife, which limits how far the ascetic diagnosis is meant to bind a householder

note: In Puhar Madhavi received by the king's rule the thousand and eight kalanju (ஆயிரத்து எண்கழஞ்சு ... எட்டுக்கடை நிறுத்த) with the talaikkol, and Kovalan bought her garland; in Madurai the talaikkol dancers receive the same sum (எட்டுக் கடைநிறுத்த ஆயிரத் தெண்கழஞ்சு) every day by fixed rule, and both passages praise the house as வடுநீங்கு சிறப்பின்.
teaches: The price that marked Madhavi's debut as a singular royal honour, and began Kovalan's ruin, turns out in Madurai to be the standing daily fee of a whole profession, and Kovalan walks past it as a man who has already paid it.

note: The couplet says those whose knowledge is refined by good sense do not sink into the common charms of women who are everyone's; the epic says that in the net of the dancers' glances even ascetics' hard-won wisdom turns to something else.
teaches: The Kural makes refined knowledge a protection against the courtesan, and the epic's street denies the guarantee by naming ascetics among those caught, so the pair shows the rule holding only for the wise who stay away, not for any wisdom that walks into the street.

gains.a: the epic's hyperbole gains its edge from the rule it breaks: the ascetic's fall matters because wisdom was supposed to protect
gains.b: the couplet gains a limit: its protection is a claim about who abstains, and the epic shows a learned art that even the disciplined are said to fall before

note: The Maduraikkanchi's courtesans of Madurai drain the wealth of rich young men and leave them like bees leaving a spent flower; the epic's courtesans of the same city are masters of the two styles of dance and its treatises, paid a fixed fee by rule, before whom kings bow.
