teaches: The Sangam poem sees Madurai's courtesans as the drain on the young rich, while the epic sees them as an institution of learned art with a royal tariff, so the pair shows the epic recasting a city's vice as its high culture, the very shift that made Madhavi's art and Kovalan's ruin the same thing.

gains.a: the epic's dancers' quarter gains its older picture, in which the same women of the same city appear as takers of wealth, which the epic's praise silently suppresses
gains.b: the Sangam poem's courtesans gain an account of their art and its rules, which the poem, seeing them only from the side of the spent lover, does not give

note: Madurai's gem street is full of men who tell gems apart by the flaws the treatises name; before the king Kannaki says her anklet holds gems, the queen's holds pearls, and when she breaks it a gem flies to the king's mouth and he declares himself the thief.
teaches: The city Kovalan admires is one where every stone is judged by rule, yet the king condemns him on a goldsmith's word without testing the anklet, and the truth comes only when Kannaki breaks it, so the pairing shows the failure was not of the city's knowledge but of the king's will to use it.

note: The Maduraikkanchi lists in Madurai's four streets (நால்வேறு தெருவினும்) the shell-cutters, gem-borers, goldsmiths, gold-assayers and cloth-sellers; the epic closes its tour with the gold-assayers, cloth street, grain street and the four streets (நால்வேறு தெருவும்).
teaches: The epic follows the Sangam catalogue of Madurai's trades down to the four streets, but where the Sangam poem lists them as the plenty of a victorious Pandya, the epic shows them through a stranger about to be condemned by one of these trades, so the inherited praise of the city becomes the setting of its fall.

gains.a: the epic's tour gains a source and a measure: it is the classic praise of Madurai, which makes its turn toward ruin a turn against a known tradition
gains.b: the Sangam catalogue gains a later reading in which the gold-assayers it lists among the city's glories include the trade that will bring about the city's burning

note: Kovalan reports a Madurai free of evil whose kings' sceptre is straight (கோலின் செம்மை, தீதுதீர் மதுரை); the Pandya, after killing him, declares himself the thief and his guarding failed.
teaches: The straightness of the Pandya sceptre is first vouched for by the man it will kill, on the day before his death, so the epic lets the victim's trust in the city's justice set the measure by which the king condemns himself.

note: Maadalan, finding no cause for Kovalan's suffering in his good deeds of this life, asks whether it is the fruit of a former birth; the patikam's goddess names that cause, a curse from a former birth.
teaches: The epic reaches its doctrine of former deeds by elimination: a witness who knows only Kovalan's good acts can explain his ruin only by a past birth, and the patikam later confirms the guess with a named curse, so the karmic cause is offered as what remains when the visible life acquits the sufferer.

note: The crossroads spirit of Puhar announces that it seizes false witnesses and others with its noose and devours them; here it seizes one and refuses Kovalan's offer of his own life in exchange.
teaches: The spirit's announced punishment proves rigid in practice: it will not take a good man's life even when he offers it, so the pair shows its justice as exact matching of deed to doer, with no place for the substitution that Kovalan's generosity proposes.

note: Kovalan dreams of his wife's distress, his seized garment and a death-ride, then release and his daughter's renunciation; the Pandya queen dreams of the umbrella and sceptre falling and the sky in disorder.
teaches: The same ruin is dreamed from both sides of the verdict: the victim's dream runs past death into release and his daughter's turn to the Buddha, the queen's stops at the fall of the sceptre, so the dreams divide between them the epic's two morals of ripening deeds and failed kingship.

note: The couplet says a wife who worships her husband rather than a god can bid the rain fall; Kavunthi calls Kannaki a deity fairer than any she has seen and quotes a saying that where chaste wives live the sky never fails and kings' victory never decays.
teaches: Where the couplet keeps the wife below the gods yet gives her command of the rain, Kavunthi makes the chaste wife herself the deity and extends her power from rain to the king's victory, which is the very extension the epic will turn against the Pandya when that power destroys his city.

gains.a: Kavunthi's saying gains a source for its rain clause in a couplet that ties the wife's power to her refusal of other gods
gains.b: the couplet gains a reading in which the chaste wife's power reaches past nature to the fortunes of kings, and so becomes a threat as well as a blessing

note: Kavunthi quotes the saying that where chaste wives live the kings' victory does not decay; the patikam says that because Kannaki was a pathini she burned Madurai and the Pandya fell.
teaches: The saying Kavunthi offers as a pledge of the king's safety is reversed in the same city, where a pathini's presence ends the king, so the pair shows that the epic makes the chaste wife's power conditional on the king's justice rather than a blessing that protects any throne.

note: The couplet holds that giving is good even if there were no higher world; the charana proves the worth of a gift by showing the god it produced, with the monkey's hand still on him.
teaches: The Kural deliberately cuts giving loose from any reward in a higher world, while the Jain tale makes a visible heavenly body the evidence for the gift's worth, so the pair separates two defences of giving, one that needs no world beyond and one that rests on it.

gains.a: the tale's proof by reward is set against a view that does not need the proof, which shows how much its case rests on the heaven it displays
gains.b: the couplet's hypothetical 'even if there were no higher world' gains a concrete rival: a contemporary teaching that answers the hypothetical by producing the higher world as witness

note: Tirumular says merit and sin both come with one into birth and both must be cut at the root to reach the Lord; the Jain tale shows merit carrying a monkey to a human birth and then to a god's body that keeps the monkey's hand.
teaches: The god who still bears a monkey's hand makes visible Tirumular's point that merit, too, works by giving births: the reward of the gift is another body marked by the last one, which is why the Saiva verse ranks merit as a bond to be uprooted rather than a road to the Lord.

gains.a: the tale's god with the monkey's hand gains a reading as a sign that merit's fruit is still a birth, not only a proof of the gift's power
gains.b: Tirumular's abstract claim that merit binds gains a concrete image of a merit-made body that carries the history of its former birth

note: The Jain debater in the Manimekalai says release is to block the inflow of both good and bad deeds and wear out past ones; the Jain charana of the Silappathikaram tells a gift whose merit leads to a god's birth.
teaches: Held together, the Jain doctrine stated in debate and the Jain tale told for lay hearers show the two levels of the same teaching: the doctrine counts good deeds among the bonds, while the tale for householders displays the heavenly birth that good deeds bring, and Kavunthi reserves release itself for those who turn to dharma (line 197).

note: The couplet calls a fort that which cannot be taken by siege, storm or work on those inside; Madurai's gate is lined with every engine against attack as Kannaki passes through it.
teaches: The epic fills Madurai's walls with the defences the Kural's fort requires at the very moment it lets in the woman whose wrong will burn the city from within, so the pair shows a danger the couplet's three threats do not name: an injustice of the king's own that no engine on the wall can repel.

gains.a: the list of engines gains a measure: by the Kural's standard the city is a perfect fort, which sharpens the irony of its fall
gains.b: the couplet's account of impregnability gains a case where the fort is lost through no siege at all, but through the king's own wrong

note: Kavunthi gave Kannaki as a ward to the herdswoman and charged her to bathe, dress and mother her; Maadari here receives her as a ward, has her bathed and settles her.
teaches: The ascetic's charge is carried out point by point, so the refuge fails not through any lapse of the guardian but on the very day she is kept as promised, and the harm comes from the city's justice, not the host's house.
audit_text_issue: silappathikaram:15:130-147 is not a marked unit; it straddles 15:115-130 and 15:131-148.

note: Kannaki sprinkles water on the ground as if to clear the earth-woman's distress (மண்ணக மடந்தை, line 40); at the killing the earth-woman's grief grows as Kovalan's blood pours over her (line 215).
teaches: The earth that Kannaki soothes with water at his last meal is soaked with his blood the same day, so the poet makes one figure measure the distance between her care and his death.

note: The herders liken Kovalan and Kannaki to the dark god and the lamp of their clan who relieved his distress; in the next kaathai Maadari dances the kuravai of Krishna and Pinnai so that Kannaki may see it, to ward off a coming harm.
teaches: The herders' wonder at their guests becomes a rite: having seen the couple as Krishna and his consort, they dance that pair's kuravai to avert the harm their omens foretell, which has already fallen.

note: Kovalan asks whether his ruin is illusion or a strong former deed (வல்வினை கொல்லோ); at his death the narrator answers that his former deed came in wrath (பண்டை ஊழ்வினை உருத்து).
teaches: The question the victim cannot answer is answered by the narrator only over his body, so the karma he half suspects is confirmed only when it can no longer be acted on, and he had meanwhile blamed himself.

note: The couplet says one who slipped by not guarding beforehand will grieve later over his own fault (தன்பிழை); Kovalan, now in Madurai, grieves that he grew heedless (பொச்சாப் புண்டு) and failed his parents and his wife.
teaches: The couplet makes late regret the heedless man's whole penalty and puts the fault in him alone, while the epic has the heedless man grieve and still lose his life, and lets him ask in the same breath whether karma rather than his own lapse has brought him here.

gains.a: Kovalan's confession gains a name and a rule: his is the heedlessness whose fruit is regret that comes too late
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where regret is not the end of the penalty, and where the one who grieves over his own fault also suspects a former deed

note: In Puhar Kovalan blamed his ruin on sporting with a deceitful woman and the shame of lost wealth; in Madurai he blames his own heedlessness, bad company and disobedience to his parents.
teaches: Between the two confessions the blame moves from Madhavi to himself, so the road to Madurai is shown changing his account of his fall even as it carries him to his death.

note: The couplet makes the householder the support of renouncers, the needy and the dead; Kannaki says that without her husband she lost giving to the virtuous, tending Brahmins, receiving ascetics and welcoming guests.
teaches: The couplet speaks of the householder as one person, while Kannaki shows that a wife alone could not keep those duties, so the householder's dharma the Kural assigns depends on the pair being together.

gains.a: Kannaki's list gains its standing: what she lost is the very support the Kural makes the householder's office
gains.b: the couplet gains its cost when the house is broken: the wife left at home cannot be the support it describes

audit_text_issue: 16:65-66 are doubtful, but the link doesn't rest on them.

note: The couplet defines the woman who guards herself, tends her husband, keeps their good name and does not flag; Kannaki hid her grief before his parents and followed him without gainsaying him though his conduct was unworthy.
teaches: The couplet does not say what such a wife owes a husband who wrongs her; Kannaki's answer is to name his fault and follow him all the same, so the epic shows the couplet's tireless wife carried into the ruin her husband makes.

gains.a: Kannaki's hidden grief and silence before her in-laws gain a name as keeping the household's good name, part of what defines the wife in the couplet
gains.b: the couplet gains the hard case it leaves open, a husband who has failed her, and one answer to it

note: In Puhar, Kannaki offered her anklets and Kovalan resolved to recover his lost wealth with them as capital in Madurai; here he takes one anklet to exchange.
teaches: The plan made in the bedchamber as a fresh start is carried out here and leads straight to the goldsmith, so the means of recovery chosen in Puhar becomes the instrument of his death.

note: Kovalan meets a humped bull in the street and does not know it as an ill omen; in the next kaathai the herdswomen see the tears of their humped bull and say a harm is coming.
teaches: The same beast gives the same warning to two kinds of people, and only the herders, whose knowledge it is, read it, so the epic makes reading the omen a matter of birth and has the warning understood only after the harm is done.

note: The goldsmith declares that the anklet fits none but the queen; in the court Kannaki's anklet, broken, shows gems where the queen's holds pearls.
teaches: The craftsman's expert verdict, the only evidence against Kovalan, is shown false by the anklet itself, so the case is undone by the very object it was built on.

note: The quatrain says that when people who know what should be known still do blameworthy things, it comes from their own former deeds; the epic says the king inquired into nothing because it was the time for a deed to ripen.
teaches: The quatrain traces the knowing man's wrong to his own deeds, while the epic leaves open whose deed ripens, the king's or Kovalan's caught in its net, so one man's karma may be what makes another man err.

gains.a: the king's failure gains a received explanation: knowing men do wrong when former deeds press them, and blame still attaches
gains.b: the quatrain gains a case where the deed that ripens may not be the wrongdoer's own, which its wording does not consider

note: The couplet calls stealth a dark knowledge (காரறிவாண்மை) absent in those who love measure; the goldsmith, the real thief, lectures the guards on the eight arts of thieves as an unmatched skill.
teaches: The Kural grants that stealth is a kind of knowledge, and the epic shows that knowledge turned from taking goods to taking a life, as the thief's expertise in theft persuades the guards to kill an innocent man.

gains.a: the goldsmith's lecture gains a name for what it displays: cleverness that is still darkness
gains.b: the couplet's dark knowledge gains a use it does not mention, deceiving those who keep the law

note: The patikam sets as the epic's third moral that a former deed comes in wrath and makes its doer eat (ஊழ்வினை உருத்துவந்து ஊட்டும்); Kovalan's death is told in the same words (பண்டை ஊழ்வினை உருத்து).
teaches: The moral stated as a thesis at the outset is spoken again in its own words at the death, and in the same line as the king's bent sceptre, so the epic gives its first and third morals as two causes of one event.

note: The quatrain says an old deed seeks out its doer as a calf finds its mother among many cows; Kovalan's former deed reaches him through a goldsmith's lie, a king's hasty word and a drunken guard's sword.
teaches: The quatrain's deed finds its doer by itself, while the epic shows it arriving through other people's free and blameworthy acts, so karma here does not excuse the hands it works through.

gains.a: Kovalan's death gains the quatrain's image of the deed that cannot miss its doer, which explains why every escape fails
gains.b: the quatrain's calf gains a path: the seeking deed travels through other people's lies and violence

note: The venba says both deeds will reach their doer and bids men turn to good dharma; Tirumular says that when the two deeds stand balanced, grace comes as the guru and frees the soul from them.
teaches: The venba's remedy for the two deeds is to do more good, which on its wording still returns to the doer, while Tirumular's is grace that comes when good and evil are balanced and ends them, so the pair sets merit-making against release by grace; the conflict holds if நல்லறம் is read as producing good fruit.

gains.a: the venba's moral gains a contrast that shows it offers no escape from deeds, only better ones
gains.b: Tirumular's balancing of the two deeds gains a plain statement of the view it moves beyond, that good deeds are the answer to karma

note: The Kalittokai's herders open their bull-catch by praising the Pandya who removed the tiger and the bow and set his fish in their place; the epic's herders open their kuravai on the Pandya whose fish is inscribed on the Himalaya beside the tiger and the bow.
teaches: The same herders' praise of the Pandya emblem is kept in the epic but with the boast of conquest removed, so a work that follows all three kingdoms keeps the mullai custom of beginning with the king while setting the three emblems side by side.

gains.a: the opening's praise of the king gains a precedent: Sangam herders already began the bull-catch songs with the Pandya and his fish
gains.b: the poem's claim that the fish displaced the tiger and the bow gains a later telling that does not keep it, so the claim reads as praise rather than settled history

note: Both pledge a herd girl to the man who, unafraid of the black bull's fury, takes it (காரி கதன் அஞ்சான்); in the Kalittokai her kin give her to the catcher, in the epic no bull is penned.
teaches: The epic keeps the bull-catch pledge word for word but drops the contest, so a herders' marriage custom survives as the names of dance roles in a rite against ill omen.

gains.a: the pledge gains its origin in a real contest in which a girl's kin give her to the man who takes the bull
gains.b: the custom gains a later life, recited over girls as a ritual formula with no bull and no catcher

note: In the idyll the old women seek an omen and hear a herd girl tell a distressed tethered calf that its mothers will soon come; in the epic the herd's own signs foretell sorrow and the herdswoman dances so that the cows' and calves' distress may pass.
teaches: Both read a calf's distress among the herds as a sign about an absent man, but the idyll's chance word promises a return and the epic's signs announce a death the herders do not yet know, so the mullai omen-scene is turned from hope to loss.

gains.a: the rite gains its convention: in mullai poetry an omen among the herds speaks of an absent husband, which lets the signs point at Kovalan without naming him
gains.b: the idyll's comforting omen gains a counterpart in which the same kind of sign foretells a husband's death and a rite fails to turn it

note: The first signs, milk that will not set and a weeping bull, come on the morning after Kovalan has been cut down at the king's word.
teaches: Read after the killing, the omens are no forecast but the herd registering a death its keepers have not heard of, so the reader holds the meaning the characters lack.

note: The herders' omens fall in the cowshed (the cattle's bells drop, the cows tremble); the queen's fall in the court (the falling umbrella and sceptre, the trembling gate bell).
teaches: The same wrong is signalled first in the house of the victim's hosts and later in the king's own house, each through the things of its own life, so the omens move from the cowshed to the throne as the consequence nears the king.

note: The kuravai is danced so that the coming distress may pass; at the dance's end an uproar from the town brings the news of Kovalan's death.
teaches: The rite meant to turn the sorrow away becomes the frame in which the sorrow arrives, so the herders' remedy is shown powerless against a deed already done.

note: Aiyai and her mother likened Kannaki to the one of their clan who relieved the gem-coloured god's distress in the Yamuna; here the girl cast as Pinnai garlands the girl cast as Mayavan while Kannaki looks on.
teaches: Because the herdswomen had already seen Kannaki as Pinnai and Kovalan as the dark god, the dance's Pinnai garlanding Mayavan plays out before Kannaki the union that has, unknown to her, already ended.

note: The herdswomen pray that the Pandya's drum bring victory day after day; the same day that king's verdict has killed Kovalan, and the next morning he names himself the thief and dies.
teaches: The closing blessing is the stock wish of a herders' song, but placed on the day the sceptre has bent it becomes a prayer for a king already doomed, so the reader hears the epic's justice theme inside a rite meant only to save the cattle.

note: Kalittokai 104 ends its herders' kuravai by praising the god of the ancient bright discus and wishing that the world take the one word of the Pandya with the thunder-loud drum; the epic's kuravai to the discus-holder (கதிர்திகிரி, line 99) ends in the same wish for the Pandya's drum.
teaches: The epic keeps the Sangam mullai close, god first and then the Pandya's drum, but moves the kuravai from the joy after the bull-catch to a rite against ill omens, so the inherited blessing now carries dread rather than celebration.

gains.a: the epic's close is shown to be a set form of the Madurai herders' kuravai, not Ilango's invention, which makes its irony a turn on a known convention
gains.b: the Kalittokai's conventional wish for the Pandya is shown to be one that a story could test: the epic sets it on the day the same dynasty's justice fails

audit_text_issue: The note cites கதிர்திகிரி at line 99, outside the printed unit 148-159.

note: Patitruppattu 11 likens Cheralathan's sea-raid and felling of the guarded kadambu to Murugan cutting down Sur in the sea; the epic's herdswomen tell the same Chera deed and say he churned the sea, Vishnu's deed.
teaches: Both poets lift the Chera's kadambu raid into a god's sea-deed, but each picks the god of its own setting: the Patitruppattu's war poem chooses Murugan, the herders' kuravai chooses Maal, so the same royal memory is divinised differently by genre.

gains.a: the epic's bare 'the Chera who threw down the kadambu' gains the Sangam record of who did it and how it was praised, while the epic itself does not name Neduncheralathan
gains.b: the Patitruppattu's comparison gains a later witness showing the kadambu raid still famous enough to be sung by Pandya herdswomen beside the other two crowns

note: Kural 9 says a head that does not bow at the feet of the eight-qualitied one is as useless as a sense organ without its power; the kuravai asks what ear it is that has not heard Thirumaal's praise, and goes on to the eye and the tongue.
teaches: The couplet's simile, an organ without its function, becomes in the kuravai a definition carried through ear, eye and tongue, so the claim that the body's parts exist for worship is spelled out organ by organ and bound to one named god.

gains.a: the epic's refrain gains a recognised ethical form: it is the Kural's argument that an organ is defined by its proper act, applied to devotion
gains.b: the couplet's unnamed god and single organ gain a sung extension, where the same test is applied to each sense and given a sectarian object

note: Paripadal 3 says the god is everything and the essence within everything and calls him one full of maayam (மாயமார் அனையை); the kuravai asks whether the churner of the sea bound by Asodhai's churning rope is maayam, for it bewilders.
teaches: The hymn treats the god's maayam as a doctrine to be stated, his being all things at once, while the herdswomen meet it as an unanswered question in a domestic scene, so the same paradox is shown both as learned theology and as village wonder.

gains.a: the kuravai's question gains an answer it does not give: the hymn's account of why one god can be both the cosmic churner and a bound child
gains.b: the hymn's abstract claim gains a concrete case, a single hand that churned the ocean and was tied with a butter-churn's cord

note: The kuravai ends praising the Pandya's victorious drum and asking the god to remove the herd's distress; the woman who led it comes back from the river with news of the Pandya's guards killing an innocent man.
teaches: Set side by side, the herdswomen's blessing on the king's victory is overtaken within lines by the report of his injustice, so the rite meant to avert evil omens is shown failing at the very moment it is completed.

note: The townsfolk say Kovalan is a thief (கள்வனாம்); the sun's voice answers கள்வனோ அல்லன்.
teaches: The kaathai sets the hearsay of men, which the king acted on, against the testimony of the all-seeing sun, so the case against Kovalan is answered by a higher witness before it ever reaches the king's court.

note: The rumour says he stole an anklet from the palace; in the next kaathai Kannaki tells the women of the city that he was no thief and was killed for the price of her own anklet.
teaches: Kannaki turns the private news she received into a public counter-charge, correcting the one fact the rumour got wrong (whose anklet it was), which is the fact the trial will turn on.

note: The sun's voice says bright fire will eat this city; in the vow, the fire god appears and says he was ordered long ago to eat the city on the day it wronged the great pathini.
teaches: The burning of Madurai is announced twice by gods, first by the sun as witness and then by the fire as agent, so Kannaki's act fulfils a sentence already spoken from above rather than a private revenge.

note: Here Kannaki names only the king's error as the cause; before the king she says her husband came to the city driven by ஊழ்வினை.
teaches: In private grief Kannaki blames the king alone, but in court she joins karma to his fault, so the two causes the patikam names are shown held by one speaker at two moments, not only by narrator and character.

note: The queen of Bhoothapandiyan refuses the widow's life of alli food and the gravel bed and chooses the pyre; Kannaki asks whether she too must waste away like the widows who keep those observances.
teaches: Both widows refuse the observances of kaimmai, but the Sangam queen turns to the pyre while Kannaki turns to the sun and the king, so the epic moves the wife's refusal of widowhood from death beside the husband to a demand for justice.

gains.a: the lament gains the Sangam measure of what the widows' observances were and that a high-born wife could reject them
gains.b: the poem's choice between widowhood and the pyre gains a third way, a widow who rejects both to accuse the king

audit_text_issue: The marker flags the sense of 41 (அறனென்னும் மடவோய்); the link does not rest on it.

note: Kannaki's vow to see her husband and hear a faultless word from him is kept in the vision, where he speaks only of her faded face and bids her stay.
teaches: The vow is fulfilled in form but not in substance: the dead husband's word clears no one, so the proof of innocence has to come from Kannaki's own plea at court.

note: The townspeople's bent sceptre and cool umbrella breeding heat are the omens the queen sees falling in her dream in the next kaathai.
teaches: The same signs of ruin appear first as the street's verdict in waking speech and then as the palace's dream, so the city knows the king's fall before the court does.

note: The city sees Kannaki weeping beyond bearing (அல்லலுற் றாற்றா தழுவாளை), the very condition the couplet names as the force that wears away a king's wealth.
teaches: The couplet's tears work slowly as an abrasive on wealth, but the epic makes one woman's tears the moment the people themselves declare the sceptre bent, the first step to the city's burning.

gains.a: the citizens' grief gains a known rule that such tears are a weapon against the ruler
gains.b: the couplet's general 'those who suffer' gains a single witnessed scene in which a whole city reads the tears as a verdict on the king

note: In Puram 72 the Sangam Pandya Nedunjeliyan of Talaiyalanganam curses himself, should he fail in his vow, to be a king whose people find no cool shade and spread his blame (குடிபழி தூற்றும்); the epic's Madurai spreads the blame of its king (மன்பழி தூற்றுங் குடி) and finds his cool umbrella breeding heat. The two kings share a title, not an identity: the epic's Nedunjeliyan is not the Sangam one.
teaches: The Sangam king's conditional self-curse, a boast of what will never happen, becomes in the epic a description of what has happened to a later Pandya, so the formula of royal disgrace moves from oath to fulfilment.

gains.a: the citizens' words gain the weight of an old Pandya oath that names exactly this disgrace
gains.b: the oath's imagined penalty gains a story showing a Pandya city actually blaming its king

note: The quatrain's old deed seeks out its own doer as a calf finds its mother among many cows; Kannaki laments a deed to be eaten that reached her husband through the king's fault.
teaches: Where the quatrain sends the deed straight back to the one who did it, the epic interposes a guilty king between deed and fruit, so karma and the ruler's fault both stand as causes of one death.

gains.a: Kannaki's 'deed that must be eaten' gains the quatrain's account of how a deed finds its owner
gains.b: the quatrain gains a case where the deed arrives through another's wrongdoing, which its image of the calf leaves out

note: Both show a wife at her husband's wounded chest at the edge of night; the Puram wife reads the omens and dreads the widow's life, while Kannaki asks who will name the deed and blames the king.
teaches: The Sangam lament by the wounded body looks ahead to widowhood, but Kannaki's lament at the same scene turns outward into a charge against the king, so the old mourning form becomes the opening of a plea.

gains.a: Kannaki's lament gains the old shape of the wife's watch by the wounded husband, against which its turn to accusation shows
gains.b: the Puram wife's private grief gains a counterpart in which the same scene is made public and political

audit_text_issue: The marker flags both units as uncertain in sense.

note: Kannaki says she does not know the cruel deed behind her loss; the patikam's goddess tells the grieving pathini it was a curse laid in a former birth by the wife of Sangaman.
teaches: The heroine laments in ignorance of the cause the poem's frame has already disclosed, so the reader judges her accusation of the king knowing a second cause she does not.

note: The patikam's goddess says Kannaki will see her husband only in the form of the gods; here he rises among a host of immortals (பல்லமரர் குழாத்துளான்) on the day of his death.
teaches: The vision anticipates the reunion the goddess limits to divine form, and Kannaki's refusal to join him until her anger cools shows the reunion withheld by her own choice, not only by the curse's term.

note: The closing lines recall the evil dream (இடருற்ற தீக்கனா) in which Kannaki saw a false word laid on her husband in a great city.
teaches: Kannaki goes to the king remembering the dream that foretold the false charge, so the dream that was dismissed now becomes her warrant for the confrontation it did not foresee.

note: The queen's dream of the falling umbrella and sceptre is fulfilled in the king's lowered umbrella and slack sceptre at the verdict.
teaches: The omen comes first in the queen's private dream and is fulfilled the same hour in public, so the fall of justice is shown as already decided before Kannaki speaks.

note: Both use the falling star and the broken royal umbrella as signs of a king's death.
teaches: The epic borrows the Sangam stock of royal death-omens but moves them into a dream before the death, turning the elegist's after-the-fact proof of grief into a warning that comes too late to be heeded.

gains.a: its dream gains a traditional sense: these are the recognised signs that a king will die, not private fears
gains.b: the poem's omens gain a narrative use, where the same signs foretell a death caused by the king's own wrong

note: Kannaki vowed to see the cruel king and ask him the reason; here she stands at his gate and sends in her charge.
teaches: The vow made beside the body is kept as a legal summons through the gatekeeper, so her grief is shown taking the form of a formal case rather than a lament.

note: Kannaki's 'he who relieved the distress of the bird' repeats the Purananuru's praise formula for the Chola's ancestor (புள்ளுறு புன்கண் தீர்த்த).
teaches: The epic takes a genealogical compliment that a Sangam poet paid a Chola king and turns it into a legal precedent that a Chola woman holds against a Pandya, showing the ancestor-legend working as a standard of justice across kingdoms.

gains.a: Kannaki's precedent gains the weight of an established praise-formula of the Chola line
gains.b: the formula gains a use beyond flattery: it becomes the measure by which another king is judged

note: The narrator says the king did not inquire because it was the hour of karma's fruit (தேரான் ஆகி); Kannaki calls him the king who did not inquire (தேரா மன்னா).
teaches: The same failure to inquire is excused by karma in the narrator's voice and charged as guilt in Kannaki's, and she herself also names karma, so the epic holds both causes together rather than choosing one.

note: The couplet makes inquiry (தேர்ந்துசெய்) part of what justice is; Kannaki's first words to the king name him as the one who did not inquire.
teaches: The couplet treats inquiry as within the ruler's power, while the epic shows a ruler failing it in an hour the narrator calls karma's ripening, and still holds him answerable for it.

gains.a: Kannaki's charge gains a definition: what the king failed is the first step of justice itself
gains.b: the couplet gains a case that tests it: a king fails to inquire under the press of former deeds and is still judged by the couplet's standard

note: Kannaki dreamed that she spoke before the king and that harm came to the king and the city with him; here she speaks before the king and he falls.
teaches: Her dream foretold both the plea and the harm beyond the king, so the king's fall here is only the first part of what the dream foretold, with the city's burning still to come.

note: The narrator's venba says the never-bent sceptre bent as the fruit of former karma; the king says only that he heeded the goldsmith and is himself the thief.
teaches: The narrator assigns the bent sceptre to karma while the king, judging himself, assigns it wholly to his own act, so the epic lets the wrongdoer refuse the excuse its narrator offers.

note: The couplet says a ruler who does not examine and do justice perishes by himself (தானே கெடும்); the Pandya, who did not examine, pronounces his own death.
teaches: The epic makes the couplet's 'perishes by himself' literal: no enemy or court condemns the king, he passes the sentence on himself the moment his error is shown, and he was easily approached, so only the failure to examine undoes him.

gains.a: the king's self-sentence gains a rule behind it: ruin comes from within to the king who does not examine
gains.b: the couplet gains a scene that separates its two conditions, an accessible king who still fails to examine, and shows the ruin as self-inflicted in act as well as in result

note: The patikam's first moral, that dharma becomes death to those who err in kingship, is restated here as a common saying proved true.
teaches: The moral announced at the outset as the poem's thesis is here called a saying of the assemblies now proved, so the book frames its plot as the demonstration of a received maxim.
audit_text_issue: The venba's sense is flagged uncertain, but the line the link rests on (92-93) is clear.

note: The venba's 'queen of the king' and the speaker 'of harsh deeds' recur at the opening of the next kaathai, where Kannaki addresses the queen and calls herself கொடுவினை யாட்டியேன்.
teaches: The next kaathai's opening supports reading this venba as Kannaki's words to the queen, and shows the threat 'see what I will do' carried into the vow against the city.

note: The couplet says all pains rest on those who caused pain; the venba says dharma is death to the wrongdoer, but the speaker, who did no wrong, calls herself one of harsh deeds and the wrongdoer's queen suffers too.
teaches: The epic agrees that harm returns to the one who did it, but shows it spreading to the innocent queen and to the victim who names her own karma, so the couplet's neat return of pain to its doer becomes a wider ruin.

gains.a: the venba's maxim gains the couplet's general rule that harm returns to its doer
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where pain does reach the doer, yet also those around him, which its own wording does not consider

audit_text_issue: Marker flags the venba's sense as uncertain; the addressee/subject of வயவேந்தன் தேவி is ambiguous.

note: The couplet calls the tears of those who cannot bear their suffering a weapon that wears away wealth; here a widow's tears and words take the king's life.
teaches: The couplet's slow wearing-away of a bad king's wealth by the people's tears becomes, in the epic, the instant death of the king at one wronged woman's tears and words.

gains.a: the venba gains a moral law behind its marvel: tears of the wronged are a force against an unjust king
gains.b: the couplet gains an extreme case, where the weapon of tears acts at once and on the king's life, not slowly on his wealth

audit_text_issue: Bridge to the Kural printed with no gains clause.

note: Kannaki states the forenoon-afternoon law of returning harm, in other words than the couplet's, as her warning to the Pandya's house.
teaches: The couplet's தாமே says the harm returns of itself with no agent, but the epic puts the law in the mouth of the woman who will herself bring the harm back that same day, so the impersonal return of a deed is shown working through a wronged person's act.

gains.a: her threat gains the standing of a known moral law rather than private revenge
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where the returning harm has a human executor and falls on a whole city, not only on the doer

note: Both tell of the husband of Karikal's line seized by the Kaveri flood at a festival; the akam poem leaves him taken, the epic has the sea bring him back to the wife who followed.
teaches: The Sangam memory of a lover lost to the river, which an akam courtesan uses as an image of a man taken away for good, is completed in the epic with a restoration won by the wife's steadfastness, turning a story of loss into an exemplum of chastity's power.

gains.a: the clipped allusion gains its back-story: the flood at Kazhar before Karikal in which the husband was seized
gains.b: the akam image gains a later ending in which the sea gives back what the river took, showing how the tale was retold as a chastity legend

note: Both are vanjinam vows in the conditional form 'if I do not, may I', one by a Pandya Nedunjeliyan before battle, one by Kannaki against a Pandya; the epic's king is not shown to be the Talaiyalanganattu victor of the puram poem.
teaches: The puram king stakes his own name as a just king on winning, while Kannaki stakes her name as a pathini on unmaking a king, so the epic turns the royal oath-form against the royal house and makes a widow's virtue the thing pledged.

gains.a: her vow gains the recognised form and force of the warrior's pledge, which explains the kaathai's name
gains.b: the puram oath-form gains a use outside war and kingship, showing that its penalty of being called a cruel king could be fulfilled by another's vow

note: Puram 9's Pandya warns cows, Brahmins, women, the sick and the sonless to take shelter before he attacks; Kannaki tells the fire to spare Brahmins, the virtuous, cows, chaste women, elders and children.
teaches: The protected classes of the just king's war reappear as the limit a wronged woman sets on her own vengeance against a Pandya city, so the code meant to restrain kings now restrains the one punishing a king, and is applied to his own capital.

gains.a: her list of the spared gains a precedent: it is the established rule of righteous attack, not a sudden mercy
gains.b: the poem's battle rule gains a case where it binds a non-king and is turned against the Pandya line whose ancestor proclaimed it

note: The couplet's wife commands the rain; Kannaki commands the fire god, who waits on her word.
teaches: Where the couplet's wife who worships no god has the rain at her word, the epic shows a god coming in person to take her orders, and the power that brings rain turned to burning a city, so the same claim for the chaste wife's word is shown in its most destructive extent.

gains.a: her command over the fire gains a known doctrine behind it: the chaste wife's word moves the elements
gains.b: the couplet gains a test case showing that the power it grants is not only beneficent and can set a god to destroy

note: Kannaki's dream of a harm to the city with the king, which she would not speak of, is fulfilled in the burning of the Pandya's house and Madurai.
teaches: The harm she refused to name in her dream turns out to be her own act, so the omen foretold not only the city's fall but the part the dreamer would play in it.
audit_text_issue: silappathikaram:21:61 மாத்துவத் தான் is insecure; 9:51-54 is dense.

note: The patikam traces the ruin to a curse of a former birth ripening; the fire god here says he held an old order to burn the city, while Kannaki claims the act as her own rage.
teaches: Read together, the burning is caused three ways at once, by a karmic curse, by a standing divine order and by the wife's own deliberate act, and the epic does not choose between fate and her choice.

note: The venba's challenge to the queen to see what the woman of harsh deeds will do is made explicit as a vow to destroy the kingdom and Madurai.
teaches: The vague threat that closed the plea becomes a sworn vow with a condition on her own chastity, so the step from grievance to destruction is taken as an oath, not as a sudden fury.

note: In the court the Pandya calls himself the thief and dies; here the narrator says he gave his life for the bent sceptre and so showed the earth a straight one.
teaches: The narrator turns the king's self-condemnation into his last act of just rule, so the same death that proves the sceptre bent is counted as straightening it.

note: The couplet says the king who does not examine and do justice perishes by himself (தானே கெடும்); the Pandya, having failed to examine, dies by his own sentence.
teaches: The epic takes the couplet's 'perishes by himself' literally, as a king's own verdict on himself, and adds what the couplet does not allow for: that the ruin can be read as redeeming the rule it ends.

gains.a: the unit's claim that the death showed a straight sceptre gains a rule behind it: a non-examining king's fall is self-caused, not an enemy's work
gains.b: the couplet gains a case in which self-caused ruin is chosen and becomes the king's one act of justice, which a bare 'he will perish' cannot show

note: Kannaki bids the fire god go to the wicked (ஏவ); this kaathai opens by naming the fire as ஏவல் தெய்வம், the god under command.
teaches: The title the fire bears here carries over from her command, so the burning of Madurai is presented as a god's obedience to a woman rather than as divine wrath.

note: The couplet likens a king's killing of the cruel to weeding a crop; the royal bhuta's office is to put down cruel deeds (கொடுந்தொழில் கடிந்து), and the Pandya killed Kovalan as a thief under that office.
teaches: Held together, the two show the licence to kill wrongdoers, which the Pandya invoked, being the very office whose guardian spirit now abandons his city, so the Kural's weeding image is shown to depend on the king knowing which are the weeds.

gains.a: the royal bhuta's charter gains a pointed sense: its duty of putting down the cruel is the duty the Pandya misused
gains.b: the couplet gains its failure case, a king who weeded out an innocent and whose own guardian spirit then left

audit_text_issue: silappathikaram:22:37-50 marked in the edition as doubtful; link rests on 51-61

note: Tirumular says a land where Brahmins make the oblation dusk and dawn does not decline and its king prospers; here the Brahmin bhuta of the unfailing three-fire life leaves Madurai because its king erred.
teaches: Tirumular makes the Brahmins' rites the protection of king and land, while the epic makes the king's justice the condition of the guardian of those rites staying, so the two run the dependence in opposite directions.

gains.a: the Brahmin bhuta's departure gains its weight: it withdraws what the Saiva text holds to be the land's very safeguard
gains.b: the verse gains a limit: in the epic even the guardian of the three fires cannot keep a city whose king has done wrong

audit_text_issue: Lines 17-33 are marked in the edition as doubtful; the departure the note relies on is outside the unit.

note: The couplet says that if the king bends justice the sky withholds rain; the bhutas say that on the day the king errs in the order of rule the city is eaten by fire.
teaches: Both bind nature's order to the king's justice, but the epic replaces the slow withdrawal of rain with an immediate fire on the city and gives the city's own guardian spirits the knowledge of the rule, so the couplet's consequence becomes a sentence carried out the same night.

gains.a: the bhutas' rule gains a recognised doctrine: misrule upsets the order of nature, which the Kural already states
gains.b: the couplet gains a sharper instance where the penalty falls at once on the city as a whole, and the guardians themselves stand aside for it

audit_text_issue: Lines 89-96 are doubted in the edition; the claim at 103-106 lies outside them.

note: The patikam's first moral is that dharma becomes death to those who err in kingship (அரைசியல் பிழைத்தோர்க்கு அறம்கூற்று); the bhutas name the same fault (கோமுறை பிழைத்த) as the cause of the city's burning.
teaches: The patikam promises death to the erring king; this unit extends the penalty from the king to his city and makes it a standing law the guardian spirits obey, which the moral as first stated does not say.
audit_text_issue: lines 89-96 of the unit are doubted in the edition; the link does not rest on them

note: Kannaki bids the fire spare Brahmins, the virtuous, cows, chaste wives, elders and children and go to the wicked; here the flame spares the side of the virtuous, the cows and calves escape, and the warriors' quarter burns.
teaches: The exemptions she named are carried out street by street, so the fire is shown as a discriminating judgment rather than a blind disaster, and the warriors' quarter is put among those she called the wicked.
audit_text_issue: In 22:113 விடாது could be read the other way. Line 111 is doubted in the edition, and kaathai 22 has lines marked as later additions. | Line 113 விடாது can be read either way; line 111 is doubted in the edition, though the link does not rest on it.

note: Tirumular says the king whose task is to protect cows, women, the virtuous and the holy goes to endless hell if he fails them; in the burning Madurai the cows and the virtuous are protected not by the king, who is dead, but by the fire itself.
teaches: The two list the same protected beings, but the Saiva verse punishes the failing king after death while the epic transfers his duty of protection, in this life, to the wronged wife's fire.

gains.a: the fire's sparing gains a recognised code: these are the beings any king is bound to protect
gains.b: the verse gains a case where the duty survives the king's failure and is fulfilled by another power, which its threat of hell does not consider

audit_text_issue: 113 (விடாது) is read as sparing; the marker flags the alternative. Line 111 is doubted in the edition.

note: Kannaki says that if she is truly a pathini she will not let the king and Madurai live; the city's housewives, keepers of household dharma, declare her breast-battle no cruelty and worship the fire.
teaches: Her conditional oath is answered not by a god but by the wives of the city she burns, so her standing as a pathini is confirmed by the very household virtue she claimed.

note: The couplet says that if the guardian does not guard, the cows' yield fails and those of the six duties forget their books; in burning Madurai the Vedic chant and the fire offering cease.
teaches: The couplet's warning that Vedic learning lapses under an unguarding king is shown happening in a single night, and with the cows spared, so the epic keeps one half of the couplet's penalty and lets the other fall.

gains.a: the stopping of the rites gains its doctrinal reading: it is the Kural's named sign of a king who failed to guard
gains.b: the couplet gains a scene in which its two penalties are separated, the cows spared by the pathini's command while the books' recitation still falls silent

note: In Puhar's evening the women parted from their lovers sigh like a smith's bellows (ஊதுஉலைக் குருகின் உயிர்த்தனர்); here Kannaki, parted from Kovalan by his death, sighs like the bellows (ஊதுலைக் குருகின் உயிர்த்தனள்) amid a burning city.
teaches: The same formula moves from the passing grief of lovers apart for a night to a widow's grief that has set a city alight, so the forge in the image becomes a real fire.

note: Madurapathi appears before Kannaki here; in the next kaathai she names herself and tells her that the harm came to her husband as ஊழ்வினை, a deed come to fruit.
teaches: The goddess who comes because she cannot bear the fire is the one who will give karma as the cause, so the poem brings in its karmic account only after the pathini's justice has run its course.

note: The venba gives Madurapathi the powers of Lakshmi, Saraswati and the slayer of Mahisha; the next kaathai shows her body half dark and half gold, lotus in one hand and sword in the other.
teaches: The venba's union of gentle and warlike goddesses is drawn in the next kaathai as a body divided down the middle, so the reader sees the city goddess's double nature first named, then pictured.

note: The Alarpadu Kaathai ends with the goddess of Madurai appearing before (முன்) the pathini, unable to bear the fire; here she will not stand before her and appears behind her, being the Pandya's family goddess.
teaches: Read together, the goddess's first coming is driven by the fire, but her place behind Kannaki shows that the city's deity arrives as an embarrassed advocate of the guilty king's house.
audit_text_issue: silappathikaram:22:134-157 is not a marked unit; it spans 22:119-137 and 22:138-157.

note: Kannaki shamed the Pandya with the Chola whose gate bell's tongue trembled for the cow; the goddess replies that the Pandya kings' ears heard the Veda's tongue (மறைநா) and never the bell's tongue (மணிநா).
teaches: The goddess turns Kannaki's proof of the Chola's justice into evidence for the Pandya: a line whose bell no one ever had to ring needed no such exemplar, so the dispute over the king's justice becomes a dispute between two dynasties' records.

note: The patikam's third moral is that the former deed comes in wrath and makes one eat it; the goddess says ஊழ்வினை came to her king as well as to Kannaki's husband.
teaches: The patikam keeps karma for the story's sufferers and the death-dealing dharma for the king, but the goddess applies ஊழ்வினை to the king himself, so the first and third morals meet in one person.

note: The couplet says those born of good family do not slip (இழுக்கார்) in conduct; the goddess says those born in the Pandya line joined to conduct (ஒழுக்கொடு) suffer no fault (இழுக்கம்) even in untamed youth.
teaches: The couplet's rule about good birth is spoken by the dynasty's own goddess while she excuses its present king, so the epic shows the rule used as a family's defence at the moment its member has failed.

gains.a: the goddess's boast gains a recognised maxim behind it, which is why it carries weight against Kannaki's charge
gains.b: the couplet gains a test: the chapter itself tells of a king of that line who erred, so good birth does not guarantee what the couplet claims

note: Kannaki cited the Chola who killed his own son under the wheel when the cow's tears burned his heart (நெஞ்சுசுட); the goddess answers with a Pandya who cut off his own hand when a woman's reproach burned his heart (நெஞ்சஞ் சுடுதலின்).
teaches: The two speeches match self-punishment for self-punishment, son for hand, showing that the argument over Kovalan's death is being fought with rival royal legends of the same pattern.

note: Parasaran hails the Chera who cut the kadamba in the sea (கடற்கடம் பெறிந்த) and carved his bow on the hill; Patitruppattu 11 tells the felling of the guarded kadamba after reaching the sea by Imayavaramban Neduncheralathan, whom the Himalaya marks.
teaches: The epic keeps the Sangam Chera's signature deed as a blessing formula in a brahmin's mouth, and strings it with Mantharam Cheral and the Porunai's Poraiyan, so the separate Cheras of the decades become one praised house.

gains.a: the brahmin's blessing gains a real deed and a named king behind its epithet
gains.b: the decade's battle gains an afterlife as a stock title, cited in a Pandya village by a Chola-land brahmin as the Chera's fame

note: The officers seize Vaarthikan because his son wears jewels a stranger gave; the goldsmith tells the king that the stranger with the anklet is the thief of the palace anklet.
teaches: The goddess's precedent is the same case as Kovalan's, a man holding valuable jewels wrongly taken for a thief by the king's men, chosen so that the old king's remedy can be measured against the present king's haste.

note: The old Pandya asks whether his sceptre has bent, admits his rule strayed through ignorant men and makes amends; Nedunjeliyan, shown the gem, says he is the thief and dies.
teaches: Both kings confess the fault as their own, but the ancestor's confession comes before any death and repairs it with land, while Nedunjeliyan's comes after and can only be paid with his life: the difference is when the king inquires.
audit_text_issue: Lines 121-122 of 23:103-122 are of unclear word division.

note: The goddess cites a saying that fire will eat Madurai and its king on a fixed day of Aadi; the fire god says he had a command long before (பண்டே) to burn the city on the day the pathini was wronged.
teaches: Two separate voices, the omen and the fire god's standing order, make the burning predetermined, so Kannaki's act is shown as the trigger of a sentence already fixed.

note: Bharatan seized a stranger merchant with goods as a spy, showed him to the king and had him killed; in this life Kovalan, a stranger with an anklet, is shown to the king as a thief and killed without inquiry.
teaches: The former deed is the present crime with the roles reversed, so Kovalan suffers exactly the false accusation he once made, and the goldsmith takes the place he once held.

note: Neeli cried through the halls and streets asking whether this was justice and cursed the killers to suffer her sorrow; Kannaki cries through Madurai asking whether there are women, wise men or a god in the city.
teaches: Neeli's curse asked for the same sorrow, and Kannaki's lament fulfils it in form as well as fact, a widow's public cry against an unjust killing repeated in a new birth.

note: The quatrain says sin cannot stand before austerity while merit lasts; the goddess says that when a former deed rises in wrath penance does not help those not upright.
teaches: Both limit what austerity can do, but the quatrain makes merit run out with time, while the goddess makes the bar moral: penance fails against a ripened deed for those who lack uprightness.

gains.a: the goddess's saying gains a measure: austerity does guard, but only on terms
gains.b: the quatrain's limit gains a second condition and a case, the ascetic-guarded couple who still meet the deed of a former birth

audit_text_issue: செம்மையிலோர் (172) is not identified in the unit, and the verse's sense was flagged uncertain. | Unit flagged uncertain; who the செம்மையிலோர் are is not stated.

note: At the burning Kannaki declared to the gods that she was without fault (குற்றமிலேன் யான்); under the vengai she laments that she is a woman of fiery deeds (தீத்தொழி லாட்டியேன் யான்).
teaches: Kannaki's own judgment of the burning reverses once the goddess has shown her the former deed, so the epic lets its heroine see her vengeance as a deed with its own weight just before it raises her to heaven.

note: The couplet says the wife who worships her husband rather than a god can command the rain; the venba takes its words and says the gods themselves worship such a wife.
teaches: The epic reads Kural 55 through Kannaki's end: the wife's power over nature becomes a claim on the gods, who now worship her, and the reward follows the burning of a city rather than a gift of rain.

gains.a: the venba gains the authority of the couplet's own words for its praise of Kannaki
gains.b: the couplet gains a case that tests it: its pathini wields fire and destruction, not rain, yet is still praised in its words

note: The verdict scene ends with the Pandya saying 'am I king? I am the thief', falling dead, and his queen falling at his feet saying there is nothing to show those who have lost their husbands; the summary recalls this as the king who slept on his throne-couch with his queen of flawless chastity.
teaches: The summary turns the king's self-condemnation and his wife's instant death into one dignified image of a royal pair at rest, and gives its only epithet of chastity to the queen and does not name Kannaki, so the book's official memory honours the Pandya's atoning death as the thing its whole story is viewed with.

note: The couplet says that if the ruler bends justice the sky, bending its rain, will not pour; the summary credits the Pandya land, whose king bent justice in this book, with a sky that never fails to pour new rain.
teaches: Read against the couplet, the summary's line of unfailing rain claims for the Pandya land the very sign the Kural withdraws from a bent sceptre, so the epic's punishment for the bent sceptre falls on the king's own life and the city by fire rather than on the rain, and its stock praise of the land survives the verdict intact.

gains.a: the formula line about rain gains a political charge: under the couplet it is a claim that the king ruled justly, which the book itself has refuted
gains.b: the couplet gains a case in which the bent sceptre is answered by a different penalty than drought, the king's death and his city's burning, which limits the couplet's rain as the only sign of misrule

note: Bhoothapandiyan's queen rebukes the elders who hold her back and chooses the pyre over the widow's austerities, calling fire and a lotus pond one to her; the summary sets the Pandya Nedunjeliyan's queen of flawless chastity lying with him on the throne-couch, her death having come at once at his feet.
teaches: Both remember a Pandya queen who would not outlive her husband, but the Puram queen must argue her way to the pyre against counsel, while the epic's queen dies without fire or argument and the summary counts that death as flawless chastity, so together they show the widow's death moving from a chosen and contested act to a sign of karpu that needs no choosing.

gains.a: the summary's praise of the queen gains the older Pandya precedent of a wife who refused widowhood, which shows what kind of chastity புரைதீர் கற்பின் is honouring
gains.b: the Puram poem gains a later version of its scene in which no elders object and no pyre is needed, which shows the queen's resolve becoming an ideal assumed rather than argued

note: The Madurai goddess told Kannaki that a deed of the former birth had come and pressed (உம்மை வினைவந் துருத்த காலை) and that after fourteen days she would see her husband only in a god's form; here Kannaki uses the same words of herself and the gods bring her husband.
teaches: Kannaki takes the goddess's karmic account into her own mouth when strangers ask who she is, so the explanation offered to her in Madurai becomes the one she gives of herself, and the prophecy is fulfilled before witnesses outside the city.

note: The patikam's hill kuravar report to Ilango that they saw a pathini taken to heaven under a vengai; this unit is the hill women's own telling of that sight.
teaches: The frame says the epic began from the hill folk's report; the kaathai shows that report already as a cult with drums, incense and a prayer for the hill's wealth, so the poem's source is presented as a worship before it is a story.

note: Kural 380 says nothing is stronger than oozh, which arrives before any device; Kannaki blames the strong deed that pressed on her but also names herself the woman of cruel deeds.
teaches: Kannaki grants karma the force the couplet gives oozh yet keeps the burning of Madurai as her own act, so the epic holds fate and the agent's deed together where the couplet speaks only of fate's priority.

gains.a: her double phrase (வல்வினை, கடுவினையேன்) is set against a flat statement of fate's power, which brings out that she does not hide behind it
gains.b: the couplet's abstract fate is shown working through a person who still owns what she did

note: In Kuruntokai 111 the mother takes the velan's word that Neduvel caused the girl's sickness, and the friend wants the lover to come so the household may see a great laugh (பெருநகை); here the friend's refrain is இதுநகையாகின்றே over the same mistake.
teaches: The laugh at the mother's misreading, a friend's private aside in the short poem, becomes the sung refrain of a public round dance, which shows the old akam situation turned into communal performance.

gains.a: the epic's refrain gains a source: the joke on the velan was an established akam situation, not the hill girls' invention
gains.b: the short poem's single laugh is shown as a convention strong enough to carry four stanzas of a festival song

note: Natrinai 34's friend tells Murugan that, knowing the sickness is not his seizure, he came to the veri house at the velan's call, and so, though a god, he is truly foolish (மடவை மன்ற); the kuravai ranks the god as more foolish than the velan if he comes.
teaches: The single daring address to the god in the Sangam poem becomes a graded series (the velan foolish, the god more so) sung inside a hymn to the same god's spear, so the mockery of his coming to the rite sits beside praise of his power without contradiction.

gains.a: the stanza's charge against the god is seen to be a received akam boldness, not irreverence peculiar to the epic
gains.b: the poem's address gains a setting in worship: the same girls who call the god foolish here have just sung his victories

note: Paripadal 5 praises the spear that cut Sur's mango in the sea and split the crane-named mountain and says the velan's praises and veri are neither true nor false; the kuravai names the same crane-mountain killer and calls him foolish if he comes to the velan's rite.
teaches: Both texts hold the god's deeds fixed while keeping the velan's rite at a distance: the hymn suspends judgement on the rite, and the kuravai laughs at it, which shows that doubt about the diviner was compatible with full praise of Murugan.

gains.a: the friend's mockery gains a temple-hymn parallel that also refuses to vouch for the veri
gains.b: the hymn's guarded 'neither true nor false' is shown in a folk voice that goes further and laughs

note: Thirumurugatruppadai places the god at Erakam among Brahmins who chant the six-syllable mantra at the hours; the kuravai names Erakam with Senthil, Sengodu and Venkunru as hills the god never leaves.
teaches: The same shrine is claimed by the guide poem for a Brahmin rite and by the hill women for their kuravai, and their list differs from the six seats, so the roster of Murugan's hills was not yet fixed when the epic was made.

gains.a: the epic's four names gain a comparison that shows they are a distinct list, with Sengodu and Venkunru outside the six
gains.b: the guide poem's Erakam is seen also as a hill folk's god's seat, not only a Brahmin site

note: In Paripadal 19 maidens who do not eat the leftover of the god's elephant at Parankunram fail to win husbands; the hill girls pray to Murugan not for marriage in general but that their friend be spared another's match and given her own lover.
teaches: The temple poem treats Murugan as giver of husbands to all maidens who honour him, while the kuravai bends the same belief to the akam crisis of the secret union, asking him to prevent the family's match.

gains.a: the girls' prayer is seen to rest on an established belief that Murugan grants marriages
gains.b: the hymn's general belief is shown turned to one lover and against one feared marriage (அயல்மணம்)

note: The kuravai girls call Murugan's kurava wife their own clan's daughter; Thiruppugazh 1000 tells Valli guarding the hunters' millet from her platform and Murugan entering the field.
teaches: The epic's hill women claim Valli as kin and pray to Murugan as an in-law of the clan, while the later devotional song keeps the millet field and the hunter girl but makes the story a model of the god's grace to the devotee, so the kin claim comes first and the theology after.

gains.a: the clan claim gains a view of what the Valli story would later carry in devotion
gains.b: the song's millet field and hunter girl are seen rooted in a hill people's claim to the goddess as their daughter

audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 1000 is flagged uncertain in its syntax.

note: Ainkurunuru 250 tells the beads that the one who afflicted the girl is not Vel, lord of their valli forest; the friend here tells the lover that he comes with kadamba and spear but has no six faces, no peacock and no kurava bride.
teaches: The Sangam friend's bare denial that the god caused the sickness is worked out here as a point-by-point comparison of the man with the god's attributes, which shows the denial leaning on an iconography of Murugan already settled.

gains.a: the friend's list gains a precedent: denying the god's seizure was a set move of the friend's speech
gains.b: the short poem's 'not Vel' is spelled out in the god's own marks, making plain what the girl's lover is being measured against

audit_text_issue: 24:99-100 (கடம்பூண் தெய்வமாக நேரார் மடவர்) can be read two ways.

note: Kannaki names a strong deed of the past and her own cruel deed as the cause of Madurai's ruin; the hill women sing that she burned Koodal because the royal order failed.
teaches: Within one kaathai the burning is put down to karma in the victim's voice and to the king's broken justice in the worshippers', so the chapter repeats the patikam's two morals as two voices rather than choosing one.

note: Kural 55 says the wife who rises worshipping her husband and not a god can bid the rain fall; here the pathini, who held to her husband alone, has become the god whom chaste wives worship, and the hill women ask her to keep their hill fruitful.
teaches: The couplet's power of the chaste wife's word passes, after her death, into a cult in which other chaste wives worship her, so the woman the couplet exempts from worshipping a god is herself made one.

gains.a: the epic's deification gains a basis in a stated ethical claim about the chaste wife's power over rain and plenty
gains.b: the couplet is tested at its edge: its own ideal, once dead, becomes an object of the worship the couplet set her free from

note: The patikam promises to show that the high praise a renowned pathini (உரைசால் பத்தினிக்கு உயர்ந்தோர் ஏத்தல்); here the gods of heaven worship her and the hill women sing her praise.
teaches: The second moral is first fulfilled among the gods and the hill girls of a love song, before any king hears of her, so the praise of the pathini begins at the margin of the kingdom and travels to the Chera court in the next kaathai.

note: Akananuru 127 credits Cheralathan with driving off the sea-foe, cutting the kadamba and carving his bow on the Himalaya; the kuravai's closing blessing hails the king of the Kudavar who ruled Kolli and the Himalaya where the bow was carved.
teaches: A deed the akam poem ties to one named Chera becomes, in the epic's blessing, an epithet of the reigning king of the Kudavar without a name, which shows a Sangam memory turned into a dynastic title; the Tamil does not say the two kings are one.

gains.a: the blessing's 'bow-inscribed Himalaya' gains its Sangam source and reads as inherited fame, not a deed of the king now ruling
gains.b: the poem's single feat is shown surviving as a formula for the whole line in a later work

note: The hill kuravar's report of the one-breasted woman taken to heaven, made to Ilango in the patikam, is made here to the reigning king.
teaches: The same witnesses tell the same wonder twice, to the prince who renounced and to the king who rules, and only the king's hearing turns it into a cult and a war, so the epic's frame and its last book answer each other.

note: To Ilango, Saathan explains the former-birth curse behind the deed; to the king he tells only the anklet, the case, the vow and the burning.
teaches: Saathan tailors the story to his hearer: the renouncer is told the karmic cause, the king is told the public case of a bent sceptre, so the epic keeps its two explanations of the disaster apart by audience.

note: In the Vazhakkurai the queen trembles and falls at the dying king's feet; Saathan reports that she resolved to go where the king went and died with him.
teaches: The scene of the verdict leaves the queen's end open, and the report to another court completes it as a chosen death, which is what lets the Chera queen weigh her against Kannaki in the next units.

note: The Pandya named himself the thief and died; Senguttuvan reads that death as the dying life straightening a sceptre bent by strong former deeds.
teaches: A second king supplies the interpretation the Pandya scene leaves unstated: the fault is laid on வல்வினை, yet the remedy is the king's own death, so karma and royal responsibility are both kept in one verdict.

note: Vellaikkudi Naganar tells the Chola that the world blames kings when rain fails and bids him ignore such talk and guard the ploughmen; Senguttuvan names rain failing and a life wronged as the protector-king's two great fears.
teaches: The Sangam counsellor treats blame for drought as unfair public talk a just king can bear, while the epic king takes the same burden inward as fear and ranks one wronged life above drought, so that kingship itself becomes suffering.

gains.a: the king's lament gains a known royal topos, the king answerable for rain, against which his ranking of a wronged life above drought stands out
gains.b: the poem's advice to set aside blame gains a counter-voice: a king who, after seeing a Pandya die of one wrong verdict, finds the burden unbearable rather than ignorable

note: The Kural says the king who does justice and protects is set apart as இறை for the people; Senguttuvan says birth into a line that guards the people is suffering and nothing to be revered.
teaches: Read with தொழுதக as 'worthy of reverence', the two judge the same office oppositely: the couplet awards the protector divine standing, while the epic king, speaking after a just king's fall, denies that the office deserves reverence at all.

gains.a: the lament gains a sharp opposite: the standard honour of the just king that it refuses
gains.b: the couplet's conditional honour gains the view from inside the office, where the same duty of protection is felt as fear and suffering

note: The patikam's second moral, that the great praise a renowned pathini, begins to be enacted when the Chera queen proposes worshipping her.
teaches: The moral is fulfilled first by a queen's judgment that sets the Pandya queen's death aside for heaven and chooses Kannaki for worship on earth, so the praise of the great begins in a comparison of two wives.

note: Bhuthapandiyan's queen Perunkoppendu rejects the elders and chooses the pyre after her husband; the Chera queen grants the Pandya queen who died with her king heaven, but chooses Kannaki for worship.
teaches: The Sangam queen's death after her husband is the summit of a wife's virtue in its own poem, while the epic, granting such a death its heavenly reward, ranks above it the wronged wife who survived to accuse a king.

gains.a: the queen's verdict gains the Sangam model of the widow's chosen death that it puts in second place
gains.b: the poem gains a later judgment in which following one's husband in death is honoured yet ranked below the pathini's wrath

note: The Patitruppattu preface to the fifth decade lists among Senguttuvan's deeds that he went for a stone for the goddess Pattini and bathed it in the Ganges; the epic shows him choosing the Himalaya stone over the one from Pothiyil.
teaches: The preface records the stone as one conquest among many, while the epic gives its reason, a king's honour that refuses the near southern stone, so the pairing shows the pathini's cult being written into the Chera king's record of war.

gains.a: the king's resolve gains independent witness that the stone for Pattini belonged to the tradition of Senguttuvan's deeds
gains.b: the preface's bare phrase கடவுள் பத்தினிக் கற்கோள் gains a scene, a debate over which stone and why

note: Villavan Kothai credits Senguttuvan with making the sea-fenced land Tamil (இமிழ்கடல் வேலியைத் தமிழ்நா டாக்கிய); the Patitruppattu preface uses nearly the same phrase of his father Imayavaramban.
teaches: The minister applies to the son the formula the preface gives the father, so the Chera line's fame works as a shared inheritance that the campaign for the stone is said to renew.

gains.a: the minister's praise gains its source, a formula of the Chera line rather than a fresh boast
gains.b: the preface's phrase gains a later use as an argument that the northern kings will yield without war

note: Patitruppattu 43 praises Kuttuvan whose army broke kings from the Himalaya to Kumari; Villavan Kothai argues that because of such victories none in the world will resist him.
teaches: The Sangam poem praises conquest as done, while the epic minister uses the same fame as a reason no new conquest is needed, so the reputation of past war is offered as the means of a bloodless one.

gains.a: the minister's claim that none will resist gains the Sangam record of conquest it rests on
gains.b: the poem's praise gains a political use, fame as a weapon that spares battle

note: The kadambu thrown down in the sea and the bow set on the Himalaya, epithets of the Chera line in the opening lines, return in the drum's proclamation.
teaches: The same two feats change use within one kaathai: at the start they adorn a king going to see the hills, at the end they are a threat sent to northern kings, which marks how far the news of the pathini has turned the pleasure trip.

note: The Kural warns that honouring a spy openly lets out the king's secret; Azhumbil Vel counts on the enemy's spies at Vanchi's gate to carry the proclamation.
teaches: The couplet treats exposure to spies as a leak to be prevented, while the epic court makes the leak its instrument, so the pairing shows intelligence used as a channel of open threat.

gains.a: the counsel gains the norm of secrecy that it deliberately inverts
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where a king wants his purpose known, which marks the limit of its rule

audit_text_issue: The spy lines the link depends on (173-176) fall outside the moved unit.

note: Purananuru 39 praises the Chola who made the Chera of the Himalaya-carved bow fall and withered வாடா வஞ்சி; the epic's king enters வாடா வஞ்சி and the drum boasts of the carved bow.
teaches: The epithets 'unwithering Vanchi' and 'the bow carved on the Himalaya' are the Chera line's own glory in the epic and the measure of a Chola victory in the Sangam poem, so the pairing shows one stock of Chera fame used by both its owners and its enemies.

gains.a: the proclamation gains the knowledge that its boasts were stock epithets that rival poets also used
gains.b: the poem's paradox of withering the unwithering city gains the Chera's own use of the same name for a city at the height of its power

note: The vow to bring a stone for a god on the northern kings' heads is kept when the king takes the Himalayan stone after capturing Kanakan and Vijayan.
teaches: The vow names only a god to be carved and a royal insult to be avenged, and the close names the stone as the pathini's, so the epic joins a war of royal honour to the worship of Kannaki only once the vow is kept.

note: Both are royal vows in the conditional form whose penalty is the king's own sceptre turning cruel to his people; the Chera's line almost repeats the Pandya's.
teaches: The Pandya's vow names only his own subjects as the sufferers of a failed king, while the Chera's sets the choice out plainly, a sceptre that makes either foreign kings or his own people tremble, showing that the vow form took the king's power to terrify as fixed and staked the people's peace on a war abroad.

gains.a: the Chera's penalty clause is shown to be the old vanjinam formula, குடிபழி தூற்றும் கோலேன் ஆகுக, carried almost word for word into குடிநடுக் குறூஉங் கோலேன் ஆகென
gains.b: the formula gains a use against an insult reported from far away by ascetics rather than spoken to the king's face, so the vow answers a rumour of scorn

note: Both kings open a northern march by moving sword and umbrella at a chosen hour: the Chola with his drum to find foes for his arms, the Chera toward the Himalaya for a stone.
teaches: The Chola went north wanting only enemies for his shoulders, was stopped by the mountain and left his tiger carved on it, while the Chera goes with a cause, a pathini and an insult to Tamil, and carries a stone away from the mountain, so the epic's second northern march gives a moral reason to the rite the first performed for glory alone.

note: The couplet says the six-duty men forget their books if the guardian does not guard; the sages charge the Chera to guard the Veda-keepers of the Himalaya, which lies outside his kingdom.
teaches: The couplet ties the Brahmins' learning to their own king's protection, and the epic stretches that duty across the border, so that a king marching to punish northern kings is made guardian of the northern Brahmins, and he keeps the charge in victory (lines 248-250).

gains.a: the sages' charge gains a reason: without a guardian the Veda-keepers' learning fails, so the Chera's protection keeps the northern Vedas alive
gains.b: the couplet gains a case beyond the king's own realm, where the guardian of learning is an invader and the protection is owed to the enemy's Brahmins

note: Both cook a battlefield meal on hearths of crowned heads stirred with bangled arms (முடித்தலை அடுப்பு, தொடித்தோள் துடுப்பு), and both set it beside the king's care for Vedic Brahmins.
