teaches: The puram poem makes the battlefield cooking the Pandya's own rite beside his completed Vedic sacrifices, and the epic gives the cooking to demons who call the field an அறக்களம் and then has the king order the fire-keeping Brahmins protected, so the epic keeps the old pairing of war-rite and Vedic rite and adds the name of dharma to the slaughter.

gains.a: the demons' feast is recognised as the formal battlefield sacrifice of the Pandya praise poem, not loose description of gore
gains.b: the puram image gains a later life in which the cooks are demons and the field is named a field of dharma, showing the formula become a convention that could be given to any Tamil conqueror

note: The couplet's spy goes in the guise of renouncers to get in and see; the defeated northern kings put on the guise of ascetics and performers to get away.
teaches: The couplet treats the renouncer's dress as a tool of the king's intelligence, and the epic shows the same dress used by kings themselves to escape a lost battle, so the guise that hides a spy's purpose also hides a king's shame, and it works because no one strikes a man who looks like a renouncer.

gains.a: the kings' flight gains a known device, the renouncer's dress as cover for passing through hostile ground, rather than a chance escape
gains.b: the couplet's technique gains a case where it is used not by a servant to enter but by the defeated to leave, turning a spy's skill into a mark of a king's disgrace

audit_text_issue: விச்சைக் கோலத்து (230) is uncertain in sense.

note: The patikam's second moral, that the great praise a renowned pathini, begins to be acted out when the Chera takes the stone for the pathini from the Himalaya.
teaches: The patikam promises only that the high will praise the pathini, and this kaathai shows the praise has to be won by humbling northern kings, so the honour paid to Kannaki and the Chera's conquest are made one act.

note: The decade's preface says Senguttuvan went for the stone of the goddess pathini, defeated the Aryan lord and bathed the stone in the Ganga; the kaathai tells the expedition at length. The epic here does not name the king's parents, so the identity rests on name and deed.
teaches: The preface compresses the campaign to a stone sought, one Aryan lord defeated and a bathing in the Ganga, while the epic gives the war a cause in an insult to Tamil, names two kings Kanakan and Vijayan, and brings the army over the Ganga on allies' boats, so the two show a shared tradition of the pathini's stone told with different enemies and routes.

gains.a: the epic's campaign gains an independent notice in the Chera decade's preface, showing the stone for the pathini was part of the Chera king's remembered deeds
gains.b: the preface's bare clause கடவுட் பத்தினிக் கற்கோள் gains its story: why the stone was sought, from whom it was taken, and that the god was Kannaki

note: The decade's preface lists among Senguttuvan's deeds that he sought the stone of the goddess-pathini (கடவுள் பத்தினிக் கற்கோள்) and bathed in the Ganga; the epic opens this kaathai with the same phrase and the same river.
teaches: Set beside the preface, the epic's நீர்ப்படை is seen to rest on a Chera tradition that already called the pathini a goddess and joined her stone to the Ganga, and the epic's contribution is the story that makes her one: who she was and why a king would march north for her.

gains.a: the bathing gains outside witness: a Chera praise tradition that names the pathini's stone among the king's conquests
gains.b: the bare line of the preface gains the woman behind the title and the reason the stone was wanted

note: Maadalan says Madhavi's seaside song crushed the crowns of Kanaka and Vijaya; the earlier unit is the moment she takes up the yazh in a sulk to answer Kovalan's songs.
teaches: The scene of a lovers' misreading of each other's songs on the beach turns out, in Maadalan's riddle, to be the first link in a chain that ends in a northern war, so the poem asks the reader to see a small private quarrel and a campaign as one sequence of cause.

note: Kannaki told the Pandya that Kovalan came to Madurai driven by former deeds; here Madari cries that Kovalan was blameless and the king erred, and Maadalan puts the parting under karma.
teaches: Kannaki in her plea names both karma and the king's failure to inquire, and this report splits those causes between witnesses, the Brahmin naming karma and the herdswoman naming the king, so the epic keeps both explanations alive in the story's aftermath rather than letting either replace the other.

note: The patikam promises that the deed of the past comes in wrath to be eaten and that the great praise a pathini; Maadalan uses the same verb (ஊழ்வினை உருத்தெழ) and says the woman has risen onto the crowns of the northern kings.
teaches: The patikam's morals are fulfilled here in a messenger's words: the praise of the high is made literal as kings carrying her stone on their crowns, and the wrathful deed is placed at a courtesan's song, a smaller and more human moment than the former-birth curse the patikam gives as its cause.

note: The Charana taught Kavunthi that the strong deed comes back to face its doer; here she asks whether the couple's deed has risen against her too and dies by fasting.
teaches: The doctrine she heard says a deed returns to its own doer, but the nun who led the couple treats their deed as falling on her as their guide, so the epic shows a Jain ascetic acting on a shared responsibility that the Charana's rule of individual return does not name.

note: Both tell a death by refusing food: the Chera Perunjeralathan, ashamed of a wound in his back, sits facing north with his sword; Kavunthi, after the deaths of her wards, gives up life by the vow of not eating.
teaches: The fasting death that the Sangam poem shows as a warrior king's answer to shame is in the epic taken up by a Jain nun as an answer to failed guardianship, so the same act carries the honour code into the renouncer's vow.

gains.a: Kavunthi's brief death gains a Tamil precedent that makes it read as an answer to dishonour, not only as grief
gains.b: the king's death gains a counterpart outside the warrior class, showing the act could be chosen by a renouncer for a failure of care rather than of valour

note: The quatrain says the best renounce home and wealth after slowly seeing that nothing lasts; here Kannaki's father and Madhavi renounce on hearing of deaths, and the two mothers simply die of the same news.
teaches: The quatrain's renunciation comes from calm reflection on impermanence, while in the epic it comes from the shock of bereavement and is only one of two outcomes of the same grief, so the pair shows the distance between the ethics book's ideal path to renunciation and the way the story's people actually reach it.

gains.a: the epic's renunciations gain a standard by which they look sudden and grief-driven rather than reasoned
gains.b: the quatrain's ideal gains a case showing that the same knowledge of loss can end in death as well as in renouncing

note: The preface says Senguttuvan, son of the Chola Manakkilli, felled Pazhaiyan's neem and made nine heirs of the Chola house fall at the gate; Maadalan praises him for destroying the nine umbrellas that would not bear his cousin Killi's young rule and for felling Pazhaiyan's neem.
teaches: Read together, the preface's nine Chola kin felled at the gate are given a cause in the epic, a war over the succession of a young Chola who was the Chera's cousin through his Chola mother, so the Sangam list of victories becomes a family quarrel among the crowned houses.

gains.a: Maadalan's allusions gain the record of the same deeds and of the Chola mother that explains the word மைத்துனன்
gains.b: the preface's bare list gains a reason for the war on the nine and a sense of why a Chera would fight in Chola affairs

note: The couplet likens a king's killing of the cruel to weeding the crop; the new Pandya kills a thousand goldsmiths in one day as an offering of lives to the pathini.
teaches: The couplet's punishment by death is of the cruel, one by one, as care for the crop, while the epic's new king kills a whole craft for one goldsmith's lie and calls it an offering, so the pair shows royal punishment sliding from justice into collective sacrifice to restore a king's standing.

gains.a: Cheliyan's act gains a measure from the ethics of the sceptre against which its scale and its form as offering stand out
gains.b: the couplet gains a case that asks who counts as the weed when a king must atone for a predecessor's wrong

note: Both recite the Chola line's ancestors, the king who entered the scale for the dove and the one who destroyed the hanging fort; the puram poem praises a Chola who withered the Chera's unwithering Vanchi, the epic has a Brahmin recite the same lineage in the Chera's own court.
teaches: The praise of the dove-king's line, which in the Sangam poem celebrates a Chola's victory over Vanchi, is spoken in the epic before the king of Vanchi as a pledge that the Chola's sceptre is sound, so the formula once used against the Chera now serves an alliance between cousins.

gains.a: Maadalan's assurance gains its source: a fixed Chola praise in which the dove, the fort and the just sceptre go together
gains.b: the puram formula gains a later use in which the rival it once mocked hears it as reassurance

note: Kannaki threw the Chola who relieved the bird's distress at the Pandya as a reproach; Maadalan offers the same ancestor to the Chera as proof that the Chola sceptre cannot bend.
teaches: The one exemplum works in two directions within the epic, as an accusation of a king who failed and as a guarantee for a king who has not been tested, which shows how the ancestor's deed stands in for an inquiry into the living king's justice.

note: The Chola of the puram poem entered the scale with his own body to save a dove from a hawk; the Chera here gives the Brahmin gold measured against his own weight fifty times over, just after the Brahmin has praised that very dove-king.
teaches: The scale in which a Chola ancestor weighed his flesh against a bird becomes in the Chera's court a scale in which the king's weight is matched in gold for a messenger, so the body-as-measure moves from self-sacrifice to royal gift.

gains.a: the weighing gains the Tamil memory of the royal scale, which makes the gift an answer to Maadalan's praise of the dove-king
gains.b: the dove story gains a later royal practice in which the king's body is weighed for giving, not for suffering

note: The bard of the puram poem hails Athiyaman as the ploughman who yokes white-mouthed donkeys on the bloody fields of captured forts and sows white varagu and horse-gram; the Chera's ploughmen sing their king as the donkey-plough ploughman who sowed kavadi on the northern kings' forts.
teaches: The terror title that a Sangam bard gives a patron at his gate is in the epic sung by real ploughmen in their field song, beside their oxen's holiday, so the conqueror's mock ploughing of enemy ground is absorbed into the farming folk's festival of his return.

gains.a: the ploughmen's epithet gains the rite behind it: ploughing a ruined fort with donkeys and sowing it with poor seed
gains.b: the bard's title gains a later setting where the king's own ploughmen own it as a song of joy

note: When the Chera Perunjeralathan sits north to die, the ploughmen's cry is forgotten and the village festival forgotten; when Senguttuvan returns, the ploughmen's song and the bathing festival fill the land.
teaches: Holding the two Chera poems together shows the ploughmen's song as the land's own measure of its king, silenced by a king's shameful death and loud at a king's triumph, so the epic's return scene answers the Sangam lament with its exact reverse.

gains.a: the field songs gain a Sangam frame in which the ploughmen's voice is a sign of the king's fortune
gains.b: the lament gains its opposite case, showing what the forgotten songs were when the king lived and won

note: The beaten Aryan kings fled the field disguised as matted, ash-smeared ascetics, singers and dancers; here the Chola names that disguise கொல்லாக் கோலம் and denies the Chera any glory for taking them.
teaches: The ruse that saved the northern kings' lives in battle becomes, in the rival Tamil kings' mouths, the reason the Chera's triumph counts for nothing, so the escape and the taunt together show a victory spoiled by the vanquished's change of dress.
audit_text_issue: The b span 26:214-228 is not a marked unit; the disguise lines 225-228 belong to unit 26:225-246.

note: Puram 9 praises a Pandya who before battle bids cows, brahmin-natured men, women, the sick and the sonless take shelter; the Chola's dictum spares, after battle, men who have made themselves look like non-killers.
teaches: The old dharma of war spares people by what they are, but the epic shows warriors claiming that shelter by what they wear, and a king using the rule not to restrain himself but to belittle another king's captives.

gains.a: the Chola's taunt gains its ground: an old Tamil rule that war is not waged on those who do not fight
gains.b: the poem's list gains a hard case it does not foresee, defeated fighters who step into the spared class by disguise

note: Maadalan's list of the king's victories runs close to the wording of the fifth decad's preface on Senguttuvan: சிறுகுரல் நெய்தல் வியலூர், இடும்பின் புறத்து இறுத்து, the nine kings beaten at the gate in standing battle, the sea driven back, the Aryan beaten at the Ganges.
teaches: The preface's bare record of conquests, which names the pathini's stone only as its occasion, becomes in the epic the praise a brahmin recites to cool the king's anger just before telling him that such conquests pass, so the same list serves first as glory and then as the premise of a sermon on impermanence.

gains.a: the epic's list gains an independent Sangam witness for the same campaigns in nearly the same words
gains.b: the preface's terse கடவுள் பத்தினிக் கற்கோள் gains the story of who the pathini was and what the stone became

note: After the northern battle the Chera is hailed as one who made a field of dharma (அறக்களஞ் செய்தோன்) having finished the field of war; Maadalan tells him he has made only the war-field sacrifice and never the dharma-field one.
teaches: The epic sets the battlefield hailed as a field of dharma against a brahmin's verdict that the same wars were sacrifice of the wrong field, so the king's highest praise and his counsellor's rebuke use the same two words to opposite ends.
audit_text_issue: 26:225-246 is flagged uncertain in sense; the link rests on line 246, which is plain.

note: Among the ancestors Maadalan cites are the king who took a four-Veda man's poem and sent him to the upper world, and (lines 144-146) the one who struck Agappa and bathed in Ayirai and the two seas; the third decad's preface and colophon give Palyanai Selkezhu Kuttuvan these feats and the brahmin poet's reward of heaven through sacrifices.
teaches: The Sangam tradition's sacrifice that sent a brahmin poet to heaven becomes Maadalan's precedent for the sacrifice he urges on the king, yet the same preface says that king went away to the forest, and the epic's counsellor leaves out the renunciation and keeps only the rite.

gains.a: Maadalan's allusions gain the stories behind them: the poet Gautamanar, his reward and the king who gave it
gains.b: the preface gains a later reading in which its king's sacrifice is remembered and his going to the forest is not

audit_text_issue: The poet's reward of heaven is in the colophon (பாடிப்பெற்ற பரிசில்), not in the printed preface lines; Agappa and Ayirai (144-146) are outside the unit.

note: The couplet ranks not killing one creature to eat above a thousand oblations; Maadalan ranks the sacrifice of dharma above the war-sacrifice in which the king has killed for fifty years.
teaches: Read together they make a three-step ranking that neither states: the Kural puts abstaining from killing above the Vedic rite, while the epic's brahmin puts the Vedic rite above the killing of war and offers it as the remedy for that killing.

gains.a: Maadalan's remedy is shown to rest on a ranking the Kural itself would not grant
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where the oblation is urged as the cure for killing, not as its rival

note: Both tell a king that the rulers before him, many and mighty, are all gone; Puram 363 concludes that he must renounce the whole sea-bounded world before death, Maadalan that he must perform a great sacrifice and rule for aeons.
teaches: The same proof from dead kings yields opposite counsel: the Sangam poet's impermanence ends in giving up the kingdom, the epic's brahmin's in a rite that keeps the king on the throne, so the argument alone does not decide between renunciation and ritual.

gains.a: Maadalan's sermon is seen to stop short of the conclusion the older poem draws from the same premise
gains.b: the poem's call to renounce is set against a counsellor who uses its argument for a royal sacrifice

audit_text_issue: Maadalan's counsel of sacrifice falls after line 154 (it is at 176-178), outside this cut; the unit holds only the premise. | The counsel of a great sacrifice lies after line 154, outside the linked unit.

note: The patikam opens with the Chera prince Ilango, who gave up kingship and lives at the eastern gate; here a Chera king is told that body and wealth do not last and is led to a sacrifice, not to the forest.
teaches: Within one royal house the epic shows the two answers to impermanence, the prince who left the throne and the king who is counselled to stay on it and sacrifice, without saying which is right.

note: The Naladiyar quatrain calls the life a dancer (கூத்தன்) who leaves the skin bag, after which the body's fate does not matter; Maadalan's soul is like dancers who do not stay in one costume but go by their deeds into the bodies of gods, men, beasts or hell-beings.
teaches: The quatrain uses the dancer to make the abandoned body worthless, while the epic follows the dancer to its next costume, which its deeds choose, so the same figure moves from indifference to the corpse to anxiety about the next birth.

gains.a: Maadalan's simile gains a known ethical use of the dancer image to test against
gains.b: the quatrain's dancer gains a destination: the epic says where the performer goes after leaving the costume

note: The beaten Aryan kings escaped as ascetics and as dancers (ஆடு கூத்தர்) in a changed guise (விச்சைக் கோலம்); Maadalan tells their conqueror that the soul too is like dancers who change their கோலம்.
teaches: The kings' change of costume to save their lives, mocked by the king's rivals, returns in the sermon as the image of every soul's passage from body to body, so the mockery of the disguised kings recoils on the mocker.

note: In the previous kaathai the king gave Maadalan gold to his own weight, counted as ஐயைந்து இரட்டி; here Maadalan says he is not one who seeks rich gifts.
teaches: The counsellor's disclaimer comes after the largest gift in the story, so the epic leaves the reader to weigh whether the sermon is disinterested, without itself saying so.
audit_text_issue: silappathikaram:27:173-187 the count ஐயைந்து இரட்டி is uncertain

note: The couplet says do aram without saying 'later'; Maadalan says if the king says 'we will do aram tomorrow', life may leave today, and the aram he means is the Vedic royal sacrifice.
teaches: The epic keeps the couplet's urgency but narrows aram from the whole of virtue to one rite performed by priests for a king, showing how the ethical maxim could be recruited for a particular religious practice.

gains.a: Maadalan's urgency gains the authority of a general rule about not deferring virtue
gains.b: the couplet's unspecified aram is shown filled with one school's content in a court setting

note: The patikam's three morals are that dharma becomes death to kings who err, that the great praise a pathini, and that former deeds come to fruit; here the pathini gives three lessons, one to each crowned king.
teaches: The epic's late summary turns the patikam's morals into lessons addressed to the three kings and drops karma for the Chera's fulfilled vow, so the story's close weighs kingship more than the former deed the patikam put among its causes.

note: The couplet gives the wife who worships her husband power over the rain on her own; the ancients' saying quoted here makes the glory of famous women's chastity depend on kings doing justice.
teaches: The couplet's chastity commands nature unaided, but the epic's closing saying makes its public glory wait on the king's justice being tested, so the pathini's power is tied to a failure of the sceptre.

gains.a: the saying is set against the best-known claim for a chaste wife's unaided power
gains.b: the couplet gains a condition the Kural does not state: chastity's power shows itself through the state's justice or injustice

note: The Chera vowed that unless he took a stone for the goddess on the heads of the northern kings his sword should be counted shameful; here the narrator says the pathini taught the western king that kings' anger does not cool until their vow is fulfilled.
teaches: The Chera's vow, made in anger at reported scorn, is in the end credited to the pathini as one of her lessons, so the king's campaign is retold as her teaching rather than his own design.

note: Puram 264 tells of a hero-stone set up on gravelly ground, crowned with a red flower garland and peacock feathers, with the fallen man's name carved; the epic's kaathai named நடுகல் installs a stone from the Himalaya as a jewelled image with priests and daily rites.
teaches: The epic takes the hero-stone rite, raised by herdsmen for a fallen fighter, and gives it to a woman whose power is chastity, enlarging it with Brahmin sacrifice and a temple, so the old rite of the warrior becomes the founding of a goddess's cult.

gains.a: the kaathai's title gains its source in the rite it adapts: stone, garland, offering
gains.b: the poem's simple rite is shown transformed into temple worship of a pathini

audit_text_issue: The unit (222-234) starts after the stone has been brought; the stone itself is not in the cut.

note: The decade preface on Senguttuvan, son of Nedunjeralathan by the Chola Manakkilli, says in one phrase that he went north wanting a stone for the goddess pathini and bathed it in the Ganga; the epic's prose gives the same parentage and campaign, and adds the Aryan kings' taunt and the stone carried on their heads.
teaches: Held together, the two show the Sangam colophon tradition already knew a Chera king's northern stone for a pathini, and the epic turns that bare record into a cause and a ritual: the stone becomes a goddess only after it is won by humbling the kings who mocked Tamil kingship.

gains.a: the epic's prose gains an outside witness for the king's parentage and his stone-seeking campaign, so the cult is set in remembered Chera history
gains.b: the preface's terse phrase கடவுள் பத்தினிக் கற்கோள் gains the story of whose stone it was and why the king went for it

audit_text_issue: 'Already knew' assumes the patikam is earlier than the epic, which the texts do not settle.

note: The second decade's preface credits Imayavaramban Nedunjeralathan with carving the bow on the Himalaya; the epic's Aryan kings recall the day bow, tiger and fish were all carved there, and say no such kings are left.
teaches: The epic widens one Chera's boast into the shared emblem of the three Tamil crowns and makes the memory a reproach, so the son's campaign is shown as the redeeming of a glory the north said had lapsed.

gains.a: the taunt's 'day the bow was carved' gains a named Chera, Senguttuvan's own father, as its author
gains.b: the preface's single deed gains a later afterlife as a standard that northern kings could throw back at his heirs

note: Neeli's curse in the former birth is the deed the prose says rose up against Kovalan (வினையுருத்து); the prose also names the goldsmith and the king.
teaches: The retelling at Vanchi keeps the goddess's karmic explanation but sets it beside the petty man and the king as agents, and beside Kannaki's reviling of dharma, so the karmic cause is told without excusing the human ones.

note: In the dream kaathai Devanthi read Kannaki's dream as the fruit of a vow broken in a former birth and prescribed a bath in the tanks; here she says she heard the dream and did not grasp what it would bring.
teaches: The friend who once explained the dream by past karma and a ritual remedy now confesses she misread it, so her earlier karmic diagnosis is shown to have been the wrong kind of answer to a warning of the future.

note: The quatrain says the best renounce without delay after slowly considering that home, youth, wealth and strength do not last; Maasaathuvan gives his wealth away and renounces only when the news of his son's death makes life seem death.
teaches: The pair separates renunciation reached by reflection from renunciation forced by bereavement: the epic's fathers come to the quatrain's act by the road the quatrain hopes to spare, after the loss has already happened.

gains.a: the father's turning gains a measure: it is the right act done late, under grief rather than insight
gains.b: the quatrain's counsel gains a case showing what the delay it warns against costs, a house emptied before its master leaves it

note: Kavunthi told Maadhari that a charge held for the ascetics, however small, yields very great joy; Maadhari, who could not guard that charge, gave up her life.
teaches: The promise of joy from keeping a trust is reversed into death from failing it, and the failure was not hers: the pair shows the epic laying on a guardian the full weight of a duty that the king's act made impossible to keep.

note: At the palace gate Kannaki called the Pandya a king of ruined sense who strayed from right rule (இறைமுறை பிழைத்தோன்); in the sky she calls him faultless (தீதிலன்) and herself his daughter.
teaches: The same speaker gives opposite verdicts on the same king, and the epic means both: the turn shows that in its eyes the king's death of his own sentence has cancelled the fault she rightly charged him with.

note: The king's own sentence, யானோ அரசன் யானே கள்வன், and his death are what Kannaki now rewards by declaring him Indra's guest.
teaches: Read together, the scenes show the self-condemnation as the act that wins the king heaven: the confession that he was the thief is what makes him faultless in the goddess's word.

note: The couplet says a ruler endures by just rule and without it his lustre does not endure; the Vanchi women sing that Pandyas do not live once the sceptre bends, and praise the Pandya for that.
teaches: The epic grants the couplet's link between a bent sceptre and the king's end but reverses its outcome for fame: the Pandya's dying of his own injustice is exactly what makes his line's glory endure and be sung by a rival kingdom.

gains.a: the women's saying gains a general rule behind it, so the Pandya's death reads as the law of kingship and not a private collapse
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where losing life for a bent sceptre restores the lustre it says is lost, a limit on its simple equation

note: The patikam's morals are that dharma becomes death to those who err in kingship and that an old deed comes to make its doer eat its fruit; the blessing names the old deed as the cause of her suffering and hails the king dharma killed.
teaches: The closing blessing keeps both of the patikam's causes but changes the moral's tone: the king to whom dharma became death is not left as a warning but praised with his whole line, because he died of it.

note: Devanthi's friend born on the Himalaya and bathed in the Ganga and the blessing's doll born of the mountain king are the same Himalaya stone, spoken of as Kannaki.
teaches: The Himalaya origin is given to Kannaki twice, once in a friend's grief and once in a royal blessing, and the second, with its echo of the mountain king's daughter, shows the woman of Puhar being absorbed into the figure of the great goddess.

note: The Puram poem tells Killivalavan that giving, conquest and justice are not his own fame, since his line already holds the king who entered the scale for the dove and the ancestors who destroyed the hanging fort; the ammanai answers its riddle with the Chola who destroyed the hanging forts and names no living Chola.
teaches: Read together, the Puram poet's warning that the ancestors' deeds swallow a living Chola's fame comes true in the epic, where Chola praise sung at the Chera court consists of nothing but those ancestral deeds and the city of Puhar.

gains.a: the riddle's answer gains its old standing: the hanging fort was already the Chola line's inherited title in the Sangam praise of a named king
gains.b: the Puram poem's claim that ancestral glory outshines the present king gains a later case in which the line is remembered only by it, in a rival kingdom's women's game

note: Kannaki before the Pandya recalls the Chola who relieved a bird's distress and the one who crushed his son under the wheel for a cow, to accuse a king who did not inquire; the ammanai sings the dove-king and the cow's justice as the glory of Puhar, after Kannaki has declared the Pandya blameless.
teaches: The same two Chola precedents change use across the story: in Madurai they are Kannaki's weapon against a Pandya, and in Vanchi, once she has cleared him, they are a girls' refrain beside ball songs hailing that same Pandya, so the standard of justice survives the verdict while losing its edge.

note: The Puhar book tells how Thirumavalavan went north, was stopped by the Himalaya and carved his tiger on it; the ammanai sings a king who stamped his tiger on the northern mountain while the eight mountains of the quarters watched, and ruled all eight directions under his umbrella.
teaches: Set beside the narrative, the song shows the epic's praise turning a halt into a triumph: the mountain that ended Valavan's march becomes a witness, and one carving on one peak becomes rule of the eight quarters.

note: Kannaki, appearing in the sky to Senguttuvan, says the Southerner is blameless and has become a guest in the palace of the king of the gods, and that she is his daughter; the ball songs that follow hail the Southerner with the gods' necklace at every stroke.
teaches: The ball songs are the public form of Kannaki's acquittal: only because she has called the Pandya blameless can the women of the Chera city hail the king who killed her husband, and his old title of the gods' necklace now reads as his place in Indra's hall.

note: The Patitruppattu poem names Neduncheralathan as the king who went against his foes on an island in the sea and cut down the kadamba at its root (கடம்புமுதல் தடிந்த); the swing song sings the guardian who cut the kadamba at its root (கடம்பு முதல் தடிந்த) and the emblem of the bow, and names no king.
teaches: The pair shows the Patitruppattu's title for one Chera king passing into the epic as an unnamed dynastic refrain, so that in Senguttuvan's court a deed the Sangam decade credits to Neduncheralathan is sung as the house's own.

gains.a: the swing song's unnamed guardian gains an identity: the phrase is the title of Neduncheralathan in the Chera court poetry
gains.b: the Patitruppattu's title gains evidence of its afterlife, as a stock phrase of the Chera line sung by women at play rather than a bard's praise of one patron

note: Murinjiyur Mudinagarayar praises Uthiyan Cheralathan as the one who gave the great feast without limit while the Five and the hundred fought until the hundred fell; the swing song gives the feast at the war of the Five and the twice fifty to the Chera, Poraiyan, Malaiyan, by house names only, and pairs it with the kadamba deed.
teaches: The Puram poem binds the feast to one named king, while the epic gives it to the Chera house in general and sets it beside another king's deed, so the pair shows a single patron's distinction becoming an heirloom any Chera can be sung by.

gains.a: the swing song's line gains its source and the king it belonged to, Uthiyan Cheralathan, whom it does not name
gains.b: the Puram poem's claim gains a measure of its fame: generations later it is still the Chera line's mark, though detached from the king it praised

note: The Madurai herdswomen's book opens on the Pandya whose fish is written on the brow of the Himalaya with the tiger and the bow written beside it; the Vanchi swing song sings the king of the bow who holds the fish and the tiger and rules from the Yavana land to Kumari.
teaches: The two songs claim the same three emblems for different kings: Madurai sets the Pandya's fish first with the Chola and Chera signs beside it, and Vanchi folds fish and tiger into the Chera's bow, so the epic's praise of the three crowns is a set of rival boasts that its songs leave standing side by side.

note: The couplet asks what learning is worth to those who do not bow at the good feet (நற்றாள் தொழாஅர்) of the one of pure knowledge; the close says kings who do not bow at the good feet (நல் தாள் தொழார்) of Poraiyan find it hard to live, and Kannaki too praises Senguttuvan.
teaches: The close moves the Kural's phrase for bowing to the god's feet onto a living Chera king and makes the penalty for not bowing the loss of life rather than of learning's fruit, while the deified Kannaki joins the praise, so the epic ends by turning a devotional formula into a political one.

gains.a: the closing boast gains the weight of the formula it borrows: bowing at the good feet is the Kural's posture before the god
gains.b: the couplet's phrase gains a case of its wording transferred from the god to a king, which shows how its language of worship could be turned to royal praise

audit_text_issue: Line 172 வாழ்த்தல் may be a slip for வாழ்தல்; the song number for 174 is misprinted.

note: Kovalan's midnight dream at Madurai has Kama casting his flower arrows on the bare ground and Madhavi giving Manimekalai before the dharma-one of the Bodhi; in the last kaathai Devanthi reports both as done, Kama flinging his bow and arrows on bare ground as Madhavi gives her daughter at the Bodhi.
teaches: The dream Kovalan feared as a sign of coming harm is fulfilled after his death in its other half, his daughter's renunciation, so the poem treats the dream as true in every part and lets the bad omen and the good one come out of a single night.

note: In the dream kaathai Saathan, having grown up as Maalathi's child and married Devanthi, shows her his ageless youth, tells her to come to his shrine and leaves, and she keeps worship there to win him back; in the last kaathai Maadalan retells this and the god returns by possessing her.
teaches: Devanthi's long worship to get her husband back is answered, but not as she asked: the god returns as a voice that takes over her body to reveal others' former births, so the husband she waited for comes back only as an oracle.

note: Maadalan once praised Kovalan as the compassionate hero who entered the rogue elephant's trunk to free an old Brahmin; in the last kaathai Maadalan says that this man, who entered the elephant's trunk to end the Brahmin's distress, has won the form of the gods.
teaches: The poem names one deed of Kovalan's, the elephant rescue and not his life with Madhavi or his wasting of wealth, as the deed whose fruit is his heavenly form, so the man the story often blames is judged at the end by his single act of risking his life for a stranger.

note: In the Manimekalai the materialist answers the question whether some have known a former birth by saying that the minds of those deluded by a god or by dreams are changed and such knowledge is mere doubt; in the last kaathai of the Silappathikaram former births are shown through a god possessing a woman and a sprinkled water, before a king's whole court.
teaches: The materialist's objection names exactly the means the Silappathikaram uses to prove former birth, a god's possession, so the sister epic records the reply a sceptic would make to this scene, and the scene offers as public proof what that sceptic rejects as the delusion of the possessed.

note: The patikam's third moral is that the deed of the past comes in wrath and makes one eat its fruit; the last kaathai states the law of births in full: the good reach the golden world, the loving go where their attachment leads, the fruits of virtue and wrong both ripen, and the born die and the dead are born.
teaches: The poem opens with karma as a vengeance that falls on Kovalan and closes with karma as an even law that also rewards and that lets love carry the mothers to rebirth beside the pathini, so the frame turns the threat of the opening into a consolation by the end.

note: The couplet says griefs that never let go hold those who hold attachment and do not let go; Maadalan says those whose hearts are full of love go where their attachment leads, and the mothers, held by love for Kannaki, are reborn near her temple.
teaches: The epic agrees with the couplet that attachment binds one to birth, but shows what the couplet does not: a bond of love that leads to a new birth beside the one loved, told without blame, so attachment's hold is the cost the mothers pay for staying near the pathini rather than only a grief.

gains.a: the epic's phrase பற்றுவழிச் சேறல் gains from the couplet the warning that the same hold is what keeps a soul from release, which Maadalan's calm statement does not say
gains.b: the couplet gains a case of attachment that is love for a virtuous woman and whose fruit, a rebirth near her, is told as a mercy, which tests its flat equation of holding with grief

note: Pattinathar's verse begins its list of the world's reversals with the born dying and the dead being born and turns from them to Siva, who frees from coming and going; Maadalan says the born die and the dead are born and calls it nothing new, the ancient way of life.
teaches: The same saying about the born and the dead serves the epic as a reassurance that the order of deeds holds and the Siddhar as a reason to loathe that order and seek Siva, so the line itself carries no verdict and its meaning depends on whether release or a good rebirth is the goal.

gains.a: the epic's law gains from Pattinathar the reminder that a round of births ordered by deeds is still a round, so the mothers' reunion is not release
gains.b: the Siddhar's formula gains a setting where it is said without disgust, as the Brahmin's comfort to a king, which shows that its horror in the Siddhar comes from his frame and not from the saying

note: The preface to the Patitruppattu's fifth decade says Senguttuvan, seeking a stone for the goddess-pathini, went through the forests, defeated the Aryan lord and bathed it in the Ganga; the last kaathai has the Chera endow the pathini's temple and the freed Aryan kings and Gajabahu of Lanka beg her to come to their lands.
teaches: The Sangam preface records the pathini stone as one deed among a king's conquests; the epic carries the story past the conquest, to the defeated kings themselves asking for the goddess, so the war for the stone becomes the way her worship spreads beyond the Chera land.

gains.a: the epic's scene gains from the preface an independent record that a Chera named Senguttuvan was remembered for fetching a pathini's stone from the north, though the preface itself is late
gains.b: the preface's single phrase about the pathini gains the cult that the epic says grew from it: a temple, a daily festival and a boon asked by foreign kings

note: The patikam opens with Ilango living at the eastern-gate shrine after giving up kingship; in the last kaathai the goddess tells why: when a man said he bore the mark of a future king, he looked at him in anger and put away the earth's burden to end Senguttuvan's distress.
teaches: The poet's renunciation, stated without cause in the first line of the poem, is explained only in its last unit and by the goddess herself, so the poem's frame makes the poet's giving up of a throne one more past act whose meaning the pathini reveals, like the former births of the mothers.

note: The Naladiyar quatrain, in its chapter on youth not lasting, says that since merciless Death roams looking for his people one should take provisions for the journey in good time; the epic's last lines say youth, wealth and body do not last and bid the hearers seek a true companion for the land they will go to.
teaches: The epic folds the Naladiyar's three opening themes, wealth, youth and body not lasting, into one line and draws the same conclusion of provision for the journey, but sets it after a list of concrete deeds, so the provision is named as truthfulness, not killing, giving and the rest rather than left as a figure.

gains.a: the epic's closing line gains from the quatrain the image of Death as a hunter who takes even the unborn, which is the urgency behind உளநாள் வரையாது
gains.b: the quatrain's undefined provisions (தோட்கோப்பு) gain a list of the deeds that make them up, given just before in the epic's commands

note: The couplet bids one do virtue without putting it off, because when one perishes it is the companion that does not perish; the epic bids its hearers not wait on their remaining days but seek the true companion for the land they will go to.
teaches: Read with the couplet, the epic's உறுதுணை is aram, the Kural's undying companion, and the epic adds that the companion must be sought before youth, wealth and body fail, after a story in which the dead carried only their deeds and loves into their next births.

gains.a: the epic's unnamed companion gains its identity from the couplet: it is virtue, not a person or a god
gains.b: the couplet's companion at the hour of perishing gains a destination, the land one goes to, which the epic has just shown as a new birth shaped by deeds and attachments

note: Maadalan told how a poor man who bore false witness against a chaste wife was caught in the noose of the devouring spirit, which would not take Kovalan's life in his place; among the poem's closing commands is never to bear false witness.
teaches: The command against false witness is the one rule in the final list that the poem had already shown punished on stage, by a spirit that refused even a willing substitute, so the bare imperative carries the weight of a remembered scene in which no one could pay another's penalty.

note: Senguttuvan rejects a stone from the Podiyil hill bathed in the Kaveri as unworthy of those born in his line of valour, and resolves that if the Himalaya's king will not give a stone to carve the great Pattini goddess, he will march north; the summary views the book as one with the king whose army fought with valour fitted to aram and reached the Ganga.
teaches: The king's own reason for the northern war was the honour of his line of valour, with the goddess's stone as its occasion, and the summary keeps exactly that reason and drops the occasion, so the book that began with worship for Kannaki is remembered as a Chera conquest called righteous.
audit_text_issue: The b end is not a marked unit; it spans 25:110-121 and 25:122-136.

note: Both summaries open with the same frame (aram, maram, the old city, festivals, the gods' visits, the land's wealth); the Madurai summary keeps the river and the unfailing sky and ends with the Pandya who lay dead on his throne-couch with his chaste queen, the Vanchi summary drops river and sky and ends with Senguttuvan's army at the Ganga, adding valour fitted to aram.
teaches: The shared frame lets the difference show: the Pandya book is summed up in a king undone by a wrong verdict, the Chera book in a king whose war is declared righteous, so the epic's last word on aram passes from the court of justice to the battlefield, and neither summary names the woman both books turn on.

note: The preface to the fifth decad names Senguttuvan, who drove back the sea, as the king who went north to take a stone for the goddess Pattini, defeated the Aryan lord and bathed it in the Ganga; the epic's summary names him by the same epithet (கடல்பிறக் கோட்டி) and the same Ganga, and says nothing of the stone.
teaches: The decad's preface and the epic's summary give the same king the same two marks, the sea driven back and the Ganga reached, but only the Sangam preface keeps the Pattini stone as the purpose of the march, so the epic, which tells the stone's story at length, lets its own summary remember the expedition as the preface's bare royal conquest.

gains.a: the summary's epithet gains its source: கடல்பிறக் கோட்டி is the name under which a Patitruppattu decad was sung for this king, which shows the summary closing the book in the older praise-poets' terms
gains.b: the preface's brief clause on the Pattini stone gains the epic's full account of why and for whom the stone was sought, and a case where the epic's own closing formula leaves that clause out

note: The patikam's opening frame names three morals the poem will show (dharma as death to the erring king, the praise of the pathini, the past deed that comes to fruit) and calls the poem a பாட்டுடைச் செய்யுள்; the closing summary describes the finished work by its land, its akam and puram matter, its three aims and its music, dance and song forms, and repeats none of the morals.
teaches: The two frames of the epic describe it in different terms, the opening as a story built to prove three moral claims and the close as a compendium of Tamil poetics, music and dance, so the work presents itself at the start as an argument and at the end as an art, and the morals are left for the story itself to carry.

note: The Silappathikaram's last line calls it the work whose story's matter is completed in Manimekalai; the Manimekalai patikam closes by saying that Saathan set out Manimekalai's renunciation (மணிமேகலை துறவு) in thirty songs, with Ilango hearing it, reversing the Silappathikaram patikam, where Ilango sang and Saathan heard.
teaches: Each work's frame names the other's author as its listener, and the Silappathikaram declares its own story finished only in a sequel whose subject is a daughter's renunciation, so the pair presents the two epics as one story whose tale of justice and chastity reaches its end in the turn from household life to the robe.
audit_text_issue: Line 17 can be read as the work or the person Manimekalai; the link holds on either reading.

note: Both call the human body rare (அரிய, அரும்பெறல் யாக்கை); the Valayapathi derives the rarity from karma's long series of bodies, the Naladiyar draws the duty of pressing virtue from it.
teaches: The Naladiyar's command to use the rare body gains its urgency from the fragment's account of how many karma-driven bodies come before a human one, and the fragment's second rarity, wealth to enjoy, is what the quatrain says to turn into virtue instead.

gains.a: the fragment's statement of rarity gets the practical conclusion it leaves unsaid
gains.b: the quatrain's bare 'rare body' is given its cause in the cycle of deeds

note: Both say rain falls at the chaste wife's word; the Kural makes it her one power, the Valayapathi sets it in a list of honours with the praise of country and town and credits it to what the learned of Koodal say.
